rows: Introduction to MCC Clinical Presentations The Medical Council of Canada organises medicine around clinical presentations — what the patient walks in with — rather than diagnoses. The one idea: sort a presentation by how specific it is to one body system and how urgent it is . A sign is found by the practitioner on PEx; a symptom is what the patient perceives as abnormal for them. Undifferentiated presentations (fatigue, malaise) point to no one system; single typical ones (abdominal pain, knee swelling) do. Life-threatening presentations are handled by the ABCs first. Preventive care (pap test, fecal blood test, glucose, lipids) is itself a presentation. Signs vs symptoms Sign : what the health care practitioner identifies on PEx Symptom : what the patient perceives as “not normal” for them Types of clinical presentation Presentation type Meaning Examples Undifferentiated Symptom not specific to one body system Fatigue, malaise Single typical Symptom very specific to one body system Abdominal pain, diarrhea, knee swelling Multiple problems / multisystem Multiple symptoms across body systems; may have one or multiple causes Fever, cough Life threatening Managed by the ABCs — Preventive care / health promotion Cancer and metabolic screening Pap test, fecal blood test, blood sugar, serum lipids
02 Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach

Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach The frameworks a physician uses to structure an encounter — from the patient-centred clinical method and the diagnostic pathway through prescribing, prevention and ethics. The organising idea: every step attends to both the disease and the person's illness experience . Check stability and vitals first , then Hx → PEx → Ix → DDx → Tx. FIFE (feelings, ideas, function, expectations) explores the illness experience. VITAMIN C&D generates a DDx. Choosing Wisely : least invasive test first, and only tests that change management. The prevention paradox : population-wide prevention brings large community benefit but little to each individual. The four physician-patient models run from informative (technical expert) to paternalistic (guardian). Patient-centred clinical method Exploring both disease and illness experiences – Hx, PEx, Ix, FIFE Understanding the whole person – proximal (modifiable) and distal (non-modifiable) contexts Finding common ground – problems, goals, roles, mutual decisions Incorporating prevention and health promotion Enhancing the patient-physician relationship Being realistic FIFE – the illness experience Feelings – How does your disease/symptom make you feel? Ideas – What do you think is wrong? Function – How are your symptoms impacting your function/enjoyment of life? Expectations – What do you hope to get out of the medical visit? Ethics Two accounts of how people reach a moral judgement. The organising idea is where reasoning sits : after the judgement (social intuitionism) or before it (ethical deliberation). Social intuitionism : dilemma → judgement → rationalization (reasoning justifies a gut call). Ethical deliberation : dilemma → rational deliberation → judgement (reasoning produces the call). Social intuitionism : moral dilemma → moral judgement → rationalization Ethical deliberation : moral dilemma → rational deliberation → moral judgement

History of Medicine How medicine moved from the humoral theory to the germ theory , and the figures who made the physician a diagnostician. The organising idea: disease explained by natural causes , not religion or magic. Humoral theory: blood, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm . Germ theory's program: identify the organism → develop a lab diagnostic test → discover a chemotherapeutic agent . Hippocrates rejected religious/magical healing; Galen set Hippocratic medicine in an anatomy and physiology framework. Theories of disease Humoral theory : blood, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm Germ theory : identify the micro-organism, develop a laboratory diagnostic test, discover a chemotherapeutic agent Key figures Hippocrates – rejected religious/magical healing; introduced the medical practitioner as a diagnostician/therapist Galen – took clinical Hippocratic medicine and set it within a wider anatomy and physiology framework
10 Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees

Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees Cultural competence as a continuum running from destructiveness to proficiency, then what the WHO says every clinician should know about refugee and migrant health. The organising idea: moving along the continuum means recognising differences and acting on them , not treating everyone the same. Cultural blindness (treating everyone the same) is still low on the continuum – it meets only the dominant group's needs. Cultural humility : our own perspective is not the only, or necessarily the “correct”, one. Refugees/migrants are generally healthy , have lower risk of all cancers except cervical , but more diabetes and more PTSD than the host population; labour migrants are the largest group. The cultural competence continuum Stage Features 1. Cultural destructiveness Forced assimilation, subjugation, rights and privileges for dominant groups only 2. Cultural incapacity Racism, maintained stereotypes, unfair hiring practices 3. Cultural blindness Differences ignored, everyone treated the same, only the needs of dominant groups met 4. Cultural pre-competence Exposes cultural issues, committed, assesses needs of organization/individuals 5. Cultural competence Recognizes individual/cultural differences, seeks advice from diverse groups, interacts effectively 6. Cultural proficiency Implements changes to improve services based upon cultural needs Related concepts Cultural safety : fostering an environment that is spiritually, socially, and emotionally safe Cultural humility : recognition that our own perspective is not the only and not necessarily the “correct” perspective 10 things to know about the health of refugees and migrants (WHO) The health of refugees/migrants is important – a basic human right The numbers of migrants are often overestimated Refugees/migrants are likely to be healthy in general They can face challenges accessing health care – legal status, language barriers, discrimination Lower risk for all forms of cancer, except cervical cancer , but more diabetes than the host population Breakdown in health systems in the country of origin PTSD seems more prevalent among refugees and asylum seekers than the host population Labour migrants are the largest group of migrants globally – more work-related injuries Children without parents or a guardian are especially vulnerable Making health systems refugee- and migrant-friendly

Muscle Tissue Basic biochemistry and histology, the three muscle types and the sarcomere, the cells of the nervous system, and the body's fluid compartments. The organising idea: structure predicts function – striations, nuclei and fibre shape tell you which muscle you are looking at and how it behaves. Skeletal = striated, voluntary, multinucleated (peripheral nuclei); cardiac = striated, involuntary, single central nucleus, intercalated disks; smooth = not striated, spindle-shaped. During contraction the I band and H zone shorten and the sarcomere shortens (the A band does not). Schwann cells myelinate one segment of one axon (PNS); oligodendrocytes myelinate many axons (CNS). TBW = 60% of body weight : ICF 2/3, ECF 1/3; in Darrow-Yannet diagrams the ECF always changes first . Types of Connective Tissue Connective tissue classified from embryonic mesenchyme through connective tissue proper to the specialized tissues (fat, cartilage, bone, blood-forming tissue), and how its fibres are made. The organising idea: each type is defined by its cells, its fibres (collagen type), and its ground substance . Loose CT carries vessels and nerves under epithelia; dense regular (tendons, ligaments) = type I collagen in rows for stress resistance. Brown fat = multilocular, many mitochondria, newborn thermoregulation; white fat = unilocular. Cartilage is avascular : hyaline and elastic use type II collagen, fibrocartilage types I and II . Articular hyaline cartilage lacks perichondrium, so regenerates poorly (osteoarthritis). Reticular fibres = type III collagen. Cellular Communication How cells hold together, move substances across membranes, signal one another, and fire and transmit an action potential all the way to muscle contraction. The organising idea is a single chain: resting potential → action potential → NMJ → excitation-contraction coupling . RMP = -70 mV , set mainly by K + leak; the Na + /K + pump moves 3 Na + out, 2 K + in . The AP is all-or-none: threshold -55 mV, peak +45 mV, undershoot to -90 mV. Absolute refractory period = Na + channels inactivated. At the NMJ, Ca 2+ influx releases ACh (more Ca 2+ = more ACh); ACh on nicotinic receptors → EPP → muscle AP. In ECC, Ca 2+ binds troponin so tropomyosin uncovers myosin-binding sites on actin. Myopathy : normal nerve conduction, reduced muscle amplitude; neuropathy : abnormal conduction. Anatomy Terminology The three anatomical planes. The organising idea: each plane is named for how it divides the body . Coronal = anterior/posterior; sagittal = left/right; transverse (axial) = superior/inferior. Anatomical planes Plane Divides the body into Coronal Anterior / posterior Sagittal Left / right Transverse / axial Superior / inferior

Body System Organization Cartilage and bone biology, how the body is organised into regions and systems, the imaging modalities used to see it, and the evidence-based-medicine toolkit for judging studies. The organising idea: know the normal structure, and know how trustworthy the evidence about it is . Osteoblasts build bone (osteoid); osteoclasts (fused monocytes/macrophages, in Howship's lacunae) resorb it. Intramembranous ossification has no cartilage template (skull, clavicle); endochondral replaces one (long-bone length). CT = x-ray slices, big radiation dose, avoid in pregnancy; MRI: T1 short TE/TR , T2 long TE/TR – fluid bright ; MRI is contraindicated with pacemakers, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic implants. Intention-to-treat analyses patients as assigned, not as treated. NNT = 1 / (rate in untreated − rate in treated) ; power = 1 − β . Child Development The well-baby assessment, the red flags of abnormal development, and the theories (attachment, Erikson, conditioning, Piaget) used to describe how a child develops. The organising idea: development follows a predictable sequence , so missing a stage on time – or losing a skill – is the signal . Use WHO growth charts and correct for prematurity until 24 months if born < 37 weeks. Failure to thrive : weight < 3rd percentile and family norm, or crossing 2 major percentile lines. Loss of previously acquired skills is a red flag at any age ; so is hand preference before 2 years. Secure attachment (60-65%) comes from prompt, consistent caregiving; disorganized attachment from frightened/frightening caregiving. Piaget: sensorimotor (object permanence) → preoperational (symbolic play) → concrete operational (conservation) → formal operational (abstract thought). Goals of the “well baby” assessment Growth – length, weight, head circumference; correct age until 24 months if born < 37 weeks gestation; use WHO growth charts Failure to thrive : weight less than 3rd percentile and family norm; weight trajectory crosses 2 major percentile lines Short stature : height less than 3rd percentile and family norm BMI > 85th percentile = overweight; BMI > 95th percentile = obese Parent/caregiver concerns Nutrition – feeding, supplementation, stool pattern/urine output Education and advice – injury prevention, behaviour and family issues, environmental health, other issues Development – inquiry and observation of milestones Physical examination Problems and plans / current and new referrals – medical specialist, dietician, speech, audiology, PT, OT, eyes, dental, social Investigations/screening and immunization Ontario routine schedule (Jan 2021): note the 2, 4, 6 month infant series, the 1-year MMR/Men-C/Pneu-C-13 visit, the 4-year boosters, and school-based grade 7 HB, Men-C-ACYW and HPV-9. Genetics The vocabulary of genetic variation and the patterns of inheritance, each with its signature pedigree. The organising idea: who is affected, in which generations, and whether males pass it to sons tells you the mode of inheritance. AD : every generation, both sexes, all forms of transmission (including male-to-male). AR : usually one sibship in one generation; consanguinity ↑ risk; trans compound variants cause disease, cis do not. X-linked : almost only males; no male-to-male transmission ; carrier females can be affected by skewed X-inactivation. Anticipation = triplet repeat disorders (fragile X CGG, Huntington CAG, myotonic dystrophy CTG, Friedreich GAA). Gonadal mosaicism explains recurrence of an apparently new dominant mutation (~1%). Mitochondrial disease = maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy, threshold effect. Genetics terminology Allelic heterogeneity – different variants in the same gene; different phenotypes Locus heterogeneity – mutations in different genes at different chromosomal loci cause the same phenotype Penetrance – fraction of individuals carrying a gene who manifest a specific phenotype; complete = always shows signs, incomplete = may not show signs Anticipation – symptoms become more apparent/severe with each new generation; triple repeat disorders Patterns of inheritance Pattern Features Autosomal dominant (incl. new dominant) People with the condition in each generation Males and females affected in equal proportions All forms of transmission present Variable expression and penetrance Dominant negative : mutant protein adversely affects the function of the normal protein from the other allele, usually by interacting with it Haploinsufficiency : one functioning allele is not enough for a normal phenotype; the other may be a null allele (non-functional protein, reduced mRNA/gene product, or deleted) Gain of function : increased activity of the normal gene product Pleiotropy : a pathogenic variant in one gene causes multiple effects in different organs Autosomal recessive People with the condition usually in one sibship in one generation Males and females affected in equal proportions Consanguinity increases the number of individuals affected Cis : one allele contains more than one variant – individual NOT affected Trans : two different mutations on different alleles of the same gene – individual affected X-linked Males affected almost exclusively Transmitted from female carriers to sons Affected males cannot transmit the condition to their sons Carrier females may be mildly or fully affected due to skewed X-inactivation X-inactivation : one X is inactivated in females; genes in pseudoautosomal regions are NOT inactivated, so usually two copies X-autosomal translocation : if the translocated X is inactivated, partial monosomy of the autosomal segment is lethal to the cell Triplet repeat disorders Fragile X (CGG) – transcriptional silencing, loss of function Friedreich ataxia (GAA) – impaired transcription, loss of frataxin function Huntington disease, cerebellar ataxia (CAG) – gain of function Myotonic dystrophy I (CTG) – gain of function Mosaicism Gonadal : mutation only in the gonads; may account for recurrence of apparently new dominant mutations; no phenotypic effect but ~1% recurrence risk in offspring Somatic : may account for a less severe, tissue-limited presentation of an AD disorder Epigenetic Genomic imprinting : differential expression of a gene depending on whether it was inherited from mother or father, maintained by methylation Uniparental disomy : both chromosomes inherited from the same parent – via trisomy rescue or monosomy rescue Mitochondrial Polyplasmy – multiple copies of mtDNA per cell Heteroplasmy – mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA in a cell Threshold effect, random mitotic segregation of mitochondria, maternal inheritance of mitochondria Many mitochondrial disorders are coded in nuclear DNA – autosomal recessive Digenic Phenotype manifests only when two non-allelic controlling genes interact Multifactorial More than one factor causes the trait, including factors that are NOT genes (lifestyle, nutrition) Autosomal dominant : every generation, both sexes, and male-to-male transmission. Autosomal recessive : affected siblings in one sibship, unaffected parents. X-linked : affected individuals are almost exclusively male, and affected males do not pass it to their sons.

Genetic Screening When to suspect a genetic disorder, and the screening programs that run from preconception through pregnancy to the newborn. The organising idea: screening tests estimate risk; only invasive tests (CVS, amniocentesis) diagnose . Suspect a genetic disorder with DD/dysmorphism/malformations , family history, 3+ miscarriages , consanguinity/ancestry, or early/multiple cancers. Folic acid 0.8-1 mg/day from 3 months before pregnancy through the 1st trimester . NT > 3.5 mm → ↑ risk of aneuploidy, CHD, skeletal dysplasia, Noonan. eFTS (11-13w6d) screens T18/T21 at a 1:350 cut-off; NIPT (> 9 wk) screens cell-free placental DNA. CVS 11-13 wk, 1/100 miscarriage ; amniocentesis 15-20 wk, 1/200 . Ontario newborn screening covers 30 metabolic disorders, mostly AR . When to consider a genetic disorder Developmental delays, dysmorphic features, or congenital malformations Positive family history of a genetic disorder History of 3+ miscarriages/stillbirths , infertility, neonatal deaths Consanguinity / ethnic background: Ashkenazi Jewish – Tay-Sachs, BRCA1, Canavan disease, familial dysautonomia French Canadian – Tay-Sachs Mediterranean – β-thalassemia Southeast Asian – α-thalassemia Amish/Mennonite and Arab – various rare disorders African – sickle cell anemia Caucasian – cystic fibrosis Cancers – multiple family members, early onset (< 50), multiple primaries in 1 individual, occurrence in the less commonly affected sex Early-onset heart disease / sudden deaths Ontario newborn screening Screens for 30 metabolic disorders – most are autosomal recessive Wilson & Jungner criteria : disease (serious, natural Hx understood, asymptomatic stage), screening test (acceptable, economical, reliable), management (treatable, available) movement of oxygen in the blood Cystic fibrosis (CF) – causes problems with breathing and growth Severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) – affects the body's ability to fight infections Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) – causes muscle weakness and wasting Critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) – affects the quantity of oxygen in the blood Congenital hearing loss Preconception counselling Chromosome Disorder Testing The classic chromosome syndromes and the cytogenetic tests that detect them, followed by the basics of nutrition – macro- and micronutrients, vitamins and minerals, dietary reference intakes, and Canada's Food Guide. The organising idea for testing: a karyotype shows chromosome structure; a microarray shows gene content . Turner 45,X – webbed neck, coarctation, short stature, primary amenorrhea, normal intelligence. Klinefelter 47,XXY – tall, gynecomastia, small testes. DiGeorge 22q11.2 deletion – cleft palate, CHD, hypocalcemia, immunodeficiency. 15q11-q13: paternal deletion = Prader-Willi , maternal deletion = Angelman . Energy: carbohydrate and protein 4 kcal/g , fat 9 , alcohol 7 . Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K . RDA = EAR + 2 SD (meets 97.5% of the population). Developmental Milestones How development is monitored (surveillance and screening), what counts as global developmental delay, and the milestone chart by age across four domains. The organising idea: speech and language is the domain most predictive of cognition; gross motor the least . Surveillance = Rourke Baby Record; screening = Nipissing/LookSee ( one “no” = positive screen ) or ASQ. Global developmental delay : failure to meet milestones in 2+ areas at ≤ 5 years . Start early intervention as early as possible (brain plasticity). Anchors: sits 6 mo, pincer grasp 10 mo, walks and first words 12 mo, 2-word phrases 24 mo , stands on one foot 36 mo, hops/skips 60 mo. Monitoring development Surveillance : Rourke Baby Record Screening : Nipissing/LookSee (one “no” = positive screen), ASQ (compare scores to age-expected norms) Global developmental delay : failure to meet expected developmental milestones in 2+ areas of function at ≤ 5 years Early intervention works best when started as early as possible – brain plasticity Goals: optimize growth and developmental trajectory, prevent secondary problems, optimize participation Milestones by age – gross motor is least predictive of cognition; speech and language is most predictive. Nutrition How infants are fed – breast milk, formula, and the transition to solids from 6 to 24 months. The organising idea: exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months, then iron-containing foods , with supplements covering what breast milk lacks. Exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months (continue up to 2 years) + 400 IU/day vitamin D + iron-containing foods after 6 months . Breast milk and formula are both 20 kcal/oz (0.67 kcal/mL), 50% fat . Mixing formula incorrectly risks failure to thrive, electrolyte imbalance, dehydration . No honey before 12 months (infant botulism). Do not delay allergenic foods (egg, peanut). Breast milk vs formula Feature Breast milk Formula Energy 20 kcal/oz, 0.67 kcal/mL 20 kcal/oz, 0.67 kcal/mL Composition 50% fat, 40% lactose, 10% protein (60-80% whey, 20-40% casein) Colostrum (IgA, IgM, IgG) → transitional milk → mature milk 50% fat; higher vitamin and mineral content than human milk; iron absorbed less Feeding Every 2-3 hours for 10-20 min/side – high-fat hind milk is important Ready to feed, concentrate, powder – must be mixed correctly to avoid failure to thrive, electrolyte imbalance and/or dehydration Supplements / stools Exclusive up to 6 months, continue up to 2 years + 400 IU/day vitamin D + iron-containing foods after 6 months Fewer stools than breastfed babies Special formulas Hydrolyzed whey – lower osmolality, improves gastric emptying Soy – vegetarians, lactase deficiency, galactosemia Lactose free Protein hydrolysate – cannot digest/allergic to intact protein, fat malabsorption Iron supplementation for high-risk groups Birth weight < 3 kg Premature infants < 37 weeks gestation Prenatal alcohol exposure Maternal diabetes Infants of iron-deficient mothers Canadian feeding guidelines, 6-24 months Open cups support development of mature feeding skills from > 6 months Bottles and sippy cups are discouraged > 12 months Homo milk can be given, but cannot replace breast milk or formula Start lumpy Iron-containing foods – iron-fortified infant cereals, meat, tofu, legumes, poultry, fish, whole eggs No delay in starting allergenic foods – eggs, peanut products Parents decide what foods are available and when; children decide whether to eat and how much No honey before 12 months Honey under 12 months of age risks infantile botulism .

Normal Infant Growth The rules of thumb for normal weight, length and head growth from the newborn period to puberty. The organising idea: growth is judged by velocity against a few memorable anchors. Newborns lose 5-10% of birth weight in days 1-3 and regain it by 10-14 days . Birth weight doubles by 4-5 months and triples by 1 year . Weight anchors: 10 kg at 1 y, 20 kg at 5 y, 30 kg at 10 y . Length 50 cm at birth, 100 cm at 4 y . Head circumference 35 cm at birth, +2 cm/month for the first 3 months . Normal infant and child growth Measure Rule of thumb Newborn weight 5-10% weight loss on days 1-3 of life; regain birth weight by 10-14 days Infant weight Calculate growth velocity (g/day); double birth weight at 4-5 months, triple at 1 year Child weight 1 year = 10 kg, 5 years = 20 kg, 10 years = 30 kg Average gain 2-3 kg/year from 2 years to puberty Length / height Supine length < 2 years, stadiometer height > 2 years Birth = 50 cm, 4 years = 100 cm Average increase 5-8 cm/year from 4 years to puberty Head circumference Birth = 35 cm; increases 2 cm/month in the first 3 months

Common Childhood Behaviors Two halves: the basics of inflammation and immunity (innate vs adaptive, MHC, antibodies, immunization), then a general approach to common childhood behaviours – colic, night waking, tantrums, aggression, school avoidance. The organising idea for behaviour: take a careful Hx and PEx first, then decide typical (anticipatory guidance) vs atypical (further Ax and Tx) . Innate immunity acts within hours via PRRs recognising PAMPs/DAMPs; adaptive immunity develops over time via antigen-specific TCR/BCR and clonal selection. MHC I – all nucleated cells, presents cytosolic peptides to CD8 ; MHC II – APCs, presents external peptides to CD4 . Behaviour Hx uses the ABCs: antecedent, behaviour, consequence . Colic = crying > 3 h/day, > 3 days/week, > 3 weeks, peaks at 6 weeks. Tantrums peak 18-36 months and last < 5 min. Inflammation A general term for a wide range of immune responses within a localized tissue; systemic = sepsis Cardinal signs: swelling, redness, heat, pain, loss of function Acute inflammation – tissue repair, healing, and clearance of local pathogens Resolution – shifts in cytokines, M1 to M2 macrophages Chronic inflammation – tissue remodelling and loss of function over time Innate vs adaptive immunity Feature Innate immunity Adaptive immunity Onset Immediately or within hours of a pathogen's entry Develops over time – infection with a pathogen, or following immunization Recognition General evidence of infection or injury PAMPs – viral/bacterial DNA/RNA, lipid/carbohydrate components Danger signals / DAMPs – parts of cells in the wrong place, signals from damaged cells and tissues Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) – Toll-like, C-type lectin, NOD-like, RIG-I family receptors Initiates non-specific measures – inflammation Very specific targets; antigen is often a unique version of a protein Mutations in the antigen can reduce adaptive recognition Antigen-specific receptors – T-cell receptors (TCR), B-cell receptors (BCR) Clonal selection Vaccine component Adjuvant: alum, PAMPs Isolated or purified protein; killed/attenuated virus/bacteria Phagocytosis Macrophages and neutrophils recognize targets through PRRs Macrophages and neutrophils recognize antibody-bound targets through Fc receptors – opsonization Cytotoxicity NK cells – perforin/granzyme, FasL; recognize evidence of cell stress CD8 T-cells (cytotoxic/killer) – perforin/granzyme, FasL; recognize specific antigen on MHC class I NK cells – antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity Inflammation Tissue-resident cells produce cytokines and other pro-inflammatory agents to activate local vasculature and recruit immune cells; triggered by PAMPs, danger signals/DAMPs CD4 T-cells produce cytokines and other pro-inflammatory agents to maintain inflammation and drive tissue remodelling; complement activation, NK activation Major histocompatibility complexes Feature MHC class I MHC class II Chains α chain paired with β2-microglobulin α chain paired with a β chain Binds CD8 T-cells / cytotoxic T-cells CD4 T-cells / helper T-cells Expressed on All nucleated cells Immune cells (APCs) – dendritic cells, macrophages; some at baseline, can be induced by cytokines Pathway Endogenous – presents peptides from cytosolic proteins; usually self, but also intracellular pathogens Exogenous – presents peptides from external proteins; usually self, but also extracellular pathogens or anything taken up by phagocytosis Gene products HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C DPαβ, DQαβ, DRαβ Antibody functions Neutralize – block the biological activity of the antigen by binding to its surface Opsonize – bind the pathogen's surface antigen to facilitate phagocytosis Facilitate pathogen recognition and antigenic responses – bind to specialized immune cells Activate complement – phagocytosis and attraction of other immune cells towards the pathogen Immunization Immunologic memory : the immune system's ability to remember an infectious agent, giving an effective and rapid response on later exposure to the same or similar agents Passive immunity – transfer of immunoglobulins from human or animal sources; placental transfer Active immunity – the body produces pathogen-specific antibodies after an antigen is introduced through vaccines General approach to childhood behaviours Take a detailed history including the ABCs – antecedent, behaviour, consequence Assess development – make use of assessment tools PEx – consider underlying physical conditions Management plan – typical behaviour = anticipatory guidance ; atypical behaviour = further Ax and specific Tx Hidden causes of discomfort in young children Headache, undiagnosed seizures, entropion, otitis media, sinusitis, dental caries, mouth ulcers, pharyngitis, medication for asthma, GERD, constipation, UTI, renal stones, arthralgia/arthritis, occult fracture, hair tourniquet, eczema/dermatitis, skin breakdown/ulcer. Common childhood clinical presentations Behaviour Features Management Colic (5-20%) ↑ frequency/intensity of crying in young infants with no underlying illness Prolonged (> 3 hours/day), persistent (> 3 days/week for > 3 weeks), especially evenings; peaks at 6 weeks Careful evaluation of causes for discomfort, reassurance, support/respite Night waking (25%) Sleep patterns highly variable in infancy; cultural expectations have a significant influence Sleep hygiene, appropriate limit setting, eliminate bottle at 12 months, reassurance/nurturing Headbanging (under 2 years) Typically attention seeking, avoiding a request, or self-soothing Careful Hx and PEx, encourage “time-in”, redirection/distraction Infant masturbation (most children) May be mistaken for seizures/movement disorder; children quickly learn to keep it “private” Careful evaluation, caregiver education, encourage “time-in”, redirection/distraction Temper tantrums (18-36 months) Out-of-control behaviour – screaming, stomping, hitting, headbanging, falling down, frustration/distress; breath-holding Part of the normal assertion of independe

Social Pediatrics Health Canada's social determinants of health, the life-course models of how early adversity shapes later health, and the three levels of intervention. The organising idea: upstream interventions change the causes-of-the-causes; downstream ones change the effects . Childhood experiences matter: toxic stress alters brain development and ACEs act across the lifespan. Three life-course models: latency (one exposure, effect decades later), accumulation (exposures add up), pathways (early exposure sets off a chain of later adversity). Upstream = macro policy, midstream = micro policy/living conditions, downstream = service-level access. Health Canada social determinants of health Income and social status – low income, income inequality, social exclusion Employment and working conditions – safety at work, stress at work, social environment Education and literacy – job opportunities, social-psychological status, healthy lifestyle Childhood experiences – toxic stress alters brain development, negative coping skills, ACEs effects across the lifespan Physical environments – walkability, housing, neighbourhood density Social supports and coping skills – system supports, personal coping style, adverse life events Healthy behaviours – smoking and substance abuse, diet Access to health services – proximity, privileges, competing pressures Biology and genetic endowment – epigenetics, gene-environment interaction, genetic predisposition Gender – discrimination, gender pay gap, childcare responsibilities Culture – religious beliefs, cultural views on illness and health, cultural healing practices Race and racism – vulnerable populations, marginalization, discrimination Life-course models of childhood experience Latency : exposure at one point in the life course affects health years to decades later, despite any intervening experiences Accumulation : multiple exposures over the life course have individual health effects, but also combine to create more significant effects Pathways : a sequence of exposures in which one stage of life influences the probability of later exposures; the early exposure sets off a pathway towards further adversity Types of interventions to address social health problems Feature Upstream Midstream Downstream Aim Reform the fundamental social and economic structures that distribute wealth, power, opportunities, and decision-making Reduce exposure to hazards by improving material working and living conditions, or reduce risk by promoting healthy behaviours Increase equitable access, at an individual or family level, to health and social services Level Macro policy – national, transnational Micro policy – regional, local, community, organizational Service level Target Diminish the causes-of-the-causes Change the causes Change the effects of the causes

School Age Development between 6 and 12 years and what a child needs to be ready for school. The organising idea: rising academic demands unmask deficits that were invisible before school. Preschoolers' semi-logical thinking produces misconceptions (“my parents divorced because I was bad”). School-age children differentiate from parents; peers and rule-based games matter. Learning disabilities, behaviour disorders and intellectual disability often surface at school; a specific learning disability requires a significant deficit – 2 grades below expectations . School readiness spans physical, attitudinal, attentional, emotional, cognitive, cultural and academic domains. School-age development (6-12 years) In pre-school years, semi-logical thinking leads to misconceptions – “my parents divorced because I was bad” School-age children start to differentiate from their parents; peers important, rule-based games, increased attention span Learning disabilities, behaviour disorders, and intellectual disability may become evident during the school years Increasing difficulty may appear as educational demands increase; mild learning deficits may not present until school age Diagnosing a specific learning disability requires a “significant” academic deficit – 2 grades below expectations Factors affecting school readiness Readiness What it involves Physical health and fitness Hearing, vision, chronic conditions (surgical repairs of congenital disorders, medications) Attitude and motivation Understands school is important and will be hard; able to delay gratification to some degree Attentional Sits and attends, knows when to interrupt, listens without eye contact, assimilates verbal information Emotional Tolerates separation from parent, allows correction, makes friends Cognitive Achievement of previous milestones Cultural Family feels school is important; school and family are congruent Academic Reading (rhyming), writing (fine motor dexterity), arithmetic (symbolic thinking, number concepts) If a child will not be ready Learning in smaller groups (preschool) Remediation of identified deficits Delaying school entry Specialized programming

ADHD What ADHD is, how it is diagnosed, and how it is treated. The organising idea: the diagnosis needs enough symptoms, for long enough, starting early enough, in more than one setting, with real impairment – and nothing else that explains them better. 6+ inattentive and/or 6+ hyperactive-impulsive symptoms for ≥ 6 months , several present before age 12 , in 2+ settings , with clear functional impairment, and not better explained by another disorder. ADHD is highly heritable . Assessment: parent and child interviews across settings, rating scales (SNAP-IV) , psychological tests. Tx: psychoeducation, parent training/behavioural management, school accommodation, stimulants , non-stimulants. ADHD Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) : a neurodevelopmental disorder defined by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development Causes : highly heritable, gene-environment interaction, neurochemical/structural/functional brain abnormalities Assessment : thorough Hx (parent interview, child interview, consider multiple settings), rating scales (SNAP-IV), psychological tests Tx : psychoeducation, parent training/behavioural management, school accommodation, stimulants, non-stimulants Diagnostic criteria A. 6+ inattentive symptoms and/or 6+ hyperactive-impulsive symptoms persisting for at least 6 months , inconsistent with developmental level, with direct negative impact on social and academic/occupational activities B. Several symptoms were present prior to age 12 years C. Several symptoms are present in two or more settings – home, school, work, with friends/relatives, other activities D. Clear evidence that the symptoms interfere with, or reduce the quality of , social, academic, or occupational functioning E. Symptoms do not occur exclusively during schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder and are not better explained by another mental disorder – mood, anxiety, dissociative, or personality disorder, substance intoxication, withdrawal Symptom lists – count each column separately (6+ needed in either) # Inattention Hyperactivity-impulsivity a Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes in schoolwork, at work, or during other activities Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat b Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected c Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate d Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly e Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities Often “on the go,” acting as if “driven by a motor” f Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort Often talks excessively g Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed h Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn i Often forgetful in daily activities Often interrupts or intrudes on others

Adolescent Development The well-adolescent visit and the biological, psychological and social changes of adolescence, with the HEADSS interview as the tool for exploring them. The organising idea: adolescence runs from a physical event (puberty) to a psychological one (a restructured identity) . Adolescence spans 11-22 years . Girls' growth spurt at 10.5 y (peak 12), boys' at 12.5 y (peak 14). The prefrontal cortex matures later than limbic regions – reward seeking before emotion regulation. HEADSS : home, education/employment, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide/depression. Interview without parents after explaining confidentiality and its limits. Acculturation: integration keeps heritage and accepts the receiving culture; marginalization rejects both. Goals of the “well adolescent” assessment Growth Patient concerns Sexual health – 7 Ps : partners, practices, protection from STIs, past Hx of STIs, pregnancy, permission, personal identity Concerns with physical, social, mental, and emotional health – risk-taking behaviours Develop a therapeutic relationship – confidentiality and its limitations Definition Adolescence : the period of development that begins with the onset of puberty (physical event) and ends with the formation of a restructured identity and the ability to assume the tasks of young adulthood (psychological event); age 11-22 years . Biological development Biological Females Males Physical growth Growth spurt at 10.5 years, peak velocity at 12 years Increase fat, gain muscle, increase hip size Growth spurt at 12.5 years, peak velocity at 14 years Lose fat, gain more muscle, increase shoulder size Sexual characteristics (Tanner stages) Onset of breast development at 8-13 years Puberty = breast development, pubic hair, menarche Onset of testicular enlargement at 9-14 years Puberty = testicular size, penile growth, pubic hair Neurodevelopment Executive function – prefrontal cortex matures later than limbic regions; emotion regulation and reward seeking Same as females Psychological and social development Domain Topic Key points Psychological Freud (psychosexual stages) Id = instincts; ego = reality; superego = morality – stages below Piaget (cognitive) See Child Development – theories of development Erikson (psychosocial) See Child Development – theories of development Identity formation Psychosexual development – crushes vs. experimenting with sexual roles vs. intimacy and long-term relationships Sexuality, gender identity, gender expression, physical/emotional attraction Mental health Risk factors – heritability, early attachment patterns, noticeable differences in physical/pubertal development, substance abuse (CAGE questionnaire, CRAFFT interview), self-harm/suicidality, trauma/ACEs Social Peer relationships Close friendships with same-sex peers vs. strong peer group vs. individual meaningful friendships Culture Acculturation : adaptation that occurs as a result of intercultural contact – strategies below Racism and discrimination Reactive ethnicity : discrimination by another culture can lead ethnic minorities to remain separated and hold even more tightly to their heritage culture Freud's psychosexual stages Stage Age Description 1. Phallic 3-6 years Boys more attached to their mother; girls more attached to their father 4. Latency 6 years-puberty Children spend more time and interact mostly with same-sex peers 5. Genital Beyond puberty Individuals are attracted to opposite-sex partners Acculturation strategies Strategy Receiving culture Heritage culture Assimilation Accepts Rejects Separation Rejects Maintains Integration Accepts Retains Marginalization Rejects Rejects H.E.A.D.S.S. psychosocial interview for adolescents H ome and environment E ducation and employment A ctivities D rugs S exuality S uicide/depression The developmental approach Explain confidentiality and capacity to make treatment decisions Interview without parents – encourage collaboration with parents when possible/safe Ask open-ended questions, avoid medical jargon, be genuine/curious Elicit/check the youth's understanding of their health concerns when providing health education Be mindful of self-image, treatment adherence, transition care (pediatric to adult), and outcomes

Introduction to Vaccines What an ideal vaccine looks like, how vaccines protect individuals and populations, the main vaccine types, and pre- vs post-exposure prophylaxis. The organising idea: live vaccines give stronger, broader immunity but cannot be given to the immunocompromised, pregnant or neonates; non-live vaccines are safe but need adjuvants and boosters . Efficacy = controlled studies; effectiveness = real world. The herd-immunity threshold rises with transmissibility – high R0 (measles) needs higher coverage . Live attenuated: measles, OPV, rota, varicella, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid. Rotavirus is the only routine oral vaccine in Canada . Measles PEP: vaccine within 72 h if immunocompetent > 6 months; IG within 4-6 days if immunocompromised, pregnant, or < 6 months. HIV PEP within 72 h for 28 days . Ideal vaccines Safe with minimal adverse effects Effective – lifelong protection after a single dose that can be given at birth Inexpensive Stable during shipment and storage Easy to administer What vaccines do Individual level – protect the immunized person against the specific disease Population level – reduce the incidence of disease; reduce exposure of susceptible individuals and consequent illness Vaccine efficacy : ability to prevent illness in people vaccinated in controlled studies Vaccine effectiveness : ability to prevent illness in people in the real world Herd immunity Herd immunity : the immunity of a population against a specific infectious disease A population's resistance to spread depends on the percentage of people who are immune and the probability that those still susceptible will contact an infected person The proportion that must be immune depends on the transmissibility of the agent – from a symptomatically infected person or an asymptomatically colonized person High R0 = highly infectious diseases that require higher immunization coverage – measles Live vs non-live vaccines Feature Live attenuated Non-live Advantages Immune response similar to natural infection Longer-lasting and broader immunity Produces immunity in most recipients when injected Safe – cannot replicate or cause the disease they are intended to prevent More stable – minimal interference from circulating antibody; less impact of a break in the cold chain Disadvantages May result in vaccine-strain disease Circulating antibody may interfere with the response Unstable – requires careful storage and handling Weaker response than live vaccines – may need adjuvants; usually a primary series to prime the immune system Response is mostly humoral Less sustained – antibody titre falls over time, so booster doses are needed Contraindications Immunocompromised, pregnant women, neonates — Live vaccines: who must not get them Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in the immunocompromised, pregnant women, and neonates . Vaccine types Class Type Examples Live attenuated Viral Measles, oral polio vaccine (OPV), rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever Bacterial Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), oral typhoid Non-live Inactivated whole cell Viral: inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), hepatitis A Bacterial: pertussis, cholera Inactivated bacterial toxin (toxoid) Tetanus toxoid, diphtheria Subunit / purified Protein-based viral: hepatitis B, HPV, Shingrix recombinant protein vaccine Protein-based bacterial: acellular pertussis, injectable typhoid Polysaccharide: pneumococcal 23 Conjugate: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), pneumococcal, MCV-4, meningococcal C Vaccine facts Healthy children can shed vaccine virus in stool for up to 1 month The only oral vaccine in the routine Canadian schedule is rotavirus NOT routine in Canada: oral polio, yellow fever, shingles, salmonella, Japanese encephalitis, hepatitis A, meningococcal B, pneumococcal polysaccharide, BCG Pre- and post-exposure immunoprophylaxis. PrEP : preventive strategies in vulnerable persons BEFORE an anticipated high-risk activity/event that could lead to substantial exposure. PEP : preventive strategies AFTER a high-risk activity/event but before the onset of disease. Disease Pre-exposure (PrEP) Post-exposure (PEP) HIV Chemoprophylaxis: anti-HIV drugs (Truvada) taken daily Chemoprophylaxis: HIV PEP started within 72 h for 28 days Measles IG: N/A Vaccine ONLY, 2 weeks before: unvaccinated immunocompetent, infants > 6 months, previously vaccinated immunocompetent non-pregnant hosts without lab evidence of immunity IG within 4-6 days : immunocompromised, pregnant women, infants < 6 months Vaccine within 72 h : immunocompetent, > 6 months Varicella (chickenpox) IG: N/A Vaccine ONLY, 4-6 weeks before: unvaccinated immunocompetent, > 1 year, previously vaccinated immunocompetent non-pregnant hosts without lab evidence of immunity IG within 96 hours : immunocompromised, pregnant women, neonates of mothers without immunity Vaccine within 3-5 days : immunocompetent, > 1 year Hepatitis A IG, 2 weeks before: immunocompromised, infants < 6 months, chronic liver disease or > 40 years, travelling to endemic countries Vaccine: > 6 months travelling to endemic countries in > 2-4 weeks IG within 2 weeks: immunocompromised, infants < 6 months, chronic liver disease or > 40 years Vaccine within 2 weeks: immunocompetent, 6 months-40 years Rabies IG: N/A Vaccine, 30 days before: travel to countries with a high prevalence of rabid animals, work with wildlife, spelunkers/hunters IG ASAP: unvaccinated with high-risk exposure Vaccine ASAP after a high-risk bite/scratch/bat exposure: unvaccinated get a 4-dose primary series (5 doses if immunosuppressed); previously vaccinated get 2 booster doses

Which one of the following statements on diagnostic tools in incorrect ? Pathology involves the interpretation of cells and tissues. Ultrasound does not expose the patient to radiation. Microbiology identifies bacteria, viruses, and parasites. X-ray, CT, and MRI produce signals based upon tissue density. Biochemistry includes metabolic tests and tumour markers. The correct answer is D. MRI does not produce a signal based on tissue density, but instead on the prevalence of hydrogen atoms.

Which one of the following approaches is not in alignment with Choosing Wisely principles? A patient presents with a concerning mole and is concerned about skin cancer. The physician performs a punch biopsy for pathologic diagnosis. A patient presents with lower back pain since last week after moving heavy boxes. The physician orders an MRI for further investigation. A patient with good overall health has no symptoms and wants blood tests to confirm that she does not have any unseen conditions. The physician emphasizes that there does not appear to be any concerns and does not run the blood tests. A hospital implements a policy to reduce the number of pre-operative laboratory tests for low-risk surgeries to save both time and money, particularly when the tests do not change patient management. The correct answer is B. In the Choosing Wisely framework, the use of costly testing is avoided if it won’t change patient management. As well, other lower cost options should be followed in this scenario first before any expensive testing/investigation

Which of the following is considered the strongest evidence in the context of evidence-based management plans? Expert opinion Observational studies Non-randomized control study Systematic review Randomized control study The correct answer is D. A systematic review analyzes many different peer-reviewed articles and is considered the strongest form of evidence in evidence-based decision making.

Which of the following accurately describes the indicated strategy for prevention and disease control? Primordial prevention is geared toward the entire population. Primary prevention has the ultimate goal of reducing disease prevalence. Tertiary prevention is geared toward people with one or more risk factors. Secondary prevention intends to reduce complications for patients with advanced disease. Health promotion applies mainly to patients with one or more risk factors. The correct answer is A. Primordial prevention (Health promotion) is geared toward the entire population with a goal of reducing risk factors.

Two approaches for disease prevention include the clinical approach and the public health approach. Which of the following statements is incorrect ? The clinical approach identifies high-risk individuals and offers individual protection. The public health approach may lead to poor motivation for individual patients. The public health approach involves altering behaviours in the entire population. The prevention paradox is the phenomenon that, with the public health approach, many people need to make changes that may only provide a relatively small benefit to individuals. The clinical approach is effective in widespread reduction of disease incidence. The correct answer is E. The clinical approach involves treating individuals who have highly elevated risk factors or who already have a condition, but it is not as valuable in the widespread reduction of disease incidence.

Concerning the epidemiological transition, which of the following statements is correct? The typical life expectancy in the receding pandemics stage is >70 years. The pestilence and famine stage is largely associated with malnutrition and infectious diseases. In the degenerative and man-made diseases stage, there is an increase in chronic disease, but less than 50% of deaths are due to cardiovascular disease. In the delayed degenerative diseases stage, cardiovascular disease is largely absent and cancer dominates as the primary cause of death. The pestilence and famine stage typically has more than 50% of deaths as the result of cardiovascular disease. The correct answer is B. The pestilence and famine stage is the first stage of the epidemiological transition, where major causes of death include malnutrition and infectious diseases.

Which of the following statements applying Emanuel’s models of the physician-patient relationship (1992) is true? A patient presents to a family practice who trusts that the physician knows best and will follow the physician’s instructions. This patient is seeking an informative model. A patient presents to a family practice with conflicting values about treatment options. The patient wants the physician to provide advice and counselling to arrive to the best treatment option. This patient is seeking a paternalistic model. A patient wants to hear all the options for treating high blood pressure before making his own decision according to his own fixed values. This patient is seeking an interpretive model. A patient comes into the clinic seeking sleeping pills. The physician attempts to convince the patient that they should first attempt a behavioural modification approach, including introducing appropriate sleep hygiene. This is an example of the deliberative model. When a patient and physician are close friends, it’s an example of the fraternalistic model. The correct answer is D. In the deliberative model, the physician acts as a teacher, articulating and persuading the patient of appropriate values and treatments.

Jerry has forgotten about a sum of $1000 in cash left under his mattress. His neighbour, Keith, breaks in and finds the $1000, and takes it home to feed his starving family. Because Jerry has forgotten about this, the money was never missed. Which of the following statements about Keith’s action is correct? According to social intuitionism, it is important to understand the reasons for Keith’s actions and other contextual information before reaching a conclusion about the rightness/wrongness of the act. If Keith was practicing casuistry, the decision to take the money would have been the result of an outside-the-box solution to his current financial problems. To decide if there is any wrongdoing, a proponent of ethical deliberation immediately> arrives at a conclusion regarding this situation, and then finds reasons to justify it. A deontologist would not find Keith’s actions to be wrong because the decision to take the money from Jerry treated him as an end in-and-of-himself. According to utilitarianism, there is no wrongdoing in this situation as happiness and utility is maximized. The correct answer is E. In utilitarianism, actions strive to improve utility and happiness. Since Jerry has forgotten about the cash under his mattress, he will not suffer any pain if it is stolen, and this cash can help Keith and Keith’s family.

Which was not a significant contribution toward the history of medicine in the Medieval period? The printing press allowed for the dissemination of a lot of medical knowledge. Universities began teaching medicine The importance of a working knowledge of anatomy was first introduced Diagnostic tests involved examining bodily fluids, such as urine. The correct answer is C. The importance of anatomy in medicine was a key advancement made by Galen of Pergamum, a Greek Physician, about 150 years BCE.

What type of cartilage is found in the epiglottis and the larynx? Elastic cartilage Hyaline cartilage Loose cartilage Fibrous cartilage The correct answer is A. Elastic cartilage forms epiglottis, larynx and is made of Type 2 collagen and elastin.

You are examining a newborn child 1 hour after birth and you check for their red reflex using an ophthalmoscope. You do not find a red reflection in their eyes. Which of the following is the next best step? Proceed with your examination. A red reflection should not be seen in the child’s eyes. Proceed with your examination as this is normal in newborn children. Check the baby for a red reflex 1 month after its birth, at which point it should have developed. While most children are born with a red reflex, some children will develop this within the first year of life. If it has not been developed then, this is problematic and further services may be needed. The absence of a red-reflex is abnormal. Consult with an ophthalmologist immediately. The correct answer is D. The absence of a red reflex indicates that there is obstruction of visual input to the retina. This is essential for normal visual pathway development in infants.
