Hemostasis and Coagulation Testing Hemostasis runs in four stages — platelet plug, thrombin generation, fibrin stabilization, then inhibition and fibrinolysis — and the lab probes each with a clotting-time test that maps onto the old intrinsic/extrinsic/common scheme. vWF–GPIb = adhesion; fibrinogen–GPIIb/IIIa = aggregation. TF/VIIa initiates; thrombin amplifies (V, VIII, XI); tenase (IXa+VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa+Va) propagate; FXIII cross-links . Vitamin K-dependent: II, VII, IX, X . aPTT = intrinsic + common, PT = extrinsic + common. Mixing study: corrects = deficiency, doesn't = inhibitor . A negative D-dimer rules out VTE ; a positive one means little. Definitions Bleeding : to emit or lose blood Hemostasis : activation of multiple clotting-system components in response to vessel injury to control bleeding; four stages below 1. Primary hemostasis — vasoconstriction + platelet plug Triggered by vessel-wall injury exposing subendothelial collagen Vasoconstriction at the injury site ↓ flow (reflex neurogenic mechanisms) Adhesion : vWF tethers platelets to collagen via platelet GPIb/IX ; platelets also bind collagen directly through other receptors Activation / contraction : shape change (discoid → spheroid), granule secretion, calcium influx; the plug offers a negatively charged phospholipid surface for coagulation factor assembly Thromboxane: arachidonic acid → (cyclooxygenase) → endoperoxides → (thromboxane synthase) → thromboxane A2 Aggregation : fibrinogen bridges platelets by binding activated GPIIb/IIIa → platelet plug 2. Secondary hemostasis — coagulation factors generate thrombin and fibrin Initiation Tissue factor (TF) released from injured tissue cells, endothelium and monocytes TF + FVIIa form the TF/VIIa complex, which activates a little FIX and FX → a small amount of thrombin FXII and other contact factors play only a minor role (activating FXI) Amplification Thrombin activates FV → Va , FVIII → VIIIa , FXI → XIa , and more platelets Propagation TF/VIIa activates FIX; IXa + VIIIa = tenase complex → converts much more FX to Xa Xa + Va + Ca2+ + phospholipid (activated platelets) = prothrombinase complex → prothrombin (FII) to large amounts of thrombin (IIa) 3. Fibrin clot formation and stabilization Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin monomers, which polymerize into a soluble clot Thrombin activates FXIII , which cross-links fibrin and stabilizes the clot 4. Inhibition — limit thrombin and break down the clot Block initiation : tissue factor pathway inhibitor ( TFPI ) targets TF-VIIa and Xa Block further thrombin generation : protein C and protein S inactivate FV and FVIII Block thrombin already generated : antithrombin (also binds FIX, X and XI) Fibrinolysis : t-PA converts plasminogen → plasmin , which breaks cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers Brakes on fibrinolysis: TAFI (thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor) suppresses plasmin formation; α2-antiplasmin and PAI-1 inhibit plasmin and t-PA Cell-based model: TF-VIIa starts it, thrombin feeds back to activate V, VIII and XI, and FXIIIa turns soluble fibrin into cross-linked fibrin. Coagulopathy in Adults A bleeding disorder found in adulthood is usually one that was mild enough to be missed , one whose lab values overstate it, or one that was acquired . Severe congenital disorders are found in childhood; adults present with mild-moderate phenotypes , with low factor levels that need not bleed badly , or with acquired hemophilia A, vWD or platelet disorders. What turns up in adults Mild-moderate congenital phenotypes — severe forms are usually identified earlier in life Congenital deficiencies with clinico-laboratory discrepancy — a low factor level may not confer a severe bleeding phenotype Acquired bleeding disorders — acquired hemophilia A, acquired vWD, platelet disorders Schulich Reviews FVIII is made mainly by endothelium, not liver → normal or ↑ in liver disease while the liver-made factors fall

Coagulopathy in Children A newborn's hemostatic system is still maturing, so normal neonatal coagulation values are not adult values . Hemostasis matures over the first 6 months . An immature liver means lower vitamin K-dependent factors, protein C and protein S , so PT and aPTT are physiologically longer in neonates and premature infants — interpret against age-specific ranges. Neonatal hemostasis Hemostatic system matures over the first 6 months of life Liver immaturity → lower levels of most factors: vitamin K-dependent factors, protein C, protein S PT and aPTT are physiologically longer in premature infants and neonates than in adults Schulich Reviews vWD = most common hereditary bleeding disorder (0.1-1% of population); vWF recruits platelets and carries FVIII

Thrombocytopenia, Anticoagulants and VTE A low platelet count is sorted by mechanism — made too few, destroyed, pooled, or miscounted . The destructive causes split on whether they bleed or clot, which is why several of them must never be given platelets. The lecture then covers the anticoagulants and VTE. < 10 = spontaneous bleeding risk. ITP: isolated low platelets, diagnosis of exclusion, steroids/IVIg. Schistocytes + low platelets: low ADAMTS-13 = TTP (plasma exchange) , normal + diarrhea/AKI = HUS , deranged coags = DIC . LMWH/fondaparinux: anti-Xa not aPTT; UFH safe in renal failure, reversed by protamine; dabigatran by idarucizumab. Negative D-dimer excludes VTE. Approach to Leukocytosis and Myeloproliferative Neoplasms A high white count is sorted by which lineage, how mature, and whether it is clonal . The clonal mature myeloid disorders are the MPNs, most driven by a JAK2 switch stuck "on". Blasts = acute leukemia (AML/ALL); mature clonal = CML/CLL/MPN; reactive = infection, drugs, inflammation. Reactive neutrophilia: left shift, toxic granules, Döhle bodies, no blasts ; primary: blasts, WBC > 30, ↑ eos/basos. PV = JAK2 in 90-95% , aquagenic pruritus, low EPO; manage with ASA + Hct < 0.45 , hydroxyurea if ≥ 60 or prior clot. ET: platelets ≥ 450. PMF: teardrops, leukoerythroblastic film , ruxolitinib. Leukopenia and Febrile Neutropenia Neutropenia is graded by the ANC and matters because of infection risk; its most urgent form, febrile neutropenia , is treated as an emergency before the source is known. ANC < 1.5 = neutropenia; < 0.5 severe . Acquired causes: infection, drugs ( chemo, clozapine , antithyroid), autoimmune (Felty), B12/folate/copper, marrow failure, spleen. Febrile neutropenia = > 38.3°C once or ≥ 38.0°C for 1 h : stabilize, culture, no DRE , empiric imipenem or pip-tazo , add vancomycin for line/skin infection or instability. Definitions Leukopenia : ↓ WBCs below the reference range (4-10 × 10 9 /L) Neutropenia : ANC < 1.5 × 10 9 /L — mild 1-1.5 · moderate 0.5-0.99 · severe < 0.5 Causes of neutropenia Congenital Acquired Constitutional neutropenia Cyclic neutropenia Severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann syndrome) Chediak-Higashi syndrome Shwachman-Diamond syndrome Barth syndrome Infection — viral (EBV, CMV, HAV/HBV/HCV, HIV, influenza); bacterial (sepsis, mycobacteria, Salmonella , Brucella , Rickettsia ) Toxins — chemotherapy, radiation, drugs (antibiotics, antithyroid, clozapine , antiepileptics) Autoimmune — primary (autoimmune neutropenia); secondary (SLE, RA, Felty syndrome) Nutritional — B12, folate, copper, malnutrition Marrow failure — MDS, AML, lymphoma in marrow, metastatic solid tumour Splenic sequestration Complications Bacterial : gram-negative ( E. coli , Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Klebsiella pneumoniae ); gram-positive ( S. aureus , streptococci, enterococci) Viral reactivation : HSV, CMV, VZV Fungal : Candida , Aspergillus , mucormycosis Febrile neutropenia — oncologic emergency Single oral temperature > 38.3°C , or ≥ 38.0°C sustained over 1 hour , in a neutropenic patient. Stabilize : ABCs, IV fluids, O2 for hypoxia Investigate : CBC + differential, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, transaminases, total bilirubin, blood and urine cultures , CXR Hx/PEx : head and neck (oral/pharyngeal mucosa, sinuses), respiratory, GI ( no DRE ), GU, skin and IV catheter sites, mental status/neuro Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics : a carbapenem (IV imipenem) or IV piperacillin-tazobactam Add IV vancomycin if skin or catheter-site infection, or hemodynamic instability Febrile neutropenia cannot wait Start empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly once cultures are drawn. No digital rectal exam in a neutropenic patient.

Approach to Leukemia Leukemias are classified on two axes — myeloid vs lymphoid and acute (blasts) vs chronic (mature cells) — and the acute ones bring their own emergencies: APL bleeding, tumour lysis and leukostasis. AML = adults, ALL = children (~90% cured). CML = t(9;22) BCR-ABL → imatinib. CLL = most common, elderly, smudge cells, CD5+ B cells , AIHA/ITP; do not treat asymptomatic disease. APL = t(15;17) PML-RARα, multiple Auer rods, DIC → ATRA + arsenic . TLS = ↑ K, PO4, urate, ↓ Ca → hydrate, rasburicase/allopurinol. Leukostasis → leukapheresis. Leukemia WBC cancer localized to blood and marrow Most common cancer in younger patients; drops out of the top 6 with age Risk factors : male, older age, smoking, obesity; prior hematologic disease (MDS, PV, ET, CML); chemicals (benzene, alkylating agents, topoisomerase inhibitors); radiation; hereditary (Down, Bloom, Fanconi anemia, ataxia telangiectasia) Sites : blood, skin ( leukemia cutis ), gums, behind the eyes Myeloid sarcoma : extramedullary AML mass made of myeloblasts Complications : leukocytosis and infiltration, tumour lysis syndrome , DIC Radiation and surgery are not treatment options The four leukemias Feature AML ALL CML CLL What it is Myeloid cells fail to differentiate beyond the blast stage FAB: M3 = APL; Erythrocytosis Too many red cells is sorted by one test — serum EPO : low means the marrow is driving itself (PV), normal/high means something is driving EPO. Erythrocytosis: Hb > 170 (M) / > 160 (F) . Low EPO = primary (PV) ; normal/high EPO = secondary — hypoxia (COPD, OSA, smoking, altitude), renal hypoxia, EPO-secreting tumours (RCC, HCC, cerebellar hemangioblastoma) , EPO/androgens. All three lines high → treat as erythrocytosis. Erythrocytosis ↑ RBCs : Hb > 170 g/L in men , > 160 g/L in women Congenital causes are very uncommon Split on EPO : low EPO = primary (the marrow is autonomous); normal/high EPO = secondary (something drives EPO) → treat the cause High Hb + high platelets + high WBC If Hb, platelets and WBCs are all high, treat it as erythrocytosis (think PV). Type Congenital Acquired Primary (low EPO) EPO receptor mutations (ECYT1) Polycythemia vera Secondary (normal/high EPO) Defects in the oxygen-sensing pathway; left-shifted Hb-O2 dissociation curve Systemic hypoxia : COPD, R→L shunt, smoking, OSA, high altitude Local (renal) hypoxia : renal artery stenosis, renal cysts, post-renal transplant Pathologic EPO : cerebellar hemangioblastoma, RCC, HCC, pheochromocytoma Drugs : EPO, androgens Other — Splenectomy, hyposplenism

Thrombocytosis and Pancytopenia A high platelet count is usually reactive , occasionally clonal, sometimes not real; pancytopenia is sorted like any cytopenia into production, destruction and sequestration . Thrombocytosis ≥ 450 , extreme ≥ 1000; secondary is more common — infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, bleeding, asplenia. Primary = MPNs. Spurious = fragments, cryoglobulins, bacteria. Pancytopenia = fatigue + bleeding + infections ; causes: marrow failure/infiltration, immune/drug destruction, splenomegaly. Thrombocytosis Platelets ≥ 450 × 10 9 /L ; extreme ≥ 1,000 (up to 5% of cases) Secondary (reactive) is more common → treat the underlying cause Type Causes Primary — congenital Familial thrombocytosis Primary — acquired MPN (PV, ET, PMF, CML); MDS/MPN overlap syndromes Secondary (more common) Infection (bacterial most common); inflammation (IBD, RA, SLE); tissue damage (trauma, surgery, burns); hemorrhage; iron deficiency anemia ; hemolysis; hyposplenism (functional asplenia, splenectomy); non-hematologic malignancy; rebound after myelosuppression Spurious (falsely high count) Red cell fragments (microspherocytes, schistocytes), cryoglobulin crystals, neoplastic cell fragments, bacteria Pancytopenia ↓ all hematopoietic lines Anemia (fatigue) + thrombocytopenia (mucocutaneous bleeding) + leukopenia (recurrent infection) Fever : core temperature > 38°C (100.4°F) Causes of pancytopenia ↓ Production ↑ Destruction Sequestration Aplastic anemia / congenital marrow failure MDS , CMML, AML Myelofibrosis Myelophthisis (marrow infiltration) Vitamin deficiencies Idiopathic Immune Medications Infections Connective tissue disorders Splenomegaly

Specialized Testing for Hematological Malignancies One marrow sample feeds four tests — morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics — plus a core biopsy for architecture. Sample the PSIS ; never core the sternum . Normal M:E ratio 1:1-3:1 ; cellularity ≈ 100 − age . Flow: FSC = size, SSC = granularity ; needs fresh (< 24 h) sample. Cytogenetics finds chromosome changes; molecular testing finds mutations. Morphology of the marrow aspirate Assesses all stages of hematopoiesis Site: posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) ; if necessary sternum (children and adults) or tibia (children only) Never take a core biopsy from the sternum (too close to the heart) or tibia; never take any marrow sample from the skull or ribs Normal aspirate : mixed erythroid and myeloid cells at all stages; myeloid:erythroid ratio 1:1 to 3:1 ; no dysplasia Normal core biopsy Subcortical acellular zone often present Cellularity ≈ 100 − age (%) Cell composition similar to the aspirate Flow cytometry Characterizes cell populations in a mixture: light scatter gives physical properties ; fluorescent antibodies detect antigens on or in cells Forward scatter = size ; side scatter = complexity/granularity Samples: fresh (< 24 h) liquids (blood, marrow aspirate, CSF, ascites), or solid tissue disaggregated into suspension (lymph node, biopsy) Immunophenotype = pattern of antigen expression: immaturity, myeloid, B-cell, T-cell and NK markers Cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics Cytogenetics : chromosome changes in structure, location or function Molecular genetics : mutations in the genetic material of cells Pathology of the core biopsy Architecture and cellularity (see normal core above). Cytogenetics example: two interstitial deletions of chromosome 5q, del(5)(q13q31) and del(5)(q13q33), with their commonly deleted regions. Marrow morphology (arrows mark abnormal cells) with a chromosome ideogram marking the altered band.

Approach to Lymphadenopathy Most enlarged nodes are reactive; the job is to use location, character and red flags to find the few that need a biopsy. > 98% of enlarged nodes in primary care are benign ; only inguinal nodes are normally palpable in adults. Supraclavicular = think abdominal/thoracic malignancy. Red flags: fixed, non-tender, matted, ≥ 2 cm , not settling after 2 weeks of antibiotics, B symptoms, abnormal CBC/CXR. T-cell activation needs TCR + CD28–CD80/86 + cytokines ; germinal centres make high-affinity antibody by somatic hypermutation. Lymph nodes Contain lymphocytes that filter lymph to detect and fight infection Lymphoid tissue mass peaks in adolescence In adults, nodes are normally not palpable except inguinal In primary care, > 98% of enlarged nodes are non-malignant Lymph node anatomy: B-cell follicles with germinal centres in the cortex, T-cell zone in the paracortex, lymph in through afferent and out through efferent vessels. Primary vs secondary lymphoid tissue Primary = bone marrow (B cells), thymus (T cells) — where antigen-specific lymphocytes differentiate Secondary = spleen, lymph nodes, GALT/MALT — where immune responses start Mature but naive B and T cells leave the primary tissues and recirculate looking for antigen Starting a response in the node T cells need an APC (TCR binds peptide-MHC) Immature dendritic cells mature by innate recognition of pathogens, move to the T-cell zone and express CD80/86 (B7.1/B7.2) 3-signal hypothesis : (1) antigen-specific signal (TCR); (2) co-stimulation ( CD28 ↔ CD80/86 ); (3) cytokines B cells become plasma cells : T-independent (low-affinity IgM) or T-dependent (high-affinity) Germinal centre makes high-affinity BCRs by proliferation and somatic hypermutation of the variable region Timeline in the node: antigen arrives day 0-1, T cells proliferate day 1, germinal centre and low-affinity antibody by day 4, high-affinity antibody by day 8-10. Classification and Testing for Lymphomas Lymphomas split first into Hodgkin (RS cells in a mostly reactive background) and non-Hodgkin (a sheet of one malignant B or T clone); NHL is then classified by cell type, maturity, size, architecture and behaviour. Classical HL = RS cells, CD15+/CD30+ ; nodular sclerosis is most common (young adults, mediastinal mass); lymphocyte-depleted is worst. NLPHL = popcorn cells, CD20+ , no EBV. HL: early stage chemo + radiation; advanced ABVD . DLBCL = most common NHL, rapidly enlarging mass, R-CHOP , IPI. Follicular = t(14;18) , indolent, watch and wait, BR + rituximab. SLL/CLL: smudge cells, don't treat asymptomatic. Approach to Lymphoma Lymphoma is diagnosed on tissue , sorted into Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin, and staged by where it is relative to the diaphragm ; staging and type decide treatment. HL : young, nodal, contiguous spread , RS cells in inflammation, always treated to cure. NHL : older, extranodal possible, monoclonal. Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies Surgery diagnoses, radiation treats locally, and systemic drugs do the rest — from classic cytotoxics that hit every dividing cell to targeted and immune therapies aimed at one molecule on the tumour. Classic chemo: myelosuppression, alopecia, mucositis ; organ toxicities — cisplatin ears/kidneys, vincristine neuropathy, bleomycin lungs, doxorubicin heart, cyclophosphamide bladder . Rituximab = CD20, daratumumab = CD38. Imatinib → CML; ibrutinib → CLL (AF, bruising); bortezomib → myeloma; lenalidomide → del(5q) MDS, myeloma; ATRA → APL . Checkpoint inhibitors block PD-1/PD-L1; treat their immune toxicity with steroids. Treatment modalities in hematologic malignancy Therapy Use Example Surgery (local) Diagnosis ONLY Resect a lymph node Radiotherapy (local) Palliation Myeloma bone pain Cure Limited-stage lymphoma; CNS prophylaxis in ALL Chemotherapy (systemic) Classic, targeted, immune and hormonal therapies See tables below Classic chemotherapy — all share myelosuppression (infection risk), alopecia and mucositis Class Drugs Mechanism Alkylating agents Cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, cisplatin, carboplatin Cross-link guanine → strands cannot separate or enter S phase → arrest → apoptosis Antimetabolites Methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, 6-mercaptopurine, 6-thioguanine Interfere with normal nucleic-acid metabolism Antitumour antibiotics Doxorubicin, daunorubicin, bleomycin Inhibit topoisomerase II → DNA cannot relax, stays broken; intercalate between base pairs; generate ROS → apoptosis Topoisomerase inhibitors Etoposide, anthracyclines Inhibit topoisomerase I → DNA cannot uncoil/relax → no replication (as written in source) Antimicrotubule agents Paclitaxel (Taxol), docetaxel (Taxotere), vincristine (Oncovin) Vinca alkaloids block microtubule assembly in metaphase; taxanes bind and stabilize microtubules so chromosomes cannot separate → M-phase arrest → apoptosis Organ-specific chemotoxicities: cisplatin/carboplatin — ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity; vincristine — neuropathy; bleomycin/busulfan — pulmonary fibrosis; trastuzumab/doxorubicin — cardiotoxicity; cyclophosphamide — hemorrhagic cystitis; methotrexate/5-FU/6-MP — myelosuppression. Radiation Oncology, Quality Improvement and Critical Appraisal Radiation kills by DNA damage and is given in fractions so normal tissue can recover between doses while tumour cannot. The lecture closes with the QI cycle and the vocabulary of trial appraisal. Fractionation works through the 4 Rs — repair and repopulation spare normal tissue; redistribution and reoxygenation sensitize tumour. Fast-growing tumours are most radiosensitive. Radiation pneumonitis at 6-12 weeks → steroids; late hypothyroidism, infertility, second cancers. QI: root cause analysis is the forgotten step ; outcome/process/ balancing measures. ITT is conservative, PP inflates ; confounders are not on the causal path; power = 1 − β; NNT = 1/ARR . Radiation therapy Ionizing radiation to treat tumours: damages DNA so cells cannot reproduce — normal and cancer cells alike Every tissue has a tolerance dose beyond which damage is irreparable; spinal cord, bowel, kidney and lung are often limiting Delivered externally or internally Modality How it works External beam (EBRT) Photon (x-ray) or electron beams; 10-15 min, 5 days/week for 1-10 weeks Painless; worst side effects near the end of the course Slight risk of a secondary cancer years later Brachytherapy Decaying isotopes placed next to the tumour (gynecologic, GU) LDR permanent implants : dose over days-months · HDR temporary implants : dose over minutes Modern: minimally invasive, 3D image-guided (prostate, gynecologic) IMRT (intensity-modulated) Maximizes the therapeutic ratio by sparing uninvolved tissue from high dose SABR / SRS (stereotactic) Highly focused external beam (~1 mm accuracy) with very high doses in 1-5 treatments ; e.g. Gamma Knife, CyberKnife, TrueBeam Fractionation and the 4 Rs Fractionation : total dose split into small daily fractions over weeks Exploits the difference in repair : normal cells recover by repair and repopulation ; cancer cells are sensitized by redistribution and reoxygenation and repair less well Cells are most vulnerable in G2-M , when DNA is exposed → fast-growing tumours are more radiosensitive and respond sooner The 4 Rs of radiobiology Repair of sublethal damage between fractions Repopulation (regrowth) between fractions Redistribution of cells into radiosensitive cell-cycle phases Reoxygenation of hypoxic cells, making them more radiosensitive Clinical uses Cure : destroy localized tumours; adjuvant — kill microscopic residual disease after surgery/chemo. Sites: breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, pancreas, esophagus, head and neck, brain, skin, gynecologic, lymphoma, bladder, sarcoma Palliation : shrink tumours to relieve pain or neurologic symptoms; Which statement on the topic of reticulocytes is true? A patient presents to your clinic complaining of fatigue. He is anemic, with MCV of 85 fL [normal 80-96 fL]. Retic count is very low, and blood film analysis is positive for teardropshaped RBCs. What is the likely diagnosis? Pure red cell aplasia Aplastic anemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Myelophthisis Hemolysis The correct answer is D. In myelophthisis, bone marrow is replaced with other cells. This condition is associated with teardrops in the blood film.

Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology for megaloblastic anemia? A lack of Vitamin B12 leads to the rapid division of the red blood cell precursor Cholesterol and phospholipids are deposited into the plasma membrane of the red blood cell The cell cycle cannot progress from the G2 growth phase into mitosis, so there is cytoplasmic growth without division Plasma concentration becomes hypotonic, which leads to fluid flowing into the cell leading to an enlarged appearance and dysfunction The correct answer is C. Option C explains the pathophysiology of megaloblastic anemia. Option A is incorrect – Megaloblastic anemia is characterized by halted replication and fewer red blood cells overall. Option B is characteristic of a type of non-megaloblastic anemia, liver disease.

Which statement on the topic of macrocytic anemia below is true? Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with non-megaloblastic anemia. Folate deficiency is associated with elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. Liver disease results in primarily spherocytes on the blood film. Nutritional deficiencies associated with macrocytic anemia result in blood cell progenitors arrested in G2 phase. A patient with hypothyroidism will present with a history of weight loss and elevated heart rate. The correct answer is D. Nutritional deficiencies associated with macrocytic anemia are vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies. These result in an arrest in G2 phase, leading to megaloblastic anemia.

What type of red blood cell would be observed in a blood film of a patient with alcoholrelated anemia? Elliptocytes Schistocytes Target cells Sickle cells Spherocytes The correct answer is C. Alcohol consumption increases lipid concentrations in the blood, which incorporate themselves into red blood cells. With an increased membrane, the red blood cell adjusts its shape into a more energy-efficient one, leading to target cells.

A physician orders a reticulocyte count and then a Coombs test which comes back positive for IgG. Which of the following pathologies is the most likely diagnosis? A positive coombs test (DAT) rules in immune related conditions, and the presence of IgG on the surface of RBCs suggest Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia.

How does a G6PD deficiency lead to hemolysis? The absence of G6PD leads to structural protein defects creating a more spherical cell shape. The absence of G6PD prevents the formation of certain globin chains The absence of G6PD leads to the cells clumping together in circulation. The absence of G6PD leads to the production of free radicals. The correct answer is D. G6PD plays a role in reducing oxidative stress by inactivating free radicals, and without it, oxidative stress would increase leading to hemolysis.

From gestation to the first year of life a child’s hemoglobin F is replaced with hemoglobin A. Which of the following changes normally occur in the globin chains around birth? A decline in the synthesis of the β-globin around birth A rise in the synthesis of the α-globin around birth A decline in the synthesis of γ-globin around birth A decline in the synthesis of δ-globin around birth The correct answer is C. The α-subunit and the β- subunit form Hemoglobin A (adult hemoglobin which is a tetramer composed of 2 α- and 2 β-g

A 4-year-old female patient has symptoms of β-thalassemia major. Genetic analysis confirms the diagnosis. Which statement below is true? Due to the high severity of symptoms at a young age, the patient likely has mutations in three of the four β-globin genes In red blood cells, this patient has an excess of Hb S hemoglobin molecules It is likely that both of this patient’s parents are heterozygous carriers of β- thalassemia Hemoglobin molecules in this patient likely have two α-subunits and two γ-subunits This patient likely has a qualitative mutation of the β-globin gene The correct answer is C. β-thalassemia major is mainly a recessive condition in contrast to β-thalassemia minor observed in heterozygotes. Since this patient’s symptoms are severe, this patient likely has two deficient copies of the β-globin gene. This means that the parents must be carriers. Thalas

Which statement below on the topic of sickle-cell anemia is false? Sickle-cell disease was the first genetic disorder whose molecular basis was known. Genetic screening for sickle-cell disease is mandatory for newborns in Canada. Sickle-cell anemia geographically coincides with regions of higher rates of malaria. Sickle-cell anemia is the result of a mutation causing a Val-->Glu transition of β- globin. A diagnosis for sickle-cell anemia in adults involves Hb electrophoresis/HPLC. The correct answer is D. Sickle-cell anemia is the result of a mutation causing a Glu-->Val transition in the 6th amino acid of the β-globin chain.

Which of the following markers would you use to distinguish a folate deficiency from a Vitamin B12 deficiency? Methionine Homocysteine Methylmalonic acid None of the above The correct answer is C. Homocysteine is converted into methionine, and since both Vitamin B12 and Folate play a role in methionine synthesis, a reduction in Methionine or an increase in Homocysteine cannot be used to distinguish the two. Only Vitamin B12 assists in the production of Succinyl CoA fr

Which of the following relationships between globin and oxygen are true? Fetal hemoglobin has a stronger affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin Myoglobin has a stronger affinity for oxygen than adult and fetal hemoglobin Carbon monoxide has a stronger affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen. i, ii iii only i, ii, iii ii, iii The correct answer is C. Fetal hemoglobin has a stronger affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin so it can take oxygen from the mother’s hemoglobin. Myoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin and fetal hemoglobin, so that the oxygen can be transferred to muscles from circulat

Which pair of lab results indicates a folate deficiency? Elevated homocysteine, elevated methylmalonic acid Elevated homocysteine, normal methylmalonic acid Normal homocysteine, elevated methylmalonic acid Normal homocysteine, normal methylmalonic acid The correct answer is B. Elevated methylmalonic acid is associated with a vitamin B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency would not have elevated methylmalonic acid but would have elevated homocysteine.

The body has several proteins responsible for iron storage and iron transport. Which definition or function below is true? Transferrin is a membrane protein that transfers iron from intestinal cells to blood. Ferritin is only found within cells. Hepcidin is an iron-storage complex that can be seen with Perl’s stain. Divalent metal transporter proteins uptake Fe2+ from the intestines. Each hemoglobin subunit binds to four iron atoms. The correct answer is D. Transferrin transports iron in the blood. Ferritin is an iron storage inside the blood. Hepcidin helps in the transport of iron from intestinal cells to the blood. Finally, each hemoglobin subunit binds to one iron atom, for a total of 4 iron atoms per hemoglobin molecule.

Which of the following would you NOT see in a patient with Myelodysplastic Syndrome? Thrombocytopenia Immature blood cells in peripheral circulation MCV below normal Acquired mutations in bone marrow cells The correct answer is C. An MCV below normal would indicate microcytic anemia – Myelodysplastic Syndrome is often characterized by macrocytic anemia, with a reduction in all blood cells (including platelets), immature cells in the bloodstream and can be acquired through genetic mutations in the bone

Which of the following therapies is appropriate for patients with high-risk Myelodysplastic Syndrome, but not appropriate for low-risk Myelodysplastic Syndrome patients? Blood transfusion Transfusing Hematopoietic growth factors (such as erythropoietin) Hematopoietic stem cell transplant Lifestyle changes The correct answer is C. Blood transfusion and transfusing hematopoietic growth factors are options available for both high risk and low risk MDS patients. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant is a therapy only available to high-risk patients with MDS that are relatively healthy.

A 76-year-old frail patient presents with fatigue. Blood tests suggest normocytic anemia, and reticulocyte count is low. A bone marrow biopsy is performed, and the bone marrow appears abnormal with dysplasia in at least 2 lineages but no indication of infiltrating tumour cells. Ferritin and serum iron are both high. The patient also has poor prognostic factors as evaluated by the IPSS scoring system (Hemoglobin 82, Platelets 78, complex cytogenetics, 7% blasts in BM). Which option below correctly identifies a diagnosis and a suitable treatment? Myelodysplastic syndrome – hypomethylating agents Myelodysplastic syndrome – hematopoietic stem cell transplant Myelophthisis – blood transfusions Myelophthisis – iron chelating reagents Pure red cell aplasia – aggressive chemotherapy The correct answer is A. An abnormal bone marrow indicates myelodysplasia. The patient has poor prognostic factors (IPSS) in addition to his old age and frailty. He would not qualify hematopoietic stem cell transplant but would qualify for hypomethylating agents.

A patient presents with suspected myelodysplastic syndrome. Which observation is most likely to rule out a diagnosis? Leukopenia Pancytopenia Thrombocytopenia Elevated reticulocytes Normocytic anemia The correct answer is D. Myelodysplastic syndrome is associated with pancytopenia, and accordingly, reduced reticulocytes. Myelodysplastic syndrome can present as normocytic/macrocytic anemia.

A patient has the following conditions: macrocytic anemia, hyper-segmented neutrophils, significant weight loss and substantial atrophy of brain tissue. Out of the following causes for his presentation which is the most probable? Liver disease Folate deficiency Vitamin B12 deficiency Alcohol abuse The correct answer is C. Macrocytic anemia, hyper-segmented neutrophils and significant weight loss are all signs of Megaloblastic macrocytic anemia, which primarily has two culprits listed: folate deficiency and vitamin B12 deficiency. Only Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to defect in neurological tis

Key feature question: Select two answers. A prescription of erythropoietin would be MOST beneficial for patients with the following conditions: Hereditary spherocytosis Folate deficiency Myelodysplastic syndrome Acute renal failure Vitamin B12 deficiency Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia Aplastic anemia The correct answer is C, D. Erythropoietin (EPO) is a growth factor mainly produced by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell growth. Patients with acute renal failure may have reduced endogenous erythropoietin (EPO), and patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) could use extra erythropoieti

Which of the following connects the correct main site of absorption for each supplement? Iron in the duodenum, folate and B12 in the terminal ileum Iron and folate in the duodenum, B12 in the terminal ileum Iron, folate, and B12 in the duodenum Iron, folate, and B12 in the terminal ileum The correct answer is B. Iron and folate in the duodenum, B12 in the terminal ileum. Recall that iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Folate is absorbed in the duodenum. Although vitamin B12 can be absorbed by passive diffusion throughout the gastrointestinal tract, the main site o

Which of the following would be the MOST likely cause for B12 deficiency anemia? Chronic blood loss Trauma of the spleen Surgical resection of the colon and part of the small intestine attached to the colon Hypothyroidism The correct answer is C. Surgical resection of the terminal ileum which is the part of the small intestine attached to the colon. Chronic blood loss would lead to iron deficiency anemia. Trauma to the spleen would cause acute blood loss and a normocytic anemia. Hypothyroidism is associated with a ma

What are the two premetabolites that will be increased if vitamin B12 is deficient? Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine Methylmalonic acid and succinyl acid Homocysteine and methionine Methionine and succinyl acid The correct answer is A. Vitamin B12 is involved in only 2 metabolic pathways in the human body. It converts methylmalonic acid to succinyl CoA and homocysteine to methionine. With vitamin B12 deficiency, these premetabolites methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine build up and are elevated.

A 45-year-old man has had progressive weakness and dyspnea with exertion for 3 months. He appears malnourished; the conjunctivae are pale, and there are scattered petechiae. He has been under stress from the pandemic and lost his job 6 months ago. His diet consists of water and occasional scraps he can find. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 98 g/L (N: 135-180); MCV: 109 fL (N: 80-100); leukocyte count: 4.5 E9/L (N: 4-10) with hypersegmented neutrophils; reticulocyte count: 0.5%; platelet count: normal. The MOST likely cause of his condition is deficiency of which of the following? Folic acid Iron Vitamin B12 Vitamin B6 The correct answer is A. Folic acid deficiency. Although, it is very likely that he could be deficient in multiple nutrients and minerals, his macrocytic anemia and hyper-segmented neutrophils point to a megaloblastic anemia. Of the choices, only folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency could do this. H

Which of the following is a complication of folate deficiency? Microcytic anemia Koilonychia Neural tube defects Peripheral neuropathy The correct answer is C. Folic acid deficiency can lead to neural tube defects. This occurs in neonates born to a mother with folic acid deficiency.

With regards to sleep hygiene, which of the following is a good practice? Take naps throughout the day to alleviate tiredness and maintain your sleep cycle Eat a light bedtime snack if you are hungry Consume fluid before bed to wake up refreshed Think about going to sleep when you are in bed The correct answer is B. Eating a light bedtime snack if you’re hungry promotes sleep by reducing hypoglycemia. It’s important to keep an anchored wake time and not to take naps if you haven’t gotten enough sleep as this will reduce your sleep deficit, and possibly alter your sleep cycle. Reduce flu

Which of the following sleeping disorders is correctly characterized? Insomnia: snoring/gasping, daytime sleepiness, unrefreshed sleep Obstructive sleep apnea: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep or early morning awakening Narcolepsy: Recurrent periods of irrepressible need to sleep REM sleep behavior disorder: urge to move legs, unpleasant sensation in legs relieved by movement The correct answer is C. The description in option A applies to Obstructive sleep apnea, and the description in option B applies to insomnia. Option D refers to restless leg syndrome.

Key feature question: Select four answers. Which of the following conditions would warrant a referral for polysomnography? Schizophrenia Bipolar disorder Insomnia Narcolepsy PTSD Hypersomnolence disorder Major depressive episode Parasomnia Generalized anxiety disorder Obstructive sleep apnea The correct answer is D, F, H, J. These answers were taken from the notes for a psychiatrist’s approach to fatigue. Normally, you would not order polysomnography testing for a patient with insomnia, however, this can be considered if traditional management of insomnia is unsuccessful.

Which of the following is not a central tenet when using cognitive behavioural therapy to treat insomnia? Never try to fall asleep Recognize the high importance of sleep Do not catastrophize after a poor night’s sleep Develop tolerance to the effects of insomnia Keep your expectations realistic The correct answer is B. All of these are central tenets for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia except B. Instead, patients should try not to overemphasize the importance of a good night’s sleep, or else they may have elevated anxiety about sleep which may exacerbate their insomnia.

Which of the following complexes is necessary for the pathway that propagates (amplifies) the coagulation cascade? Extrinsic Xase Intrinsic Xase Prothrombinase Fibrinogenase The correct answer is B. The intrinsic Xase complex is necessary for facilitating the intrinsic pathway which is often regarded as amplifying the cascade that is initiated by the extrinsic pathway (mediated by extrinsic Xase.

Which of the following pathways INCORRECTLY describe a stage of a platelet feature in the primary hemostasis pathway? The contraction phase involves a change in the shape of the platelet from a spherical shape to a disc shape The adhesion phase is characterized by surface glycoproteins binding to the sub endothelial area of the injured tissue The secretion phase involves the influx of calcium inside the cell followed by a release of platelet granules In the aggregation phase, aggregation is mediated by glycoproteins, including GP IIb/IIIa The correct answer is A. The contraction phase involves the platelets changing from a disc-shape to a spherical shape.

Which of the following markers is elevated as a result of fibrinolysis? Thrombin Antithrombin Cross-linked fibrin D-dimer The correct answer is D. D-dimer is the final product of the fibrinolysis pathway. Cross-linked fibrin present in clots is broken down to D-dimer by plasmin. Thrombin is a procoagulant, and anti-thrombin is an anticoagulant (it stops coagulation but does not play a role in fibrinolysis)

For which of the following genetic abnormalities would a patient be expected to bleed more readily? A mutation in the gene encoding Protein S which reduces Protein S activity A mutation in the gene encoding antithrombin, which reduces antithrombin activity A mutation in the gene encoding Factor XIII, which increases Factor XIII activity A mutation in the gene encoding Factor V, which reduces Factor V activity A mutation in the gene encoding Factor XII, which reduces Factor XII activity The correct answer is D. Protein S and antithrombin down-regulate clot formation, so reduced activity of these will increase clot formation. Factor XII deficiencies do not result in increased bleeding risks. Factor V and Factor XIII are involved in creating and maintaining blood clots. Reduced activ

Why could the presence of splenomegaly result in thrombocytopenia? Thrombopoietin is manufactured by the spleen Thrombocytes are stored in the spleen Many clotting factors are stored in the spleen Antithrombin is produced by the spleen Antithrombin is stored in the spleen The correct answer is B. Platelets (thrombocytes) are stored in the spleen. Splenomegaly, or enlarged spleen, could result in excessive storing of platelets, reducing availability in the body.

Which variant of Heparin would you provide an elderly patient who is at risk of adverse health outcomes and cannot risk an uncertain drug response? High Molecular Weight Heparin Low Molecular Weight Heparin Unfractionated Heparin None of the above The correct answer is B. Low molecular weight heparin has a more predictable pharmacokinetic profile, and would provide more predictability of treatment outcomes.

Which variant of Heparin would you provide for a patient with kidney disease due to ongoing micro vascular hemorrhage? High Molecular Weight Heparin Low Molecular Weight Heparin Unfractionated Heparin None of the above The correct answer is D. You would not provide an anticoagulant to a patient who is actively bleeding.

Which of the following correctly describes the process by which Vitamin K antagonists act as anticoagulants? They increase the affinity of antithrombin for thrombin They deactivate activated factors in the coagulation cascade They prevent the activation of certain factors in the coagulation cascade They decrease platelet aggregation in primary hemostasis The correct answer is C. Vitamin K antagonists inhibit Vitamin K reductase which is needed to carboxylate and activate factors II, VII, IX, X.

You are treating a patient with a known genetic mutation that impairs antithrombin function. This patient is also noncompliant with his medication often taking too many or too few pills at a time. Which of the following anticoagulants would you prescribe him? Unfractionated Heparin Low molecular Weight Heparin Vitamin K antagonist Direct oral anticoagulant The correct answer is D. Heparin works by increasing the affinity of antithrombin for thrombin, thus in this patient heparin would be ineffective. A patient who may overdose requires a larger therapeutic window thus direct oral anticoagulants would be the best choice. Warfarin, has many interactions

For which patient would anticoagulation not be a suitable treatment? Patient with venous thromboembolism Patients with mechanical heart valves Prophylactic stroke prevention Patients with immune thrombocytopenia Patients with arterial thrombosis The correct answer is D. Patients with immune thrombocytopenia have a reduced ability to form blood clots. Administration of anticoagulants for such patients would exacerbate their blood clotting issues.

Which option below is a correct antidote to be used for drug reversal? An antidote for warfarin is Vitamin B12 An antidote for Dabigatran is idarucizumab An antidote for Fondaparinux is Factor XII An antidote for Argatroban is Factor XIII An antidote for Rivaroxaban is warfarin The correct answer is B. This is the only correct antidote listed. An antidote for warfarin , a vitamin K antagonist, is prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC.. Fondaparinux is an activator of antithrombin. Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor, and Rivaroxaban is a Factor Xa inhibitor.

Which of the following is a contraindication for Argatroban, an IV-direct thrombin inhibitor? A previous history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia A patient with elevated thrombin levels A patient with chronic or acute hepatic failure A patient with a sizeable gastric resection The correct answer is C. Argatroban is the treatment of choice of patients with a past history of HIT. It is excreted by the liver, so it would not be a good choice for patients with hepatic failure. Argatroban is safe for patients with renal failure. Since it is administered by IV, the presence of

A patient with severe kidney injury presents with reduced platelet counts, normal ADAMTS-13 level, and a peripheral blood smear shows the presence of schistocytes. His coagulation tests INR and PTT are normal. Which of the following diseases are most probable? Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic purpura Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation Immune Thrombocytopenia The correct answer is B. Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome and Thrombotic Thrombocytopenia Purpura both fit with the symptoms in the patient (kidney disease, peripheral blood smear, schistocytes). However kidney disease is more severe in Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome making it more probable, and TTP would be as

Which of the following illustrates the correct pathway to confirm a Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia? Perform a 4T score followed by an ELISA/Serotonin release assay Perform an ELISA/Serotonin release assay followed by a 4T score Diagnosis of exclusion rule other causes of thrombocytopenia ADAMTS-13 level test and presence of schistocytes on blood film The correct answer is A. The 4T test is performed to assess probability of HIT. Based on the results, follow-up tests are necessary. The most diagnostic tests available are the ELISA or serotonin release assay.

Which of the following pathologies can be attributed to decreased production of platelets? Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) Liver disease i, ii ii, iii i, ii, iii iii The correct answer is C. Myelodysplastic syndrome affects the bone marrow which plays a central role in platelet production, the liver secretes thrombopoietin (TPO) which plays a large role in the stimulating platelet production and this process can be impaired by liver disease. Immune Thrombocytope

You are a hematologist assessing a patient referred for easy bruising. CBC results indicate normal RBCs and WBCs and severe thrombocytopenia. Liver function is normal. A blood film indicates the presence of schistocytes, and subsequent lab tests suggest low levels of ADAMTS-13. He is not taking any medications. What is your recommended treatment? Warfarin after three months D-Dimer administration Intravenous immune globulin Platelet transfusion Plasma exchange The correct answer is E. With a low ADAMTS-13 level, this patient has thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). The treatment of choice for TTP is plasma exchange with or without glucocorticoids. Subsequently, rituximab may be added in addition to plasma exchange or used for relapsed disease. TTP i

A patient is not taking any medications and presents with thrombocytopenia. Blood tests indicate elevated levels of D-Dimer and low fibrinogen. What is the likely diagnosis? ITP TTP HUS DIC HIT The correct answer is D. In DIC, there is a systemic activation of all clotting factors, leading to elevated D-Dimer and low fibrinogen. Note that heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) can also produce clotting (and therefore elevated D-Dimer), but this is unlikely in this case as the patient is no

After a treatment with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) such as dalteparin (Fragmin), a patient presents with moderate thrombocytopenia. A 4T score indicates a high probability of HIT, and the diagnosis was confirmed with a serotonin release assay. What is the next course of action? Change treatment immediately to UFH Change treatment immediately to warfarin Perform a platelet transfusion Change treatment immediately to argatroban Perform a splenectomy The correct answer is D. With HIT, all heparin-based treatments should be stopped immediately. Warfarin could be a safe alternative after a patient is adequately treated with an alternate anticoagulant (such as argatroban, fondaparinux or danaparoiD. and the platelets have recovered. If used too ear

A patient presents with severe Von Willebrand disease where there are inadequate levels of Von Willebrand factor. Which of the following markers/processes would be significantly affected? Primary hemostasis Secondary hemostasis Prothrombin time (PT) Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) i, ii, iii ii, iv i, ii, iv i, ii, iii, iv The correct answer is C. Primary Hemostasis would be affected as vWF plays a role in platelet recruitment in formation of the platelet plug. vWF acts as a chaperone for factor VIII extending its halflife, and factor VII plays a central role in the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade measure

Which of the following scenarios would warrant a platelet transfusion? A patient going for invasive surgery with a low platelet count A patient with a low platelet count and diagnosed with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura A patient with a low platelet count and diagnosed with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia A patient with Hemophilia A The correct answer is A. TTP and HIT are contraindications for platelet transfusion as the addition of platelets can increase thrombosis without reducing bleeding risk. A patient with hemophilia A would require factor VIII medication, not platelet transfusion.

Which transfusion below is safe for all patients if their blood type is unknown? Plasma from individuals with Type O- blood Red blood cells from individuals with Type AB- blood Red blood cells from individuals with Type O+ blood Plasma from individuals with Type AB+ blood Red blood cells from individuals with Type A- blood The correct answer is D. Type O- is the universal RBC donor because the RBCs do not have antigens on the cells. However, Type AB+ plasma does not have any antibodies toward these antigens and is safe for all recipients.

For the next five questions, choose ONE of the following options for transfusion. Assume informed consent. Options may be used more than once, or not at all. A bleeding patient presents with TTP. Platelets are 96 E9/L [normal = 150-400 E9/L] Packed RBCs Platelets Plasma Fibrinogen concentrates Prothrombin complex concentrates The correct answer is C. First, the patient's platelets are not low enough for platelet transfusion. Second, TTP is a contraindication for platelet transfusion. Plasma is transfused for patients with TTP if plasma exchange is not available.

For the next five questions, choose ONE of the following options for transfusion. Assume informed consent. Options may be used more than once, or not at all. A bleeding patient presents with anemia (Hb = 64 g/L) [normal = 115-160 g/L] Packed RBCs Platelets Plasma Fibrinogen concentrates Prothrombin complex concentrates The correct answer is A. For severely anemic patients (ie. hemoglobin less than 70 g/L), red blood cells are the best transfusion

For the next five questions, choose ONE of the following options for transfusion. Assume informed consent. Options may be used more than once, or not at all. A patient requires warfarin anticoagulation reversal. Packed RBCs Platelets Plasma Fibrinogen concentrates Prothrombin complex concentrates The correct answer is E. Warfarin anticoagulation reversal requires PCC transfusions. Note that this should also be supplemented with Vitamin K.

For the next five questions, choose ONE of the following options for transfusion. Assume informed consent. Options may be used more than once, or not at all. A bleeding patient presents with hypofibrinogenemia. Packed RBCs Platelets Plasma Fibrinogen concentrates Prothrombin complex concentrates The correct answer is D. Fibrinogen concentrates are the transfusion of choice for patients with afibrinogenemia or hypofibrinogenemia.

For the next five questions, choose ONE of the following options for transfusion. Assume informed consent. Options may be used more than once, or not at all. A bleeding patient presents with acquired hemophilia B. Packed RBCs Platelets Plasma Fibrinogen concentrates Prothrombin complex concentrates The correct answer is C. Plasma transfusion is an option for patients with single factor deficiencies, such as Hemophilia B (Factor IX) where specific factor replacements are NOT available.

Which of the following is an incorrect description of the expiry of a type of transfusion? Red blood cells can be stored at 4 °C for up to 42 days. PCC can be stored at room temperature for up to 5 years Plasma can be stored in a freezer (-18 °C. for up to a year Platelets can be stored at room temperature for up to 7 days Cryoprecipitate can be stored at room temperature for up to 5 years The correct answer is E. Cryoprecipitate should be stored in the freezer (-18 °C. and can be stored for up to 1 year.

Von Willebrand deficiency can reduce the half-life of factor VIII in the coagulation cascade. Which of the following markers can be affected in Von Willebrand disease? Prothrombin time (PT) Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) Thrombin time (TT) Platelet count The correct answer is B. Factor VIII is a component of the intrinsic pathway which is measured by the PTT; it is important to note that a normal PTT may not exclude VWD as not all VWD is associated with a low FVIII. Measuring the VW antigen, VW activity and FVIII activity would be pertinent when ass

Which of the following markers would be significantly affected in severe liver disease? Prothrombin Time (PT) Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT) Platelet count i, ii i, iii ii, iii i, ii, iii The correct answer is D. The liver produces all the coagulation factors except FVIII (that are involved in both the intrinsic, extrinsic pathway and common pathway), thus the PT,PTT and TT (as fibrinogen can also be low) would be affected. The liver also produces thrombopoietin which stimulates plat

A patient presents with Petechiae, wet purpura and bleeding at several mucocutaneous sites. Which of the following causes are most likely for this presentation? An impairment in the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade An impairment in the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade An impairment in formation of the platelet plug An impairment in the fibrin cross-linking The correct answer is C. Mucocutaneous (oral cavity, nasal, uterine, skin) sites of bleeding, petechiae, wet purpura, ecchymoses are all signs of defects in primary hemostasis. The formation of the platelet plug occurs during primary hemostasis, while the impairments in the coagulation cascade belon

Key feature question: Select four answers. In which of the following is an elevated aPTT most likely? Patients with deficiency in clotting factor VII Patients with acquired Hemophilia A A mixing test performed for patients with a deficiency in clotting factor IX A mixing test performed for patients with an inhibitor to clotting factor XI Patients with a Lupus anticoagulant Patients with mutations in clotting factor XIII Patients with severe von Willebrand's disease (vWD) Patients with afibrinogenemia Patients with immune thrombocytopenia Patients with splenomegaly Patients with pseudothrombocytopenia Patients with mutated Protein C The correct answer is B, D, E, G. The aPTT involves the intrinsic coagulation pathway (Factors XII, XI, IX, and VIII). Hemophilia A is associated with Factor VIII; the lupus anticoagulant is an antibody that targets the phospholipids which initiate the intrinsic pathway. vWD has reduced levels of vo

A recent newborn from a homebirth presents with easy bruising, but blood counts (RBCs, WBCs, platelets) are normal. A physical exam is unremarkable, and there are no indications of liver disease or family history for an inherited bleeding disorder. Further testing is performed to elucidate the cause of the bruising. The patient has an elevated INR and prolonged aPTT. Based on the above, which of the following diagnoses are most likely? Factor VII deficiency Severe Vitamin K deficiency von Willebrand’s disease Factor XII deficiency Presence of factor IX inhibitor The correct answer is B. Options C, D, and E are associated with elevated aPTT only, and also, factor XII deficiency does not increase bleeding risk! Option A would be associated with elevated PT (or INR) only. In the case of vitamin K deficiency, there are Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in th

Which of the following would NOT be significantly lower (relative to an adult) in a newborn? Factor VII Factor VIII Factor IX Factor X The correct answer is B. Factor VIII is actually elevated in the newborn and plays a protective role in bleeding. The liver in children less than 6 months of age are immature and the coagulation factors produced by the liver are in smaller quantities – however factor VIII is not produced by the live

Which of the following would be most beneficial to treat an undiagnosed coagulopathy? Aspirin DDAVP Tranexamic acid Fresh frozen plasma The correct answer is D. Fresh frozen plasma is helpful in emergent situations when a factor card (or in this case diagnosis) is not readily available. Fresh frozen plasma contains most factors and fibrinogen.

Tyler is a newborn who bleeds excessively after circumcision. Tyler’s father and paternal grandmother have Hemophilia B. Tyler’s mother and maternal grandfather have von Willebrand disease. Based on this information, what is the most likely diagnosis for Tyler? Hemophilia B, because it can be inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. Hemophilia B, because it can be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. von Willebrand disease, because it can be inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. von Willebrand disease, because it can be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The correct answer is D. Hemophilia disorders are X-linked, whereas vWD is autosomal (either dominant or recessive depending on the sub-typE.. Note that Tyler could not have inherited an X-linked disorder from his father.

Which of the following deficiencies would not lead to a bleeding disorder? Factor VIII deficiency Factor IX deficiency Factor XII deficiency Factor II deficiency Factor X deficiency The correct answer is C. Factor XII is a contact factor affects the aPTT in vitro. It is not significant in vivo and does not present a bleeding risk if there is a deficiency.

You perform a clinical assessment to determine if a patient has DVT, and you conclude that it is unlikely. What is the next best step? Order a compression ultrasound Order an ascending venogram Order a D-Dimer test No further tests are needed The correct answer is C. A negative D-dimer test can be used rule out DVT. If the D-dimer comes test back positive you can use a Compression Ultrasound to diagnose DVT.

You perform a V/Q scan in a patient you suspect has pulmonary embolism. The test results come back as “Non-Diagnostic”. What is the next best step? Order a compression ultrasound Order an ascending venogram Order a D-Dimer test No further tests are needed The correct answer is A. If the test comes out as non-diagnostic, you would then order a bilateral compression ultrasound (on both legs) to determine if they have DVT, as DVT is associated with pulmonary embolism.

A patient presents with edema in their left leg, associated with pain. You suspect a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). What is the first test you order to diagnose this patient when DVT is likely? Ventilation/Perfusion scan Determine D-Dimer levels CT pulmonary angiogram Ascending venogram Compression ultrasound The correct answer is E. A positive result for compression ultrasound indicates DVT. A negative result is inconclusive and further testing is necessary.

Based on the Wells criteria, a patient is unlikely to have deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE). What statement on subsequent testing is true? A positive D-Dimer test confirms DVT. A negative D-Dimer test leads to additional testing for DVT A positive D-Dimer test leads to additional testing for PE A negative D-Dimer test leads to additional testing for PE The correct answer is C. If a patient is unlikely to have DVT or PE based on the Wells criteria, a negative D- Dimer test will rule out DVT or PE. A positive D-Dimer test requires additional testing to arrive at a definitive diagnosis.

A male patient is being treated for a venous thromboembolism. Which statement below on treatment options is true? If it was determined that his DVT was idiopathic, his anticoagulant treatment should be continued indefinitely. For DVT, physical activity is encouraged, but for PE, physical activity is discouraged. Patients with elevated INRs should receive higher doses of warfarin. If the underlying cause of DVT was cancer and the cancer was cured, the patient should continue the treatment for DVT for at least six months after the cancer cure. The correct answer is A. For idiopathic DVTs, anticoagulant treatment is prescribed indefinitely, even after the DVT is addressed.

Which abnormal cell morphology is observed in the following blood film? Toxic granules Toxic vacuoles Auer rods Döhle bodies Reactive lymphocytes The correct answer is D. The blue structure in the blood film is a Döhle body, which is typically light blue-gray, basophilic, leukocyte inclusion located in the cytoplasm of neutrophil. They are thought to be remnants of the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

A patient’s CBC-Differential indicates significant eosinophilia with no other leukocytosis. What is the most probable diagnosis? Hypothyroidism Parasitic infection Bacterial infection Viral infection Allergic infection The correct answer is B. Eosinophils target parasites and are involved in the allergic response. However, basophils are also involved in the allergic response. A parasitic infection is likely to increase eosinophil levels only. Additionally, eosinophilia tends to be very mild in allergic response.

Which of the following clinical findings is inconsistent with tumour lysis syndrome? Hypokalemia Gout Hypocalcemia Increased presence of cytokines Acute renal failure The correct answer is A. In tumour lysis syndrome, components inside tumour cells are released into the bloodstream. Since potassium is found in higher concentrations in the cytoplasm, tumour lysis syndrome would result in hyperkalemia .

A 25-year-old patient presents with lymphocytosis. You suspect he is fighting a viral or bacterial infection. Which clinical observation is inconsistent with your working diagnosis? An elevated neutrophil count The patient has had a fever for a week Lymphocytes on the peripheral blood smear Lymphoblasts on the peripheral blood smear The correct answer is D. Viral infections are the most common cause of lymphocytosis. It’s common to see an elevated neutrophil count and lymphocytes in the peripheral blood smear if this patient is fighting a viral/bacterial infection. If the patient had a fever past 4-6 weeks this would be concern

Use the following options below to answer the next THREE questions. A patient presents with basophilia, eosinophilia, and neutrophilia. Their blood film also shows a few immature neutrophils, particularly myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Which of the following conditions best align with this condition? Chronic myeloid leukemia Acute myeloid leukemia Acute lymphocytic leukemia Infection/Trauma Hyposplenism Chronic lymphocytic leukemia The correct answer is A. Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (a myeloproliferative neoplasm) often presents with these symptoms. While there are immature WBCs in the peripheral blood (left shift), the vast majority of cells are mature which rules out Acute Myeloid Leukemia.

Use the following options below to answer the next THREE questions. A patient’s blood smear shows a significantly elevated level of monoblasts with very few mature macrophages. Which of the following conditions best align with this condition? Chronic myeloid leukemia Acute myeloid leukemia Acute lymphocytic leukemia Infection/Trauma Hyposplenism Chronic lymphocytic leukemia The correct answer is B. Having an elevated level of monoblasts or myeloblasts points to Acute Myeloid Leukemia where myelocytes/monocytes (eosinophils, basophils, neutrophils) have an arrest in maturation.

Use the following options below to answer the next THREE questions. A patient presents with an elevated level of mature neutrophils. Cytogenetic and molecular testing were conducted and ruled out any bone marrow pathology. No secondary issue could be identified. Which of the following conditions best align with this condition? Chronic myeloid leukemia Acute myeloid leukemia Acute lymphocytic leukemia Infection/Trauma Hyposplenism Chronic lymphocytic leukemia The correct answer is E. The lack of bone marrow pathology or secondary causes that can lead to increased neutrophils, points to decreased destruction of neutrophils to explain the elevated count. The spleen plays a large role in the sequestration and destruction of blood cells, thus a reduction in

What is the current standard of care for patients with a t(9,22) translocation leading to chronic myeloid leukemia (BCR-ABL fusion protein)? Stem cell transplant Gleevec (Imatinib) ATRA ATRA + Arsenic Steroids The correct answer is B. Imatinib is an oral inhibitor of the BCR-ABL fusion protein. ATRA and arsenic are treatments for acute promyelocytic leukemia.

Which option correctly describes a treatment option for different leukemias? The treatment of CLL is prophylactic chemotherapy immediately after diagnosis The treatment of CML involves prophylaxis for sanctuary sites such as the CNS and testes The treatment of ALL is Gleevec / imatinib The treatment for APL is ATRA The treatment for AML is Arsenic The correct answer is D. All-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic is the treatment for APL. Imatinib is the treatment for CML. Prophylaxis for sanctuary sites is the treatment for ALL. Note, in CLL, patients are treated only after symptoms develop

Which of the following cells would be significantly altered in acute myeloid leukemia? Neutrophils Myeloblasts Lymphocytes B-cells The correct answer is B. Acute leukemia signifies immature blood cells which rules out mature cells (Neutrophils, B- cells) while the myeloid component rules out cells from the lymphoid lineage (lymphoblasts and B-cells)

According to the World Health Organization, acute myeloid leukemia is identified by which condition? The frequency of blast cells in your peripheral blood Morphological characteristics of white blood cells Certain recurrent genetic mutations Bone Marrow Biopsy The correct answer is C. If you have certain genetic abnormalities regardless of your blast count you have Acute Myeloid Leukemia, according to WHO’s classification system.

A 70-year old hospital volunteer requires a blood film examination prior to starting placement. The following blood film is obtained despite the patient feeling entirely well. Which of the following pathologies is most likely? Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Acute Myeloid Leukemia Chronic Myeloid Leukemia Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia The correct answer is D. Most patients with CLL are often asymptomatic in the early stages of the disease. Note: The presence of smudge cells is an artifact in blood films. Often lymphocytes “smudge” easier so conditions such as CLL with lots of lymphocytes will have more “smudge” cells.

What is not an underlying reason why treatment success rates for ALL in children have increased in the past 30 years? Personalized treatments based on risk assessments Prophylactic support for CNS/testicular involvement Improved ability to provide supportive care during treatment Increased radiation therapy instead of intrathecal therapy Post-treatment flow cytometry to assess for residual disease The correct answer is D. Treatments for ALL in children have generally improved for several reasons. One of these is the replacement of radiation therapy with intrathecal therapy.

A child presents with abnormal bruising and bilateral leg pain in the absence of any obvious injuries. Which observation during the physical exam would support a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia over acute lymphoid leukemia? Gingival swelling and bleeding Hyperpigmentation of the skin Double palmar crease Thumb polydactyly Splenomegaly The correct answer is A. Gingival swelling is indicative of AML in children. Splenomegaly would be observed in both AML and ALL.

Which of the following best describes the function of the intensification stage of treatment in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia? To induce a remission state in the patient often times using multi-agent chemotherapy Treat the remaining microscopic cancer to overcome resistance often using moderate intensive chemotherapy To continue the remission of the patient and maintain a cancer free state To prevent the infiltration of leukemia into the CNS or other organs The correct answer is B. The Intensification stage is conducted after the patient reaches a remission state and is done to treat any lingering cancer cells.

A patient with intracerebral hemorrhage presents with abnormal fibrinolysis activity and disseminated intravascular coagulation. A peripheral blood smear from the patient is shown below. Which leukemia would best explain these symptoms? Acute promyelocytic leukemia Acute myeloid leukemia Chronic myeloid leukemia Acute lymphoblastic leukemia The correct answer is A. Patients with Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a type of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), often present with increased fibrinolytic activity, disseminated intravascular coagulation and have a high risk of hemorrhage relative to other types of AML. Also, the presence of multi

Which diagnostic technique cannot be performed on a bone marrow aspirate? Morphology Pathologic Assessment Flow cytometry Cytogenetics Molecular genetics The correct answer is B. A pathological assessment is performed on a bone marrow biopsy. Flow cytometry can be performed on bone marrow aspirate and peripheral blood.

Key feature question: Select two answers. A new patient arrives with erythrocytosis. You conduct a thorough patient history and some lab tests. Which two statements are inconsistent with a secondary erythrocytosis? The patient recently climbed Mount Everest The patient takes anabolic steroids The patient has low erythropoietin levels The patient has obstructive sleep apnea The patient smoked 1.5 packs per day for the last 20 years The patient has a mutation on exon 12 of JAK2 The patient is a competitive marathon runner and partakes in EPO doping The correct answer is C, F. These statements are consistent with a primary erythrocytosis. Activities in the patient’s history which lead to an elevated erythrocyte count (high altitude, EPO doping, reduced oxygen intake due to smoking or OSA).

What is a correct description of the etiology of polycythemia vera? The bone marrow no longer responds to erythropoietin and erythropoiesis is halted. The kidneys no longer produce erythropoietin and erythropoiesis is halted. The kidneys produce extra erythropoietin and erythropoiesis is upregulated. Erythropoiesis continues in the absence of erythropoietin Hypoxia in the kidneys increases the production of erythropoietin The correct answer is D. In polycythemia vera, the kidneys continue to produce erythropoietin even in the absence of erythropoietin. This is caused by a mutation in JAK2 (JAK2 V617F, or exon 12 mutation) which constitutively expresses JAK2 signaling.

A new patient presents to your clinic with hypertension and headache, and the CBC indicates panmyelosis despite low levels of erythropoietin. Cytogenetic testing is positive for a JAK2 V617F mutation. You assess that the patient is at high risk for thrombosis. What is your immediate and long-term treatment respectively? Aspirin and hydroxyurea for cytoreduction Aspirin and referral to Canadian Blood Services for blood donation Heparin and watchful waiting for worsening symptoms Treat the underlying anemia with O- red blood cells Treat the underlying cause of secondary erythrocytosis and repeat CBC after the condition resolves. The correct answer is A. For patients with high-risk erythrocytosis, aspirin is immediately taken to reduce DVT risk, and cytoreduction via hydroxyurea is a long-term treatment. Note that phlebotomy is a suitable treatment for low-risk patients. Phlebotomy could be appropriate for a high-risk patien

Which of the following diagnostic tests would NOT be appropriate for a patient that presents with erythrocytosis? Testing for a JAK2 V617F mutation for a patient with low EPO Conducting an echocardiogram for a patient with low EPO Conducting a pulmonary function test for a patient with high EPO Conducting a sleep study for a patient with high EPO The correct answer is B. An echocardiogram is offered for patients with a high EPO who have secondary erythrocytosis (no BM pathology); this can be used to see if there are shunts in the heart which misdirect blood from entering the lungs to be oxygenated thus leading to hypoxia.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. A patient’s blood sample is taken and when centrifuged the hematocrit is large and the buffy layer is normal. Which pathology best explains this result? Chronic myeloid leukemia Primary erythrocytosis Secondary erythrocytosis Aplastic anemia The correct answer is C. In Secondary Erythrocytosis the patient is producing higher quantities of erythrocytes which would explain the elevated hematocrit. However the white blood cells and the platelets (which make up the buffy layer) are unaffected.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. A patient’s blood sample is taken and when centrifuged the hematocrit is large and the buffy layer is large. Which pathology best explains this result? Chronic myeloid leukemia Primary erythrocytosis Secondary erythrocytosis Aplastic anemia The correct answer is B. In Primary Erythrocytosis there is often an acquired genetic mutation that leads to panmyelosis (where RBC, WBC and platelet counts are elevated). Thus the hematocrit and the buffy layer would both be proportionally larger.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. A patient’s blood sample is taken and when centrifuged the hematocrit is normal and the buffy layer is large. Which pathology best explains this result? Chronic myeloid leukemia Primary erythrocytosis Secondary erythrocytosis Aplastic anemia The correct answer is A. In chronic myeloid Leukemia there is an overproduction (abnormal growth) of myeloid lineage granulocytes (eosinophil, basophils, neutrophils). These would lead to a larger buffy layer.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. A patient’s blood sample is taken and when centrifuged the hematocrit is low and the buffy layer is small. Which pathology best explains this result? Chronic myeloid leukemia Primary erythrocytosis Secondary erythrocytosis Aplastic anemia The correct answer is D. In aplastic anemia there is reduced cellularity of the bone marrow and there is a significant reduction in the production of all blood cells (erythrocytes and leukocytes) which leads to a low hematocrit and low buffy layer.

A 15-year-old male presents to a walk-in clinic concerned about a new fever suspecting an infection. On visual examination, there are patches of hyperpigmentation on his back and there are defects in the fingernails. When the CBC results come back, the patient has low erythrocytes, low thrombocytes, and low leukocytes. What is the likely diagnosis? Fanconi anemia Acute promyelocytic leukemia Polycythemia vera Dyskeratosis congenita Chronic lymphoid leukemia The correct answer is D. Dyskeratosis congenita is a hereditary disorder that can lead to aplastic anemia, characterized by pancytopenia, hyperpigmentation of the skin, fingernail defects, and additionally, leukoplakia.

A patient presents with polydactyly and eye and ear defects. A CBC+ differential shows pancytopenia and a bone marrow core biopsy shows reduced cellularity. Which of the following pathologies fit best with the symptoms and lab findings? Fanconi anemia Dyskeratosis congenita Myelodysplastic syndrome Chronic myelogenous leukemia The correct answer is A. The reduced cellularity within the bone marrow coupled with the pancytopenia point towards aplastic anemia. Fanconi Anemia is a hereditary disorder that can lead to Aplastic Anemia and is associated with eye and ear defects and polydactyly (extra finger or thumb).

Which option below is not considered a myeloproliferative neoplasm? Polycythemia vera (PV) Essential thrombocytosis (ET) Myelofibrosis (MF) Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) Dyskeratosis congenita (DC) The correct answer is E. Dyskeratosis congenita is a hereditary disorder that can lead to aplastic anemia, which is not considered a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

Myelofibrosis is characterized by the presence of mutations in CALR, JAK2, and MPL. Which of these genes is a mutation most commonly associated with myelofibrosis? CALR JAK2 MPL BCR/ABL The correct answer is B. Most mutations leading to myelofibrosis are caused by JAK2 mutations [50-60%].

A 60-year-old patient presents with pancytopenia and an enlarged spleen. Upon taking a peripheral blood smear the following image is obtained. Which of the following pathologies best fit this patient? Polycythemia vera Essential thrombocytosis Chronic myeloid leukemia Myelofibrosis The correct answer is D. In patients with myelofibrosis there is fibrosis of the bone marrow leading to pancytopenia. There is an excess maturation of myeloid progenitors including granulocytes and erythroid progenitors spilling out into the peripheral blood leading to the leukoerythroblastic pictur

Which of the following statements regarding the natural progression of myeloproliferative neoplasms is INCORRECT? Patients with Myelofibrosis can be at risk of developing Acute Myeloid Leukemia Patients with Essential Thrombocythemia can be at risk of developing Myelofibrosis Patients with Essential Thrombocythemia can be at risk of developing Acute Myeloid Leukemia Patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia can be at risk of developing Polycythemia vera The correct answer is D. Patients with Polycythemia vera are at risk of developing Acute Myeloid Leukemia.

A 24-year-old female comes into your family practice with chronic fatigue. A CBC test reveals leukocytosis. The blood film results are shown below. Based on the results, you suspect acute promyelocytic anemia. What test result would confirm your suspected diagnosis? JAK2 V617F mutation Karyotypic observation of t(15;17) Karyotypic observation of t(9;22) Insensitivity to vancomycin Inhibition of CTLA-4 on T-cells The correct answer is B. APL is the result of a translocation of chromosomes 15 and 17 leading to a fusion of the PML/RAR-alpha genes. This can be diagnosed through karyotype, FISH or by molecular genetics testing.

When a patient presents with secondary thrombocytosis, which reactive (or secondary) condition is unlikely?
