Acute liver disease Infection Trauma Iron deficiency anemia Hyposplenism The correct answer is A. Thrombopoietin is produced by the liver. Acute liver disease would result in thrombocytopenia. The rest of the answers would lead to thrombocytosis.

A patient’s lab findings are suggestive of thrombocytosis. Which of the following options can potentially explain this lab finding? The patient is experiencing inflammation and tissue damage The patient is positive for the Philadelphia chromosome The patient’s blood also contains red blood cell fragments i, ii I i, ii, iii ii, iii The correct answer is C. Inflammation and tissue damage within the body can lead to stimulated production of platelets by the bone marrow (secondary thrombocytosis). Patients who are positive for the Philadelphia chromosome have Chronic Myeloid Leukemia where they can have either thrombocytosis or t

Which of the following cancer drug classifications would Microtubule Inhibiting Drugs fall under? Cell-cycle specific conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy Non-cell-cycle specific conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy Cell-cycle specific targeted therapy Non-cell-cycle specific targeted therapy The correct answer is A. Microtubule Inhibiting Drugs inhibit microtubule activity during the M phase of the cellcycle, preventing cancerous cells from further dividing. These drugs are cell-cycle specific as they primarily function in the M phase.

Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which the cancer drug Bevacizumab impairs tumour angiogenesis? It acts as an antibody which binds Vascular endothelial Growth Factor and prevents its interaction its receptors It acts as a small molecule inhibitor that enters the cell and leads to the downregulation of VEGF receptors on the cell surface It acts as an antagonist by binding to VEGF receptors and preventing the VEGF- VEGF receptor interaction It acts as a CDK inhibitor to prevent cell progression from the G1 to S phase The correct answer is A. Bevacizumab acts as an antibody (most antibody drugs end with –MAB) that bind to VEGF and prevent it from binding to its receptor thereby preventing tumour angiogenesis.

Targeted therapy is a means to treat cancer. Which option demonstrates a true mechanism of action of a targeted cancer therapy treatment? Aromatase inhibitors block the conversion of estrogen to androgen. Drugs that target VEGF receptors halt angiogenesis. Some cancer cells inhibit CDKs, and CDKs halt the cell-cycle progression. Drugs that target estrogen receptors increase the proliferation rates of non- cancer cells. The correct answer is B. The VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) binds to receptors to stimulate angiogenesis. Drugs can prevent this by targeting the VEGF receptors. For option A, Aromatase inhibitors block the conversion of androgens to estrogens. For option C, CDKs promote cell cycle progre

A patient is currently on immunotherapy. Which of the following drugs amplify the T cell response via an interaction between T cells and antigen presenting cells? CTLA-4 Inhibitors PD-L1 Inhibitors CTLA-4 inhibitors and PD-L1 inhibitors None of the above The correct answer is A. CTLA-4 inhibitors bind to the CTLA-4 protein on tumour cells and prevent interaction with B7 (found on antigen presenting cells) which allows the T cells to mount a more robust response). PD-L1 inhibitors work by binding to PD-L1 on tumour cells, preventing PD-1 (found on T

Key feature question: A patient with a neutrophil count of 0.2 E9/L presents at the emergency department with a fever of 39 °C. What are the best three treatments? Carbapenem Leukocyte transfusion Piperacillin-tazobactam Imatinib Vitamin B12 supplement Cytoreduction with hydroxyurea The correct answer is A, C. When a patient presents with febrile neutropenia (low WBC count with a fever), the infection and is considered an oncologic emergency. The patient is immediately placed on broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Key feature question: Which two leukocyte sub-types are not considered granulocytes? Basophil Eosinophil Lymphocyte Monocyte Neutrophil The correct answer is C, D. Lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes. Basophils, eosinophils, and neutrophils are granulocytes.

Which of the following is considered the main complication of leukopenia? Leukostasis Bleeding risk Infection System inflammation The correct answer is C. Leukopenia is having a reduced number of WBCs – often neutrophils. Without an adequate titer of neutrophils, the body is unable to fight off infection. Leukostasis is often seen in patients with a very high white cell count due to conditions such as acute myeloid leukemia wh

A randomized, double-blind control study took place to determine the efficacy of a new drug, miterbitinib in patients with terminal, incurable, pancreatic cancer. 1000 patients received placebo treatment, and 1000 patients received miterbitinib. At the end of six months, 950 patients receiving placebo died, whereas 900 patients receiving miterbitinib died. In this study, what is the number needed to treat (NNT) to avoid death after 6 months? Assume perfect adherence to the treatment regimen for all 2000 individuals. 2 5 10 20 50 The correct answer is D. The absolute risk of death at 6 months with placebo and miterbitinib are 0.95 and 0.90, respectively (or, in other words, absolute survival is 0.05 vs 0.10 at 6 months). The absolute risk reduction in death is 0.05 (0.95-0.90). The NNT is calculated by 1/ARR, and 1/0.05 = 20

Which statement on the topic of critical appraisal is true? Bias reduces the precision of a study’s findings. Equipoise dictates that it is only ethical to conduct clinical trials in areas of uncertainty. Confounding can be avoided completely in a randomized control trial. A per protocol analysis studies individuals based on the protocol they were assigned. The correct answer is B. Precision is a term that generally refers to ‘standard error’. Standard error can be reduced with large sample size but the study can still be inaccurate if there is bias. Bias is systematic error that leads to INACCURATE results rather than imprecise results. Randomized con

A drug pharmaceutical company has made an alternative to the cancer drug Bevacizumab, with the primary intention being to reduce the accompanying nausea and discomfort with the original drug. Their hope is that this drug is not less efficacious than Bevacizumab. Which of the following trials are best suited for this alternative? Superiority Trial Non-inferiority Trial Equivalence Trial Non-equivalence Trial The correct answer is B. A non-inferiority trial is designed to assess if a drug is not less efficacious than the standard therapy, and this would be the design of choice to ensure the alternative is not less efficacious than Bevacizumab. A superiority trial is designed to assess if a drug is more e

Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to prefer the “Intention to Treat Analysis” over the “Per-Protocol Analysis”? Intention to treat analysis is more like the “real world” With the Per Protocol analysis, exclusions of non-adhering patients can introduce a bias With the Per Protocol analysis, if too many patients are excluded the sample size can be reduced and thereby reduce study power Intention to treat analysis is generally more likely to capture a greater treatment effect The correct answer is D. Intention to treat analysis is more likely to register a treatment effect that is too conservative because of non-adherence by patients enrolled in therapy group

Which of the following characteristics of lymphadenopathies is NOT characteristic of a malignancy? Supraclavicular nodes Generalized lymphadenopathy Tender nodes Fixed (immobile) nodes The correct answer is C. Non-tender nodes are usually indicative of a malignancy.

Use the following answers to answer the next THREE questions. A patient has an Inguinal lymphadenopathy, which cause is most likely? Tuberculosis Breast carcinoma Sexually transmitted infection The correct answer is C. Sexually transmitted infection From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Where a node sits tells you what it drains, and so what to look for. Inguinal nodes drain the lower abdomen, external genital skin, anal canal, lower third of the vagina and lower limb. The lecture's ingui

Use the following answers to answer the next THREE questions. A patient has an axillary lymphadenopathy, which cause is most likely? Tuberculosis Breast carcinoma Sexually transmitted infection The correct answer is B. Breast carcinoma From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Axillary nodes drain the breast, upper limb and chest wall. The lecture lists breast cancer (adenocarcinoma) first among axillary causes, with melanoma and lymphoma. Axillary adenopathy should prompt a breast exam. A tu

Use the following answers to answer the next THREE questions. A patient has a mediastinal lymphadenopathy, which cause is most likely? Tuberculosis Breast carcinoma Sexually transmitted infection The correct answer is A. Tuberculosis From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The lecture's causes of mediastinal nodes are Mycobacterium tuberculosis , sarcoidosis, and primary or secondary malignancy. Hilar or mediastinal adenopathy on CXR is also one of the features concerning for malignancy. B br

A 15-year-old presents to your family practice with a lymphadenopathy of the submandibular area. The patient history is suggestive of a bacterial infection. What is your best course of action? Select two answers. Follow-up in one month CBC + Differential Assess LDH and bilirubin levels Infection work-up plus antibiotics Fine-needle aspiration biopsy Core needle biopsy Excisional biopsy Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy The correct answer is A, D. Since the lymphadenopathy is likely to be caused by an infection, the infection should be treated. The follow-up is meant to confirm that treatment worked and confirm that something more sinister like lymphoma is not causing the enlarged lymph node.

A patient is concerned about a suspicious lump in their supraclavicular region. What aspect of the patient’s history decreases the likelihood of the lump being neoplastic? The patient has been having drenching night sweats. The patient has rapid unexplained weight loss. The patient has a 40 pack-year smoking history. The patient’s lump has been present for 7 days. The patient has a family history of early onset breast cancer. The correct answer is D. The sudden onset of lymphadenopathy indicates that infection or inflammation is a more likely cause. Drenching night sweats and unexplained weight loss are B-symptoms and indicate neoplasm, and a past history of smoking plus a family history of early onset cancer indicates a

A 50-year-old woman presents with a suspected malignancy. A CT scan shows a mass in her anterior mediastinum. Which of the following pathologies is at the top of your differential diagnosis? Hodgkin Lymphoma Thymoma Esophageal tumour Thoracic spine lesions The correct answer is B. Thymoma is the most prevalent tumour in the anterior mediastinum for women in that age group. Hodgkin’s lymphoma is more common in younger women (ages 10-39). An esophageal tumour would be interpreted as mass in the middle mediastinum and a thoracic spine lesion would be int

Which of the following structures are found in the middle compartment of the mediastinum? Heart Thoracic aorta Spine Esophagus Thymus The correct answer is A. The thymus is located in the anterior compartment, and the spine, esophagus, and thoracic aorta are located in the posterior compartment.

A patient presents with a positive Pemberton’s sign. Which statement below is true? A mass may be obstructing their inferior vena cava A mass may be obstructing their superior vena cava A mass may have severed their inferior vena cava A mass may have severed their superior vena cava The correct answer is B. The Pemberton’s sign is associated with an obstruction of the superior vena cava.

A 50 year old patient presents to your clinic for a periodic health encounter. The patient describes shortness of breath, cough and difficulty swallowing. Upon further examination you also notice this patient has one constricted pupil and one dilated pupil, and one of their eyelids is drooping. Which of the following conditions is a likely cause for the signs and symptoms? Superior Vena Cava Obstruction from a mediastinal mass Horner’s syndrome from a mediastinal mass Laryngeal Nerve compression from a mediastinal mass Vagus Nerve compression from a mediastinal mass The correct answer is B. Horner’s syndrome is characterized by miosis (constricted pupil), partial ptosis drooping of eyelid) and anhidrosis (inability to sweat), and oftentimes this occurs unilaterally in the body. SVC obstruction would present as edema in the face and neck and would be accompanied

What is the most common cause of lymphadenopathy? Autoimmune disorders Metastatic neoplasm Primary lymphoid neoplasm Infection Sarcoidosis The correct answer is D. Infection is by far the most common cause of lymphadenopathy.

Which of the following is an accurate difference between lymph nodes and the spleen? The lymph node contains follicles whereas the spleen does not Lymph node receives afferent lymphatics where the spleen has an afferent blood supply The spleen contains antigen presenting cells where the lymph node does not The lymph nodes can swell due to an infection whereas the spleen does not The correct answer is B. Lymph nodes and the spleen both contain follicles (germinal center, marginal zone, mantle layer). Both contain antigen presenting cells. The lymph nodes and the spleen (splenomegaly) can be enlarged during an infection. The spleen contains an afferent blood supply whereas th

Which of the following techniques is most valuable in terms of diagnostic ability for biopsying a lymph node? Surgical excision Core needle biopsy Fine Needle Aspiration Punch biopsy The correct answer is A. Surgical excision where the entire lymph node is extracted is invasive however provides the most diagnostic yield. Core needle biopsy is better for diagnostic purposes than Fine Needle Aspiration which has a high false negative rate. Punch Biopsy is only used for skin lesion

You are performing a lymph node biopsy for a patient you suspect to have Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Which of the following principles do you use to perform this biopsy? Select the most superficial lymph node to minimize the invasiveness of the procedure. With surgical excision, remove a small part of the lymph node as opposed to the whole lymph node. Select the largest lymph node as this contains the most tissue for diagnostic purposes Excise a large lymph node and a smaller lymph node to compare diagnostically. The correct answer is C. Many of the superficial lymph nodes are often benign or atypical, however the deeper and larger lymph nodes are better suited for diagnostic purposes. The larger the lymph node the more likely it is to contain diagnostic tissue.

A pathologist receives an excised lymph node for pathologic investigation. Using immunohistochemical staining, the pathologist noted a region rich in T-cells. Based on the location of these T-cells, the pathologist concluded that the lymph node was completely normal. Where were these T-cells? Germinal centre Mantle zone Marginal zone Interfollicular region Fibrous capsule The correct answer is D. T-cells are rich in the interfollicular region, but sparse in the germinal center, mantle zone, and marginal zone.

A pathologist examined a lymph node sample but based on sample size, could not rule out lymphoma as a diagnosis. What sampling technique did the pathologist likely receive? Fine needle aspiration Core needle biopsy Punch biopsy Incisional biopsy Excisional biopsy The correct answer is A. A FNA has reduced diagnostic ability, but is sometimes used as a first diagnostic technique because of its non-invasive nature and low cost.

Which of the following flow cytometry findings is NOT characteristic of a malignancy? B-lymphocytes that are monoclonal (express either kappa or lambda light chains) B-lymphocytes that are polyclonal (express both kappa and lambda light chains) B-lymphocytes that express CD5 (which is commonly found on T cells) B-lymphocytes that lose their normal CD markers (CD19, CD20) The correct answer is B. B lymphocytes that are polyclonal are benign. It is worth noting that in Hodgkin lymphoma, the flow cytometry shows a polyclonal pattern, as there are too few ReedSternberg cells to be detected by flow.

You suspect a patient has a malignancy and biopsy a lymph node. A histological sample from the biopsied lymph node is shown below. How would you classify this patient’s pathology? Large cell lymphoma Diffuse lymphoma Hodgkin lymphoma Non-Hodgkin lymphoma The correct answer is C. Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells with a binucleate cell.

Which option below INCORRECTLY differentiates Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) from nonHodgkin lymphoma (NHL)? Reed-Sternberg cells are only observed in HL, never in NHL. NHL can spread contiguously or non-contiguously, HL usually spreads contiguously. HL cannot be detected by flow cytometry but NHL can. NHL is more common than HL. Patients with NHL have better prognoses than patients with HL. The correct answer is E. Hodgkin Lymphoma is treatable and often curable. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is treatable and some subtypes are curable but not all of them are.

The next three questions relate to the same clinical case scenario. A 25-year-old male patient presents with several enlarged lymph nodes in the supraclavicular region. The patient remarked feeling easily fatigued, with mild shortness of breath upon physical activity, and bloating. He denied fever, weight loss or night sweats. An excisional biopsy reveals the patient has Hodgkin Lymphoma. Subsequent PET-CT scans indicate that the lymphoma is limited to his supraclavicular lymph nodes, axillary lymph nodes, a small mediastinal mass, and abdominal lymph nodes. What is the stage of the patient? Stage IIA Stage IIB Stage IIIA Stage IIIB Stage IVA Stage IVB The correct answer is C. The patient’s Lymphoma is stage IIIA. He has more than two nodal areas affected, both above and below the level of the diaphragm. There is no extra-nodal involvement indicated by the PETCT scan, and in addition, the patient has not reported any B-symptoms.

The case. A 25-year-old male patient presents with several enlarged lymph nodes in the supraclavicular region. The patient remarked feeling easily fatigued, with mild shortness of breath upon physical activity, and bloating. He denied fever, weight loss or night sweats. An excisional biopsy reveals the patient has Hodgkin Lymphoma. Subsequent PET-CT scans indicate that the lymphoma is limited to his supraclavicular lymph nodes, axillary lymph nodes, a small mediastinal mass, and abdominal lymph nodes. Which of the following treatments would you suggest to the 25-year-old patient? ABVD chemotherapy CHOP-R chemotherapy Radiation Surgical excision Watch and wait The correct answer is A. ABVD chemotherapy is the first line treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma, which is highly responsive to both radiation and chemotherapy. CHOP-R is used in diffuse B cell lymphoma. Radiation alone is not standard treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma, but is sometimes used after chemother

The case. A 25-year-old male patient presents with several enlarged lymph nodes in the supraclavicular region. The patient remarked feeling easily fatigued, with mild shortness of breath upon physical activity, and bloating. He denied fever, weight loss or night sweats. An excisional biopsy reveals the patient has Hodgkin Lymphoma. Subsequent PET-CT scans indicate that the lymphoma is limited to his supraclavicular lymph nodes, axillary lymph nodes, a small mediastinal mass, and abdominal lymph nodes. The 25-year-old patient completes their recommended treatment. Which of the following techniques would is most appropriate when reassessing the patient for residual lymphoma? CT Scan MRI PET scan Physical exam to palpate lymph nodes The correct answer is C. A PET scan is better at assessing for residual active tumor than a CT scan or MRI; CT scan or MRI cannot distinguish tumors from residual scar tissue, whereas PET scans can. A PET scan is appropriate as it determines which regions are consuming radiolabeled fluorodeoxyglucos

Which option below correctly describes a potential treatment option for lymphoma? Chemotherapy (CHOP-R) cannot be followed by radiation due to adverse effects. Stem cell treatments are not used because there is not enough evidence of efficacy. “Watch and wait” is used for slow-growing, incurable non-Hodgkin-lymphomas. Immune therapy is only available for lymphomas involving polyclonal B-cells. The correct answer is C. When a lymphoma is slow-growing and cannot be cured, watch and wait is the best strategy for treatment. Chemotherapy can be followed by radiation therapy, usually after a short break. Stem cell treatments can be used to treat lymphoma. Immune therapy involves monoclonal anti

A patient with known lymphoma has several affected lymph nodes. The areas affected are the supraclavicular region, the mediastinal region, and the inguinal region. A PET/CT reveals extra-nodal spread to the kidneys. On patient history and examination, he denies night sweats and any recent weight loss. He has been experiencing intermittent fevers up to 38.5 °C. Based on the above, what is the most likely type of lymphoma and what stage of lymphoma does this patient have? Select TWO answers. Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma Hodgkin Lymphoma Stage IIA Stage IIB Stage IIIA Stage IIIB Stage IVA Stage IVB The correct answer is A, H. The non-contiguous spread of the lymphoma is more in keeping with non-Hodgkin Lymphoma, though it does not totally exclude Hodgkin lymphoma. This patient has nodal involvement both above and below the diaphragm and extra-nodal involvement, signifying Stage IV. Based on th

A 40-year-old patient presents asymptomatically with bilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. There are no other sites of disease. A biopsy confirms follicular lymphoma and blood work confirms a normal LDH level and a Hemoglobin of 130 g/L (normal). With regards to the Follicular Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (FLIPI), which risk group does the patient fall into? Low (0-1 risk factors) Intermediate (2 risk factors) High (3-5 risk factors) The correct answer is A. The patient does not have any risk factors. Her lymphoma involves less than 4 nodal areas, she is below 60 years of age, her stage is 2 (axillary and supraclavicular nodes are both above the diaphragm) and her LDH and hemoglobin levels are normal.

The case. A 40-year-old patient presents asymptomatically with bilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. There are no other sites of disease. A biopsy confirms follicular lymphoma and blood work confirms a normal LDH level and a Hemoglobin of 130 g/L (normal). Which of the following treatment options is most appropriate for the 40-year-old patient in the previous question? ABVD chemotherapy BR Chemotherapy Radiation Watch and wait The correct answer is D. This patient is presenting asymptomatically with stage II follicular lymphoma so observation is appropriate. If the patient was stage I, radiation would be recommended. If a patient had stage II+ and was symptomatic BR chemotherapy would be the first line chemotherapy option

Which of the following correctly describes a process by which fractionation helps in radiation therapy? Fractionation allows healthy cells to reoxygenate between radiation doses which will impair DNA repair. Fractionation leads surrounding cells to exit the cell cycle and stop proliferating, halting tumour growth. Fractionation allows tumour cells to reoxygenate between radiation doses, which makes the treatment more lethal. Fractionation allows tumours to repair themselves in an incorrect manner leading to their own death. The correct answer is C. Reoxygenation of hypoxic cells makes them more sensitive to radiation, and when radiation is fractionated cancerous cells are able to reoxygenate. Reoxygenation does not help with repair in healthy cells. Fractionating the radiation doses thereby providing time between doses

A patient is scheduled for radiation therapy for a lymphoma in their neck and head region. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be a side effect? Shortness of breath Dry mouth Skin redness Mucositis The correct answer is A. Side effects during radiation therapy are often localized to the site of radiation. You would not expect shortness of breath unless radiation was administered to the chest region.

Britney Spears has lymphoma and requires a modest dose of radiation therapy to her bilateral neck and larynx spread out over 20 daily sessions. Which treatment modality would be used? External beam radiation Brachytherapy Stereotactic Ablative Body Radiation (SABR) Intensity modulate external beam radiation The correct answer is A. Lymphoma is almost never treated with SABR because the microscopic area of the spread is too broad for a tiny target. Furthermore, the doses required for lymphoma are too modest to be appropriate for SABR. The treatment modality for lymphoma is external beam radiation.

Key feature question: On the subject of radiation oncology, which two statements below are true? Large radiation doses are broken down into several smaller doses spread out over a longer period of time – this process is called fractionation. Brachytherapy involves the use of a linear decelerator to slowly administer radiation. In radiation therapy, the ultimate goal is for the cancer cells to die but for normal cells to self-repair. The side-effects of radiation therapy are often immediately apparent. Radiation therapy is used for cancer cure, but the toxic side-effects make it a poor choice for palliative care. The correct answer is A, C. Brachytherapy involves decaying radioactive isotopes placed near the tumour. Sideeffects of radiation treatment typically manifest near the end of the treatment regimen. Lastly, radiation therapy is used with curative and palliative intent.

A patient’s blood test shows the presence of Monoclonal protein (M Protein). The physician conducts a bone marrow biopsy and notices the bone marrow contains 15% plasma cells. The patient is not reporting any symptoms. Which stage best fits the patient's description? MGUS Smoldering multiple myeloma Overt multiple myeloma Plasma cell leukemia The correct answer is B. Smoldering multiple myeloma is characterized as asymptomatic, bone marrow is more than 10% plasma cell and the presence of Protein M in urine or blood samples.

Which of the following is NOT a symptom of Multiple Myeloma? Anemia due to bone marrow infiltration from plasma cells Hypocalcemia due to increased osteoclast activity Renal failure from elevated levels of M protein Increased risk of infection from neutropenia The correct answer is B. Osteoclast activity is increased due to inflammatory cytokines produced by plasma cells, which consequently leads to bone reabsorption and higher serum calcium (hypercalcemia).

Which of the following tests could be performed to identify a patient with MGUS or smoldering Myeloma? Complete Blood Count Skeletal survey Protein electrophoresis Renal function tests The correct answer is C. Protein Electrophoresis would identify the presence of a Monoclonal protein (M protein) from a urine or blood sample. Patients with MGUS and smoldering Myeloma are asymptomatic thus it is unlikely to find significant findings such as neutropenia, anemia (from a CBC) or reduc

Which lab test results and their respective indications help in the diagnosis of multiple myeloma? Select TWO answers. Elevated calcium levels indicating bone lesions Reduced creatinine levels indicating impaired renal function Pancytopenia indicating reduced bone marrow infiltration Rouleaux cells in the blood film indicating presence of M-protein X-ray, CT, or PET-CT indicating elevated osteoblast activity The correct answer is A, D. Impaired renal function results in elevated creatinine levels. Pancytopenia is the result of increased bone marrow infiltration. In multiple myeloma, increased osteoclast activity results in bone lesions.

Which of the patients below is most likely to have plasma cell leukemia? A patient with renal damage and anemia, with 15% monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow. A patient with renal damage and bone lesions with 25% monoclonal plasma cells in the peripheral blood. An asymptomatic patient with 15% monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow. An asymptomatic patient with 7% monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow. A patient with depositions of insoluble M-protein in organs and other tissues. The correct answer is B. Plasma cell leukemia is characterized as symptomatic with end organ damage and plasma cells in the peripheral blood (>20%).

5-Fluorouracil is a chemotherapy agent which works by inhibiting the production of thymine within tumour (and non-cancerous) cells. Which of the following is the best classification of this drug? Alkylating agent Anti-metabolites Antitumour antibiotics Topoisomerase inhibitors Antimicrotubule agents The correct answer is B. Antimetabolites interfere with the normal cellular metabolism of nucleic acids.

Zevalin is a chemotherapy agent used in relapsed follicular lymphoma. Zevalin is unique in that it is an antibody that also delivers radiation. Which of the following is the best classification of this drug? Naked monoclonal antibodies Conjugated monoclonal antibodies Bi-specific monoclonal antibodies CAR-T monoclonal antibodies The correct answer is B. Conjugated monoclonal antibodies contain an attachment to the antibody which contains additional therapeutic properties.

Which of the following drugs would be used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia? Bruton Kinase Inhibitor (interferes in B cell antigen receptor signaling) ATRA/Arsenic (allows cells to differentiate into mature granulocytes) Imatinib (inhibits constitutive activity of BCR-Abl receptor through competitive inhibition) Velcade (proteasome inhibitor) The correct answer is A. Bruton Kinase Inhibitor is used to treat CLL, as it interferes in signaling that is necessary for B cell tumour expansion. ATRA/Arsenic is used to treat Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia. Imatinib is used to treat Chronic Myeloid Leukemia. Velcade is used to treat multiple myelom

Which option below incorrectly describes the mechanism of action of chemotherapy drug used to treat non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHOP-R)? Cyclophosphamide alkylates DNA preventing strand separation. Hydroxyadriamycin (aka doxorubicin) intercalates DNA preventing replication. Oncovin (vincristine) prevents microtubule formation. Prednisone decreases inflammation. Rituximab is a DNA topoisomerase inhibitor. The correct answer is E. Rituximab is an immune therapy which targets CD-20 on B-cells.

Which statement on cancer treatments are true? Select all that apply. Ibrutinib is a Bruton’s kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of relapsed CLL. Imatinib is a conjugated antibody used in the treatment of CML. CAR-T therapy involves editing the genes of T-cells and infusing back into the patient. Rituximab is highly specific for B-lymphocyte cells. Glucocorticoids alkylate DNA and arrest the cancer cell in G1 phase. The correct answer is A, C, D. Imatinib is used in the treatment of CML, but it is not a conjugated antibody. Glucocorticoids do not alkylate DNA - these are steroidal treatments to reduce inflammation.

Taylor has ordered a 23andMe test which reveals she has a genetic variant of NUDT15 which makes her a poor metabolizer of thiopurine drugs. This variation is present in approximately 2% of the East Asian population. Both of Taylor’s parents have taken the test and are heterozygotes for this variant. Which of the following is the likely the best classification of Taylor’s NUDT15 variation? Germline mutation Somatic mutation Germline polymorphism Somatic polymorphism The correct answer is C. Since her parents have this variant, it’s likely germline instead of somatic. Given that this genetic variant has a frequency greater than 1%, it is classified as a polymorphism. A mutation is prevalent in less than 1% of the population.

In the absence of genetic testing, which of the following are appropriate methods to determine the dosage and type of medication a patient should receive? Taking into account a patient’s race Taking into account a patient’s age, weight, and disease factors Empirically determining the safe and effective dose for an individual patient i, ii ii, iii i, iii i, ii, iii The correct answer is D. It’s appropriate to take into account a patient’s race, age and weight when determining drug dosage/type. With certain drugs like Warfarin the safe and effective dose can be determined empirically.

The therapeutic effect of cancer drugs is influenced by a patient’s genetic profile. Which patient would likely yield a smaller-than-average therapeutic response based on their genetics? Andrew, who is receiving clopidogrel (a pro-drug platelet inhibitor) and has lossof-function mutations in both of his copies of the gene encoding CYP2C19. (CYP2C19 metabolizes clopidogrel) Brandon, who is receiving 5-fluorouracil (a fluoropyrimidine) and has loss-of function mutations in both of his copies of the gene encoding dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase. (Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase metabolizes 5-fluorouracil) Charlie, who is receiving azathioprine (a thiopurine) but has loss-of-function mutations in both of his copies of the gene encoding thiopurine methyltransferase. (Thiopurine methyltransferase metabolizes thiopurines) David, who is receiving warfarin treatment but has SNPs in both of the genes encoding Vitamin K Epoxide Reductase (VKOR). Specifically, his SNPs increase his VKOR sensitivity to warfarin. Ernie, who is receiving simvastatin (a statin) and is homozygous for normal activity statin transporter gene SLCO1B1. (SLCO1B1 encodes the gene for the transporter that facilitates statin entry into the liver) The correct answer is A. Clopidogrel is a pro-drug that needs to be metabolized into a pharmacologically active metabolite. Reduced metabolism of clopidogrel through mutated CYP2C19 enzymes will result in a smaller response to standard treatment doses.

Which option below correctly describes a type of complementary medicine? Herbal medications to treat recurrent cancer Traditional Chinese Medicine to help deal with the side effects of chemotherapy Homeopathy for control of diabetes Naturopathy for management of an ear infection Body-mind techniques to deal with a compound fracture The correct answer is B. This is complementary therapy - the others are actually alternative medicine, which is used instead of conventional management.

There are a great many kinds of white blood cells circulating about in the blood stream. When observing the blood as part of a blood smear, which cell types do you expect to observe as part of the “granulocyte” class of white blood cell? Neutrophils B lymphocytes Myeloblasts Megakaryocytes Eosinophils Basophils A, E, and F. Only E and F. The correct answer is G. A, E, F . All are part of the granulocyte group of white blood cells. A quick trick for memorization could be that the granulocytes end in -phil.

Hematopoiesis is the production of blood cells in the body. The location of this production changes throughout fetal development. Which of the following options showcases the correct sequence of hematopoiesis throughout fetal development? (Starting from the left and ending with the final location of hematopoiesis on the right.) Yolk sac (YS), Aorta/gonad/mesonephros (AGM), Liver, Spleen, Bone marrow, Lymph plexuses and Thymus. Yolk sac (YS), Aorta/gonad/mesonephros (AGM), Bone marrow, Lymph plexuses and Thymus, Spleen, Liver. Yolk sac (YS), Aorta/gonad/mesonephros (AGM), Bone marrow, Liver, Spleen, Lymph plexuses and Thymus. Yolk sac (YS), Aorta/gonad/mesonephros (AGM), Liver, Spleen, Lymph plexuses and Thymus, Bone Marrow. The correct answer is D. The correct order is D, followed by the rapid loss of most hematopoiesis outside of the bone marrow shortly after birth.

White blood cells are instrumental in fighting various pathogens that invade the body. Of these white blood cells, which are the best equipped to mediate an allergic response and fight parasites? Neutrophil Monocytes Eosinophils Basophils Lymphocytes The correct answer is C. Eosinophils along with mast cells give rise to allergic reactions. They also play a major roll in parasitic infection resistance.

There are numerous red blood cell morphologies. While some variation in RBC shape can be expected, other forms may be more indicative of disease. Which of the following disease states would be most associated with elliptocytes? Thalassemia Lead Poisoning Blood Loss Severe Iron Deficiency The correct answer is D. sever iron deficiency can lead to elliptocytes. It can also lead to brittle finger nails, pica, and difficulty swallowing.

Which term defines the attitude that cisgender heterosexuality and heterosexual sex is the normal and natural expression of sexuality? Cisgender Heteronormative Gender Expression Attitudinal Bias The correct answer is B. Heteronormative. This term defines the attitude that cisgender heterosexuality and heterosexual sex is the normal.

The process of focusing on specific information about an individual, as opposed to categorizing someone based on their social, racial, or other group is called? Perspective Taking Broadening Opening Individuating The correct answer is D. Individuating. This is the process of focusing on specific information about an individual, as opposed to categorizing someone based on their social, racial, or other group.

Of the following disease states, which are potential causes of microcytic anemia? Iron Deficiency anemia Hemolytic anemias Sideroblastic anemia Lead poisoning All of the above A, C, and D The correct answer is F. A, C, D. All can cause microcytic anemia. From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Microcytosis means Hb synthesis has fallen behind cell division, from too little heme or too little globin. The differential is TAILS : thalassemia, anemia of chronic inflammation, iron defici

A patient presents with mild microcytic anemia. Their ferritin level is normal, and stainable iron stores are found within the patients’ macrophages. They also present with a chronic pulmonary infection. What is likely the form of microcytic anemia the patient is presenting with? Thalassemia Lead poisoning Anemia of Chronic Inflammation Sideroblastic anemia The correct answer is C. Anemia of chronic inflammation leads to a widespread signalling within the body to retain the body’s iron stores. This can lead to the contradictory result of high iron levels, but anemic presentation.

You observe a blood smear containing a leucoerythroblastic picture. This smear is full of immature white blood cells and red blood cells. The Bone marrow biopsy shows fibrotic tissues instead of the normal marrow tissues expected. Which of the following normocytic anemias is most likely? Hemolytic anemia Blood loss Myelodysplastic syndrome Myelophthisis Anemia of Chronic Inflammation The correct answer is D. Myelophthisis. This is essentially the case where normal cell production is progressively occluded by fibrotic tissue buildup in the bone marrow. This can be caused by other diseases that have infiltrated the bone marrow.

You would expect to see all the following results from lab work taken from a patient with hemolysis except: Decreased LDH Increased indirect bilirubin Decreased haptoglobin Increased reticulocytes The correct answer is A. Hemolysis is most likely to present with an increase LDH, not decreased.

Generally, the main cause behind megaloblastic anemia is: Decreased DNA synthesis Increased availability of Vitamin B12 Increased Folate Increased metabolic efficiency The correct answer is A. Decreased DNA synthesis leads to bloated cells with little in the way of DNA to compensate. This is typically the result of little building blocks for DNA, but continued cell development.

Which of the following is an indicator of macrocytic anemia? Reticulocytosis Thalassemia Biochemical markers of hemolysis Autoimmune hemolytic anemia A, C, and D The correct answer is E. A, C, D. Thalassemia is more exclusive to microcytic anemias.

Effective goals have the following characteristics, except: Measurable Time-sensitive Achievable Relevant The correct answer is B. Effective goals include SMART: smart, measurable, achievable, relevant and timedependent. Time-sensitive is a made up trait.

Quality Improvement includes 3 phases. Which of the following lists these phases in the correct order? Root cause analysis, analysis, solution generation & selection Solution generation & selection, root cause analysis, and analysis Analysis, solution generation & selection, root cause analysis Root cause analysis, solution generation & selection, and analysis The correct answer is D. The correct order is root cause analysis, solution generation/selection, and then analysis after.

When should parenteral iron be administered? When the patient cannot tolerate oral iron When oral iron cannot be absorbed adequately by the patient When losses exceed that of which oral iron can provide All of the above The correct answer is D. All of the above are true and legitimate reasons to administer IV iron as opposed to oral.

Which of the following statements correctly pairs the organ with the correct stage of absorption of B12? Stomach - acidic pH degrades B12 Duodenum - pancreatic enzymes in the acidic environment digest R protein, releasing B12 Terminal ileum - B12 and Intrinsic factor (IF) bind to IF receptors Stomach - Parietal cells bind intrinsic factor (IF) The correct answer is C. The terminal ileum is where B12 and intrinsic factor bind to the IF receptors. Stomach is where the acidic pH releases B12, the duodenum is where pancreatic enzymes in the ALKALINE environment digest R protein, releasing B12. Lastly, the parietal cells release IF.

Which of the following can be clinical presentations can be present in MDS? Anemia Thrombosis Neutropenia Constitutional symptoms A, C, and D The correct answer is E. A, C, and D are true. MDS can also cause thrombocytopenia.

What management procedures can be given to those with lower risk MDS? Supportive stem cell transplants EPO Epigenetic modifiers Chemotherapy The correct answer is B. EPO is given to low risk patients. The remaining treatments are given to high risk patients.

What is folate essential for? DNA synthesis Helps in red blood cell synthesis Methylates DNA All of the above A and B only The correct answer is D. Folate is essential for all of the above processes. From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias and 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome . Folate does all three jobs: A DNA synthesis - as tetrahydrofolate it is the cofactor for uracil → thymine; deficiency hits rapidly dividing

Which of the following is true of Vitamin B12? Cannot be produced by mammals The daily requirement is high The body only stores about 1 year supply in the liver The body only stores about 3-5 years supply in the gallbladder The correct answer is A. B12 cannot be produced by animals. The daily requirement is low, and the body stores 3- 5 years worth in the liver, not the gallbladder.

In Beta Thalassemia, there is a lack of Beta chains, causing alpha chains to aggregate. This can result in which of the following? Ineffective erythropoiesis Iron overload Hemolysis All of the above The correct answer is D. All of the above can result from Beta Thalassemia. From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. In beta thalassemia the unpaired excess alpha chains precipitate in red-cell precursors and circulating cells. The lecture lists all three consequences under thalassemia: ineffective

For patients with sickle cell disease, lifestyle coaching should include which of the following? Do not swim in warm water Do not use warm compress on injury Do not use cold compress on injury None of the above The correct answer is C. Injuries should not be cold-compressed. From the sickle cell disease reference note (the lecture notes cover crises but not lifestyle advice). Vaso-occlusive episodes are triggered by dehydration, cooling of the skin , stress and infection, because cold slows flow and promot

Which of the following are signs and/or symptoms of hemolytic anemia? Bilirubinemia Hemoglobinuria Hemoglobinemia Fever and chills All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above reasons can result from hemolytic anemia.

What is unique about warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) as opposed to cold? Warm AIHA is not C’ fixing Warm AIHA is caused by IgM Splenectomy is never effective Warm AIHA includes extravascular hemolysis while cold AIHA is intravascular The correct answer is A. Warm AIHA is in fact, not C’ fixating. Warm AIHA is caused by IgG, splenectomy may be effective, and both warm and cold AIHA involve extravascular hemolysis.

Which of the following is NOT a step that must be taken before giving any patient a blood transfusion? Blood Group and Screen and Crossmatch Obtain informed consent and evaluate decision-making capability Follow the Massive Transfusion Protocol Ensure that transfusion is indicated The correct answer is C. The massive transfusion protocol is useful in times of rapid bleeding to deliver transfusion products to the bedside quickly. However, it is not needed in all situations where transfusion is indicated.

You transfuse 3 units of packed red blood cells to a bleeding patient. Which of the following is NOT a possible risk of transfusion? Transfusion-associated anemia Chagas Disease Hemolysis Transfusion-associated circulatory overload The correct answer is A. Transfusion-associated anemia is not a non-infectious risk of transfusion. Transfusion is a helpful tool in managing patients with anemia.

You want to prescribe an anticoagulant to a 74 year old male patient. Which of the following is NOT a reasonable pharmacological option? Rivaroxaban Warfarin Low molecular weight heparin Idarucizumab The correct answer is D. Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for dabigatran; it is not an anticoagulant.

Which of the following sentences INCORRECTLY describes the corresponding phase of platelet activation? Adhesion – platelets are exposed to collagen, which binds vWF. Aggregation – platelets adhere to one another via phospholipid binding. vWF and fibrinogen facilitate this. Contraction – activated platelets change their shape from discoid to spheroid. Secretion – calcium influx triggers granular secretion and the formation of the platelet plug, providing a surface for fibrin deposition. The correct answer is B. Platelets adhere to one another using glycoproteins, not phospholipids.

Which of the following statements is CORRECT? DVT and PE can be diagnosed based on history and physical exam. PE and DVT are isolated events and do not usually co-exist. Compression ultrasound is the gold standard diagnostic test for DVT. Other differential diagnoses for DVT symptoms include cellulitis and bacterial cysts. The correct answer is D. DVT and PE cannot be diagnosed clinically and require specific diagnostic testing to be done. DVT can often lead to PE, and ascending venogram is the gold standard diagnostic tool for DVT.

Which of the following are management strategies for PE (select all that apply): Activity as tolerated NSAID Warfarin Edoxaban The correct answer is A, B, C, D. All are treatment and management options for PE.

For which of the following patients would you administer low molecular weight heparin rather than unfractionated heparin (select all that apply)? 76M diagnosed with diabetes and acute renal failure 87F who is mostly being cared for outpatient 24F who’s may or may not have taken a significant amount of aspirin prior to hospital admission 34F diagnosed with anemia (and therefore cannot tolerate many blood draws) The correct answer is B, D. LMWH is mostly cleared by the kidney while UFH is mostly cleared by the liver. LMWH can be given subcutaneously, and therefore administered at home, while UFH is given IV and must be administered by a healthcare professional. Aspirin is an anticoagulant and UFH is better

Which of the following anticoagulants requires anti-thrombin to function: Fondaparinux Hirudin Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) Warfarin The correct answer is A. Fondaparinux binds to anti-thrombin to form the scaffold needed to inhibit factor X. Hirudin and DOACs can bind directly to thrombin, and Warfarin inhibits the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors.

Which of the following is NOT a cause of an isolated elevated PTT? Von Willebrand disease Lupus anticoagulant Hemophilia A Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) FXI deficiency The correct answer is D. An isolated elevated PTT indicates something is wrong with the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. Von Willebrand protein acts as a chaperone for FVIII, a part of the intrinsic pathway. Lupus anticoagulant acts as an antiphospholipid antibody, which prevents the ac

A patient presents with a history of heavy bilateral epistaxis that takes 30+ mins to resolve. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be the cause? Ehlers Danlos syndrome Hypersplenism Hemophilia B Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) Antiplatelet medications The correct answer is C. Ehlers Danlos syndrome is a connective tissue disease and vascular disorder. Hypersplenism will result in sequestration of platelets and reduce the number of circulating platelets. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) causes increased destruction of platelets and will reduce the nu

Which of the following is the LEAST likely to indicate a patient may have an underlying bleeding disorder? Heavy bleeding after dental work Menorrhagia Weekly bilateral epistaxis Hemarthrosis Papercut that takes 20 minutes to stop bleeding The correct answer is B. Menorrhagia is a common condition in otherwise healthy individuals. The presence of menorrhagia alone does not indicate that an individual has an underlying bleeding disorder. Heavy bleeding after dental work, weekly bilateral epistaxis, hemarthrosis, and slow/delayed hemost

A concerned mother brings her 2-month-old son to your walk-in clinic. Her son has had his third nosebleed in the past 2 weeks and she is very worried. She did not have any prenatal screening performed. You suspect an underlying bleeding disorder. Which of the following would NOT be helpful investigations? Collect a family history of bleeding Ask whether or not her son was circumcised and if there has been any associated bleeding Examine the son’s joints, particularly the ankles and knees Inquire about the son’s dental work and if there has been any associated bleeding Examine the son for bruising The correct answer is D. It is highly unlikely that a 2-month-old will have had any dental work done. A family history of bleeding may indicate a possible hereditary bleeding disorder. Post-surgical bleeding, such as post-circumcision bleeding, may point towards an underlying bleeding disorder. Iden

Which of the following is FALSE regarding hemostasis in neonates? FIX is often significantly lower in neonates and can mimic Hemophilia B aPTT is greater in neonates compared to adults Inadequate vitamin K prophylaxis can result in hemorrhagic disease of the newborn Hemarthroses are uncommon in neonates with hemophilia up until the 6-8 month mark Neonates typically have lower levels of all coagulation factors compared to adults The correct answer is E. Neonates have lower levels of most coagulation factors, but not all of them. FVIII is typically found in greater levels in neonates than in adults. FVIII is not made in the liver. Most other coagulation factors are made in the liver, and in neonates their levels are lower du

Which of the following is FALSE regarding von Willebrand disease (vWD)? vWD is tested for with vWF antigen, vWF activity, FVIII level, and blood group vWD is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder DDAVP can be used to increase the levels of vWF and FVIII in those with vWD Women with vWD should avoid using oral contraceptives Those with type O blood typically have less vWF than non-O type blood The correct answer is D. The oral contraceptive pill has procoagulant properties can help women with vWB manage heavy menstrual bleeding. vWD the most common inherited bleeding disorder and is tested for by investigating vWF antigen, vWF activity, FVIII level, and blood group. DDVAP can be used to h

Which of the following is NOT a step in your general approach to thrombocytopenia? Consider the differential diagnosis Confirm thrombocytopenia Assess bone marrow Consider associated disorders Assess severity The correct answer is C. The 1st step when approaching thrombocytopenia should be to confirm that thrombocytopenia is present. This can be done with a CBC. Step 2 is to assess the severity. This is done clinically by identifying whether or not bleeding is present, the site of bleeding, and how sever

Which of the following is NOT a cause of decreased thrombocyte production? Liver disease von Willebrand disease B12 deficiency Aplastic anemia Myelofibrosis The correct answer is B. von Willebrand disease is a disease that affects secondary hemostasis and does not result in reduced platelet production. The liver produces thrombopoietin which stimulates thrombocyte production, and liver disease can affect thrombopoietin production. Vitamin B12 is require

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a cause of increased platelet destruction. Which of the following is NOT a commonly associated with ITP? Severe thrombocytopenia (<10 x 109/L) Schistocytes Acute presentation Mucosal bleeding and bruising Normal Hb and WBC levels The correct answer is B. When it comes to thrombocytopenia, schistocytes are seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (MAHAs), not immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

Which of the following statements regarding microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (MAHAs) is FALSE? One investigation finding that is useful in diagnosing disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is elevated D-dimer Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is caused by reduced ADAMTS-13 levels which results in large dysfunctional multimers of von Willebrand factor Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is characterized by acute kidney injury, the presence of spherocytes, and acute thrombocytopenia Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) has multiple etiologies including sepsis and malignancies There are normal levels of ADAMTS-13 in hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a condition that occurs most commonly in the setting of an infection The correct answer is C. A patient presents with erythrocytosis and low EPO levels, molecular studies show that the patient is negative for JAK2 V617F mutation. What is true about this case? What is the proper management of a 45 year old patient with polycythemia vera, who does not have a prior history of thrombosis? Which of the following is not a cause of secondary erythrocytosis: High altitude Obstructive sleep apnea Pheochromocytoma Lipoma The correct answer is D. From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. Which of the following will be seen on a blood film of a patient with myelofibrosis? Teardrop cells Leucoerythroblastic picture Reticulin fibres A and C All of the above The correct answer is E. A 38 year old female presents to your family medicine clinic for a routine physical exam. A CBC reveals an isolated elevated platelet count of 1000x109/L. Before you consider her medical history and perform a physical exam, what would be at the top of your differential diagnosis? Polycythemia Vera (PV) Chronic myelocytic leukemia (CML) Essential Thrombocytosis Reactive Thrombocytosis Myelofibrosis The correct answer is D. Secondary (reactive) thrombocytosis is the most common cause of thrombocytosis even in patients with extreme thrombocytosis (platelet count > 1000x109/L).

Leukemia can present with fatigue, bleeding, and infections due to progressive cytopenias. Leukemia can present with headaches due to leukostasis and gout due to tumor lysis syndrome. Which of the following labs results is suggestive of tumor lysis syndrome? Select all that apply. Hypercalcemia Hyperphosphatemia Hyperkalemia Hyponatremia Elevated creatinine The correct answer is B, C, E. In the blood you will see elevated phosphate and potassium as the tumor cells lyse. Additionally, there will be low serum Ca and high levels of uric acid. The high uric acid can acute renal failure leading to an increase in plasma creatinine.
What is the best prognostic indicator for ALL in pediatrics? CNS involvement Age Cytogenetics Response to treatment The correct answer is D. Response to treatment is the greatest prognostic factor.

A 6 year old boy and his parents arrive in the ER. Their primary concern is pallor, fever, and bone pain that wakes their son up at night. They have even noticed that he started limping today. CBC shows blast cells. What would be your top differential diagnosis? AML ALL CML CLL Multiple Myeloma The correct answer is B. The symptoms described and the presence of blast cells are concerning for ALL, which is the most common leukemia in children.

Which of the following correctly outlines a difference between ALL and AML? ALL treatment duration is ~6 months, whereas AML is ~2-3 years. ALL treatment involves induction, reinduction, and maintenance therapy; however, AML only involves maintenance therapy. ALL treatment involves CNS directed therapy and AML does not. ALL is unlikely to manifest in sanctuary sites. AML can relapse in sanctuary sites such as the CNS and testes. The correct answer is C. ALL treatment includes CNS directed therapy because ALL can relapse in the CNS, as it is a santuary site. Another santuary site for ALL is the testes. Santuary sites are not commonly seen in AML.

What are ways to decrease bias in research? Select all that apply. Blinding Per-Protocol Analysis Randomization Intention-to-treat analysis The correct answer is A, C, D. A per-protocol analysis includes all patients who completed the full course of the assigned treatment and yields a higher effect estimate. The concern with this is that patient exclusions in the analysis can introduce bias.

In which of the following would folate supplementation not be recommended? Methotrexate use When trying to conceive Alcoholism Pregnancy Celiac disease The correct answer is A. Methotrexate acts by antagonizing folate; supplementation would be counterproductive. Folate is recommended during pregnancy and when trying to conceive to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. Celiac disease and alcoholism can both cause folate deficiency.

Which of the following is not a significant source of vitamin B12? Eggs Cheese Shellfish Soy Milk Beef Liver The correct answer is D. Unless fortified, soy milk is not a source of vitamin B12. In general, animal products contain vitamin B12; fruit, vegetables and grain products do not.

Which of the following findings would best distinguish between alpha-Thalassemia and beta-Thalassemia in a patient you suspect has this disorder? Which of the following is most commonly used to investigate possible iron deficiency? Although ferritin mainly stores iron within cells, a small amount leaks into the circulation and is valuable clinically as a measure of how much iron is stored in the body. How long should treatment for iron deficiency continue? 1 month after return to normal hemoglobin concentration 2 months after return to normal hemoglobin concentration 3 months after return to normal hemoglobin concentration 6 months after return to normal hemoglobin concentration 1 year after return to normal hemoglobin concentration The correct answer is D. Which of the following is not associated with sideroblastic anemia? Hydroxyurea use Pyroxidine deficiency Alcoholism Lead toxicity The correct answer is A. From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Anemia directly relating to live disease is best associated with: Schistocytes Spherocytes Elliptocytes Target cells Howell-Jolly Bodies The correct answer is D. Liver disease can result in excessive incorporation of cholesterol and phospholipids in the membranes of RBCs. Increased membrane redundancy causes RBCs take on target shape.

A CBC reveals granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia and a slightly macrocytic anemia. A bone marrow examination reveals hypocellularity. What is the most likely diagnosis? The therapeutic index of many drugs used in cancer treatment approaches that of the toxic index. This means that: A toxic dose of the drug is much higher than a therapeutic dose A toxic dose of the drug is much less than a therapeutic dose There is no relationship between the drug's therapeutic and toxic dosages The toxic dose of the drug is approximately equal to the therapeutic dose In 50% of cases, the toxic dose is equal to the therapeutic dose The correct answer is D. When the therapeutic index of a drug is close or approaches that off the toxic index that suggests the drug has a narrow therapeutic index – whereby slightly increases of the therapeutic dose can cross the boundary into the toxic dose and elicit toxic side effects.

Which of the following is not a possible cause of iron deficiency? Veganism Celiac disease Bleeding gastric ulcer Colonic resection Pregnancy The correct answer is D. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the colon.

Which of the following is true about platelets? The Microbiology Laboratory How a specimen becomes a result: the lab's value depends on getting the right specimen, before antibiotics, to the lab fast , and then on choosing between direct methods (microscopy, culture, molecular, antigen) and indirect ones (serology). Collect specimens BEFORE antibiotics , from the site of infection, avoiding normal flora. Blood culture: volume is the most critical factor ; catheter-drawn cultures contaminate more. Gram-positive = purple (thick peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid → TLR2); Gram-negative = pink (outer membrane, LPS → TLR4). Serology: IgM+ = acute/recent; IgG alone = immunity ; a fourfold rise between acute and convalescent sera confirms. S. aureus is catalase+/coagulase+ in clusters; S. pyogenes is catalase–, β-hemolytic, in chains, and its M-protein drives rheumatic fever. The Human Microbiome The same microbe can be harmless or pathogenic depending on where it is : the organising idea is the spectrum from commensal → coloniser → infection , plus dysbiosis when the community itself shifts. Commensal = usual habitat; coloniser = unusual habitat, no disease; infection = wrong compartment or outside invader causing disease; dysbiosis = changed composition, diversity or metabolites. Most infections here are a compartment breach by the site's own flora (cellulitis, peritonitis, PID). Normally sterile: bladder, blood, CSF, lower respiratory tract . Definitions Human microbiome : the bacteria, archaea, fungi, parasites and viruses living in and on the body Microbiota : the microorganisms found in a specific environment Commensal : microbe in its usual habitat Coloniser : microbe in an unusual habitat, not causing disease Infection : microbe in a site causing disease (wrong compartment or unusual invader) Dysbiosis : a change in the composition, diversity or metabolites of the microbiome Sterile sites (and the infection when breached) Bladder (urobiome), bloodstream (bacteremia), CSF (meningitis), lower respiratory tract (bronchitis, pneumonia) Site Commensals Colonisers Infection Dysbiosis Skin Staphylococcus , Streptococcus , Propionibacterium , Corynebacterium , Lactobacillus , Candida Wounds colonised with Pseudomonas Compartment breach → cellulitis, impetigo, erysipelas, abscess ( S. aureus , GAS) Eczema (less CoNS producing antimicrobial peptides) Mouth S. pneumoniae , S. anginosus , Peptostreptococcus , Fusobacterium , Parvimonas micra , Candida S. aureus , S. pneumoniae , Moraxella catarrhalis , Haemophilus influenzae Compartment breach → dental abscess, deep neck space infection Pharyngitis : GAS, adenovirus Poor dental hygiene → plaque, gingivitis — Gut S. anginosus , Enterococcus , E. coli , Klebsiella pneumoniae , Proteus , Bacteroides fragilis , Candida — Colitis : Salmonella , Shigella , Campylobacter , C. difficile Compartment breach → peritonitis : E. coli , K. pneumoniae , Enterobacter , B. fragilis IBD (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's), IBS, C. difficile Vagina Lactobacillus , Candida — Compartment breach → PID : E. coli , anaerobes Outsider infection: gonorrhea, chlamydia Bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis
09 Approach to a Patient with Fever

Approach to a Patient with Fever A fever workup runs in a fixed order — safety, then stability and sepsis screen, then history, exam, differential, investigations and treatment — with the thresholds and the history shifting by age group (children, adults, older adults). Screen for sepsis first : qSOFA ≥ 2 (RR ≥ 22, BP ≤ 100/60, altered mentation) in adults; SIRS ≥ 2 in pediatrics. Fever: 38°C in children; 37.2°C (6 AM) or 37.8°C in adults; in older adults 37.8°C once, 37.2°C persistent, or ≥ 1.1°C above baseline — and fever is absent in 30–50% of frail older adults with infection (look for falls, delirium). Always send 2 sets of blood cultures. Positive urine culture ≠ UTI; no urinalysis in patients over 65 . 1. Safety check Routine: handwashing + COVID precautions (gown, gloves, face mask, eye protection) — PPE 2. Is the patient stable? Vitals and sepsis check Airway, breathing, circulation; BP, HR, RR, temperature, O2 saturation qSOFA (quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) — adults: RR ≥ 22/min, BP ≤ 100/60, altered mentation ; 2+ points = high risk SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) — pediatrics: temperature < 36°C or > 38°C, HR > 90, RR > 20/min, WBC > 12,000/mm³ or < 4,000/mm³ or > 10% bands; 2+ = SIRS criteria What counts as fever Group Site Threshold Pediatrics Rectum, armpit 38°C Adults Oral/tympanic 37.2°C (6 AM) or 37.8°C Older adults Oral/tympanic 37.8°C single or 37.2°C persistent , or rise ≥ 1.1°C above baseline 3. When? Diagnosis? Treatment? Management Treat the underlying cause: bacter

Important Gram-Negatives and Mycobacteria E. coli shows how one species causes different diseases by which adhesin it carries and which toxin it secretes ; mycobacteria, by contrast, are defined by a mycolic-acid wall that makes them acid-fast and drives chronic infection. PapG → galactose glycolipids → pyelonephritis; FimH → mannose → cystitis. LPS O-polysaccharide blocks MAC assembly ; a sialic acid capsule blocks complement (mimicry). STEC O157:H7 : intimin/Tir actin pedestal → Shiga toxin → Gb3 → retrograde transport to ER → rRNA damaged → protein synthesis stops. Mycobacteria are acid-fast because acid-alcohol cannot wash out the stain from their mycolic-acid wall. Escherichia coli E. coli Classification Gram-negative bacilli, aerobic Grows on sheep blood agar; oxidase – Diseases UTI Pyelonephritis : PapG adhesin binds a galactose-containing glycolipid in the upper urinary tract and kidney → tissue tropism Cystitis : FimH adhesin at the pilus tip binds the bladder mucosal surface Colitis · bacteremia · sepsis Transmission Contact, contaminated food/water Colonises Gut microbiome Virulence: adhesion Fimbriae — pyelonephritis = glycolipids ; cystitis = mannose Immune evasion O-polysaccharide of LPS can prevent assembly of the complement MAC E. coli K12 capsule contains sialic acid, which prevents complement activation Uropathogenic E. coli (K1) make a sialic acid capsule (mimicry) STEC (Shiga toxin-producing), E. coli O157:H7 Adhesin intimin binds its receptor Tir , which the bacterium inserts into the intestinal epithelial membrane → actin pedestal , from which Shiga toxin is secreted (B-subunit pentamer + A-subunit toxin) B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) → endocytosis Retrograde transport through the Golgi to the ER, where the toxin component leaves the vesicle and modifies ribosomal RNA → protein synthesis stops → cell death Other enteric Gram-negatives Salmonella , Shigella and Yersinia cause colitis by injecting proteins into intestinal epithelial cells — some promote uptake by a ruffling mechanism , others promote inflammation (IL-1β) Gram-negative ID: aerobic bacilli split on growth on sheep blood agar, then oxidase, then glucose or lactose fermentation — E. coli and Klebsiella are oxidase-negative lactose fermenters. Patterns of Acute Inflammation Acute inflammation takes four morphological patterns , and what distinguishes them is what leaks out of the vessels : pus (neutrophils), fibrin, cell-poor fluid, or a breach of the mucosa itself. Purulent = pyogenic bacteria ( Staphylococcus ) → liquefactive necrosis; an abscess is walled off and avascular, so antibiotics penetrate poorly — drain it . Fibrinous = marked permeability lets fibrinogen out (e.g. fibrinous pericarditis : post-MI/Dressler's, cardiac surgery, uremia, SLE). Serous = cell-poor fluid: effusion, ascites, blister. Ulcer = a local mucosal defect. Pattern Features and examples Purulent / suppurative Most often from pus-producing pyogenic bacteria ( Staphylococcus ) → liquefactive necrosis Common sites: skin (groin, axilla, perianal), mouth (teeth), GI (around the gut), lung Abscess : pus ( neutrophils ) localised to a cavity created by tissue destruction Tx: incision and drainage ; deep organ abscesses may need a more invasive surgical approach Antibiotics penetrate poorly — the process is walled off, with an avascular pus-filled necrotic centre Example: acute appendicitis Fibrinous Greatly ↑ vascular permeability lets fibrinogen through inter-endothelial spaces → fibrin deposition Occurs in spaces or potential spaces: pleural, pericardial, meninges Fibrinous pericarditis : exaggerated immune response after MI (Dressler's syndrome), cardiac surgery, uremia, autoimmune disease (SLE) Serous Exudation of "cell-poor" fluid Pleura/pericardium = effusion · peritoneum = ascites · skin = bulla/blister Ulcer Local defect on a mucosal surface creating a breach in the mucosa Sites: skin, oral mucosa (canker sore), GI tract (stomach/duodenum in peptic ulcer disease, colon in IBD) Abscesses need drainage An abscess is walled off with an avascular necrotic centre, so antibiotics alone struggle to reach it — incision and drainage is the treatment.

Clostridial Species Clostridia are anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli , and each species is best remembered by what its toxin does — from colitis ( C. difficile ) to spastic (tetanus) or flaccid (botulism) paralysis. Spores are metabolically inactive and hard to destroy. C. difficile : TcdA/TcdB (TcdB most potent) + binary toxin CDT (CDTb pore, CDTa ribosylates actin) → pseudomembranous colitis; diagnose by NAAT or ELISA, not culture. Tetanus blocks GABA/glycine release → spasm (trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonos); botulinum blocks ACh release → flaccid paralysis (honey in infants, home canning, prison brew). C. perfringens → gangrene. General features Gram-positive bacilli, anaerobic, spore-forming , ± toxin-producing Spore : a unit of sexual or asexual reproduction, adapted for dispersal and long survival in unfavourable conditions; metabolically inactive; hard to destroy Ix: NAAT ( C. difficile toxin gene), ELISA ( C. difficile common antigen, C. difficile toxin); difficult to culture Species Disease and mechanism C. difficile Diarrhea; pseudomembranous colitis Large clostridial toxins TcdA and TcdB (TcdB most potent) enter epithelial cells → IL-1β and chemokines, neutrophil influx, tight-junction disruption, fluid secretion, cell death Binary toxin: CDTb binds an epithelial receptor, is endocytosed, oligomerises and forms a pore; CDTa is translocated through the pore into the cytoplasm as the endosome acidifies (vacuolar ATPase) and ribosylates actin → cytoskeleton destroyed, loss of cell shape and tight junctions, cell death C. perfringens Gangrene : blood flow to a large area of tissue is cut off → tissue breaks down and dies (greenish-black) C. tetani Tetanus : trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus (sardonic grin), opisthotonos (backward arching) Inhibits release of GABA/glycine → uncontrolled neurotransmitter release → muscle contraction/spasm C. botulinum Infant botulism (flaccid paralysis): gut colonisation; honey contaminated by spores; dust/soil with spores Foodborne : self-canned products, prison brew (pruno, hooch, moonshine, bootleg) Wound and iatrogenic botulism Inhibits acetylcholine release → no muscle contraction C. septicum Gangrene, sepsis, soft tissue infections C. sordellii TSS, gynecological infections, soft tissue infections Two neurotoxins, opposite paralysis Tetanus Botulism Blocks release of GABA/glycine (inhibitory) Acetylcholine Result Spastic: spasms, trismus, opisthotonos Flaccid paralysis

Viruses, Fungi, Parasites and Prions A survey of the non-bacterial agents. For viruses the organising idea is that the genome defines the virus — the Baltimore system classifies them by nucleic acid type and strand sense, and every virus runs the same seven-step replication cycle. mRNA is always the (+) strand ; its complement is (–). Enveloped viruses bud through the host membrane and carry glycoproteins; naked viruses resist harsh conditions better. Replication: attach → enter → uncoat → translate → replicate genome → assemble → release . Fungal wall = mannoproteins, β-glucans, chitin; membrane = ergosterol . Parasites: cultures generally not an option — use smears, O&P, PCR, antigen. Prions are not microbes — misfolded proteins that template their shape. Viruses → acute and chronic infections Viruses : infectious obligate intracellular parasites — DNA or RNA inside a protein coat and/or membrane Virions : mature particles that can be released from the cell Capsid : protein shell encasing the genome, held by non-covalent interactions; capsid + genome = nucleocapsid Enveloped viruses : outer lipid bilayer acquired by budding through the host cytoplasmic membrane; glycoproteins on the envelope surface Naked viruses : no envelope; often more resistant to harsh conditions Morphology: helical , icosahedral (hollow, symmetrical, quasi-spherical), complex (non-symmetrical) Virion components: polymerases, proteases, integrases, topoisomerases, capping enzymes, proteins, lipids The genome defines the virus It encodes gene products and signals for replication, assembly and packaging, timing of the replication cycle, modulation of host defences, and spread to other cells and hosts mRNA is always the (+) strand ; Fever Fever is a raised hypothalamic set point driven by pyrogens and cytokines through PGE2 — which is exactly what separates it from hyperthermia , where the set point is normal and the body simply cannot shed heat. Fever: ≥ 37.2°C at 6 AM or ≥ 37.8°C any time (oral/tympanic). Exogenous pyrogen = LPS lipid A; endogenous pyrogens = IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ → PGE2 → set point ↑ ; cryogens limit it. FUO = ≥ 101°F on several occasions with a negative initial workup. Fever rarely exceeds 41°C and responds to antipyretics; hyperthermia can exceed 41°C and does not. Alarm features: very high fever, rash, altered mental status, dizziness, recent chemotherapy, dyspnea/chest pain. Definition Fever : elevated core temperature that is often, but not necessarily, part of host defence against microorganisms or inanimate matter recognised as pathogenic or foreign Early morning (6 AM) oral/tympanic temperature ≥ 37.2°C (99.0°F) , or any oral/tympanic temperature ≥ 37.8°C (100°F) Benefits: inhibits growth of many microorganisms, ↑ antibody production, stimulates innate and adaptive responses Common symptoms: rise in temperature (then sweating and falling temperature), chills, rigors; variable: headache, malaise, anorexia Fever of unknown origin : ≥ 101°F documented on several separate occasions, with an appropriate initial workup failing to find the cause Physiologic basis of fever Mediator Examples and actions Exogenous pyrogens Bacterial endotoxin — LPS of Gram-negative bacteria; its lipid A induces fever Endogenous pyrogens IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ → PGE2 raises the thermostatic set point → hypothalamus → heat-seeking behaviour and release of noradrenaline, acetylcholine and thyroid hormones Triggers: infection, inflammatory disease (gout, cancer, vasculitis), tissue injury (ischemia, trauma), cell death (necrosis) Cryogens Anti-inflammatory cytokines, hormones, neuroendocrine products — lower temperature, protecting against unchecked fever Classifying fever Axis Categories Onset Acute (< 7 days) : viral infection, SSTI, UTI, pneumonia Subacute (1–2 weeks) : intra-abdominal abscess Chronic/persistent (> 2 weeks) : TB, HIV, cancer, connective tissue disease (SLE) Height Low > 37°C · moderate 38–39°C · high grade > 39°C Pattern Continuous, intermittent, remittent Alarm symptoms (URGENT) Alarm symptom Consider Benign causes High fever (> 105.8°F) CNS infection, NMS, heat stroke — Rash Meningitis, bacteremia with septic shock, rickettsial disease, bacterial endocarditis Viral exanthem, drug fever Change in mental status / sensorium Meningitis, encephalitis, NMS, heat stroke, bacterial infection with septic shock — Dizziness / light-headedness Bacterial infection with septic shock, adrenal insufficiency, PE Viral infection with labyrinthitis Recent chemotherapy Nosocomial infection with neutropenia — Shortness of breath and chest pain PE, pneumonia, empyema — Fever vs hyperthermia Fever Hyperthermia Mechanism Acute phase reactants; activation of many physiologic, endocrine and immune systems Dysregulated thermoregulation, insufficient heat dissipation; lacks normal diurnal fluctuation Set point Reset upward Unchanged (normal) Temperature Rarely > 41°C Can exceed 41°C Periphery Intact heat generation and loss Excess heat production, diminished heat loss Antipyretics Respond No response Causes Infection, inflammation, trauma Drugs, exercise, heat exposure

Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Antibiotics are organised by the bacterial process they hit — cell wall, nucleic acid, protein or folate synthesis — and choosing one wisely means naming the syndrome, the target bugs, the narrowest empiric drug, then narrowing again when cultures return. The lecture closes on resistance, penicillin allergy, and the three big respiratory viruses. β-lactams bind PBPs (bactericidal) and are the safest antibiotics in pregnancy ; carbapenems are the broadest and should be reserved. Vancomycin covers MRSA but is nephrotoxic; aminoglycosides (30S) are nephro- and ototoxic; fluoroquinolones carry tendon, aortic and CNS warnings — avoid when alternatives exist. > 90% of reported penicillin allergies are not true allergy ; skin testing has > 95% NPV, and never challenge severe type II–IV reactions . MRSA = mecA/PBP2a ; VRE = D-Ala-D-Lac . Drift → epidemic; shift (reassortment) → pandemic , and only influenza A shifts. Cell wall synthesis — β-lactams : most commonly prescribed class; relatively safe therapeutic index — safest antibiotics in pregnancy ; low levels in eye and CSF/brain (cross the BBB when meninges are inflamed); therapeutic levels in lung, liver, kidney, urine, prostate, bone. Bind penicillin-binding proteins (which cross-link peptidoglycan) → bactericidal . Resistance rising with overuse: β-lactamases hydrolyse the β-lactam ring before it reaches the target; PBP modification .
