Warnings: CNS (anxiety, delirium, dizziness), C. difficile , hypo/hyperglycemia, myasthenia gravis crisis, peripheral neuropathy, tendon injury (tendinitis, rupture) , aortic aneurysm rupture . Avoid if other suitable options exist. Staphylococcus , Streptococcus Avoid if other options exist (penicillins) Part of combination therapy for some infections — necrotizing fasciitis (source: "parasitic infections") Tetracyclines Tetracycline , doxycycline , minocycline Four-ring structure; bind 30S , block incoming charged tRNA → bacteriostatic Oral only Broad, including cell-wall-deficient organisms and parasites ( Plasmodium ) Rising resistance Sulfonamides (folate) e.g. TMP-SMX Folate synthesis inhibition; bactericidal in combination H. influenzae , S. pneumoniae , Neisseria , S. aureus (some MRSA), Pneumocystis jirovecii Rising resistance Choosing antibiotics wisely — four questions What infection/clinical syndrome am I treating? Introduction to Infection Prevention and Control Infection spreads along a six-link chain — agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host — and every IPAC measure works by breaking the weakest link . Additional precautions are chosen by the mode of transmission . Hand hygiene is the single most important infection-control measure — ABHR unless hands are visibly soiled (then soap and water). Droplets ≥ 5 μm travel < 2 m → mask + eye protection; airborne particles < 5 μm → fit-tested N95 + negative-pressure room (TB, measles, varicella, VHF). Doffing order: gloves, gown, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene. LHSC: alert level 1 = pre-outbreak , level 2 = outbreak (threshold met, health unit notified, admissions stopped). Vaccine Adverse Events and Reporting An AEFI is any unwanted health event within 6 weeks of immunisation, whether or not the vaccine caused it — so the lecture is about classifying causes, knowing the real (usually tiny) frequencies, and the mandatory reporting chain from provider to WHO. AEFI = within 6 weeks ; cause may be the vaccine component, a defect, the process (error or anxiety), or coincidence. Notable rates: rotavirus → intussusception 1–2/10⁵ ; MMR → febrile seizures 3–9/10⁴ ; whole-cell pertussis → prolonged crying/seizures < 1/10² . Reporting is mandated for immunisers under Section 38 of the Health Protection and Promotion Act. VISP compensates serious, permanent injury from vaccines given on or after Dec 8, 2020. Vaccine Development, COVID-19 Vaccines and Hesitancy How a vaccine gets from the lab to the arm in Canada, how the COVID-19 platforms differ, and how to counsel a hesitant patient — where the organising idea is that a provider's sound advice is one of the strongest influences on the decision . Conventional development takes 8–15 years : exploratory → preclinical → phase I (10s, safety/dose) → II (100s, efficacy/dose) → III (10,000s, disease prevention) → Health Canada review → approval → distribution → monitoring. Adenoviral vectors : fridge-stable; rare TTS clots , capillary leak, GBS. mRNA : lipid nanoparticles, cold chain; rare myocarditis (young males, within 2 weeks of dose 2, mostly self-resolving). No safety signal in pregnancy; keep breastfeeding . Do not dismiss vaccine refusers ; use presumptive and motivational interviewing. Vaccine development and approval in Canada — conventional development takes 8–15 years. Antivirals for Herpesviruses and Influenza Two drug families: herpesvirus antivirals block viral DNA polymerase (guanosine analogues, or foscarnet as a pyrophosphate analogue), and influenza antivirals mostly block neuraminidase , trapping new virus on the infected cell. Acyclovir/valacyclovir → HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV; ganciclovir/valganciclovir → CMV ; foscarnet → drug-resistant viruses and CMV . The oral prodrugs (valacyclovir, valganciclovir) raise bioavailability to 55% (acyclovir 10–20%). All are renally cleared → renal dose adjustment ; watch renal dysfunction and cytopenias (foscarnet: electrolytes). Neuraminidase inhibitors shorten symptoms by only ~1 day in healthy people; zanamivir is inhaled and needs no renal adjustment ; baloxavir targets RNA replication. Introduction to Sepsis Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection — inflammation that is no longer local. Management rests on four principles, and the one that saves the most lives is early, appropriate antibiotics . Mortality 30–40% ; organ failure comes from microcirculatory dysfunction → MODS. Septic shock = hypotension that does not respond to fluids (arteriolar vasodilation + capillary leak) → add vasopressors. Every hour of antibiotic delay after hypotension ≈ 8% ↑ mortality — draw cultures first only if they will not delay antibiotics . Then find and control the source (drain, operate, remove the device); life support buys time but fixes nothing. Many targeted therapies (anti-TNF, activated protein C, anti-endotoxin, vitamin C…) have failed. What sepsis is Sepsis : life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — bacteria, viruses or fungi Common, deadly and an emergency — mortality 30–40% Loss of balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators → cellular injury → multiple organ dysfunction (MODS) ; inflammation is no longer localised but systemic Any organ can fail because of microcirculatory dysfunction in arteriolar–capillary networks: Cardiovascular: ↓ BP, ↑ HR, myocardial dysfunction Respiratory: hypoxia, ARDS Brain; coagulation (thrombocytopenia, DIC); liver; kidneys; muscles; nerves Septic shock : low BP that does not respond to fluids Arterioles vasodilate and intravascular fluid leaks into the interstitium Add vasoconstrictors to raise BP and avoid "salt-water drowning"/edema Recognise it clinically — hypothermia or fever, tachycardia, ↑ RR, warm/flushed, ↓ BP — and look for the cause Therapies studied that do NOT work Activated protein C / heparin / antithrombin III; tissue factor pathway inhibitor; nitric oxide synthesis blockade Anti-TNF antibodies / TNF receptor blockers; interleukin receptor antibodies; platelet activating factor (GCSF) Anti-endotoxin/LPS inhibition; vitamin C and other antioxidants; immunonutrition; hemofiltration Basic principles of sepsis management Step What to do 1. Early recognition Wherever you work, if you see sick patients you need a plan to NOT miss sepsis Physiology : tachypnea/hypoxia (lung), tachycardia/hypotension, oliguria (kidney) Symptoms : rapid decline in performance status, family is concerned, major change in cognition/confusion, looks/feels very unwell High-risk groups : recent surgery, recent chemotherapy, immunosuppressed, elderly 2. Early treatment Nothing saves lives in sepsis like early, appropriate antibiotics — get the drug into the blood ASAP From onset of hypotension minutes count: ~8% ↑ mortality per hour of delay Broad spectrum , often multidrug Draw cultures before antibiotics only if this WILL NOT DELAY antibiotics 3. Source control Find the source promptly — exam (wound, rash), imaging (CT, ultrasound) Control it promptly — surgery, drainage, removal of infected foreign body 4. Life support Invasive support for failing organs buys time for therapy to work — it does not fix the problem Cardiovascular: vasopressors, inotropes Pulmonary: mechanical ventilation, prone positioning, lung-protective ventilation, ECMO Renal: dialysis, CRRT Neurologic: sedation, delirium medication Do not let cultures delay antibiotics Once hypotension starts, each hour without appropriate antibiotics adds ~8% mortality . Cultures matter, but only if drawing them does not hold up the first dose.

Choosing an Antimicrobial Agent Choosing an antimicrobial means matching the likely organism and its likely susceptibility to host and drug factors — and deciding when to start, which depends on how sick the patient is. Septic shock, acute bacterial meningitis, febrile neutropenia → start immediately , with or right after specimen collection. Stable subacute infections (osteomyelitis, diskitis, subacute endocarditis) → collect samples first . Mild infections in healthy patients → no antibiotics unless the diagnosis is sure and bacterial. Indirect harms matter: disrupted bowel flora and selection of resistant pathogens . Oral options: fluoroquinolones, macrolides, clindamycin, doxycycline, TMP-SMX. What you need to know The identity (or likely identity) of the organism, from clinical information Its susceptibility (or likely susceptibility), as accurately as possible Host factors Drug allergies, site of infection, pregnancy, regional susceptibility data, renal/hepatic function (eGFR), recent antibiotic exposure, community vs hospital acquisition, drug–drug interactions, comorbidities, immunocompromise, older age Drug factors Safety record, success record, microbial etiology, bactericidal vs bacteriostatic, penetration into the site, adverse effects Direct adverse effects : neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity, DDIs, allergic reactions Indirect adverse effects : effects on normal bowel flora; ↑ risk of infection with drug-resistant pathogens Timing of initiation Situation Approach Examples Urgent Start antimicrobials immediately after or concurrently with collecting diagnostic specimens Septic shock, acute bacterial meningitis, febrile neutropenia Subacute infection, clinically stable Avoid starting antibiotics before appropriate samples are collected Osteomyelitis, diskitis, subacute endocarditis Mild infection, otherwise healthy Refrain from antibiotics unless sure of the diagnosis and the likely etiology is bacterial — Mechanisms by target: cell wall (β-lactams, vancomycin), membrane (polymyxins), folate (sulfonamides, trimethoprim), DNA gyrase (quinolones), RNA polymerase (rifampin), 50S and 30S ribosomal subunits. Oral options Fluoroquinolones, macrolides, clindamycin, doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) Organisms placed by Gram-positive vs Gram-negative and aerobe vs anaerobe; resistance increases toward the outer edges (MRSA on the left, Pseudomonas on the right). Antibiotic spectrum on the same map: penicillin narrowest, carbapenems broadest; vancomycin for MRSA; Flagyl for anaerobes; aminoglycosides for Gram-negatives.

Outbreak Management and Healthcare-Associated Infections Outbreak management follows ten ordered steps , from verifying that there is an outbreak to debriefing the team — and because outbreaks are sociological as much as medical , the fix must reach root causes. Reportable diseases are legislated: they feed surveillance, trigger the medical officer of health's authority, and meet Canada's International Health Regulations obligations. Case definition + line list (updated daily) + epidemic curve . Common source (point, continuous, intermittent) vs propagated (more than one incubation period). Isolation separates the sick; quarantine restricts the exposed. HAIs: 1 in 31 inpatients on any day; 35–55% preventable (most for CLABSI and CAUTI); 8,000 Canadian deaths/year . Principle Outbreaks are sociological as much as medical phenomena — solutions must address root causes Steps in outbreak management Step Actions 1. Verify the outbreak Reportable diseases : diseases/syndromes that legislation requires specified people to report to public health; obligations fall on clinicians, labs, institutions, public health and governments Critical for surveillance — gives risk-factor information Empowers public health action — individual-level information for interventions (contact tracing); triggers the legislative authority of medical officers of health Fulfils Canada's obligations under the International Health Regulations Shifting risk groups: MSM, illicit drug use, homeless/under-housed, incarceration 2. Confirm the diagnosis Laboratory results 3. Assemble the team Interdisciplinary — physicians, nurses, inspectors, epidemiologists, communications, administrative support 4. Define and find cases Case definition : clinical signs/symptoms plus laboratory confirmation criteria; varies by jurisdiction Line list : tracks cases; facilities and public health update it daily; shows outbreak status (under control, ready to declare over) 5. Orient the data By person, place (maps) and time (epidemic curves) Epidemic curve : cases plotted over time — shows changes in prevalence and incidence, supports analysis of transmission 6. Generate hypotheses Who is exposed, what is the source? Patterns: common source (point, continuous, intermittent) vs propagated (more than one incubation period) 7. Test hypotheses — 8. Prevention and control Know the mode of transmission Isolation : separates sick, contagious people from the well Quarantine : separates and restricts movement of exposed people to see if they become sick Enhanced precautions — gown, gloves, mask/eye protection Environmental cleaning and decontamination PEP for contacts and at-risk people — vaccination, IVIg Vector control — needle disposal, mosquito control 9. Communicate the findings — 10. Debrief the team — Healthcare-associated infections (HAI) On any given day, 1 in 31 hospital patients has at least one HAI 35–55% are preventable — highest for central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI) and catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) ; lower for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and surgical site infection (SSI) Each year 8,000 Canadians die from hospital-acquired infections; 220,000 more are infected Treatment costs more than prevention ( $129 million/year ) — prolonged stays, special control measures, costlier drugs, extensive surveillance (MRSA)

Approach to Fever in the Immunocompromised Host Different conditions impair different arms of the immune system , and immune deficiency is dynamic — it is all about timing . The differential is the usual one + opportunistic infections + context , remembering that the presentation (even the fever) may be blunted. Diabetes : ↓ C4, ↓ cytokine response, chemotaxis, killing and phagocytosis. Uremia : defective APC co-stimulation (poor hepatitis B vaccine response). HIV CD4 < 50 → MAC, CMV retinitis, lymphoma; > 500 → infections like the general population, plus TB. Allogeneic HSCT: neutropenia pre-engraftment → NK recovery → CD4 recovery late . Cytokine blockers can mask fever. Vaccinate — before immunosuppression where possible, and avoid live vaccines . Which condition, which defect Diabetes mellitus : low C4; ↓ cytokine response after stimulation, ↓ chemotaxis, killing and phagocytosis Renal failure : uremia → defective co-stimulatory function of antigen-presenting cells (thought to explain poor vaccine response, e.g. hepatitis B); ↓ lymphocyte numbers in dialysis patients HIV : CD4 < 50 → M. avium , CMV retinitis, lymphomas; CD4 > 500 → infections similar to uninfected people, TB High risk of invasive mould infection : chronic granulomatous disease, allogeneic HSCT, lung/heart transplant, AML/MDS Immune deficiency is very dynamic — it is all about timing Allogeneic stem cell transplant Patient receives healthy donor stem cells to replace their own, which have been conditioned (radiation or high-dose chemotherapy) Phases: pre-engraftment (neutropenia) → post-engraftment (NK cells recover) → late phase (CD4 T cells recover) After graft infusion, neutrophils, monocytes and NK cells recover within weeks; B and CD8 T cells over months; CD4 T cells take years. Approach Fever may be absent on cytokine-blocking drugs: anakinra, rilonacept, tocilizumab, infliximab, golimumab, adalimumab Build the differential around immune status: same differential + opportunistic infections + context Presentation commonly differs between immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients Prevention Vaccination is imperative in immunocompromised patients; live virus vaccines are generally unsafe Give vaccines before immunosuppressive medications when possible Give antimicrobial prophylaxis to HIV patients and transplant recipients for infections with no vaccine Live vaccines Live virus vaccines are generally unsafe in immunocompromised patients — vaccinate before immunosuppression starts where possible.

Opportunistic Infections Opportunistic infections occur more often and more severely when immunity is compromised. Five organisms anchor the lecture, and each is tied to a specific immune threshold or risk group . TB : airborne; 3 sputa (≥ 1 early morning); RIPE (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). MAC : water sources, not person-to-person; disseminated at CD4 < 50 ; azithromycin + rifampin + ethambutol. CMV : 40–50% infected; reactivates at CD4 < 100 and in transplant; ganciclovir/valganciclovir, letermovir prophylaxis. Cryptococcus : meningitis; amphotericin B + flucytosine → fluconazole . PJP : CD4 < 200 or long-term steroids; ↑ LDH, ground glass; TMP-SMX ± steroids if severe. Antifungals Fungi are eukaryotes, so selective drugs must hit what humans lack: the cell wall (echinocandins) or the ergosterol-based membrane (azoles block ergosterol synthesis; polyenes bind the membrane directly). Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (a CYP450) → no ergosterol; they also inhibit human CYP450s → drug interactions , plus QT prolongation and hepatotoxicity . Fluconazole is limited for non- albicans Candida. Echinocandins (caspofungin) block 1,3-β-D-glucan synthesis; reliable for Candida , few DDIs, IV only, poor eye/CNS/urine penetration . Amphotericin B is broad spectrum but nephrotoxic with infusion reactions. Approach to Immunodeficiency, Hypersensitivity and Allergy The pattern of infection points to the broken arm of immunity : phagocyte defects → catalase-positive bacteria and fungi; complement → Neisseria ; T cells → opportunists in the first 6 months; antibodies → encapsulated bacteria after maternal IgG wanes. The second half turns the problem around — an immune system that overreacts (Gell and Coombs, anaphylaxis, common allergies). Secondary immunodeficiency is the commonest in practice. CGD = NADPH oxidase defect → catalase+ infections; DHR 123 assay. Terminal complement (MAC) deficiency → recurrent Neisseria . SCID is detected by TRECs on newborn screening and is fatal without BM transplant. Selective IgA = commonest humoral (mostly asymptomatic); CVID = commonest symptomatic (IgG replacement). Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000, max 0.3 mg, repeat q5–15 min — everything else comes after. Introduce allergenic foods early ( 4–6 months ). Approach to Allergy Testing and Autoimmunity Allergy tests only mean something in the light of the clinical history — the best allergy test — because interpretation rests on pre-test probability and likelihood ratios. The lecture then turns to autoimmunity as a breakdown of tolerance , with rheumatoid arthritis as the worked example. History is the best allergy test ; oral challenge is the gold standard . LR+ = Sn/(1–Sp); LR– = (1–Sn)/Sp. Skin prick or intradermal: positive = wheal ≥ 3 mm over the negative (saline) control , with histamine as positive control; intradermal is for drugs and venom. Cross-reactivity needs ~70% homology . Tolerance is central (deletion in BM/thymus) and peripheral (ignorance, anergy, deletion, Treg suppression). RA : HLA-DRB1 shared epitope binds citrullinated self-proteins → ACPA ; smoking and periodontal disease ( P. gingivalis ) are risk factors. Principles of allergy testing Testing helps diagnose type I hypersensitivity The best allergy testing tool is the clinical history Sensitivity and specificity differ by allergen and test type Interpret using pre-/post-test probability and likelihood ratios, in the context of the history Pre-test probability : clinical impression of the chance of a diagnosis — clinical experience, epidemiology, comorbidities, risk factors, exam findings Likelihood ratio (LR) : how much more likely a result is in someone with the disorder than in someone without it LR+ = Sn / (1 – Sp) : odds of a positive test in someone with the condition vs someone without LR– = (1 – Sn) / Sp : odds of a negative test in someone with the condition vs someone without Calculate from Sn and Sp, or use a nomogram Cross-reactivity : occurs with ~70% homology between antigens (tertiary structure conserved) — e.g. birch pollen-food syndrome → oral pruritus with almond Test reagents Food allergen proteins for skin prick and serum IgE tests are commercially prepared Purified food protein : should contain all relevant allergens; amount of each varies batch to batch Recombinant extract : known allergens made in bacterial vectors; contains major known allergens but not lesser-known ones (false negatives); can spike purified extracts with clinically important low-concentration allergens Environmental allergens: dust mites (feces), cat/dog (dander), seasonal (pollen), mould (spores) Skin prick test Intradermal test Use Foods, environmental allergens, immediate drug allergy (penicillin) Drugs, venom (patients who have had anaphylaxis) Sensitivity 57–97% 60–95% Specificity 70–94% 32–89% Method Several allergens introduced into the skin; positive control: histamine ; negative control: saline Antigen injected just below the epidermis to raise a bleb Positive test Wheal ≥ 3 mm larger than the negative control Wheal ≥ 3 mm larger than the negative control Common errors Tests < 2 cm apart → overlapping reactions Bleeding → false positive Insufficient penetration → false negative Solutions spreading during the test or when wiped Commercial food extracts → more false negatives than fresh food Sites too close → false positive Volume too large (> 0.1 mL) High allergen concentration → false positive Splash reaction from injected air Subcutaneous injection → false negative Intracutaneous bleeding → false positive Too many tests at once → systemic reactions Prick tests (standardised needle or modified prick) break only the epidermis; the intradermal test injects antigen into the dermis. Prick tests are simpler, faster, safer, more specific and usable in infants; intradermal tests are more sensitive and reproducible but give more false positives. RAST (radioallergosorbent test) Blood radioimmunoassay detecting allergen-specific IgE Extract proteins from the allergen Fix the extract to a solid-phase surface and send to the lab Add the patient's serum; wash it away, leaving bound IgE Add a marker and measure how much IgE is bound Component-based IgE testing : pinpoints the specific proteins causing symptoms — a newer test to better predict food reactions and cross-reactivity and identify major food and aeroallergens Oral challenge — the gold standard Foods : 5–7 steps, dose increased every 15–30 min, aiming for a full age-appropriate serving (dry foods 8–10 g, wet foods 100 mL) Drugs : single step (full dose, observe) or two-step/graded (10%, wait, then remaining 90%) High-risk patients : start with very low doses unlikely to cause a reaction; optimise comorbidities; avoid in pregnancy; β-blockers can interfere with treatment of a reaction ; do it in hospital and consider an IV beforehand Who does what Provider Role Pharmacist Often first contact for possible mild reactions (severe ones go to the ER) Advises on choosing an antihistamine; recommends follow-up, allergen avoidance and seeing the family physician Does NOT diagnose — gives treatment and advice Family physician Presumptive diagnosis, recommendations and treatment plan, weighing many factors Refers to an allergist Allergist Considers the same factors; confirms the allergy, counsels/educates, builds the treatment and management plan Immune tolerance Immune tolerance : antigen-specific unresponsiveness to self-antigens Central tolerance : immature self-reactive lymphocytes are negatively selected/deleted in the BM and thymus; Chronic Inflammation, Granulomas, Herpesviruses and Fungi Chronic inflammation is inflammation that persists for weeks to months alongside attempts at repair , driven by macrophages and lymphocytes; its signature structure is the granuloma , the body's attempt to wall off what it cannot clear. The lecture then catalogues two persistent pathogen groups — latent herpesviruses and medically important fungi . Causes of chronic inflammation: persistent infection (TB), hypersensitivity (RA, asthma, IBD), chronic toxin exposure (silicosis, atherosclerosis) . Granuloma = epithelioid macrophages ringed by T cells , ± Langhans giant cells and caseation. Rule out TB before immunosuppression. Herpesviruses are dsDNA and latent , reactivating with stress, fever, UV, immunosuppression: HSV-1/2 and VZV in ganglia, CMV in WBCs (commonest congenital infection in Canada), EBV in B cells (malignancy). Mucor/Rhizopus thrive in hyperglycemic, acidotic states ; invasive Aspergillus → voriconazole . Chronic inflammation Inflammation present for weeks or months , usually with attempts at tissue repair Causes: persistent infection/injury (TB), hypersensitivity (RA, asthma, IBD), chronic toxin exposure (silicosis, atherosclerosis) Cells of chronic inflammation Cell Role and appearance Macrophages Dominant cell in many chronic inflammatory reactions Eosinophils Allergic reactions and parasitic infections Granules contain major basic protein — toxic to parasites and host epithelium; can cause tissue damage in allergy Bright red (eosinophilic) granules, bilobed nuclei Lymphocytes (B, T, NK) Major players in adaptive immunity, activated by microbes and environmental antigens Release cytokines that amplify and sustain inflammation Appear as just a purple nucleus (minimal cytoplasm) Plasma cells (differentiated B cells) Make antibodies Eccentric nuclei with a "clock face" chromatin pattern Granulomas Granuloma : aggregate of macrophages surrounded by T lymphocytes , formed in chronic inflammation Activated macrophages accumulate cytoplasm and resemble epithelium — epithelioid histiocytes ; nuclei sometimes look like footprints in the sand Macrophages may fuse into multinucleate giant cells (Langhans cells) Often an attempt to contain something hard to eradicate — talc in IV drug use, sutures White nodule with a chalky/cheesy centre — necrotising/caseating from hypoxia and free-radical injury Common sites: lungs, lymph nodes, GI tract Causes: mycobacterial (TB), fungal (histoplasmosis), bacterial (cat scratch disease); sarcoidosis, vasculitis, Crohn's disease, foreign body reaction, malignancy Screen for TB before immunosuppression Make sure the patient does not have TB before starting immunosuppressive treatment for a non-infectious condition — the granulomas containing it depend on an intact immune response. Which of the following cytokines is alone sufficient to promote all the properties of toxic shock? TNF IL-10 IL-8 TGF-β The correct answer is A. Which of the following interactions are responsible for the “rolling” stage of neutrophil at the site of inflammation – where the neutrophil slows down in circulation through a low affinity interaction with the endothelium? PSGL-1 binding to P-Selectin on the endothelium IL-8 binding to CXCR1 on the neutrophil ICAM ligand binding to LFA1 integrin on the neutrophil All of the above The correct answer is A. IL-8/CXCR1 interaction is responsible for leading the neutrophils to the inflammation. ICAM/LFA1 interaction is a high affinity interaction which is consequently proceeded by neutrophils exiting circulation and entering the interstitial fluid.

A and B A and C The correct answer is A. Natural killer cells would target cells indiscriminately, but non-pathogenic cells have inhibitory membrane-bound proteins that protect them from NK cells. NK cells do not phagocytose particles, but secrete enzymes to destroy target cells.

Which is NOT a mechanism by which macrophages kill a cellular target after phagocytosis? Acidification of the phagosome An efflux of copper and zinc (oxidizing metals) from the target cell Mobilizing killing enzymes from the Golgi-apparatus Removing iron and manganese from the target cell The correct answer is B. B. Copper and zinc have a large oxidative potential and one mechanism by which target cells are digested is by influxing copper and zinc. Iron and manganese are critical metals in enzymes and proteins and effluxing them helps to kill the target cell.

B-cells can bind directly to an antigen it recognizes without presentation on MHC, unlike T- cells.

An epithelial cell lining the gut epithelium is infected with a viral agent. An activated T cell is able to recognize that particular viral antigen and mount a response. Which option below is a correct difference between T-cells and B-cells? B-cells recognize intact antigens; T-cells recognize epitopes presented by HLA. Which statement below is a correct description of how antibodies can assist the immune response? Macrophages recognize the variable regions of the antibody and subsequently phagocytose the infectious particle/cell. T-cells present antigens to antibodies on bacterial cells and signal to macrophages to engulf the target cell. Antibodies can coat the target pathogen and physically block the interaction of the pathogenic target with host cells. A and C. All of the above. The correct answer is C. This is an example of neutralization of hosts by antibodies. Note that macrophages recognize the constant region of antibodies, not the variable region, and note that MHC cells present antigens that antibodies on T-cells recognize.

A patient with a suspected systemic bacterial infection undergoes blood cultures to help in determining the identity of the pathogenic bacteria. The bacteria stained pink after a Gramstain. Based on this limited information, what is true about the bacteria? The bacteria has a single cell membrane and a thick peptidoglycan layer. The bacteria has membrane-bound lipoteichoic acid that is recognized by TLR2. The bacteria has membrane-bound lipopolysaccharide that is recognized by TLR4. The bacteria has mycolic acid in its membrane. The bacteria is resistant to penicillin and forms a reticulocyte body inside host cells. The correct answer is C. The pink Gram-stain indicates a Gram-negative organism. Gram-negative organisms have a double membrane with a thin peptidoglycan layer containing lipopolysaccharides. LPS is recognized by TLR4. Which of the following viruses require reverse transcriptase for survival? Single-stranded RNA(-) virus Single-stranded RNA(+) virus Single-stranded RNA retro-virus Single-stranded DNA(+) virus The correct answer is C. Retroviruses rely on reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA, which is then integrated into the host genome.

A new viral therapy involves antibodies that neutralize viral envelope glycoproteins. Which stage of the virus replication cycle does this predominantly affect? Assembly Attachment Uncoating Genome Replication The correct answer is B. Attachment is the first stage where the viral envelope binds to receptors on the cell surface promoting entry. With this interaction neutralized, virus cannot enter the cell.

Which option below correctly matches a viral classification with an example virus? Hepatitis B is a single-stranded RNA virus. Influenza is a single-stranded DNA(+) virus. SARS-CoV-2 is a double-stranded DNA virus. HIV is a single-stranded RNA retrovirus. Herpes simplex virus is a single-stranded RNA(-) virus. The correct answer is D. Hepatitis B is a partially double stranded DNA virus that uses reverse transcription in its replication cycle. Influenza is a single-stranded RNA(-) virus. SARS-CoV-2 is a singlestranded RNA(+) virus. Herpes simplex virus is a double-stranded DNA virus.

Which class does the following Aspergillus fungi belong to? Yeasts Moulds Thermally dimorphic Gram-positive The correct answer is B. Moulds are characterized as multicellular and have Hyphae – a branching structure.

Which of the following categories best characterize the parasite that causes Malaria? Protozoa Helminths Ectoparasites None of the above The correct answer is A. Plasmodium is the parasite that causes Malaria, and it is a protozoa (unicellular). Helminths are multicellular and worm-like parasites. Ectoparasites live on the surface of your skin (lice, scabies).

Which option below INCORRECTLY describes a feature of a non-bacterial pathogen? Protozoa are unicellular organisms. Fungal moulds have hyphae. Ectoparasites like scabies and lice live on the skin. Which of the following sites would the presence of microbes be most concerning? On the surface of our skin In our blood Within our colon Inside the vagina and cervix The correct answer is B. The presence of bacteria in healthy equilibrium in the vagina/cervix, skin, and colon is expected and plays a role in our health, however microbes should not be found in our blood. The blood is a sterile site.

Which example below correctly describes a commensal bacteria species in humans? Lactobacillus in the vagina Staphylococcus in the lungs E. coli in the urinary tract Pseudomonas in the guy E. coli in the lungs The correct answer is A. Lactobacillus is commonly found in the vagina and does not cause disease. The other bacteria and location combinations would either be considered a colonization or infection based on the disease status.

In which of the following categories does Staphylococcus aureus differ from Streptococcus pyogenes? Choose as many as applicable. Gram stain (positive, negative) Catalase status (positive, negative) Cell shape (cocci, bacilli, spirochetes) Cell arrangement (clusters, lines, tetrad) The correct answer is B, D. Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive bacteria, cocci shaped (exist in clumps), catalase positive and coagulase positive. Streptococcus pyogenes is a Gram-positive bacteria, cocci shaped (exist in lines) and catalase negative.

Betty White has developed a bladder infection from E. coli. What physical component of coli made Betty susceptible to a bladder infection? FimH adhesion on the fimbrial tip of the E. coli PapG Adhesion on the fimbrial tip of the E. coli M protein on the E. coli The rod-shaped cell of E. coli The correct answer is A. The type of E. coli infection is dictated by the specificity of the fimbrial tip adhesion. FimH suggests a bladder infection, and PapG suggests a kidney infection. M-protein is on the surface of Streptococcus pyogenes .

Which of the following best encapsulates the pathophysiology of C. difficile binary toxin? This toxin leads to sepsis from overstimulation of the immune system This toxin interferes with muscle contract by inhibiting acetylcholine release This toxin glycosylates ribosomal RNA leading to the inhibition of protein synthesis and cell death The toxin is endocytosed into epithelial cells which eventually leads to the destruction of the cytoskeleton and loss of cell shape The correct answer is D. The toxin is an actin-specific ribosyl transferase that causes depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton and loss of cell shape. Option B is characteristic of Botulinum Toxin. Option C is characteristic of the Shiga toxin.

Which option below correctly describes a likely patient presentation associated with a Clostridium infection? Clostridium tetanus produces a gangrenous infection. Clostridium botulinum produces spastic paralysis. Clostridium difficile produces pseudomembranous colitis Clostridium septicum produces severe diarrhea Clostridium perfringens produces flaccid muscle paralysis. The correct answer is C. Clostridium difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis which can progress to toxic megacolon if not treated properly. Clostridium tetani results in spastic paralysis, Clostridium botulinum results in flaccid paralysis, Clostridium septicum results in sepsis, and Clostridium p

Which option incorrectly describes a mechanism by which S. aureus evades the immune response? Protein A binds to the variable regions of antibodies preventing phagocytosis. Protein A binds fibronectin, which reduces the ability of C3b to bind to the membrane. S. aureus secretes CHIPS, which blocks macrophage C5a receptors. S. aureus secretes α-hemolysin, which lyses neutrophils. S. aureus releases TSST1 which dysregulates T-cell response and leads to septic shock. The correct answer is A. Protein A binds to the constant region of antibodies, preventing recognition of antibodies by macrophages, thereby preventing phagocytosis.

Which of the following factors does Streptococcus pyogenes use to bind fibrinogen? Coagulase Clumping factors M-protein Collagen The correct answer is C. M-protein is present on the surface of S. pyogenes and produces a fuzzy appearance and along with binding to fibrinogen it also binds complement regulatory proteins

Which statement regarding of S. pyogenes is false? Repeated S. pyogenes infections can lead to an auto-immunity to tropomyosin. S. pyogenes infections that are M-protein positive are reportable diseases. Toxic shock syndrome caused by S. pyogenes is the result of a cytokine storm resulting from the presence of SpeA and SpeC. Wildtype S. pyogenes have a fuzzy coat appearance when visualized by electron microscopy. S. pyogenes has a commensal relationship with the armpits and groin area. The correct answer is E. S. pyogenes is commensally found in the mouth and throat, but S. aureus is found in the armpits and groin area. All the other options are true.

Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which a superantigen can lead to septic shock? A superantigen leads to a significant proportion of T-cells becoming activated (since it stabilizes non-specific T cell interactions via the MHC/antigen complex) which leads to a drastic production of inflammatory cytokines. A superantigen binds to numerous innate receptors in a nonspecific manner which lead to a drastic production of inflammatory cytokines. A superantigen binds to a TCR that is specific for that antigen, leading to a mass proliferation of that T cell and consequent production of inflammatory cytokines. A superantigen acts as coagulase and “clumps” the blood leading to a dramatic decrease in Blood pressure. The correct answer is A. Superantigens can bind to and stabilize the MHC-TCR interaction leading to T-cell activation in the absence of MHC-specific antigen presentation. This can cause activation of up to 20% of T cells consequently leading to mass production of inflammatory cytokines.

Which of the following types of Influenza is most likely to cause pandemics and infect a variety of species? Influenza A Influenza B Influenza C Influenza D The correct answer is A. Influenza A is most likely to cause pandemics and mortalities in youngest people as well as infect humans, pigs, horses and birds.

Zanamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor used in influenza treatment. Which of the following does this drug target? The lipid envelope Viral proteins on the lipid envelope The capsid RNA-dependent RNA polymerase The correct answer is B. Neuraminidase is a viral protein expressed on the surface of the lipid envelope of Influenza.

Which of the following scenarios best exemplifies influenza antigenic drift? One subtype infects someone and rapidly evolves into two unique subtypes. Two different subtypes co-infect someone simultaneously and one subtype assimilates into the other Two different subtypes co-infect someone and a new unique subtype is produced consequently One subtype acquires genetic mutations over time to become a different version of that subtype over a long period of time The correct answer is D. Antigenic Drift is the slow accumulation of point mutations over an extended period of time. Antigenic shift typically occurs when two influenza viruses exchange their genetic segments and produce a new subtype altogether. For instance, H1N1 and H3N2 infect a pig, and reasso

Which statement below describes an advantage that a virus has against humans? The SARS-CoV-2 virus has relatively low genetic diversity. The influenza A virus has a segmented genome allowing rapid antigenic shift. Respiratory syncytial virus is resistant to many conditions including humidity and temperature. The SARS-CoV-2 virus overpowers the immune response in the first 5-6 days of infection. The Influenza B virus binds to ACE2 in the lungs making it a highly contagious respiratory infection. The correct answer is B. While option A is true, this is a weakness of SARS-CoV-2. The respiratory syncytial virus is labile to many conditions, including temperature and humidity. Option D is false - patients are asymptomatic for 5-6 days. Option E is also false - the influenza virus binds to siali

A virus with a reproductive number of 2 and an incubation period of 10 days can be interpreted as: Every two cases will lead to one case of this virus, and every 10 days the number of cases will double Every two cases will lead to one case of this virus, and people with this virus must be incubated for 10 days to prevent infection of others Every one case of this virus will produce two more cases, and every 10 days the number of cases will double Every one case of this virus will produce two more cases, and it takes 10 days from exposure to become symptomatic The correct answer is D. The incubation period is the time from point of exposure to when you develop symptoms. The effective reproductive number is in a completely susceptible population how many cases will one case causes.

Which of the following is primarily responsible in raising the thermostatic set point in the fever response? TNF Prostaglandin E2 Noradrenaline Acetylcholine The correct answer is B. Prostaglandin E2 signals to the hypothalamus to increase the set-point temperature of the body.

Which option correctly describes a homeostatic response in regulating temperature? Brown adipose tissue is elevated in newborns and its metabolism generates heat. Blood vessel dilation near the surface of the skin reduces heat loss via the skin. Evaporative warming occurs through water exhaled in the lungs. A and B A, B, and C The correct answer is A. Blood vessel dilation near the skin increases heat loss, and the lungs are a site of evaporative cooling.

Which of the following statements are true regarding Fever and Hyperthermia. Select all that apply. Fever involves raising the thermostatic set point; in Hyperthermia, this is unchanged Fever involves the inability to dissipate heat; in hyperthermia thermoregulation is possible Body temperature is more likely to exceed 41 degrees in hyperthermia compared with fever Fever responds to antipyretics while there is no response in hyperthermia Fever and hyperthermia both commonly originate from infection The correct answer is A, C, D. In hyperthermia, thermoregulation is often not possible where heat can’t be displaced, but in fever these mechanisms are still possible. Fever commonly originates from infection, inflammation and trauma, while hyperthermia commonly originates from drugs, exercise and h

Assuming the absence of infection, which statement below on physiological body temperature is true? Men have a higher body temperature than women. Patients with an elevated body temperature have an elevated heart rate. The highest body temperature in a 24-hour period occurs just after waking up. In the same patient, an axillary temperature will be higher than a rectal temperature. The correct answer is B. Elevated body temperatures result in elevated heart rates. Women tend to have slightly higher body temperatures than men. The highest body temperature occurs around 1-4 in the afternoon. Finally, the rectal temperature is higher than the axillary temperature.

An 87-year-old male patient from your family practice comes into your examination room with his wife, with symptoms of a fever. During the history, his wife claims that he has been uncharacteristically “out of it” since the onset of the fever. During the physical examination, the oral temperature was recorded as 38.6 °C, heart rate was 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 19 breaths per minute, and blood pressure was 90/60. You put in a requisition for white blood cell count and are awaiting results. Does this patient have sepsis? No, according to his qSOFA and SIRS scores. Yes, according to his qSOFA score. Yes, according to his SIRS score. Yes, according to his qSOFA and SIRS scores. There is not enough information to diagnose sepsis without the WBC count. The correct answer is D. Sepsis according to the qSOFA requires two of: respiratory rate >22, blood pressure <100/60, and altered mentation (NEED 2 of 3). The patient has altered mentation and a low blood pressure. Sepsis according to the SIRS criteria requires two of: temperature outside of 36-38,

When a patient has an infection, several lab tests can be ordered. Which description below is accurate? CBC + differential can help elucidate if the infection is viral or bacterial. A urinalysis (urine analysis) can identify bacteria causing sepsis. PCR can help in differentiating bacterial or viral infections. When submitting fungal cultures, one sample collection is enough. Testing for fungal cultures has a rapid turnaround time (1 day). The correct answer is A. A urinalysis can help diagnose bladder infections or UTIs. PCR can be used to confirm a suspected diagnosis, but since it requires known primers, it is not used to determine an unknown pathogen. When submitting cultures, at least two samples are always submitted. Lastly, fun

Taylor comes into your clinic with suspected bacteremia. To confirm your diagnosis, how many blood cultures would you order in this scenario? 1 2 3 4 The correct answer is B. Bacteremia involves bacteria in the blood. 2 sets should always be ordered. Ordering only 1 culture leaves the possibility of contamination, and makes it more challenging to rule out false positives or false negatives.

Which of the following pathologies best describes the inflammatory process of a full thickness mucosal defect in the upper palate of one’s oral cavity? Purulent Fibrinous Serous Ulcer The correct answer is D. Ulcers are breaches/holes in the mucosa, in this scenario there is a breach in the oral mucosa.

Which of the following pathologies best describe the inflammatory process of a clear blister that forms after one slightly burns their finger on the stove? Purulent Fibrinous Serous Ulcer The correct answer is C. Serous inflammation is characterized by “cell poor” fluid occupying spaces such as skin blisters or pleural/pericardial spaces. This is in contrast with purulent inflammation where pus (neutrophils) primarily occupy the space.

What is the optimal treatment for an abscess caused by infection? Broad-spectrum antibiotics Anti-fibrinolytics Fibrinolytics Watch and wait None of the above The correct answer is E. An abscess usually has a poor blood supply and may be walled off, so antibiotics will have difficulty reaching the center of the abscess. The optimal treatment for an abscess is incision and drainage of the cavity. If the abscess is not superficial, a more invasive surgery m

Taylor presents with a fever and rashes on her right wrist. Which of the following investigations should be conducted to determine if medication would be effective against the suspected microbe? Culture Serology Molecular studies The correct answer is A. A culture would give susceptibility results whereas serology and molecular studies would not.

Taylor is planning on doing an OCLO in a rural health clinic, but prior to that the physician wants to determine if Taylor has ever been exposed and can mount a response against an endemic pathogen in the area. Which of the following investigations should be conducted? Culture Serology Molecular studies The correct answer is B. Serology would examine if Taylor developed antibodies against this pathogen. Molecular studies and Culture would only indicate if Taylor is currently infected with the pathogen in the present moment.

Which statement(s) describe a limitation of molecular analysis of microbes via PCR? PCR is only valuable if you know which primers to use PCR is only valuable if there are a lot of lipids in the blood PCR is only valuable if there is a sufficient amount of DNA present A and B A, B, and C The correct answer is A. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is a cycle of denaturing DNA with heat, annealing primers, and extending off of these primers with a thermostable polymerase. PCR works best if you know what to look for -- requiring knowledge of which primers to use. Note that PCR fails if th

Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding immunization? Passive immunization offers relatively short protection for the patient Active Immunization involves the transfer of pre-formed antibodies to the patient Vaccine effectiveness refers to the vaccine’s ability to prevent illness in real world settings Vaccine efficacy refers to the vaccine’s ability to prevent illness in controlled studies The correct answer is B. Active immunization (vaccines) elicit an immune response from the host.

Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine is an mRNA vaccine that transfers synthetic mRNA that encodes for the spike protein on SARS-CoV-2. The human cells translate and produce this spike protein and the adaptive immune system develops a response against this. Which of the following categories does this vaccine best fall under? Live Attenuated Vaccine Non-Live inactivated whole cell vaccine Non-live inactivated bacterial toxin vaccine Non-live subunit vaccine The correct answer is D. The covid vaccine is a subunit vaccine. From 06 - New Vaccine Platforms and 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. A subunit vaccine uses one component of the pathogen as the antigen rather than the whole organism. The Pfizer vaccine makes the immune system respond to a single prote

Which of the following statements correctly elucidates a difference between conjugate vaccines and pure polysaccharide vaccines? Conjugate vaccines are more immunogenic than pure polysaccharide vaccines and are as safe as pure polysaccharide vaccines Conjugate vaccines are more immunogenic than pure polysaccharide vaccines but are slightly more dangerous Pure polysaccharide vaccines contain a sugar (polysaccharide) component, but conjugate vaccines do not Conjugate Vaccines are live attenuated vaccines whereas Pure polysaccharide vaccines are not The correct answer is A. From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines (Block 1). Both are non-live subunit vaccines. A polysaccharide vaccine uses capsular sugar alone and is not immunogenic in children under 2 . A conjugate joins that polysaccharide to a protein, which gives a T-cell-dependent response , so

A patient who engages in intravenous drug use is at high-risk for contracting HIV. A physician is strongly considering giving the patient Truvada (a nucleotide analogue that functions as an anti-HIV drug). Which of the following therapies does this best fall under? Pre-exposure Chemoprophylaxis Pre-exposure Immunoprophylaxis Post-exposure Chemoprophylaxis Post-exposure Immunoprophylaxis The correct answer is A. Giving the drug before potential exposure is pre-exposure chemoprophylaxis.

Which of the following statements regarding herd immunity is the most accurate answer? 90% of the population must be vaccinated to reach herd immunity for any given infectious disease 75% of the susceptible population must be vaccinated to reach herd immunity for any given infectious disease The threshold for herd immunity varies from pathogen to pathogen based on the infectiousness of the disease The threshold for herd immunity varies from pathogen to pathogen based on the mortality associated with the pathogen The correct answer is C. The threshold for herd immunity depends on the pathogen’s infectiousness.

Which of following diseases pre-exposure prophylaxis strategies only consists of a vaccine strategy? i. Measles ii. Varicella iii. Hepatitis A i, ii ii, iii i, iii iii The correct answer is A. Hepatitis A has a Prep IG option. From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines (Block 1). The lecture's PrEP table gives each disease's pre-exposure options. Measles : IG is N/A, so the only pre-exposure option is vaccine , given 2 weeks before. Varicella : IG is N/A, so the only opti

The measles vaccine is an attenuated vaccine. Which of the following is most likely to be true based on this information? The immune response from the measles vaccine will be weaker than the immune response for inactivated vaccines. A booster dose will be required in middle-adulthood. This vaccine contains purified protein components of the measles virus. The vaccine should be avoided in immunocompromised individuals. The correct answer is D. Live vaccines can cause adverse effects in immunocompromised individuals.

In the context of cancer treatment, “adjuvant” refers to a treatment after the primary treatment, to destroy remaining cancer cells. What does “adjuvant” mean in the context of vaccinations? Adjuvants are chemicals added to inactivated or killed pathogens to boost a weaker natural immune response. Adjuvant doses are the doses that are required after an initial dose to guarantee immunity. Adjuvant refers to prophylactic vaccinations after an exposure to a pathogen. Adjuvant refers to the phenomenon that live attenuated vaccines evoke immune responses similar to a natural infection. Adjuvant effects are the adverse side-effects that occur after vaccineadministration. The correct answer is A. Adjuvants are added particles that enhance the immune response to a vaccine.

Which of the following viruses can become latent within the host and reactivate years later causing disease? Hepatitis A Mumps virus Varicella Measles virus The correct answer is C. Varicella can cause Shingles. From 11 - Herpes. Varicella zoster virus is a herpesvirus, and the defining feature of herpesviruses is lifelong latency . After primary chickenpox, VZV persists as a silent episome in the sensory ganglia, with no replication. It reactivates yea

Which of the following vaccines are NOT a part of Ontario’s routine immunization program? BCG Varicella Influenza Pertussis The correct answer is A. From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. The lecture lists what is NOT routine in Canada : oral polio, yellow fever, shingles, Salmonella , Japanese encephalitis, hepatitis A, meningococcal B, pneumococcal polysaccharide and BCG . BCG is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine agains

Which of the following infectious agents would have the highest threshold to reach herd immunity? Measles - A virus with a high reproductive number Influenza A - A virus with a small incubation period Ebola - A virus that can have deadly effects on the host Covid-19 - A virus that is unlikely to mutate into different strains The correct answer is A. Measles would have a higher degree of infectiousness. From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents and 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. Herd immunity protects the few susceptible people because the pathogen is unlikely to find them. The proportion who must be immune depends on

Which of the following symptoms is NOT characteristic of Sepsis? Low blood pressure Decreased heart rate Urine output decreased Hypoxia Tissue hypoperfusion The correct answer is B. Increased heart rate is characteristic of sepsis. From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. Sepsis is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. The cardiovascular picture is tachycardia with hypotension, as the heart compensates for arteriolar vasodilation and capillary l

A patient presents with C. difficile and localized pain in their abdomen. Within a short time frame the patient develops sepsis. The surgeons do an urgent abdominal surgical resection and remove sections of their intestine. Which of the following basic principles of sepsis management is displayed in this situation? Early recognition Early treatment Source control Life support The correct answer is C. Removing the source of infection is called source control for sepsis management.

Which of the following therapies would NOT be classified as “life-support” for a patient on life support following sepsis? Vasopressors Dialysis Mechanical ventilation Vancomycin The correct answer is D. Vancomycin is antibody treatment. From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture separates early treatment (early, appropriate, broad-spectrum antibiotics) from life support , which is invasive support for failing organs that buys time and fixes nothing. Vancomycin is an anti

Which of the following outlines how an E. coli cell is mostly likely able to become ESBL (Extended Spectrum Beta-Lactamase) positive? An E. coli cell is able to evolve within its lifetime and gain this ability to circumvent β-lactam antibiotics. In the presence of other E. coli they can work cooperatively to produce ESBL. Local environments provide signals to up regulate the expression/production of ESBL in E. coli E. coli is able to uptake a plasmid found in their local environment. The correct answer is D. From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture explains ESBL as a bacterium “hanging around a bunch of bad guys” that picks up a plasmid carrying the instructions for extended-spectrum β-lactamase. That is horizontal gene transfer, and it is the fast route to r

Which of the following antibiotics would you use for a patient with a suspected MRSA infection? Cloxacillin Amoxicillin Vancomycin Carbapenem The correct answer is C. Vancomycin is effective against MRSA. From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. MRSA carries mecA , which makes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein that β-lactams cannot bind. Every β-lactam therefore fails. Vancomycin binds peptidoglycan directly and covers most Gram-po

Which of the following drugs can NOT be used to treat Pseudomonas? Amoxicillin Carbapenem Aminoglycosides Piperacillin-tazobactam The correct answer is A. Amoxicillin is not broad spectrum. From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin with no anti-pseudomonal activity. The lecture's anti-pseudomonal penicillin is piperacillin/tazobactam , and Pseudomonas sits at the resistant outer edge of th

Which of the following bacteria is Penicillin capable of treating? E. coli Streptococcus pyogenes Staphylococcus aureus MRSA The correct answer is B. Penicillin is used to treat GAS. From 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 2. In the cellulitis case the lecture says penicillin covers group A strep ( S. pyogenes ) but is too narrow on its own because it lacks anti-staphylococcal activity. Penicillin is the lecture's e

Annalise is a 25-year-old medical student at McMaster University doing a clerkship rotation in infectious disease. She is seeing a patient with a past MRSA infection who was treated with oral Clindamycin. Following this treatment, the infection by MRSA resolved, but the patient developed extreme gastrointestinal pain coupled with chronic diarrhea. Suspecting a second bacterial infection, what next antibiotic is Annalise most likely to recommend? Piperacillin-tazobactam Cloxacillin IV Vancomycin Oral Vancomycin Imipenem The correct answer is D. Oral vancomycin is used to treat C.difficile infections.

Vanessa is an 83-year-old living in a long-term care facility who has recently developed a urinary tract infection caused by E. coli . Which antibiotic is least appropriate to use against E. coli ? Assume Vanessa has no allergies or renal issues. Aminoglycosides Metronidazole (Flagyl) Amoxicillin Meropenem Piperacillin-tazobactam The correct answer is B. Flagyl treats anerobic bacteria From 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 2 and 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. E. coli is an aerobic Gram-negative bacillus. Metronidazole (Flagyl) is the anaerobe drug on the spectrum map. In the peritonitis case it is added to c

Which of the following correctly describes a mechanism in which β-lactams are able to affect susceptible bacteria? They bind with high affinity to enzymes that promote cross-linking of peptidoglycan They bind to terminal residues on the peptidoglycan and prevent further crosslinking They block formation of the 50s + 30S subunit They inhibit enzymes involved in bacteria DNA synthesis and inhibit further growth The correct answer is A. B-lactams exert their function by binding the enzymes that promote cell wall crosslinking.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which bacterial modification prevents antibiotics from entering into the cell? “ D -Ala- D -Ala” peptide altered to “ D -Ala- D -Lactate” peptide E. coli uptakes a plasmid which codes for ESBL Porins become mutated Efflux pumps on the cell surface The correct answer is C. Porins allow entry into cell. If mutated, this process is inhibited.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which bacterial modification leads to enzymatic degradation of the antibiotic? “ D -Ala- D -Ala” peptide altered to “ D -Ala- D -Lactate” peptide E. coli uptakes a plasmid which codes for ESBL Porins become mutated Efflux pumps on the cell surface The correct answer is B. From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Enzymatic degradation means the bacterium makes an enzyme that destroys the drug. ESBL (extended-spectrum β-lactamase) inactivates most β-lactams except carbapenems, and ESBL E. coli is the lecture's example. This is a major resis

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which bacterial modification increases an antibiotic’s removal from the cell? “ D -Ala- D -Ala” peptide altered to “ D -Ala- D -Lactate” peptide E. coli uptakes a plasmid which codes for ESBL Porins become mutated Efflux pumps on the cell surface The correct answer is D. Efflux pumps pump out antibiotics from the cell. From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Efflux pumps actively move antibiotic back out of the bacterial cell. This is one arm of “preventing antibiotic accumulation”, whose net effect is lower intracellular drug levels. P

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which structural change directly prevents antibiotic interference in cell wall synthesis? “ D -Ala- D -Ala” peptide altered to “ D -Ala- D -Lactate” peptide E. coli uptakes a plasmid which codes for ESBL Porins become mutated Efflux pumps on the cell surface The correct answer is A. From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Vancomycin works by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the peptidoglycan precursor and blocking cell-wall cross-linking. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci change that terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac , a structural change to the binding site it

Which antibiotic targets nucleic acid synthesis at the level of nitrogenous bases? Fluoroquinolones Trimethoprim Metronidazole Carbapenem Ciprofloxacin The correct answer is B. Trimethoprim impacts folate synthesis. From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Trimethoprim is a folate-synthesis inhibitor, the partner of sulfamethoxazole in TMP-SMX. The lecture notes that folate is “vital for DNA”. Blocking the folate pathway starves the cell of

You are volunteering in a vaccination awareness campaign and your role is to converse with parents who are refusing vaccines for their children. Which argument brought up by one of these vaccine-refusers is most valid? “My 4-year-old child cannot get the varicella vaccine because they have acute lymphoid leukemia, and they won’t be able to fight off the virus.” “My 6-year-old child cannot get the influenza virus. She just had a really bad cough and I don’t want her to get the flu too.” “My 3-year-old child cannot get the influenza virus. Her older sister is currently on immunosuppressive therapy to treat her diabetes.” “My 12-month-old should not get her MMR vaccine because she was born two months pre-mature.” “My precious 4-month-old should not get the flu shot because she is so physically weak. I want to wait until she is older.” The correct answer is A. Cancer patients are immunocompromised and thus can have adverse reactions to live vaccines such as varicella.

Which of the following antibiotics function by directly interfering with protein synthesis? β-lactams Carbapenems Macrolides Fluoroquinolones The correct answer is C. Macrolides inhibit the 50s subunit of ribosomes. From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture sorts antibiotics by the process they hit. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and are bacteriostatic protein-synt

Which option below correctly describes the target of an antibiotic? Vancomycin targets the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan. Tetracyclines target enzymes responsible in the synthesis of folate. Fluoroquinolones bind to the 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes. Carbapenems such as imipenem are substrates for penicillin-binding proteins. Clindamycin targets the cell membrane and forms pores in the cell membrane. The correct answer is D. Carbapenems bind PBP. From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem) are β-lactams, and every β-lactam works by binding penicillin-binding proteins , the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan. So D is right. A fails: vancomycin

Which of the following antibiotics has the broadest spectrum of activity? Vancomycin Meropenem Penicillin Sulfonamides Aminoglycosides The correct answer is B. Meropenem is a carbapenem, which is a broad spectrum antibiotic.

Tuberculosis rates are 40 times higher in First Nations living on reserves compared to the Canadian born non-Indigenous population. This is a persistent problem that can often be attributed to poorly ventilated/overcrowded homes, food insecurity and smoking. Which of the following levels of infectious disease does this reality best fall under? Sporadic Endemic Epidemic Pandemic The correct answer is B. From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Endemic means the constant presence of a disease in a population, or its usual prevalence there. A TB rate that has stayed persistently high on reserves for years, driven by lasting structural conditions (overcr

Taylor recently tested positive for COVID-19 the same day she started experiencing symptoms. Taylor works in close proximity to her co-worker Drake. Drake says he feels fine and has no symptoms. Which of the following are the next best steps for Taylor and Drake? Taylor should go into quarantine and Drake should go into isolation Taylor should go into isolation and Drake should go into quarantine Taylor and Drake should both go into quarantine Taylor and Drake should both go into isolation Taylor and Drake should both go to a party The correct answer is B. Isolation is for those who already have the disease. From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Isolation separates sick people with a contagious disease from those who are not sick, and it lasts for the period of communicability. Quarantine restricts th

Recently there was an outbreak of Salmonella that originated from a shipment of pet Hedgehogs. Any measures to eliminate the source of infection could not be taken until extensive epidemiologic data could be collected to implicate the hedgehogs. The epidemic curve is shown below. Which of the following epidemic outbreak patterns does this scenario best fall under? Point common-source Continuous common-source Intermittent common-source Propagated The correct answer is A. From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Every option except propagated is a common-source outbreak, so the discriminator is how long exposure lasted . In a point source, exposure is brief and all cases fall within one incubation period, giving a sharp

If you have had exposure to another person who has tested positive for COVID-19, the government of Canada recommends quarantining for 14 days. If you develop symptoms of COVID-19, the government of Canada recommends isolation. Which statement below is correct? Quarantine is a measure to prevent the possible spread of COVID-19 from affected individuals. Quarantine is a measure to reduce the symptoms of COVID-19 in affected individuals. Isolation is a measure to prevent the possible spread of COVID-19 from affected individuals. Isolation is a measure to reduce the symptoms of COVID-19 in affected individuals. The correct answer is C. From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Both measures exist to stop spread , and neither treats symptoms. Isolation separates sick people with a contagious disease from people who are not sick, for the period of communicability, so it is the measure f

Which option correctly describes a pattern of spread of transmissible diseases? Select all that apply. A continuous-source outbreak is indicated when public health measures to control the spread of a contagious disease are unsuccessful. A point-source outbreak involves a single source, such as a pathogenic E. coli that was consumed by several patrons in a restaurant three weeks ago. A propagated-source outbreak has an epidemic curve with multiple peaks separated by approximately one incubation period. An intermittent-source outbreak has an epidemic curve that shows elements of continuous-source transmission and propagated source transmission. The correct answer is B, C. From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Check each statement against the lecture's four curve patterns. A false : a continuous common source means cases exposed to the same source over an extended period , a property of the exposure, not a verdict

Which of the following antivirals would you prescribe to a patient with Cytomegalovirus (CMV) who would prefer an oral tablet? Acyclovir Valacyclovir Ganciclovir Valganciclovir The correct answer is D. From 09 - Antivirals. CMV needs the ganciclovir family: ganciclovir and valganciclovir cover CMV, while acyclovir and valacyclovir cover only HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV. Ganciclovir is IV only . Valganciclovir is its oral prodrug (bioavailability 55%), so it is the answer for a pa

Which of the following antivirals directly inhibits the budding phase in Influenza? Acyclovir Baloxavir Marboxil Foscarnet Zanamivir The correct answer is D. From 09 - Antivirals. Neuraminidase frees newly formed influenza particles from the cell surface as they bud off. Neuraminidase inhibitors, oseltamivir (oral) and zanamivir (inhaled), therefore prevent budding and release. Acyclovir : a guanosine analogue that inhibits herpe

Which option correctly contrasts two antiviral medications? Valacyclovir is a pro-drug, acyclovir is not. Ganciclovir targets viruses specifically, valganciclovir does not. Acyclovir is used to treat Herpes Simplex Virus 1 and 2, Valacyclovir is not. Ganciclovir is used to treat cytomegalovirus, valacyclovir is not. Foscarnet targets DNA polymerase, acyclovir does not. The correct answer is D. From 09 - Antivirals. Spectrum is the dividing line. Ganciclovir covers CMV (plus HSV and VZV), while valacyclovir , like acyclovir, covers HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV and not CMV . Which option correctly describes a feature of an antiviral medication? Drugs that target hemagglutinin on Influenza A prevent the release of virions from an infected cell. Acyclovir requires modification by virally encoded enzymes for activity. Foscarnet prevents viral envelopes from binding to cells. Given identical oral doses, more ganciclovir reaches the bloodstream compared with valganciclovir The correct answer is B. From 09 - Antivirals. Acyclovir must be triphosphorylated before it can act on viral DNA polymerase, and the first phosphorylation is done by viral thymidine kinase . Anti-CTLA-4 drugs are a commonly-used medication in cancer therapy, but have been associated with the development of autoimmune conditions through disrupting T-cell tolerance in the periphery. Which of the following modes of T-cell tolerance do anti[1]CTLA-4 drugs disrupt? Immunologic ignorance Deletion Inhibition Suppression The correct answer is C. Inhibition provides an inhibitory stimuli to the T-cell so they become anergic. CTLA-4 from the T-cell binding to CD80 on the APC provides this inhibitory stimuli. With antiCTLA-4 drugs, this interaction cannot take place, and self-reactive T-cells can go on to become activa

Use the following options for the next FOUR questions . A patient emerges from a surgery with complications where the Blood brain barrier was permeated and CSF proteins were able to flow into the periphery. Which mechanism of autoimmunity is the patient susceptible to? Modification of Self-antigen Release of sequestered self-antigens Molecular mimicry Defective deletion The correct answer is B. T-cells that are self-reactive for CSF proteins (and weren’t deleted during central selection) may be capable of mounting an autoimmune response against these CSF antigens that were (prior to the surgery) sequestered from the periphery.

Use the following options for the next FOUR questions . In rheumatoid arthritis, smoking plays a large role in the citrullination of proteins. How does this process contribute to the development of autoimmunity and breakdown of tolerance? Modification of Self-antigen Release of sequestered self-antigens Molecular mimicry Defective deletion The correct answer is A. The post-translational modification of self-antigens creates modified peptides that may become new targets for an immune response, as T-cells that can recognize this new peptide would not have been negatively selected for in the thymus.

Use the following options for the next FOUR questions . A patient with a genetic defect is unable to express the Fas Ligand on APCs. Which mechanism of autoimmunity is the patient susceptible to? Modification of Self-antigen Release of sequestered self-antigens Molecular mimicry Defective deletion The correct answer is D. The Fas ligand binding to Fas on T-cells leads to T-cell apoptosis and is a key mechanism for tolerance in the periphery. With a defective Fas ligand the patient’s ability to delete selfreactive T cells is diminished.

Use the following options for the next FOUR questions . A patient infected with the herpes simplex virus develops antibodies against a glycoprotein on the virus. These antibodies have cross-reactivity with Acetylcholine receptors in neuromuscular junctions. Which mechanism of autoimmunity is the patient susceptible to? Modification of Self-antigen Release of sequestered self-antigens Molecular mimicry Defective deletion The correct answer is C. Molecular Mimicry is when certain proteins on foreign substances have similarities with self-peptides, so when antigens are developed to target those foreign proteins they can inadvertently also mount an immune response against those self-peptides due to their similarity.

Which of the following therapies would NOT be helpful for a patient with rheumatoid arthritis? Physician counselling on smoking cessation Rituximab (reduces B cell count) Glucocorticoids B and C A, B, and C The correct answer is E. Smoking plays a key role in the citrullination of proteins that when presented by MHC- SE to the appropriate T-cells can lead to an autoimmune response. Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that works by decreasing B-cell levels by targeting CD-20 - this is important because B

Which option below incorrectly pairs an autoimmune disease with its antigen target? In Myasthenia gravis, antibodies target acetylcholine receptors in muscles. In Graves’ disease, antibodies target TSH receptors in the thyroid. In Systemic Lupus erythematosus, antibodies target phospholipids on platelets. In Diabetes Mellitus (Type 1), T-cells target β-cells in the pancreas. In Multiple sclerosis, T-cells target myelin in the central nervous system. The correct answer is C. Systemic lupus erythematosus is the result of antibodies targeting DNA. This autoimmune condition can be the result of viral infections such as CMV, EBV, or HZH.
