Taylor is a 3-year-old who was immediately brought to the ER after eating a peanut butter cookie for the first time. Taylor is experiencing hives, difficulty breathing and her blood pressure starts dropping. Which option describes the correct order of therapy? Remove the cookie, then administer intramuscular epinephrine, then administer supportive therapy (fluids, antihistamine, etc) if necessary Remove the cookie, then administer supportive therapy (fluids, antihistamine, etc), then administer intramuscular epinephrine if necessary Remove the cookie, and wait up to 1 hour to see if self-resolves, then administer supportive therapy if necessary Remove the cookie and wait up to 1 hour to see if it self-resolves, then administer epinephrine if necessary The correct answer is A. Taylor is experiencing anaphylaxis (2 symptoms in two systems within 1 hours of allergen). The first step involves discontinuing the suspected trigger (cookie), then providing epinephrine and repeating as necessary. Other supportive therapy must only be provided after epinep

Which of the following treatments would you most likely prescribe as a daily medication for a patient with allergic rhinitis? First generation antihistamines (Benadryl) Second generation antihistamines Decongestant nose sprays Epinephrine The correct answer is B. Patients should generally receive second generation antihistamines. First generation antihistamines such as Benadryl have a sedating effect and interfere with sleep – this could have adverse effects if taken on a daily basis. Decongestant Nasal sprays make congestion worse i

Harry is 4 months old. His two parents, James and Lily, are discussing whether they should start him on solid foods. James thinks that now is a good time to start, but Lily argues that they should wait a bit more as she is happy breast-feeding. Which food below is NOT safe to introduce to Harry? Tree nuts Honey Eggs Fish Cow milk The correct answer is B. Honey is not safe for infants less than 1 year old due to risk of botulism. However, the other foods can and should be recommended between 4 and 6 months. Early exposure to possibly allergenic foods reduces the likelihood of a food-allergy.

Which of the following children is LEAST at risk for developing a food allergy? A 6-month-old child with atopic dermatitis A child who is sensitized to peanuts (as determined by skin testing) A child who is not exposed to peanuts in their first year of life A toddler who regularly eats peanuts but stops consuming them abruptly after turning 5 A mother rubs peanut butter on their 4-month-old child’s skin to help him get exposure The correct answer is D. Introducing food early on within the first 6 months of life can prevent a food allergy even if that food is later discontinued. Atopic dermatitis is a risk factor for food allergy as there is a disruption in the skin in which food antigens can invade and be recognized as a h

Taylor was recently stung by a hornet. A large rash appeared on her neck (where she was stung), and in addition, similar rashes appeared on her thigh and abdomen. What type of reaction is this? Normal local reaction Large local reaction Systemic extracutaneous Systemic cutaneous The correct answer is D. Systemic cutaneous reactions are characterized by skin only symptoms that are not contiguous with the original site of the sting. In this situation her rash spread from her neck to her arm which was not stung. Systemic extracutaneous reactions involve multiple organ systems.

Which of the following best explains the purpose of granulomas in a chronic inflammatory response? They serve as a precursor to scar tissue formation They serve as extra nodal sites where APCs can present antigens to naïve T cells They aim to contain foreign bodies that cannot be eradicated from the body They are a site of production for pro-inflammatory cytokines The correct answer is C. Granulomas often aim to contain something that can’t be eradicated from the body.

Which of the following descriptions best describe the structure of a granuloma? Activated macrophages surrounded by T lymphocytes Activated neutrophils surrounded by B lymphocytes Activated lymphocytes surrounded by monocytes Malignant neoplasms surrounded by lymphocytes The correct answer is A. Granulomas consist of activated macrophages, sometimes fused to form multinucleated giant cells (called Langhans cells), surrounded by a rim of T-cells.

Isabella has suffered from chronic allergic rhinitis for the past two months. Upon visual examination of her nasal cavities, the doctor notices what he thinks are nasal polyps. If the polyps were surgically resected and sent to a pathologist, what would the pathologist see after H+E staining? Red-coloured lymphocytes Eosinophils with a bi-lobed nucleus Eosinophils with a “clock-face” nucleus Lymphocytes with a large nucleus and a thin cytoplasm Plasma cells with multi-lobed nuclei The correct answer is B. One of the major cell types responsible for inflammation in nasal polyps is the eosinophil. These leukocytes are usually associated with allergic / atopic responses. They have a bilobed nucleus and cytoplasmic granules which appear red (eosinophilic) on H+E stain.

A 7-year-old patient presents with dysmorphic facial features, mild failure to thrive and a repetitive history of Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli infections. The physician, suspecting an immunodeficiency, performs a neutrophil count which turns out to be abnormally low. Which of the following classification of immunodeficiencies is most likely? Primary humoral immunodeficiency Primary phagocytosis immunodeficiency Secondary humoral immunodeficiency Secondary phagocytosis immunodeficiency The correct answer is B. This patient’s dysmorphic facial features and failure to thrive suggest a primary immunodeficiency over a secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency. Furthermore the low neutrophil count and repetitive history of staphylococcal and gram negative bacterial infections suggest a pha

Which of the following conditions is NOT an underlying condition that can contribute to the development of a secondary immunodeficiency? Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Atopic dermatitis Radiation treatment Allergy The correct answer is D. Allergy is an exaggerated immune response against an antigen that is intrinsically not harmful for your body. Atopic Dermatitis can lead to a disruption of the epithelial surface comprising the barrier function and possibly leading to SID. Radiation treatment and other medic

Which of the following methods regarding T cell allorecognition is correct? Direct allorecognition involves T cells recognizing donor MHC peptides presented on a recipient (self) antigen presenting cell Direct and indirect allorecognition is MHC restricted, so activated T cells are able to recognize foreign alloantigens solely through MHC presentation Indirect allorecognition involves T cells recognizing foreign MHC on donor cells Naïve T cells are capable of being activated through recognizing foreign MHC peptides on donor epithelial cells The correct answer is D. Direct allorecognition is not MHC restricted so T-cells are capable of becoming activated through recognizing foreign MHC on donor cells (donor APCs/epithelial cells). In the absence of any immunosuppressive agents a graft from Albert is given to Bobby, and this is the first time Bobby is receiving any graft. Albert is also giving a graft to Charlie for the second time after the graft was slowly rejected the first time. In which patient is the graft able to survive for a longer period of time? Bobby Charlie The graft survival will be the same in both patients The correct answer is B. Since Bobby is receiving a graft for the first time it’s very likely they don’t have any preexisting antibodies, however they will still mount an immune response against the graft over an extended period of time. Charlie who rejected the graft the first time, likely has anti

Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next THREE questions. Sarah Hyland is an American actress who played Haley Dunphy in the comedy TV show, Modern Family. In 2012, her kidneys failed due to a congenital condition known as kidney dysplasia. Her father stepped up and became a living donor. Then, in 2016, her body began to reject her father’s kidney. In 2017, she started regular hemodialysis treatments, three times per week, each lasting 4 hours. In 2018, she received an organ transplant from her brother. Sarah and her father are directly related. Why would Sarah’s immune system reject her father’s kidney? Sarah inherited 50% of her HLA-epitopes from her father, and HLA-epitopes are expressed in an incomplete dominant pattern. Sarah inherited 25% of her HLA-epitopes from her father, and HLA-epitopes are expressed in an incomplete dominant pattern. Sarah inherited 50% of her HLA-epitopes from her father, and HLA-epitopes are expressed in a co-dominant pattern. Sarah inherited 25% of her HLA-epitopes from her father, and HLA-epitopes are expressed in a co-dominant pattern. The correct answer is C. HLA-epitope alleles are codominant, with both maternal and paternal alleles being completely expressed.

Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next THREE questions. Sarah Hyland is an American actress who played Haley Dunphy in the comedy TV show, Modern Family. In 2012, her kidneys failed due to a congenital condition known as kidney dysplasia. Her father stepped up and became a living donor. Then, in 2016, her body began to reject her father’s kidney. In 2017, she started regular hemodialysis treatments, three times per week, each lasting 4 hours. In 2018, she received an organ transplant from her brother. What is the likely etiology of Sarah Hyland’s rejection of her father’s kidney? The kidney was rejected due to pre-existing donor-specific antibodies already found in Sarah’s systemic circulation. This caused the graft to clot. The kidney was rejected due to infiltration of the kidney by Sarah’s T-cells, causing tubulitis. The kidney was rejected due to the presence of pre-existing donor-specific antibodies which activated the Sarah’s complement system. The kidney was rejected due to antibody- or T-cell-mediated neointimal thickening of arterial walls in the donor kidney and reduced arterial lumen space. The correct answer is D. Chronic rejection of a graft is gradual, occurring more than three months after transplantation. This type of rejection involves neointimal thickening of arterial walls and a subsequent reduction in arterial lumen space.

Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next THREE questions. Sarah Hyland is an American actress who played Haley Dunphy in the comedy TV show, Modern Family. In 2012, her kidneys failed due to a congenital condition known as kidney dysplasia. Her father stepped up and became a living donor. Then, in 2016, her body began to reject her father’s kidney. In 2017, she started regular hemodialysis treatments, three times per week, each lasting 4 hours. In 2018, she received an organ transplant from her brother. What is likely true about Sarah Hyland’s medication history? She was likely treated with rituximab immediately after receiving her father’s kidney. She likely received long-term immunosuppressive agents such as tacrolimus or prednisone between 2012 and 2016. She likely received powerful immunosuppressants such as thymoglobulin before the transplant, but probably not when her body was rejecting the kidney. After receiving her brother’s kidney, she likely was not prescribed any antibiotics since most antibiotics are cleared renally. The correct answer is B. Transplant recipients are prescribed immunosuppressive agents long-term to prevent the rejection of the transplant organ. Rituximab is used in special situations, such as an ABO- incompatible transplant. Thymoglobulin is a powerful immunosuppressive agent that can be used be

With regards to immunosuppression within the context of a transplant, which type of rejection does Induction therapy aim to prevent? Hyperacute rejection Acute T-cell-mediated rejection Acute antibody-mediated rejection Chronic rejection The correct answer is A. Induction therapy often involves the use of powerful immunosuppressant (monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies) at the time of the transplant to prevent hyperacute rejection. Hyperacute rejection is often caused by pre-existing donor-specific antibodies that target the graft.

Which of the following best explains how immunosuppressants contribute to EBV-induced Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD)? Immunosuppressants weaken protective and innate barriers allowing EBV entry into the host cell which consequently leads to PTLD Immunosuppressants reduce immune surveillance which lead to reactivation of dormant EBV and consequently leads to PTLD) Immunosuppressants contribute to pro-inflammatory environments where EBV is able to proliferate and lead to the development of PTLD Immunosuppressants reduce B cell count allowing EBV to proliferate and contribute to the development of PTLD The correct answer is B. PTLD often comes in the form of B cell proliferation due to EBV infection in the context of immunosuppression. Most individuals contract EBV in adulthood and it remains dormant in memory B cells due to ongoing immune surveillance. However in the presence of immunosuppressant

Which of the following statements about Fungi is NOT correct? Fungal cell membrane contains ergosterol Fungal cell wall contains peptidoglycan Fungal cells are eukaryotic Most fungi live off dead and decaying cells The correct answer is B. Fungal Cell wall contains chitin, glucan and mannan proteins. Bacteria often contain peptidoglycan in their cell wall. Most fungi are saprophytes, meaning that they feed off of dead and decaying materials.

Which of the following classes of fungi would you consider doing a serology assay for? Yeasts Moulds Dimorphic fungi None of the above The correct answer is C. Unlike other fungi, serology is a key component of the diagnosis for dimorphic fungus. However, it’s important to know that there may be cross-reactivity between dimorphic fungi, thus the presence of antibodies may not signify the body has encountered that specific dimorphic

Tinea versicolor is a fungal infection of the skin resulting in hyper- or hypo-pigmented patches. Bernadette went to her family doctor suspecting Tinea versicolor, and the doctor prescribed Lamisil, a topical cream containing terbinafine. Which organism was the cause of the fungal infection? Candida spp. Saccharomyces cerevisiae Malassezia furfur Aspergillus niger Tinea corporis The correct answer is C. From 03 - Important Fungal Infections. The lecture makes the exception explicit: tinea versicolour is NOT a dermatophyte infection; it is caused by Malassezia furfur . The other “tinea” conditions (capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium) are dermatophyte infections. A Can

Tinea versicolor is a fungal infection of the skin resulting in hyper- or hypo-pigmented patches. Bernadette went to her family doctor suspecting Tinea versicolor, and the doctor prescribed Lamisil, a topical cream containing terbinafine. What is the mode of action of terbinafine? Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase Terbinafine inhibits glucan synthesis Terbinafine damages fungal DNA Terbinafine forms pores in the fungal cell membrane The correct answer is A. Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase, an important first step in the synthesis of ergosterol. Ergosterol is found in fungal membranes.

Clotrimaderm is an anti-fungal topical cream containing clotrimazole. It is a prescribed medication for vaginal yeast and Candida infections. What aspect of clotrimazole’s mechanism of action makes it target fungal yeast cells but not human cells? (Note, clotramidazole belongs to the azole class of antifungals.) Fungal cells contain peptidoglycan, human cells don’t. Fungal cells contain glucan, human cells don’t. Fungal cells contain membrane-bound proteins, human cells don’t. Fungal cells contain ergosterol, human cells don’t. Fungal cells contain mycolic acid, human cells don’t. The correct answer is D. Azoles inhibit the formation of ergosterol, which is found only in fungal cells. Note, fungal cells do not contain peptidoglycan - bacterial cells do. Echinocandins inhibit glucan synthesis. Human cells and fungal cells contain membrane-bound proteins. Mycolic acid is found

A patient is placed on immunosuppressive therapy following a heart transplant. Within the first month the patient develops a severe viral infection however is not presenting with a fever. Which of the following options best explain the absence of a systemic fever? Their immune response is still focused on mounting a response against the donor graft, it is unable to mount a fever response to address the viral infections Immunosuppressive agents interfere with white blood cells’ ability to produce endogenous pyrogens that contribute to fever development Immunosuppressive agents can produce an inflammatory environment leading to a disruption in homeostasis and the body’s ability to mount a fever response The immunosuppressive agents are able to redirect the inflammation associated with a fever through chemotaxis to create a more localized “fever response” as opposed to a systemic response The correct answer is B. Immunosuppressive agents interfere with WBCs ability to produce endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, IL-6, IFN-gamma, TNF) which are necessary in leading to a fever response. Immunosuppressive agents generally promote an anti-inflammatory environment to diminish any immune responses.

Which of the following infections is best characterized as an opportunistic infection? A patient with a necrotizing fasciitis infection who must have one of their limbs amputated to survive A patient who contracts Pneumocystis jirovecii and is able to mount an effective immune response against it A patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 558 cells/mL who develops Influenza A patient with Diabetes Mellitus develops Mucormycosis, an infection that thrives in a Diabetic ketoacidosis state The correct answer is D. An opportunistic infection is an organism that can cause fatal outcomes in immunocompromised individuals, but are relatively harmless in immunocompetent individuals. Patients with Diabetes are more prone to fatal outcomes when they contract Mucormycosis as this organism thri

Which option correctly describes the pathophysiology of a patient with a compromised immune system? Patients with liver cirrhosis have a reduction in Kupffer cells, which inhibit the immune response mediated by NK cells and neutrophils. Patients with Type 1 Diabetes produce antibodies that target B-cells. Patients with recent stem-cell transplants have received immunosuppressant medications which irreversibly reduce immune cell counts. Patients with acute myeloblastic leukemia have an increased quantity of white blood cells, but these white blood cells have limited immune activity. The correct answer is D. AML is associated with leukocytosis (increased white-blood-cell count), but most of these white blood cells are immature and non-functional. Kupffer cells are produced by the liver but are involved in phagocytosis of foreign particles. The pancreas secretes proteins which sy

What clinical manifestation may be expected in an immunocompromised individual? Antibiotics are less effective in killing pathogenic bacteria. A dysregulated immune system could lead to hyperthermia (>41 °C) following a viral infection. Inactivated vaccines may demonstrate reduced efficacy in an immunocompromised host and may require repeated administrations. Live vaccines may demonstrate increased efficacy and are relatively safer in immunocompromised hosts. The correct answer is A. With a compromised immune system, T-cells are less able to mount a strong response against inactivated pathogens. Repeated administrations are sometimes necessary. Live vaccines are not used in immunocompromised individuals as these patients may not be able to mount an immun

Which of the following antifungal classes would you be hesitant to give a patient who is currently taking Warfarin (warfarin is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 enzyme and has a narrow therapeutic window)? Azoles Echinocandins Amphotericin B All of the above are fine to administer The correct answer is A. Azoles are known to inhibit CYP450 enzymes in fungi, but can also inhibit human CYP450 enzymes. Therefore, prescribing an Azole could reduce metabolism of Warfarin and lead to toxic concentrations of this drug in circulation.

Which option below correctly describes a strength or limitation associated with an antifungal medication? Fluconazole is safe for patients with renal impairment. Amphotericin B can be administered both orally or intravenously. Renal dose adjustment is required for echinocandins. Echinocandins are not suitable for Candida albicans infections of the CNS. The correct answer is D. Echinocandins such as caspofungin have poor penetration into the eye, CNS, and urine. Fluconazole requires renal dose adjustment and would not be safe for patients with renal impairment. Amphotericin is available intravenously only. Echinocandins do not require renal dose ad

Julian is a 54-year-old male who developed a severe Candida spp. infection in his eye following a corneal transplant surgery. He has liver cirrhosis from chronic drinking of 6+ beers per day for the past 20 years. What is the best antifungal of choice for Julian? Fluconazole, an azole Caspofungin, an echinocandin Amphotericin B, a pore former Voriconazole, an azole The correct answer is C. Azoles can cause liver damage and would not be appropriate for patients with preexisting liver damage such as Julian. Additionally, echinocandins have poor penetration into the eye, CNS and urine, and would also not be a good choice. The best remaining choice is amphotericin

Which chemokines and cytokines are involved in TLR signaling? (Select 5) IL-6 IL-12 TNF IL-13 IL-8 IL-1 IL-9 IL-4 The correct answer is A, B, C, E, F. IL-13 and IL-9 are not components of the innate immune response. IL-4 is an important cytokine in the differentiation of naïve T-cells into Th2 cells.

Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the role of acute phase proteins in the inflammatory response? They are produced by the liver upon stimulation by IL-7 and TNF. Examples include mannose-binding lectin/protein, C-reactive protein, fibrinogen and complement. They have immunomodulator functions relevant to sepsis Complement proteins aid in bacterial phagocytosis through opsonization The correct answer is A. The production of acute phase proteins from the liver is stimulated by IL-6 and TNF, not IL-7.

B-cell receptor rearrangement and affinity maturation: Occurs in the thymus Involves the selection of highly self-reactive BCRs Begins with low affinity BCR binding which becomes higher affinity due to AID- induced somatic hypermutation Involves VDJ recombination followed by RAG-driven class switch recombination The correct answer is C. This statement correctly describes BCR selection and affinity maturation, which occurs in the bone marrow. BCR recombination is a different mechanism than VDJ recombination – it uses the enzyme AID instead of RAG.

Which of the following is NOT a B-cell or plasma cell effector mechanism? Act as antigen presenting cells (APCs) in the periphery to activate T-cells Production of IL-6 and IL-10 Production of neutralizing antibodies Production of antibodies that are a targeting mechanism for dendritic cells to perform ADCC The correct answer is D. This answer is almost true, expect the Natural Killer cells (NK cells) perform ADCC as an effector function, not dendritic cells.

You send a nasopharyngeal sample to the microbiology lab for culture. Later, you are notified that the sample was rejected. What is the most likely reason for this? The specimen leaked from its transport container The specimen was not collected in accordance with the Lab Test Information Guide (LTIG) or improperly labelled The specimen was collected from the wrong patient The microbiology lab determined that testing the specimen was not clinically indicated The correct answer is B. Pre-analytical errors are the most common reason that the microbiology lab will reject a sample. Since it was not a liquid, it is unlikely to have leaked during transport.

You suspect that a patient has bacteremia. You collect two samples of blood and send the specimen to the microbiology lab for diagnostic testing. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be least helpful if performed on this sample? Culture – a direct way to determine the organism’s susceptibly to select antibiotics. Microscopy – used to provide pre-culture information and determine what tests/methods should be used. Gram stain – can help rapidly identify the pathogen and determine the quality of the specimen. Molecular testing – conducting a respiratory viral PCR panel to detect and amplify nucleic acid sequences. The correct answer is D. In a patient with suspected bacteremia, molecular PCR for a respiratory virus panel would not be as helpful as the other options, which all facilitate bacterial identification and treatment of bacteremia.

Thermoregulation is the homeostatic balance between heat dissipation and heat production. Categorize each term below as an effector, thermoreceptors, regulated variable, or feedforward system. The pairings: Term Category Body temperature at 37C Regulated variable Primary sensory neurons in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, and brain Thermoreceptors Body temperature during hyperthermia Feedforward system Sweat glands Effector From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. The n

When Golda was in Jamaica on vacation, she noticed that her body was responding physiologically and behaviorally to the warmer climate. Which of the following is NOT a homeostatic response mechanism that would been seen in Golda? Exhalation of warm air NO-mediated vasodilation of blood vessels supplying the skin Movement to a shaded area Contraction of skeletal muscle (i.e., shivering) The correct answer is D. Shivering generates heat – Golda’s body would be responding in a way that maximizes heat dissipation.

Which of the following general statements about infection and infectious agents is FALSE? Superficial fungal infections are often diagnosed based on visual assessment. Mycobacteria are stained using the Ziehl-Nielsen stain or Auramine phenol. The steps of the viral replication cycle are: transmission, attachment, entry, uncoating, genome replication, protein synthesis, assembly, and release. Adenoviruses are non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses. The correct answer is C. Transmission is not one of the steps of the viral replication cycle. Additionally, protein synthesis (i.e., translation) must occur before the viral genome can be replicated, so the order of those steps is reversed.

Which of the following statements correctly captures a difference between gram-positive (GP) and gram-negative (GN) bacteria? GP bacteria have a thinner layer of peptidoglycan in their cell wall than GN bacteria GP bacteria have a single phospholipid bilayer membrane whereas GN bacteria have inner and outer membranes GP bacteria have proteins that control membrane permeability and influence antibiotic efficacy GP bacteria have lipopolysaccharide while GN bacteria have lipoteichoic acid as an endotoxin The correct answer is B. Gram positive bacteria have a single phospholipid membrane while gram-negative bacteria have two membranes (an outer and inner membrane).

Which of the following regarding Group A Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS) is incorrect? Beta hemolysis pattern Catalase positive Found in chains Gram positive Round shape The correct answer is B. GAS is not catalase positive, it is catalase negative. It is a gram positive cocci (round) that is found in chains and has a beta hemolysis pattern.

Group A Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS) is responsible for many different types of infections. Which of the following is incorrect? GAS can cause invasive disease including necrotizing fasciitis Rheumatic heart disease can result from untreated GAS infections in childhood GAS commonly forms biofilms on foreign bodies like pacemakers and prosthetic joints resulting in severe infection Pharyngitis – more commonly known as strep throat – is a common non-invasive disease caused by GAS The correct answer is C. While it is possible for GAS to form a biofilm, it is not a common cause of severe infection. This is more typical of Staphylococcus aureus.

Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes utilize several different virulence factors to evade the immune system, most of which involve the coagulation system. Which of the following virulence factors is incorrect? M-protein – found on the surface of Streptococcus pyogenes , binds fibrinogen, complement regulatory proteins, and IgG Coagulase – secreted by Staphylococcus aureus , binds and activates prothrombin ClfA – found on the surface of Staphylococcus aureus , binds fibrinogen and causes cell clumping SpyCep – a protease produced by Streptococcus pyogenes that degrades chemokines and prevents their detection by neutrophils Protein A – found on the surface of Staphylococcus aureus , binds complement proteins in a way that makes it impossible for phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils The correct answer is E. Protein A is found on the surface of Staphylococcus aureus and orients IgG – not complement proteins – in a position that is unfavourable for phagocytosis.

Which of the following is NOT a normal colonizer of the intestines? Proteus E. coli Pseudomonas Klebsiella Enterococcus sp. The correct answer is C. Pseudomonas is not a normal colonizer of the gut. It is usually the result of regular exposure to the healthcare system or repeated use of antibiotics.

A bacteria whispers in your ear: “I am Gram negative. I am rod shaped and I am lactose positive. Who could I be?” Vibrio cholera Pseudomonas Neisseria meningitidis Klebsiella Staphylococcus aureus The correct answer is D. Klebsiella is a Gram negative rod (bacilli) that is lactose positive. Vibrio cholera is Gram negative but is “common-shaped.” Pseudomonas is a gram negative rod but is lactose negative. Neisseria meningitidis is Gram negative but is round (cocci). Staphylococcus aureus is Gr

Which of the following regarding E. coli and urinary tract infections (UTIs) is FALSE? Depending on the type of fimbrial adhesions it uses, E. coli can cause cystitis or pyelonephritis E. coli is the most common causative agent of UTIs Longer O-polysaccharide chains can help E. coli avoid complement binding Shiga toxins produced by E. coli are internalized and activate programmed cell death signaling in cells that line the bladder E. coli can mimic our own cells and avoid immune detection by producing sialic acid The correct answer is D. Shiga toxins are produced by E coli and are internalized, undergo retrograde transport from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum, and the toxin component is shed. The shed toxin glycosylates ribosomal RNA resulting in inhibition of protein synthesis and cell deat

Which of the following definitions regarding the microbiome is incorrect? Infection – an exogenous microbe is in a site causing disease Coloniser – a microbe in its usual habitat that is causing disease Commensal – a microbe in its usual habitat that is not causing disease Dysbiosis – a change in the composition or diversity of the microbiome from a normal healthy population to one that causes disease or predisposes to disease Infection – a normal commensal microbe is in a different compartment than usual and causing disease The correct answer is B. A coloniser is a microbe that is in an unusual habitat but not causing disease. An example of a coloniser is Pseudomonas in a chronic wound.

There are many body compartments that are either sterile or have their own unique microbiota. Which of the following statements is false? Impetigo is an example of a skin infection that results from a break in the skin C. difficile colitis can occur following prolonged antibiotic usage and is often the result of dysbiosis of the intestine microbiota Bacterial vaginosis is an infectious state where there is an overabundance of the coloniser Lactobacillus Different areas of the skin have different microbiota, and commensals include Corynebacterium, Lactobacillus, and Staphylococcus A perforated appendix can result in a breach in compartments and infection of the peritonitis with microbes from the intestines The correct answer is C. Bacterial vaginosis is an infectious state that occurs when there is a decrease in the presence of Lactobacillus – a normal commensal bacteria, not a colonisor – and an increase in other anaerobes, which can be symptomatic.

You are a clerk on your very first rotation in the emergency department. A patient presents with signs that point strongly towards meningitis. They are currently stable with normal vitals. Which of the following approaches to gastroenteritis is correct? In cases of travel-acquired diarrhea, your number one suspicion should be C. difficile colitis It is impossible to perform cultures from GI specimens because of the abundant microbiota present in the intestines One possible viral cause of gastroenteritis is Giardia Mild watery diarrhea does not typically require additional testing and can be treated with supportive management The presence of E. coli is indicative of a GI infection The correct answer is D. Unless watery diarrhea is severe or occurs in the context of a known outbreak (e.g., cholera) it does not require further investigation and can be treated symptomatically. Which of the following serological results indicates immunity to a particular pathogen in an immunocompetent patient? IgG +, IgM + IgG +, IgM - IgG -, IgM + IgG -, IgM - None of the above The correct answer is B. IgG + and IgM - indicates immunity to a particular pathogen. IgG + and IgM + indicates an acute or recent infection. IgG - and IgM + may also indicate an acute or recent infection or may represent a non-specific reaction; you must consider the clinical picture to determine t

Rubor, calor, dolor, tumor, and functio laesa are the cardinal signs of inflammation. Which of the following descriptions of each sign is incorrect? Dolor – stimulation of sensory nerve endings by chemical mediators released in inflammatory process Tumor – fluid accumulation in affected tissue Rubor – vasoconstriction and reduced blood flow Functio laesa – loss of function of affected site Calor – heat from warm blood entering cooler site The correct answer is C. In inflammation there is vasodilation and increased blood flow to the affected site, not vasoconstriction and decreased blood flow. This is what causes erythema (redness) in inflamed tissue.

There are several different types of inflammation. Identify the type of inflammation that is incorrectly matched to its description. Serous inflammation – results from a cell-rich exudate and is commonly seen in serous carcinoma Fibrinous inflammation – fibrin deposition that occurs when fibrinogen escapes the circulation during inflammatory response Ulcer – defect in a mucosal surface that most commonly occurs in the GI tract Purulent inflammation – caused by pyogenic bacteria and can result in abscess formation The correct answer is A. Serous inflammation is a cell-poor exudate. It is seen in conditions like ascites and in skin blisters and is unrelated to serous carcinoma.

Which of the following are accurate differences between fever and hyperthermia (select all that apply): Fever is the resetting of the thermoregulatory control centre while hyperthermia is dysregulation of the set point Fever does not respond to antipyretics while hyperthermia does Fever can be caused by infection, inflammation, and trauma while hyperthermia is caused by heat exposure, drugs, and exercise Fever is best treated with acetaminophens while hyperthermia is best treated with NSAIDs The correct answer is A, C. Fever responds to antipyretics while hyperthermia does not. As a result, acetaminophens and NSAIDs are both treatments used for fever.

What PPE would be required for a routine examination of a patient with mumps during the COVID-19 pandemic (select all that apply): Gloves Gown Surgical-grade mask N95 mask Eye protection The correct answer is A, B, C, E. Mumps is transmitted via droplets while COVID-19 is transmitted via contact and droplet (airborne transmission is debatable). As such, only droplet/contact precautions are required, which constitutes gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection. An N95 mask would only be

Which of the following causes of a fever + rash presentation are considered a medical emergency (select all that apply)? Necrotizing fasciitis Endocarditis Meningococcemia Toxic shock syndrome The correct answer is A, B, C, D. All of these are considered medical emergencies and can be discerned based on the type of rash present, where the rash is located, and how widespread it is.

Clyde is an ex-con currently working as a cashier at Home Depot. He experienced numbing and tingling in his face around a week ago, which has now spread to his neck. He has also recently started finding it difficult to smile or frown. He has a smoking history of 10 pack years, and has been drinking 2 glasses of wine every week (including when he was in prison) for the past 15 years. His tests results indicate infection. What microbe is likely causing Clyde’s symptoms? C. difficile Cryptococcus C. botulinum Peptostreptococcus The correct answer is C. Descending paralysis is a key feature of botulism. Botulism can be acquired from prison brew.

Which image is indicative of a Clostridial species? A. B. C. D. The correct answer is B. Clostridums are gram-positive bacilli. A shows gram-positive cocci, C shows gramnegative bacilli, and D shows gram-negative cocci.

Which geriatric patient likely has an UTI? 87F with malodorous urine and pelvic pain 79F with worsening confusion over the past week and increased incontinence 81F with increased urgency and frequency of urination over the past week 68F with a test result indicating bacteriuria The correct answer is B. Malodorous urine is not correlated with infection. Clinical suspicion should only be piqued when a patient presents with multiple symptoms suggesting UTI (C only had one symptom). Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not mean UTI. This is common in older women and individuals livin

Which of the following is NOT a reason why geriatric populations are more susceptible to infection: Alterations in skin barriers Urethral shortening Increased vaginal mucosal secretions Impaired antibody production The correct answer is C. Old age is associated with vaginal mucosal atrophy, which decreases population of mucosa-resident immune cells in that region.

Which of the following is not a symptom suggestive of Kawasaki disease? Conjunctivitis Rash Adenopathy Strawberry tongue Hepatosplenomegaly & burn (Fever) The correct answer is E. The H in CRASH&burn stands for hands; the hands will exhibit palmar and/or plantar erythema and swelling.

When should antipyretics be administered in children? Immediately upon detection of a fever Only after the diagnostic samples have been collected Only when children start to become uncomfortable Never, antipyretics are not effective in children The correct answer is C. Most fevers are not dangerous and so do not require treatment unless the child is uncomfortable. Antipyretics are safe to administer in children, and administration does not interfere with diagnostic testing

Which of the following is not a component in the chain of infection? Mode of Transmission Reservoir Susceptible Host Virulence of organism Portal of Exit The correct answer is D. Virulence of the organism impacts its probability of transmission and infection but is not a component in the chain of infection. The chain of infection is: Infectious Host Reservoir Portal of Exit Means of Transmission Portal of Entry Susceptible Host

Which of the following statements is false Ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone) has excellent activity against Gram negative bacteria Vancomycin is a weakly bactericidal agent that binds to the bacterial cell wall Vancomycin is effective against MRSA Aminoglycosides (like gentamycin and tobramycin) are active against Gram positive bacteria Macrolides can be used against respiratory tract infections The correct answer is D. Vancomycin Penicillin Cefazolin Pip-Tazo Amoxicillin The correct answer is C. Cefazolin/Cephalexin is great for most SSTI. (Here, S Aureus is a likely pathogen, so Penicillin is not sufficient)

A 35-year-old female patient has an intra-abdominal bacterial infection. Which of the following may not be a sufficient treatment for this patient? Pip-Tazo Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone Metronidazole + Ceftriaxone Aminoglycoside + Metronidazole Carbapenems The correct answer is B. With intra-abdominal infections, bacteria from the gut need to be covered. This includes aerobic and anaerobic gram-negative organisms. Vancomycin does not have gram negative coverage

Which of the following statements is incorrect? I. Effective reproductive number is dependent on population behavior II. Antigenic shift involves one virus III. Hemagglutinin protein on the influenza virus plays a role in binding to the target cell IV. NA (Neuraminidase) is important in replicating the viral genome i, ii iii, iv i, ii, iv ii, iv The correct answer is D. Antigenic shift involves two viruses while drift is mutations within one virus. NA is important in the release of the virus.

Which of the following does the SARS-CoV-2 virus cause? Respiratory failure VTE (Stroke, DVT) Acute cardiac injury, arrythmias A & B All of the above The correct answer is E. Of the following cases, identify which individuals are vaccine hesitant (select all that apply) Kendra refuses to allow any of her children to receive vaccines and has petitioned the school board for vaccine exemption Andrew has received vaccines for the “deadly” diseases but prefers natural immunity against diseases like chicken pox and COVID-19 Brittany and her children have not been vaccinated against COVID-19 because she has not been able to take time off from work. Andrew and Miley are vaccine hesitant.

The following epidemic curve is an example of Intermittent common-source outbreak Propagated outbreak Continuous common-source outbreak Point common-source The correct answer is B. Occurs when transmission is from one person to another; Cases occur over more than one incubation period

What is true about the viral lifecycle and antivirals? It is easy to create antivirals as viruses utilize molecules that are very different from host molecules, making it easy to find targets. HA is a protein on the virus envelope that binds sialic acid to gain entry into cells.

What is FALSE about Vancomycin resistance? High level resistance occurs when the cell wall alters its structure from D-Ala-D- Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac, thus preventing the antibiotic from binding to the cells wall Intermediate resistance occurs when the cell wall gets thicker, thus preventing the efficacy of the antibiotic High level resistance is an adaptive response, depending on the mutation of existing genes High level resistance depends on the acquisition of new genes on a mobile genetic element High level resistance exists in S. aureus The correct answer is C. High level resistance is a plasmid acquisition related response. It is not adaptive. Intermediate resistance is adaptive.

What is TRUE about septic shock? It is defined as low blood pressure that could respond to fluids 50% of the time Sepsis can only be caused by bacteria that affect humans Sepsis can cause reduced heart function by decreasing heart rate and blood pressure The qSOFA score is used to recognize sepsis clinically It is unimportant to identify the cause of the sepsis, only important to treat it right away The correct answer is D. qSOFA is used to diagnose sepsis clinically. What are the main roles of the immune system? Removal of pathogens Removal of foreign cells Removal of lactate Removal of damaged cells A, B, D The correct answer is E. A, B and D are all functions of the immune system. The removal of lactate is done primarily by the liver.

What are some of the clinical features of a phagocytic disorder? Which of the following can be performed to help diagnose an autoimmune condition? Antibody testing Genetic testing Biopsy All of the above The correct answer is D. All of the above are methods used to diagnose autoimmune conditions.

Which of the following is true regarding autoimmune diseases? Females are more likely to have them than males Symptoms happen at an early age Symptoms are typically the result of inflammation A and C None of the above The correct answer is D. Females are more likely than males to have autoimmune conditions, and symptoms are a consequence of ongoing inflammation as well as resulting organ dysfunction. Symptoms can happen at any age.

What can cause false positive and negative results in food allergy testing? Choose the most correct option. Not having enough antigen, which can lead to false positives The extract does not contain the relevant protein – false negatives Spiked extracts have very little antigen and have weak responses None of the above The correct answer is B. Not having the relevant protein can lead to false negatives. Not having enough antigen would lead to false negatives, not false positives. And spiked extracts have too much antigen, leading to too strong responses, and thus, false positives.

Which of the following correctly outlines the sequence of events of RAST testing? This is the correct sequence of events. Proteins are extracted, fixed to solid phase surface, and then the patients’ serum is isolated, added to protein adhered to the solid phase. Which of the following is true in terms of treating patients with allergies? Education at each touchpoint with a healthcare provider is unimportant Family doctors are often the first point of contact for mild allergies Severe allergic reactions often present to their family physician None of the above The correct answer is B. Family doctors as well as pharmacists are often the first point of contact for patients experiencing allergic reactions. Education at each touchpoint IS important, and severe reactions often present to the emergency room.

Which of the following is false? An allergist can provide education to a patient presenting with suspected allergies An allergist only considers different factors that a family doctor did not consider before The role of the family doctor is to provide a presumptive diagnosis Pharmacists do not provide a diagnosis The correct answer is B. Which of the following is true regarding the comparing of an HIV patient with a CD4 of less than 50 (patient A) and an HIV patient with a CD4 of great than 500 (patient B) Patient A is more at risk of mycobacterium avium infections, CMV rhinitis, and lymphoma Patient A and B are at equal risk of mycobacterium avium infections, CMV rhinitis, and lymphoma Patient A could be at risk of developing TB whereas patient B is not at risk of developing TB Both patient A and B could be at risk of developing TB. A and D The correct answer is E. Patient A is much more immunocompromised compared to patient B, thus they are at much higher risk of developing mycobacterium avium infections, CMV rhinitis, and lymphoma. The patients are also at risk of developing TB at any CD4 T cell count.

Which one of the following is the best approach to protecting a patient undergoing allogeneic stem cell transplant against infections? Vaccinate the patient before the transplant Vaccinate the patient Vaccinate the patient after the transplant, particularly in phase III, where they have regained their T cells and B cells Vaccinate the patient after the transplant, particularly in phase II, where they have recovered their NK cells The correct answer is A. Vaccine effectiveness greatly relies on T cell and B cell mediated adaptive immunity. Which of the following are features of cells in chronic granulomatous inflammation Langhan cells Cells with eccentric nuclei that have a “clock face” appearance Epithelioid histiocytes A and C All of the above The correct answer is D. Which of the following is not a potential cause of chronic inflammation TB Malnutrition Rheumatoid arthritis Silicosis The correct answer is B. Persistent infection (TB), hypersensitivity (Rheumatoid arthritis) and chronic exposures to toxins (silicosis) are all potential causes for chronic inflammation.

A patient comes in with suspected cryptococcus infection, what are your next steps? A 50 year old women with HIV presents to your family medicine clinic with fever, shortness of breath, and a cough. You take her vitals and realize that she is hypoxic, with an O2 saturation of 92%. Which of the following is not a key characteristic of HSV? Can develop latency Double stranded DNA virus Transmitted by airborne transmission Can manifest as oral or genital herpes The correct answer is C. HSV is transmitted through contact with active lesions or asymptomatic shedding.

A 25 year old women comes to your family medicine clinic and is quite upset because she just found out that her partner has HSV-2. There is no vaccine for HSV. cefazolin and cloxacillin are antibiotics that are not used for the treatment of HSV. Antivirals including acyclovir and valacyclovir are possible treatments.

Which of the following matches the class of antifungals with its mechanism of action? Which of the following statements is true of antifungals? Echinocandins should be used for CNS fungal infections as they can easily cross the BBB Amphotericin B should be used for a patient with renal failure as it is not nephrotoxic Fluconazole can be prescribed as both IV and oral formulations Dimorphic fungi are primarily treated with antibiotics rather than antifungals The correct answer is C. Echinocandins are not used for eye, CNS or urine fungal infections as they poorly penetrate those systems; Amphotericin B is nephrotoxic so is contraindicated in a patient with renal failure. Dimorphic fungi are treated with antifungals.

A 45-year-old has a fluctuant, pus-filled lesion on his thigh. Gram stain of the drained pus shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters; the isolate is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which organism is it? Staphylococcus aureus Streptococcus pyogenes Enterococcus faecalis Streptococcus pneumoniae Staphylococcus epidermidis The correct answer is A. Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase + and coagulase + are S. aureus , which tends to cause abscesses and purulent infection. S. pyogenes is catalase −, β-hemolytic, in chains; S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative.

A sputum smear from a man with chronic cough and night sweats is stained with Ziehl-Neelsen. Thin rods stain red against a blue background. What property of the organism explains the red staining? Thick peptidoglycan retaining crystal violet Outer membrane lipopolysaccharide Mycolic acid in the cell wall A polysaccharide capsule Absence of a cell wall The correct answer is C. Mycobacteria are acid-fast: the waxy mycolic acid in their wall resists acid-alcohol decolourisation, so they keep the red carbol fuchsin (acid-fast positive = red; negative = blue). Crystal violet retention is the Gram-positive trait.

Ten days after stepping on a rusty nail, a farmer has jaw stiffness (trismus) and painful generalised muscle spasms. What does the responsible toxin do? Blocks acetylcholine release Forms pores in neutrophils Ribosylates actin in colonocytes Cleaves ribosomal RNA Blocks GABA/glycine release The correct answer is E. Tetanus toxin blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters GABA/glycine → spastic paralysis (trismus, opisthotonos). Blocking acetylcholine release is botulinum toxin → flaccid paralysis; actin ribosylation is the C. difficile binary toxin.

A marathon runner collapses on a hot day with a core temperature of 41.8 °C. Acetaminophen given en route has not lowered it. Which feature best separates this from fever? The set point is unchanged Endogenous pyrogens are elevated Peripheral heat loss is intact PGE2 has reset the thermostat Temperature follows a diurnal pattern The correct answer is A. Hyperthermia is dysregulated heat balance with a normal set point: excess production, diminished loss, can exceed 41 °C and does not respond to antipyretics. Fever is a set point raised by pyrogens via PGE2, rarely exceeds 41 °C, keeps peripheral mechanisms intact and respon

A 60-year-old has had fevers for 10 days after a bout of diverticulitis. By timing of onset, how is this fever classified, and which cause does that category point to? Acute; viral infection Subacute; intra-abdominal abscess Chronic; tuberculosis Acute; urinary tract infection Chronic; connective tissue disease The correct answer is B. Acute fever is < 7 days (viral, SSTI, UTI, pneumonia); subacute is 1–2 weeks, classically an intra-abdominal abscess; chronic is > 2 weeks (TB, HIV, cancer, connective tissue disease).

A 70-year-old with pneumonia is confused, RR 26 and BP 88/50. Blood cultures cannot be drawn for another hour because of difficult venous access. What is the best next step? Wait for blood cultures, then start antibiotics Start oral antibiotics after chest CT Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics now Give antipyretics and reassess in an hour Start vasopressors and hold antibiotics The correct answer is C. Nothing saves lives in sepsis like early, appropriate antibiotics: from the onset of hypotension each hour of delay adds ~8% mortality. Draw cultures first only if doing so will not delay antibiotics. The review makes the same point: do not delay treatment while waiting for

A patient with urosepsis remains at BP 78/44 after 3 L of IV crystalloid. What defines this state, and what is added? Severe sepsis; add a second antibiotic SIRS; observe on the ward Hypovolemic shock; give more fluid Septic shock; add vasopressors Septic shock; stop the fluids The correct answer is D. Septic shock is low blood pressure that does not respond to fluids — arteriolar vasodilation plus capillary leak — so vasopressors are added as life support while antibiotics and source control treat the cause. Mortality is 30–40%.

Six weeks after a kidney transplant, a patient develops fever, leukopenia and CMV viremia. Which antiviral is first line? Acyclovir Valacyclovir Zanamivir Oseltamivir Ganciclovir The correct answer is E. Ganciclovir (IV) or its oral prodrug valganciclovir is the CMV drug; acyclovir/valacyclovir are for HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV; foscarnet is reserved for drug-resistant virus. Neuraminidase inhibitors are for influenza.

A man with advanced HIV has headache and fever; CSF India ink and cryptococcal antigen are positive. What is the induction regimen? Amphotericin B + flucytosine Caspofungin Liposomal amphotericin B alone Fluconazole alone Itraconazole The correct answer is A. Cryptococcal meningitis: induction with amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole for consolidation and maintenance. The review adds: test for HIV, especially with meningitis. Voriconazole is the Aspergillus drug; caspofungin covers Candida .

A patient with prolonged neutropenia after chemotherapy develops fever and nodular lung lesions; bronchoalveolar lavage grows a filamentous mould, Aspergillus fumigatus. Which drug is first line? Fluconazole Voriconazole Caspofungin Topical nystatin Flucytosine The correct answer is B. Invasive aspergillosis → voriconazole (second-generation azole, 6–12 weeks), with amphotericin B as an alternative. Fluconazole does not cover moulds; caspofungin is the reliable Candida agent.

A patient with candidemia is started on caspofungin. What does this drug inhibit? Lanosterol 14α-demethylase Fungal DNA synthesis 1,3-β-D-glucan synthesis Ergosterol in the membrane Squalene epoxidase The correct answer is C. Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) block 1,3-β-D-glucan synthesis → defective cell wall; IV only, few interactions, reliable for Candida . Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase; polyenes bind ergosterol; flucytosine hits DNA/RNA synthesis.

An ICU patient on gentamicin for Gram-negative sepsis develops tinnitus and hearing loss, and his creatinine doubles. Which antibiotic class caused this? Macrolide Carbapenem Tetracycline Fluoroquinolone Aminoglycoside The correct answer is E. Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside: it binds 30S (bactericidal), covers aerobic Gram-negatives, and is nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Fluoroquinolones carry tendon, aortic and CNS warnings; macrolides and tetracyclines are bacteriostatic.

An Enterococcus faecium bloodstream isolate is resistant to vancomycin. How has the organism changed the drug's target? It produces a β-lactamase It expresses PBP2a from mecA It methylates its 23S ribosomal RNA target D-Ala–D-Ala is altered to D-Ala–D-Lac It mutates DNA gyrase The correct answer is D. Vancomycin binds the D-Ala–D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan; VRE swap it for D-Ala–D-Lac so the drug cannot bind. PBP2a/ mecA is MRSA; 23S methylation is macrolide resistance; gyrase mutation is fluoroquinolone resistance.

A 55-year-old has a perforated sigmoid colon with peritonitis. Which empiric regimen covers the Gram-negative aerobes and the anaerobes? Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole Oral cephalexin plus amoxicillin Vancomycin alone Azithromycin plus doxycycline Nitrofurantoin The correct answer is A. Intra-abdominal infection needs Gram-negative plus anaerobic cover: ceftriaxone (or an aminoglycoside) for the aerobes, plus metronidazole for the anaerobes. Metronidazole covers anaerobes only, which is why it is paired.

A 32-year-old has had three pneumonias and recurrent sinusitis over two years. Her serum IgG is low. What is the most likely diagnosis? Selective IgA deficiency Common variable immunodeficiency Chronic granulomatous disease Terminal complement (C5–C9) deficiency Severe combined immunodeficiency The correct answer is B. CVID is the most common symptomatic primary immunodeficiency: it can present in adulthood with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and is treated with IgG replacement. Selective IgA deficiency is the most common overall but mostly asymptomatic; SCID presents in the first 6 mo

A newborn's Ontario screen is flagged for a low T cell receptor excision circle (TREC) count. Which condition is the screen designed to catch? Chronic granulomatous disease Selective IgA deficiency Terminal complement (C9) deficiency Common variable immunodeficiency Severe combined immunodeficiency The correct answer is E. TRECs are the DNA circles cut out during T cell receptor rearrangement, so low or absent TRECs mean few T cells. SCID — the most severe immunodeficiency, fatal without bone marrow transplant — is screened for this way so infants can be transplanted before infection.

A 3-year-old boy has had a liver abscess, S. aureus skin abscesses and Aspergillus pneumonia. Biopsies show granulomas. Which is the most likely disorder? Common variable immunodeficiency Selective IgA deficiency Chronic granulomatous disease Terminal complement deficiency Severe combined immunodeficiency The correct answer is C. Phagocytic disorders are the most common primary innate immunodeficiency, and CGD is the most common of them: an NADPH oxidase defect leaves phagocytes unable to kill catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, with abscesses and granulomas. Nine days after starting a sulfonamide, a patient develops fever, mucosal erosions and widespread skin detachment (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Which hypersensitivity type is this? Type I, IgE-mediated Type II, antibody against cell surface Type III, immune complex Type IV, T cell-mediated Not a hypersensitivity reaction The correct answer is D. SJS/TEN are type IV (delayed, cell-mediated) reactions: CD8+ CTLs lyse targets and CD4+ cells drive cytokine inflammation, with onset over days. Type I is minutes (IgE, mast cells), type II is antibody against cells (drug-induced cytopenia), type III is immune complexes (ser

Minutes after eating a cashew, a 19-year-old has hives, lip swelling, wheeze and BP 82/50. What is given first? IM epinephrine IV diphenhydramine Nebulised salbutamol IV methylprednisolone Oral cetirizine The correct answer is A. Anaphylaxis is treated with prompt IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000, max 0.3 mg, repeat every 5–15 min); antihistamines, salbutamol and steroids come only after. The review: EpiPen is the treatment.

The day after a bee sting on the forearm, a 40-year-old has swelling of 14 cm spreading continuously from the sting site, with no hives elsewhere and no breathing or GI symptoms. How is this reaction classified? Normal local reaction Systemic cutaneous reaction Systemic extracutaneous reaction Anaphylaxis Large local reaction The correct answer is E. Swelling at the sting site greater than 10 cm is a large local reaction. A systemic cutaneous reaction is skin-only and not contiguous with the sting; a systemic extracutaneous reaction involves other organ systems (bronchospasm, hypotension, GI).

A 30-year-old gets bloating and diarrhea after milk. Lactase deficiency is confirmed and skin prick testing to milk is negative. How is this reaction classified? Food allergy Food intolerance Food aversion Type I hypersensitivity Non-immediate food allergy The correct answer is B. An intolerance has a known, non-immune mechanism (lactose intolerance). An allergy has an immunological explanation; an aversion has no mechanism and is not reproducible when the food is given blinded.

Parents of a 5-month-old with severe eczema ask how to lower her risk of peanut allergy. Which principle guides the advice? Oral exposure sensitises, skin exposure builds tolerance Avoiding all allergens until age 3 prevents allergy Skin exposure sensitises; eating builds tolerance Eczema protects against food allergy Breast milk alone prevents all food allergy The correct answer is C. The dual antigen hypothesis: sensitisation to foods occurs through inflamed, broken skin (eczema is a risk factor), while tolerance develops when the food is eaten. Hence early oral introduction of allergenic foods.

A 50-year-old on high-dose prednisone and mycophenolate for lupus nephritis is due for vaccines. Which vaccine should be avoided? Inactivated influenza Tetanus-diphtheria toxoid Pneumococcal conjugate Measles-mumps-rubella Hepatitis B The correct answer is D. MMR is a live attenuated vaccine, and live vaccines are generally unsafe in immunocompromised patients (vaccinate before immunosuppression where possible). Inactivated, toxoid, conjugate and subunit vaccines are safe, though responses may be weaker.

A 35-year-old needs perioperative cefazolin but reports a childhood 'penicillin allergy' (a rash). What is true about this label? Most such patients are truly allergic Over 90% are not allergic on skin testing Delayed reactions usually wane over time It must never be tested Skin testing is unreliable for IgE allergy The correct answer is B. More than 90% of patients reporting penicillin allergy are not allergic on skin testing; immediate reactions wane (80% not allergic after 10 years of avoidance), while delayed reactions persist for life. Skin prick testing is the most reliable test for IgE-mediated penicilli

Circulation, the Cardiac Cycle & Cardiac Electrical Physiology How blood moves through a series pulmonary circuit and a parallel systemic circuit, how one cardiac cycle fills and empties the ventricle, and the ion currents that make the heart beat. The organising idea: pressure gradients open and close the valves , and ion gradients set the rhythm. EF = SV/EDV (normal 50–60%; EDV 120 mL, ESV 50 mL). S1 = AV valves close, S2 = semilunar valves close. Veins hold ~70% of blood volume. Capillary pressure ~20 mm Hg – any compartment above that compromises perfusion. Cardiac AP: phase 0 Na+ in, phase 2 Ca2+ plateau, phase 3 K+ out ; SA node self-excites from -55 to -60 mV to a -40 mV threshold, and the AV node delay (0.13 s) is the longest step. Blood flow through the heart Venous return → atria → AV valves → ventricles → semilunar valves → arteries Right heart Left heart Atrium → valve Right atrium → tricuspid valve Left atrium → mitral valve Ventricle → valve Right ventricle → pulmonary valve Left ventricle → aortic valve Outflow To lungs (pulmonary artery) To systemic circulation (aorta) Circuit Pulmonary circulation – low pressure • Oxygenation • Carbon dioxide removal/ventilation Systemic circulation – high pressure • Oxygenated blood • Redistribution The four chambers and their valves: right side (blue) receives venous return, left side (red) ejects to the aorta. Oxygen delivery Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × oxygen content Oxygen content = oxygen bound to Hb + dissolved oxygen Oxygen content = (O2 saturation × Hb × 1.34) + (pO2 × 0.3) Microvascular perfusion at the tissue level is important for oxygen delivery at a cellular level Oxygen delivery must meet requirements for oxygen consumption 200 mL of O2 in every 1 L of blood, but only use 250 mL Venous pO2 depends on the balance between supply and demand Pathways of blood flow Pulmonary circulation Systemic circulation Role Separates the right and left ventricle Organ and tissue perfusion Pressure Low pressure system (20/10) – RV less muscular than LV High pressure system (120/80) – can change blood-flow distribution • Dehydration/hypervolemia: less skin and kidney perfusion to retain water • Exercise: vasodilation of skin and muscles Arrangement In series – output of RV and LV matched In parallel Resistance R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 + R4 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + 1/R4 The pulmonary and systemic circuits are in series, so RV and LV output must match. Organ beds of the systemic circulation sit in parallel, which lets flow be redistributed between them. Distribution of blood to organs at rest: share of the 5 L/min cardiac output and flow per 100 g for each organ. The vasculature – 100 000 miles! Vessel Features Arteries • High pressure system ( 120/80 ) • Rapid transit • Distensible – become less elastic with increasing age • Elastic arteries = conducting arteries ; elastic fibres (pressure reservoir) • Muscular arteries = distributing arteries ; smooth muscle (vasoconstriction) Arterioles • Resistance vessels – vasoconstriction, vasodilation • Thick, elastic, muscular walls • Control of microvascular blood flow to various organs Capillaries • Large cross-sectional area • Exchange system – nearby cells extract nutrients/deposit wastes • Slow, non-pulsatile flow • Length = 0.3–1 mm • Capillary pressure = 20 mm Hg • Capillary refill evaluates microvascular flow clinically; chronic vasoconstriction, hypovolemia, or obstructive shock will delay the refill Venules and veins • Capacitance vessels – hold 70% of blood volume • Low pressure system • Compliant • Able to contract and dilate • Valves propel blood back to the heart – varicose veins if incompetent Where’s the blood? Most of it sits in the veins. Compartment % of blood volume Heart 10% Systemic arteries 12% Capillaries 6% Large veins 15% Small veins 45% Lungs 12% The biggest pressure drop is across the arterioles – the resistance vessels. Cross-sectional area peaks at the capillaries, which is why flow there is slow. Capacitance Total body fluid = 60% of body weight Blood volume = 5 L Vasodilation → increased capacitance Vasoconstriction → decreased capacitance Only a finite ability to compensate: after maximum constriction, any additional blood loss will unmask hypovolemia, which may present as a sudden deterioration Compensation in a low-flow state Arteriolar vasoconstriction Venoconstriction Redistribution of flow to vital organs Increased oxygen extraction Decrease in venous pO2 The cardiac cycle SYSTOLE = CONTRACTION (atrial systole, ventricular systole) DIASTOLE = RELAXATION AND FILLING OF VENTRICLES Graph below is of the L side of the heart; the R side looks very similar but with much lower pressures Electrocardiogram = electrical conduction; phonocardiogram = heart sounds Ventricular systole: isovolumetric contraction → rapid ejection → reduced ejection Ventricular diastole: isovolumetric relaxation → rapid filling → reduced filling → atrial systole Line up each valve event with the ECG and heart sounds: S1 at AV valve closure, S2 at aortic valve closure. Step Events Volume Pressure 1. Atrial systole a wave · P wave · S4 may be heard • AV valves open • Pulmonary/aortic valves closed • There is a delay between electrical and mechanical events in the heart • Normally a small contribution to ventricular filling • Increased ventricular volume • In some clinical situations atrial systole is more important for filling: – High HR: less diastolic time – Stiff ventricle: does not fill well passively • Atrial fibrillation : atria have no organized contraction; HR irregularly irregular; no atrial systole • Slight increase in atrial pressure 2. Isovolumetric contraction c wave · QRS complex · S1 • Ventricles begin to contract • AV valves close • Pulmonary/aortic valves closed • Maximum ventricular volume unchanged • End-diastolic volume (EDV) : volume in the ventricle at the end of diastole, before the heart contracts; 120 mL • Increase in ventricular pressure closes the AV valves •

ECG Basics and Interpretation The ECG records the heart’s depolarization as seen from 12 viewpoints; a wave moving toward a positive electrode writes an upward deflection . Everything else – leads, axis, localising an infarct – follows from that one rule, read in a fixed order: rate, rhythm, axis, hypertrophy, ischemia. PR 120–200 ms, QRS 80–120 ms, QT ≤ 440 ms (M) / ≤ 460 ms (F). Rate by 300-150-100-75-60-50. Normal axis -30° to +90° (leads I and aVF). Localise STEMI by lead group: anterior V1–V4 = LAD, inferior II/III/aVF = RCA, lateral I/aVL/V5–V6 = circumflex , confirmed by reciprocal changes. Mobitz I = progressive PR (benign); Mobitz II = constant PR with drops (pacemaker). Electrocardiogram basics Electrocardiogram (ECG, EKG) : records the electrical activity of the heart – myocardial contraction As a wave of depolarization (positive charges) within the myocytes flows TOWARD a positive electrode, a positive (upward) deflection is recorded Most of the QRS reflects the LV because of its high mass – current flows from top to bottom, then R to L P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; ST (plateau) and T (rapid phase) = ventricular repolarization. Depolarization moving toward the electrode (the eyes) records an upright deflection. Moving away from the electrode records a negative deflection. Travelling perpendicular to the electrode gives a small biphasic complex. ECG paper Smallest divisions = 1 × 1 mm ; heavy black squares = 5 × 5 mm Horizontal axis = time : 1 mm = 40 ms, 5 mm = 200 ms Vertical axis = amplitude/voltage : 10 mm = 1 mV Calibration signal = 1 box wide × 2 boxes high Lead changeover marker = small spike A normal 12-lead ECG: note the grid, the calibration pulse and the lead changeover markers. ECG waves Wave / interval Represents Normal / notes P wave Atrial depolarization and contraction PR interval Pause at the AV node before ventricular depolarization 120–200 ms QRS complex Ventricular depolarization and contraction 80–120 ms • Q: first downward deflection; often absent • R: first upward deflection • S: any downward wave preceded by an upward wave • QS: no upward wave ST segment Plateau phase of ventricular repolarization Normally level with baseline – pathology if elevated or depressed T wave Late phase of rapid ventricular repolarization QT interval Duration of ventricular systole Less than half the R-to-R interval at normal rates Males ≤ 440 ms; females ≤ 460 ms Prolonged by genetics, drugs, electrolytes, hypothermia U wave Ventricular repolarization Can be normal or a sign of hypokalemia Depolarization (1), plateau (2) and repolarization (3) of the myocyte map onto QRS, ST segment and T wave. The 12 standard ECG leads 6 limb leads (R arm, L arm, L leg) + 6 chest leads . Lead Positive electrode Negative electrode Bipolar limb leads (Einthoven’s triangle) Lead I Left arm Right arm Lead II Left leg Right arm Lead III Left leg Left arm Augmented limb leads (unipolar) aVR Right arm Left arm + left leg (common ground) aVL Left arm Right arm + left leg (common ground) aVF (II + III) Left leg Left arm + right arm (common ground) Pushing the leads to the centres of their triangles forms six intersecting lines of reference Lie in a flat frontal (coronal) plane Each limb lead records from a different angle – a different view of the same cardiac activity Lateral leads (left arm positive): I, aVL Inferior leads (left leg positive): II, III, aVF → QRS should be positive aVR → QRS should be negative Modified electrode positions on the trunk (shoulders, abdomen) are commonly used to monitor patients in various settings Each limb lead looks at the heart from a different angle in the frontal plane. Chest wall leads (unipolar) – lie in a horizontal (transverse) plane ; each chest electrode is positive, projects through the patient’s back (negative), and is oriented through the AV node. Lead Views Position V1 Right chest 4th intercostal space, R sternal border V2 Right chest 4th intercostal space, L sternal border V3 Interventricular septum (RV) Midway between V2 and V4 V4 Interventricular septum (LV) 5th intercostal space, L midclavicular line V5 Left chest 5th intercostal space, L anterior axillary line V6 Left chest 5th intercostal space, L mid-axillary line Standard layout: I, aVL, V5, V6 lateral; II, III, aVF inferior; V1–V2 septal; V3–V4 anterior. ECG interpretation Work through the tracing in the same order every time. Rate Count large boxes between beats: say “300, 150, 100” … “75, 60, 50” Or calculate: rate = cycles per 10-second strip × 6 Sinus bradycardia : rate < 60/min · sinus tachycardia : rate > 100/min 1 large box = 0.2 s: 1 box → 300, 2 → 150, 3 → 100, 4 → 75, 5 → 60, 6 → 50 bpm. Rhythm Identify the basic rhythm, then scan for prematurity, pauses, irregularity and abnormal waves Check for: P before each QRS, QRS after each P, PR intervals (for AV blocks), QRS interval (for BBB) If axis deviation, rule out hemiblock Axis Normal = -30° to +90° ; check lead I and aVF; check lead II for left axis QRS above or below baseline gives the axis quadrant For axis in degrees, find the isoelectric QRS in a limb lead of the axis quadrant – use the “Axis in Degrees” chart Axis rotation in the horizontal plane – find the transitional QRS Lead I and aVF both upright = normal; I up, aVF down = LAD; I down, aVF up = RAD; both down = extreme RAD. Find the isoelectric limb lead, then read the axis in degrees for that quadrant. Hypertrophy – check V1 Location Leads Look for Right atrium II, III, aVF Tall P wave Right ventricle V1–V3 Large R wave Left atrium I, II, V1 Long notched or biphasic P wave Left ventricle V1, V6 Large S in V1 + large R in V6 > 35 mm Ischemia and infarction Check for: Q waves (necrosis/past infarction), inverted T waves (ischemia), ST elevation (infarction), ST depression (ischemia) Reciprocal changes : ST elevation ± ST depression on the mirror side of the STEMI location = true STEMI Find the location of the pathology, then identify the occlud
