Anatomy of the Mediastinum and the Heart A map of the chest’s middle compartment and the heart inside it. The organising idea is the sternal angle : it splits superior from inferior mediastinum, and from there each structure – chamber, valve, coronary branch, nerve – has a fixed place and a fixed job. Sternal angle (T4/T5) separates superior from inferior mediastinum and marks the carina. L recurrent laryngeal loops under the aortic arch; the R loops the subclavian. Pericardial pain refers via the phrenic (C3–C5) ; cardiac ischemic pain via T1–T4/5 . LAD = anterior 2/3 of the septum; posterior interventricular (RCA) = posterior 1/3. VSD is the most common heart defect. Bundle of His is the only electrical link between atria and ventricles. Anatomy of the mediastinum Mediastinum : the middle space between the two pleural sacs All thoracic structures are within the mediastinum except the lungs The sternal angle to the T4/T5 disc divides superior from inferior mediastinum. Division Boundaries Contents Superior mediastinum Superior thoracic aperture to the sternal angle anteriorly and the inferior border of T4 posteriorly Thymus gland · brachiocephalic veins · SVC · arch of aorta and branches · vagus nerve · L recurrent laryngeal nerve · ligamentum arteriosum · phrenic nerve · trachea · esophagus Inferior mediastinum Sternal angle to the diaphragm Divided into anterior, middle and posterior: Anterior : between the sternum and pericardial sac Thymus gland (children, adolescents) · fat (adults) · lymph nodes · internal thoracic vessels and branches Middle : within the pericardial sac Heart · ascending aorta · pulmonary vessels · terminal SVC · phrenic nerves Posterior : from the pericardial sac and lung roots to the thoracic vertebral bodies Descending aorta · thoracic duct · azygos venous system ( collateral pathway from the IVC in the abdomen ) · esophagus · sympathetic trunk · thoracic splanchnic nerves Arteries and veins of the mediastinum Left: aortic arch branches. Right: brachiocephalic veins, SVC and the azygos/hemiazygos system. Nerves of the mediastinum R/L phrenic nerves : arise in the neck from C3–C5 to innervate the diaphragm; often embedded in fat around the pericardial sac R/L vagus nerves : descend from the neck into the superior mediastinum; found posterior to the root of the lung , which distinguishes them from the phrenic nerves L recurrent laryngeal nerve : branch of the L vagus supplying many laryngeal muscles; loops under the arch of the aorta and ascends between trachea and esophagus to the larynx R recurrent laryngeal nerve : loops around the R subclavian artery and ascends between trachea and esophagus; it is NOT in the superior mediastinum Sympathetic chain : bilateral trunks either side of the vertebral column from skull base to coccyx Typically 12 ganglia (postsynaptic cell bodies) in the thoracic portion of each trunk Most presynaptic sympathetic fibres synapse in ganglia along the trunk Thoracic splanchnic nerves : presynaptic nerves that pass through the thoracic sympathetic trunk without synapsing , continue through the diaphragm into the abdomen to supply abdominal organs Greater : 5th–9th ganglia · lesser : 10th–11th · least : 12th thoracic ganglion Other structures in the mediastinum Trachea : from the larynx into the superior mediastinum, anterior to the esophagus; ends at the carina at the level of the sternal angle , bifurcating into R and L primary bronchi; it is NOT part of the posterior mediastinum Ligamentum arteriosum : remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosum, which shunted blood from the pulmonary trunk to the inferior surface of the aortic arch Esophagus : from the pharynx, posterior to the trachea; runs the entire length of the thorax before piercing the diaphragm to enter the stomach Thoracic duct : main lymphatic duct; begins in the abdomen, enters the thorax to the R of the aorta, ascends to the base of the neck and drains at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins Pericardium Pericardial sac : protective, fluid-filled, triple-layered sac around the heart and roots of the great vessels Fibrous pericardium (outer): dense, inelastic connective tissue attached to the diaphragm to anchor the heart; protects it and prevents overstretching Serous pericardium : thin, double-layered membrane that secretes serous fluid Parietal pericardium : lines the internal aspect of the fibrous pericardium Visceral pericardium : lines the heart and roots of the great vessels Pericardial cavity : serous fluid between the layers reduces friction as the heart moves Sensory : phrenic nerve (C3–C5) – pain radiates to the ipsilateral supraclavicular region (top of the shoulder) Sympathetic : cardiopulmonary splanchnic nerves (T1–T4) · parasympathetic : vagus nerve The arrow marks the infrasternal approach for pericardiocentesis. Clinical note Pericarditis : painful inflammation making the pericardial surface rough → friction heard as a rustling sound with a stethoscope Pericardial effusion : passage of fluid into the pericardial cavity Cardiac tamponade : compression of the heart; potentially lethal Can occur from cardiomegaly, or an illness/wound that lets blood or fluid enter the pericardium With extensive effusion the sac cannot let the heart fully expand → limits filling and reduces CO Pericardiocentesis removes fluid to relieve pressure: wide-bore needle into the 5th or 6th intercostal space near the sternum or via the infrasternal angle Anatomy of the heart Located in the inferior, middle mediastinum; rests on the diaphragm between the lungs and the ribs The apex lies on the left Generates and conducts electrical impulses for contraction so blood can be transported to the lungs and throughout the body Chambers of the heart Chamber Key features Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body • R auricle and anterior portion contain pectinate muscles • Crista terminalis separates the pectinate muscles from the smooth posterior wall • F

Normal Heart Sounds and Classifying Cardiac Murmurs Two normal sounds mark valve closure; two extra sounds and every murmur point to a specific abnormal load or valve. The organising idea: describe a murmur by timing, location, intensity and shape , and the diagnosis narrows itself. S1 = mitral + tricuspid close; S2 = aortic + pulmonary close. S3 = volume-loaded ventricle (early diastolic, can be normal when young); S4 = stiff ventricle (late diastolic, atrial kick). Regurgitant = leaky, stenotic = tight. Grade IV = thrill ; diastolic murmurs top out at IV. Normal and additional heart sounds Sound Cause Timing Significance S1 (LUB) Mitral and tricuspid valves closing Start of systole Normal S2 (DUB) Aortic and pulmonary valves closing End of systole Normal S3 (ken-TUC-ky) Rush of blood into the LV Early diastolic Volume-loaded ventricle : mitral regurgitation, severe diastolic dysfunction Can be normal in young patients S4 (ten-nes-SEE) Atrial contraction forces blood through the AV valves, striking the LV Late diastolic Stiff, non-compliant ventricle Classifying cardiac murmurs Murmur : an audible sound from increased blood flow through normal cardiac structures, or turbulent flow through abnormal ones Regurgitant valve = leaky · stenotic valve = tight Describe every murmur by: Timing : systole, diastole, or both Location of maximum intensity : sternal border (tricuspid), base (aortic, pulmonary), apex (mitral) Intensity : grading scales (below) Shape : ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) or holosystolic for systolic murmurs; decrescendo for diastolic murmurs Intensity grading – systolic murmurs go to VI, diastolic only to IV. Grade Systolic murmurs Diastolic murmurs I Barely audible Barely audible II Audible Audible III Loud but without palpable thrill Loud but without palpable thrill IV Thrill present Thrill present V Audible with stethoscope tilted off the chest wall — VI Audible with stethoscope away from the chest — Split first by timing, then by where it is loudest; the tables separate the candidates by radiation, apex beat, S2 and extra sounds (e.g. AS radiates to the carotids with a single S2; MR radiates to the axilla).

Determinants of Cardiac Output: The Heart as a Pump Cardiac output is heart rate × stroke volume , and stroke volume is set by three levers – preload, afterload and contractility . Each lever helps a normal heart; the recurring lesson is how a failing heart stops responding to them. CO = HR × SV (5 L/min; SV 60–70 mL). Tachycardia shortens diastole, when the LV is perfused → demand ischemia. Frank-Starling: ↑ EDV → ↑ SV up to an optimal sarcomere length. Afterload by Laplace: tension = P × r / (2 × wall thickness) ; pressure overload → concentric, volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy . Contractility is independent of preload and afterload. A failing heart is insensitive to preload but very sensitive to afterload. Determinants of cardiac output Cardiac output (CO) : blood pumped in one minute; increases with oxygen demand (exercise, fever); normal = 5 L/min CO = HR × SV Cardiac index : relates heart performance to body size – CI = CO/body surface area (L/min/m2) CO = HR × SV, and SV is set by preload, afterload and contractility – the structure of this lecture. Heart rate Heart rate (HR) : contractions per minute; normal resting HR = 70–80 bpm The SA node pacemaker sets HR; normal intrinsic resting SA node rate = 110 Parasympathetic input (vagus) decreases HR – athlete resting HR = 50–60 bpm Sympathetic input increases HR Heart transplants are denervated : No PSNS innervation – higher HR from the intrinsic SA node rate No SNS innervation – circulating catecholamines can still cause tachycardia Force-frequency relationship (Bowditch/treppe phenomenon): ↑ HR increases the force of contraction, but only up to a maximum rate; not as effective for failing ventricles ↑ HR decreases diastolic time → decreased CO and decreased cardiac perfusion Force rises with rate up to ~180/min in normal muscle; the failing heart gains almost nothing. Left coronary flow happens mainly in diastole – so tachycardia, which shortens diastole, starves the LV. Changes in HR Bradycardia = HR too low → low CO if SV does not increase Tachycardia = HR too high → ↑ myocardial oxygen consumption, ↓ myocardial perfusion (occurs mainly during diastole for the LV), ↓ time for diastolic filling; demand ischemia Increasing age → ↓ maximal HR ( 220 – age ) and maximal oxygen consumption; stiffer aorta and ventricles Stroke volume and preload Stroke volume (SV) : blood pumped in one contraction; normal = 60–70 mL Preload (EDV) : the blood that fills the ventricles during diastole and stretches them to their greatest dimensions Starling’s law : the more a muscle fibre is stretched, the greater its contractile energy There is an optimal sarcomere length ; beyond it there is no further increase in tension ↑ preload/EDV → ↑ SV Frank-Starling curves : show how changes in ventricular preload change SV SV climbs with EDV as sarcomeres approach their optimal length, then plateaus. Determinants of preload Determinant Effect on preload Blood volume ↑ volume → ↑ preload Venous tone ↑ venous tone → ↑ preload Ventricular compliance A more compliant ventricle holds more blood at a given pressure than a noncompliant one Afterload ↑ afterload → ↑ preload: less blood ejected, more residual blood adds to EDV Contractility More blood ejected in systole → less left to add to EDV Atrial contraction Atrial “kick” forces extra blood into the ventricle Intrathoracic pressure Excessive thoracic pressure can reduce venous return to the RV Clinical relevance of preload EDV cannot be easily measured or monitored Too little EDV → the heart is underfilled Too much EDV → the heart is overstretched → decompensation, ↑ LV diastolic pressure and congestion ( pulmonary edema ) A failing ventricle is less responsive to EDV The failing heart's curve is flat: more preload pushes it past the congestion line without adding much stroke volume. Case: hockey player with acute blood loss who feels faint Expected vital signs Heart rate : increased to help maintain CO Blood pressure : initially maintained by the sympathetic nervous system, then decreased from blood loss Oxygen saturation : normal – the lungs are functioning Respiratory rate : increased due to fear Temperature : decreased; may become hypothermic, especially if given blood products Urine output : decreased to preserve water and circulating volume How is he compensating? Reduced urine output and vasoconstriction to maintain SV Decreased capillary refill – blood is sent to vital organs rather than the extremities Management: stop the bleed (pressure); elevate the legs and give fluids or transfusions to increase SV; surgical intervention The case: acute hemorrhage in a previously healthy athlete. Afterload Afterload : the wall tension or stress the ventricle must develop to open the aortic valve and eject blood into the aorta Law of Laplace: tension = (pressure × radius)/(wall thickness × 2) Clinically simplified to pulmonary arterial pressure (right) or MAP (left) RV = lower afterload – generates less pressure to eject Decrease afterload clinically by decreasing pressure – vasodilator, intra-aortic balloon pump for LV failure; beware hypotension A normal heart tolerates afterload changes well; a failing heart is very sensitive to afterload ↑ RV afterload : pulmonary embolism with R heart failure – acute response : ventricular dilation, ↑ EDV + ESV, ↓ SV ↑ LV afterload : hypertension (↑ aortic pressure) – chronic response : concentric hypertrophy, ↑ wall thickness Good → compensatory, decreases afterload (wall stress) Bad → stiffer ventricle, more prone to ischemia, difficult to perfuse The more the heart fails, the more steeply SV falls as afterload rises. Hypertrophy : an increase in ventricular mass and cell volume. Hypertrophy type Stimulus Wall Physiologic (athlete’s heart) Training – normal, lower HR Changes are reversible Concentric Pressure overload ↑ relative wall thickness Eccentric (dilated) Volume overload Normal relative wall thickness Ventricular remodeling Changes in mass, volume and shape of t

Microcirculation, Vascular Flow and BP Regulation How the capillary bed exchanges material and fluid, and how flow and pressure are controlled – from Poiseuille’s law through the baroreflex to local metabolites. The organising idea: Flow = ΔP/R , and nearly every control mechanism works by changing R at the arterioles . R = 8ηl/πr⁴ – radius to the fourth power dominates. Optimal O2 delivery at hematocrit ~40% . Net fluid out at the arteriolar end, in at the venous end ; small ↑ interstitial pressure → 10-fold ↑ lymph flow. Aortic baroreceptors = vagus; carotid sinus = glossopharyngeal. Parasympathetics do not innervate vessels. Neurogenic shock = hypotension + bradycardia from lost T1–T4 sympathetic outflow. NO → cGMP → vasodilation; sildenafil blocks PDE5; bosentan blocks endothelin receptors. Macro- vs microcirculation Macrocirculation : transports material between organs – long distances, movement within vessels Microcirculation : distributes and exchanges material within organs – short distances, movement within capillaries; a network of arterioles, capillaries and venules Precapillary sphincters regulate blood flow into the capillary beds Arteriovenous anastomoses shunt blood directly to the venules – temperature regulation Precapillary sphincters gate the bed; the metarteriole and AV anastomosis let blood bypass it. Bulk flow and diffusion Bulk flow : movement of fluid along a vessel due to a pressure gradient ; resistance depends on vessel geometry and blood viscosity Diffusion : movement of material across a vessel wall due to a concentration gradient Factors: blood flow, concentration gradient, endothelial area, endothelial permeability Capillary endothelia have a high permeability; molecular movement depends on molecular weight, temperature and viscosity Major factors of material exchange: diffusion distance, capillary density Fick principle : ↑ flow → more arterial O2 available per minute → more exchange by diffusion (dO2/dt) Uptake = flow × ([arterial O2] – [venous O2]) Used to assess CO by measuring arterial and venous O2 Multi-directional flow in adjacent capillaries enhances uniform exchange The lung is an ideal exchange organ: large surface area, short diffusion distances, fast flow Poiseuille’s law Q = πPr⁴ / 8ηl or R = 8ηl / πr⁴ Q = flow rate · R = resistance · P = perfusion pressure · r = vessel radius · η = blood viscosity · l = vessel length Blood flow in vessels is generally laminar ; entering a smaller vessel, a parabolic flow profile develops Plasma skimming : natural separation of RBCs from plasma at bifurcations, dividing blood into relatively concentrated and dilute streams → low hematocrit entering the smaller capillaries Factors increasing turbulence: low/high blood viscosity (disrupt laminar flow), vessel obstructions (increased CO in pregnancy, atherosclerotic plaques, stenotic heart valves) The branch taking the cell-free edge layer gets fewer RBCs – the basis of plasma skimming. Hematocrit and viscosity Hematocrit : volume of blood occupied by packed RBCs; men = 45%, women = 40% Makes blood viscosity 3–4× that of water; provides the basis for laminar flow Low hematocrit: not enough O2-carrying capacity per volume High hematocrit: viscosity too high for adequate flow Optimal O2 delivery occurs when the hematocrit/viscosity ratio is maximized ↑ hematocrit in normal RBCs → small ↑ viscosity; in sickle cells → huge ↑ viscosity – they cannot deform at low PO2 The hematocrit/viscosity ratio peaks near 40% – the optimum for oxygen delivery. Sickle cells at low PO2 behave almost like rigid spheres: viscosity climbs steeply. Determinants of fluid exchange Transmural differences in tissue/capillary fluid pressures and oncotic pressures: Net fluid OUT at the arteriolar end of the capillary Net fluid IN at the venous end Changes in resistance in one vascular bed alter perfusion pressure and flow: ↑ vascular resistance → ↓ perfusion pressure and capillary flow ↓ vascular resistance → ↑ perfusion pressure and capillary flow Ultrafiltration : capillary pressure drives fluid out of the vessels Some returns to the circulation by plasma oncotic pressure Some remains in the interstitium – high capillary hydrostatic pressure and loss of large molecules from vessels (capillary damage, angiogenesis) lead to edema Lymphatics A one-way drainage returning lymph to the bloodstream to maintain circulatory homeostasis Distal endothelial cells overlap, letting proteins and fluid enter the lymphatic vessel Lymph reaches the subclavian veins mainly via surrounding muscle contraction and elastic recoil of the lungs Distal lymphatics = valves, no smooth muscle · tubular lymphatics = some smooth muscle Overlapping endothelial flaps open to let fluid and protein in, then close as one-way valves. Interstitial compliance High interstitial compliance: ↑ volume → small ↑ interstitial pressure – subcutaneous tissue Low interstitial compliance: ↑ volume → large ↑ interstitial pressure – brain When interstitial pressure is increased by -5 mm Hg (i.e. from about -5 toward 0 mm Hg), lymphatic flow increases 10-fold , which helps reduce edema Lymph flow rises 10-fold as interstitial pressure climbs from normal (-8 to 0 mm Hg). Cardiovascular Pharmacology A physiology review (flow, resistance, blood pressure control) followed by the drugs that act on it: the RAAS blockers, digoxin, nitrates, vasodilators, calcium channel blockers and beta blockers , then the autonomic (cholinergic and adrenergic) drugs . The organising idea: know where each drug acts in the pathway , and its effects, indications, contraindications and toxicities follow. Digoxin is the one HFrEF drug (vs ACEI, ARB, MRA, beta blockers) that does not reduce mortality — it reduces admissions for pulmonary edema. ACEI block bradykinin breakdown (dry cough, angioedema); ARBs have no effect on bradykinin and are used when ACEI cause cough. ACEI, ARBs and MRAs all predispose to hyperkalemia ; nitrates do not. Nitrates are contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors and need a nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance. Non-dihydropyridine CCBs are contraindicated in systolic heart failure. Anticholinergic toxidrome = dry skin; sympathomimetic = sweaty ; AChE inhibitors (sarin) = muscarinic + nicotinic effects. Circulatory system: function and organization Function: transport materials required by cells; transport hormones and metabolites; transfer heat from the core of the body to the surface; remove nitrogenous wastes and CO 2 from the body Organization: cardiopulmonary circulation (in series), systemic circulation (in parallel); arterial system (high pressure), venous system (low pressure) Overall goal: provide blood flow to organs in response to their needs Vessels Elastic arteries — closest to the heart; most elastin to withstand high pressure and recoil Muscular arteries — less elastin, more smooth muscle Arterioles — significant smooth muscle content; the greatest change in pressure occurs in the arteriole bed Capillary beds — link arterioles and venules; lined by a single layer of cells, allowing diffusion of materials from capillary to tissues and vice versa; in direct contact with the single-cell-layered alveolar sacs in the lungs Venules, veins — move blood back to the heart Flow, pressure and resistance Flow = ΔP / R ; SVR = ΔP / CO R = 8ηl / πr 4 (η = viscosity, l = vessel length, r = radius) Worked example: renal blood flow 500 mL/min, renal arterial pressure 100 mm Hg, renal venous pressure 10 mm Hg → R = ΔP / flow = (100 − 10 mm Hg) / 500 mL/min = 0.18 mm Hg/mL/min Mean arterial pressure — the average arterial pressure through one arterial cycle: MAP = CO × SVR = DP + 1/3(SP − DP) = 93 mmHg Laminar vs turbulent flow Laminar: slowest flow closest to the vessel wall, increasing velocity towards the centre Turbulent: disorganized flow at points of vessel obstruction; flow rate decreased, perfusion pressure increased Increases turbulence: low blood viscosity, high blood viscosity (as written in source) Hematocrit, viscosity and resistance Hematocrit contributes to blood viscosity, which is why blood flow is laminar Resistance is directly proportional to viscosity → an abnormally high hematocrit raises viscosity and vessel resistance In anemia, reduced hematocrit → reduced resistance Acute vs chronic blood pressure regulation Acute — neuronally controlled, responds rapidly to changes in BP → baroreceptors Chronic — hormonal, through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system → primary role of the kidneys AVP and ANP AVP: dehydration detected as increased extracellular osmolality → AVP released from the posterior pituitary → increases water permeability of the collecting ducts and water reabsorption → ↑ blood volume, ↑ BP ANP: peptide hormone released by atrial muscle cells in response to increased stretch from increased blood volume → increases GFR and decreases sodium reabsorption in the collecting ducts → ↓ blood volume, ↓ BP Local control of blood flow Metabolites — metabolic hypothesis: vasodilator metabolites regulate vascular tone Autoregulation — constant blood flow over a wide range of blood pressures Active regulation — in response to changes in blood flow reflecting metabolic demand Reactive regulation — occurs “after the fact” Reactive hyperemia — when flow in a vessel stops and then resumes, flow rises above the pre-blockage level Vascular smooth muscle tone Vasoconstriction: increased intracellular calcium initiates a second messenger pathway that results in decreased cGMP Vasodilation: decreased intracellular calcium leads to increased cGMP Nitric oxide maintains high cGMP in smooth muscle by increasing guanylyl cyclase activity (GTP → cGMP) ACE inhibitors (ACEI) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) ACEI (“-pril”) — block ACE: ↓ production of angiotensin II and block metabolism of bradykinin (bradykinin → vasodilatation is enhanced) ARB (“-sartan”) — block the AT 1 (angiotensin II) receptor; no effect on bradykinin Both impair angiotensin II actions: vasoconstriction, ↑ aldosterone (→ ↑ Na+ retention), ↑ sympathetic activity Mineralocorticoid antagonists (MRA) Aldosterone is an adrenal steroid hormone, stimulated for release by angiotensin II Binds mineralocorticoid receptors → Na+ and water retention, K+ excretion; also inflammatory and fibrosis effects MRAs have a cardioprotective effect in systolic heart failure — stop aldosterone from retaining water ACE inhibitors act at ACE (blocking both angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdown); AT 1 antagonists act at the receptor. The boxed actions below are what both impair. Where each RAAS step happens: liver → angiotensinogen; kidney → renin; ACE on the endothelium; angiotensin II → adrenal aldosterone. Investigations in Cardiovascular Disease How to investigate suspected ischemic heart disease, from history to catheter. The organising idea: match the test to the pretest probability and to the question (anatomy vs. function vs. viability) – no testing when risk is low, functional stress testing when it is intermediate, angiography when non-invasive results are high-risk. Hx and PEx are the most important investigations ; don't test asymptomatic low-risk patients (Framingham < 10%). Troponin is the most sensitive and specific marker of myocardial injury (rise 2-4 h, peak 12 h, normal by 5-10 days). Gold standards: MRI for chambers/global function, echo for valves, cardiac catheterization for coronary anatomy. CTCA is a test of exclusion (NPV 99%) . Withhold caffeine/theophylline 48 h before dipyridamole; dobutamine is preferred for stress echo. LV function is the strongest predictor of survival – LVEF normal > 50%, prognosis falls below 30-35%. Ischemia: insufficient blood supply to a specific organ The ischemic cascade — abnormalities appear in a fixed order as supply falls behind demand: First detectable abnormality: a perfusion abnormality at the cellular level Abnormalities of ventricular function Abnormalities detected on an ECG – ischemic ST depression Angina : chest pain related to myocardial ischemia, caused by coronary arterial narrowing/reduced blood flow to the heart The ischemic cascade: as exercise and myocardial O 2 demand rise, perfusion abnormality comes first, then regional diastolic → regional systolic → global LV dysfunction, then ischemic ST depression, and angina last. Symptoms and ECG are late markers. Approach to suspected ischemic heart disease Hx and PEx are the most important investigations for ischemic heart disease. Testing is NOT recommended in asymptomatic, low-risk patients → use the Framingham risk score Severe CAD requiring intervention in asymptomatic patients is rare False positive tests result in: inappropriate anxiety, adverse consequences related to work and insurance, complications from further diagnostic testing History Predictors of CAD: age, male gender, chest pain symptoms – most powerful Also: diabetes, smoking (½ ppd), hypercholesterolemia, ECG changes (Q waves, ST-T changes) Physical exam Angina pectoris : substernal squeezing chest pain (5-30 minutes); occurs with stress, emotion, or physical activity; relieved with rest or nitroglycerin Levine sign : chest hand-clutching; the universal sign of distress in angina pectoris and myocardial infarction; pain > 20 minutes Framingham risk score : estimated 10-year CVD risk, based on age, sex, smoking status, total cholesterol, HDL, and systolic BP. Framingham risk 10-yr CVD risk Management Low < 10% Lifestyle interventions; retest in 5 years with risk estimation Intermediate 10-19% Lifestyle interventions + moderate-potency statin High ≥ 20% Lifestyle interventions + high-potency statin; consider ASA ECG assesses electrical activity; an important tool in the diagnosis of myocardial ischemia or infarction. The ECG may be normal or nonspecific. Presentation ECG findings Classic angina Normal; ST segment depression and T wave abnormalities; Q waves STEMI ST elevation, T wave inversions, Q waves, LBBB NSTEMI ST segment depression and T wave inversions ECG limitations Underdiagnosis : a normal ECG does not exclude myocardial ischemia/infarction (though a normal ECG throughout the course of an acute MI is uncommon) → leads to undertreatment Overdiagnosis : ST elevation from other conditions – acute pericarditis, acute myocarditis, Brugada syndrome, early repolarization (normal), Prinzmetal's angina → exposes the patient to unneeded risk from overtreatment Laboratory investigations Complete blood count : hemoglobin Renal function : creatinine, microalbumin (especially if using contrast) Electrolytes : Na + , K + Glucose : diabetes, HbA1c Hypercholesterolemia : LDL, HDL, apolipoprotein B-100 (ApoB; main protein in LDL; not in ER) High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP): inflammation marker; atherosclerosis Cardiac biomarkers reflect acute damage to the myocardium: chemicals/enzymes are irreversibly released from injured muscle cells over a period of hours-days. Biomarker Kinetics Notes Troponin (acute chest pain) Initial rise 2-4 h Peak 12 h Normal by 5-10 days Most sensitive and specific for myocardial injury Larger MI = longer detection in blood Can also be elevated by contusion, myocarditis, stretch from PE, and arrhythmias Creatine kinase (CK-MB) Peak 10-24 h Specific if no skeletal muscle injury LDH Peak 24-72 h Myoglobin Peak 2 h Low specificity for MI Biomarker curves (multiples of the AMI cutoff vs. days after onset): troponin after a large MI rises highest and stays above the 99th-percentile cutoff for over a week; CK-MB peaks around day 1 and normalizes within a few days; a small MI gives only a low troponin rise. Interpreting troponin > 99th percentile URL: a rise and/or fall with acute ischemia = acute MI (type 1: plaque rupture/erosion; type 2: supply-demand imbalance, e.g. severe hypertension, sustained tachyarrhythmia); without ischemia = acute myocardial injury (acute HF, myocarditis); a stable level = chronic injury (structural heart disease, CKD). Case example – one patient, escalating investigation as pretest probability rises. Pericardial Disease Three pericardial syndromes – acute pericarditis, effusion (with or without tamponade) and constriction – compared across the same headings. The organising idea: inflammation causes pain, fluid and stiffness each impair diastolic filling , and the rate of change decides how sick the patient is. Viral is the most common cause. Acute pericarditis = 2 of 4 (pleuritic pain, rub, widespread ST elevation/PR depression, effusion); treat with NSAID + colchicine 3 months . Rate of accumulation, not volume , decides symptoms (200–300 mL fast vs 2 L slow). Tamponade: Beck’s triad, pulsus paradoxus > 10–12, electrical alternans → drain. Constriction: Kussmaul’s sign, pericardial knock, equalized pressures, square root sign ; pericardiectomy earlier is better. Function of the pericardium Prevents spread of infection between the lungs and heart Maintains cardiac position within the thorax Lubricates the movements of the heart Causes of acute pericarditis and pericardial effusion Category Cause Examples Infectious Viral (most common) Enteroviruses, herpesviruses, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HIV, COVID-19 Bacterial Mycobacterium tuberculosis , Borrelia burgdorferi , Pneumococcus spp, Staphylococcus spp Fungal, parasitic Very rare Non-infectious Autoimmune Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis Malignant Primary tumours (rare), metastatic tumours (lung cancer, breast cancer, lymphoma) Metabolic Uremia (severe renal failure), myxedema (severe hypothyroidism) Traumatic, iatrogenic Direct injury (penetrating trauma), indirect injury (non-penetrating trauma), post-pericardiotomy syndrome, radiation-induced Drug-related Lupus-like syndromes (methyldopa, INH, phenytoin), chemotherapy agents Other Post-MI (acute, Dressler syndrome), amyloidosis, aortic dissection Causes of constrictive pericarditis Pericarditis/idiopathic (45% of cases) Post-pericardiotomy syndrome (25%) Chest irradiation (mantle radiation for lymphoma; 20%) Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, end-stage renal disease, malignancy Mycobacterium tuberculosis (most common in developing countries) Acute pericarditis Pericardial effusion Constrictive pericarditis Definition Inflammation of the pericardium Complications: • Recurrent pericarditis • Chronic pericarditis • Constrictive pericarditis • Associated myocarditis Increased pericardial fluid (normal = 50 mL) Slower accumulation = better tolerated – up to 2 L before symptoms Faster accumulation = more symptomatic – symptoms with only 200–300 mL Compromised cardiac function from a thickened, rigid, fibrous pericardium secondary to acute pericarditis Thickened, calcified, stiff; loses compliance: • Cannot expand when the heart fills (diastole) • Impaired cardiac filling • High intracardiac pressures • Equalization of pressures in all 4 chambers Symptoms Chest pain: sharp, pleuritic • Worse with inspiration • Worse supine, better leaning forward ± fever ± signs of systemic disease (malignancy, autoimmune conditions, hypothyroidism) “Tamponade physiology” when fluid impairs cardiac filling (30% of patients) Pre-syncope, syncope Dyspnea Pedal edema Hiccups (phrenic nerve irritation) Dysphagia Symptoms of the underlying cause From elevated filling pressures: Fatigue/weakness · ↓ exercise tolerance RHF: pedal edema, ascites LHF: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, cough Similar to other CVD states – need a high index of suspicion Signs Pericardial friction rub : triphasic (atrial contraction, ventricular expansion – diastole; ventricular contraction – systole), scratchy, can be transient ↑ WBC ↑ inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) ↑ myocardial injury markers (CK, troponin) Small–moderate: no signs on exam Large: Ewart’s sign below the L scapula (dullness, ↓ breath sounds) Tamponade: • Beck’s triad – low BP, high JVP (prominent x, blunted y), muffled heart sounds • Pulsus paradoxus > 10–12 mm Hg : BP variation with respiration ↑ JVP (prominent y descent) • Kussmaul’s sign : no expected fall, or a rise, in JVP on inspiration Pericardial knock : early diastolic, loud, high-pitched – rapid equalization of filling pressures Hepatomegaly/features of cirrhosis Ascites, peripheral edema Diagnosis ESC 2015 – need 2 of: • Pleuritic chest pain • Pericardial rub • New widespread ST elevation or PR depression • Pericardial effusion Supportive: ↑ inflammatory markers; pericardial inflammation on CT or MRI CXR : ↑ cardiac silhouette if > 250 mL; “water bottle heart” if very large Echo : presence and size of effusion; signs of cardiac compression/tamponade ECG : LA enlargement, AF, non-specific T changes, low voltages Echo : normal systolic function, diastolic dysfunction, plethoric IVC, septal bounce, respirophasic septal motion; pericardial thickness hard to see on TTE CXR/CT : pericardial calcification Cardiac MRI : thickness, enhancement after gadolinium, respirophasic septal motion Catheterization : elevated, equalized pressures in all 4 chambers; “square root sign” (early diastolic filling); ventricular interdependence Treatment • High-dose NSAIDs (1–2 weeks) + proton pump inhibitor to prevent ulcers • Colchicine (3 months) – ↓ recurrences • Steroids (tapering) – autoimmune • Immune modulators – anakinra, IVIG, azathioprine • Pericardiectomy • Exercise restriction for 3 months Treat the underlying cause Drain the fluid : pericardiocentesis (percutaneous) or pericardial window (surgical) Therapeutic : tamponade physiology (IV fluids or pressors stabilize BP while preparing to drain); suspected purulent effusion Diagnostic : large effusions where malignancy or infection is suspected Treat the heart failure: diuretics, low-salt diet Treat inflammation, especially with late gadolinium enhancement on MRI: NSAIDs/colchicine/steroids/anakinra (IL-1 inhibitor)/azathioprine Surgical pericardiectomy – earlier is better Beck’s triad = tamponade Low BP + high JVP + muffled heart sounds , with pulsus paradoxus > 10–12 mm Hg and electrical alternans. Infective Endocarditis (and Atherosclerosis) Infective endocarditis is infection of a damaged endocardial surface : injured endothelium forms a sterile platelet-fibrin thrombus that transient bacteremia seeds into a vegetation. Everything follows from the vegetation: it destroys valves (heart failure), throws septic emboli (the peripheral signs) and hides in biofilm (weeks of IV antibiotics). The notes finish with atherosclerosis, a different chronic injury-and-repair disease of the arterial intima. Diagnose with Duke criteria : definite = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; majors are typical organism in 2 blood cultures, persistent bacteremia, Coxiella , or a positive echo. TTE first (sens 70%, spec 99+%); TEE (> 90%) for negative TTE with high suspicion, complications or devices. Early prosthetic IE is CNST ; IVDU is S. aureus on the tricuspid valve . Treat with 6-12 weeks IV antibiotics ; operate for HF, persistent infection, abscess/heart block, or vegetation > 10 mm , but delay at least 4 weeks after a major stroke or ICH. Atherosclerosis begins as chronic endothelial injury → fatty streak → fibrous plaque, and combined risk factors raise risk exponentially. Definition Endocarditis : infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, one or more heart valves, or an indwelling cardiac device, with local collection of fibrinous material and superimposed infection. Epidemiology Incidence 1970-2000: 5-7 cases per 100 000 person-years Incidence since 2000: 15 cases per 100 000 person-years Typical patient: male, mean age 67 years Younger patients: developing countries, underprivileged socioeconomic demographic Category Risk factors Cardiac Congenital heart disease : bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, ventricular septal defect Acquired valvular heart disease : rheumatic heart disease, previous endocarditis, prosthetic cardiac valves Patient Immunocompromised, IVDU , indwelling vascular catheters or devices, septicemia Potentially infective procedures Dental procedures, body piercing, skin wounds, systemic sepsis, genitourinary instrumentation, endoscopies Microorganisms: native valve Streptococcus : S. pneumoniae , S. bovis Staphylococcus aureus Enterococcus HACEK organisms (7-21 day incubation time): Haemophilus parainfluenzae , Haemophilus aphrophilus , Haemophilus paraphrophilus ; Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans ; Cardiobacterium hominis ; Eikenella corrodens ; Kingella kingae Culture negative : Q fever ( Coxiella burnetii ), Bartonella quintana , Brucella , Chlamydia , Legionella , Tropheryma whipplei Microorganisms: IVDU S. aureus , G-ve rods; usually the tricuspid valve (right side) Prosthetic valve endocarditis : organisms in order of frequency (CNST = coagulase-negative staphylococci). Timing Organisms (most to least common) Early (< 60 days) CNST > S. aureus > G-ve bacilli > Enterococcus = fungi = diphtheroids > HACEK > polymicrobial > Streptococcus spp Intermediate CNST > S. aureus = Enterococcus = fungi > Streptococcus spp > HACEK = polymicrobial > G-ve bacilli = diphtheroids Late (> 60 days) Streptococcus spp > S. aureus > CNST > Enterococcus > G-ve bacilli = HACEK = polymicrobial > diphtheroids > fungi Pattern to remember Early prosthetic valve IE is dominated by CNST (skin flora seeded at surgery); by late (> 60 days) the order reverts toward the native-valve pattern, led by streptococci . Pathophysiology: how a vegetation forms Normal valvular endothelium is smooth and resistant to bacterial colonization Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) follows damage to the vascular surface: Systemic disease states (rheumatic carditis) Mechanical injury by catheters or electrodes Injury from repeated injections of solid particles in IVDU Transient bacteremia → microorganism-NBTE interaction Platelet aggregation and evolution of the vegetation Biofilm formation : makes the vegetation more resistant to antibiotic therapy Pathogenesis: pathogens gain transient access to the bloodstream (IV line, injection, mouth), then (b) adhere to an injured or inflamed valve surface, (c) persist, (d) proliferate into a vegetation and (e) disseminate as emboli. Symptoms Acute : fulminant septic illness with emboli, valve destruction, and cardiac decompensation Subacute : non-specific constitutional symptoms: anorexia/weight loss, fevers/chills/night sweats, fatigue/general malaise, flu-like illness, cardiac decompensation (shortness of breath, edema) Clinical findings Peripheral stigmata : septic emboli, finger clubbing, subungual hematoma, splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots, Janeway lesions Cardiac decompensation : tachycardia, new murmur, peripheral edema, weight gain (fluid retention), pulmonary edema Sepsis : fever, organ-specific infective syndromes secondary to emboli History and physical exam : search every system for emboli and heart failure. System Ask about Examine General Level of consciousness, mental status, vitals HEENT Fundoscopy for Roth spots , conjunctival hemorrhage, neck stiffness, oral mucosal petechiae CNS Stroke, focal neurological symptoms (vegetations may have spread systemically) Full neuro exam Cardiac CHF: dyspnea, ankle edema, PND JVP, S3, regurgitant murmur, volume status Respiratory Septic emboli to lungs: cough, sputum production Signs of pneumonia MSK Septic emboli to joints: joint pain Joint exam GU Hematuria GI Bloody diarrhea from septic emboli, abdominal pain Hepatosplenomegaly, masses Skin / peripheral Skin rash (peripheral septic emboli) Clubbing, splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes (painful) , Janeway lesions Where the emboli land: Roth spots (retina), embolic stroke with hemorrhagic conversion and pyogenic brain abscess, septic pulmonary emboli, splenic infarcts, peripheral infarcts of the fingers; in the heart, a perforated aortic leaflet, a mitral vegetation and a vegetation on a pacemaker lead. Differential diagnosis With bacteremia : intravascular catheter infection, cardiac device infection, prosthetic joint infection, hematogenous o

Tests for the Heart Schulich Reviews Pretest probability: age, sex, and chest pain type – typical angina = all 3 : substernal, provoked by exertion/stress, relieved by rest or nitro Can exercise + normal ECG → exercise stress test Cannot exercise or abnormal ECG (LBBB, paced) → stress imaging (stress echo, perfusion); dobutamine stands in for exercise High suspicion or high-risk features → CCTA or invasive angiography

Coronary Artery Disease, Myocardial Infarction & Complications of Acute MI Coronary atherosclerosis becomes an emergency when a vulnerable plaque ruptures and thrombus forms : an occlusive thrombus gives a STEMI (reperfuse now), a non-occlusive one an NSTEMI (stabilize, then angiography). The note then follows the damage through healing and its complications, and closes with aortic aneurysm and dissection. Most MIs arise from plaques < 50% stenosed – rupture, not stenosis, is the trigger. STEMI is diagnosed on ECG, not troponin : ASA 162-325 mg, then primary PCI (gold standard) or fibrinolysis within 12 h ; benefit is maximal within 1 h. Inferior MI + hypotension, JVD, clear lungs = RV infarct – fluids, no nitro. Post-MI: ASA + P2Y12 (12 months) + beta-blocker + ACEI + high-intensity statin regardless of LDL . AAA: repair at ≥ 5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women, or growth > 1 cm/yr ; the leading cause of death on surveillance is cardiovascular, not rupture. Dissection: type A = surgery, type B = medical . Coronary artery disease (CAD) Coronary artery disease / ischemic heart disease : a group of cardiovascular diseases characterized by reduced blood supply to the heart – angina, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, sudden cardiac death Death from heart disease has decreased due to less smoking, the importance of exercise, and pharmacological management (statins, antiplatelet agents) – but it still remains a common cause of mortality Canada compares fairly well with other countries for heart-disease mortality Every 26 seconds someone has an event; every 60 seconds someone dies from one 1/5 deaths are from atherosclerotic disease; 37% of those who have an event die within a year Heart-disease death rates fall steadily from 1970 to 2002 but remain the highest of the six leading causes. Coronary anatomy Epicardial coronary arteries : run along the outer surface of the heart on the epicardium – right and left coronary arteries Subendocardial zone : furthest from the blood supply; suffers first when circulation is compromised The arrangement of the coronary circulation varies Vascular territories overlap because of collateral vessels and anastomoses – the myocardium can tolerate some reduction or blockage without tissue damage Coronary artery dominance : defined by the vessel that gives rise to the posterior descending artery , which supplies the myocardium of the posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum – RCA (85%) , left circumflex (15%) Right coronary (red) gives the AV nodal and posterior descending arteries; the left coronary (purple) divides into LAD and circumflex. Territories: anterior wall = LAD; septum = LAD (anterior 2/3) + RCA (posterior 1/3); lateral = circumflex; posterior = RCA. Coronary atherosclerosis Vessels initially expand to accommodate plaque growth ( compensatory enlargement ) but eventually become stenosed No symptoms until late in plaque formation – angina patients usually have > 70% narrowing Disease is often in the proximal portions of medium and large arteries – reachable by surgery or catheters Atheroma can be very focal along a coronary artery – the rate-limiting step for flow; normal flow can be restored locally with surgery Many patients have severe disease in multiple vessels, which makes treatment much more challenging Investigation of angina: treadmill stress testing (ECG), coronary angiography (contrast dye) Measuring stenosis Pathological assessment : percent reduction of cross-sectional lumen area compared with the normal vessel Angiographic assessment : percent narrowing compared with the least stenosed area High-risk anatomic patterns – the thresholds that define them differ: 50% for left main, 70% elsewhere. Pattern Stenosis Vessels Left main coronary stenosis – “widow maker” > 50% Left main Left main equivalent > 70% Proximal LAD + circumflex Triple vessel disease > 70% LAD + circumflex + RCA Double vessel disease > 70% Proximal LAD + circumflex or RCA Left main stenosis. Left main equivalent: proximal LAD + circumflex. Triple vessel disease: LAD + circumflex + RCA. Double vessel disease: here LAD + RCA. Surgical management: coronary angioplasty and stenting (PCI) A catheter carrying a deflated balloon with a deployable stent around it is inserted and guided to the blocked artery The balloon is inflated and expands the stent, which pushes the plaque against the sides of the artery and holds the vessel open Plaques are intentionally ruptured and expanded by angioplasty, and may even dissect the vessel wall Patients are anticoagulated to prevent thrombosis Previously angioplastied and stented vessels can develop re-stenosis Drug-coated stents are designed to reduce inflammation and slow re-stenosis Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) – who benefits Left main coronary stenosis , abnormal LV function , class III/IV angina Survival gain from CABG is largest with left main disease (~19 months), then abnormal LV function; small for one/two-vessel disease. Pooled trials: mortality is lower with CABG than medicine for most of follow-up, with the curves converging by about 12 years. CABG procedure A healthy vessel from elsewhere in the body is harvested and attached above and below the plaque to bypass the blockage Most commonly the saphenous vein , radial artery , or internal thoracic (mammary) artery 1998: endoscopic bypass-graft technique for taking out the saphenous vein – limited pain, infection and edema; quality identical to the open technique Vein harvest : incision above the knee; a fiberoptic scope is slid between the fat layer and the top of the vein. If more vein is needed, a counter-incision is made, the scope reinserted, and dissection continues towards the groin. Once dissection is complete and all branches divided, the vein is pulled out of the original incision and divided Median sternotomy (“mediastinotomy” in the source) with a reciprocating saw; sternal edges opened Internal thoracic artery is taken down and its branches divided;

Cardiac Rehabilitation, Secondary Prevention and Peripheral Vascular Disease What happens after the first vascular event: cardiac rehab and drugs to prevent the next one, then the limb version of the same disease. The organising idea: collaterals decide the presentation – an embolus into a normal artery is catastrophic, while slow atherosclerotic occlusion is often tolerated. After MI, risk of another MI is 5–7×. Cardiac rehab is class I, level A (18–26% ↓ mortality in trials; ~50% in real-world programs); prescribe by F.I.T.T. Acute limb ischemia: 6 Ps, necrosis within 6–8 h , heparin then revascularize, watch for compartment syndrome → fasciotomy. ABI < 0.5 = rest pain, < 0.3 = tissue loss. PAD management is ABCDES – smoking cessation most important . Fibrinolyse STEMI if PCI cannot happen within 120 min; RV infarct: no nitrates, give fluids . Why secondary prevention matters – one vascular event multiplies the risk of the next. Outpatient: evaluate → prescribe exercise → modify risk factors → set physical, vocational and psychological goals. Valvular Heart Disease and Surgical Management The four big left-sided lesions — aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation — each load the heart in a characteristic way (pressure vs volume, LV vs LA/pulmonary circulation), and that load predicts the symptoms, the signs and the timing of surgery. The organising surgical idea: regurgitant valves can usually be repaired, stenotic valves must be replaced — and the best valve is your own. Echocardiography is the gold standard for every valve lesion; ECG is never diagnostic. Severe AS: valve area < 1 cm², mean gradient > 40 mm Hg ; once symptoms start, 50% survival is 5 y with angina, 3 y with syncope, 2 y with heart failure — there is no medical therapy, so replace (SAVR, or TAVI in elderly moderate-to-high-risk patients). Operate on asymptomatic severe AR when LVEF < 50%, LVESD > 50 mm or LVEDD > 65 mm . Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic (Jones: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor); balloon valvuloplasty is contraindicated with LA thrombus or significant MR. For MR, repair beats replacement and early surgery before NYHA III-IV symptoms preserves survival. Mechanical valves last but need lifelong anticoagulation (INR 2-3 aortic, 2.5-3.5 mitral); bioprosthetic valves need none but deteriorate (~15 years). Aortic valve Three cusps Ventricular systole: isovolumetric contraction, then the aortic valve opens and blood is rapidly ejected into the aorta; normally opens with a very small pressure gradient Large pressure is generated across the valve → a lot of wear and tear over time Aortic sclerosis : thickening/calcification of the valve without obstruction to flow; increases with age (50% of patients over 85 years) Stenotic aortic valve: calcific nodules on a tricuspid valve (main) vs a congenital bicuspid valve (inset) — the two main causes of AS. Mitral valve Allows passage of blood from the LA to the LV and prevents its return Mitral annulus – fibrous ring attached to the leaflets Two leaflets – anterior and posterior Chordae tendineae Papillary muscles – attached to the LV (The moderator band is not part of the mitral apparatus — it carries conduction fibres through the RV.) The mitral apparatus: annulus, anterior leaflet, posterior leaflet (3 lobes), commissures, chordae tendineae and the lateral and medial papillary muscles — dysfunction of any part causes MR. Aortic valve disease: stenosis vs regurgitation Aortic stenosis is the most common acquired heart (valve) disease — a pressure load on the LV. Aortic regurgitation is a volume load. Aortic stenosis Aortic regurgitation Patho-physiology Obstruction to flow from LV into aorta ↑ pressure gradient LV → aorta ↑ afterload on LV ( Law of Laplace ) Compensatory hypertrophy: • Good: maintains normal afterload • Bad: ↓ LV compliance, ↓ coronary blood flow, ↑ O₂ demand • Contractility maintained until late in course Backflow from aorta into LV through a leaking valve Annuloaortic ectasia : dilatation of the aortic root/valve annulus • Usually idiopathic; may be associated with chronic hypertension • ↑ risk of aortic dissection (tear/laceration) Chronic AR : volume overload → LV dilatation, ↑ wall stress, compensatory hypertrophy; LV systolic function preserved initially, CHF eventually Acute AR : sudden onset (endocarditis, dissection) into a normal-sized, normally compliant LV → sudden ↑ LV pressure; LVEDP transmitted back to LA and pulmonary circulation → pulmonary edema ; dyspnea, hypotension, short (possibly inaudible) murmur; emergency surgery usually indicated Causes Degenerative/calcific (etiology unclear) • Pathophysiology similar to atherosclerosis; calcium deposition • Presents later in life (60s-80s) – wear and tear • Genetic markers being identified • Statins (atherosclerotic regression) have no benefit Congenital/bicuspid • 1% of population, male preponderance • Presents in 40s-50s • 1/3 AS, 1/3 AR, 1/3 clinically insignificant • Abnormal, dilated aortas – intrinsic defect in the media Leaflet : calcific degeneration, bicuspid valve, endocarditis, lupus Root enlargement (leading cause in the Western world): • Age-related degeneration/enlargement – most common • Hypertension – stretches the annulus • Cystic medial necrosis – Marfan syndrome • Bicuspid aortic valve aortopathy Acute AR : endocarditis, dissection Symptoms "ASD" : A ngina, S yncope, D yspnea (CHF) Asymptomatic: survival similar to general population; < 1% SCD Symptomatic: 10% SCD with angina, higher with CHF Overall survival 75% at 3 years; normalises with AVR Dyspnea/HF carries the worst prognosis Long asymptomatic period – good prognosis Early: exertional dyspnea , fatigue CHF as LV systolic function fails: orthopnea, PND Angina can occur – low diastolic pressure, LVH Signs Systolic murmur at the base ; later peak = more severe (loudness does not grade severity) Soft S2: stenotic valve does not close properly, so only P2 is heard S4 : stiff hypertrophied LV Pulsus parvus et tardus : reduced, delayed LV heave: strong apical impulse; apex may be displaced Diastolic murmur at the (left sternal) border ; later peak = more severe LVH with dilated LV: apex displaced down and out S3 : CHF; S4 : stiff LV Widened pulse pressure – narrows as CHF develops: • Quincke : capillary pulsations • Müller : systolic pulsation of the uvula • Duroziez : systolic murmur when femoral artery compressed proximally, diastolic when compressed distally • Traube : pistol-shot sounds over the femoral artery • Corrigan : collapsing pulse Diagnosis ECG: not diagnostic Echocardiogram: gold standard – valve gradients, valve area, LV function (EF), other valve disease, LVH, aortic root size ECG: not diagnostic CXR: may show LVH or enlarged aorta Echocardiogram: gold standard – etiology, severity, LV response (EF), aortic root size, other valve disease Management Asymptomatic: watch and wait; Heart Failure: Physiology, Classification and Management Heart failure is a clinical syndrome , not a disease: symptoms and signs plus structural heart disease. Its engine is neurohormonal activation (SNS, RAAS, AVP) – an appropriate response to dehydration turned harmful – and nearly every HFrEF drug blocks one limb of it. EF is not needed for the diagnosis; symptoms are always the last stage. HFpEF is 60%, HFrEF 40% (ischemic 65% of HFrEF). AHA stages never go backwards; NYHA class can. Low BNP rules out HF; a normal ECG makes it very unlikely. Cold and wet has the worst prognosis. HFrEF: ACEI/ARB→ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i , ivabradine if sinus HR ≥ 70 ; ICD/CRT if LVEF ≤ 35% . HFpEF has no proven therapy beyond diuretics. Definitions of heart failure Historic physiologic : the heart cannot maintain a cardiac output adequate for metabolic requirements and cannot accommodate venous return – no mention of EF Clinical : a syndrome in which reduced heart function is associated with diminished exercise capacity, a high incidence of ventricular arrhythmia and shortened life expectancy Better clinical definition : a clinical syndrome of typical symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling, fatigue), possibly with signs (elevated JVP, pulmonary crackles, peripheral edema), caused by a structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality, resulting in reduced cardiac output and/or elevated intracardiac pressures at rest or during stress Layman's terms : the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's oxygen and nutrient demands 2005 clinical definition = symptoms of HF (rest or exercise) + objective evidence (echo) of systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction + (if in doubt) response to HF-directed treatment 2008 clinical definition = symptoms (breathlessness at rest or on exercise, fatigue, tiredness, ankle swelling) + signs (tachycardia, tachypnea, pulmonary rales, pleural effusion, raised JVP, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly) + objective evidence of structural/functional abnormality at rest (cardiomegaly, S3, murmurs, echo abnormality, raised natriuretic peptide) HF is a clinical syndrome, NOT a disease – a constellation of signs and symptoms + some type of structural heart disease. Ejection fraction is NOT required to make the diagnosis. Compensated vs decompensated Compensated : asymptomatic despite ↓ pumping function – enlarged heart, ↑ HR Decompensated : symptomatic; can no longer compensate; needs treatment and often hospitalization Epidemiology Fastest-growing global CVD – substantial morbidity, mortality and economic burden; 40 million affected worldwide 42-50% die within 5 years of diagnosis 74% have ≥ 1 comorbidity (renal disease, diabetes, hematological) 27% re-hospitalized within 30 days #1 reason for hospitalization in patients > 65 ; number one driver of unplanned admission; 1.4 million hospital days/year Canada: > 600 000 affected and rising; > 50 000 diagnosed each year ; 1 in 2 Canadians touched by HF Costs Canadians > $2.8 billion/year; 10 billion spent annually on HF hospital costs Annual HF deaths in Canada exceed breast + colon + prostate cancer combined There is no cure for HF Pathophysiology Over time, damage to any major structure/system – ventricles, atria, coronary arteries, valves, electrical system, pericardium, pulmonary arteries/lungs – alone or together can result in HF Patients often develop HF after the heart has been weakened or damaged by other cardiovascular conditions The cardiovascular continuum: risk factors → CAD → MI → remodeling → HF → end-stage disease. LV dysfunction ↓ cardiac output → neurohormonal activation → Na+ retention, arrhythmia, further remodeling → congestion, sudden death, pump failure. Stages of HF development Injury/induction – all at once (MI, inflammation) or slow cumulative effects (risk factors, genetics) Cellular changes – lead to anatomic changes (cardiac remodeling) Functional changes – cardiac dysfunction and physiologic responses to accommodate the damage Symptomatic HF ± acute pulmonary edema/shock – clinical signs and symptoms are always the last thing to occur Renal function also declines as HF worsens. Survival is poor in both HFpEF and HFrEF, slightly worse with HFrEF. Left vs right heart failure Biventricular HF : both sides affected; LHF can lead to RV disease. Left-sided HF Right-sided HF (cor pulmonale) Types Systolic = failure to pump : reduced EF (HFrEF); LV loses normal contraction, less ejection force; ↑ preload Diastolic = failure to fill : preserved EF (HFpEF); LV does not relax fully between beats; ↑ afterload Most commonly from pulmonary hypertension due to chronic lung disease – COPD, PE, pulmonary fibrosis, sleep apnea, myasthenia gravis, poliomyelitis Causes RV dilation and RVH Mechanism of symptoms Reduced forward flow (fatigue, ↓ exercise tolerance, lightheadedness, low BP) and reduced filling from the lung (SOB, orthopnea/PND) Blood backs up in the veins from the RV → venous congestion Symptoms (Q5) Fatigue, ↑ capillary wedge pressure, pulmonary congestion, PND, confusion, restlessness, orthopnea, tachycardia, exertional dyspnea, cyanosis Fatigue, ↑ peripheral venous pressure, ascites, enlarged liver/spleen, distended jugular veins, dependent/pitting edema, anorexia/GI complaints, swelling of legs, ankles, abdomen Left HF: reduced forward flow and lung congestion; right HF: venous congestion. Left-sided failure: pulmonary congestion, PND, orthopnea. Orthopnea: sitting up to breathe, with pulmonary edema on CXR. Right-sided failure (cor pulmonale): distended neck veins, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, dependent edema. Right heart failure: raised venous pressure and dependent edema. HFrEF: enlarged ventricles that contract poorly. HFpEF: thick, stiff ventricle that fills poorly. Cardiac hypertrophy in heart failure (see also Q9) Systolic HF (HFrEF) Diastolic HF (HFpEF) Load Volume overload (↑ preload) Pressure overload (↑ afterload/EDP); hypertrophy normalizes wall stress Remodeling Eccentric – sarcomeres added in se
Heart Failure Treatments Schulich Reviews Symptomatic HFrEF despite GDMT → ARNI in place of ACEI/ARB Ivabradine (I f blocker, sinus node): benefit when sinus HR ≥ 70

Hypertension: Diagnosis, Causes and Risk Hypertension is defined by treatment benefit , not a number alone. The lecture follows the four-step approach: confirm it is really hypertension, find a cause, estimate CV risk, then plan treatment. One high reading ≠ hypertension ; clinic BP runs 9/6 mm Hg high , and ABPM is the gold standard (night-time BP best predicts events). SBP rises with age; DBP falls after ~55 . OSA (10%) is the commonest secondary cause, then renal disease, primary aldosteronism, alcohol/substances and medications (5% each). Lowering BP cuts CHF 60%, stroke 40%, CAD 15% . Definitions Elevated blood pressure : a BP level associated with an increase in long-term risk Hypertension : a BP level at which treatment is associated with a decrease in long-term risk Why it matters Most attributable risk factor for global disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) Leading reason patients present to primary care and specialty offices Second most important risk factor for stroke, after atrial fibrillation BP variability BP varies throughout the day, which makes assessment a challenge; white coat hypertension is also a problem Readings vary with who takes them – retraining is important for normalization BP and age Systolic BP rises linearly with age Diastolic BP begins to fall around age 55 due to loss of compliance → widened pulse pressure 1) Determine that the patient with high BP has hypertension One high BP reading ≠ hypertension Manual BPM accuracy is affected by device, provider and patient factors: conversation during the reading, only one reading recorded, no rest period, rapid cuff deflation, rounding to 0 or 5, patient anxiety in a healthcare setting Routine clinical BP is 9/6 mm Hg higher than standardized research BP Proper BP procedure Sit in a comfortable chair, back supported, feet flat on the floor, arm at heart level 5-minute rest; take a first and second reading, and a third if they differ significantly NEVER record BP on an exam table or supine in a hospital bed to determine future CV risk BP measurement methods – HBPM and ABPM predict CV risk better than office BPM; night-time BP correlates best with future CV events . Method Abbreviation Note Office OBP Office automated AOBP Ambulatory ABP Gold standard Home HBP Fun fact: standing upright One adaptation that lets humans stand on two legs is increased afterload : nerves to the leg arteries constrict the vessels on standing so BP does not fall. BP can change beat to beat as the body adapts it to what we are doing. BP and cardiovascular risk MRFIT : SBP 120-129 → ↑ CV risk; SBP > 140 → significant ↑ CV risk; a drop in DBP → ↑ CV risk High-normal BP increases the risk of developing CVD SHEP : a 12 mm Hg drop in SBP was associated with a 40% reduction in stroke In general, lowering SBP lowers stroke risk – trials use a baseline of 140-160 mm Hg 2) Determine the cause of the hypertension Workup cycle: history → physical exam → blood and urine tests → special tests if required. Secondary causes of hypertension Secondary cause Prevalence Obstructive sleep apnea 10% Chronic renal disease 5% Primary aldosteronism 5% Alcohol or substance use 5% Medications 5% Renovascular disease 2% Cushing syndrome 0.1% Pheochromocytoma 0.1% Coarctation of aorta 0.1% Secondary “aggravating” causes Self-inflicted Doctor-inflicted Fate Salt NSAIDs Stimulants – Rx, OTC, street drugs Alcohol Withdrawal from Rx or non-Rx drugs Pain Wearing a white coat Not measuring BP correctly Medications: glucocorticoids, NSAIDs, stimulants, estrogens/androgens, cyclosporine/EPO, nasal decongestants Obstructive sleep apnea – ↑ aldosterone/NE Hyperaldosteronism – low serum K+ Intrinsic kidney disease – urinalysis Renal artery stenosis – atherosclerosis Thyroid/parathyroid disease – TSH, serum Ca2+ Endocrine: pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, acromegaly Modifiable aggravating factors : alcohol, excess salt, recreational drugs, NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, anabolic steroids, erythropoietin, calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), ephedrine/pseudoephedrine, black licorice (glycyrrhizic acid ↑ cortisol levels), sleep apnea Preliminary Ix : urinalysis; blood chemistry (K+, Na+, Cr); serum Ca2+ and albumin; TSH; HbA1c; lipid profile; standard 12-lead ECG 3) Determine the risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes Hypertension is a risk factor for cerebrovascular disease (dementia), CHF, AF, renal failure, CAD, peripheral vascular disease, erectile dysfunction Benefits of lowering BP: ↓ CHF 60%, ↓ stroke 40%, ↓ CAD 15% Risk assessment: clinical impression, risk factor counting/equation tools, Framingham risk score, cardiovascular age score 4) Make a plan to lower risk with lifestyle and medications Lifestyle management for all More aggressive management for higher CV risk – early pharmacotherapy, lower BP targets Choose medications by patient factors (drug plan, adverse events), disease factors (ACEI for CHF), drug factors (long-acting once daily; low, fixed-dose combinations) Details: see Management of Hypertension Practice questions 37. Treatment of Hypertension Treatment intensity follows global CV risk : thresholds and targets tighten as risk rises. Most patients need several drugs combined (RAAS stimulator + RAAS inhibitor), added rather than dose-doubled. Start drugs at ≥ 160 (low risk), ≥ 140 (moderate), ≥ 130 (diabetes, high risk) ; targets < 140/90, < 130/80 diabetes, ≤ 120 high risk . > 10 mm Hg above target → low-dose single-pill combination. Add a drug rather than double one – half dose gives 80% of the effect. Preferred 3-drug cocktail: diuretic + ACEI/ARB + long-acting CCB . No RAAS blockers in pregnancy or renovascular disease ; no BB first line at ≥ 60. Usual office BP thresholds for starting pharmacological treatment Population SBP DBP High risk (SPRINT population) ≥ 130 NA Diabetes ≥ 130 ≥ 80 Moderate risk ≥ 140 ≥ 90 Low risk (no TOD or CV risk factors) ≥ 160 ≥ 100 Treatment thresholds by risk group. Recommended office BP treatment targets Population SBP DBP High risk ≤ 120 NA Diabetes < 130 < 80 All others < 140 < 90 Treatment targets by risk group. Options for pharmacotherapy First-line treatment of systolic/diastolic hypertension without compelling indications Target < 135/85 (automated): health behaviours, then thiazide/thiazide-like, ACEI, ARB, long-acting CCB, beta blocker, or a single-pill combination (ACEI+CCB, ARB+CCB, ACEI/ARB+diuretic). BP > 10 mm Hg above target → start 2 medications as a low-dose single-pill combination Plan for most patients to be on a 3-drug cocktail : RAAS inhibitor (ACEI/ARB) + diuretic/dihydropyridine CCB Longer-acting (thiazide-like) diuretics are preferred over shorter-acting (thiazide) diuretics RAAS inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy ; caution in women of childbearing potential Beta blockers are not recommended first line for patients ≥ 60 without another compelling indication (angina, CHF) Avoid diuretic-induced hypokalemia by using K+-sparing agents when possible (ACEI, ARB) ACEI are not used as monotherapy for Black patients without another compelling indication – higher rates of low-renin hypertension, so drugs that stimulate renin are preferred first line Combination therapy If BP does not improve on one drug, add a second drug rather than doubling the first – much more effective, fewer side effects ALLHAT : BP control rates depend on physician willingness to escalate (use of 3+ drugs) Adding a second drug gives the full additive SBP reduction (ratio ~1.0); doubling the dose gives only ~0.2 of it. Column A: RAAS stimulation Column B: RAAS inhibition Diuretic Beta blocker Long-acting CCB Direct renin inhibitor ACEI ARB MRA ENaC inhibitor (amiloride) Case example 60-year-old man; annual check-up BP 165/95 by AOBP, confirmed with multiple HBPM readings FHx of hypertension in parents and siblings; no OSA or other secondary causes Initial investigations normal; S4 present Best recommendation? All are reasonable: (a) Na+ < 2000 mg; (b) exercise ≥ 30 min, 5/7 days; (c) lose weight; (d) vegetables and high-K foods; (e) avoid eggs. Despite complying, readings are identical. Medications? Yes – the usual office threshold to start drugs in low/moderate risk is ≥ 160 mm Hg. Preferred long-acting medication? (a) ACEI (perindopril, trandolapril); (b) ARB (telmisartan, candesartan, irbesartan); (c) diuretic (indapamide, chlorthalidone); (d) DHP CCB (amlodipine, nifedipine); (e) beta blocker (bisoprolol). What dose of the first medication? (a) ¼ dose (start low, go slow); (b) ½ dose (80% of the effect); (c) full dose (go big or go home). Dose-response: half the maximum dose gives ~80% of the SBP lowering of the full dose. Go ahead with combination therapy now? (a) No, starting two is dangerous; (b) absolutely, go big or go home; (c) yes, but as a low-dose single-pill combination – starting point 165/90 vs target 140/90: 25 points away = 3+ drugs. If you add a second drug : ACEI + diuretic or ACEI + CCB.
