Congenital Heart Disease CHD is sorted with two questions: pink or blue? and how much pulmonary blood flow? The answers group the lesions (left-to-right shunts, obstructions, right-to-left shunts, mixing lesions, separate circulations), and each group follows from where development went wrong. The lecture also covers pediatric murmurs, chest pain and Kawasaki disease. CHD affects 1% of births . Cyanosis needs > 5 g/dL deoxygenated Hb ; a hyperoxia PaO2 < 100-150 points to the heart. ASD: wide fixed split S2 , often found in adults; VSD: pansystolic murmur, congestion at 6-12 weeks; PDA: continuous murmur, bounding pulses . TGA is the commonest cyanotic lesion in neonates; ToF the commonest overall . 98-99% of pediatric murmurs are innocent (Still's most common). Kawasaki: fever ≥ 4-5 days + 4/5 features; IVIG + ASA within 10 days cuts aneurysms from 25% to 4% . Congenital heart disease (CHD) : any alteration in the structural development of the heart. The most common congenital defect – 1% of all births , not counting bicuspid aortic valve and small muscular VSDs. Embryology of the heart Day 14 : primary heart field in a crescent on the cranial side of the embryo; as the embryo grows, the heart tube rotates on the transverse axis to lie ventral and caudal Day 20 : bilateral endocardial tubes filled with cardiac jelly Day 21 : tubes bulge towards each other at the dorsal end and fuse in the midline Day 22 : primitive heart tube with precursors of the main structures – truncus arteriosus + bulbus cordis → great arteries; primitive ventricle → ventricles; primitive atrium → atria; tube elongates by proliferation of secondary heart field cells Day 24 : cardiac looping anterior and to the right, as top and bottom are anchored Day 35 : atria move cranially, giving a common AV canal; RV gives rise to both outflow tracts Septation : muscle walls grow toward the middle between atria, ventricles and outflow tracts; foramen ovale forms in the atrial septum; the outflow septum spirals down to the ventricles, giving blood two paths out of the heart Then valve formation and branching of the great arteries and veins Heart development from the cardiogenic area (day 18) to four chambers (8 weeks). Fetal circulation Goals: deliver oxygenated placental blood to the coronaries and brain; protect the non-aerated lungs Shunts bypass the lungs (in parallel): oxygenated blood to head/heart, deoxygenated back to the placenta 100% of blood goes to the body, only 10% to the lungs Ductus venosus – placental blood bypasses the hepatic circulation Foramen ovale – placental blood bypasses the right heart Ductus arteriosus – deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs into the descending aorta What can go wrong? Looping stage : different connections between atria, ventricles and great arteries; different heart orientations Septal stage : septal defects – “holes in the heart” (ASD, VSD) Later stages : valve stenosis/regurgitation, abnormal venous connections, distal aorta and PA abnormalities Persistent fetal circulation : patent shunts Fetal circulation: ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus. Cardiac hemodynamics The impact of a shunt depends on the pressure gradient (location), resistance of the capillary beds (PVR/SVR), and resistance of the hole/tube (radius, length) Approach to CHD 1) Pink (acyanotic) or blue (cyanotic)? Deoxygenated Hb is blue-toned; oxygenated Hb red-toned Cyanosis appears when deoxygenated Hb > 5 g/dL in the systemic circulation – there must be deoxygenated blood in the systemic circulation Requires desaturation, but is less prominent with anemia 2) Degree of pulmonary blood flow (PBF) ↑ PBF = lighter lungs (fluid); vascular markings reach the lung edges; proximal branch PAs more prominent ↓ PBF = darker lungs; proximal branch PAs look smaller Increased pulmonary blood flow: vascular markings extend to the periphery. Decreased pulmonary blood flow: dark lung fields, small branch PAs. 3) Associated findings Symptoms: congestive symptoms Signs: abnormal precordium, pulses, heart sounds, murmurs – lesion specific Ix: ECG and CXR (less specific, more available); echocardiogram (usually definitive, less available) Congestive symptoms and signs by age Infants Older children Symptoms Failure to thrive Respiratory distress, especially with feeds Excessive diaphoresis with feeds Poor feeding Exercise intolerance Malaise SOB on exertion or orthopnea Signs Tachypnea, tachycardia Pallor, hepatomegaly, hyperdynamic precordium ↑ work of breathing Failure to thrive – low weight Tachypnea, tachycardia Pallor, hepatomegaly, hyperdynamic precordium Edema Crackles rare Pink, normal PBF: valve lesions and arterial obstruction. Acyanotic lesions: left-to-right shunts Communication between the right and left heart In isolation, blood moves left → right because of higher left-sided pressures and lower pulmonary vascular resistance Normal heart for comparison. Left-to-right shunt lesions – pink with ↑ PBF Lesion Shunt and epidemiology Findings and course ASD L→R across the atrial septum (↑ RA compliance, ↑ LA pressure) 10% of CHD; 30% of CHD newly diagnosed in adults Hemodynamics: ↑ flow – volume overload of the pulmonary circulation Generally asymptomatic in children; presents in adults with arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, HF and congestion RV heave (RV enlargement) Wide fixed split S2 – extra flow delays pulmonary valve closure Blowing systolic ejection murmur at LUSB (↑ flow across the pulmonary valve) May close spontaneously in the first 2 years Tx: repair around 5 years – surgical patch or interventional device VSD L→R across the ventricular septum (↑ LV systolic pressure, ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance) 5% of newborns; 20-30% of CHD Hemodynamics: ↑ pressure and/or flow ; shunting in systole (RV and LV pressures similar in diastole) Presentation depends on defect size – larger defects shunt more at higher pressure Congestive symptoms often at 6-12 weeks May close spontaneously in 1-2 years, but may n

Pediatric Palpitations In an adolescent with palpitations, the task is separating sinus tachycardia (gradual, rate-appropriate) from SVT (abrupt, > 200 bpm) – and the exam rarely helps, so the diagnosis comes from history and capturing the rhythm. An ECG during symptoms is diagnostic ; Holter 24-48 h or 3-8 week monitors capture it. SVT: abrupt onset (1-5 s), usually > 200 bpm ; sinus tachycardia: slow onset (> 10-30 s), < 150-180 at rest. Resting ECG may show WPW . VT presents with syncope rather than palpitations. Pediatric cardiology case 3 A 15-year-old male is referred for palpitations. First question: what is meant by “palpitations” – fast? irregular? hard? slow? Approach to pediatric palpitations Step Considerations Hx What the palpitations feel like (fast? irregular?), onset and offset, triggers, actual heart rate if measured PEx Not particularly helpful – usually not having palpitations in clinic Ix Try to capture the rhythm while symptomatic Resting ECG may be normal, but may show patterns predisposing to arrhythmia ECG during palpitations is diagnostic Longer-term rhythm monitoring: Holter (2-lead continuous ECG, 24-48 hours, rarely 1-2 weeks) or longer continuous/intermittent monitors (3-8 weeks) DDx Sinus tachycardia – exercise, anxiety, presyncope (dehydration, position changes, prolonged standing), organic (hyperthyroid, hypertension) Sinus rhythm – increased awareness of a normal heart rate Supraventricular tachycardia Ventricular tachycardia is more likely to present with syncope than palpitations Sinus tachycardia vs SVT Feature Sinus / sinus tachy Arrhythmia / SVT Rate Less than maximal HR; usually < 150-180 bpm at rest Usually > 200 bpm (slightly slower in older adolescents); too fast to count Onset Slow (> 10-30 seconds) Rapid (1-5 seconds) Offset Slow Rapid (may be slower if anxiety adds a sinus tachycardia) Associated May have presyncope or SOB with or before palpitations; normal exam Presyncope, chest pain or SOB follow the onset of palpitations; usually normal exam ECG Normal May see WPW Monitoring Sinus rhythm or sinus tachycardia SVT or other arrhythmia captured Source table: sinus tachycardia vs SVT – rate, onset and offset separate them.
09 Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant

Advanced Heart Failure Advanced (stage D) heart failure is recognized when standard therapy stops working – the patient is cold . The decision is then which durable option fits: transplant, VAD, or palliation , with inotropes as a bridge. I NEED HELP flags advanced HF. Cold + wet = cardiogenic shock. Inotropes improve symptoms but do not prolong life – bridge or palliation. Referral ≠ listing; transplant needs desire, severity, no contraindications . Post-transplant: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisone , graft half-life ~12 years; late death from allograft vasculopathy . VADs are pulseless ; driveline infection is nearly universal. Recognizing advanced heart failure Low perfusion at rest = COLD Cold + wet = cardiogenic shock HF stages A-D: therapies escalate step by step; stage D (refractory) adds inotropes, VAD/transplant, hospice. A patient approaching end-stage HF will tell you – I NEED HELP : Letter Marker Criterion I Inotropes Previous or ongoing dobutamine, milrinone or dopamine N NYHA class / natriuretic peptide Persistent NYHA III/IV symptoms or persistently high BNP E End-organ dysfunction Worsening liver or renal function E Ejection fraction Very low EF (< 20%) D Defibrillator shocks Recurrent shocks/ATP for VT/VF H Hospitalizations ≥ 2 HF hospitalizations in 12 months E Edema / escalating diuretics Persistent edema or frequent diuretic dose adjustments L Low blood pressure Consistently low SBP (< 90 mm Hg) P Prognostic medications Need to reduce / inability to uptitrate goal-directed therapies Referral Once advanced HF is identified, refer to a centre providing advanced care – mechanical devices (ventricular assist devices) or transplant Being referred or seen at a transplant centre does NOT mean the patient is “listed” – one of the options will be considered Very few advanced HF patients meet transplant criteria – only 50 people on the waitlist in Ontario Patients approaching stage D Recognize your limits as a physician in treating a complex condition Allow your patient to be considered for specialized therapies, usually concentrated in a few centres Inform your patient about the seriousness of their condition and provide information on prognosis and outcomes Inotropic therapy Most HF therapies slow or reverse progression, but beyond a point they may give no benefit – cold patients Beta blockers may not help at this stage because of their negative inotropy (which tries to preserve ventricular function) – consider reducing them, recognizing this marks advancing disease Inotropes improve symptoms but do NOT prolong life and may precipitate arrhythmias Inotropy is a bridge to a durable therapy (transplant/LVAD) or palliation Cardiac transplantation Orthotopic : recipient heart explanted and the donor heart implanted in its place Heterotopic : recipient heart left in situ; donor heart placed in series Orthotopic transplant: aorta, pulmonary artery, SVC and IVC connections. Components of transplant assessment Does the patient want transplant/advanced options? Is the condition advanced enough to warrant transplant? Severe symptoms, supplemented by cardiopulmonary exercise testing and invasive hemodynamics Any contraindications? Significant comorbidities, psychosocial considerations, immunological issues, surgical considerations, age The ethical principle of justice matters – there are usually too few donors for those who might benefit Post-transplant care Patients are often frail and deconditioned – intensive rehabilitation pre- and post-operatively Immunosuppression: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisone Prophylaxis against opportunistic infection – pneumocystis, CMV Routine endomyocardial biopsies to assess for rejection Outcomes Graft half-life: at 12 years, 50% of hearts are no longer functioning Early deaths : infection, rejection, vasoplegia, cerebrovascular events Later deaths : cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, infection/rejection Transplant numbers rose in the mid-1980s with better immunosuppression (cyclosporine) Transplant survival by era: median 8.4 years (1982-1991) and 10.7 years (1992-2001). US heart transplants rose sharply from the mid-1980s. Ventricular assist devices (VAD) Surgically implanted, electrically driven pump moving blood from the ventricle(s) into the arterial circulation Durations: temporary and durable Designs: axial and centrifugal Brands: HeartMate II and III, HeartWare HVAD Axial flow Centrifugal flow Blood travels in the same direction as the rotor's orientation Blood enters perpendicular to the rotor's orientation Blood can contact static devices – stators Rotor need not contact any static surface – magnetic levitation Less sensitive to physiological factors like afterload More sensitive to afterload changes because of the 90° entry May provide better ventricular offloading Physiological changes affect the device's ability to offload VAD components Well-positioned, unimpeded pump – inflow cannula, rotor (propeller), outflow cannula Intact driveline – delivers power and operating information to the pump Functioning controller – tells the pump what to do and monitors it Power supply – battery or wall socket Batteries and controller are outside the patient; the driveline tunnels in to the pump Indications Bridge to another therapy (temporary → durable VAD) or to transplant Destination therapy for non-transplant candidates – a patient may not qualify for transplant but may for a VAD Complications Foreign body providing non-physiologic flow – pulseless Driveline infection – most patients develop this; surface or deep GI bleeding Stroke/intracranial hemorrhage Device thrombosis Pump malfunction Palliative care in advanced HF No advanced therapy cures HF (not even transplant) – at best it trades an imminently lethal condition for a manageable one Patients need to understand the main goal: improving symptoms, which may prolong longevity Patients often die from HF itself or an HF-related complication Palliative care traditionally focused

Mechanisms of Arrhythmia Every arrhythmia is a failure of one of two functions – impulse initiation or impulse conduction . Failure of either gives bradycardia; abnormal excess of either (automaticity, triggered activity, re-entry) gives tachycardia. Pacemaker hierarchy: sinus 40-90 → junction 35-50 → His-Purkinje 20-40 → ventricle <30 bpm . Re-entry causes tachycardia, never bradycardia , and needs two limbs with different refractoriness, slow conduction and a uni-directional block triggered by a premature beat. Orthodromic AVRT (90%) is narrow, antidromic is wide ; AVNRT is narrow, scar VT is wide. Long QT → early afterdepolarizations → Torsades , treated with Mg2+ and faster heart rate. Functions of the electrical system Impulse initiation Failure to initiate an impulse → bradycardia Abnormal rapid repetitive initiation → tachycardia Impulse conduction Failure to conduct to all parts of the heart → bradycardia (conduction block) Circular conduction (short circuit) → tachycardia Automaticity Automaticity : specialized cardiac tissue can initiate impulses and spontaneously depolarize SA node determines when and how quickly the heart beats Under normal physiologic stimuli the heartbeat accelerates and decelerates – neural control (autonomic input) Hierarchy of pacemaker automaticity – each lower site is slower. Pacemaker Rate ECG findings Sinus node 40-90 bpm P waves before each QRS complex Atrium (abnormal) AV node and junction 35-50 bpm Narrow regular QRS complex without a preceding P wave His-Purkinje 20-40 bpm Wide regular QRS complex Ventricular (abnormal) < 30 bpm Abnormal automaticity Pathologically suppressed automaticity → bradycardia Sinus node disease – scarring with age, fibrosis, sick sinus syndrome Metabolic conditions reducing sinus node automaticity – electrolyte disturbances, thyroid disease Tissues can become automatic under pathologic conditions Atrial tachycardia – an atrial focus rapidly and repetitively fires During myocardial ischemia/infarction, ventricular muscle may develop automaticity → ventricular tachycardia Case example A 78-year-old woman is monitored for syncope. AF stops, then a 6-second pause with no atrial activity and no junctional escape. Rhythm strip shows reduced automaticity → a 6-second pause Initially HR is rapid, irregular, with no P waves (atrial fibrillation) When AF stops, nothing happens in the atrium for 6 seconds and no junctional escape beat takes over Suppressed automaticity → bradycardia, dizziness, syncope A pacemaker may be indicated to depolarize during the pause Re-entry Re-entry : re-stimulation of cardiac muscle due to circular conduction abnormalities. Impulse conducts abnormally (usually circularly around an obstacle) and perpetuates itself Common cause of tachycardia; does NOT cause bradycardia Refractoriness protects against re-entry Cardiac tissue has a long absolute refractory period after activation, caused by the long recovery phase of the AP All ventricular muscle depolarizes in 80 ms , but repolarization takes 400 ms (QT interval) This prevents re-stimulation of tissue and is anti-tachycardic Depolarization of the ventricle takes 80 ms (QRS); repolarization takes 400 ms (QT). Requirements for re-entry A potential circuit – usually two halves (limbs) Different refractoriness in each limb Slow conduction in one region – lets previously activated tissue recover and be re-activated Temporary conduction block in one direction – uni-directional block A premature beat blocks in the longer-refractory β limb, conducts slowly down α, then returns retrograde up β once it has recovered. 1) AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) – Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Extra short circuit: an accessory pathway connecting atrium to ventricle outside the AV node Sinus conduction goes normally down the AV node, around the ventricular conduction system, and back up the accessory pathway Forms a circuit that re-stimulates the AV node, creating a heartbeat each time – 120-250 bpm Circuit: down the AV node into the ventricle, back up the accessory pathway to the atrium. Possible accessory pathway locations around the mitral and tricuspid annuli. Orthodromic AVRT (90%) Antidromic AVRT (10%) Uni-directionally blocked first beat comes down the AV node (slows conduction) and up the accessory pathway , back to the AV node Uni-directionally blocked first beat comes down the accessory pathway and up the AV node, opposite to normal conduction Conduction to the ventricle uses the AV node and His-Purkinje system Conduction to the ventricle uses the accessory pathway Narrow complex regular tachycardia Wide complex tachycardia Orthodromic AVRT. Orthodromic: antegrade down the AV node, retrograde up the accessory pathway. Antidromic: antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the AV node. 2) AV node re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) Both limbs of the circuit are within the AV node (small microcircuit) One limb moves slowly down towards the ventricle; the other travels around and re-enters Narrow complex regular tachycardia – common in young people Responds to beta blockers, CCB, or catheter ablation of the slow pathway in the AV node 3) Ventricular tachycardia in myocardial infarction scarring Limb 1: slow conduction through the scar Limb 2: outside and around the scar Wide complex regular tachycardia Can be life-threatening with poor EF and prior MI Management: medications (sotalol, amiodarone) or catheter ablation of the scar tissue Scar VT: slow conduction through the peri-infarct zone, returning around the scar. Re-entrant tachycardias at a glance Re-entrant rhythm Circuit QRS Orthodromic AVRT Down AV node, up accessory pathway Narrow, regular Antidromic AVRT Down accessory pathway, up AV node Wide AVNRT Two limbs within the AV node Narrow, regular Scar VT Through and around MI scar Wide, regular Triggered activity: abnormality of impulse initiation Abnormal ion currents produce an abnormal AP Re-depolarizations are triggered after depolarizations → repetitiv

Bradycardia Bradycardia is either a battery problem (sinus node dysfunction – too few P waves) or a wiring problem (AV block – P waves without QRS). Whether to pace depends on mortality risk and symptoms , not the heart rate alone. SSS = symptomatic sinus node dysfunction; asymptomatic dysfunction needs no treatment. Lower (infra-nodal) blocks carry a worse prognosis. Mobitz II and complete heart block are paced for mortality even if asymptomatic. AF with a regular QRS means complete AV block. LBBB is negative in V1, RBBB positive. The two categorical mechanisms of bradycardia: sinus node dysfunction (a problem with the battery → not enough P waves) and AV block (a problem with the wiring → normal P waves, not enough QRS complexes). Sinus node dysfunction = problem with the battery Not enough P waves Degenerative process that becomes more prevalent with aging 1) Sinus bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence Inappropriate response to sympathetic drive – adrenaline, exercise Symptoms: fatigue, exertional limitation Chronotropic incompetence (CI): peak heart rate with exercise is blunted compared with controls. 2) Sinus pauses, sinus arrest Intermittent pauses of the SA node Symptoms: presyncope, syncope 3) Conversion pauses Sinus pause triggered by conversion of a tachycardia Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome Tachy = AF with rapid rates Brady = sinus conversion pauses Management challenges Rapid AF treated with metoprolol, then conversion to a slow sinus rhythm with long pauses. Sick sinus syndrome vs asymptomatic dysfunction Sick sinus syndrome (SSS) = symptomatic sinus node dysfunction → treatment is appropriate (pacemaker) Asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction ≠ SSS → no indication for treatment AV block = problem with the wiring Normal P waves, not enough QRS complexes Site of block: AV node or infra-nodal (His bundle, bundle branches) – lower levels of block have a worse prognosis Degrees of AV block Degree Definition Features 1st degree PR interval > 200 ms All P waves are conducted 2nd degree At least 1 non-conducted P wave; more P waves than QRS Group beating: QRS complexes appear bunched in groups Site of block: AV node or infra-nodal; pacemaker likely indicated Mobitz I (Wenckebach) Gradual PR prolongation before the block Mobitz II No PR prolongation preceding the block 2:1 AV block Every second P wave non-conducted; no consecutive PR intervals to judge whether they prolong or are fixed 3rd degree (complete) No conducted P waves; more P waves than QRS AV dissociation – QRS regular, PR variable Regular escape rhythm: junctional (narrow QRS) or ventricular (wide QRS) Site: AV node (> 40 bpm) or infra-nodal (< 40 bpm) AF with complete AV block Regular QRS with fibrillatory waves at baseline (AF is normally irregularly irregular) Bundle branch blocks (BBB) Warning sign of degenerative conduction disease, which may evolve into complete heart block Same number of P waves and QRS complexes, because the other bundle branch still works Wide QRS > 120 ms – left and right bundles depolarize consecutively instead of together Block ECG sign Left bundle branch block Wide QRS, negative in V1 Right bundle branch block Wide QRS, positive in V1 Left anterior fascicular block Left axis deviation Left posterior fascicular block Right axis deviation Torsades de Pointes / polymorphic VT = long QT interval Usually triggered by a premature ventricular contraction landing on the T wave – “ R on T phenomenon ” Bradycardia management Treat for mortality (risk of sudden death): 2nd degree AV block type II, 3rd degree AV block Treat for morbidity (symptomatic): sinus node dysfunction, 2nd degree AV block type I No need for treatment (asymptomatic): sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, Mobitz I Wenckebach, 1st degree AV block, BBB Acute treatment Chronic treatment IV atropine (anticholinergic): ↑ HR, improves conduction Permanent pacemaker IV isoproterenol (sympathomimetic): ↑ HR, improves conduction Wire passed through L subclavian vein, SVC, tricuspid valve, into RA and/or RV Temporary transcutaneous pacing : pads stimulate the heart through the chest wall Attached to a generator housing a battery and computer chip Temporary transvenous pacing wire : through the jugular vein into the RV ECG: sharp spikes followed by a wide QRS Practice questions The 2 main categorical mechanisms of bradycardia are: sinus node dysfunction and AV block All of the following (sinus arrhythmia, sinus bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence, sinus pauses) are manifestations of sinus node dysfunction EXCEPT: sinus arrhythmia – physiologic sinus variation with respiration; normal First degree AV block is defined by: a long PR interval > 200 ms, but all P waves are conducted Types of second degree AV block include all EXCEPT: (a) intermittent non-conducted P waves preceded by prolonging PR intervals; (b) … preceded by fixed PR intervals; (c) AV dissociation – a manifestation of third degree (complete) heart block; (d) 2:1 AV block This ECG shows: sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and normal axis – QRS wide and positive in V1; QRS positive in leads I and II Question 13: RBBB – wide QRS, positive in V1. The following patients should have pacemaker implantation, EXCEPT: (a) symptomatic sinus node dysfunction; (b) asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction – no high mortality risk and not symptomatic; (c) symptomatic complete AV block; (d) asymptomatic complete AV block

Syncope Syncope is transient LOC from reduced cerebral blood flow. Most is benign reflex (vasovagal) syncope ; the job is to find the minority with cardiac syncope , which carries the worst prognosis, and the history does most of that sorting. Reflex syncope is 75% ; cardiac syncope (15%) has the worst survival . Simultaneous sinus slowing + AV block is diagnostic of vasovagal reflex. VVS treatment is reassurance, salt and water, trigger avoidance, counter-pressure ; pacemakers rarely help because they miss the vasodepressor component. Red flags: exertional or sudden syncope, structural disease, abnormal ECG, FHx of sudden death . Definitions Syncope : a transient loss of consciousness (LOC) with spontaneous recovery that does not require intervention Blackout, faint, spell, collapse; not the same as coma, cardiac arrest, drowsiness or generalized seizure Usually due to a reduction in cerebral blood flow (hypotension) Presyncope : sensation of impending loss of consciousness without progression to LOC Dizzy, lightheaded; must be differentiated from vertigo May be a less severe manifestation of reduced cerebral blood flow Prodrome : the symptoms that precede syncope Differential diagnosis of syncope Category Cause Notes Reflex syncope (75%) neurally-mediated / neurocardiogenic Vasovagal (75%) Usually structurally normal hearts, otherwise healthy; any age Situational Vasovagal variant with a recognized trigger – micturition, cough, pain Orthostatic Postural tachycardia syndrome, postural hypotension Carotid sinus hypersensitivity Baroreceptors in the carotid vasculature become stimulated Cardiac syncope (15%) worst prognosis Structural/obstructive (1%) Aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumours Arrhythmia (25%) Bradycardia, tachycardia Neurologic Seizure Can mimic syncope CVA or TIA (affecting RAS) Intracranial hemorrhage Other Metabolic Hypoglycemia, hypoxia Pulmonary embolus Psychogenic (factitious) Survival by cause of syncope: vasovagal tracks no-syncope; cardiac syncope has the worst survival. Vasovagal pathophysiology Taking a syncope history Confirm LOC – not a fall/trip, weakness or dizziness Circumstances – standing for long periods, dehydration, warm weather Prodrome or sudden (vasovagal vs arrhythmic) – HR, sweating, chest pain, flushing, nausea, SOB Recovery (post-drome) – heart racing, chest pain, SOB, fatigue Witnesses PMHx – structural heart disease FHx – sudden, unexplained death Case example A 65-year-old woman with recurrent syncope – 6 events over 17 years. PMHx: high cholesterol, osteoarthritis. Medications: simvastatin, ibuprofen. What does this patient need first? (a) echocardiogram, (b) ambulatory monitor, (c) tilt table test, (d) more history – ask questions that push towards or away from a neurally-mediated (benign) cause, (e) straight to pacemaker. Clinical presentation and management of vasovagal syncope (VVS) Step Vasovagal syncope Hx Common situations : post-prandial, warm day, prolonged standing; post-exertion, post-cough, post-micturition; triggered by pain, anxiety, stress, illness Prodrome (seconds-hours before): fatigue, weakness, nausea, sweating, pallor, visual disturbance, abdominal discomfort Post-episode : fatigue, malaise – whereas cardiac syncope with heart block may feel back to normal after the episode ECG Absence of QRS complexes – the heart is affected by the vasovagal reflex, it does not cause it Parasympathetic tone hits the sinus node and AV node at the same time: sinus node → P waves slow; AV node → Wenckebach or AV block Simultaneous sinus slowing and heart block is diagnostic of a vasovagal reflex Tilt table Vasovagal reflex ↓ systemic vascular resistance → BP falls Pure vasodepressor – HR stays stable Cardioinhibitory/mixed – HR also drops Lifestyle Reassurance – VVS is generally benign (simply a bodily reflex) Salt (electrolytes) and water (hydration) Trigger avoidance Counter-pressure Feeling a prodrome – do NOT stand to “walk it off”; sit/lie down Squeeze/cross the legs to increase perfusion to the brain Drugs Beta blockers – block the SNS overdrive that leads to the reflex PNS surge Fludrocortisone – retains salt in the kidney, ↑ BP Midodrine – ↑ vascular resistance, ↑ BP Pacemaker Generally not warranted; rare instances – refractory patients, occupations where an event is high risk Patients often still faint: pacing addresses only the cardioinhibitory component, not the vasodepressor component Surgical placebo is very effective at treating VVS Counter-pressure maneuvers (leg crossing, squatting, foot on a stool) raise BP. Clinical approach to cardiac syncope Step Cardiac syncope Initial screening Routine bloodwork ECG Echocardiogram; cardiac MRI or CT if high suspicion – structural heart disease increases the risk of malignant arrhythmia Ambulatory monitoring Patients are often seen AFTER the event – only useful if another episode occurs during monitoring Symptom-rhythm correlation diagnoses arrhythmic causes (brady, tachy); the patient keeps a symptom diary to compare with the rhythm Monitors: Holter (24-48 h); external loop recorder; implantable loop recorder (2-3 year battery) Provocation Tilt test, stress test, drug infusions Electrophysiology testing (invasive): catheters through the veins into the heart; stimulate and measure electrical activity; look for conduction disease or inducible tachycardia Management Treat the underlying cardiac condition: Structural – surgical correction of the obstruction Bradycardia – pacemaker Tachycardia – medications, cardiac ablation, implantable defibrillator Red flags that warrant additional investigation Red flag Why it matters Exertional syncope Fainting during exercise is NOT vasovagal – suggests cardiac causes; obstruction and arrhythmia can be provoked by exertion/↑ demand Aortic stenosis 3-year survival after the onset of symptoms Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Diagnosed by echocardiogram; cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy people Inherited arrhythmias

Tachycardia: SVT and VT Tachycardia sorts first by QRS width : narrow = supraventricular (benign, no sudden death), wide = VT until proven otherwise (can cause collapse and sudden death). For SVT, the next question is whether it depends on the AV node . SVT has an excellent prognosis; VT can kill. AV node–dependent SVTs (AVNRT, AVRT) terminate with AV block ; atrial tachycardia, flutter and AF continue. WPW = delta wave + fused QRS. For an uncertain wide complex tachycardia, adenosine then cardioversion – cardioversion is always appropriate if unstable or uncertain. Polymorphic VT presents with syncope/arrest, and acute ischemia is its most common cause. VT prognosis tracks LV function. Supraventricular vs ventricular tachycardia Feature SVT VT QRS Narrow (< 120 ms) Wide Origin Top chambers (atria) – activates both ventricles together via AV node and His-Purkinje Bottom chambers (ventricles) HR 100-200 bpm 100-200 bpm Prognosis Recurrent symptoms but NO sudden death ; excellent prognosis Can cause hemodynamic collapse and sudden death if untreated Pitfall Can mimic VT if QRS is wide (bundle branch block) Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) SVTs are classified by whether the arrhythmia needs the AV node – which is what blocking the AV node (adenosine, vagal maneuvers) reveals. Classification of SVT Class Type Notes Sinus tachycardia Sinus Hyperthyroidism, fever, anemia, exercise Atrial tachycardia AV node independent – continues when the AV node is blocked Ectopic atrial tachycardia Atrial flutter P (flutter) waves continue to circulate Atrial fibrillation QRS complexes rapid and irregular Junctional re-entrant AV node dependent – terminates when the AV node is blocked AV node re-entry (AVNRT) Circuit localized within the AV node Atrioventricular re-entry (AVRT) Uses an accessory pathway Conduction system: SA node, AV node and His-Purkinje – the origin of the P wave sets its axis. P wave morphology: sinus vs atrial tachycardia Sinus rhythm: upright P waves in I, II and III. Atrial tachycardia: P wave axis differs from sinus. Lead Sinus tachycardia Atrial tachycardia (likely LA) I SA node activates atrium R → L (+ P wave) Atrium activated L → R (– P wave) II Top → bottom (+ P wave) Bottom → top (– P wave) III Top → bottom (+ P wave) Bottom → top (– P wave) Clinical management of SVT Acute management Chronic management AV node blockade : Vagal maneuvers – carotid sinus massage IV adenosine – short-lasting, 10 seconds IV verapamil, IV diltiazem – long-lasting IV amiodarone No therapy if spells are infrequent and minimally symptomatic Restore sinus : Cardioversion Procainamide – slow atrium Ibutilide – slow atrium Empirical drug therapy: beta blockers, CCB Catheter ablation : destroy the cardiac tissue contributing to the arrhythmia Fluoroscopy of electrophysiology catheters positioned for mapping and ablation. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome Conduction occurs over both the AV node and an accessory AV pathway Fused QRS complex with a preceding delta wave Pre-excitation: the degree of accessory pathway conduction changes how much of the QRS is fused into a delta wave. Accessory pathways and their ECGs A : down the normal pathway, up the accessory pathway → narrow QRS SVT B : SVT with bundle branch block → wide QRS tachycardia C : down the accessory pathway, up the normal pathway → wide QRS tachycardia D : conduction down the normal pathway + accessory pathway (AF) → irregularly irregular Panels A-D match the four accessory pathway patterns above. Bundle branch block vs SVT with aberrancy ECG Rate Features Typical LBBB 80 bpm Wide QRS; lateral leads: rabbit ears Typical RBBB 75 bpm V1: R, S, R′; normal axis SVT with LBBB aberrancy 200 bpm Small R, deep S wave; lateral leads: rabbit ears Typical LBBB. Typical RBBB – RSR′ in V1. SVT with LBBB aberrancy – rate 200 with an LBBB pattern. Wide complex tachycardia. Wide complex tachycardia. Wide complex tachycardia of uncertain origin If you do not know whether a wide complex tachycardia is VT, SVT over an accessory pathway, or SVT with bundle branch block, give adenosine to establish AV dependency, then perform cardioversion . Cardioversion is always appropriate for deteriorating hemodynamics or uncertainty. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) Monomorphic VT – QRS complexes all look identical Associated with organic heart disease – CAD, cardiomyopathy Idiopathic VT – structurally normal heart; primary electrical problem Monomorphic VT. Polymorphic VT – QRS complexes change beat-to-beat in a single lead Repolarization (QT) syndromes With ischemia, cardiomyopathy, “genetic” heart disease Generally presents with syncope and cardiac arrest, NOT palpitations Prolonged QT Torsades de Pointes can lead to polymorphic VT Polymorphic VT. Polymorphic VT / Torsades de Pointes. Ventricular fibrillation Rapid, disorganized rhythm that can lead to cardiac arrest Ventricular fibrillation. Prognosis with VT Depends mainly on ventricular function – good LV = good prognosis Extent and degree of coronary stenosis is a major factor – treatable (statins, risk reduction) vs fixable (revascularization) Sudden death can occur with QT syndromes despite a good LV Clinical management of VT Acute management Chronic management IV adenosine to assist diagnosis if uncertain Oral antiarrhythmics (sotalol, propafenone, amiodarone) IV lidocaine – monomorphic ischemic VT Implantable defibrillator (ICD) IV procainamide – any monomorphic VT Catheter ablation IV amiodarone – refractory VT (polymorphic not related to QT syndrome) or VF Unique considerations for QT syndrome and other repolarization syndromes Cardioversion is always appropriate for deteriorating hemodynamics or uncertainty Case example 1 A 32-year-old previously well woman notes sudden-onset heart racing after dropping her son off at hockey Light-headed, neck pounding, anxious No medications except an assortment of vitamins and “herbal” remedies with unlisted ingredients Comes to the ER after 2 hours, beginning to panic Case 1: SVT –

Atrial Fibrillation AF is chaotic re-entry in the atria producing an irregularly irregular rhythm. It harms in three ways – stroke, rapid rate, lost atrial kick – and management matches each: anticoagulate, rate-control, rhythm-control . Irregularly irregular with fibrillatory waves. 10% of over-80s have AF. CHADS2 : CHF, HTN, age > 75, diabetes (1 each), stroke/TIA (2); mitral stenosis is also very high risk. Rate control = beta blocker, CCB, digoxin ; rhythm control = class I/III drugs or DC cardioversion . > 48 h or unknown → 3 weeks anticoagulation before cardioversion. ECG manifestations Multiple re-entrant circuits meander through the atria – multiple waves in the atrium Fibrillatory waves – disorganized, continuous; can be very small Irregular RR intervals – irregularly irregular ventricular rate Etiology Age-dependent : risk rises after 50; 10% of those 80+ have AF Cardiac : hypertension, ischemic heart disease, valvular disease (MS, MR, AS), sick sinus syndrome, cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic) Non-cardiac : alcohol, metabolic (thyroid disease), pulmonary (COPD, pneumonia, sleep apnea) Reversing the underlying disease can make AF easier to treat Classification of patient presentation Type Features Paroxysmal Highly symptomatic self-terminating episodes, minutes to hours Patients are well when back in sinus rhythm Persistent Does not stop spontaneously – antiarrhythmic agents or DC cardioversion required Chronic (permanent) In AF all the time – agents slow the ventricular rate and control symptoms No attempt is made to restore sinus rhythm AF causes harm through three consequences , and each has its own therapy: thromboembolism → anticoagulation; rapid irregular ventricular rate → rate control; loss of atrial kick → rhythm control. 1) Thromboembolic events Rapid, chaotic atrial activation → disorganized mechanical function and stasis of blood Causes of AF also cause LA enlargement, adding to stasis Once formed, clots can embolize → stroke and other thromboembolic events Mitral stenosis is also a very high risk factor for stroke Stroke prophylaxis (any 1 risk factor): anticoagulation (warfarin) or antiplatelet therapy (ASA) CHADS2 item Points C HF 1 H ypertension 1 A ge > 75 years 1 D iabetes 1 Prior S troke or TIA 2 Annual stroke risk (%) rises with CHADS2 score: 1.9% at 0, 4.0% at 2, 18.2% at 6. Where anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, fondaparinux, dabigatran) and antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) act. 2) Rapid irregular ventricular rate The AV node allows rapid ventricular activation: 130-170 bpm Symptoms: palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort Tx: rate control with AV nodal blocking drugs – beta blockers, CCB, digoxin AF can also give a normal rate or bradycardia; rate slowing may or may not be needed depending on AV node function 3) Loss of atrial-ventricular synchrony Loss of atrial mechanical function removes the atrial contribution to ventricular filling – the atrial kick In some heart diseases this ↓ LV filling and cardiac output → breathlessness, exertional dyspnea, fatigue Tx: rhythm control Class I (Na+ channel blockade): flecainide, propafenone Class III (K+ channel blockade): sotalol, amiodarone, dronedarone DC cardioversion: synchronized electrical shock to return AF to sinus – patient anaesthetized (propofol), paddles anterior and posterior, 50-200 J, patient wakes in sinus rhythm AF > 48 hours or of unknown duration Rate-control and give 3 weeks of anticoagulation before cardioversion – thrombus may already have formed. Antiarrhythmic Pharmacology Antiarrhythmics act on specific phases of the action potential (Vaughan Williams classes I-IV), and every one can also cause arrhythmias. Therapy starts with precipitating factors and a clear goal, not with the drug. Class I = Na+ (phase 0, widens QRS); II = beta blockers (phase 4); III = K+ (phase 3, prolongs QT); IV = Ca2+ (phase 2, AV node). CCBs are not for ventricular arrhythmias and are avoided in HF. Amiodarone: long half-life, lung, thyroid, cornea, skin toxicity , little proarrhythmia. Digoxin does not convert AF and fails with high sympathetic tone. Adenosine terminates AVNRT, slows AF/sinus tachycardia, can cause bronchospasm. In emergencies: stable → drugs, unstable → electricity, dead → CPR + electricity + drugs . Torsades: Mg2+, correct K+ slowly, stop QT drugs, raise HR. Lidocaine does not slow AF ; TCA overdose widens the QRS. Vaughan Williams classes mapped to the action potential: class 1 phase 0 (Na+), class 2 phase 4 (β), class 3 phase 3 (K+), class 4 phase 2 (Ca2+). Drug effects on the ECG Changing the slope of phase 0 → widening of the QRS Prolonging the plateau phase → prolonged QT Basic principles of therapy 1) Identify and treat precipitating factors Electrolyte abnormalities – low K+, Mg2+, PO4 3– Myocardial ischemia Hypoxemia Catecholamines – endogenous (anxiety, pain, fever), exogenous (epinephrine, dopamine) Other modifiable risk factors – weight reduction, alcohol, smoking cessation Medications – drugs may prolong QT; antiarrhythmics may be proarrhythmic 2) Decide on your goal Not all arrhythmias need treatment – sinus tachycardia (treat the underlying cause) AF – rate control vs restoring sinus rhythm; thrombosis prophylaxis if indicated 3) Minimize risk Drug-drug interactions Renal dysfunction – many drugs are renally excreted; know renal function and the drug's pharmacology to avoid side effects or toxicity Non-pharmacologic therapy may be most appropriate – pacemaker, implantable cardiac defibrillator Proarrhythmia Proarrhythmia : the ability of drugs (including antiarrhythmics) to cause arrhythmias. Digoxin – toxicity may cause virtually any arrhythmia, including triggered activity QT-prolonging drugs – Torsades de Pointes Drug-induced bradyarrhythmia – beta blockers, CCB Vaughan Williams classification of antiarrhythmics Class Drug Effects Clinical use I: Na+ channel blocker phase 0 1a: Procainamide Prolongs AP duration – widens QRS Active metabolite has class III action (prolonged QT) SVT Convert AF to sinus Ventricular arrhythmias 1c: Lidocaine Caution: hepatic metabolism; half-life 1-2 hours Toxicity: CNS toxicity, cardiovascular collapse VT (ischemia) Local anesthetic II: Beta blockers phase 4 Metoprolol Slows sinus rate, ↓ AV node conduction, modulates SNS Ischemic heart disease, systolic HF ↓ rate in AF III: K+ channel blocker phase 3 Amiodarone Prolongs plateau – ↑ QT Oral: long-term therapy, loading dose required IV bolus: ↓ BP Half-life 24+ hours; accumulates in tissue with half-life 2-6 months SVT Ventricular arrhythmias Emergency rate control in rapid AF Amiodarone adverse effects Not very proarrhythmic despite class III effect Pulmonary toxicity – inflammation, fibrosis Thyroid – hyper- or hypothyroidism Corneal microdeposits, skin discoloration, GI effects, neuropathy Sotalol Prolongs repolarization – ↑ QT, can be proarrhythmic ↓ automaticity, slows AV node conduction IV: Ca2+ channel blocker phase 2 Verapamil Diltiazem IV bolus: acute situations, ↓ BP Oral: long-term therapy; avoid in HF Supraventricular arrhythmias Slow AV node conduction NOT for ventricular arrhythmias Many drugs act in multiple classes – sotalol is a beta blocker (II) with K+ channel blockade (III); amiodarone is class III but has class I, II, III and IV effects Some drugs are metabolized to active components in a different class Some drugs fit no class – atropine (bradycardia), digoxin (slows rate in AF), adenosine (AV nodal blocker) Digoxin Adenosine Mechanism Inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → ↑ contractility Indirect vagal effect ↓ intrinsic SA node rate Prolongs AV conduction – rapid but very short response Uses Rate control in AF, but: will not convert AF to sinus; Wide complex tachycardia. Case 1 monitor: wide complex tachycardia. ECG Review: New Atrial Fibrillation A case of palpitations in a 65-year-old woman worked from ECG to management. The ECG settles the diagnosis (AF: narrow, irregularly irregular); management then rests on two principles – anticoagulation and rate vs rhythm control . Palpitations workup: exam, CBC/electrolytes/TSH, ECG, Holter – all reasonable . Narrow + irregularly irregular = AF ; narrow + regular = SVT; F waves in inferior leads = flutter; wide + regular = VT. Stable new AF → anticoagulate (CHADS2 2 = 4%/yr) + rate control . No cardioversion if > 48 h/unknown and not anticoagulated , unless unstable or TEE excludes thrombus. Meet the patient: palpitations A 65-year-old woman with a week of “palpitations” – skipped, irregular heartbeats. No chest pain, SOB or syncope. Personal stress (caring for her husband after his stroke); attributes symptoms to stress. Recently diagnosed hypertension; diet-controlled diabetes. Appropriate next step? (e) All of the above – all are reasonable starting points: a) Physical exam – pulse regularity, vitals, clues of structural heart disease b) Bloodwork (CBC, electrolytes, TSH) – palpitations can signal common systemic disease such as anemia or thyroid disease c) ECG – shows rhythm or clues to structural heart disease d) Holter monitor – captures the rhythm during symptoms Based on the ECG, what is the diagnosis? Narrow complex, irregularly irregular rhythm – atrial fibrillation. Option ECG clue a) Atrial fibrillation ✔ Narrow complex and irregularly irregular b) Supraventricular tachycardia Narrow complex and regular c) Atrial flutter Flutter or “F waves” in the inferior leads d) Ventricular tachycardia Wide complex and regular Findings AF at 110 bpm in the office; otherwise unremarkable exam – no murmurs, no elevated JVP BP 130/80; currently well and asymptomatic, but concerned by the new diagnosis Echocardiogram: no structural disease What are the next appropriate steps? (a) anticoagulate; (b) beta blocker for rate control; (c) antiarrhythmic medication; (d) elective electrical cardioversion; (e) A and B . For THIS patient: anticoagulation + beta blocker for rate control . All answers can be acceptable in certain situations. The question highlights the two key AF principles: (1) the need for anticoagulation and (2) rate vs rhythm control . Stroke risk uses the CHADS2 score: hers is 2 (age and hypertension) → annual stroke risk 4% Stable, new AF → no need for emergency cardioversion or an urgent antiarrhythmic Rate control with a beta blocker or CCB is a good first step – it controls the ventricular rate during exercise Duration unknown and could be > 48 hours → high thrombus risk → anticoagulate Cardioversion in AF of unknown duration If AF has lasted, or may have lasted, > 48 hours and the patient is not appropriately anticoagulated, cardiovert only for hemodynamic instability or once an intracardiac thrombus is excluded by imaging (transesophageal echocardiogram).

Right ventricular hypertrophy is associated with a large R wave in leads V1, V2, and V3. Left ventricular hypertrophy is associated with a large S wave in V1 and a large R wave in V6.

If a patient’s ECG shows abnormalities in leads II, III, and lead aVF, which of the following is a reasonable interpretation? There is an error in the ECG reading There is an abnormality in the anterior portion of the heart There is an abnormality in the inferior portion of the heart There is an abnormality in the lateral portion of the heart The correct answer is C. Leads II,III and lead aVF all have at least one component of their vector which point down (inferiorly). Thus an abnormality in those leads may suggest an abnormality in the inferior portion of the heart.

A recent heart attack survivor presents to the clinic for his 6-month follow-up. The patient seems to be doing well and is on his way to recovery. Which of the following pathologic signs would you expect to see in this patient’s ECG today? ST elevation ST depression T wave inversion Wide Q waves There should be no abnormalities given the patient is currently healthy. The correct answer is D. Q waves are persistent even after a patient has recovered from a heart attack and will be persistent on future ECGs. ST elevation signals a current myocardial infarction. ST depression and T wave inversion are indicative of ischemia.

Consider the ECG below for a patient with complete (third-degree) AV-block. Which statement regarding the 12-lead ECG below is true? The heartbeat is irregularly irregular The heart rate is above 60 bpm Leads I, II, and aVF demonstrate right-axis deviation There is a regular P wave The correct answer is D. The heartbeat is regular at about 50 bpm. With positive signals in leads I, II, and lead aVF, this is a normal axis ECG. Careful analysis of the rhythm strip indicates regular P waves and slower (but also regular) QRS waves characterized by complete (third-degree) AV block.

All of the following drugs are vasodilators EXCEPT: Digoxin Losartan (an angiotensin receptor blocker) Nitroglycerin Benazepril (an ACE-inhibitor) Amlodipine (a calcium channel blocker) The correct answer is A. Digoxin is not a vasodilator. Digoxin functions in the heart by increasing contractility. All other drugs listed are vasodilators.

Sildenafil was originally developed by Pfizer for the treatment of hypertension and angina. During its clinical trials, researchers discovered that the drug was more effective at inducing erections than treating angina, and thus, Viagra was born. What is the mechanism by which Viagra induces penile erections? Viagra inhibits the enzyme that converts GTP to cGMP. Viagra decreases the intracellular concentration of calcium in endothelial cells. Viagra inhibits the enzyme that breaks down cGMP. Viagra increases the cellular concentration of nitric oxide. Viagra blocks the release of aldosterone from the adrenal glands. The correct answer is C. Viagra works by preventing the breakdown of cGMP, a vasodilator. It does this by inhibiting phosphodiesterase-5, the enzyme that converts cGMP into GMP.

Bradykinin is a vasodilator that, in excess amounts, can lead to a cough and edema of the tongue and airways. Which drug prescribed for hypertension is most likely to increase blood concentrations of bradykinin? Digoxin Losartan (an angiotensin receptor blocker) Nitroglycerin Benazepril (an ACE-inhibitor) Amlodipine (a calcium channel blocker) The correct answer is D. Angiotensin-II is a vasoconstrictor and stimulates the release of aldosterone from the adrenal glands. In addition to this, angiotensin II degrades bradykinin. ACE-inhibitors such as benazepril prevent the formation of angiotensin II, leading to elevated levels of bradykinin

The patient has chronic hypertension and has a respiratory illness which makes them particularly susceptible to pulmonary edema and coughing. Which of the following medications would you prescribe this patient to manage their cardiac condition? Lisinopril (ACE-inhibitor) Valsartan (angiotensin receptor blocker) Lisinopril and valsartan Spironolactone (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) The correct answer is B. ACE-inhibitors and ARBs are both indicated in patients with hypertension and postmyocardial infarction. Choose as many as applicable Diastolic murmur with an S3 sound Systolic murmur with an S4 sound Enlarged valve area (> 4 cm2) Reduced valve area (< 1.5 cm2) Right ventricular hypertrophy Fatigue and weight loss Angina and syncope Weak and delayed pulse The correct answer is B, D, G, H. Aortic stenosis manifests as a systolic murmur with an accompanying S4 sound in late diastole. A shrunken valve area is indicative of aortic stenosis. 2. Johanna is a 77-year-old patient coming to your clinic. For the past three years, she has been noticing increasing shortness of breath and fatigue, especially after climbing stairs. Her blood pressure is 170/80, and during a physical exam, you hear a diastolic murmur. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis? Mitral stenosis Mitral regurgitation Aortic stenosis Aortic regurgitation Pericarditis The correct answer is D. The presence of a widened blood pressure range (the range between diastole and systole) in addition to a diastolic murmur strongly indicates aortic regurgitation. A patient with aortic regurgitation can also present with dyspnea following exertion.

Chest X-Ray Echocardiography MIBI scan Cardiac MRI Computed tomography Cardiac CT’s provide a detailed picture of cardiac vessel anatomy and can pinpoint calcifications and occlusions. The image below represents the jugular venous pressure throughout the cardiac cycle for a patient with cardiac tamponade (a wave=atrial contraction, x descent =atrial emptying, v wave= ventricular contraction, y descent= ventricular filling). Which of the following components of the image are abnormal relative to a healthy patient? The a-wave is too high The v-wave is too low The v-wave is too high The y-wave is blunted The correct answer is D. In patient with cardiac tamponade, ventricular filling is compromised as pericardial effusions extrinsically compress the ventricle making it difficult to fill the ventricle. This is reflected on the Jugular venous pressure as a blunted y-wave.

Which of the following invasive imaging modalities provide physicians the ability to treat the pathology while conducting the imaging test? Trans esophageal Echocardiogram Transthoracic Echocardiography Nuclear Scintigraphy Cardiac Catheterization The correct answer is D. With inspiration there is negative thoracic pressure which draws venous return into the heart. Which of the following imaging modalities involve subjecting a patient to ionizing radiation? Select all that apply. Chest X-Ray Echocardiogram Nuclear Scintigraphy Computed Tomography Magnetic Resonance Imaging Cardiac Catheterization The correct answer is A, C, D, F. These imaging modalities involve subjecting a patient to ionizing radiation, and occasionally contrasting agents which are excreted renally. These are disadvantages to these imaging modalities.

Which imaging modality is considered non-invasive and best suited for excluding coronary artery disease? Chest X-Ray Echocardiogram Nuclear Scintigraphy Computed Tomography Magnetic Resonance Imaging Cardiac Catheterization The correct answer is D. Computed Tomography is a non-invasive technique that can be used to exclude coronary artery disease. Cardiac catheterization can also be used to assess for coronary artery disease, but this is an invasive technique.

Which of the following symptoms is NOT characteristic of mitral regurgitation? Systolic murmur with an S3 sound Decrease in stroke volume Left ventricular dilatation Decrease in left atrial pressure Pulmonary edema The correct answer is D. In mitral regurgitation, it's common to find an increase in left atrial pressure as blood can flow up into the left atrium during systole, giving the marked raise in pressure.

Which condition is most consistent with an ECG that reveals QRS waves of alternating intensity? Acute pericarditis Pericardial effusion Constrictive pericarditis Tricuspid valve regurgitation Mitral valve regurgitation The correct answer is B. In pericardial effusion leading to tamponade, compression of the heart leads to the heart “swinging” within the pericardium. This swinging leads to electrical alternans, where QRS waves alternate in signal intensity.

Upon listening to the patient’s heart you hear a systolic murmur loudest at the base of the heart. The sound radiates to the patient’s carotids, and you hear an S4 sound and a single S2. There is sustained palpitation at the apex. Which of the following murmurs best describe this? Aortic stenosis Atrial septal defect Tricuspid regurgitation Mitral regurgitation Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy The correct answer is A. The characteristics – single S2, located at the base, radiating to the carotid and sustained palpitation – are indicative of aortic stenosis.

Upon listening to the patient’s heart you hear a systolic murmur loudest at the border. The sound does not change with inspiration and palpitation of the precordium reveals a parasternal thrill. Which of the following murmurs best describe this? Aortic stenosis Atrial septal defect Tricuspid regurgitation Mitral regurgitation Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy The correct answer is D. The characteristics – systolic murmur loudest at the border, no change in inspiration and parasternal thrill at the precordium – are indicative of a ventral septal defect.

Which of the following best explains the etiology of rheumatic fever-induced mitral stenosis? A streptococcal infection leads to the production of antibodies against a particular antigen on the pathogen, which is molecularly similar to an antigen in the valvular structure of the heart. How can mitral valve stenosis and mitral valve regurgitation be differentiated? Select all that apply. Timing of murmur (systole/diastole) Ventricular hypertrophy (Left/right/none) Volume of cardiac output Presence of Pulmonary edema Patient reporting angina The correct answer is A, B. Mitral stenosis manifests as a diastolic murmur, while mitral regurgitation manifests as a systolic murmur. In which of the following conditions are you most likely to observe an S3 sound during auscultation of the heart? Select TWO answers . Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Mitral regurgitation Mitral stenosis Aortic stenosis Aortic regurgitation The correct answer is B, E. An S3 sound is observed with a volume-loaded ventricle. This can be caused by regurgitation of the aortic and mitral valves.

Arthritis Arthralgia Elevated acute phase reactants Central nervous system involvement A and D All of the above The correct answer is F. A patient presents with fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance, and peripheral edema. Additionally, they have an increased jugular venous pressure on inhalation. Based on this presentation the physician suspects constrictive pericarditis. Which of the following is the best modality to assess the thickness of the calcification of the pericardium? ECG Chest X-ray Transthoracic echocardiogram Auscultation The correct answer is B. Chest X-ray, CT scan, or MRI are all good imaging modalities to observe calcification of the pericardium.

A patient presents to your clinic with mitral stenosis. Which of the following conditions would you NOT commonly find in a patient with this disease? Left atrium dilation Left ventricle hypertrophy Pulmonary hypertension Reduced cardiac output Thrombus development in left atrium The correct answer is B. In mitral valve stenosis left atrium dilation is common as less blood is able to make it past the stenotic mitral valve and remains in the left atrium. Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next TWO questions. Andrew is a 65-year-old man who presents to your walk-in clinic with dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and angina. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and regularly consumes alcohol. When auscultating his heartbeat, you notice a systolic murmur loudest at the base, and the presence of S4. Based on this presentation, you suspect aortic stenosis. What is the best test to confirm the diagnosis? Electrocardiogram Chest X-ray Transthoracic echocardiogram Transesophageal echocardiogram MRI The correct answer is C. Echocardiograms are diagnostic imaging tests for valvular diseases. A trans-thoracic echocardiogram would be preferred to a trans-esophageal echocardiogram because the transthoracic cardiogram is non-invasive.

You are seeing a patient complaining of chest pain. After a comprehensive patient history and physical exam, you suspect mitral valve stenosis. Which observation is inconsistent with this working diagnosis? The patient has chest pain from pulmonary hypertension. The patient’s heartbeat includes a diastolic murmur. The patient has arthritis and a rash on his skin. The patient’s ECG indicates atrial fibrillation. The patient has left ventricular hypertrophy. The correct answer is E. In mitral valve stenosis, narrowing of the mitral valve would result in reduced volume supplied to the left ventricle. This would not lead to left ventricular hypertrophy.

There is no medical therapy available for Aortic Stenosis, which leaves SAVR and TAVI. You are a third-year medical student doing a rotation in the emergency department. Your patient is Saul, who presented with rapid-onset severe chest pain. Heartbeat auscultation reveals a systolic murmur, best heard at the apex. Suspecting a pathology associated with the heart valves, you perform a bed-side echocardiogram. Based on the clinical presentation, which diagnosis is the echocardiogram most likely to reveal? Acute mitral stenosis Acute mitral regurgitation Acute aortic stenosis Acute aortic regurgitation Acute pericarditis The correct answer is B. A patient with mitral regurgitation presents with a systolic murmur loudest at the apex. Acute mitral regurgitation is sudden in onset and leads to a presentation of pulmonary edema. This can be caused by endocarditis.

Which of the following statements is NOT true? The “MitraClip” is an emerging therapy used to treat selected patients with mitral regurgitation In general, there are more benefits to doing complete valve replacement over valve repair In most scenarios stenotic valves must be replaced Bioprosthetic valves in older individuals last longer than bioprosthetic valves in younger individuals Patients with mechanical valves must stay on lifelong anticoagulation The correct answer is B. There are significant advantages to repairing a repairable valve over replacing the entire valve. There is increased durability, decreased risk of infection, thrombosis, thromboembolism, and less bleeding complications.

Which of the following is not a risk factor for aortic stenosis? Old age (> 60 years) Increased dietary source of calcium Congenital bicuspid aortic valve Rheumatic fever leading to aortic valve scarring The correct answer is B. Old age, congenital bicuspid aortic valve, and rheumatic fever that leads to scarring are all risk factors for aortic stenosis. An increase in dietary calcium is not a risk factor.

Which of the following causes of aortic regurgitation do NOT usually lead to left ventricle hypertrophy? Leaflet calcification Chronic hypertension Rheumatic fever Marfan’s syndrome The correct answer is C. Rheumatic fever is a cause of acute aortic regurgitation, where enough time usually does not pass for left ventricle hypertrophy to develop. The leaflets of the aortic valve can deteriorate causing a backflow of blood into the left ventricle.

Which of the following is a complication of myocardial Infarction? Choose the best FIVE answers. Which of the following is not a risk factor for atherosclerosis? Older age Female sex Diabetes mellitus Hypertension Smoking The correct answer is B. Female sex is not a risk factor for atherosclerosis – male sex is a risk factor for atherosclerosis. Estrogen provides a protective effect against the development of atherosclerotic plaques.

Which of the following aneurysms have an etiology that stems from atherosclerosis or inflammation? Berry aneurysm in the brain Saccular aneurysm in the thoracic aorta Fusiform aneurysm in the abdominal aorta B and C A, B, and C The correct answer is D. Berry aneurysms in cerebral vessels are not related to atherosclerosis or inflammation. Their etiology is not well understood but it is believed to be an inherent weakness within the cerebral vessels and can rupture from transient increase in blood pressure.

Which of the following pathologies does NOT require an invasive intervention? Which of the following statements is false regarding aneurysms? Which of the following stenoses is generally be the most fatal? Left Main coronary stenosis Left Main Equivalent stenosis Triple Vessel Disease Double Vessel Disease with proximal LAD The correct answer is A. Left main coronary stenosis occurs when there is a 50% (or greater) reduction in the lumen of the left coronary artery and often carries the worst outcomes.

Which of the following complications of Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery does not increase a patient’s mortality? Cerebrovascular accident (which can result from an emboli), mediastinitis, and hemorrhage (with increasing need for transfusion) are all associated with increased

Which statement regarding coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery is true? During CABG surgery, the heart is injected with a high sodium solution to pause the heartbeat. The internal thoracic artery is the best artery to use for long-term survival. Finally, CABG is ideal for long-term management of hea

Use the following passage to answer the next TWO questions. A 70-year-old patient presents to your clinic with leg pain in both calves. Acute Arterial Embolic Ischemia Acute Arterial Thrombotic Ischemia Intermittent Claudication Chronic Limb Ischemia The correct answer is C. These patient’s symptoms align with intermittent claudication – there is pain in his calf that is brought upon by exertion and relieved by rest. This patient might have narrowing of both of his femoral arteries from atherosclerotic plaques.

Use the following passage to answer the next TWO questions. A 70-year-old patient presents to your clinic with leg pain in both calves. Watchful waiting Aspirin medications Surgical bypass Statin medication Establishing an exercise routine Smoking cessation Percutaneous revascularization The correct answer is B, D, E, F. For patients with intermittent claudication the focus should be on Antiplatelet therapy (prescribing Aspirin), Blood pressure control, Cholesterol management (prescribing Statins), Diabetes management, Exercise and smoking cessation – the acronym ABCDE’S is useful t

A patient with ongoing tissue loss, gangrene and resting pain in their lower limbs presents to your clinic. After a thorough investigation the physician diagnoses the patient with chronic limb Ischemia. The physician and patient are deciding on a management option. Which of the following statements are accurate? The physician should consider a surgical bypass surgery if the patient prefers a minimally invasive procedure The physician does not need to consider medical therapy (exercise, antiplatelet therapy) as it’s not relevant for this patient’s pathology The physician should consider a surgical bypass surgery with an autogenous vein graft for its high durability The physician should consider a surgical bypass surgery if the patient has diabetes and is susceptible to chronic infections The correct answer is C. If the patient wants a minimally invasive procedure the physician should consider percutaneous revascularizat

The normal diameter of the descending thoracic aorta is 2.5 cm, and the normal diameter of the abdominal aorta is 2 cm. Francisco is a patient who just received a CT scan to assess for bone lesions caused by multiple myeloma. During the CT scan, the radiologist noted that Francisco’s descending thoracic aorta had fusiform growth to a diameter of 3.4 cm, and his abdominal aorta had fusiform growth to a diameter of 3.2 cm. Which statement is true? The descending aorta has an aneurysm and the abdominal aorta has an aneurysm The descending aorta has an aneurysm and the abdominal aorta has ectasia The descending aorta has ectasia and the abdominal aorta has an aneurysm The descending aorta has ectasia and the abdominal aorta has ectasia The correct answer is C. An aneurysm is defined as a growth in diameter of more than 50% of the normal diameter. Growth less than 50% is defined as ectasia.

Which of the following modalities is currently used to screen patients for abdominal aortic aneurysm? CT scans Ultrasounds X-rays Catheter-based angiography Physical Exam The correct answer is B. Ultrasounds are used to screen patients for abdominal aortic aneurysms. CT scans are the gold standard however they are also more expensive.

Which of the patients below would not qualify for a screen for an abdominal aortic aneurysm? Albert, a 55-year old male with whose father died of an AAA rupture Betsy, a 65-year old female with a 30 pack-year smoking history Charlie, a 70-year old male without any symptoms David, an 80-year old male whose previous AAA screen at age 65 was negative The correct answer is D. The current Canadian guidelines for AAA screening are a one-time ultrasound for men between ages 65 and 75, a one-time ultrasound for women with risk factors, or a one-time ultrasound for patients older than 55 with a family history. Bill is a 55-year-old patient who has been suffering from a severe chronic infection and was recently diagnosed with a mycotic abdominal aneurysm. The diameter of the aneurysm is 3.5 cm. The patient’s chronic infection has also deteriorated several of his organs. Which of the following management options is best suited for this patient? Operative Intervention Antibiotics Statin medication (for aneurysm size reduction) Observation The correct answer is A. For patients with a pseudoaneurysm or mycotic aneurysm there is a need to operate despite size as they grow faster and rupture at smaller sizes – even with antibiotic treatment. The endovascular repair is preferable to an open surgical repair, as it’s less invasive. Furtherm

Which of the following aneurysms would an endovascular repair be least appropriate? Suprarenal aortic aneurysm Juxtarenal aortic aneurysm Infrarenal aortic aneurysm Popliteal aneurysm The correct answer is D. Popliteal aneurysms are usually repaired with an open bypass operation, as endovascular repair is less frequently used due to the risk of occlusion. For suprarenal, juxtarenal and infrarenal aortic aneurysms, endovascular repair is indicated in most patients.

Which statement below concerning aneurysm rupture is false? Aneurysm rupture risk increases as the diameter of the aneurysm increases Aneurysms remain stable or are degenerative - they never regress Aneurysm rupture is associated with an overall 40-50% mortality rate Aneurysms are repaired as prophylactic treatment to avoid rupture The correct answer is C. The overall mortality rate of an aortic aneurysm rupture is 80%. Among those who are able to make it to the hospital, the mortality rate is 40-50%. The rest of the statements are true.

Use the following answers for the next THREE questions. A patient has been experiencing worsening symptoms of pulmonary congestion and palpitations. A physician orders an echocardiogram which reveals cardiomegaly associated with eccentric cardiomyopathy anterolaterally. What is the likely diagnosis? Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction Left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction Right-sided heart failure The correct answer is B. Pulmonary congestion and palpitations are associated with left-sided heart failure. Eccentric cardiomyopathy indicates a volume-overloaded ventricle, consistent with leftsided HFrEF.

Use the following answers for the next THREE questions. A patient has been experiencing prolonged peripheral edema and upon physical examination it is noted that she has an elevated jugular venous pressure, and presence of ascites. Lung sounds are normal. What is the likely diagnosis? Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction Left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction Right-sided heart failure The correct answer is C. The absence of lung pathology and lung sounds indicates right-sided heart failure. Peripheral edema and elevated JVP are consistent with right-sided heart failure: with reduced blood outflow from the right ventricle, blood volume pools in the veins.

Use the following answers for the next THREE questions. A patient came into your clinic with some concerns of his health following his heart attack last year. He feels winded after climbing the stairs, and his partner has been complaining recently of his loud snoring. Suspecting heart failure, you order an echocardiogram, which reveals concentric hypertrophy. What is the likely diagnosis? Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction Left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction Right-sided heart failure The correct answer is A. Dyspnea on exertion and obstructive sleep apnea indicate left-sided heart failure, and concentric hypertrophy is associated with preserved ejection fraction.

Sacubitril and valsartan when combined are an example of the ARNI class of heart failure medications. What is the mode of action of sacubitril? What is the mode of action of valsartan? An ARNI (angiotensin receptor / neprilysin inhibitor) includes valsartan as the angiotensin receptor inhibitor (blocks the binding of angiotensin II) and sacubitril (inhibits neprilysin). Neprilysin is an enzyme which catalyzes the break-down of natriuretic peptides such

A 55-year-old patient who has persistent COPD presents to your clinic with ascites and severe swelling of the foot. Upon physical examination you to notice this patient has a distended jugular vein. You are suspecting heart failure; which of the following types of heart failure is most likely in this scenario? Systolic left-sided heart failure Diastolic right-sided heart failure Right-sided heart failure Biventricular heart failure The correct answer is C. Right-sided heart failure can arise from chronic lung diseases such as COPD, where there is an increase in pulmonary pressure. Increased pulmonary pressure leads to fluid back-up into the right ventricle and back into the venous system, which can manifest as a distended jugu

“Heart A” and “Heart B” are both hearts from patients who had heart failure. Which of the following statements are likely true? Choose THREE answers. Heart A likely belonged to a patient with systolic heart failure; Heart B likely belongedto a patient with diastolic heart failure Heart B likely belonged to a patient with systolic heart failure; Heart A likely belongedto a patient with diastolic heart failure Heart A shows concentric hypertrophy; Heart B shows eccentric hypertrophy Heart B shows concentric hypertrophy; Heart A shows eccentric hypertrophy The individual with Heart A likely experienced reduced ejection fraction, but theindividual with Heart B likely did not The individual with Heart B likely experienced reduced ejection fraction, but theindividual with Heart A likely did not The correct answer is B, C, F. Heart A shows concentric hypertrophy where sarcomeres develop in parallel leading to increased ventricular wall thickness, and this is often the case in diastolic heart failure where the heart is unable to fill properly and there is increased afterload – ejection fract

Which of the following statements regarding medications for heart failure is false? IF channel inhibitors block the sodium/potassium channels in the SA node leading to a reduction in heart rate, however contractility is not impaired. Beta Blockers reduce both heart rate and contractility in addition to reducing hypertrophy and fibrosis.

Despite treatment with heart failure medications, a 70-year-old patient with worsening left sided heart failure is now unable to go on his daily walks without feeling out of breath. Bill is a 79-year-old patient who suffered an anterior wall myocardial infarction three years ago. Despite rapid treatment, Bill was left with some mild damage to his heart. Which of these patients are expected to have the worst prognosis upon presentation to a hospital with heart failure? The presence of which of the following signs/markers after a thorough investigation is enough to exclude a diagnosis of Heart Failure? Which of the following physiologic changes would you NOT expect to see in a patient with left-sided systolic heart failure? Which of the following patients are suffering from restrictive cardiomyopathy? A patient who suffered from myocardial infarction, which led to necrosis of their myocardium and ultimately dilation of the left ventricle with a resultant wall motion abnormality A patient with long standing aortic regurgitation which has led to a dilated left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction Significant hypertrophy of myocardium, possibly of a genetic etiology resulting in hypertrophied and a stiff ventricle. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is when the wall of the ventricles are stiff but not necessarily thickened. This can result from cardiac amyloidosis or be idiopathic. Commonly the atria are enlarged. Which option below correctly describes a contraindication for a drug used to treat heart failure? A contraindication for treatment with ARNIs is current treatment with ACE- inhibitors. A contraindication for treatment with beta-blockers is bilateral renal arterial stenosis. A contraindication for treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors is the presence of diabetes.
