In 2019, dapagliflozin was approved for the treatment of heart failure. Dapagliflozin is a SGLT2 inhibitor that was originally approved for the treatment of diabetes. For which of the patients below is Dapagliflozin recommended? Select all that apply. A patient with HFrEF and diabetes A patient with HFrEF and no diabetes A patient with HFpEF and diabetes A patient with HFpEF and no diabetes The correct answer is A, B, C. Dapagliflozin is used to treat diabetes, so options A and C are correct. Data also suggests that Dapagliflozin is effective in the treatment of HFrEF even in patients without diabetes, making option B also correct.

Which of the following combination treatments is currently recommended for initial management of patients with Heart Failure with reduced ejection fraction (<40%)? Angiotensin Converting Enzyme inhibitor, Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists Angiotensin Converting Enzyme inhibitor, Beta-Blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists Angiotensin receptor / Neprilysin inhibitor, Beta-Blockers and mineralocorticoid receptors Angiotensin receptor / Neprilysin inhibitor, Beta-Blockers and Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors The correct answer is B. Initial management for these patients is triple therapy – ACEi (or ARB if the patient is intolerant to ACEi), Beta blockers and MRA. Patients should not be on both ACEi and ARBs. ARNI is introduced later in therapy for patients with NYHA classifications II-IV.

Which of the following therapies primarily targets the pathological effects of Aldosterone in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction? Angiotensin II Converting Enzyme inhibitor Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists Beta Blockers ARNI Implantable Cardiac Device The correct answer is B. MRAs such as spironolactone and eplerenone counteract the effects of Aldosterone in Heart Failure.

Which of the following therapies primarily prevents sudden cardiac death for patients with heart failure? Angiotensin II Converting Enzyme inhibitor Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists Beta Blockers ARNI Implantable Cardiac Device The correct answer is E. Sudden Cardiac Death originates from arrhythmia. An ICD is implanted within a patient to prevent abnormal rhythms (ventricular arrhythmia specifically) that can lead to sudden cardiac death.

Which patient below should be referred to advanced care for end-stage heart failure? Abigail, whose heart failure is NYHA Class II with an ejection fraction of 30% Brenda, who consistently has elevated BNP and has required 3 hospitalizations for heart failure in the past year Corina, who has pitting edema and a blood pressure of 110/75. Deborah, who wants a heart transplant despite good management with her current meds. The correct answer is B. For referral for advanced care, a patient should have two of the symptoms or signs in the I NEED HELP acronym. Abigail would qualify if her heart failure was NYHA Class III or IV and her ejection fraction was less than 20%. Corina would qualify if she had pitting edema and a

Which statement concerning the care of advanced heart disease is false? Even though a patient may feel better after cutting back on beta-blockers, this will not prolong their life. In a heart transplant, the donor’s heart is usually connected to the recipient’s heart in series. Common complications of a ventricular assist device are driveline infection and thrombosis. In 50% of cases, a transplanted heart survives 12 years following transplantation. The correct answer is B. Donor hearts are not connected in series to the recipient’s heart. The recipient’s heart is removed, and the donor heart is anastomosed with the patient's aorta, pulmonary veins, and venae cavae. The remaining options are true.

Which statement on the variability of blood pressure (BP) is true? A routine clinical BP measurement is likely to underestimate a patient’s BP. The best predictor of cardiovascular risk are BPs measured by highly trained nurses. The gold standard for accurate BP measurements is an ambulatory BP measurement. The correct answer is D. Option A is false - routine clinical BP typically measurements overestimate a patient’s BP by (on average) 9 mmHg. Option B is false - a patient should not be talking while taking a BP measurement. A patient comes to your clinic concerned they have high blood pressure after a close relative received that diagnosis. As the physician you take his blood pressure while he is sitting and still – the patient’s blood pressure is 160/100. Which of the following is an appropriate next step? Diagnose the patient with hypertension and discuss next steps Reassure the patient they don’t meet the threshold for hypertension Reassure the patient they don’t have hypertension but ask them to follow up in 1 year Arrange for an out of office assessment to be done (Ambulatory or Home Blood Monitor) The correct answer is D. In this scenario the patient’s blood pressure is below the 180/110 threshold to diagnose hypertension, but still significantly high to warrant further investigation. This can be done by arranging ABP or HBP. If the ABP is >135/85 or the HBP is >140/90 this is enough for furt

Which of the following is NOT a typical initial investigation for a patient with hypertension? Urinalysis Blood chemistry 12-lead ECG Echocardiogram Hbg-A1c levels The correct answer is D. An echocardiogram is useful for diagnosing valvular pathologies, but not so valuable when investigating a patient with hypertension.

With a highly elevated blood pressure of 180 mmHg (systole), Felicia’s target BP is 140 mmHg (40 mmHg difference). Clark is a 66-year-old patient with hypertension (BP 170/110 mmHg). Three months ago, his doctor prescribed both ramipril (an ACE-inhibitor) and indapamide (a diuretic). He has diligently taken all medication as prescribed, and today, his blood pressure is 155/104 mmHg. Assuming Clark is low risk, what would be the next course of action for Clark’s management? Continue the current treatment – blood pressure takes more than 3 months to adjust following a medication change. Double the current doses of ramipril and indapamide Supplement the current medication regimen with candesartan (an ARB) Supplement the current medication regimen with amlodipine (a CCB) The correct answer is D. If a patient has not completely responded to double-therapy, a third antihypertensive agent should be prescribed. For a patient on triple therapy, the drug classes are normally an ACE-inhibitor OR an angiotensin receptor blocker, a diuretic, and a calcium channel blocker.

For a patient with severe hypertension, triple-therapy is recommended. How should a physician approach triple therapy for severe hypertension? Prescribe one medication at a time, and check for symptoms continually before and after adding another medication Prescribe one medication from the cocktail at a low dose, and then continue to increase that dose until you’ve reached maximal efficacy. Prescribe all the medications at once at maximal dose and monitor for symptoms. Prescribe all the medications initially in a combination pill at a moderate dose and monitor for symptoms as you reach the maximal dose The correct answer is D. Often it’s better to prescribe multiple medications at once, perhaps in a single pill, and then increase the dosage as you monitor for symptoms. Prescribing the medications one at a time, will eliminate the enhanced response that comes with combination therapy.

Elizabeth is four weeks old. She was born following an uncomplicated pregnancy and returned to the hospital today due to cyanosis of the skin. Truncus arteriosus Transposition of the great arteries Tricuspid atresia Tetralogy of Fallot Total anomalous pulmonary venous return The correct answer is E. There are no curative surgeries available for this condition; however, some palliative surgeries exist to prolong life until early adulthood.

Which of the following cardiac structures within a fetus is pathological? The increased volume in the right ventricle gets pumped

Within the first week of life a child presents mildly cyanotic. Upon examination the physician can hear a systolic ejection murmur. Furthermore, the VSD present allows for the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood leading to mild

Which of the following murmurs is most likely to be pathologic? A 4-year-old with a soft (2/6) systolic ejection murmur at the lower left sternal border that is louder in the supine position. Option A is consistent with Still’s murmur, Option B is consistent with benign peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, and option D is consistent with venou

Both can be the result of a bicuspid aortic valve There is an increase in afterload in the left ventricle in both conditions Both have a systolic murmur on physical exam Degenerative calcified valves can cause either aortic stenosis or aortic regurgitation Both result in left ventricular hypertrophy The correct answer is C. There is a diastolic murmur in aortic regurgitation and a systolic murmur in aortic stenosis. It is best heard in the 3rd intercostal space at the end of expiration and when the patient is leaning forward.

Which of the following is a possible physical exam, symptom, or investigation finding in aortic regurgitation? Chest xray will be unremarkable ECG will help assess the severity of regurgitation The loudness of the murmur is a strong indicator of the severity of the regurgitation Orthopnea can occur in long-standing aortic regurgitation The heart apex will be normally located The correct answer is D. Orthopnea is a sign of congestive heart failure, which can occur in the setting of chronic aortic regurgitation. A chest xray will likely reveal an enlarged left ventricle from left ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation. The most an ECG will tell you is that there is left ve

A patient presents with a previous history of untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis and you are concerned about rheumatic fever. Which of the following does NOT meet the criteria of rheumatic fever? Fever Involuntary movements of the limb and trunk Carditis Shortness of breath Elevated CRP The correct answer is D. Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis and is diagnosed using the Revised Jones Criteria, which consists of major criteria (arthritis, carditis, central nervous system involvement, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum) and minor criteria (arthralgia, fe

Which of the following is NOT a consequence of mitral stenosis? Increased stroke risk Right-sided heart failure Hemoptysis Exertional dyspnea Left ventricular dilatation The correct answer is E. Left ventricular dilatation is not one of the symptoms, signs, or consequences of mitral stenosis. Increased stroke risk comes from dilatation of the left atrium, which can cause atrial fibrillation. This promotes blood stasis and thrombus formation, which can embolize. Righ

Which of the following is NOT a cause of acute mitral regurgitation? Mechanical failure of a prosthetic mitral valve Dilatation of the left ventricle due to myocardial ischemia Rheumatic fever Mitral valve prolapse/myxomatous mitral valve disease The correct answer is D. While mitral valve prolapse/myxomatous mitral valve disease may be acute, it is much more commonly a cause of chronic mitral valve regurgitation.

While rounding, you notice that 78 year-old patient named Mr. Cristae has been diagnosed with chronic mitral valve regurgitation. Which of the following signs and symptoms is unlikely to be observed? Abnormal carotid upstroke Dyspnea, fatigue and orthopnea Palpitations High-pitched, pansystolic or holosystolic murmur audible at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position The correct answer is A. The carotid upstroke is expected to be abnormal in a patient with aortic stenosis, not mitral regurgitation. In fact, this sign can be used to distinguish the two conditions.

While auscultating a patient’s precordium, you notice a scratchy, triphasic sound throughout systole and diastole. The patient also reports pleuritic chest pain which worsens when they are supine. What is the most likely diagnosis? Aortic regurgitation Acute mitral valve regurgitation Infective endocarditis Pericarditis The correct answer is D. The triphasic, scratchy character of the sound is a hallmark of the pericardial friction rub. Thus, this patient likely has pericarditis.

Which of the following sequences correctly describes the lines of treatment for acute pericarditis? First line: NSAIDs, colchicine and exercise restriction. Second line: steroids. Third line: immune-modulating agents. Fourth line: pericardiectomy. First line: steroids, NSAIDs exercise restriction. Second line: colchicine. Third line: immune-modulating agents. Fourth line: pericardiectomy. First line: pericardiectomy. Second line: immune-modulating agents. Third line: steroids. Fourth line: NSAIDs, colchicine and exercise restriction. First line: NSAIDs and colchicine. Second line: immune-modulating agents and exercise restriction. Third line: steroids. Fourth line: pericardiectomy. The correct answer is A. The first line of pericarditis treatment is NSAIDs, colchicine and exercise restriction (for 3 months). Steroids are generally a second line treatment; however, they may be a first line treatment in patients with autoimmune conditions. Immune-modulating agents like anakinra,

A 40 year-old women with mitral valve stenosis is deciding whether she should select a bioprosthetic valve or a mechanical valve for her valve replacement surgery. She has endstage renal disease and is dependent on dialysis. Which valve would you recommend and why? Bioprosthetic – this will avoid the need for anticoagulation. Bioprosthetic – mechanical valves have a higher risk of thrombosis, which could lead to severe end-organ damage in this patient’s kidneys. Mechanical – evidence strongly indicates that mechanical valves confer a greater survival benefit than their bioprosthetic counterparts. Mechanical – dialysis accelerates the degeneration of bioprosthetic valves, making mechanical valves the better choice. The correct answer is D. Dialysis accelerates the degeneration of bioprosthetic valves, therefore, a mechanical valve would be the more durable option. It is true that bioprosthetic valves are less thrombogenic. However, the risk of thrombosis is comparable if mechanical valves are paired with antic

Which of the following characteristics would NOT make a patient with myxomatous mitral valve disease a good surgical candidate? Asymptomatic with moderate, but declining, left ventricle function New onset atrial fibrillation Symptomatic with severe left ventricle dysfunction Severe pulmonary hypertension The correct answer is C. Mitral valve repair surgery is indicated if patients are asymptomatic and have mild or moderate left ventricle dysfunction. It is not favourable (and has poor outcomes) if left ventricular dysfunction has become severe.

Which of the following would NOT increase one’s risk of developing endocarditis? Bicuspid aortic valve Previous endocarditis Intravenous drug use Coronary artery disease The correct answer is D. Although the presence of CAD increases the risk of subsequent CV events, this does not directly relate to endocarditis. The risk of endocarditis increases with cardiac-related, patient-related and procedure-related factors that increase infection risk.

The diagnosis of endocarditis relies on the fulfillment of Duke’s Criteria. Which of the following is a major criterion? Fever above 38 degrees Celsius Echocardiogram showing vegetation, abscess, new growth on a prosthetic valve, or new valve regurgitation Osler nodes and Janeway lesions observed upon physical exam Predisposing heart conditions or intravenous drug use The correct answer is B. Duke’s criteria requires either 2 major criteria, 1 major + 3 minor criteria, or 5 minor criteria to diagnose infective endocarditis. All of the options – apart from visualization of the heart and valves using an echocardiogram – are minor criteria.

Which of the following layers of the heart is the first to be compromised in an ischemic event? Myocardium Pericardium Sub-endocardium Epicardium The correct answer is C. The sub-endocardial zone is the farthest away from blood supply; when blood supply is compromised, this zone suffers first.

Which of the following statements is false: The proximal parts of the coronary arteries are usually affected by coronary artery disease It always takes a large focus for coronary artery disease to become a problem Multifocal coronary artery disease is easier to treat Fibrofatty plaque is more unstable and prone to thrombose The correct answer is B. Atheroma can be very focal along a coronary artery From 02 - Pathology of Ischemic Heart Disease. The lecture says atheroma can be very focal . One short, tight segment limits flow through the whole vessel, so a small focus can be a big problem. That makes B false. A : true.

Match the coronary artery to the location of infarction The pairings: Coronary artery Location of infarction Left Anterior Descending Artery Anterior MI Right Coronary Artery Inferior MI Left Circumflex Artery Posterior MI From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. These come first and precede ST elevation. ST elevation : transmural inj

Which of the following are absolute contraindications for administering thrombolytics (choose all correct options): Pregnancy Use of warfarin Intracranial bleeding episode 1 year prior Ischemic stroke 2 months ago Intracranial malignancy Blood pressure 160/90 The correct answer is C, D, E. From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The lecture splits contraindications to thrombolysis into absolute and relative. The absolute ones include: Any prior intracranial bleed (C) , however long ago. Ischemic stroke within 3 months (D) : 2 months qualifies. After 3 months it

Which of the following signs is not typically seen in a patient suffering from an RV infarction? ST elevation Elevated JVP Chest crackles Hypotension The correct answer is C. Lungs are clear in a setting of RV infarction (Triad: Hypotension, JVP, clear lungs)

Which of the following statements is false: Acute mitral regurgitation occurs in the setting of an anterior MI due to rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscles Ventricular septal rupture can be heard as a pan-systolic murmur A patient with an LV free-wall rupture may present with an elevated JVP There is a high risk of thrombogenesis in settings of LV aneurysms The correct answer is A. Posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied by the PDA branch of RCA. Inferior MI is caused by occlusion of the RCA in most cases

Which of the following cases would benefit the least from a CABG? Triple vessel disease RCA stenosis Stenosis of LAD and LCx Left Main Equivalent The correct answer is B. From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. CABG improves survival as well as symptoms when a large territory of LV is at risk. The lecture's list: left main , left main equivalent (70% or more in the proximal LAD plus the circumflex), triple-vessel , and double

Which among the following interventions are beneficial for post-CAPG patients? (choose all that apply) Smoking cessation Anti-platelet therapy ACE-inhibitors Statins Beta blockers The correct answer is A, B, C, D, E. (all are beneficial interventions for patients post-CABG)

In the examples provided below, choose the patient who will benefit the most from an exercise stress test 55-year-old man who presents with chest pain which started while he was shovelling snow 70-year-old woman who has shortness of breath and chest pain 28-year-old man who came in for his annual physical 48-year-old who has high blood pressure and cholesterol The correct answer is D. Treadmill Exercise stress tests are indicated when there is intermediate pretest probability (based on age, sex, and chest pain)

A 60-year-old male presents to the ER with acute chest pain and shortness of breath precipitated by climbing a flight of stairs. Which test(s) from the options below would be the next steps? Persantine-MIBI EKG Cardiac CTA Coronary Angio The correct answer is B, D. From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. Acute chest pain in the ER is ACS until proven otherwise. The first test is a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, and it decides the pathway. A STEMI goes to reperfusion by primary PCI. An NSTEMI or unstable angina is stabilized, the

Which of the following is NOT conventional practice for cardiac rehabilitation: Begin counselling patients on smoking cessation even in the inpatient setting Incorporate physical, pharmacological, and nutritional practices into the rehabilitation process Encourage aerobic and resistance training that significantly stresses the heart to build up fitness tolerance Address anxiety and/or depression concerns The correct answer is C. Exercise should be sensible and tailored to the patient’s exercise tolerance, functional capacity, disease burden, and symptom status. The goal is not to place the heart under extreme stress each, but to slowly build up the patient’s endurance. Aerobic and resistance trainin

What is the recommended intensity for resistance training? 40-85% increase in heart rate 50-60% of the patient’s 1 rep-max in the upper body 50-60% of the patient’s 1 rep-max in the lower body Continued sets until the patient can no longer continue The correct answer is C. A is the intensity recommended for aerobic training, B is the intensity recommended for resistance training of the lower body, and C is not in any official recommendations.

What is the role of smooth muscle cells in the development of atherosclerosis? Aberrant smooth muscle cells in the media intima can cause irritation to the endothelial layer, leading to endothelial dysfunction Circulating smooth muscle cell precursors are recruited to the site by an increase in endothelial cell adhesion molecules Smooth muscle cells proliferate and differentiate into foam cells, which store lipid molecules Smooth muscle cells deposit extracellular matrix and collagen which form the basis of the plaque The correct answer is D. Endothelial dysfunction can be caused by hemodynamic stress from hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, toxins, or immune reactions. The increase in endothelial cell adhesion molecules serves to attract circulating leukocytes, not smooth muscle cells, and foam cells are deri

Which of the following patients is LEAST likely to develop an aortic dissection? Abe is a 19-year-old male diagnosed with Marfan’s syndrome Bob is a 62-year-old male with longstanding hypertension Cris is a 23-year-old gender-neutral individual with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus Diane is a 3-month-old female with suspected bicuspid aortic valves The correct answer is C. Diabetes is a cardiovascular risk factor but may not directly contribute to aortic dissection. All other conditions are part of the disease etiology.

A patient presents to your clinic complaining of chronic limb ischemia in the form of claudication. Select all of the possible management strategies you may employ: Oxygen Beta blockers Surgical bypass Balloon angioplasty Anticoagulants ACE inhibitors Statins The correct answer is A, C, D, E, G. Beta blockers are absolutely contraindicated for chronic limb ischemia and ACE inhibitors are not part of the standard management protocol either.

For which of the following patients would you consider surgical bypass over percutaneous revascularization? Ed, a 73-year-old patient with no other comorbidities Felicia, a 19-year-old patient with a large arterial blockage Gok, a 45-year-old patient who is adamant against having surgery Hamad, a 23-year-old patient who is severely anemic The correct answer is B. Large blockages are best managed using bypass if there are no other contraindications to surgery. For A, durability of the stent is not a concern given the patient’s advanced age. For C, patient preference must be taken into account when making medical decisions. For D, anem

What is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosing an abdominal aortic aneurysm? Ultrasound CT Catheter-based angiography MR-angiography The correct answer is B. CT scan with IV contrast is the diagnostic gold standard.

When should mycotic aneurysms be repaired? When the aneurysm is greater than 5.5cm in men or 5cm in women When there is significant growth When it has ruptured As soon as it is identified The correct answer is D. Mycotic aneurysms are fast growing and can rupture at smaller sizes, and so be repaired regardless of size.

A 70 year old man comes to your clinic. He is frustrated because for the last 4 weeks he has been unable to walk up the stairs in his house without becoming mildly short of breath. He does not experience this at rest. With further questioning you learn that he had an MI two years ago. What AHA and NYHA stage of heart failure would this patient fall under, respectively? Stage B, Class 1 Stage C, Class 2 Stage C, Class 1 Stage B, Class 2 The correct answer is B. Stage C because the patient has structural heart disease with current symptoms; Class 2 because he has mild impairment of physical activity and is comfortable at rest.

The NYHA classification of heart failure is irreversible, meaning once you attain one class, you can not go backward. True False The correct answer is B. False, throughout the heart failure progression a patient may wax and wane through the NYHA classes. A patient may present at class 3, but with treatment can revert to class 2, for example.

In pregnancy, the ventricle may dilate to adapt to the volume overload. This is: Pathologic concentric remodeling Physiologic concentric remodeling Pathologic eccentric remodeling Physiologic eccentric remodeling The correct answer is D. Ventricular dilation in pregnancy is adaptive, physiologic remodeling to accommodate the increased volume (ie preload). When ventricles dilate, sarcomeres are added in series, eccentric remodeling.

A patient has symptoms of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and orthopnea. They are given a diuretic, which improve their symptoms. An echo is performed, which is unremarkable. Does this patient meet the diagnostic criteria for heart failure? Yes No The correct answer is B. This patient does not meet the diagnostic criteria for heart failure, as there is no objective evidence because the echo is negative.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy would be described as: Structurally or functionally abnormal heart muscle most commonly due to parvovirus B19, HHV6, or coxsackie virus. Stiff and thickened heart in the absence of coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular and congenital heart disease Structurally abnormal heart where the atria may be larger than the ventricles Cardiomyopathy whereby the ventricles and surrounding structures dilate. The correct answer is C. A characteristic finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is atria larger than the ventricles. RCM involves a stiff, but not necessarily thickened heart. It is most commonly idiopathic or due to cardiac amyloidosis.

There are several ways to classify heart failure. Which of the following is correct? HFpEF occurs when the EF is less than 40% Stage B of the AHA stages of heart failure corresponds to clinical heart failure A patient in class IV of the NYHA classification of heart failure may improve to class III with treatment Left sided heart failure may present with an ascites, an elevated JVP, and reduced appetite The correct answer is C. From 02 - Heart Failure Causes and Classification. NYHA class describes function, so it waxes and wanes as symptoms are controlled. A class IV patient can therefore improve to class III with treatment. The AHA/ACC stages, by contrast, only move forward. A : HFpEF is EF ≥ 50%

A patient presents to the ER with SOB at rest, orthopena, confusion and dizziness. On examination you hear crackles in the lungs, and find a narrow pulse pressure. A chest x ray reveals pulmonary edema. How would you classify this patient based on their congestion and perfusion? Warm and Dry Warm and Wet Cold and Dry Cold and Wet The correct answer is D. This patient has signs of pulmonary congestion (orthopnea, crackles in lungs, pulmonary edema) and poor perfusion (confusion, dizziness, narrow pulse pressure)

The case. A patient presents to the ER with SOB at rest, orthopena, confusion and dizziness. On examination you hear crackles in the lungs, and find a narrow pulse pressure. A chest x ray reveals pulmonary edema. For the patient mentioned in question 7, what additional initial tests would you order? Select all that apply. Blood work: CBC, Cr, electrolytes ECG Echo Endomyocardial biopsy Cardiac MRI The correct answer is A, B, C. Endomyocardial biopsy and cardiac MRI are more invasive tests that would not be done initially.

Which of the following medications would be considered first line therapy for NYHA class III, HFrEF? Select all that apply. ACE inhibitors ARNI ARB B-blocker Aldosterone antagonist The correct answer is A, D, E. From 04 - Heart Failure Treatments. First-line HFrEF therapy is triple therapy : A (ACE inhibitor) : indicated in virtually all patients with LV dysfunction. D (beta blocker) : for all stable mild-to-moderate HF. E (MRA) : indicated outright in NYHA III-IV. B (ARNI) :

Your patient with HFrEF has been stable in the NYHA class III classification on the standard triple therapy. His HR is 80 bpm. Which additional medication could you consider adding to this patients regimen? Ivabradine Hydralazine Nitrates ACEi The correct answer is A. Ivabradine is recommended for patients who remain symptomatic despite guideline directed medical therapy (triple therapy: ACEi, B-blocker, aldosterone antagonist) with a HR greater than or equal to 70 bpm.

Which of the following statements is incorrect ? SGLT2 inhibitors have cardio-protective effects independent of blood glucose levels. Ivabradine inhibits the Ca channel in the AV node to decrease heart rate ARNI promotes the vasodilatory and diuretic properties of BNP by inhibiting neprilysin Aldosterone antagonists decrease blood pressure in part by increasing Na secretion. The correct answer is B. Ivabradine inhibits a mixed Na/K channel in the SA node thereby decreasing pacemaker activity and heart rate.

Which of the following is not a sign of end-stage heart failure? Ejection Fraction <40% End-organ dysfunction >/= 2 hospitalization in 12 months Previous or ongoing use of inotropes such as dobutamine Edema/escalating diuretics The correct answer is A. An ejection fraction <20% is a sign of end-stage heart failure.

You confirm that your patient is in end-stage heart failure and need to consider whether they could be a candidate for a heart transplant. What should you consider when assessing a patient for a heart transplant? Select all the apply. Does the patient want a transplant? Is the patient’s condition advanced enough to warrant a transplant? Does the patient have significant co-morbidities? Does the patient have any immunological issues? Are there any surgical considerations that could complicate surgery or bring about unnecessary risk to the patient? The correct answer is A, B, C, D, E. From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. The lecture lists three components of transplant assessment, and every option falls under one of them: A : does the patient want transplant or advanced options? B : is the condition advanced enough ? That

Which of the following is not a common complication of a VAD? GI bleeding Stroke Pump malfunction Myocardial infarction Driveline infection The correct answer is D. The lecture's VAD complications, most to least common, are driveline infection (E), GI bleeding (A), stroke or intracranial hemorrhage (B), device thrombosis, and pump malfunction (C) . They follow from a foreign bod

Which of the following statements is false regarding hypertension? Obstructive sleep apnea is a cause of hypertension Similar to systolic pressure, diastolic blood pressure continuously increases with age Even for those considered to have a normal blood pressure, an increase of systolic blood pressure over 120 mmHg is still associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease Blood pressure taken by experienced clinicians is more accurate in predicting future risk of cardiovascular diseases than blood pressure taken at home Hypertension is a risk factor for renal failure, but not dementia ii, iii, iv ii, iii, v iii, iv, v ii, iv, v The correct answer is D. Diastolic pressure increases with age, reaches a peak between 50s and 60s, and decreases afterwards due to lack of vessel stiffening and decreased vessel compliance. Blood pressure taken at home is a better predictor of future risk of cardiovascular events compared to blood

Order the following steps in prescribing multiple anti-hypertensive medications Choosing between a diuretic or calcium channel inhibitor by assessing the volume status and serum potassium levels Choosing between spironolactone, beta blocker, and doxazosin by assessing the heart rate and serum potassium levels. Choosing a RAS inhibitor: choose between an ACEi or angiotensin blocker by assessing the likelihood of coughing in patient Adding either the diuretic or calcium channel inhibitor that wasn’t selected in the previous step If patient remains hypertensive, assess whether the patient is adhering to all prescribed medications before prescribing further medications. The correct answer is C, A, D, B, E. From 06 - Management of Hypertension. The lecture builds the multi-drug regimen in numbered steps: Step 1 (C) : a RAAS inhibitor, ACEI or ARB, chosen by the odds of a cough. Step 2 (A) : a diuretic or a CCB, chosen by serum K+ and volume status (pedal edema). Nor

For a hypertensive patient who is 70 years old, with no other compelling indications, which of the following is the most preferred drug regimen Calcium channel inhibitor, ARB, ACEi Beta blocker, ACEi, calcium channel blocker ACEi or ARB, calcium channel inhibitor, thiazide-like diuretic ACEi or ARB, Thiazide like diuretic, SGLT2 inhibitor The correct answer is C. The preferred drug regime for most patients with no other compelling indications is a 3 drug regime which contains an inhibitor of the renin-angiotenin-aldosterone system (ACEi or ARB), a diuretic, and a calcium channel blocker. Beta blockers are not a first line treatment f

A 3 month old baby presents to the emergency room appearing “dusky”. A harsh systolic ejection murmur is present. The echocardiogram shows a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary outflow tract obstruction, and an overriding aorta. There is also right ventricle hypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis? Transposition of the great arteries Tetralogy of fallot Coarctation of the aorta Total anomalous pulmonary venous return Pulmonary atresia The correct answer is B. The “dusky” appearance is indicative of cyanosis, thus ruling out coarctation of the aorta, which is a acyanotic lesion. Transposition of the great arteries can also be ruled out, because it usually presents very early on in newborns. The VSD, pulmonary outflow tract obstruc

Which of the following congenital heart lesions is associated with an increased pulmonary flow? Atrial septal defect Ventricular septal defect Bicuspid aortic valve Tetralogy of Fallot Truncus arteriosus i, ii, iv, v i, ii ii, iv, v i, ii, v The correct answer is D. Atrial septal defect and ventricular septal defect will lead to a left to right shunt due to high pressure in the left heart and lower pressure in the right heart. More blood will flow into the right heart, resulting in more blood pumped into the lungs. Truncus arteriosus in

A 5-year-old child presents with a harsh diastolic murmur, accompanied with a thrill. The murmur is best heart in the left lateral decubitus position. What is the most likely diagnosis? Still’s murmur Venous hum Benign peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis Mitral stenosis The correct answer is D. A harsh, diastolic murmur with a thrill is indicative of a pathological murmur, thus ruling out ABC, which are innocent murmurs. Innocent murmurs are systolic, without a thrill, and usually heard louder in a supine position (except venous hum).

A 7-year-old child presents to the clinic with sharp chest pain. The onset of pain is random, even while at rest. The pain is also discretely palpable around the sternum. What is the most likely cause of the chest pain? Cardiomyopathy Costochondritis Bronchitis Lung tumour The correct answer is B. Benign/MSK causes of chest pain can be aggravated at random and can have a sharp quality. Discrete palpable pain also indicates a MSK related cause. Costochondritis is the most common cause of chest wall pain and involves the normal development of the sternum and ribs.

What is the correct hierarchy of pacemaker automaticity? Sinus node, atrium, AV node, His-purkinje, ventricular Sinus node, AV node, atrium, His-purkinje, ventricular Atrium, sinus node, AV node, His-purkinje, ventricular Atrium, sinus node, His-purkinje, AV node, ventricular The correct answer is A. The correct hierarchy is sinus node (40-90bpm), atrium, AV node (35-50 bpm), Hispurkinje (20-40bpm), and ventricular

Which of the following examples of tachycardia are caused by re-entry? Scar related ventricular tachycardia AV re-entrant tachycardia Both A and B None of the above The correct answer is C. Both scar related ventricular tachycardia and AV re-entrant tachycardia involved circuit re-entry. Circuit re-entry requires slow conduction in one region of the circuit, which allows previously activated tissue to recover and become re-excited. Temporary conduction block in

What are correct treatment options for bradycardia? IV atropine (anti-cholinergic) Permanent pacemaker Temporary transcutaneous pacing All of the above The correct answer is D. All of the options are reasonable treatments for bradycardia. IV atropine and temporary transcutaneous pacing are treatment options for acute bradycardia. IV atropine can increase heart rate by blocking the effects of the vagus nerve. Pacemakers can increase heart rate by se

What are some findings on an ECG that are indicative of a Left bundle branch block? Positive V1 Wide QRS Left axis deviation All of the above The correct answer is B. Wide QRS is indicative of left bundle branch block (LBBB). Although, this may be indicative of right bundle branch block as well. However, the remaining options do not point towards LBBB. A positive V1 represents right bundle branch block (RBBB), and left axis deviation show

What is the most common form of syncope? Situational Orthostatic Carotid sinus hypersensitivity Vasovagal The correct answer is D. Vasovagal is the most common form of syncope. All options are forms of reflex syncope as opposed to cardiac causes of syncope.

What are potential treatment options for vasovagal syncope? Reassurance, as this is generally benign Avoid known triggers Treatment with salt and water All of the above The correct answer is D. All options can help with syncope. Reassuring the patient, telling them to avoid known triggers, and treating hypotension with salt and water can go a long way in preventing syncope

What of the following differences between SVT and VT are true? VT is electrical activity directed from the top down of the heart, while SVT is bottom up SVT causes hemodynamic instability while VT rarely causes it VT causes hemodynamic instability while SVT rarely causes it Only VT causes discomfort in patients The correct answer is C. Ventricular tachycardia causes far more hemodynamic instability. The ventricles are in a state where they cannot pump the normal large volume of blood they push into the body, whereas the atria pump a miniscule amount of blood, and their fibrillation is not as deleterious.

What is the difference between AV node re-entry tachycardia and atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia? AV node re-entry tachycardia is not affected by blocking the AV node AV node re-entry tachycardia is caused by a shorted circuit running through an extra electrical pathway through the ventricles back into the atrium Atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia is caused by a short circuit in the AV node itself and cycles within the node None of the above The correct answer is D. None of the above. Their names can be confusing due to their similar sounding content, what should be noted is that the atrioventricular re entry re enters the atria from the ventricles through the extra pathways. AV node re-entry is contained to the AV node and is a short c

What is the difference between atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation? Atrial fibrillation is an organized electrical wave that sweeps across the atria while atrial flutter is a disorganized series of electrical waves in the atria Atrial fibrillation is a disorganized series of electrical waves in the atria while atrial flutter is an organized electrical wave that sweeps across the atria atrial fibrillation is noted as being a series of saw tooth like patterns on an ECG while atrial flutter is seen as disorganized noise atrial flutter is noted as being a series of saw tooth like patterns on an ECG while atrial fibrillation is seen as disorganized noise B and D The correct answer is E. Fibrillation can be seen as a bunch of sporadic electrical discharges across the atria while flutter is also disorganized but is a sweeping discharge across the top of the atria and has more organization.

Which of the following is consistent with a description of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation? highly symptomatic self terminating episodes DC cardioversion is required minutes to hours in duration A and C The correct answer is D. Paroxysmal AF is self terminating, meaning that it ends without intervention. Cardioversion is not required for this process, and it only lasts up to a few hours.

Beta Blockers: able to slow the sinus rate and AV node conduction only antiarrhythmic drugs that decrease cardiac mortality and sudden death in patients with heart failure or ischemic heart disease blocks K+ channels and prolongs repolarization A and B only The correct answer is D. Beta blockers do nothing in the interference of the K+ channels.

Adenosine: Is used to slow atrial fibrillation which can be used to deduce a specific diagnosis Works in VT is an endogenous nucleoside A and C only The correct answer is D. Adenosine causes a momentary pause in cardiac activity but does nothing in the case of ventricular tachycardia.

What is the pericardial cavity? A potential space between the serous parietal and visceral pericardium that contains a thin film of blood for oxygenation of the pericardium. A potential space between the serous parietal and visceral pericardium that contains a thin film of serous fluid for lubrication between the layers. A potential space between the fibrous and serous pericardium that contains a thin film of serous fluid for lubrication between the layers. A potential space between the fibrous and serous pericardium that contains a thin film of blood for oxygenation of the pericardium. The correct answer is B. The pericardial cavity lies between the internal serous layers of the pericardium and contains fluid not blood. The pericardium and heart receive blood from the coronary circulation.

Which features can be found in the ventricles? i) Chordae tendinae. ii) Papillary muscle. iii) Crista Terminalis. iv) Trabeculae carnae. v) Moderator band. i, ii, iii, iv, v i, ii, iii, v i, ii, iv, v ii, iii, iv, v i, ii, iii, v The correct answer is C. Trabeculae carnae are raised irregular muscle ridges found in both the ventricles and atria; however, the atria also contain smooth ridges, and the ridge that separates that in the atria is called the Crista terminalis. Trabeculae carnae can extend into papillary muscles, wh

Which of the following is incorrectly matched with its definition? Capacitance = volume of blood that can be contained in a vessel. Compliance = change in volume / change in pressure. Which of the following is the major pathophysiological mechanism for acute myocardial infarction? Plaque rupture with thrombus formation. Embolism. Cocaine. A healthy 45-year-old has a blood pressure of 120/60 mm Hg. Using the formula from the vascular flow lecture, what is his mean arterial pressure? 60 mm Hg 70 mm Hg 80 mm Hg 90 mm Hg 100 mm Hg The correct answer is C. MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3 = (120 + 120) / 3 = 80 mm Hg . Diastolic pressure is weighted double because the heart spends longer in diastole; simply averaging SBP and DBP gives the wrong answer of 90.

A 79-year-old man with HFrEF and persistent atrial fibrillation is started on digoxin. Which effect should you expect? Digoxin inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase (↑ intracellular Ca2+, so contractility rises) and has an indirect vagal effect that slows AV nodal conduction, so it is a rate-control drug in AF. A 24-year-old woman with severe asthma is found to have hypertension. Which drug is contraindicated? Amlodipine Propranolol Ramipril Chlorthalidone Valsartan The correct answer is B. Propranolol is a nonselective beta blocker: beta 2 blockade causes bronchoconstriction, so severe reactive airway disease is a listed contraindication (with bradycardia and hypotension). A 70-year-old has a holosystolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla, with a displaced apex beat. What is the most likely lesion? In the murmur schema, systolic + apex + radiation to the axilla + holosystolic + displaced apex = mitral regurgitation . AS radiates to the carotids; TR and VSD are border murmurs (RV heave, parasternal thrill); MVP is late-peaking with a mid-systolic click.

A 78-year-old with severe aortic stenosis asks which symptom would mean the worst outlook. Which symptom carries the shortest average survival once it appears? A 74-year-old man has had two episodes of exertional syncope. Echo confirms severe aortic stenosis with preserved LV function. What is the best management? The natural history of AS turns on symptoms : asymptomatic patients are followed, but symptomatic AS → valve replacement , which restores survival. A 45-year-old man receives a mechanical aortic valve. What does this choice commit him to? Mechanical valves have a long life expectancy but need oral anticoagulation for life (INR 2-3 in the aortic position). Bioprosthetic (porcine or bovine) valves need no long-term anticoagulation but have a limited lifespan of about 15 years, which is the trade-off.

A 55-year-old smoker with weight loss has BP 85/73, HR 120, an elevated JVP and muffled heart sounds. The ECG shows electrical alternans. What is the next step? Beck's triad (low BP, high JVP, muffled heart sounds) with electrical alternans = tamponade. Stabilize with IV fluids or pressors and drain urgently (pericardiocentesis). Diuretics and rate-slowing drugs worsen it: the heart depends on preload and on tachycardia.

A 34-year-old who injects drugs has a typical organism in 2 separate blood cultures (1 major criterion) plus 3 minor criteria. How is this classified by the modified Duke criteria? Majors are a typical organism in 2 separate cultures (or persistent bacteremia, Coxiella ) and a positive echo. Draw 3 sets of cultures before antibiotics.

A 66-year-old has 2 hours of chest pain, ST depression in V4-V6 and an elevated troponin. The pain settles on medical therapy. When should he have coronary angiography? This is NSTEMI (a non-occlusive thrombus). Treat the ischemia and the thrombus (antiplatelets, anticoagulant), then risk-stratify → angiography within 24-48 h and revascularization as appropriate. Immediate primary PCI is the pathway for STEMI , diagnosed on the ECG.

A 68-year-old woman with non-valvular atrial fibrillation has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. No heart failure, stroke or TIA. What is her CHADS2 score? 0 1 2 3 4 The correct answer is C. A score ≥ 2 means oral anticoagulation; the lecture recommends it with any 1 risk factor, and mitral stenosis is very high risk on its own.

A 19-year-old with episodes of palpitations has a resting ECG showing a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke to a slightly widened QRS. What is the diagnosis? Right bundle branch block Left bundle branch block First-degree AV block Ventricular tachycardia Pre-excitation (WPW) The correct answer is E. In Wolff-Parkinson-White , an accessory pathway conducts around the AV node, so the ventricles are pre-excited: short PR and a delta wave fused into the QRS. The pathway can support re-entrant tachycardia, and AF conducted over it is irregularly irregular and wide.

Which feature of a syncope history most warrants a cardiac workup? Most syncope is reflex (vasovagal, about 75%), with a prodrome and a trigger such as standing or needles. The red flags for cardiac syncope are exertional syncope, sudden syncope with no prodrome, structural heart disease, an abnormal ECG and a family history of sudden death

A 60-year-old woman had an anterior MI last year. Echo shows an LVEF of 35%, but she has never had symptoms of heart failure. What is her ACC/AHA heart failure stage? Stages describe progression and do not go backwards, unlike NYHA functional class.

A 70-year-old with HFrEF has orthopnea, an elevated JVP and leg edema. He is drowsy, with cool extremities and a narrow pulse pressure. Which hemodynamic profile is this? Cold and wet is the sickest profile.

A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes has repeated office BP readings around 144/92 mm Hg. Diabetes counts as high risk , so the target is < 130/80 (other patients < 140/90). Higher cardiovascular risk means earlier drug therapy and lower targets; lifestyle change is for everyone.

A 72-year-old has newly diagnosed, uncomplicated hypertension. Which drug class is least appropriate as first-line therapy? A 30-year-old with chronic hypertension controlled on ramipril finds she is 8 weeks pregnant. What should be done with the ramipril? Continue the ramipril Stop the ramipril Switch to valsartan Double the ramipril dose Add spironolactone The correct answer is B. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic) , so the ramipril is stopped and her BP managed with an agent safe in pregnancy. Swapping to an ARB does not help: it carries the same contraindication.

A newborn becomes increasingly cyanotic on day 2. Echo shows tetralogy of Fallot with severe pulmonary stenosis and reduced pulmonary blood flow. What is the immediate therapy? IV furosemide IV beta blocker Prostaglandin Emergency ASD closure Observe and reassess The correct answer is C. When cyanosis comes from reduced pulmonary blood flow (tetralogy of Fallot, tricuspid atresia), the ductus arteriosus is the lifeline: prostaglandin keeps the PDA open and raises pulmonary blood flow until palliative or corrective surgery.

A 3-year-old boy has had 6 days of fever with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue, red swollen hands and a rash. What treatment reduces his risk of coronary artery aneurysms? Oral amoxicillin Supportive care only IV vancomycin IVIG and ASA Oral steroids alone The correct answer is D. Kawasaki disease: at least 4-5 days of fever + 4 of 5 (conjunctivitis, mucosal changes, rash, red indurated hands/feet, unilateral cervical node). Untreated, 25% develop coronary aneurysms; IVIG with ASA within 10 days of fever onset cuts this to 4%.

A well 4-year-old has a 2/6 vibratory, low-pitched systolic ejection murmur at the lower left sternal border that is louder supine. The rest of the exam is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis? Ventricular septal defect Pulmonary valve stenosis Venous hum Atrial septal defect Still's murmur The correct answer is E. Innocent murmurs are soft (1-3/6, never a thrill), musical or vibratory, and louder supine ; Still's is the most common. A VSD is pansystolic, valvar stenosis is harsh with a click, and a venous hum is continuous and softens lying down. A diastolic murmur is never innocent.

Ventilation, Lung Mechanics, Gas Transport and ABGs How air gets in and out (compliance, surface tension), how much of it reaches gas exchange (dead space, V/Q), and how the result is measured — PFTs for the mechanics and the ABG for the gases. The organising idea: obstruction traps air (↓ FEV1/FVC, ↑ volumes); restriction shrinks the lung (normal/↑ ratio, ↓ volumes) . FEV1/FVC < 0.7 = obstruction ; static volumes then split hyperinflation (> 120%) from restriction (< 80%), and DLCO separates parenchymal (↓) from extraparenchymal (normal) restriction . Shunt (V/Q = 0) does NOT correct with 100% O2; dead space (V/Q = ∞, e.g. PE) does. Surfactant ↓ surface tension (Laplace ΔP = 2Υ/r) so small alveoli do not collapse. Right shift = ↓ affinity, ↑ unloading (↑ H+, temperature, PCO2, 2,3-BPG). CO2 travels mostly as bicarbonate (70%) . The body never overcompensates; lungs compensate in minutes, kidneys in a day. Ventilation — moving air in and out of the lung Inspiration — active; contraction of the inspiratory muscles Diaphragm — phrenic nerves (C3-5); referred pain to shoulder and trapezius ridge External intercostals — intercostal nerves ↑ thoracic cavity volume → ↑ negative intrapleural pressure → lung expands → intrapulmonary pressure -1 mm Hg → air flows in Expiration — passive ; elastic recoil of lung and chest wall to their equilibrium positions Becomes active during exercise and voluntary hyperventilation, using: Abdominal wall muscles (rectus abdominis, internal and external obliques, transversus abdominis) Internal intercostals Compliance and surface tension Pulmonary compliance = ΔV / ΔP ; normal = 22 mL/cm H2O ↑ compliance = lung easier to fill — emphysema, older adults ↓ compliance = lung harder to fill — pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS Pressure-volume (PV) curves — non-linear; lungs most compliant between 10-20 mm Hg Hysteresis : inflation and deflation curves differ because of surface tension forces during inflation — ↑ volume during deflation 1/3 of the pressure to fill the lung overcomes elastic forces; 2/3 overcomes surface tension at the air-liquid interface Law of Laplace: ΔP = 2Υ / r (Υ = surface tension, r = radius) Small lung volumes = small r = small Υ; large lung volumes = large r = large Υ When surface tension is high, alveoli collapse easily, especially when the radius is small Surfactant forms a lipid film at the air-liquid interface → ↓ surface tension → ↓ alveolar collapse, ↓ lung recoil, ↑ compliance Lung volumes and capacities Volume or capacity Definition Volumes Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) Air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal inspiration Tidal volume (TV, VT) Air inhaled with each quiet breath; normal = 500 mL Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) Air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal expiration Residual volume (RV) Air remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration Capacities (sum of ≥ 2 volumes) Inspiratory capacity (IC) = IRV + TV Air that can be breathed in after a normal expiration Spirogram of the lung volumes. Read the capacities off the bars: FRC = ERV + RV, VC = IRV + TV + ERV, TLC = VC + RV. Minute and alveolar ventilation Minute ventilation (VE) — air entering the lungs per minute: VE = VT × RR ; normal = 500 × 12 = 6000 mL Alveolar ventilation (VA) — air entering the respiratory zone per minute: VA = (VT − VD) × RR VA = VE × (1 − VD/VT) VA = (VCO2 × 0.863) / PACO2 VA changes with changes in VT and RR even at the same minute ventilation Physiologic dead space (VD) — inspired air that does NOT take part in gas exchange Anatomic dead space + alveolar dead space; normal = 150 mL Equals anatomic dead space in normal lungs; may be greater in lung disease with V/Q mismatch The apex of healthy lungs is the largest contributor of alveolar dead space Bohr equation: VD = VT × (PaCO2 − PECO2) / PaCO2 , where PECO2 = expired air PCO2 Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) Ventilation (V) — gas going into the alveoli; perfusion (Q) — blood flow to the alveoli Ideal V/Q = 1; normal V/Q = 0.8 V/Q = 0 — airway obstruction (shunt) : V = 0, so 100% O2 does NOT improve PaO2 V/Q = ∞ — blood obstruction (physiological dead space) : Q = 0, 100% O2 improves PaO2 — pulmonary embolism Shunt vs dead space on 100% O2 Shunt (V/Q = 0) does not respond to supplemental O2 — the added oxygen never reaches the unventilated alveoli. Dead space (V/Q = ∞, e.g. PE) does improve. Obstructive and Restrictive Lung Disease A disease-by-disease comparison of the obstructive lungs (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma, bronchiectasis, CF) and the restrictive ones (IPF, sarcoidosis, GPA, ARDS, neuromuscular and chest wall). Read each column the same way — cause → pathology → presentation → diagnosis → treatment → prognosis — and the discriminating feature usually sits in the pathology row. Pink puffer (emphysema) = matched V/Q, ↓ DLCO; blue bloater (chronic bronchitis) = V/Q mismatch, normal DLCO. Chronic bronchitis = productive cough > 3 months/year for > 2 consecutive years. Asthma is reversible (≥ 12% FEV1 rise after bronchodilator); bronchiectasis is irreversible dilation . CF sweat Cl- > 60 mmol/L (> 30 under 3 months), confirmed by a second sweat test + mutation analysis. IPF: corticosteroids are NOT effective — antifibrotics slow it. ARDS = PaO2/FIO2 < 300 , not due to HF. Other Common Respiratory Pathologies A tour of the conditions that round out respirology — hemoptysis, DVT/PE, mediastinal and pleural disease, atelectasis, pneumothorax and the Pancoast tumour. Two of them are algorithms worth knowing cold : hemoptysis (stabilize → investigate → treat the cause) and pleural effusion (Light's criteria split exudate from transudate). Hemoptysis: bleeding side DOWN , then find the source — bronchoscopy is the gold standard . The bronchial circulation is the high-pressure one. Light's criteria : fluid/serum protein > 0.5, fluid/serum LDH > 0.6, fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH → exudate. Tension pneumothorax : air enters but cannot exit → needle decompression. Mesothelioma = asbestos, not smoking . Anterior mediastinal masses = 5 Ts . Pancoast tumour → Horner syndrome, hoarseness, SVC syndrome. Approach to hemoptysis Amount/rate is variable: 100-650 mL over 24 hours; massive = 100 cc/hour Pulmonary artery circulation = low-pressure — supplies lung parenchyma Bronchial artery circulation = high-pressure — supplies bronchi and visceral pleura 1. Stabilize the patient — vitals, IV access, group and screen; reverse anticoagulation (tranexamic acid) Position lateral decubitus, bleeding side down Endotracheal tube to place an endobronchial blocker; ventilate the elevated side Control bleeding with argon plasma coagulation or catheter embolization 2. Investigate the cause — CXR, chest CT, arteriography, bronchoscopy = gold standard (direct visualization, sampling, biopsy) 3. DDx for Dyspnea The differential for dyspnea is organised by tempo first — acute (minutes to hours) vs chronic — and then by system : cardiac, pulmonary, other. Within the lung, localise by compartment: airway, parenchyma (alveoli, interstitium), vessels, pleura, pump. Acute dyspnea: rule out the life-threatening causes first — MI, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE, asthma/AECOPD, aspiration, anaphylaxis. Wheeze = lower airway; stridor = upper airway. Chronic pulmonary causes split into airways (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis), parenchyma (abnormal CXR), vessels (PE, pulmonary hypertension) and pump (chest wall, neuromuscular, pleura). Don't forget the non-cardiopulmonary causes: anemia, anxiety, deconditioning, hyperthyroidism, metabolic acidosis. Acute dyspnea (minutes to hours) * = acutely life-threatening Cardiovascular : myocardial infarction*, cardiac tamponade*, CHF Respiratory Pleural: pneumothorax (tension*) Parenchymal: pneumonia Vascular: pulmonary embolism* Lower airway ( wheeze ): asthma*, AECOPD*, CHF, ARDS Upper airway ( stridor ): aspiration*, anaphylaxis* Acute dyspnea tree: asterisks mark the acutely life-threatening causes to exclude first. Structure and Function of the Lung — Gas Exchange Gas exchange happens across the thin, vast blood-gas barrier, and Fick's law says what speeds or slows it. The clinical tool that falls out of this is the A-a gradient : it tells you whether hypoxemia comes from too little O2 reaching the alveoli (normal gradient) or O2 failing to cross into blood (increased gradient). PIO2 = FIO2 × (Patm − PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) = 150 mm Hg. PAO2 = PIO2 − PaCO2/0.8. Normal A-a gradient = (age/4) + 4. Normal gradient: high altitude, hypoventilation . Increased gradient: shunt, V/Q mismatch, diffusion impairment . Diffusion is fast with large area, large gradient and a thin interface — emphysema cuts area, fibrosis and pneumonia thicken the barrier. Hypoxic vasoconstriction can lead to pulmonary hypertension. Airway structure Gas exchange takes place at the blood-gas barrier (BGB) in the alveoli — large area, thin interface 23 generations of airway branching Large airways: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi Conducting zone : trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles; pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells; NO gas exchange — anatomic dead space; warms and humidifies air Respiratory zone (acinus) : respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs; cuboidal cells, simple squamous cells Right lung = 3 lobes ; more common site for inhaled foreign bodies (R main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical) Left lung = 2 lobes ; lingula (homolog of R middle lobe) Airway tree: trachea → main (primary) → lobar (secondary) → segmental (tertiary) bronchi. Alveolar cells Type I pneumocytes — squamous; 97% of alveolar surface ; thinly line the alveoli for optimal gas exchange Type II pneumocytes — cuboidal, clustered; stem cell precursors for type I and II (proliferate after lung damage); secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies Alveolar macrophages — phagocytose foreign material Circulation and pleura Pulmonary artery branches into a dense capillary network wrapped around the alveoli; in the capillaries blood sees the largest surface area and lowest velocity Intrapleural space : between lung and chest wall; negative pressure (-5 mm Hg) from elastic properties — lungs tend to collapse inward, chest wall to spring outward Pressure becomes atmospheric if a pneumothorax (hole in the diaphragm) is created — the lung collapses Diffusion — Fick's law V_gas = (A / T) × D × (P1 − P2) — A = area, T = thickness, D = diffusion constant, P1 − P2 = partial pressure gradient Fast : large area, large pressure gradient, thin interface Slow : small area (emphysema), small gradient, thick interface (pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis) Partial pressures Partial pressure = pressure exerted by one gas in a mixture = total pressure × fractional concentration Partial pressure of a gas in solution = partial pressure of the gas in equilibrium with that solution Inspired PO2: PIO2 = FIO2 × (Patm − PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) = 150 mm Hg (FIO2 = 21%; sea-level pressure = 760 mm Hg; water-saturated air = 47 mm Hg) PAO2 = alveolar partial pressure of O2; PaO2 = arterial partial pressure of O2 PACO2 = PaCO2 ; normal = 40 mm Hg Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = PIO2 − (PaCO2 / 0.8) A-a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2 Difference between alveolar and arterial O2 Normal = (age/4) + 4 ; lower is better Causes of hypoxemia by A-a gradient Cause Mechanism / examples Normal A-a gradient ↓ PIO2 — high altitude ↓ PB → ↑ ventilation, ↓ PaCO2, respiratory alkalosis, altitude sickness ↑ PaCO2 — hypoventilation CNS depression, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, muscular weakness Increased A-a gradient R to L shunt (normal Q, no V) Anatomic (intracardiac shunt); physiologic (Q of non-ventilated alveoli in ARDS) V/Q mismatch Normal Q, ↓ V Impaired diffusion Fibrosis, ILD; hypoxemia with exercise Hypoxic vasoconstriction ↓ PAO2 causes hypoxic arterial vasoconstriction, shifting blood away from poorly ventilated lung toward alveoli that can oxygenate it — which can lead to pulmonary hypertension . Schulich Reviews Room-air shortcut: PAO2 = 150 − (PaCO2 × 1.25) , then A-a = PAO2 − PaO2 vs age/4 + 4

Chest Radiology and Rhinology Two halves: a systematic CXR read (DRS. ABCDE) with the pattern of each common abnormality, and the rhinology comparison — allergic rhinitis, acute and chronic rhinosinusitis, epistaxis. The CXR half is about never skipping a zone; the rhinology half turns on duration (10 days, 4 weeks, 8-12 weeks). Do NOT miss : deviated trachea, pneumothorax, subdiaphragmatic free air. Adequate inspiration = anterior ribs 5-6 / posterior ribs 8-10 reach the diaphragm. Pulmonary edema = Kerley B-lines , peribronchial cuffing, cardiomegaly; LLL collapse = sail sign . Acute rhinosinusitis = 10+ days or double-worsening, < 4 weeks — watch and wait 7-10 days first; chronic = 8-12 weeks with endoscopic/CT evidence. Decongestants 3-7 days only (rhinitis medicamentosa). Anterior epistaxis (90%) comes from Kiesselbach's plexus ; do NOT biopsy a juvenile nasal angiofibroma. Pneumonia, Tuberculosis and Upper Respiratory Infections Pneumonia = inflammation of the lung parenchyma with alveolar filling by exudate. The organising split is typical vs atypical vs hospital-acquired vs TB — but because typical and atypical are hard to tell apart clinically, empiric therapy covers both , chosen by the patient's comorbidities. CXR = gold standard for diagnosing and classifying pneumonia; atypicals do NOT show on Gram stain . Empiric CAP: no comorbidities → macrolide (azithromycin) + 3rd-gen cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) or doxycycline; elderly/comorbid → fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) . Hospital-acquired ( Pseudomonas ) → piperacillin/tazobactam + vancomycin . TB: 6 months INH + B6 + rifampin, plus pyrazinamide + ethambutol for the first 2 ; secondary TB favours the apices. PCP prophylaxis when CD4 < 200 . Treat strep throat promptly to prevent rheumatic fever . Pneumonia by type Typical (bacterial) Atypical Hospital-acquired Tuberculosis Causes Lobar : S. pneumoniae , Legionella , Klebsiella Bronchopneumonia : S. pneumoniae , S. aureus , H. influenzae , Klebsiella Mycoplasma , Chlamydia , Legionella Viruses: COVID-19, influenza, RSV, adenovirus Pseudomonas aeruginosa Risk factors: extended hospital stay , decreased consciousness Usually from microaspiration of oropharyngeal contents Mycobacterium tuberculosis Airborne droplet transmission Presentation Acute onset Fever, dyspnea, productive cough Purulent sputum , may be blood-tinged or "rusty" (ruptured pulmonary microvasculature) Pleuritic chest pain Epigastric pain (elderly) Insidious onset Non-productive cough ; mucoid sputum Similar to typical pneumonia Chronic productive cough Hemoptysis Respiratory function generally well preserved Weight loss, fever, night sweats CXR pattern Lobar : consolidation of an entire lobe; can involve 1+ lobes Bronchopneumonia : patchy consolidation around bronchioles and adjacent alveoli; often multifocal and bilateral Interstitial : diffuse patchy inflammation in the interstitium at alveolar walls; Lung Nodules, Thyroid Nodules and Head and Neck Masses Three kinds of lump, one question each time: benign or malignant, and what test decides it? For the lung, size and risk set the follow-up; for the thyroid, TSH decides the next test and ultrasound features decide the FNAB; for a lateral neck mass in an adult, assume cancer until proven otherwise . Mass > 3 cm; nodule < 3 cm ; < 7 mm likely benign. Pleural or pericardial effusion = stage IV. Lung cancer: stage I-II resect or radiate, III chemoradiation, IV palliative. Thyroid nodules: 50% incidence, only 5% malignant ; papillary and follicular raise thyroglobulin, medullary raises calcitonin . Rule of 7s (7 days infection, 7 months neoplasm, 7 years congenital) and the 80% rule for lateral neck masses. Salivary tumours: the smaller the gland, the more likely malignant . HPV-16 → oropharyngeal SCC with good prognosis. Pulmonary nodules and masses Mass > 3 cm; nodule < 3 cm Benign Malignant Solitary ( < 7 mm likely benign, > 7 mm likely malignant ) Hamartoma, granuloma, abscess, rheumatoid nodule, infarction Lung cancer, lymphoid, carcinoid tumour (airway-centric) Multiple Infection (fungal histoplasmosis, TB); inflammatory (vasculitis); inhalational (silicosis, asbestosis); idiopathic (sarcoidosis) Metastatic > benign Pleural effusion = stage IV Pericardial effusion = stage IV Lung cancer Non-small cell : adenocarcinoma (most common), squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma Small cell (most common in smokers) "S" cancers are central — bulky and symptomatic Presentation : cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, constitutional symptoms, clubbing — or ASYMPTOMATIC Risk factors : age, smoking, emphysema, FHx; nodule size, spiculation, upper lobe; CT density (semisolid > solid > ground glass); calcification (↓ risk) Metastatic sites : pleura, liver (jaundice, hepatomegaly), bone (pathologic fracture), brain, adrenals Important presentations : central airway obstruction, SVC obstruction, Pancoast tumour, paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, hypercalcemia, Lambert-Eaton, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy) Follow-up of a single nodule by size and risk: < 6 mm low risk needs no routine follow-up; > 8 mm warrants CT at 3 months, PET/CT or tissue sampling. Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which type of cell “wraps” around capillaries and is the main structural cell of the lung? Type 1 Alveolar Cells Type 2 Alveolar Cells Goblet Cells Alveolar Macrophage The correct answer is A. Type 1 Alveolar Cells encapsulate endothelial cells and facilitate diffusion of gases with the capillaries.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which cells phagocytose foreign bodies? Type 1 Alveolar Cells Type 2 Alveolar Cells Goblet Cells Alveolar Macrophage The correct answer is D. These cells provide an immune function within the respiratory zones of the airway as the respiratory zones lack the mucociliary escalator.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which cells secrete surfactant into the alveolus? Type 1 Alveolar Cells Type 2 Alveolar Cells Goblet Cells Alveolar Macrophage The correct answer is B. Type 2 Alveolar cells secrete surfactant into the alveoli, which maintain surface tension and prevent alveoli collapse.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. Which cells secrete mucus into the airway of the conduction zone and contribute to the mucociliary escalator? Type 1 Alveolar Cells Type 2 Alveolar Cells Goblet Cells Alveolar Macrophage The correct answer is C. Goblet cells produce mucus and secrete this into the airways which contributes to the mucociliary escalator.

Which of the following muscle groups are used during inspiration (passive or forced)? Select all that apply. External intercostal muscle Internal intercostal muscle Innermost intercostal muscle Diaphragm The correct answer is A, D. The diaphragm contracts inferiorly providing more space for the lung to expand, assisting with inspiration. The external intercostal muscles contract superiorly and have the effect of creating more space superiorly, which assists draw air in during inspiration.

Which of the following muscle groups are required for unforced expiration? External intercostals Internal intercostals Innermost intercostals Diaphragm None of the above The correct answer is E. No muscle group is required for unforced expiration. The lungs contract through elastic recoil, gravity that lowers and compresses the thoracic cage, and relaxation of the diaphragm to relieve high abdominal pressures. During a thoracocentesis, a needle is injected through the intercostal muscles between the ribs and into the pleural cavity. Which structure is the needle least likely to puncture? Intercostal arteries Intercostal muscles Intercostal veins Intercostal muscles The correct answer is C. The structure least likely to be pierced during thoracentesis is the intercostal vein.

The alveolar wall lining can be found in which of the following locations? Select all that apply. The alveolar lining (a two-cell-membrane-thick lining composed of an alveolar cell and endothelial cell where gas exchange occurs) can be found in the acinus, which consists of respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveolar sacs.

Which of the following pleural lesions is likely a benign lesion? Metastatic carcinoma Sarcomatoid mesothelioma Pleural plaque Fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity The correct answer is C. Pleural plaques are generally a benign lesion. Pleural plaques are associated with dense fibrous tissue that arises from asbestos exposure.

Which of the following organs atrophy after you reach adolescence? Thyroid Parathyroid gland Thymus Lymph nodes in the anterior mediastinum The correct answer is C. The thymus reaches its maximum size in adolescence and begins to atrophy, involuting on itself and decreasing in size.

Which pulmonary pathology is associated with a grey parenchyma and the appearance of “honeycomb” structure within the lungs? Emphysema Asbestosis Infectious granulomas Pulmonary fibrosis Asthma The correct answer is D. Pulmonary fibrosis results in significant honeycombing of the lungs.

Which of the following changes will increase the value of PAO2? Increasing the PaCO2 Inspiration of pure (100%) O2 Increase in elevation Increased age The correct answer is B. By breathing in 100% pure oxygen, FIO2 goes from 0.21 (atmospheric oxygen fraction) to 1.0, and subsequently increases PAO2.

A patient with chronic bronchospasms is consulting with his physician for pharmacotherapy. The physician is considering prescribing Formoterol (a long acting beta agonist). She is a 57-year-old female who is recently unemployed and having trouble finding work because of Covid. If you were her primary care physician, what next step would you recommend? Ventilation rates increase as PaCO2 increases, as PaO2 decreases, and as pH decreases. The increase in ventilation is the result of various sensors that detect changes in these values. Patients with a pleural effusion who satisfy the Lights criteria can be classified as having an exudative process. Arrange the steps of COPD management in order of increasing severity: PRN SABA → Pulmonary Rehabilitation → LABA → Surgery → Oxygen Pulmonary Rehabilitation → PRN SABA → LABA → Oxygen → Surgery Oxygen → PRN SABA → Pulmonary Rehabilitation → LABA → Surgery PRN SABA → LABA → Pulmonary Rehabilitation → Oxygen → Surgery The correct answer is D. The full management plan, in order of increasingly severe COPD is: smoking cessation, exercise, self-management education → PRN short-acting bronchodilator → long-acting bronchodilator → pulmonary rehabilitation → ICS/LABA → oxygen → surgery.

Which of the following is NOT diagnostic of adult asthma: FEV1/FVC ratio <0.7 but improves >= 12% with bronchodilator PEF increases >= 20% with bronchodilator TLC >= 120% Positive provocation test The correct answer is C. Hyperinflation is not exclusive to asthma, and can be found for any obstructive lung disease (eg. COPD).

Which of the following would be considered the gold-standard to asthma management? Fluticasone Ipratropium Salbutamol Formoterol The correct answer is A. ICS is the mainstay of asthma treatment. ICS drugs end in “-one”. Antimuscarinics generally end in “-ium”, SABAs generally end in “-mol”, and LABAs generally end in “- rol”.

The effects of ICS include all of the following EXCEPT: Decrease migration and survival of inflammatory cells in the lungs Decrease mucus production Inhibits mast cell mediator release Inhibits bronchoconstriction The correct answer is D. Bronchoconstriction is regulated by the parasympathetic nervous system and smooth muscle cells, neither of which are affected by ICS.

A patient presents to the ER after experiencing significant physical trauma in a motor vehicle accident. You order a chest x-ray, but they are unable to stand upright for a PA film. Instead, an AP chest x-ray is acquired. Which of the following statements are accurate about your approach to AP film interpretation? (Select all that apply) The heart and mediastinal structures will be magnified The lung parenchyma will appear slightly washed out The resolution of the image will be high This view is helpful for assessing the lung apices The effect of gravity will influence the appearance of effusions The correct answer is A, B, E. In general, AP films are less desirable than PA films because they have poorer resolution, the heart and mediastinal structures are magnified, and they appear washed out. The lordotic view is the best for assessing lung apices.

Which of the following features is observed on a normal chest radiograph? There are 8 anterior ribs between the clavicle and the dome of the diaphragm Ribs are displaced laterally and fractured The lungs fields look progressively darker as you move inferiorly in the lateral view The cardiac silhouette is more than 50% of the diameter of the thoracic cage The correct answer is C. The lung fields appear darker as you move inferiorly because of the effect of gravity on blood flow to the different regions of the lung. Blood will pool inferiorly, making perfusion at the lower lung lobes great than perfusion at the upper lung lobes.

Which of the following inaccurately describes the functional anatomy of the thorax during respiration? The elastic recoil of the lungs expels air during quiet (i.e., not forced) expiration Intrathoracic volume and diameter increases during inspiration Intrathoracic pressure increases during inspiration The internal intercostals contract during forced expiration The correct answer is C. Intrathoracic pressure will decrease during inspiration in order to draw air into the lungs. Quiet expiration relies on the elasticity of the lungs and relaxation of the external intercostal muscles. Eparterial bronchus = left lung Lingula = right lung Horizontal fissure = left lung Esophageal impression = right lung The correct answer is D. The eparterial bronchus is the superior-most bronchus of the right hilum, therefore A is incorrect. The lingula is the inferior-most aspect of the left upper lobe, therefore B is incorrect.
