What is the function of the mucociliary blanket? Recruit macrophages to engulf foreign microorganisms and particulate matter Decrease friction between the visceral and parietal pleura Increase air flow by decreasing the radius of the airways Prevent microorganisms and inhaled particulate matter from reaching the distal airways The correct answer is D. The mucociliary blanket is secreted from glands (in the bronchi) or produced by specialized epithelial cells (in the bronchioles). Its main function is to capture inhaled particulates and microorganisms. The cilia then “sweep” the mucus layer upwards, towards the epiglottis,

A 24-year-old male presents to the ER with a 5-day history of fever, chills, chest pain, and dyspnea. He also reports a productive cough with viscous, yellow-green sputum. A chest xray and sputum culture are obtained – they are shown below. Based on the histological and radiographic features, coupled with his clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis? Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Juvenile nasal angiofibroma Bacterial pneumonia Cystic fibrosis The correct answer is C. The clinical history corroborates well with an infectious etiology. The histological image shows neutrophils filling up an alveolus – this is most consistent with inflammation and infection in the airspace, or pneumonia. The chest radiograph shows a somewhat focal, ground-gl

Which of the following bones does not contribute to the nasal cavity? Vomer Ethmoid Frontal Occipital Maxilla The correct answer is D. The occipital bone is found at the posterior aspect of the skull.

Which of the following correctly describes the drainage pattern of the paranasal sinuses? The frontal sinus drains into the middle meatus using the maxillolacrimal duct The Eustachian tube drains into the nasopharynx The semilunar hiatus of the middle meatus drains both the maxillary and sphenoid sinuses The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus The posterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoidal recess The correct answer is D. The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus. While the Eustachian tube does drain into the nasopharynx, it does not drain one of the paranasal sinuses; it connects to the middle ear.

Match the muscle of the larynx with its function. Which of the following mediastinal lesions is incorrectly matched? Neurogenic tumours – posterior mediastinum Thyroid lesions – middle mediastinum Aortic dissection – middle mediastinum Thymoma – anterior mediastinum Esophageal tumour – posterior mediastinum The correct answer is B. Thyroid lesions – typically an enlarged thyroid, or goiter – are found in the anterior mediastinum, and are a part of the 5Ts of the anterior mediastinum.

Which of the following statements regarding lung and pleural pathology is FALSE? Immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be used to identify lung adenocarcinoma metastases in other tissues Mesothelioma results in a thickened pleural membrane Talc pleurodesis is a frequent cause of pleural effusion Thoracoscopy can be used to identify nodular areas of the pleura that may represent mesothelioma or metastases Pleural plaques are benign lesions composed of basketweave-like fibrous tissue The correct answer is C. Talc pleurodesis is a procedure used to treat pleural effusions; talc irritates the pleura and causes the visceral and parietal pleura to adhere, which prevents further fluid accumulation.

Which of the following would NOT result in an increase in the affinity of oxygen to bind to hemoglobin? Decreased 2-3 DPG Decreased pH Decreased temperature Decreased[H+] The correct answer is B. Decreased pH results from increased [H+], which promotes reduced affinity of oxygen to bind to hemoglobin and a rightward shift in the oxygen dissociation curve.

Which component of the alveolar gas equation is the most readily amenable? PH2O PaCO2 FiO2 Patm RespQ The correct answer is C. FiO2 is the fraction of inspired oxygen, which is 21% (0.21) on room air. This can be improved with supplemental oxygen. PH2O is the vapour pressure in the alveolus and is not modifiable. PaCO2 is derived from the arterial blood gas. Patm can be modified, but this is depende

Different diseases of the lungs have different effects on the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio. Which of the following statements is CORRECT? Pulmonary edema results in an increased V/Q ratio Healthier lungs have large V/Q ratios Normal V/Q ratios are > 1.0 The lung apices typically have a lower V/Q ratio than do the lung bases The lung apices are most vulnerable to becoming physiologic dead space if there is a drop in arterial pressure (Q) The correct answer is E. Pulmonary edema results in reduced ventilation (V) and thus reduced V/Q ratio. Large V/Q ratios imply very low perfusion (Q), which is not seen in healthy lungs and signifies significant physiological dead space. Normal V/Q ratio is approximately 0.8. The lung apices have gr

A 30 year old woman has the following arterial blood gas values: pH 7.41 PaCO2 39 HCO3- 24 PaO2 95 Which of the following statements is true? She has an elevated A-a gradient and is hypoxemic due to a V/Q mismatch She has a normal A-a gradient and is hypoxemic due to hypoventilation She should be put on supplemental oxygen and descend from high altitude She has a compensated metabolic acidosis None of the above The correct answer is E. All of her ABG values are normal, she is not hypoxemic, and she has a normal A-a gradient.

Which of the following is false? Viral sinusitis typically resolves in 7-10 days and is best treated by getting rest and remaining nourished Bacterial sinusitis is more common than viral sinusitis Epinephrine, mast cell stabilizers and anti-histamines are all potential options for management of allergic rhinitis Use of medication for allergic rhinitis after 3-7 days of continuous use results in reduced efficacy at the same dose The correct answer is B. Viral sinusitis is more common, and typically resolves within 7-10 days. Option C lists potential treatment options, which may also include decongestants and intranasal steroids. Lastly, continuous use of medication can result in reduced efficacy, and in some cases, worse co

Which option correctly matches the medication with its clinical result? Anti-histamines – eliminates congestion in addition to reducing sneezing, throat and eye itchiness. Decongestants – reduces congestion by upregulating the effects of leukotrienes and prostaglandins. Mast cell stabilizers – prevent mast cells from releasing inflammatory mediators. Intranasal steroids – inhibit leukotrienes and prostaglandins. The correct answer is C. anti-histamines only reduce congestion. Decongestants mitigate the effects of leukotrienes and prostaglandins, and intranasal steroids prevent the synthesis of leukotrienes and prostaglandins.

Which of the following are the major criteria for diagnosis of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis? Facial pain and pressure Headache Nasal obstruction Fatigue Toothache Cough Purulent nasal discharge Anosmia The correct answer is A, C, G, H. These are the major criteria (PODS: Pain/Pressure, Obstruction, Discharge, and Smell disturbance). The remaining options are some minor criteria, which can also include ear pain/pressure and halitosis.

Which of the following are red flags for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis? Systemic toxicity Altered mental status Severe headache A and C All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are red flags. From the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology (Week 7), which carries the acute rhinosinusitis column that 09 - Acute Rhinosinusitis lacks. Which of the following is true? Intranasal corticosteroids should NOT be prescribed to all patients with chronic rhinosinusitis Bacteriology of chronic rhinosinusitis is similar to that of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) The presence/absence of nasal polyps can help differentiate between different types of chronic rhinosinusitis Chronic rhinosinusitis patients typically have positive bacterial cultures The correct answer is C. Intranasal corticosteroids SHOULD be prescribed to all patients with CRS. Bacteriology of CRS differs from that of ABRS (the main pathogens in CRS include S aureus , Enterobacteriaceae spp and Pseudomonas pp ), and CRS patients typically have negative bacterial cultures.

Which of the following is/are red flags requiring urgent referral to an otolaryngologist? Immunosuppressed patients Suspected orbital or intracranial involvement Acute sinusitis with unusually severe symptoms and/or systemic toxicity. A and C. All of the above. The correct answer is E. All of the above are red flags which require urgent referral.

What are the requirements of proper phonation? Approximation of vocal folds Forced expiration Passive vibration of free mucosal edge of vocal folds A and B All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are required for proper phonation. Partly from the larynx section of Summary Notes - Anatomy. The anatomy notes cover the structure: the vocal ligament is covered by mucosa to form the vocal folds, the lateral cricoarytenoid adducts them, and the cricothyroi

Which of the following is/are true with respect to the recurrent laryngeal nerve? It provides sensory to the lower and upper larynx Motor to all intrinsic muscles It provides sensory to the lower larynx None of the above The correct answer is C. The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory to the lower larynx whereas the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory to the upper larynx. The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides motor to all intrinsic muscles EXCEPT the cricothyroid.

When performing a clinical work up for an individual with suspected pneumonia, what are some of the items/information to gather from/about the patient? host risk factors on history travel history vitals chest examination all of the above The correct answer is E. All options contain pertinent information one should obtain on clinical assessment.

Which of the following distinguishes atypical pneumonia from bacterial pneumonia? insidious onset purulent sputum more consolidated appearance on x-ray predominantly pulmonary symptoms involved none of the above The correct answer is A. Typical causes of infection are more gradual whereas insidious is more suiting to an atypical cause.

Which of the following are complications from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis? respiratory failure pulmonary hypertension Cor pulmonale A and B A, B and C The correct answer is E. all three are potential complications From the restrictive-disease chart in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 05 - Interstitial Causes of Dyspnea. When conducting a physical exam on a cystic fibrosis patient, which of the following are key to take note of? Nasal polyps Clubbing Signs of RVF Dios/hepatobiliary disease All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are true regarding the assessment of clinical CF

Which of the following are causes of hypoxemia? An increase in sea level pressure Hyperventilation V/Q mismatch Shunt C and D The correct answer is E. Shunt and ventilation perfusion mismatch are the only options in the list that might lead to hypoxemia

Metabolic acidosis is a state in which: There is high pCO2 There is a low pO2 and a low pH There is a high pO2 There is a high HCO3 and a low pH There is a low HCO3 and a low pH The correct answer is E. Both a low bicarbonate and a low pH tell of metabolic acidosis

Pulmonary function tests assess: airways alveoli mechanical function of the lung, diaphragm and chest pulmonary vasculature all of the above The correct answer is E. All of the listed functions are tested by use of function testing

Which of the following regarding total lung capacity is true? It is the maximum amount of air that can fill the lungs If it is greater than 90%, lungs might be hyperinflated If it is greater than 80% but less than 120%, lungs might be restricted None of the above All of the above The correct answer is A. The total lung capacity is the total air capacity of the lungs. The value that suggests hyperinflation is TLC >120%, whereas the value that suggests restrictive lung disease is TLC <80%.

Which artery is highly associated with posterior epistaxis? Sphenopalatine artery Facial artery Anterior ethmoid artery Ophthalmic artery The correct answer is A. From In Class - Epistaxis and 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Posterior bleeds arise at Woodruff's plexus , where the sphenopalatine artery (maxillary artery, external carotid) enters the posterior nasal cavity. They drip down the throat, are rarely traumatic,

What is a first-line management for low volume bleeding? Nasal packing Nasal Cautery Surgical embolization Anterior nasal pressure Tranexamic Acid The correct answer is D. From In Class - Epistaxis and the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. Most bleeds are anterior, from Kiesselbach's plexus , and the lecture's first-aid step is to pinch the soft ala firmly for 10–15 minutes , head tipped forward to protect the airway. After ABCs and reversing c

Which of the following is an appropriate management of epistaxis? Embolization of anterior ethmoid artery Cauterization of both sides of septum Leaving patient with posterior packing unmonitored Doing a biopsy of a mass in patient highly suspicious of Juvenile nasal angiofibroma Ligation of anterior ethmoid and sphenopalatine arteries in setting of severe nasal bleeding The correct answer is E. From the epistaxis chart and stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology, and In Class - Epistaxis. Regarding cavitary lung disease causes: They can be classified as fungal or non-tuberculosis Tuberculosis cavitary lesion presents at the onset of infection Serial washes with vasculitis results in decreased blood in subsequent washes Vasculitis can have a systemic presentation The correct answer is D. Vasculitis often has a systemic presentation. From 01 - Hemoptysis, with 02 - Pneumonia. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the vasculitis most likely to cavitate. Which of the following is FALSE? It can present as focused, local or diffused disease. From 01 - Hemoptysis, with the bronchiectasis column in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation after repeated infection or inflammation. Its causes include diffuse ones (CF, primary cil

Which is not a systemic cause of epistaxis? Hypertension Coagulopathy HHT Barometric pressure changes None of the above The correct answer is D. This is a local cause. From the epistaxis chart in 07 - Radiology, and In Class - Epistaxis. The chart splits causes into local (trauma, foreign body, tumour, cocaine, inflammation, barometric change , nasal dryness) and systemic (coagulopathy, hypertension, atherosclerosis,

What is NOT a way to treat epistaxis? Nasal irrigation Nasal tampon Nasal packing Tranexamic acid Nasal pressure The correct answer is A. Nasal irrigation is not an option here. What is true about lung masses? Are often found when presenting with symptoms of lung cancer Multiple nodules are often a sign of malignancy Nodules less than 8mm have a lower chance of being malignant It is often preferred to biopsy two different sites to diagnose and stage the cancer M0 indicates metastasis The correct answer is C. From 04 - Approach to Pulmonary Nodules and Masses. Small nodules carry a significantly lower risk of malignancy . The chart calls solitary nodules under 7 mm likely benign: under 6 mm and low-risk needs no follow-up, while ≥ 8 mm gets CT at 3 months, PET/CT or sampling. So

Which of the following organisms can cause pulmonary abscesses (select all that apply)? Fusobacterium Klebsiella species Staph aureus Peptostreptococcus Mycobacterium tuberculosis Aspergillus The correct answer is A, B, C, D, E. All these microorganisms can cause lung abscesses

A 42-year-old man presents to the ER with worsening hemoptysis. He has fever and joint pains. He is a non-smoker. Chest exam is unremarkable. His urinalysis shows elevated creatinine levels and red blood cell casts in the urine. His anti-nuclear antibody test comes back positive. What is the most likely diagnosis? Community acquired pneumonia Tuberculosis Granulomatosis with Poly-Angiitis Lung Cancer The correct answer is C. Vasculitis presents with systemic symptoms (pulmonary-renal syndrome); the kidney involvement along with the positive ANA test leads to a likely Vasculitis diagnosis.

Which of the following situations has the highest chance of being malignant? Multiple nodules with a ground glass appearance Single semisolid spiculated nodule Single solid nodule Multiple nodules with popcorn calcifications The correct answer is B. Malignant risk of nodules is highest for semisolid densities; single nodules are more likely to be malignant than multiple nodules

Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next TWO questions. A 58-year-old woman presents with a large lung nodule and significant risk factors for cancer. Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next TWO questions. A 58-year-old woman presents with a large lung nodule and significant risk factors for cancer. Upon investigations, the lung nodule was found to be 4cm, and ipsilateral subcarinal lymph node involvement was observed. Further, a malignant pleural effusion was also present. PET/CT showed no further organ involvement. Which of the following treatment options is the best suited in this situation? Surgery Curative chemo and radiation Palliative chemo and radiation Watch and wait The correct answer is C. Since this is stage IV (advanced) cancer, the most appropriate treatment modality is palliative chemo and radiation.

The respiratory tract from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles are best called? Respiratory Zones Acinus Conducting Zones Respiratory Trunks The correct answer is C. Conducting Zone. The trachea until the terminal bronchioles are only involved in air conduction and are not involved in gas exchange, this is important because these areas represent anatomic dead zones.

You’re out for a walk at sea level and wondering about the partial pressure of your inspired oxygen inside your lungs. Which of the following is a correct calculation. Which of the following is the correct calculation? PIO2= 0.21*760mmHg PIO2=0.21* (760-47)mmHg PIO2=0.21*47mmHg PIO2=0.1*(760-47)mmHg The correct answer is B. The partial pressure of inspired oxygen is equal to the fractional proportion of oxygen in air (0.21) multiplied by the barometric pressure minus the water vapour from warming and moistening the air. It’s important to remember that the trachea warms and moistens the air, red

Which of the following is the first branching of the bronchial tree that has gas exchanging capabilities? Terminal bronchioles Bronchi Alveoli Respiratory bronchioles Alveolar ducts The correct answer is D. Once the bronchial tree branches into the respiratory bronchioles, this is the beginning of gas exchange function of the lung. It is important to remember it is not only the alveoli that are involved in gas exchange.

Which of the following about lung volumes and capacities is correct? The residual volume is the volume of gas that remains after max expiration and cannot be expelled The tidal volume is air that enters the lung during normal breathing and is only air that is involved in gas exchange The functional residual capacity is the air left after maximal expiration The residual volume does not prevent the lung from collapsing after expiration The correct answer is A. The residual volume is air that cannot be expelled from the lung after maximal expiration and is important in preventing lung collapse. C is incorrect because the functional residual volume is the air left after normal expiration. B is incorrect because the tidal volume cont

Due to a motorcycle injury, a patient suffers paralysis of their intercostal muscles. For this patient, which of the following lung volumes and capacities would still be expected to be normal? Inspiratory reserve volume Expiratory reserve volume Total lung capacity Vital capacity Tidal volume The correct answer is E. The tidal volume is normal inspiration and expiration, which only involves the diaphragm for inspiration and elastic recoil for expiration. The intercostals are used in effort breathing and therefore would affect A-D.

A patient has just had surgery and is on morphine for pain. This has caused the patients alveolar ventilation to decrease by half. What will the PACO2 be, assuming the carbon dioxide production stays the same? Doubled Halved The same Tripled The correct answer is A. Alveolar Ventilation equation stats that PACO2 α VCO2/VA, therefore decreasing the alveolar ventilation by half would double the PACO2.

Compared to systemic arterial blood, pulmonary arterial blood has a lower: Carbon dioxide content Oxygen content Haemoglobin content It is the same as systemic arterial blood The correct answer is B. Pulmonary arterial blood has the same make up as systemic venous blood, as it has not passed through the lungs yet. Therefore it would a lower oxygen content and higher carbon dioxide content (PaO2=40mmHg, PaCO2=45mmHg), where as pulmonary arterial blood has a PaO2=100mmHg a

Alveolar surfactant acts to increase: Surface tension Compliance Alveolar fluid Work of breathing The correct answer is B. Surfactant is a mixture of proteins and lipids manufactured by type 2 alveolar cells to reduce surface tension caused by water molecules in alveoli trying to collapse alveoli. Surfactant forms a monolayer on the alveoli to prevent water molecules from interacting. Reducing s

What is a normal FEV1/FVC ratio in a normal adult? FEV1 =forced expiratory volume in the 1st second, FVC= forced vital capacity. A) 0.6 B) 1 C) 0.8 D) 0.1 The correct answer is C. The normal FEV1/FVC ratio is approximately 0.8. This ratio is extremely important because it can be a marker measured in suspected lung disease. In obstructive lung disease such as COPD or asthma, the FEV1/FVC ratio decreases (patient cannot expire as much in one second as a

A 22-year-old patient arrives to you with symptoms suggestive of moderate obstructive lung disease and as a result you perform an initial spirometry, then administer salbutamol and repeat the spirometry 5 minutes later. What outcome would suggest a positive test of acute bronchodilator responsiveness? A decrease in FEV1 of 10% A decrease in FEV1 of 15% An increase in FEV1 of 10% An increase in FEV1 of 15% The correct answer is D. An increase in the FEV1 of more than 12% (and greater than 0.2 L, just FYI), suggests acute bronchodilator responsiveness.

The first step in the stepwise approach to COPD management is: Oxygen therapy Short-acting bronchodilators Smoking cessation/education Inhaled steroids None of the above The correct answer is C. Smoking cessation/education should be the first step in any COPD management. Further steps include bronchodilators, rehabilitation, inhaled steroids, oxygen therapy, and surgery.

Put the following step-wise asthma management strategies in order of suggested use: i. Addition of prednisone ii. Beta agonist iii. Environmental control iv. Inhaled corticosteroid ii, iii, iv, i iii, ii, iv, i ii, i, iii, iv iii, ii, i, iv The correct answer is B. A common practice is to utilize a long-acting beta-agonist in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid, while carrying a short-acting bronchodilator for use as needed.

Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for asthma? Family history Smoking Air pollution In utero smoke exposure All of the above can contribute to asthma The correct answer is E. Asthma has both genetic and environmental components. Smoking AND maternal smoking during pregnancy can increase the risk of asthma.

One sign of poor asthma control is: Any night-time symptoms Any daytime symptoms Any need for short-acting B2 agonist Any decrease in FEV1 The correct answer is A. If a patient complains of any night-time symptoms from their asthma, the management plan should be altered. (B) Daytime symptoms are a sign of poor control only when present for 4 or more days/week. (C) It is considered acceptable for a patient to be using their short-acting

Which of these sets of signs would be most useful in diagnosing a patient with asthma? Wheezing, coughing, and sputum production Coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath Allergic rhinitis, coughing, and shortness of breath Allergic rhinitis, wheezing, and shortness of breath The correct answer is B. Coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath are excellent signs of asthma. (A) There may be sputum production in asthma, but the cough can also be dry. (C,D) Allergic rhinitis is a condition sometimes associated with asthma, but it is not a direct sign of asthma.

Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis needs 2+ major PODS symptoms (including O or D) for 10+ days , or worsening after initial improvement. At 4 days this is a viral URTI , and most acute rhinosinusitis is viral . First line is to watch and wait (7-10 days) with symptom care: sali

A 47-year-old man has used an over-the-counter xylometazoline (Otrivin) spray every day for several weeks. His congestion is now worse than when he started, despite using it more often. What is the best management? Stop it; start an intranasal steroid Increase the spray to four times daily Add an oral decongestant to the spray Start a 10-day course of amoxicillin Refer for turbinate reduction surgery now The correct answer is A. This is rhinitis medicamentosa : regular topical decongestant use causes rebound congestion and tolerance, so symptoms worsen despite more use. A 25-year-old has sneezing, itchy watery eyes and clear rhinorrhea every spring. Exam shows pale, boggy turbinates. Pollen avoidance has not been enough. What is the first-line medication? Daily topical decongestant spray Short course of oral prednisone Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate Daily intranasal corticosteroid Oral pseudoephedrine for the season The correct answer is D. Seasonal allergic rhinitis : clear drainage, itch and sneezing, with pale, swollen, boggy turbinates . A 22-year-old has a nosebleed from the right nostril after a minor bump. He is stable. What is the first step to control the bleeding? Tilt the head back and pinch the nasal bridge Sit forward, press soft nose 10-15 min Silver nitrate cautery to both sides of the septum Posterior nasal packing with a balloon catheter Embolization of the anterior ethmoid artery The correct answer is B. Most epistaxis is anterior , from Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area , and is controlled with pressure. A 15-year-old boy has recurrent nosebleeds from the left side and increasing left-sided nasal obstruction. A vascular-looking mass is seen far back in the left nasal cavity. What is the most likely diagnosis? Nasal polyposis Allergic rhinitis Juvenile nasal angiofibroma Chronic rhinosinusitis Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia The correct answer is C. Recurrent epistaxis with ipsilateral (unilateral) nasal obstruction in an adolescent male is the picture of a juvenile nasal angiofibroma . Which of the following structures does this carotid sheath NOT encapsulate? Internal Jugular vein Vagus nerve Carotid artery Sympathetic trunk The correct answer is D. The Carotid sheath sheaths the internal jugular vein, vagus nerve and carotid artery.

Which option below correctly indicates the contents of a fascia in the head and neck? The investing fascia contains the trapezius, scalene, and cricothyroid muscles The pretracheal fascia contains the thyroid gland, esophagus, and strap muscles The prevertebral fascia contains the pharynx, retropharyngeal space, and alar space The carotid sheath contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, scalene muscles The correct answer is B. A physician suspects a thyroid cancer and a biopsy must be completed for staging and grading. To obtain superficial thyroid tissue (in the least minimally invasive manner) which of the following structures must the physician dissect to get to the thyroid? Thyroid cartilage Trachea Esophagus Infrahyoid muscles Suprahyoid muscles The correct answer is D. The thyroid is deep to the infrahyoid (strap) muscles – this muscle must be dissected to gain access to the thyroid. The thyroid is anterior to the trachea and esophagus. The thyroid is inferior to the thyroid cartilage.

At a recent visit to the emergency room yesterday, Nellie discovered that her previous 2- week history of palpitations were due to atrial fibrillation. She was prescribed anticoagulation therapy to reduce the risk of thrombosis/embolism. Today, she developed numbness and paralysis in her tongue and pallor in her face, consistent with embolism. Mentation is normal and there are no other symptoms. Based on this presentation, occlusion has likely occurred in an artery that branched off the _____. Vertebral artery Common carotid artery External carotid artery Internal carotid artery The correct answer is C. The vertebral artery runs along the spinal cord straight to the brain with minimal branching. The common carotid artery bifurcates into the internal carotid artery and the external carotid artery, and the external carotid artery has many branches which supply blood to the fa

An 80-year-old presents to your clinic with a lateral neck mass. She describes the neck mass as being present for the past 3 months. Before you begin your physical examination, what is the most likely diagnosis for this patient’s presentation? Lymphatic malformation Thyroid goiter Malignant neoplasm Suppurative lymphadenitis The correct answer is C. About 80% of lateral head and neck masses are neoplastic (and 80% of neoplasms are malignant). In addition, neoplasms become a more common diagnosis in the elderly. A lymphatic malformation is a congenital defect that is commonly associated with a longer timeline (>7 years)

Which of the following treatments is NOT an appropriate treatment recommendation for Acute sialadenitis (Infection) of the submandibular gland? Gland massage Cold compress Hydration Sialagogues The correct answer is B. Warm compresses are recommended for infection of the salivary glands, however cold compresses are recommended for stones in the salivary gland.

67-year-old Georgie presented to his family doctor concerned about a palpable neck mass slowly growing on this right cheek for the past 4 months. He has a 35 pack-year smoking history, and while recently retired, used to work in a metal-working factory. Upon physical examination, the neck mass is firm, irregular, and fixed. What would be the next best step in George’s management? This is too complicated for a family doctor – immediately refer to ENT Perform an ultrasound and request a CT scan Perform an incisional biopsy for pathologic analysis Incision and drainage for the cyst for analysis of its components The correct answer is B. A family doctor should attempt imaging of a neck mass prior to referring to an ENT doctor. For neck and head masses, common imaging modalities are ultrasound and CT scans. While a biopsy may be ordered, imaging is likely to be ordered first, and also, a less invasive FNA bio

A patient with a parotid gland tumor undergoes a biopsy which reveals the tumor is benign. Which of the following is an appropriate treatment recommendation given the patient’s findings? Surgical incision Watch and wait Sialagogues Gland massage The correct answer is A. Surgical Excision is appropriate for masses that arise within salivary glands, even if they are benign. This will relieve the patients symptoms and prevent future growth and the risk of malignant transformation.

A patient presents to your clinic with a concern about her voice – _she is unable to raise the its pitch. The physician suspects the patient has an issue with the tensor muscle in the larynx. Which of the following muscles helps with pitch raising in phonation, and how is it innervated? Posterior Cricoarytenoid muscle innervated by the Superior laryngeal nerve Lateral cricoarytenoid muscle innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve Cricothyroid muscle innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve Thyroarytenoid muscle innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve The correct answer is C. The Cricothyroid muscle is the only tensor muscle of the larynx and is innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic muscles are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Roxanne was born with a patent ductus arteriosus that required surgical correction shortly after birth. Following the surgery, her parents noticed that her crying tended to be more hoarse, consistent with an iatrogenic lesion to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. What pathology is least likely based on this lesion? Inability to adjust vocal pitch Inability to close the vocal cords Inability to open the vocal cords Inability to feel an obstruction in the larynx The correct answer is A. The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates most of the muscles of the larynx, with the exception of the cricothyroid. The cricothyroid is innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve and is responsible for tensing the vocal cords and increasing pitch.

Which of the following larynx pathologies most likely involves airway stabilization as an immediate management step? Unilateral vocal cord paralysis Bilateral vocal cord paralysis Laryngopharyngeal reflux Vocal cord nodules The correct answer is B. Bilateral vocal cord paralysis can obstruct the flow air into and out of the lungs, thus an immediate consideration is always airways stabilization. With unilateral vocal cord paralysis airway management is not an immediate concern, and a long-term approach may be taken invo

Which option correctly describes a cause and a treatment of the associated laryngeal pathology? Laryngeal nodules are caused by voice overuse and are treated surgically Laryngeal polyps are caused by laryngeal trauma and treated with voice rest Laryngopharyngeal reflux is caused by stomach acid reflux and is treated with PPIs Early vocal cord cancer is treated with complete laryngectomy The correct answer is C. In laryngopharyngeal reflux, excess stomach acid from the esophagus enters the larynx causing hoarseness. PPIs (proton-pump inhibitors) decrease the acidity of the gastric juices. Laryngeal nodules are treated with voice rest, laryngeal polyps are treated surgically, and ear

A patient presented to an urgent care clinic after an episode of choking during dinner. He thinks he may have accidentally inhaled part of a chicken wing. His vitals are currently stable, but physical examination reveals stridor when inhaling only. Based on the physical examination, the chicken wing was most likely lodged in which part of the patient’s airway? In the piriform sinuses In the supraglottis In the subglottis In the right bronchus In the left bronchus The correct answer is B. Stridor can be inspiratory, expiratory (wheeze) or bi-phasic. Inspiratory stridor is usually caused by an obstruction of the supraglottis or glottis. Biphasic stridor is usually caused by an obstruction of the subglottis. Expiratory wheeze is usually caused by an obstruction

As a physician you encounter a patient on an airplane with an airway obstruction who requires an emergency airway puncture. An intubation or tracheostomy is not possible. Which of the following membranes do you pierce to provide a temporary airway for this patient? Thyrohyoid Cricothyroid Quadrate Conus elasticus The correct answer is B. During life-threatening situations where the airways become obstructed a cricothyrotomy is performed, where the cricothyroid membrane is incised.

Covid tests involve the use of a nasopharyngeal swab to detect the presence of the SARS- CoV-2 virus. The correct method is indicated with the red O below, and the blue X indicates an incorrect method. Which statement below is true? The correct method involves passing the swab through the inferior concha The correct method involves passing the swab through the maxillary sinus The incorrect method carries a risk of puncturing the cribiform plate The incorrect method displays the tip of the swab within the sphenothemoidal recess The correct answer is C. In the correct method, the swab passes through the inferior meatus (Below the inferior concha). The Cribriform plate is a thin bone superior to the nasal cavity. The sphenoethmoidal recess is a small cavity superior to the superior concha.

Paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities that surround the nose within the skull. Sinuses create mucus that drain out of various channels within the nasal cavity, keeping the nose clean and free of bacteria. When these channels get blocked, the sinuses can become inflamed. Complete the following sentence: Inflammation of the sphenoidal sinus is caused by blockage of the ____. Frontonasal duct Semilunar hiatus Middle meatus Superior meatus Sphenoethmoidal recess The correct answer is E. The sphenoethmoidal recess is the site where the sphenoidal sinus drains. The ethmoidal, maxillary, and frontal sinuses drain through the middle meatus (or the semilunar hiatus within the middle meatus).

A child presents to your clinic with a midline neck mass. The mother reports the child recently acquired this after recovering from an upper respiratory tract infection. You notice the following on physical examination. Prior to conducting any further investigation, what is the most likely diagnosis? Recurrent pharyngeal infection Thyroglossal duct cyst Benign tumor Vascular malformation The correct answer is B. The patient’s symptoms are most in line with the presentation of a thyroglossal duct cyst – the neck mass is in the middle of the neck and occurred after an upper respiratory tract infection. A concerned mother comes into your clinic with her 5-year-old son. She explains how he recently (within the past hour) aspirated on some carrots. The mother witnessed the child aspirate the carrot and reported significant wheezing and choking for about a minute. Currently the child does not seem distressed, and a physical exam suggests the child’s airway is patent. Which of the following is an appropriate next step? Reassure the mother the child is fine, no further treatment is needed Consider airway intubation Consider performing a rigid bronchoscopy Prescribe prophylactics to address opportunistic infections The correct answer is C. Although the child is asymptomatic currently, the aspirated foreign body can lead to eventual complications such as obstruction and infections. If the history, physical exam, or radiography is indicative of an aspirated foreign body, a rigid bronchoscopy should be considered

Presence of biphasic stridor (inspiratory and expiratory) indicates an obstruction of the subglottis. Both allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis can present with reduced sense of smell. Presence of pets and timing of the congestion (eg, seasonal) would indicate allergic rhinitis. What is the best treatment for a patient who complains of odynophagia and referred otalgia, and whose physical exam demonstrates uvular deviation and unilateral peritonsillar swelling? The pain and swelling have been progressing for the past week. The rapid onset implies an infection, and the referred otalgia indicates a pathology in the oropharynx. A patient comes to your clinic with concerns about difficulty breathing through their nose. Which of the following pathologies is likely NOT the cause of the patient’s presentation? Nasal polyps Deviated septum Mucosal defect Enlarged turbinate's The correct answer is C. The constant obstruction the patient reports suggest a mechanical/ anatomical barrier as opposed to a fluctuating obstruction which is most often characteristic of a mucosal defect.

Tyrone is a patient of yours who initially presented to your family clinic a few weeks ago with a unilateral enlargement of his neck consistent with an enlarged thyroid. Follow up in 1-2 months to check for symptoms of hypo or hyperthyroidism Refer to a surgeon for unilateral thyroidectomy Refer to a surgeon for complete thyroidectomy Refer to radiology for nuclear scintigraphy of the thyroid Refer to radiology for CT/MRI of the head and neck The correct answer is D. Which patient below is the best candidate for a tonsillectomy? A patient with bilateral tonsilitis, wo has had 7 tonsil infections in the past 3 years A patient with bilateral tonsillitis, who has had 6 tonsil infections in the past 2 years A patient with unilateral tonsillitis caused by a benign cyst A patient with unilateral tonsillitis and extreme obstructive sleep apnea The correct answer is D. Tonsillectomies are absolutely indicated when malignancy is involved, or where this is airway obstruction. Tonsillectomies are relatively indicated based on frequency of tonsillitis: If there are 7 episodes in 1 year, 5 per year for two years, or 3 per year for three years,

A patient arrives at your clinic with multiple medial neck masses, each approximately 1.5 cm in diameter. He is asymptomatic aside from hoarseness. The physician orders blood work which suggests thyroid nodules. Which of the following investigations should be conducted? Ultrasound and subsequent FNA of the largest/primary nodule Ultrasound and subsequent FNA of all the nodules Ultrasound and subsequent incisional biopsy of the largest/primary nodule Ultrasound and subsequent incisional biopsy of all the nodules The correct answer is B. The correct investigation for thyroid nodules involves ultrasound followed by fine needle aspiration of all the nodules (if there are multiple nodules) to determine the nodule characteristics.

A patient arrives at your clinic with a medial neck mass (1.5 cm in diameter) suspected to be a thyroid nodule by the physician upon physical exam. He is asymptomatic aside from hoarseness. Which of the following blood markers do you order on a blood test for a suspected thyroid nodule? Thyroid stimulating hormone Thyroglobulin Calcitonin LDH The correct answer is A. TSH levels are important to include in the bloodwork as high levels could provide reason to order an ultrasound and investigate the nodules. Thyroglobulin and Calcitonin and are not in the work-up of a thyroid nodule.

A patient comes in with pain and swelling in their right submandibular gland and it gets worse when eating. Which of the following are possible complications of their condition? Which of the following comparison regarding head and neck cancer (HNC) is FALSE: HPV positive HNC occurs more commonly in patients with good health and HPV positive HNV occurs more often in patients with poorer health HPV-negative HNC is most commonly found in the tonsil and base of tongue HPV-negative HNC is associated with poorer prognosis than HPV-positive HNC. Sun exposure is a risk of HNC. The correct answer is B. HPV-positive HNC is most commonly found in the tonsil and base of tongue

Which of the following nerves of the cervical plexus nerves supplies motor innervation to the strap muscles. Phrenic nerve Vagus nerve Hypoglossal nerve Ansa cervicalis The correct answer is D. The phrenic nerve provides mixed innervation to the central part of diaphragm. The vagus nerve provides sensory and motor to the pharynx and larynx and parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and gut viscera. The hypoglossal nerve provides motor innervation to the tongue.

During a thyroid gland infection, which fascia prevents the free expansion of the swollen thyroid gland, leading to pain? Investing fascia Pretracheal fascia Prevertebral fascia Carotid sheath The correct answer is B. The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland, tracheal esophagus, and strap muscles.

Following oral trauma, a patient completely lost their ability to swallow. Which one of the following muscles is most likely injured/impaired Tensor palati Levator palati Palatopharyngeal Palatoglossus The correct answer is A. Tensor palati tenses laterally and is the most important muscle of the soft palate. It acts as an origin to all the other muscles. If the tensor palati isn’t working, then none of these other ones would work and the patient will lose the ability to swallow.

Which one of the following regarding esophageal anatomy is false: The upper esophagus is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerves and the lower esophagus is supplied by the esophageal plexus Esophageal varices could be a result of portal hypotension The middle of the esophageal muscularis is composed of both skeletal and smooth muscles. Upper esophagus is supplied by the inferior thyroid arteries The correct answer is B. Esophageal varices could be a result of portal hypertension, not hypotension.

A patient presents with chest pain and intermittent dysphagia. Their manometry shows this pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis Achalasia Distal esophageal spasm Jackhammer esophagus Scleroderma esophagus The correct answer is B. Upon swallowing of food, there is vertical pressure waves of high amplitude observed in the manometry. This is suggestive of simultaneous premature contractions, which are present in distal esophageal spasms.

What is the definitive treatment for achalasia Laparoscopic heller myotomy Pneumatic dilation Botox injection Per oral endoscopic myotomy The correct answer is A. From the achalasia column of the esophagus table in 01 - Approach to Abdominal Pain & Distension (Week 13). The table splits treatment in two. Regarding thyroid nodules, which of the following presentations are concerning for malignant masses? First degree relative with thyroid cancer Age <20 or >70 Family history of autoimmune disorders Nodules immobile with swallowing Pain Smoking A. I, II, III, IV B. I, II, IV, VI C. I, II, IV D. All of the above III and V are characteristics of benign thyroid lesions. VI is not a risk factor for thyroid cancer specifically.

The patient presents with a thyroid mass and an elevated thyroglobulin level. What is their most likely diagnosis Medullary carcinoma Papillary or follicular carcinoma Anaplastic cancer Parathyroid adenoma The correct answer is B. Papillary carcinoma and follicular carcinoma are derived from well differentiated thyroid follicles, which produce thyroglobulin.

Which of the following incorrectly describes the phase of swallowing? Esophageal: peristalsis of the bolus of food toward the lower esophageal sphincter Oral: mastication of solids to form bolus and contact of posterior tongue to palate to prevent posterior spillage. Oral: tongue “peristalsis” to propel bolus to the posterior oral cavity Pharyngeal: initiated when the bolus of food is in the esophagus The correct answer is D. The pharyngeal phase is initiated when the bolus reaches the base of the tongue, this is followed by pharyngeal “peristalsis”

A 50-year-old patient comes to your family practice complaining of drooling, choking, and nasal regurgitation. They are quite frustrated by these symptoms and feel as though their quality of life has diminished. What complications are you concerned about? Select all that apply. Aspiration Aspiration pneumonia Malnutrition Dehydration The correct answer is A, B, C, D. This patient presents with likely oropharyngeal dysphagia, give their symptoms. Aspiration if most prominent risk, however, aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and dehydration are also complications.

A patient presents to your ENT clinic with symptoms concerning pharyngeal dysphagia. Which diagnostic technique would you consider assessing this stage of swallowing? Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy, EGD) Fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) Modified barium swallow Clinical swallow assessment The correct answer is C. A modified barium swallow test can rule out aspiration, assess the pharyngeal stage of swallowing, and certain structural issues.

Which of the following statements is true regarding pediatric neck masses? >50 % of pediatric neck masses are malignant Lymph nodes >2cm in size are typical and not concerning A firm mass could indicate infection or malignancy Ultrasounds are not routinely used for neck masses The correct answer is C. From 06 - Pediatric Neck Masses. The lecture's exam box reads consistency as a differential: firm means infection or malignancy , fluctuant means cyst or abscess, and fixed means malignancy. A : most pediatric neck masses are congenital (over 50% by some sources) or inflamma

A 6-year-old male presents with a fluctuant anterior/midline neck mass. Which of the following would be on your differential diagnosis based on the location? Dermoid cyst Thyroglossal cyst Thymic cyst Saccular cyst Lymphatic malformation The correct answer is A, B, E. Dermoid cysts, thyroglossal cysts, and lymphatic malformations all present in the anterior/midline neck region.

A 2-year-old girl is brought into your family practice with the chief complaint of a neck mass. The mother explains that her daughter had an upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago, and since then she has noticed this mass. On physical exam, you notice a midline, fluctuant, painful mass that elevates with protrusion of the tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings? Thyroglossal duct cyst Branchial cleft cyst Lymphatic malformation Malignancy The correct answer is A. The clinical findings mentioned in the question align with those of a thyroglossal duct cyst.

Thyroglossal duct cysts, branchial duct cysts, and vascular malformations can all be diagnosed at birth. True False The correct answer is B. Many of these congenital masses will not present until after an upper respiratory tract infection, for example. Therefore may not be diagnosed until 3-5 years of age.

A 3-year-old is being assessed in the ER due to progressive difficulty breathing. On physical exam, you note that she is febrile, has inspiratory stridor, and a ‘barky’ cough. What is the most appropriate management? Select all that apply. Hydration Cold humidification Admit to the hospital Bronchodilators Inhaled corticosteroids The correct answer is A, B. Croup is the likely diagnosis, therefore the best management is hydration and cold humification.

A 1-year-old boy and his father are at your family practice. The father explains yesterday his son was playing with his older sister's beaded bracelet when it broke. The father had momentarily stepped away to answer the door, when he suddenly heard his son coughing. When he came back, he found the broken bracelet. The father is concerned that his son may have swallowed a bead. On physical exam the boy has decreased breath sounds over the right lower lung zone and stridor. What would your next step be? Rigid bronchoscopy to retrieve the foreign body Inspiratory/expiratory CXR Lateral decubitus CXR Bronchodilators Watch and wait The correct answer is A. the general rule of thumb is that is 1 of history, physical exam, or radiography, is positive for signs of foreign body aspiration, you can perform a rigid bronchoscopy

How would you manage a patient with a deep neck infection who has no MRSA risk factors, is not immunocompromised, and otherwise healthy? Select all that apply. Incision and drainage Vancomycin Ceftriaxone Flagyl Piperacillin-Tazobactam The correct answer is A, C, D. for an otherwise healthy patient with a deep neck infection, treatment should consist of incision and drainage, and antibiotic treatment with ceftriaxone and flagyl

Which of the following correctly describes either Lemierre’s syndrome or rhinocerebral mucormycoses? Lemierre’s syndrome is due to an angio-invasive aseptate mold Rhinocerebral mucormycoses is treated with ceftriaxone and flagyl Lemierre’s syndrome may cause fever and rigors, neck pain, and respiratory distress Rhinocerebral mucormycoses has a low mortality rate if treated with the amphotericin B and surgical debridement The correct answer is C. From 05 - Infections of the Head and Neck. Lemierre's syndrome is an infectious thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically caused by the oral anaerobe Fusobacterium necrophorum. A pharyngitis comes first; about a week later the patient develops fever and rigo

Which of the following is NOT a symptom of pediatric sleep apnea? Restless sleeping Mouth Breathing Daytime hypersomnolence Secondary Enuresis The correct answer is C. Daytime hypersomnolence (excessive sleepiness) is a common symptom in adult sleep apnea, however daytime hyperactivity is a symptom of pediatric sleep apnea.

A 78-year-old woman with lung cancer develops hoarseness when speaking. This is most likely due to the involvement of which structure? Left recurrent laryngeal nerve Left mainstem (primary) bronchus Trachea Right recurrent laryngeal nerve Superior laryngeal nerve The correct answer is A. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve runs under the aorta and above the pulmonary artery. It can be compressed due to intrathoracic spread of lung cancer, resulting in paralysis of the left vocal cord. (D) The right recurrent laryngeal nerve runs under the subclavian artery an

A 58 year old woman presents to your clinic with an enlarged thyroid nodule (>1cm). After taking a detailed history, which of the following investigations is appropriate to order? Ultrasound TSH and Ultrasound Calcitonin and Ultrasound TSH and Calcitonin The correct answer is B. The appropriate work-up for a thyroid nodule larger than 1cm in diameter is taking an ultrasound and their TSH. A high TSH does not require further planning whereas a normal/low TSH would require further assessment.

The main structural component of the adult trachea can best be described as: Incomplete cartilaginous rings Elasticized bars of cartilage in a flexible matrix Complete cartilaginous rings Incomplete bony rings Complete bony rings The correct answer is A. The adult trachea is supported by fifteen to twenty incomplete C- shaped cartilaginous rings that reinforce the anterior and lateral sides of the trachea to protect and maintain the airway. This leave a flexible, membranous wall posteriorly which is closed by the trachealis

A 6-year old child comes into the clinic with a dripping, runny nose, sneezing, itchy eyes and a scratchy throat. Which of the following is the best therapy? ASA Antibiotics Supportive care OTC cough medication Anti-histamines The correct answer is C. Supportive care, including adequate hydration, nasal irrigation, and rest, and analgesia (acetaminophen or NSAIDs) would provide symptomatic relief for this child. No ASA or ASA containing products should be used in children, due to the risk of developing Reye's syndrome, a

The third pharyngeal pouch develops into which structures? The parathyroid glands only Thymus and inferior parathyroid glands Thyroid and superior parathyroid glands Laryngeal cleft and epiglottis Thymus and hyoid bone The correct answer is B. The third pharyngeal pouch develops into the inferior parathyroid glands and contributes to the thymus. The fourth pharyngeal pouch develops into the superior parathyroid glands and contributes to the thyroid gland (parafollicular cells), as well as to the musculature and ca

The rapidly spreading cellulitis of sublingual, submental and submandibular spaces which produces swelling and elevation of the tongue, leading to upper airway obstruction: Ludwig’s Angina Epiglottitis Tonsilitis Subglottic Stenosis The correct answer is A. Ludwig’s Angina is an emergency and must be treated quickly with antibiotics or incision/drainage, or both.

Lemeirre’s Syndrome is a severe deep neck space infection. Which of the following organisms and anatomical structures are implicated in this syndrome? Fusobacterium necrophorum (oral anaerobe) invading the internal jugular vein Hemophilus influenza B invading the epiglottis Group A Streptococcus invading the pharynx Oral bacteria leading to a tooth abscess. The correct answer is A. Lemierre’s Syndrome is characterized by Fusobacterium necrophorum (oral anerobe) invading the internal jugular vein leading to infectious thrombophlebitis. This can lead to septic emboli, and intravascular abscesses and can be deadly.
The most common type of thyroid cancer is: Papillary Medullary Anaplastic Follicular The correct answer is A. Papillary thyroid cancer accounts for 55-65% of thyroid malignancy

A 74-year old patient presents to your clinic with a recently discovered 3 cm solid thyroid nodule. You perform an FNAB and the results come back indicating a “high risk” lesion. The most appropriate management of this lesion is: Nothing at the moment, follow the patient up every 6 months Radiation therapy Total thyroidectomy +/- Neck dissection Local excision of the nodule The correct answer is C. A high risk lesion is likely to harbour malignancy. As such, it would be prudent to perform a total thyroidectomy with or without neck dissection. The other listed options are not recommended for such a lesion. The other potentially appropriate management option is a diagnos

You are working in the emergency room and decide that a patient requires a cricothyrotomy. The appropriate anatomical landmark for this procedure is: Between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages Below the cricoid cartilage Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage Above the hyoid bone The correct answer is A. A cricothyrotomy is performed between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. A tracheostomy is performed below the cricoid cartilage, usually between the 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies motor innervation to all of the internal muscles of the larynx except for: Cricothyroid Transverse arytenoids Posterior cricoarytenoids Lateral cricoarytenoids The correct answer is A. The only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the RLN is the cricothyroid muscle.

A patient visits your clinic and complains of hoarseness. You recall that red flags of hoarseness include: Hoarseness persisting for >2 weeks Associated symptoms – Otalgia, dysphagia Risk factors – Smoking, trauma, previous surgery All of the above The correct answer is D. These are all red flags for hoarseness From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. Hoarseness raises the question of a laryngeal primary, and the lecture's cancer history covers each element offered: Duration (A) : the red flag is persistent hoarseness, which the lecture defines as

The most common cause of stridor in neonates is: Foreign body Vocal Cord Paralysis Laryngomalacia Subglottic stenosis The correct answer is C. Laryngomalacia is the most common, followed by vocal cord paralysis and subglottic stenosis.

Which of the following is correct regarding croup: It is the most common cause of stridor in the pediatric population It has viral etiology Occurs most often in the spring and fall All of the above are correct The correct answer is D. These are all characteristics of croup. From 07 - Pediatric Airway Pathology. All three statements come straight from the lecture: A : croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is the most common cause of stridor in children, and 3-5% of children develop it. B : it is viral , usually
The treatment of thyroglossal duct cysts is usually: Radiation Aspiration Surgery None of the above The correct answer is C. Radiation and aspiration would be ineffective treatments.

Danger signs of oral infections include all of the following except: Significant dysphagia Chest pain Loss of consciousness Unilateral, slow onset facial swelling The correct answer is D. Unilateral, slow onset facial swelling is not a danger sign of an oral infection. Bilateral or rapid onset swelling (<12 hours) are considered danger signs for oral infections. Significant dysphagia, chest pain, and loss of consciousness are also considered danger signs.

Which of the following is false regarding the nose and nasal septum? Fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone can be accompanied by CSF rhinorrhea All bones that make up the external nose are paired The septum consists of both the vomer and the perpendicular plate of ethmoid The nasal bones are the most commonly fractured bones of the face The cartilaginous septum and the bones of the nasal septum divide the nasal cavity into right and left halves. B) is incorrect as the external nose consists of the paired nasal bones and frontal processes of the maxillae. It also includes the nasal part of the frontal bone (singular) and the bony part of the nasal septum which is the vomer and perpendicular plate of ethmoid.

The facial nerve exits the skull via the: Foramen ovale Foramen spinosum Superior orbital fissure Stylomastoid foramen The correct answer is D. The mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve exits via the foramen ovale. The middle meningeal vessels pass through the foramen spinosum. Cranial nerves II, III, IV, V1 and IV exit via the superior orbital fissure. The facial nerve exits via the stylomastoid foramen.

The carotid sheath contains which of the following structures? Common carotid artery Vagus nerve External Jugular vein A & B only The correct answer is D. The carotid sheath contains the internal jugular vein not the external jugular vein.

Branches of the external carotid artery include all of the following except: Ascending pharyngeal Maxillary Inferior thyroid Posterior auricular The correct answer is C. The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery. The superior thyroid artery is a branch of the external carotid artery.

The posterior border of the anterior triangle of the neck is: The sternocleidomastoid The trapezius The spinal accessory nerve None of the above The correct answer is A. The sternocleidomastoid is the posterior border of the anterior triangle of the neck.239 Answer: A) The Mandible, midline, and back edge of the SCM make up the anterior triangle of the neck, while the trapezius, clavicle, and back edge of SCM make up the posterior triangle.

Which of the following groups are the correct boundaries of the anterior triangle of the neck? Mandible-Midline-Back of Sternocleidomastoid Trapezius-Clavicle-Back of Sternocleidomastoid Trapezius-Midline-Clavicle Clavicle-External Jugular Vein-Midline Left Sternocleidomastoid-Right Sternocleidomastoid-Mastoid The correct answer is A. From 01 - Anatomy of the Neck. The sternocleidomastoid splits the neck into two triangles. The anterior triangle is bounded above by the inferior border of the mandible , medially by the midline of the neck , and laterally by the anterior border of the SCM . A is the only op

For Questions 24 – 27, match the following nerves below (A – D) with their supply: Taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Hypoglossal Nerve Maxillary Nerve Facial Nerve Mandibular Nerve The correct answer is C. The facial nerve provides taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

For Questions 24 – 27, match the following nerves below (A – D) with their supply: Sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Hypoglossal Nerve Maxillary Nerve Facial Nerve Mandibular Nerve The correct answer is D. The mandibular nerve provides sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

For Questions 24 – 27, match the following nerves below (A – D) with their supply: Sensory innervation of the palate. Hypoglossal Nerve Maxillary Nerve Facial Nerve Mandibular Nerve The correct answer is B. The maxillary nerve provides sensory innervation of the palate.

For Questions 24 – 27, match the following nerves below (A – D) with their supply: Motor innervation to the intrinsic muscles of the tongue. Hypoglossal Nerve Maxillary Nerve Facial Nerve Mandibular Nerve The correct answer is A. The hypoglossal nerve provides motor innervation to the intrinsic muscles of the tongue.

A patient comes in with an acute onset of headaches, facial pain and nasal discharge and is diagnosed with acute bacterial sinusitis and placed on antibiotics. Which of the following are red flags to be careful about while treating this patient? Patient is immunosuppressed No response to therapy within 72 hours Symptoms go away in 72 hours Both A and B None of the above D) When treating a patient with acute bacterial sinusitis, there are 5 red flags to watch for which could indicate much more severe disease. These include no responses in 72 hours, immunocompromised patients (may have fungal cause), frontal symptoms, sphenoid symptoms, recurring symptoms and complic

What are the three most common causes of acute bacterial sinusitis? Strep pneumonia, H Influenza and M Catarrhalis Strep pneumonia, H influenza and ecoli H influenza, E.coli and rotavirus H Influenza, M Catarrhalis and Group B strep None of the above A) Strep pneumonia, H Influenza and M Catarrhalis. These three bacteria are the most common cause of acute bacterial sinusitis.

What is the most common type of nose bleed (epistaxis)? Posterior Bleed Lateral Bleed Anterior Bleed Inferior Bleed C) Anterior bleed. The most common type of nose bleed is an anterior bleed (95%). Usually these are brief and from minor trauma. Posterior bleeds are rarer, but can happen in the elderly and are very dangerous. They can be severe and bleed a lot, so it is important to recognize these as early treatm

What is the most common local cause of nose bleeds (i.e. happens in nasal cavity?). Neoplasm Trauma Infection Post surgery B) The most common cause of nose bleed is trauma (nose picking, sneeze, fracture or intubation). The rest of the answers are possible causes as well, but less common.

Which of the following is NOT a normal offered treatment in an uncomplicated nose bleed? Nasal packing Cautery Medical management (correct underlying cause) Forced expulsion of clots None of the above E) All of A-D are options offered in an uncomplicated nasal bleed. Surgical options are usually only offered if patients have bleeding despite nasal packing, patient needs a transfusion, patient cannot be packed, or has a posterior bleed.

Ernie presents to ER after playing hockey. After the game, he suddenly has bleeding from his mouth and nose and fainted, so his buddy took him to emerge. The medical clerk in the ER cannot figure out the cause of the bleed so endoscopy is used, instead of other options of viewing the nasal cavity and mouth. Which of the following is not an advantage of choosing flexible endoscopy? Can examine the entire upper respiratory tract with minimal discomfort It is cheap to use Can assess swallowing Can attach a light Can assess pharyngeal airway B). Flexible endoscopy is very valuable because it allows you to assess all of the upper respiratory system, and you can attach different tools to it. So, it is the best tool for figuring out the cause of a bleed. The biggest disadvantage is cost compared to other tools, as well as it can be difficu

What is the most common cause of sore throat? Candida albicans Viral Strep pneumonia Strep pyogens E. Coli B) 85% of sore throats are caused by viral causes. From 05 - Infections of the Head and Neck. Pharyngitis is most often viral , caused by the common upper respiratory tract viruses (rhinovirus, coronaviruses, influenza, parainfluenza), with EBV and CMV as further viral causes. Strep pyogenes (D) : g

Which of the following is an indication for a tonsillectomy? Upper airway obstruction severe dysphagia (trouble swallowing) recurrent infections neoplasm All of the above are indications for tonsillectomy E) All of the above are indications for tonsillectomies. It is important to know the indications because tonsillectomies should not be offered to every patient and only when it is appropriate.

Which of the following is true of malignant neck masses? They are more commonly found in patients over 40 years old than those under 40 They are more likely to be found on the lateral neck than benign masses which are typically midline They are more likely to grow over the course of weeks-to-months All of the above None of the above D) All of the above are true. As with other malignancies, older patients are more likely to be affected (a is true). Lateral masses on the neck should raise suspicion for malignancy as well, as most benign neck masses appear in the midline (b is true). Also, malignant growths progress from ~7weeks t

Which of the following is characteristic of a typical thyroglossal duct cyst? They are more likely found on the lateral neck They move upwards with protrusion of the tongue They usually present with severe pain They are caused by an infection of the thyroid gland They are pre-malignant lesions B) Thyroglossal duct cysts are benign, congenital lesions (as such they are usually midline, non-infectious and without malignant potential). While they can be painful, or result in dysphagia, they typically do not present with pain. They result from persistence of the thyroglossal tract which arise

Scott is a 24-year-old male who sustains an injury to his cranial nerves VII, and IX. Which of the following would he notice following his injury? Dry mouth Difficulty digesting carbs Impaired taste mediation Increased risk of oral infection All of the above E) The parasympathetic nervous system (specifically CN VII, IX, (and a slight contribution from CN V) are responsible for innervating salivary glands. Lubrication, digestion (of carbs and some fats), taste mediation, and protection from infection are all functions of saliva. This patient would be im

Which of the following is true regarding the salivary glands? Larger glands are more susceptible to malignancies The parotid gland is the most likely to develop a stone Salivary stones may lead to salivary gland fibrosis All salivary gland stones must be treated as surgical emergencies Most salivary stones are present bilaterally C) Smaller glands are more likely to be affected by malignancy. The submandibular gland is responsible for most (~80%) of salivary gland stones. Some stones (such as smaller parotid stones) may be treated conservatively. Only 25% of stones are bilateral. Salivary stones may result in secondary infec

Sandra undergoes a parotidectomy to treat a parotid gland malignancy. Following the procedure Sandra claims that she feels fine, but she is unable to smile. What is the most likely cause? Sutures used during a parotidectomy were accidentally tied through her facial muscles The anaesthetic used has not yet worn off Her cranial nerve VII was injured during the procedure The swelling resulting from the operation is causing too much pressure for her facial muscles to overcome She is unhappy with the medical student conducting her post-op interview C) The MOST LIKELY cause of a patients’ inability to control their facial muscles following a parotidectomy is an injury of the facial nerve (CN VII) which runs along the parotid. Therefore c is correct. a), b) and d) are unlikely. e) is also wrong. Everyone loves medical students.

Most head and neck malignancies: Originate from other organs and metastasize to the neck Are derived from cells of epithelial origin Are derived from the salivary glands All of the above are true None of the above are true B) Metastases to the neck are rare, malignancies of the head and neck are typically primary tumors. Most of these malignancies are derived from the lining of the upper aerodigestive tract (NOT the skin, thyroid, salivary glands etc..). Most head and neck tumors are of epithelial origin (i.e. squamou

Your patient presents with a sore throat and fever for the past three days. Upon examination, you notice an enlarged pus-filled tonsil on the right side, causing the uvula to deviate to the left. What is your most likely diagnosis? viral tonsillitis peritonsillar abscess strep throat viral pharyngitis The correct answer is B. A peritonsillar abscess would cause similar symptoms to tonsillitis, but a deviating uvula and pus-filled tonsil is more suggestive of a peritonsillar abscess.

If the hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve is injured, which direction will the tongue deviate towards? Towards the affected side Towards the unaffected side It will be completely paralyzed None of the above The correct answer is A. When the hypoglossal nerve is injured, the tongue will deviate towards the affected side.

A 52-year-old woman has a 1.5 cm thyroid nodule found on routine examination. She has no compressive or thyroid symptoms. Which initial investigations are indicated? Serum thyroglobulin and CT of the neck Serum TSH and thyroid ultrasound Serum calcitonin and RAI uptake scan Palpation-guided FNA alone Reassurance and re-examination in a year The correct answer is B. For any nodule >1 cm the lecture lists TSH and thyroid ultrasound as "definitely" indicated (the review slide also gives Ix: serum TSH, U/S). Thyroglobulin is not recommended in nodule work-up and calcitonin has insufficient evidence. An RAI uptake scan is only for a low TSH

A 40-year-old woman is assessed for a thyroid nodule. Which feature most raises concern for malignancy? Nodule moves with swallowing Soft, smooth nodule on palpation Tenderness after a recent viral illness Childhood head and neck irradiation Low TSH with a hot nodule on scan The correct answer is D. Head and neck irradiation is a high-risk history factor in the lecture, with a first-degree relative with thyroid cancer, rapid growth and hoarseness; on exam the high-risk signs are vocal cord paralysis, cervical lymphadenopathy and a fixed nodule. The review's table puts m

A 68-year-old man who smokes has a painless, firm lateral neck mass that has grown over 2 months. He has had no recent infection. What is the most likely diagnosis? Metastatic carcinoma Second branchial cleft cyst Suppurative lymphadenitis Lymphatic malformation Reactive lymph node The correct answer is A. The 80% rule : 80% of lateral neck masses are neoplastic, 80% of those malignant, 80% metastatic to cervical nodes, and 80% from a head and neck primary. Add the age rule and the lecture's conclusion is that in an elderly patient a lateral neck mass is a cancer until proven

A 45-year-old man has a lateral neck mass that has slowly enlarged over about 4 months. By the rule of 7s, which category does this time course point to? Infection Congenital lesion Neoplasm Trauma (hematoma) Endocrine (thyroid) The correct answer is C. Rule of 7s : about 7 days suggests infection, 7 weeks to 7 months suggests neoplasm , and 7 years suggests a congenital lesion. Four months falls in the neoplastic window.

A 40-year-old man has recurrent painful swelling under the angle of the jaw that comes on at mealtimes and settles over a few hours. He is afebrile with no purulence at the duct. What is the most likely diagnosis? Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid Acute bacterial parotitis Sjogren syndrome Warthin tumour Submandibular sialolithiasis The correct answer is E. Salivary stones present with pain and swelling worse with meals (salivary colic), and the submandibular gland is the most common site . About 90% of submandibular stones are radiopaque (90% of parotid stones are radiolucent). Treatment: gland massage, bimanual expression, hy

A mass arising in which salivary gland carries the highest chance of malignancy? Parotid gland Submandibular gland Minor salivary gland Same risk in every salivary gland The correct answer is C. The smaller the gland, the greater the chance of cancer : parotid about 25% malignant, submandibular 50%, other (minor) glands 75%. Most salivary tumours (>80%) still arise in the parotid, so the commonest site is not the riskiest.

A 50-year-old woman has a painless 2 cm mass in the parotid gland. Facial nerve function is normal and FNA shows a pleomorphic adenoma. What is the recommended management? Serial ultrasound surveillance Parotidectomy Radiation therapy alone Course of oral antibiotics Repeat FNA in six months The correct answer is B. The lecture's rule: a mass arising within a salivary gland should be removed surgically , even if benign (continued growth, symptom relief, risk of malignant transformation). Surgery is both diagnostic and therapeutic; the goals are complete resection with preservation of th

A 47-year-old man who has never smoked is diagnosed with an HPV-positive squamous cell carcinoma of the base of tongue. Compared with HPV-negative head and neck SCC, which is expected? Older age at diagnosis Stronger link to smoking Poor oral hygiene as the main risk Better prognosis Worse prognosis The correct answer is D. HPV-positive head and neck SCC: younger, good health, higher socioeconomic status, non-smokers/non-drinkers, lower T-stage and a good prognosis . HPV-negative : older, poorer health, poor oral hygiene, smoker and drinker, advanced T-stage, poor prognosis. HPV subtype 16 acco

A 62-year-old man who smokes and drinks has a painless red velvety patch on the floor of his mouth that has been present for 6 weeks. How should this lesion be regarded? Premalignant lesion Normal mucosal variant Benign vascular lesion Traumatic ulcer Reactive lymphoid tissue The correct answer is A. In the oral cavity, the white patch ( leukoplakia ) and the red patch ( erythroplasia ) are both premalignant . A persistent lesion in a patient with risk factors (smoking, alcohol) warrants referral to Otolaryngology, who can biopsy it in clinic.

A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with a squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx. What is the usual primary treatment for this site? Surgery alone Surgery with post-op radiation Chemotherapy alone Observation with serial imaging Radiation with chemotherapy The correct answer is E. Treatment depends on site and stage: oral cavity → surgery ± post-op radiation; oropharynx → radiation with chemotherapy ; larynx → radiation (surgery + radiation if advanced); neck nodes → surgery and/or radiation. Advanced disease needs multimodality treatment.

A 35-year-old man with a carious lower molar develops a submandibular and parapharyngeal abscess and is taken for incision and drainage. He has no MRSA risk factors and is not immunocompromised. Which empiric IV regimen is most appropriate? Vancomycin alone Ceftriaxone and metronidazole Oral penicillin V Cefazolin alone Piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin The correct answer is B. Deep neck space infections are usually polymicrobial oral flora , aerobes and anaerobes.
