A 19-year-old woman had a sore throat a week ago. She now has fever, rigors and unilateral neck pain, and looks systemically unwell. CT shows thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. Which organism is classically responsible? Streptococcus pyogenes Staphylococcus aureus Fusobacterium necrophorum Pseudomonas aeruginosa Haemophilus influenzae type b The correct answer is C. Lemierre's syndrome is infectious thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically from the oral anaerobe Fusobacterium necrophorum . It is diagnosed on CT, treated with cover for oral flora (the lecture's case: ceftriaxone + metronidazole for 6 weeks), and complic

A 5-year-old has a painless midline neck mass just below the hyoid. It became larger during a recent cold, and it moves upward when he sticks out his tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis? Dermoid cyst Second branchial cleft cyst Lymphatic malformation Thyroglossal duct cyst Thymic cyst The correct answer is D. The thyroglossal duct cyst is 70% of congenital neck cysts, midline , enlarges after a URI and elevates on tongue protrusion , reflecting the thyroid's descent from the foramen cecum. Branchial cleft and thymic cysts are lateral; the case adds that a dermoid usually does not

A 4-year-old has recurrent swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, which flares with colds, and intermittent discharge from a small opening low in the neck. It is not currently infected. What is the definitive management? Incision and drainage of the cyst Serial needle aspiration of the cyst Sclerotherapy injection Prolonged oral antibiotics alone Excision of the whole tract The correct answer is E. This is a second branchial cleft anomaly (>90% of branchial cleft lesions): lateral, recurrent swelling with URIs and discharge from the lower neck. Treatment is complete excision of the sinus and tract . Recurrence is about 3%, rising to about 20% after previous partial exc

A 2-year-old has had 2 days of coryza and a low-grade fever and now has a barking cough and inspiratory stridor at rest with moderate respiratory distress. A neck X-ray shows a steeple sign. What is the most appropriate treatment? Nebulized epinephrine and steroids Rigid bronchoscopy Intubation in the emergency room Cold humidification alone IV antibiotics covering H. influenzae type b The correct answer is A. Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is the most common cause of stridor: viral (parainfluenza, RSV, influenza), 6 months to 3 years, subglottic, with low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor and a barking "seal" cough ; X-ray shows the steeple sign . Mild disease gets hydration and

A 2-year-old boy choked and gagged while eating peanuts yesterday. He is now comfortable, with mildly decreased breath sounds on the right. Inspiratory and expiratory chest X-rays are read as normal. What is the next step? Reassure, since the films are normal Repeat chest X-ray in two weeks Rigid bronchoscopy Flexible nasolaryngoscopy in clinic Trial of an inhaled bronchodilator The correct answer is C. Airway foreign bodies peak at 1-3 years , boys more than girls, and 70-80% are vegetable matter . After the acute choking phase comes an asymptomatic phase while reflexes fatigue, which can last hours to weeks, then complications (obstruction, erosion, infection). The lectur

A 45-year-old woman has a 2 cm thyroid nodule. Her TSH is low. What is the next investigation? Ultrasound-guided FNA biopsy Serum thyroglobulin level CT of the neck with contrast Needle core biopsy of the nodule Radioactive iodine uptake scan The correct answer is E. The lecture's pathway starts with TSH . A low TSH goes to a radioactive iodine uptake scan : a hot (hyperfunctioning) nodule is benign and needs no cytology, so treatment addresses the hyperthyroidism; a cold nodule needs further assessment. A normal or high TSH goes to ultr

A 50-year-old woman has a total thyroidectomy. Several weeks later she has a persistently hoarse, breathy voice. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord does not move. Which nerve was most likely injured? Recurrent laryngeal nerve External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve Hypoglossal nerve Spinal accessory nerve The correct answer is A. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies motor to most of the laryngeal muscles and runs close to the inferior thyroid artery, so thyroidectomy can injure it: unilateral → hoarseness , bilateral → loss of voice / airway obstruction . The right RLN loops the subclavian artery a

A professional singer has a thyroid lobectomy. Afterwards her vocal cords move normally but her voice tires easily and she can no longer reach high notes. Which nerve was most likely injured? Anatomy of the Abdominal Wall & GI Tract A tour of the abdomen from the outside in: wall layers and regions, the peritoneum and its folds, then the vessels, lymphatics and nerves of the gut. The organising idea is embryological origin – it predicts blood supply, drainage and innervation (the pectinate line is the clearest example). Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus. Hesselbach’s triangle = direct hernias. Retroperitoneal organs: SAD PUCKER . Acid-Lowering, Antiemetic & Prokinetic Drugs Three drug families for the upper GI tract. Each class is best learned as which receptor it hits – that predicts its indication and its side effects. PPIs irreversibly inhibit H+/K+-ATPase , take before breakfast, and interact with clopidogrel via CYP2C19 ; long-term: C. difficile, B12, Mg/Ca, fractures. H2-blockers show tachyphylaxis; cimetidine is anti-androgenic and a CYP inhibitor. Antacids : Mg = diarrhea, Al = constipation (CHOPS), CaCO3 = milk-alkali. 5-HT3 antagonists for chemo/post-op N/V; antihistamines for vestibular/pregnancy; metoclopramide crosses the BBB (extrapyramidal), domperidone does not. Mechanisms of mucosal defence Sphincters : keep acid contained in the stomach, protecting the esophagus and intestines Bicarbonate : neutralizes the acid Blood flow : washes away some of the acid that gets into the gastric mucosa Mucus : protective layer over the epithelial cells; protects the gastric mucosa from abrasion Options for ulcer / reflux treatment ↓ gastric secretion by inhibiting histamine receptors and/or the proton pump in parietal cells ↑ mucosal defences with prostaglandin analogues (stimulate mucus and bicarbonate) ↑ tone and esophageal motility ( prokinetics ) Treat H. pylori infection with ABX Treat symptoms by neutralizing acid ( antacids ) and/or drugs that cover and soothe ulcers Acid-lowering drugs – PPIs act on the final common step, so they beat H2-blockers. Diarrhea & Malabsorption Diarrhea is a disturbance of the gut’s water balance. The approach sorts it by duration (acute = infectious, chronic = non-infectious), then blood , then mechanism (osmotic, secretory, inflammatory, motility) – the stool osmotic gap separates the first two. Diarrhea = > 3 BMs/day or > 200 g/day ; acute < 4 weeks. Osmotic gap > 50 = osmotic, < 50 = secretory. Small bowel = large volume, infrequent; large bowel = small volume, urgent. Cholera toxin ↑ cAMP → Cl– secretion. Bloody infectious diarrhea (CC-E-YSS): never give antidiarrheals . In children, oral rehydration is the key treatment. Definitions Normal bowel movements: 3/day to 1 every 3 days ; normal stools are isosmotic Diarrhea : abnormal frequency and liquidity of fecal evacuations – the water balance of the GI tract is disturbed > 3 BMs/day , stool weight > 200 g/day Acute < 4 weeks – usually infectious; chronic > 4 weeks – usually non-infectious First split by duration, then by blood: acute bloody = dysentery; chronic bloody = IBD; chronic non-bloody = IBD, celiac, microscopic colitis. Four pathophysiological mechanisms Mechanism Causes Osmotic : too much water drawn into bowels Ingestion (laxatives), maldigestion (pancreatic insufficiency, disaccharidase deficiency), malabsorption (celiac disease), Toddler’s diarrhea (juice) Inflammatory : damage to mucosal lining Infections, IBD Secretory : increased secretion or inhibited absorption Neuroendocrine tumours (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), cholera, chemical stimulants, hormones (VIP) Motility : rapid gut transit IBS Stool osmotic gap Osmotic gap = 290 – 2([Na+] + [K+]) (stool electrolytes) – measures the difference in solute types between serum and feces. > 50 mOsm/L → osmotic diarrhea < 50 mOsm/L → secretory diarrhea Most diarrheas are a mixture of secretory and osmotic components Where is it coming from? Small bowel Large bowel Volume Large Small Urgency Non-urgent Urgent Frequency Infrequent Frequent Diarrhea workup Hx : nature of diarrhea (acute/chronic, bloody/non-bloody, frequency, steatorrhea), fecal urgency, incontinence, abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, energy level; risk factors (medications/ABX, foreign travel, sick contacts, dietary Hx/water source, ethnicity); extraintestinal manifestations of IBD (mouth ulcers, perianal disease, skin rash, eye symptoms, arthritis) PEx : vital signs (fever, dehydration), weight, nutritional status, abdominal exam Ix : CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, ESR, CRP, lipid profile, glucose, pancreatic enzymes, albumin, blood cultures, AXR; microbiology (stool C&S, stool O&P, C. difficile toxin); α-1 antitrypsin, TTG, sigmoidoscopy Consider admission : severe systemic signs, cannot maintain hydration orally, infants, elderly, immunocompromised Drugs associated with diarrhea Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, alcohol, ABX, antidiabetics, cholinergic agonists, dopamine antagonists, H2-receptor antagonists, immunosuppressants, levothyroxine, laxatives, orlistat (lipase inhibitor), potassium supplements, prostaglandins, SSRIs, sulfasalazine. Non-inflammatory infectious diarrhea Enterotoxin-mediated change in fluid/electrolyte absorption/secretion; small intestine . Vibrio cholerae serotypes O1 and O139 (gram-negative rod): rice-water diarrhea (mechanism below) Tx: oral/IV rehydration, ABX (doxycycline, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin); prevention (sanitation, Dukoral vaccine) Food poisoning : E. coli O157:H7 (verotoxin), S. aureus , Bacillus cereus Watery diarrhea : norovirus, rotavirus, Giardia lamblia , Cryptosporidium , Cyclospora , Cystoisospora belli Inflammatory infectious diarrhea Cytotoxin-mediated destruction/invasion of mucosal cells; large intestine . Abdominal cramping, fever, bloody stools. Bacterial bloody diarrhea (CC-E-YSS) : Clostridium difficile , Campylobacter jejuni (poultry), E. coli O157:H7, Yersinia enterocolitica , Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi (typhoid fever), Shigella dysenteriae ; Vibrio vulnificus Parasitic bloody diarrhea : Entamoeba histolytica , Giardia lamblia Bloody infectious diarrhea NEVER give antidiarrheal agents – they prolong exposure to the organism → toxic megacolon . Malabsorption Inadequate absorption of nutrients from the GI tract – the small bowel is especially important. Constipation & GI Bleeding Two common presentations. Constipation is mostly functional – the job is to recognise the Rome IV pattern and rule out secondary causes. A GI bleed is sorted by the ligament of Treitz (upper vs lower), and in either case you resuscitate before you scope . Rome IV: ≥ 2 of 6 features, 3 months, onset ≥ 6 months . Laxatives do not cause a lazy colon; fibre alone does not treat pediatric functional constipation. Upper GI bleed = proximal to Treitz (hematemesis, melena, ↑ BUN:Cr). Variceal bleed: PPI + octreotide + ABX (mortality benefit) + banding . Unstable hematochezia → upper endoscopy first. Rome IV criteria – functional constipation Must include ≥ 2 of the following: Straining in > 25% of defecations Lumpy or hard stools ( Bristol 1 or 2 ) in > 25% of defecations Sensation of incomplete evacuation in > 25% of defecations Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage in > 25% of defecations Manual maneuvers to facilitate > 25% of defecations (digital evacuation, support of the pelvic floor) < 3 spontaneous BMs per week Plus: Loose stools rarely present without laxatives Insufficient criteria for IBS Criteria fulfilled for the last 3 months with symptom onset ≥ 6 months before Dx Bristol stool chart: types 1–2 = constipation (the Rome IV criterion), 3–4 = normal, 6–7 = diarrhea. Causes of constipation Type Causes Primary (most common) Functional/idiopathic constipation , slow transit Secondary (rule out) Metabolic : hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, diabetes Structural : colorectal cancer, benign strictures, pseudo-obstruction Neurologic / myopathies : Parkinson’s disease, MS, spinal cord injury, autonomic neuropathy, Hirschsprung’s, immobility, botulism, hollow visceral myopathy, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy Medications : opiates, anticholinergics, calcium (antacids), iron supplements, antiparkinsonian drugs (dopamine), lead toxicity Systemic : trisomy 21, cystic fibrosis, connective tissue disorders, celiac disease, cow’s milk allergy Defecatory disorders (involve GI/general surgery) Anismus : the paradoxical contraction of the anal sphincter rather than relaxing during attempted defecation Dyssynergia : any disturbance of muscular coordination, resulting in uncoordinated and abrupt movements Rectocele : a bulging of the front wall of the rectum into the back wall of the vagina Constipation workup Hx : symptoms, dietary Hx (fibre/water), adequate time for toileting, willingness to use public bathrooms, PMHx (look for 2° causes), medications, allergies, social Hx (ADLs, IADLs, abuse) PEx : DRE – inspect for anal fissures/hemorrhoids/soiling, anal tone at rest and with squeeze, palpate for rectal mass, exclude fecal impaction Ix : CBC, calcium, TSH; colonoscopy for red flags Colon transit study : 24 radio-opaque Sitz markers swallowed on day 1; AXR on day 5 Anorectal manometry + balloon expulsion : pressure catheter and balloon in the rectum measure rectal sensation, anal pressure, anorectal inhibitory reflex and ability to expel the balloon Defecating proctogram : barium instilled into the rectum, then defecation on a commode under x-ray – shows anatomic abnormalities Treatment Patient education; IBD, Colorectal Cancer & Liver Disease Three linked topics: chronic inflammatory bowel disease, the colorectal cancer it can lead to (and how we screen for it), and liver disease from acute hepatitis through cirrhosis. The thread through the liver half is the injury → fibrosis → cirrhosis progression and the tests that tell you where a patient sits on it. Crohn = skip lesions, transmural, granulomas; UC = continuous, mucosal, no granulomas, colectomy curative. Average-risk CRC screening: FIT q2y age 50–74 ; never FIT a symptomatic patient; test every CRC for Lynch. HBV: HBsAg = infection, anti-HBs = immunity, IgM anti-HBc = acute . Acetaminophen toxicity is NAPQI after GSH runs out → NAC . SAAG ≥ 11 = portal hypertension. Don’t order ammonia for hepatic encephalopathy. Antidiarrheal Drugs & GI Pearls Antidiarrheals either slow the gut (opioid agonists) or reduce secretion (bismuth, bile acid resins). The second half is a set of daily GI clinical pearls that recur across the block. Loperamide is OTC with poor CNS entry; diphenoxylate contains atropine to deter overdose; eluxadoline spasms the sphincter of Oddi. Bismuth blackens stools and tongue. Bile acid resins: separate other drugs by 1 h before / 4 h after. Pearls: always order IgA with TTG ; use ferritin, not serum iron ; resuscitate before scoping a GI bleed; don’t use ammonia for hepatic encephalopathy. Drug targets in the upper GI tract The parietal cell integrates three stimulants – ACh (M3), gastrin (CCK-B) and histamine (H2) – and two brakes – somatostatin and prostaglandins – onto one final step, the H+/K+-ATPase. Each drug class blocks a different point. Where acid-suppressing drugs act: atropine at M3, H2 blockers at H2, PPIs at the H+/K+-ATPase, antacids in the lumen; misoprostol, sucralfate and bismuth protect the mucosa. Emetic pathways and the antiemetic that blocks each: H1 antagonists for vestibular input, 5-HT3 and D2 antagonists at the chemoreceptor trigger zone and gut, NK1 antagonists for delayed CINV. GI Histology & Physiology The structure and function of the digestive tract: segment histology, the hepatic lobule, then how food is moved (motility), acid is controlled, and nutrients, water, bilirubin and bile are handled. The organising idea is that every secretion and movement is regulated by the same few signals – ACh, gastrin, histamine, somatostatin, CCK and secretin. Jejunum : long vasa recta, few large arcades, tall plicae; ileum : Peyer patches, short vasa recta, more mesenteric fat. Zone III is hit first by ischemia and alcohol; zone I by viral hepatitis. MMCs are driven by motilin during fasting. Acid: ACh, gastrin, histamine ↑; somatostatin, prostaglandins ↓ . Lipids bypass the liver via lacteals; B12 needs IF in the terminal ileum . Trypsin activates the other zymogens. Histology of the digestive tract – the jejunum vs ileum distinction is a classic. Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding epithelial cells of the stomach lining Parietal cells secrete HCl Mucus cells secrete intrinsic factor Chief cells secrete pepsinogen D-cells secrete somatostatin The correct answer is B. Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor. Mucus cells primarily secrete mucus and bicarbonate.

You find yourself in a state of panic and your sympathetic nervous system is taking over. Which of the following actions describe the correct physiology in this state? Your sympathetic nervous system releases norepinephrine which increases motility and secretion of the GI tract Your sympathetic nervous system releases acetylcholine which increases motility and secretion of the GI tract Your sympathetic nervous system releases acetylcholine which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract Your sympathetic nervous system releases substance P which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract Your sympathetic nervous system releases norepinephrine which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract The correct answer is E. The sympathetic system releases norepinephrine which in turn decreases motility, secretions, blood flow, and delays gastric emptying. In a relaxed state the parasympathetic system relies on acetylcholine to increase motility and secretion to process food throughout the GI tr

Several different hormones affect secretion and motility within the gastrointestinal tract. Which statement below is true? Cholecystokinin reduces the rate of emptying of the stomach. Motilin reduces motility within the digestive tract. Gastrin reduces the secretion of gastric acid in the stomach. Secretin reduces the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas. The correct answer is A. Cholecystokinin is a hormone that induces the pancreas to secrete digestive enzymes, and the stomach to reduce the rate of emptying. Which statement below correctly identifies the substance that an epithelial cell secretes into the lumen of the GI tract? Parietal cells secrete mucus into the stomach Goblet cells secrete mucus into the small intestines Paneth cells secrete serotonin into the small intestines Chief cells secrete trypsinogen into the stomach The correct answer is B. Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factors. Goblet cells secrete mucus into the small intestine. Paneth cells secrete antibacterial factors into the small intestine (enteroendocrine cells secrete serotonin into the small intestines). Chief cells secrete pepsinogen into

Which of the following hormones have a stimulatory effect on the intestinal motility but an inhibitory effect on stomach motility? Cholecystokinin Acetylcholine Norepinephrine Secretin Gastrin The correct answer is A. CCK is a hormone which is secreted in the duodenum primarily to stimulate the digestion of fat and protein. It has a stimulatory effect on intestinal motility while having an inhibitory effect on stomach motility by delaying gastric emptying. Acetylcholine, gastrin and serot

Which neurotransmitter or hormone does NOT increase the rate that foodstuffs move through the small and large intestines? Prostaglandin Epinephrine Acetylcholine Serotinin Gastrin The correct answer is B. Epinephrine reduces contraction in the small and large intestines. One helpful way to remember this is that epinephrine is a neurotransmitter associated with the sympathetic nervous system. When the sympathetic nervous system is activated, the body enters fight-orflight mode

Choose the correct sentence in relation to the anal sphincter The internal anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under autonomous control. The internal anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under somatic control. The external anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under autonomous control. The external anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under somatic control. The correct answer is D. The internal anal sphincter is an involuntary muscle, under autonomous control. The external anal sphincter is under somatic control and is therefore voluntary.

A patient with suspected oropharyngeal dysphagia is referred by their family physician to an otolaryngologist for further assessment. Which of the following concerns is the most concerning/necessary to workup during an assessment? Pharyngeal neoplasms Aspiration risk Infection in pharyngeal spaces Regurgitation The correct answer is B. The primary reason for a workup is to assess the risk of Aspiration, as aspirated food items can be immediately life threatening.

Which symptom is associated with functional oropharyngeal dysphagia? Weight gain Pneumonia Dry mouth Feeling of food stuck in the chest Reduced meal duration The correct answer is B. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is associated with drooling, food sticking in throat, weight loss, and increased meal duration. Food lodged in the throat presents an aspiration risk, which can lead to pneumonia.

Which of the following questions would you ask a patient with dysphagia to best distinguish oropharyngeal dysphagia from esophageal dysphagia? Do you have difficulty initiating swallowing or after the action of swallowing? Do you have difficulty swallowing solid and liquid foods or just solid foods? Have you encountered any new lumps or bumps in your oral or neck region? Is the difficulty swallowing progressive or intermittent? The correct answer is A. Esophageal dysphagia is primarily characterized by difficulty swallowing after the initiation of swallowing initiated in the oropharyngeal section. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is characterized by difficulty with the initiation of swallowing. Patients with esophageal dysphagia wi

A patient presents to your clinic with dysphagia, odynophagia and acid reflux. A swallow test administered by a speech pathologist reveals the patient has difficulty and pain swallowing both solid and liquid food. Further investigation with high resolution esophageal manometry reveals low to no tonic contractions in the lower esophageal sphincter. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely? Distal esophageal spasm Jackhammer esophagus Esophageal cancer Peptic Stricture The correct answer is C. Difficulty swallowing liquids and solids suggest a motility issue over a mechanical issue that might come from a peptic structure or esophageal cancer. The high-resolution esophageal manometry scan measures pressure in the esophagus and acts as a surrogate to measure muscle

Use the following stem to answer the next TWO Questions . You are a third-year clerk interviewing a patient during your family medicine rotation. Mr. Wiggum, a 53-year-old police officer, is concerned about some difficulty swallowing. He reports that both foods and liquids feel like they get stuck in his chest, and that this has been fairly constant over the past 4 years. Upon questioning, he admits that he rarely experiences associated heartburn or chest pain, and that his symptoms are worse at night. Of these options, what is the most likely diagnosis? Peptic stricture Adenocarcinoma Esophageal achalasia Scleroderma Jackhammer esophagus The correct answer is C. Dysphagia of solids and liquids indicates a motility issue, and the onset of four years indicates a progressive nature. This could be scleroderma or achalasia. The patient reports no heartburn and nocturnal symptoms, characteristic of achalasia. Presence of heartburn could b

Use the following stem to answer the next TWO Questions . You are a third-year clerk interviewing a patient during your family medicine rotation. Mr. Wiggum, a 53-year-old police officer, is concerned about some difficulty swallowing. He reports that both foods and liquids feel like they get stuck in his chest, and that this has been fairly constant over the past 4 years. Upon questioning, he admits that he rarely experiences associated heartburn or chest pain, and that his symptoms are worse at night. Which test would you order next to confirm Mr.Wiggum’s presumed diagnosis? High resolution esophageal manometry Exploratory surgery Biopsy of the affected esophagus Barium swallow and X-ray No other tests needed – can be diagnosed clinically The correct answer is A. Motility issues such as this (where both solids and liquids are affected) are best diagnosed with high resolution esophageal manometry. Mechanical issues (where solid foods only are affected) are best diagnosed with a barium swallow and X-ray, or endoscopy.

Adenocarcinoma of the esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD. Robert is a 59-yearold lawyer with recently diagnosed adenocarcinoma. Which treatment option is NOT an effective treatment for Robert’s esophageal adenocarcinoma? Aggressive anti-reflux therapy Esophagectomy of the offending tissue Systemic chemotherapy Radiation therapy The correct answer is A. Anti-reflux therapy is a treatment for GERD to prevent progression to Barrett’s esophagus and adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. Robert already has adenocarcinoma; antireflux therapy will not treat Robert’s cancer.

A 5-year-old child is examined by their physician which reveals hepatomegaly. A request for initial imaging is made. You can immediately tell the child is very nervous at the prospect of imaging by their constant fidgeting. Which of the following initial imaging modalities are best suited to examine the child's liver? Ultrasound X-ray MRI CT The correct answer is A. Given the child’s young age, ionizing radiation should be avoided if possible as younger patients have increased life-long risk of developing cancer due to ionizing radiation exposure. Giannina is a 25-year-old who is concerned about a progressively worse sense of constipation which is not relieved with over-the-counter laxatives. Her family physician suspects a bowel obstruction. Considering her presentation and age, what is the best imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis? Ultrasound Abdominal X-ray CT Scan MRI The correct answer is B. Abdominal X-rays are effective in diagnosing bowel obstructions. A CT-scan would also confirm the diagnosis, but as a young patient, Giannina should avoid the large amounts of radiation from a CT scan.

Damian is a 27-year-old who presents to the emergency room with acute epigastric pain consistent with cholelithiasis (gallstones). Which imaging modality should the physician order to confirm the diagnosis? Ultrasound Abdominal X-ray CT scan MRI The correct answer is A. Ultrasound as an imaging modality is effective at diagnosing solid structures, such as gallstones. This imaging modality does not expose the patient to radiation.

Identify the structure of the GI tract that is properly matched with its arterial blood supply. Which statement on the development of the GI tract is true? A surgeon is performing an appendectomy, which requires him to make an incision through the abdominal wall to remove the inflamed appendix. Which statement below is true? The most superficial muscle layer is the external oblique, the middle muscle layer is the transverse abdominis, and the deepest muscle layer is the internal oblique. An investing fascia surrounds each muscle layer of the abdominal wall. The deep-most layer of the abdominal wall is the extraperitoneal fat layer. Following the surgery, the surgeon will likely insert surgical sutures (stitches) in the Camper’s fascia. The correct answer is B. Each abdominal wall muscle (external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis from most superficial to most deep) contains its own investing fascia. Choose the correct statement below pertaining to the rectus abdominis. Superior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is enveloped by the internal obliques Superior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is deep to the transverse abdominis. Inferior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is enveloped by the external obliques. Inferior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is deep to the transversalis fascia. The correct answer is A. Superior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is found within the internal obliques. Inferior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is deep to the transverse abdominis.

Either before or slightly after birth, the testes have reached their final location. Choose the one incorrect statement regarding descent of the testes. The testes descend as a result of the gubernaculum shortening. The spermatic cord contains the testicular artery, testicular vein, and the vas deferens The layers surrounding the testes contain fascia originating from the external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis muscles During descent, the testes pass through the inguinal canal. The correct answer is C. During the descent of the kidneys, the gubernaculum shortens, pulling the testes through the inguinal canal. In doing so, the testes are enveloped by the external oblique and internal oblique muscles, but not the transverse abdominis.

The D cells produce somatostatin, which is primarily released when the stomach contents reach a pH below 3.0, and they have an inhibitory paracrine effect on G cells, ECL cells, and parietal cells to reduce the overall acidity of the stomach. A patient presents to your family clinic concerned about their persistent heartburn for the past two months. Which observation allows for a positive diagnosis of GERD? A patient’s heartburn is not relieved by antacids or PPIs An endoscopy does not show signs of erosion in the patient’s esophagus A 24-hr ambulatory pH monitoring of the patient’s esophagus indicating persistent pH values of 4 or less A patient points to the center of their chest and claims there’s a burning sensation The correct answer is C. This 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring showing esophageal pH below 4 indicates gastric acid entering the esophagus (although it would typically be used by patients who have failed a PPI trial). GERD can be erosive; however, 70% of GERD cases are nonerosive. Ordinarily, GERD i

Which of the following options would NOT be part of a potential management plan for a patient with chronic GERD? Nissen fundoplication Famotidine or pantoprazole Alcohol and smoking cessation, diet modification Esophageal dilatation Endoscopic screening for Barrett’s esophagus The correct answer is D. In GERD, stomach acid travels superiorly from the stomach to the esophagus, in part because of a dilated lower-esophageal sphincter. Dilatating the esophageal sphincter would exacerbate the patient’s symptoms of GERD.

Which of the following signs and symptoms would be the largest concern for malignancy in a patient with a gastric ulcer? A biopsy of the ulcer reveals a round, flat and “punched out” ulcerating region of the stomach A biopsy reveals the ulcer has raised edges and is an oval appearance Microscopic analysis of the tissue reveals erosion of the submucosa and the muscularis mucosa as well The patient experiences symptoms of hemorrhage, regurgitation and radiating back pain The correct answer is B. Some gastric ulcers may be ulcerating cancers. An endoscopy of the ulcer that reveals an oval appearance, with irregular edges, raised edges, and gastric folds that don’t radiate to the edge indicates an ulcerating cancer. Which of the following medications would you likely prescribe this patient for his intermittent GERD? H2 receptor antagonists Antacids Proton pump inhibitors Warfarin The correct answer is B. Antacids are likely the best choice for this patient. Antacids are fast acting and provide symptomatic relief, used in uncomplicated symptoms. There are several classes of drugs that are used to reduce the acidity in the stomach. Which statement below is true? Antacids are safe for long-term use with minimal side effects or adverse drug reactions Prostaglandins reduce the acidity in the stomach by inhibiting proton pumps in the mucosa H2 receptor antagonists are the most appropriate prescription for the elderly population PPIs irreversibly inhibit active transport of protons into the lumen of the stomach The correct answer is D. This is the mechanism of action of PPIs. Antacids can have many side effects depending on their composition, from diarrhea to constipation, to drug-drug interactions, etc. Prostaglandins increase the amount of mucus present, protecting the mucosa from stomach acid. For a patient with idiopathic gastroparesis leading to chronic nausea and vomiting, which option below would NOT be a suitable recommendation for treatment? Have more frequent, but smaller meals Reduce pop and alcohol in the diet Avoid the use of antiemetic drugs due to the rebound effect Avoid smoking The correct answer is C. For patients with gastroparesis, the patient should be educated on having smaller, more frequent meals, reducing pop and alcohol, ceasing smoking, maintaining tight sugar control. To treat the associated symptoms of nausea, antiemetics are prescribed.

Eight weeks ago, Regis was diagnosed with a gastric ulcer. Since then, he has been taking his antibiotic medications to treat the underlying bacterial cause. Today, you are working for a gastroenterologist who has asked you to perform a test to confirm that all of the bacteria has been eradicated. Which test result would indicate an abated infection and would fit with Regis’s history? Negative H. pylori IgG serology test Negative urease breath test Negative esophagogastroduodenoscopy Negative Gram-stain test The correct answer is B. If Regis had an ulcer caused by H. pylori, even if the bacteria was eradicated, the H. pylori IgG serology test would be positive. Rather, to confirm eradication of the bacterial, a urease breath test should be performed. If negative, it means the infection has subsided.

54-year-old Taylor arrives at your clinic. She describes how she recently started playing spike ball and has been enjoying it, but this activity is always accompanied by feelings of nausea. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate for Taylor? 5HT3-receptor antagonists D2 antagonists Antihistamines Cannabinoids The correct answer is C. Antihistamines (Histamine H1 antagonists) are primarily useful for motion sickness as they act on the vestibular afferents and within the brainstem. 5HT3 receptor antagonists are primarilyused for chemotherapy-induced nausea and post-operative nausea. Which of the following enzymes are responsible for the breakdown of disaccharides into monosaccharaides? Salivary amylase Pancreatic amylase Gastric amylase Brush-border amylase The correct answer is D. Brush-border enzymes break down disaccharides into monosaccharides. Salivary amylase is secreted in the mouth and breakdown starch into oligosaccharides. At the level of the small intestine pancreatic amylase breaks down oligosaccharides into disaccharides.

Five years ago, Gerry had an operation to remove a large portion of his ileum. What are some expected sequelae to this surgical resection? Select all that apply. Fatty, greasy stools Hypernatremia Increased polysaccharide content in the stool Increased reabsorption of bile salts The correct answer is A. Bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum, along with other fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) and Vitamin B12. With a resected ileum, Gerry will have reduced bile salt reabsorption, and consequently, fatty stool, called steatorrhea.

Which of the following treatment strategies is generally indicated in most cases of infectious diarrhea? Alejandro came to the emergency department with acute diarrhea, that began shortly after a barbecue yesterday. He’s worried that he caught food poisoning from some uncooked beef. As the resident emergency doctor, which is NOT one of your next actions? Request stool culture and sensitivity Request stool ova and parasites Prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics Establish IV access for rehydration The correct answer is C. In this presentation, the clinical suspicion for an E. coli infection is high, particularly due to the risk of eating uncooked beef. In such cases, antibiotics should be avoided, as this can exacerbate hemolytic uremic syndrome.

A patient presents with bloody diarrhea following a 2-week course of clindamycin to treat bacterial pneumonia. A stool culture tests positive for C. difficile . She is 34 years old and is stable. What are the next steps for this patient? Antimotility agents for symptom relief Prescribe vancomycin for the C. difficile infection Admit to the hospital, refer to gastroenterologist Refer to surgery for resection of the offending area The correct answer is B. For C. difficile infections, vancomycin is a good empiric therapy. C. difficile infections are often the result of an antibiotic course of clindamycin. A gastroenterologist may be consulted; however the patient should receive antibiotics for the C. difficile infection immedi

Which of the following patients with a history of constipation would NOT be indicated for a colonoscopy? A 65-year-old patient A 55-year-old patient with bloody stool A 45-year-old patient with hypercalcemia A 35-year-old patient with unexplained weight loss The correct answer is C. A colonoscopy for the investigation of constipation should be avoided in patients under the age of 50, unless the patient has red flags such as bloody stool, anemia, weight loss, sudden change in bowel habits or a familiar history of colon cancer.

Which of the following is NOT an appropriate first-line treatment option for a patient with constipation? An increase in dietary fiber PEG 3350 Lactulose Docusate The correct answer is D. Docusate is stool softener that is generally not recommended due to the lack of evidence for its efficacy. There is low quality evidence for increasing dietary intake and it’s an inexpensive option for many patients. PEG3350 and Lactulose (not PEGLYTE) are both osmotic laxat

Larry is a 45-year-old who has complaints of constipation. He describes his bowel movements as about once every two days, and nearly all of these require straining. His stool is described as hard and lumpy. He stays hydrated but has a lot of processed foods. His physical exam is relatively unremarkable except reduced bowel sounds. Preliminary blood work is also unremarkable. Based on this presentation, what is the next best recommended treatment for Larry? Choose the best two answers. Colonoscopy Defecating proctogram Prescribe PEG 3350 Anorectal manometry Slowly increasing fiber intake Recommend weekly enemas The correct answer is C, E. Fiber is a good first-line treatment for constipation; patients should be advised to slowly increase fiber in their diet to about 20-30g per day. PEG3350 is an osmotic laxative that retains fluids in the colon and softens stools. Given the lack of any red flags, colonosco

Which of the following drugs is NOT appropriate to prescribe for a patient with constipation? D2 antagonists 5HT4 agonists Macrolide antibiotics Delta-opioid receptor agonists The correct answer is D. Delta opioid receptor agonists is an anti-diarrheal drug which plays a large role in inhibiting motility which could further worsen motility in a patient with constipation.

Archie is a 43-year-old who arrived at his family doctor seeking medications for his ongoing diarrhea. A gastrointestinal infection has already been ruled out. Archie has a past medical history of narcotic abuse, for which he is currently in recovery. He also takes medications throughout the day to manage his bipolarism. Which medication would you recommend? Select TWO answers. None – advise Archie to drink less water Domperidone (dopamine receptor antagonist) Erythromycin (a macrolide antibiotic) Loperamide (opioid antagonist) Diphenoxylate (opioid antagonist) Cholestyramine (a resin) Pepto-Bismol (a bismuth compound) The correct answer is D, G. Diarrhea is rarely caused by too much water consumption, so A is not correct. Domperidone and Erythromycin are prokinetics - these would not help the diarrhea but make it worse! Both loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioid antagonists, but diphenoxylate has abuse potentia

You suspect one of your patients has irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following initial investigations is NOT appropriate for this patient? Complete blood count Fecal occult blood (stool test) Psychological assessment IgG Food sensitivity Colonoscopy The correct answer is D. The IgG Food sensitivity test has been widely debunked and should not part of the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected IBS. IgG production is a normal immune response to food. A fecal Occult Blood stool test can be used to detect the microscopic presence of blood i

Which of the following signs/symptoms in a patient is necessary for the diagnosis of functional dyspepsia? Pain in the upper part of the abdomen (epigastric pain) Early satiety Negative endoscopy Positive serology for H. pylori The correct answer is C. Functional Dyspepsia is dyspepsia (pain in the upper abdomen) with no evidence of organic disease. Patients can present with postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric pain or burning, however all pains must have a negative endoscopy excluding any structural diseases t

Which patient below satisfies the Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome? Anthony, who has had two months of abdominal pain associated with defecation with an increase in stool frequency Bertha, who has had constipation about twice per week, and has 6 months of continuous abdominal pain regardless of her state of constipation Christopher, who for the past six months has had unbearably painful bowel movements and has noticed streaks of blood upon wiping. All of the above None of the above The correct answer is E. For IBS according to the Rome IV Criteria, a patient requires having three months of recurrent abdominal pain, and two of: 1) the abdominal pain is related to defecation; 2) a change in stool frequency; and 3) a change in stool appearance. You are a rural family doctor seeing a new patient, Eric, who has recently moved to your small town in Northern Ontario. Shortly before Eric moved, he was diagnosed with dyspepsia but was unable to discuss treatment options. Which options below would NOT be appropriate for Eric’s management for dyspepsia? Consider antibiotics to treat a possible H. pylori infection Council the patient on diet modification Council the patient on exercise reduction to reduce exacerbation of symptoms Assess Eric’s psychosocial status and consider prescribing antidepressants The correct answer is C. Non-pharmacological treatments of dyspepsia can include lifestyle changes such as improving one’s diet and increasing exercise. Dyspepsia can be caused by an H. pylori infection or by psychosocial factors: antibiotics or antidepressants may be valuable depending on the under

A patient arrives at your clinic with concerns of dysphagia, fatigue and weight loss. The patient has previously been diagnosed with GERD. After a thorough history and physical this prompts investigation with endoscopy which reveals an abnormality in the lining of the distal esophagus. Which of the following cancerous tissues is most likely? Squamous cell carcinoma Adenocarcinoma Neuroendocrine tumor Lymphoma The correct answer is B. Esophageal neoplasms tend to be mostly adenocarcinomas in the west. It’s possible the patient’s GERD may have led to metaplasia of the distal esophageal tissue (Barrett’s esophagus) which may have developed into an adenocarcinoma. A 50-year-old patient presents to your clinic for a colonoscopy after concerns for rectal bleeding and alternating diarrhea and constipation. Lesions were found on the descending colon. Which of the following statements is correct? The lesions were likely colorectal polyps and treatment involves surgical removal The lesions were likely colorectal polyps and treatment involves medical therapy The lesions were likely serrated adenomas and treatment involves surgical removal The lesions were likely serrated adenomas and treatment involves medical therapy The correct answer is A. These lesions are likely colorectal polyps as serrated adenomas tend to be more common on the right side (ascending colon). Colorectal cancer is largely preventable through early screening and treatment involves surgical removal of the polyps.

A 50-year-old patient with chronic GERD is struggling to afford his pantoprazole prescription and asks you if there will be long tern complications if he doesn’t take his medication. What do you say to him? No, you may have long-term epigastric discomfort but will otherwise be fine. Chronic GERD could lead to Barrett’s esophagus, which can lead to esophageal cancer. Chronic GERD could lead to adenocarcinoma, which could lead to Barrett’s esophagus. Chronic GERD could lead to irritable bowel syndrome if left unchecked. The correct answer is B. GERD can have very severe consequences if untreated, including esophageal cancer (adenocarcinoma). If he cannot afford pantoprazole, perhaps there is a cheaper PPI available that would help with his symptoms, or perhaps the patient qualifies for social supports to help fund

Chadwick Boseman was an American actor who played King T’Challa in Marvel’s Black Panther . In 2020, at the age of 43, Boseman passed away from stage 4 colon cancer. Which statement regarding colon cancer is true? Stage 4 indicates that the cancer has spread to the fat surrounding the colon but not yet the serosa Colorectal cancers most commonly arise from colitis, although colorectal polyps can also cause colorectal cancers “Right-sided” colon cancer presents with rectal bleeding and a mass on digital rectal exam Diagnosis can be made with colonoscopy and biopsy but staging requires X-ray and CT of the chest and abdomen The correct answer is D. Stage 4 colorectal cancer indicates that the cancer has spread to the serosa. Almost all colorectal cancers arise from polyps. Lastly, left-sided colorectal cancer presents with rectal bleeding and a mass on DRE, whereas right-sided colorectal cancer presents with anemia and

Which of the following features is NOT a characteristic of ulcerative colitis? Shallow ulcers Inflammation at the level of the mucosa Sporadic lesions throughout the bowel Absence of granulomas The correct answer is C. Ulcerative Colitis is characterized by lesions which begin at the rectum and extend to the proximal end of the bowel. Patchy skip lesions occur intermittently throughout the colon.

Which of the following treatments is the best intervention for colonic stricture resulting from Crohn's Disease? Endoscopic balloon dilatation NSAIDs Corticosteroids Surgical resection The correct answer is A. Endoscopic balloon dilation is the most common treatment for colonic strictures, to dilate the colon. Patient’s may have to do this routinely. Surgical resections are only indicated in the most severe cases due to the risk of contributing to malabsorption.

A patient with a 3-week history of bloody diarrhea presents to your clinic. The physician suspects the patient has Ulcerative Colitis and is starting their diagnostic workup. Which of the following is not an appropriate initial investigation for the workup of Ulcerative Colitis? Colonoscopy Sigmoidoscopy Stool culture and sensitivity Fecal calprotectin The correct answer is B. Ulcerative Colitis is characterized by lesions that begin at the rectum and extend proximally, thus as an initial investigation only a sigmoidoscopy may be recommended. A colonoscopy is associated with greater risks and is generally done at a later stage to determine the ext

Ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (DC) are two forms of inflammatory bowel disease. Which statement below is true? CD is more likely to be continuous whereas UC is patchy. UC occurs mainly in the left large bowel; CD occurs mainly in the right large bowel. Fecal calprotectin will be elevated in patients with UC but not with CD. None of the above statements are true The correct answer is D. Ulcerative colitis is a continuous inflammation of the large bowel Crohn’s disease is a discontinuous inflammation of the entire GI tract (“gum-to-bum”). Both are inflammatory diseases, and blood tests for both will indicate elevated fecal calprotectin. None of the answers a

A patient presents to his family doctor with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Suspecting inflammatory bowel disease, the physician orders a colonoscopy and biopsy of the various locations in the large intestine. Which statement of the pathology report or colonoscopy report is most suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis? Pathology report: “There is abnormal mucosal physiology of the ascending colon but normal mucosal physiology of the descending colon.” Pathology report: “Hematoxylin and eosin stain of the tissue sample indicates the presence of granulomas in the mucosa.” Colonoscopy report: “Shallow ulcers line the descending colon leading to the presence of pseudo-polyps.” Colonoscopy report: “The inflamed area is patchy and discontinuous.” The correct answer is C. Ulcerative colitis is a continuous inflammation of the large bowel, beginning at the rectum and spreading proximally up the GI tract - if this was UC and there was abnormal physiology in the ascending colon, there would need to be abnormal physiology in the descending colon,

Ryan was recently diagnosed with mild Crohn’s disease. Which treatment option is most appropriate for Ryan? Ryan should avoid grain and gluten products Ryan should be prescribed budesonide or ASA Ryan should undergo endoscopic balloon dilatation Ryan should undergo surgical resection of the affected area The correct answer is B. For a mild case, Ryan can be prescribed weak anti-inflammatory drugs such as budesonide or ASA. In more severe cases, Ryan may be prescribed prednisone or biological agents. In more severe cases, balloon dilatation or surgical resection could also be warranted.

A patient presents to your clinic with rectal bleeding that has been ongoing for the past two days. An initial history shows that the patient has been losing a significant amount of blood over the past few days and a CBC shows the patient has become anemic. Which of the following interventional strategies is appropriate? Colonoscopy Endoscopy RBC scan Angiogram The correct answer is D. During an angiogram a catheter is guided into the mesenteric arteries and contrast is injected to examine the location of bleeding. The angiogram also offers therapeutic potential in circumstances where the patient’s vitals are unstable – the site of the blood site can be de

Which statement below on gastrointestinal bleeding is correct? Upper GI bleeds present with melena, whereas lower GI bleeds present with hematochezia The first step in the management for a patient with GI bleeding is to perform an endoscopy and colonoscopy Upper GI bleeds occur proximal to the jejunal-ileal junction, whereas lower GI bleeds occur distal to the jejunal-ileal junction The location of GI bleeding can be deduced at any point in the GI tract via endoscopy or colonoscopy The correct answer is A. Melena (black, tarry stool) is characteristic of an upper GI bleed, occurring proximal to the ligament of Treitz (duodenal-jejunal junction). However, hematochezia (bright red or maroon-colored blood) is characteristic of a lower GI bleed. The first step in any patient with

A patient has presented to the emergency room feeling faint after vomiting blood. What is the most effective treatment for the patient if it is determined that he has ruptured esophageal varices? Pantoloc (PPI), Octreotide and Antibiotic medication followed by an endoscopy Endoscopy positive for esophageal varices followed by Pantoloc (PPI), Octreotide medication Endoscopy positive for esophageal varices followed by Band ligation Pantoloc, Octreotide medication followed by colonoscopy The correct answer is A. The patient’s symptoms, hematemesis and the elevated BUN/creatinine ratio suggest an upper GI bleed. Esophageal variceal bleeding is an urgent condition. The proton pump inhibitors decrease fibrinolysis and stabilize platelet plugs; Octreotide decrease portal flow from the l

Which of the following options best describes the features of the jejunum? Long vasa recta, few arcades with large loops Long vasa recta, many arcades with short loops Short vasa recta, few arcades with large loops Short vasa recta, many arcades with short loops The correct answer is A. The jejunum’s blood supply can be characterized by long vasa recta followed by a few arcades with large loops. The ileum’s blood supply contains short vasa recta with many arcades with short loops.

Which of the following symptoms regarding hemorrhoid are true? Patients are likely to notice internal and external hemorrhoid as they’re both painful Patients are likely to report external hemorrhoid as they can feel it but both internal and external hemorrhoid are painless Both internal and external hemorrhoid can be associated with blood loss and are both painful Both internal and external hemorrhoid are associated with blood loss but only external hemorrhoid are painful The correct answer is D. Internal and external hemorrhoids are both characterized by a thrombus of venous circulation that either occur at the anal opening (external hemorrhoids) or occur inside the anus above the pectinate line (internal hemorrhoids). Due to the location of the internal hemorrhoids

Which of the following methods can be used to correctly differentiate the ileum and jejunum in a cadaver lab? The jejunum receives its blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery, whereas the ileum receives its blood supply from the inferior mesenteric artery The jejunum has more mesenteric fat than the ileum The jejunum has longer vasa recta and larger Arcades loops The jejunum is the location of Meckel’s diverticulum The jejunum is peritoneal whereas the ileum is retroperitoneal The correct answer is C. The jejunum and ileum both receive their blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery. The ileum has more mesenteric fat than the jejunum. Meckel’s diverticulum occurs in the ileum, about 2-feet proximal to the ileal-cecal junction. Both the jejunum and ileum are periton

A patient has a complete occlusion of their right colic artery, an artery that supplies blood to part of the large intestine. Which statement is true? The patient is highly at risk of developing ischemic bowel syndrome The patient will require endovascular surgery to restore blood flow to the transverse colon The patient’s ascending colon will be supplied fresh blood by the middle colic artery and the marginal artery The life-threatening condition requires immediate colectomy The correct answer is C. The arteries that supply the large intestine anastomose at the marginal artery (of Drummond). If the right colic artery was occluded, the ascending colon would receive blood from other colic arteries.

A. patient presents to his family doctor with constipation and an associated painful anal sphincter. Upon wiping, there are streaks of bright red blood. What type of hemorrhoid would lead to this presentation and why? Internal hemorrhoids, because of the presence of pain External hemorrhoids, because these are innervated by visceral sensory fibers Internal hemorrhoids, because the blood is bright red instead of dark red External hemorrhoids, because of their presence below the pectinate line The correct answer is D. External hemorrhoids are hemorrhoids situated below the pectinate line. These are innervated by somatic sensory fibers and a patient with external hemorrhoids will feel pain.

John is a 56-year-old man, who presents to his family doctor with concerns about colon cancer. He doesn’t report any symptoms and appears to be very healthy, but he started to worry incessantly after his brother was recently diagnosed with colon cancer. John has never had any screening for colorectal cancer in the past. Which of the following tests is most appropriate? Fecal immunochemical test Flexible sigmoidoscopy Colonoscopy CT colonoscopy The correct answer is C. John is at a greater risk for colorectal cancer than the average population due to a firstdegree relative having colon cancer. John should be referred to do a colonoscopy (the “gold standard”) as opposed to a FIT test which the average risk patient does.

Which of the following options regarding colorectal screening is correct? Colonoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy both require sedation and intensive preparation Patients who screen positive on a flexible sigmoidoscopy require a follow-up colonoscopy The feces sample from a FIT test primarily looks for microscopic cancerous tissue Average risk patients above the age of 50 are offered a colonoscopy every 2 years The correct answer is B. Flexible sigmoidoscopy requires significantly less preparation (an enema the morning of and no sedation) relative to a colonoscopy. Patients who screen positive on a FS must do a colonoscopy to remove all polyps in the distal parts of the colon, which the FS cannot reach. Th

Marc is a 44-year-old patient from northern Ontario. As part of your family medicine residency, you are performing a rotation in Marc’s isolated town. You learn from Marc that his father died of colorectal cancer at the age of 53. His health history is highly suggestive of Crohn’s disease lasting several years, and you are awaiting for some bloodwork to confirm the diagnosis. Given Marc’s family history and positive diagnosis of Crohn’s, what will you recommend for Marc in terms of screening for colorectal cancer? Marc should perform a FIT test every two years once he turns 50. Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every five years effective immediately Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every two years effective immediately. Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every two years that include biopsies effective immediately The correct answer is D. Marc would be considered high risk for colorectal cancer with a first-degree family member having had colorectal cancer. His screening should involve a colonoscopy every two years, with occasional biopsies, beginning ten years earlier than the age of diagnosis of his family

Which of the following options describes the blood supply and structure of a hepatic lobule? The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic bile duct, hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the hepatic vein The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic artery, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the bile duct, hepatic portal vein and hepatic vein The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic vein, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the bile duct, hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic vein and hepatic portal vein, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the bile duct and hepatic artery The correct answer is C. Each hepatic lobule is roughly hexagonal in shape. The corners of the lobule contain a branch of the hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein and bile duct, while the center of the lobule contains the hepatic vein.

In portal hypertension large volumes of venous blood flow through the portal-caval anastomoses in other sites of the body to enter systemic circulation, leading to the development of varicose veins and other site-specific pathologies. Which of the following pathologies are you NOT likely to see in a patient with portal hypertension? Select two options. Internal hemorrhoids External hemorrhoids Varicose paraumbilical veins (caput medusae) Esophageal varices Right ventricular hypertrophy The correct answer is B, E. External hemorrhoids are not likely because the venous blood supply for this region (below the pectinate line) does not course through the portal system. A surgeon is trying to clamp the most proximal portion of the artery that supplies the gallbladder. Where should the physician look to clamp this artery? Inside the triangle of Calot, along the hepatic artery At the porta hepatis at the common hepatic artery At the porta hepatis at the proper hepatic artery At hepatoduodenal ligament at the proper hepatic artery The correct answer is A. The cystic artery (stems of the right hepatic artery) and lies within the triangle of Calot. The borders of the triangle of Calot are the liver, the cystic duct, and the common hepatic duct.

The gallbladder’s purpose is to both store and concentrate bile. Beginning in the gallbladder, what is the order of structures that bile passes through before entering the duodenum? Cystic duct -> common bile duct -> common hepatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi Common bile duct -> cystic duct -> common hepatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi Cystic duct -> common bile duct -> pancreatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi Cystic duct -> common hepatic duct -> pancreatic duct -> ampulla of Vater The correct answer is C. From the gallbladder, bile traverses the cystic duct followed by the common bile duct. The common bile duct meets with the pancreatic duct, and bile is secreted into the duodenum through the ampulla of Vater. The rate of secretion is controlled by the sphincter of Oddi.

A pregnant patient receives some bloodwork indicating elevated levels of fractionated ALP. Based on her presentation of symptoms, the physician is concerned about the possibility of bile duct obstruction. Which of the following imaging modalities is appropriate to evaluate this patient? Ultrasound CT Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography The correct answer is A. Ultrasound is the initial modality of choice in patients with suspected biliary tract obstructions. CT and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is contraindicated in pregnant patients.

If the ultrasound of the liver is unable to detect any ductal dilations or abnormalities in the hepatobiliary tract, then the physician should screen for Primary Biliary Cholangitis by assessing the patient’s anti-mitochondrial antibody levels.

Choose the three correct statements pertaining to liver failure. In a patient with liver failure, albumin is increased In a patient with liver failure, albumin is decreased In a patient with liver failure, bilirubin is increased In a patient with liver failure, bilirubin is decreased In a patient with liver failure, INR/PT is increased In a patient with liver failure, INR/PT is decreased The correct answer is B, C, E. Decreased albumin, increased bilirubin, and increased INR/PT are indications of chronic liver disease and liver failure. A 36-year-old patient presents with epigastric pain that radiates to his back. The pain started two months ago. The patient has a history of regular alcohol use (>3 drinks per day) and admits to eating a bit too much fast food. The patient’s blood tests return show elevated ALP and GGT, but normal levels of AST, ALT, albumin, bilirubin, and a normal PT/INR. Based on this presentation, which of these conditions is most likely? Cholelithiasis Budd-Chiari syndrome Alcoholic liver disease Non-alcoholic liver disease The correct answer is A. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GTT) are liver enzymes specific to the bile ducts. A patient comes to your clinic with a fever, general malaise and pain in their upper abdomen that has lasted the past 2 days. The patient describes the onset of symptoms after having sex with a new partner who has Hepatitis A. Which of the following tests should the patient order, and if it comes back positive, what is the likely prognosis? Hepatitis A IgG test, this will likely not lead to a chronic hepatitis Hepatitis A IgG test, this will likely lead to a chronic hepatitis Hepatitis A IgM test, this will likely not lead to a chronic hepatitis Hepatitis A IgM test, this will likely lead to a chronic hepatitis The correct answer is C. The physician should order Hepatitis A IgM levels, as these antibodies are synthesized in the early stages of an infection. IgG antibodies are synthesized as the infection progresses. Hepatitis A usually does not lead to chronic hepatitis.

You are managing a patient with acute hepatitis from Hepatitis B that has recently started antiviral medications. A 45-year-old female is experiencing severe pain in their right lower quadrant region. Which of the following pathologies is least likely given the location of the pain? The sigmoid colon is located in the left lower quadrant and pain would be perceived in that region. The appendix, terminal ileum and a portion of the urinary bladder are all in the right lower quadrant region.

Which of the following pathologies is NOT an urgent medical emergency? Ruptured medical emergency Peritonitis Pancreatitis Pneumothorax The correct answer is C. A ruptured abdominal aneurysm, peritonitis and a pneumothorax are all emergencies which require medical intervention.

Which of the following bowel obstructions likely will NOT need surgical management? A 64-year-old patient was recently admitted to the hospital as an in-patient with diverticulitis. The patient has started empiric antibiotic therapy of cephalosporin and metronidazole. The presence of an abscess makes this a complicated case of diverticulitis. Operation is not indicated for abscesses smaller than 5 cm. Which of these options do not correctly describe its functions? Select a correct statement. Lateral umbilical folds convey patent inferior epigastric vessels; which are active vessels that still provide blood. These inferior epigastric vessels anastomose with superior epigastric vessels.

Which of the following are not true regarding inguinal hernias? Bile salts are recycled at the terminal ileum via the enterohepatic circulation. Mia has recently been diagnosed with inflammation in the terminal ileum. PPIs (Pantoprazole) are good to promote healing of the gastric mucosa. H2 blockers (Cimetidine) are not as efficacious as PPIs. Antacids provide symptom relief but do not heal the ulcer.

Treat with PPI Serology for Helicobacter pylori Continue use of NSAIDs Treat with steroids The correct answer is A, B. If suspicious of peptic ulcer and there are no alarming symptoms requiring endoscopy, treat with PPI and get HP serology. NSAIDs must be stopped.

First line treatment for H pylori is quadruple therapy: PPI + antibiotics.

Which of the following is true regarding treatment of Gastroparesis? A high fiber diet is helpful to move the contents within the GI tract Carbonated beverages help in reducing effects of gastroparesis One should avoid eating frequent, small meals as that would distress the GI tract Tight glucose control for people with diabetes helps progression of gastroparesis The correct answer is D. Gastroparesis treatment includes: low fat, low fiber diet; small frequent meals; avoid carbonated beverages, alcohol, smoking; tight glycemic control in diabetics.

What is NOT an alarm feature of GERD? Dysphagia Melena Iron deficiency anemia Weight loss Dental cavities The correct answer is E. Not an alarm feature but an atypical presentation From the GERD section of the GI summary notes (the alarm-feature list behind 09 - GERD). Alarm features are the ones that raise concern for cancer or a complication and send the patient to endoscopy. The list includes new dys

What is true about investigations for GERD? Endoscopy can rule out GERD Esophageal manometry cannot diagnose a motility disorder. Esophageal manometry can assess LES pressure 24 hr ambulatory pH monitoring does not rule out GERD if normal as GERD Endoscopy is not needed if there is risk factors for Barrett’s esophagus as this condition is diagnosed based on clinical suspicion. The correct answer is C. From 09 - GERD, with 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia. C. True. Esophageal manometry measures esophageal pressures, including LES pressure. It is used in refractory GERD or diagnostic uncertainty. A. False. Endoscopy does NOT diagnose GERD and cannot rule it out: 70% of patients ha

Which organ is NOT intraperitoneal? Spleen Stomach Ileum Descending Colon 1st part of duodenum The correct answer is D. From 08 - Anatomy of the Foregut. The descending colon is retroperitoneal. It is covered by peritoneum only on its front surface and is fixed to the posterior wall, because its mesentery fused with the parietal peritoneum when the gut returned from herniation. The retroperit

During gallbladder removal, a vessel was accidentally cut. Luckily it was not an arterial source. Which blood vessel was most likely cut? Splenic vein Hepatic Portal Vein Superior mesenteric vein Inferior mesenteric vein IVC The correct answer is B. From 08 - Anatomy of the Hepatobiliary & Portal System. The gallbladder lies under the liver and drains through the cystic duct into the structures at the porta hepatis . The hepatic portal vein runs there, beside the common bile duct and the hepatic artery, and enters the l

When is an ultrasound indicated? Assessing full abdomen for fluid in a time intensive setting When assessing someone with a large body habits When evaluating solid organs When needing very good spatial resolution The correct answer is C. From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's first ultrasound indication is evaluating solid organs such as the liver, spleen and kidney, along with fluid-filled structures (gallbladder, biliary tree) and ascites. The pancreas is the exception, because it lies deep behind bowel gas.

What is NOT a sign of a bowel obstruction? String of pearls sign Differential air fluid levels Dilated bowel Air only beyond obstructed segment All of the above are signs of bowel obstructions The correct answer is D. From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's obstruction signs on an abdominal series are dilated bowel, differential air-fluid levels, string of pearls, step-ladder pattern, gasless abdomen, and no air beyond the obstructed segment . D inverts the last sign. Gas cannot pass the bloc

Which of the following is the most common esophageal neoplasm in Western countries? Squamous cell carcinoma Adenocarcinoma Adenoma Squamous cell papilloma The correct answer is B. Adenocarcinoma is the most common esophageal neoplasm in Western countries, and squamous cell carcinoma is the most common for the rest of the world.

Which of the following is false: Squamous cell carcinoma occurs commonly in the distal esophagus and are usually preceded by Barrett’s esophagus Colon cancer arising from the left side are more likely to present with GI symptoms/signs than those arising from the right side. H. Pylori is a major factor for developing gastric cancer Gastric cancers usually presents in the late stage. The correct answer is A. Squamous cell carcinoma occurs commonly in the mid-esophagus and are associated with nutritional deficiencies, environmental carcinogens, smoking and alcohol. The cancer described in A is more consistent with esophageal adenocarcinoma.

A 57 year old female presents to the clinic with long standing diarrhea and RLQ abdominal pain. Investigations reveal that she has transmural inflammation. Which of the following will be least consistent with a suspected Crohn’s disease? Skip lesions throughout the small and large intestines Lesions in the small bowel alone Granulomas Shallow ulcers The correct answer is D. Crohn’s disease is associated with fissuring ulcers. Shallow ulcers are consistent with ulcerative colitis.

What is the first line treatment for severe ulcerative colitis 5-ASA Azathioprine Hydrocortisone Infliximab The correct answer is C. Steroid ( -one s) is the first line treatment for severe ulcerative colitis. 5-ASA is the first line treatment for mild-moderate ulcerative colitis. Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody used to treat Crohn’s disease.

Which one of the following is true regarding the role of treatments in upper GI variceal bleeding: PPIs stabilizes the platelet plug by decreasing fibrinolysis Octreotide decreases peptic enzyme activation, thereby preventing gastric degradation Antibiotics decrease infection-related hospitalization but does not reduce mortality in cirrhotics with GI bleeding. TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) is most effectively indicated in in patients with multiple hepatic cysts. The correct answer is A. Octreotide decreases blood flow. Antibiotics reduces mortality in cirrhotics with GI bleeding. TIPS is contraindicated in patients with multiple hepatic cysts.

A patients presents to the emergency room with hematochezia, and they are hemodynamically unstable. After checking their ABC’s, what is your next step in management? Colonoscopy Sigmoidoscopy Tagged RBC scan Upper endoscopy with possible angiography. The correct answer is D. Hematochezia is usually consistent with lower GI bleeding. However, in a hemodynamically unstable patient, upper GI bleeding could also present with hematochezia. Therefore, the first step should be performing an upper endoscopy (possibly accompanied by an angiography) to ru

Cassie is a 35 year old healthy female with no history of cancer. Her mother was diagnosed with colon cancer at the age of 55. What screening options are available for Cassie? Perform FIT every 2 years staring at 50. Perform FIT every year starting at 45. Perform colonoscopy every 5 years staring at 45. Perform colonoscopy every 10 years starting 50. The correct answer is C. Cassie’s lifetime risk of developing colorectal cancer is increased since she has one first degree relative with colon cancer. Therefore, she should start colonoscopy 10 years younger than the age of diagnosis of her mother and it should be repeated every 5 years if negative

Which of the following comparisons between FIT and FOBT is false? FIT and FOBT are both performed every 2 years on average risk asymptomatic individuals Meats could lead to false positives in FOBT, whereas FIT is only specific for human hemoglobin. FIT requires multiple sample collections while FOBT requires a single sample collection. FIT is more sensitive than FOBT. The correct answer is C. FIT only requires a single stool sample and FOBT requires multiple samples.

Which of the following is not a secondary etiology of constipation? Colorectal Cancer Hypocalcemia Parkinson's Benign Stricture Hyperthyroidism The correct answer is B. Hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia is a secondary etiology of constipation

Shelby presents to your clinic with 1-2 spontaneous bowel movements per week and a sensation of incomplete evacuation in more than half her defecations.
