Straining in more than 1/3 Hard or lumpy stools in more than 1/4th of defecations Insufficient criteria for IBS Sensation of anorectal obstruction in more than 1/4 of defecations None, Shelby already meets the criteria based on this information The correct answer is E. From 06 - Constipation. Rome IV functional constipation needs ≥ 2 of 6 features for the last 3 months, with onset ≥ 6 months before diagnosis, plus loose stools rarely present without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS. Shelby has < 3 spontaneous BMs per week (1-2)

Which of the follow is not a red flag that would indicate colonoscopy in a patient presenting with constipation? Anemia Sudden change in bowel habits Hematochezia Fever Age > 50 The correct answer is D. From 06 - Constipation. The lecture's red flags that call for colonoscopy in constipation are the CRC flags: hematochezia, anemia, weight loss, age over 50, a sudden change in bowel habits, and a family history of CRC . Fever is not on that list. In an adult it points toward

What is not an accurate disadvantage of an osmotic laxative? Milk of Magnesia: risk of hypermagnesemia Magnesium Citrate: caution with renal impairment Laxaday: very sweet taste Lactulose: may cause bloating & flatulence due to fermentation of undigested carbohydrates The correct answer is D. Magnesium based laxatives such as milk of magneia and magnesium citrate are well tolerated but must be used with caution with renal impairment due to hypermagnesimia risk. Lactulose, not PEG3350 (Laxaday) is associated with very sweet taste that may be off putting.

What type of prokinetic is procalopride? D2 Antagonist D2 Agonist Cholinergic Agonist Macrolide Antibiotic 5HT4 Agonist The correct answer is E. From 09 - Pharmacology of Prokinetics and Antidiarrheal Drugs. Serotonin promotes gut motility. Prucalopride (the stem misspells it) is a gut-selective 5-HT4 agonist , so it relieves constipation, and diarrhea is its expected side effect. D2 antagonists are metoclopramide (c

What is the mechanism of action for bismuth subsalicylate? Select all that apply. Anti-secretory effects Anticholinergic effects Anti-microbial effects Sympathetic Activation Anti-inflammatory effects The correct answer is A, C, E. From 09 - Pharmacology of Prokinetics and Antidiarrheal Drugs. The lecture classes bismuth subsalicylate as an antisecretory agent (A): it stimulates fluid and electrolyte absorption across the gut wall. It has antimicrobial actions (C): it binds E. coli toxins and is

Diane comes into your clinic and describes recurrent abdominal pain at least once a week as well as an associated increase in bowel movements. She notes her stools have been very water as well. She has been experiencing this for the past year and is otherwise healthy. What is at the top of your differential? Dyspepsia Crohn's Disease Ulcerative Colitis Irritable Bowel Syndrome Infection The correct answer is D. Diane meets the Rome IV criteria for diagnosis of IBS & there are no red flags in this case.

The case. Diane comes into your clinic and describes recurrent abdominal pain at least once a week as well as an associated increase in bowel movements. She notes her stools have been very water as well. She has been experiencing this for the past year and is otherwise healthy. What dietary advice would you give Diane? Select all that apply. Consider a low FODMAP diet Avoid caffeine Increase soluble fibre intake Schedule time for regular meals Decrease soluble fibre intake The correct answer is A, B, C, D. From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. Diane (the previous question) has IBS with diarrhea. The lecture's IBS dietary management is: avoid caffeine for anxiety and diarrhea (B); increase soluble fibre , which helps both IBS-C and IBS-D (C); and try a low-FODMAP diet sh

Which of the following are red flags to take note of when a patient presents with dyspepsia like symptoms? Age of onset <12 Vomiting Nausea Heart burn & belching Upper Abdominal Pain The correct answer is B. From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. The lecture's dyspepsia red flags are dysphagia, vomiting , nocturnal pain, GI bleeding or anemia, an abdominal mass, weight loss, and age of onset > 40 . Any of these means you investigate (endoscopy) before calling it functional. Age of

Which of the following statements is correct? The superior mesenteric artery supplies the distal duodenum, the remainder of the small intestine and 2/3rd of the large intestine up to the hepatic flexure. The intestines are completely intraperitoneal Lymphatic drainage from the anal canal below the pectinate line drains into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes Parasympathetic innervation to the intestines comes from thoracic, lumbar, sacral splanchnic nerves The correct answer is C. From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Below the pectinate line, the anal canal comes from proctodeum ectoderm. It is lined by squamous epithelium, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes . Above the line, lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. So C is

Which label on the image below is correct? The correct answer is C. From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. In the figure the transverse colon is lifted up and the small bowel has been removed. The labelled vessels are: C. Right colic artery : an SMA branch running to the ascending colon on the right. The label and its pointer match, so t

Which of the following does not contribute to the process of digestion? Chief cells in the stomach Exocrine cells of the pancreas Glandular cells in the mouth Enzymes bound to the brush border in the large intestine The correct answer is D. chief cells secrete pepsinogen to digest protein; cells of the exocrine pancreas secrete several enzymes involved in digestion of carbs, fats, and proteins; glandular cells of the mouth release salivary amylase to help break down carbs. The brush border enzymes are located i

Which of the following statements about digestion and absorption is false? A patient who is deficient in a brush border enzyme for carbohydrate digestion could experience diarrhea due to increased osmotic pressure in the colon from the unabsorbed sugars. Some digestion of fats occurs in the stomach, but the majority of lipid digestion and absorption happens in the small intestine, starting in the duodenum. Regarding the absorption of lipids, long-chain fatty acids are re-esterified into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons in the intestinal enterocyte. They are exocytosed into the systemic circulation for distribution to the body. Most vitamins are absorbed in the small intestine but B12 is absorbed in the ileum The correct answer is C. chylomicrons are exocytosed into the lymphatics because they are too large to enter the systemic circulation.

How would you classify diarrhea due to laxatives based on physiology? Osmotic Inflammatory Secretory Motility The correct answer is A. osmotic diarrhea occurs when too much water is drawn into the bowels, as in the case of laxative use.

A patient complains of blood diarrhea once/day for the last 2 weeks. They consider it to be a large amount of diarrhea that fills the toilet bowel, but it is not urgent. How would you classify this case of diarrhea? Acute, large bowel Acute, small bowel Chronic, large bowel Chronic, small bowel The correct answer is B. The case is acute because symptoms have been present for less than 4 weeks. It is likely due to small bowel pathology as it is large volume, non-urgent, and infrequent.

Which of the following statements about celiac disease is false? Celiac disease is an allergy to the protein component of grain in genetically susceptible individuals The gold standard for diagnosing celiac disease is by IgA tissue transglutaminase serology The endoscopy of a celiac disease patient on a strict gluten-free diet may be normal The main treatment for celiac disease is a gluten-free diet The correct answer is B. The gold standard for celiac disease diagnosis is a duodenal biopsy in a patient not on a gluten-free diet. Histological findings suggestive of celiac disease include absent villi, increased inflammation, and intra-epithelial lymphocytes

A patient presents with abdominal cramping, fever and bloody stools that have been ongoing for 5 days. You take a detailed history and learn that they recently completed a course of antibiotics for a UTI. You have high clinical suspicion that the patient has a C.diff infection. What diagnostic test can you use to confirm your diagnosis? Abdominal xray Colonoscopy PCR for C.diff toxin gene Stool culture and sensitivity The correct answer is C. From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea and the IBD overview chart. Only toxin-producing strains of C. difficile cause disease. The lecture warns that the GDH immunoassay is positive for toxic and non-toxic strains, so confirmation needs evidence of toxin: the chart lists PCR for the

The case. A patient presents with abdominal cramping, fever and bloody stools that have been ongoing for 5 days. You take a detailed history and learn that they recently completed a course of antibiotics for a UTI. You have high clinical suspicion that the patient has a C.diff infection. You confirm your diagnosis of Cdiff for the patient in question 8. What treatment would you offer the patient? Select all that apply. Anti-motility agents Supportive therapy – fluids, electrolytes, nutrients Antibiotic therapy: metronidazole, vancomycin, or fidaxomicin Fecal microbiota transplantation The correct answer is B, C, D. These are all reasonable treatments for a patient with C.diff. Antimotility agents are contraindicated for inflammatory, infectious diarrhea.

What are characteristics of the 5 populations at risk of cholelithiasis? Infertile Fifty Fat Female C and D All of the above The correct answer is E. The 5 characteristics of populations at risks can be remembered by thinking of the 5F’s. Female, Forty, Fat, Fertile, and Flatulent.

What are structures 1, 2 and 3 pointing to, respectively? Pancreatic duct, common bile duct, and common hepatic duct Common hepatic duct, pancreatic duct, and common bile duct Common hepatic duct, common bile duct, and pancreatic duct None of the above The correct answer is C. Common hepatic duct, common bile duct, and pancreatic duct.

Which of the following regarding cirrhosis is false? It is only the end stage process of hepatitis B It involves 3 phases: cell death, fibrosis, and regeneration It is a diffuse process All of the above are true The correct answer is A. Cirrhosis is the end stage evolution of many chronic liver diseases, including chronic viral hepatitis, alcoholism, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and even cystic fibrosis, to name a few.

Which of the following is/are true with respect to cholesterol gallstones? They are more common in women They are more present in the Latin America, North America and Europe They are composed of at least 70% cholesterol A and B All of the above are true The correct answer is D. Both A and B are true. Cholesterol gallstones are more common in women, Mexican Americans, Pima, Hopi and Navajo peoples. They are also more prevalent in Europe and North and South America. However, they are composed of at least 50% cholesterol, not 70%!

What are the 3 tests that should be performed when investigating liver function? GGT, INR, and Albumin ALP, GGT, and INR AST, INR, and Albumin Albumin, Bilirubin, and INR The correct answer is D. Low albumin may indicate liver damage/disease, elevated bilirubin might indicate liver damage, and INR (or Prothrombin Time, PT) can also indicate liver damage. While the other options include liver enzymes such as GGT, ALP, and AST, the 3 main tests to measure liver functio

There are 2 types of liver enzymes: hepatocellular and cholestatic. Hepatocellular are specific to the liver, while cholestatic are specific to bile ducts. Which enzymes are specific to the liver? Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) A and B A and C All of the above The correct answer is E. ALT and AST are hepatocellular enzymes. While helpful, these do not truly measure liver function, as they can be normal in patients with liver disease (as well as cholestatic enzymes). Synthetic liver function (INR, albumin, and bilirubin) should be considered when investiga

You are reading the serology report of a patient who visited the clinc you are working at. You read the report as follows: HBsAg – negative, Anti-HBc – positive, Anti-HBs – Positive. How you would interpret this report? The patient is susceptible to Hepatitis B The patient is immune to Hepatitis B due to vaccination The patient is immune to Hepatitis B due to natural infection None of the above. The correct answer is C. With these specific findings, the patient would be considered immune due to natural infection. To be susceptible, all serologies would be negative. If they were immune due to vaccination, both HBsAg and Anti-HBc would be negative, while Anti-HBs would be positive.

You are a specialist and a patient comes to your clinic with a chronic HBV infection, but no signs of chronic hepatitis. What are your next steps (in order)? Monitor, consider risk of extrahepatic manifestations and risk of transmission, and if concerned, start antiviral treatment Monitor, and start antiviral treatment Discharge the patient – they have chronic hepatitis and no treatment will help There is no specialist follow up – but inform the patient and general practioner about the potential risk of HBV reactivation The correct answer is A. The other options do not properly follow protocols of monitoring and assessing the patient. B states to start antiviral treatment right away, which is not necessary.

What is the purpose of doing a liver biopsy? Confirm chronic hepatitis Grade inflammation Stage fibrosis B and C All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are reasons to perform a liver biopsy.

Which of the following is true regarding Wilson’s disease? Copper transport is impaired within bile, and it accumulates in hepatocytes Patients often present with neuropsychiatric symptoms Liver disease is often discovered incidentally None of the above All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are characteristics of Wilson’s disease. Copper is impaired within bile, accumulating in hepatocytes. Patients often present with neuropsychiatric symptoms because copper deposits within the basal ganglia. This condition is often discovered incidentally.

Jaundice presents with a yellowish discoloration of the body’s tissues resulting from elevated bilirubin. Which of the following investigations would be appropriate to order for someone presenting with jaundice? AST albumin CBC total and direct bilirubin all of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above, each give some detail about the liver’s function and can point one in the direction of the cause for the jaundice

It is normal for the levels of unconjugated bilirubin levels to be initially low in a new born infant, however it is also normal for those levels to steadily increase over time. Which of the following is true regarding those levels? The levels of unconjugated bilirubin can remain high for up to 10 days It is normal for the levels of unconjugated bilirubin to be far greater than 340 micromoles per liter It is normal for the level of unconjugated bilirubin to remain somewhat high for 2-5 days after birth New borns should have their unconjugated bilirubin levels checked within two weeks of birth C and D The correct answer is E. Both are correct, this was taken from the lectures on Jaundice

Which of the following is not a consequence of malnutrition? impaired wound healing increased risk of infection increased risk of skin breakdown increased motility slower recovery The correct answer is D. In this case, malnutrition decreases most bodily activity.

What are the indications for a gastrojejunostomy tube? long term feeding required if the patient presents with a risk for aspiration peritonitis bleeding A and B The correct answer is E. Both A and B are correct, the other two options are complications of the tube

Which of the following are pathologic features of pancreatitis? Edema Fat necrosis Hemorrhage Destruction of pancreatic parenchyma All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are correct From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Acute pancreatitis is autodigestion by activated pancreatic enzymes, and each enzyme leaves its own lesion, so all four options are features: Edema (A) : from microvascular leakage. Fat necrosis (B) :

What is instrumental in the management of chronic pancreatitis? cessation of alcohol consumption treat malabsorption treat abdominal pain replace nutritional deficiencies all of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are correct From the pancreas chart in 04 - Gallbladder Disease and 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Each option is a treatment line in the lecture, so all of the above is right: Stop alcohol (A) : alcohol causes 70% of cases. Alcohol and smoking ces

Which of the following is true of IgG4 related acalculous cholecystitis? Tissue infiltrates of IgG4 producing plasma cells no elevated serum IgG4 has no effect on the gallbladder, biliary tree, or pancreas may be surgically removed as a gallbladder carcinoma A and D The correct answer is E. B and C are untrue From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. IgG4-related chronic acalculous cholecystitis is one expression of a systemic disease: True (A) : tissue infiltrates of IgG4-producing plasma cells define it. False (B) : serum IgG4 is raised, which is how the systemic diseas

Which condition is responsible for 90% of acute cases of cholecystitis? acute calculous cholecystitis IgG4 related cholecystitis fibrosis tumours non of the above The correct answer is A. This is the stone obstruction of the duct, which is the main cause of the disease

Liver abscesses are characterized by? neutrophils liquified debris of dead cells edema fluid all of the above none of the above The correct answer is D. Each are characteristic of an abscess as seen under microscopy

Which of the following are true of Hepatocellular carcinomas? used to be called a hepatoma #1 primary liver malignancy #8 cause of death world wide most commonly seen in males aged >40 yrs All of the above The correct answer is E. All of the above are correct From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. The lecture supports the core of this. HCC is the most common primary liver cancer ("C = most Common primary liver tumour" in the ABCs). It is most common in males over 40 , and 90% arise in cirrhotic livers (a

Will Smith presents to the ER with periumbilical pain, which then radiates to the RLQ. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Colonic ischemia Early appendicitis Gastritis Chronic pancreatitis The correct answer is B. Early appendicitis present with periumbilical pain, which later localizes to the RLQ.

Jada Pinkett Smith presents to the ER with involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, and pain to percussion. A preliminary diagnosis of peritonitis is made. To confirm this diagnosis, which of the following investigations should be ordered? (Select all that apply) CBC Pelvic ultrasound Colonoscopy Abdominal X-Ray series HCG Urease breath test Liver enzymes and liver function tests CT chest The correct answer is A, B, D, E, G. A CBC should be ordered to investigate the possibility of anemia and/or an infectious etiology. A pelvic ultrasound and HCG test are needed to rule out ectopic pregnancy. An abdominal X-Ray series can offer clues to a potential diagnosis, as would liver enzymes a

Chris Rock is a first year medical student at a local London hospital. He notices that a patient’s abdomen is distended, however he is unsure if it is ascites or a bowel obstruction. Which of the following factors would suggest a bowel obstruction INSTEAD of ascites? Bulging flanks Shifting dullness Moderate/severe pain Bowel habit unchanged The correct answer is C. Ascites is typically painless or presents with mild abdominal pain. Contrarily, bowel obstructions are painful. They present with central distention, tympany throughout upon percussion, central distention, nausea/vomiting, constipation, and obstipation.

Which type of bowel obstruction does NOT require immediate surgery? Adhesive small bowel obstruction Closed loop bowel obstruction Non-adhesive small bowel obstruction Complete large bowel obstruction The correct answer is A. A large proportion (85%) of adhesive small bowel obstructions resolve on their own. Surgery is not immediately indicated – doing an abdominal X-Ray and gastrograffin protocol ae appropriate next steps.

Which of the following is NOT true of extra-abdominal masses? Most malignant masses are carcinomas Examples of extra-abdominal masses include lipomas and umbilical hernias These masses are not found in the peritoneal cavity Extra-abdominal masses are more prominent to palpation when the patient contracts their abdominal wall muscles Most masses are benign The correct answer is A. Most abdominal wall masses are sarcomas, not carcinomas. This is because they usually originate from connective tissue, muscle, or adipose tissue.

A mass is palpated in the left hypochondriac region. Which of the following is the least likely cause of the mass? Pancreatic cancer Colon cancer Perforated diverticulitis Splenomegaly Gastric cancer The correct answer is C. Perforated diverticulitis occurs most frequently in the sigmoid colon, which is found in the left lower quadrant/left inguinal region. The other structures listed in the question are found in the left hypochondriac region and are more likely to present with a mass there.

Which of the following is false when investigating abdominal masses? CT and ultrasound are commonly used imaging modalities for investigating abdominal masses An asymptomatic abdominal wall mass can be observed over time Painless masses have a higher risk of malignancy than painful masses Initial bloodwork includes CBC, creatinine, and CA-125 Jaundice and weight loss are red flags associated with malignancy The correct answer is D. CA-125 should not be a part of your initial bloodwork. It is not a good diagnostic test and is used as a baseline when treating a known malignancy after its anatomic location has been determined by imaging.

Which of the following regarding peritonitis is false? Patients with peritonitis tend to involuntarily guard their abdomen Pain associated with peritonitis is constant and severe Rebound tenderness alone does not necessarily indicate peritonitis Diagnostic confirmation of peritonitis is made with peritoneal biopsy or washings Initial management includes IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and no food by mouth in the event surgery is required The correct answer is D. Peritonitis is a clinical diagnosis made based on the presenting patient’s constellation of symptoms. Although biopsy or peritoneal washings may be helpful in some cases of peritonitis, it is not necessary in all cases.

Which of the following statements regarding the 4 causes of acute abdomen are false? Perforation is commonly caused by duodenal ulcers and is often plugged using the patient’s own omentum Bowel obstruction often starts as colicky pain and can progress to obstipation Small bowel ischemia is most severe when a thrombus forms in the superior mesenteric artery GI bleeding in the small bowel often cannot be visualized and is termed obscure bleeding All of the above statements are true The correct answer is C. Embolic tend to cause more dense ischemia and cause infarction than thrombi. Emboli travel more distal through the intestinal vasculature where there is less vessel collateralization, resulting in more severe ischemia.

Which of the following is not a part of the best initial management strategy for a patient with suspected diverticulitis? 3rd generation cephalosporin + metronidazole as initial antibiotics Digital rectal exam CBC and chemistry Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound Ask patient about FIT testing and if they have inflammatory bowel disease The correct answer is D. First-line imaging for suspected diverticulitis is CT abdomen/pelvis, so abdominal/pelvic ultrasound would not be a part of the best initial management strategy. It is important to rule out other causes including colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease, so these que

In which of the following scenarios would an urgent appendectomy NOT be indicated? Septic patient with perforated appendicitis Patient with a non-drainable perforated appendiceal abscess Patient with nonperforated appendicitis and is unfit for surgery but improves with antibiotics Patient with nonperforated appendicitis and is fit for surgery Patient with phlegmon around appendix that does not require ileocecal resection The correct answer is C. A patient that is unfit for surgery should be hospitalized and put on IV antibiotics. If the patient improves, an appendectomy is not urgently indicated, and they can be discharged home with oral antibiotics. The patient will likely require an appendectomy in the future, tho

Which of the following presentations is inconsistent with anal fissures: Painful bowel movement Sentinel skin tag Hematemesis Sensation of anal spasm The correct answer is C. Hematemesis presents in upper GI diseases. Anal fissures may present with bright red blood on defecation (hematochezia).

Zeus is presenting to your family medicine clinic with a complaint of pain in his anus starting 2 days ago. He denies any bleeding, change in bowel movement, or diagnosis of IBD. What is at the top of your differential? Infection Trauma Inflammatory process Hemorrhoids The correct answer is A. Abscesses/infections are the most common cause of acute rectal pain with no bleeding. The other diagnoses have a high likelihood of causing bleeding.

Which of the following is a likely potential cause of chronic diarrhea in infants that is less likely in children and teens? Post-infectious secondary lactase deficiency IBS Cow’s milk intolerance Congenital carbohydrate enzyme deficiencies The correct answer is C. Children and teens are more likely to have general lactose deficiency, whereas the cow’s milk intolerance experienced by infants usually spontaneously resolves within 1 year. Postinfectious secondary lactase deficiency and congenital carbohydrate enzyme deficiencies are also

Why is it not recommended to give children plain water to treat dehydration caused by GI pathologies? Children enjoy high-sugar fluids more and will likely consume more of those if offered Too much plain water coupled with electrolyte imbalance can cause hyponatremia and hypoglycemia Dehydration is a necessary physiological process for recovery Oral rehydration solution (ORS) contains more nutrients, which will promote growth to combat the illness-induced weight loss The correct answer is B. From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea (with 05 - Pediatric Diarrhea). Dehydration is the main complication of diarrhea, and infants are at higher risk. Rehydration should use a balanced electrolyte solution (ORS). Diarrhea loses water and sodium. Replacing that with plain water dilu

For which of the following children with constipation would be most concerned: Arman, 3 year old, who presents with a distended rectum on imaging Belle, 3 week old, who has stooled only once in the last week Cho, 1 year old, who cries when stooling Dune, 10 year old, who presents with a perianal fissure The correct answer is B. Onset of constipation at <1 month of age is an alarm feature. All other presentations are characteristic of mild or moderate constipation.

Which of the following is NOT a good toileting habit: Scheduled toilet time Using a stool to bring legs up Rewarding stooling or attempted stooling Using the child potty instead of the adult toilet until the age of 3 The correct answer is D. There are no official recommendations for how long a child should stay on the child potty. All others are part of the recommended guidelines for toileting hygiene.

The upper half of the stomach is functionally designed for Pumping/grinding Control of acid secretion Solid emptying Reservoir The correct answer is D. The function of the stomach can be thought of in terms of halves. The lower half of the stomach is primarily responsible for pumping and grinding, metering, peristalsis, and solid emptying. The upper half is primarily responsible for storage of food (acting as a reservoir),

Acid secretion in the stomach comes from what cell type? Parietal cells G-cells Goblet cells Chief cells The correct answer is A. Parietal cells are the specialized acid-secreting cells of the stomach. These cells respond to histamine, gastrin, and acetylcholine receptor activation to produce acid. In addition to acid secretion, parietal cells also secrete intrinsic factor. Note that in the antrum, G c

H+/K+ ATPase transporters found in parietal cells are the target sites of which heartburn medication? Antacids Omeprazole Bismuth H2 antagonists The correct answer is B. Antacids are used to neutralize the acidity of stomach acid or to block acid secretion by gastric cells. Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase transporters. Bismuth (ie. Pepto-Bismol) works as a weak antacid and coats the stomach to protect the l

Which of the following is not a stimulant of stomach acid secretion? Histamine Gastrin Misoprostol Acetylcholine The correct answer is C. Misoprostol is an analog of prostaglandin E1 used in the treatment of missed abortions, for abortions and to induce labour. All of the other answers are stimulants of stomach acid secretion via the parietal cells.

What cell type in the gastric mucosa of the stomach secretes intrinsic factor (IF)? Chief cells ECL cells Goblet cells Parietal cells The correct answer is D. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase. ECL (Enterochromaffin-like) cells secrete histamine (H2). Goblet cells secrete mucin. Parietal cells secrete gastric acid and intrinsic factor, these cells are only located in the fundus.

What is the leading cause of duodenal ulcers worldwide? Helicobacter pylori infection Stress Alcohol Diet of salted and pickled foods NSAID overuse The correct answer is A. Worldwide, the leading cause of duodenal ulcers is H. pylori infection. H. pylori is a gram negative curved bacillus with flagella. Prevalence is up to 50% in developed countries and 90% in developing countries.

What is the leading cause of gastric ulcers? Helicobacter pylori infection NSAID Overuse Alcohol Stress The correct answer is B. NSAIDs are the leading cause of gastric ulcers. The pathogenesis of NSAID-induced gastric ulcers is related to the disruption of protective factors such as mucin production and prostaglandin secretion. NSAIDs directly inhibit prostaglandin production, and may exert indirect

Which of the following are complications of peptic ulcer disease? Bleeding Perforation Obstruction All of the above None of the above The correct answer is D. Peptic ulcer disease can present with obstruction, perforation and hemorrhage. It can also mimic other gastrointestinal diseases. Obstruction usually occurs at the gastric outlet due to ulcers of the antropylorus or duodenum. Perforation and hemorrhage may occur wherever ulc

Quadruple therapy to eradicate H. pylori refers, in general, to which combination of drugs? One PPI, one H2 antagonist, amoxicillin and tetracycline One PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline Two H2 antagonists, bismuth, metronidazole Two PPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin The correct answer is B. Quadruple therapy for H. Pylori eradication includes a proton pump inhibitor and either 1) bismuth, Metronidazole and tetracycline (PBMT) OR 2) amoxicillin, metronidazole, and clarithromycin (PAMC) . The proton pump inhibitor most often used is omeprazole although pantoprazo

The epiploic foramen is narrow opening in the mesentery that leads from The greater sac to the lesser sac The visceral peritoneum to the parietal peritoneum The greater sac to hepatorenal pouch Paracolic gutters to the paravertebral gutters The correct answer is A. The epiploic foramen (omental foramen) is the connection between the greater sac and the lesser sac of the abdomen. It is bordered by the hepatoduodenal ligament, the peritoneum of the IVC, the peritoneum of the caudate lobe of the liver and the peritoneum of the duodenum.

Chief cells of the stomach secrete: HCl intrinsic factor mucus pepsinogen The correct answer is D. Chief cells of the stomach secrete pepsinogen and other enzymes, such as gastric lipase. Parietal cells are responsible for HCl (A) and intrinsic factor (B) production. Goblet cells produce mucin, which becomes mucus when exposed to water (C).

Which is not a layer of the esophageal wall? Mucosa Submucosa Adventitia Serosa Muscularis The correct answer is D. Unlike much of the rest of the gastrointestinal tract, there is no serosa in the esophagus. Instead, there is an adventitia surrounding the esophagus. These structures share similar functions.

A 72-year-old patient presents to his family doctor with progressive difficulty in swallowing solid food. However, he does not experience heartburn, except on the rare occasion when he eats spicy Mexican food. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely? Achalasia Scleroderma Esophageal Carcinoma Peptic Stricture The correct answer is C. Esophageal carcinoma is suspected in an older patient presenting with progressive dysphagia of solid food without heartburn. Although patients with achalasia have progressive dysphagia without heartburn, they have trouble swallowing liquids AND solids. People with scleroderm

Barret’s Esophagus: Is the most important long-term consequence of GERD Can easily be reversed by changing one’s diet to less oily foods Occurs in 50% of patients with GERD Is generally managed with watchful waiting The correct answer is A. BE is the predisposing factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma. Patients with BE have a 30x increased risk of developing adenocarcinoma. Although Barret’s esophagus is an extremely important consequence of GERD, only 10% of patients with GERD develop BE. BE is aggressively trea

Achalasia: Involves low pressure in the lower esophageal sphincter Is generally associated with non-progressive dysphagia Can be treated with pneumatic dilatation of the lower sphincter None of the above The correct answer is C. Achalasia involves high pressure in the LES, the dysphagia is progressive.

Diffuse Esophageal Spasm is often treated with H2 – antagonists Esophageal myotomy Nitrogylcerin Nissen Fundoplication The correct answer is C. DES is a painful condition in which the muscle of the esophageal wall goes into spasm, causing intermittent dysphagia. Treatment is aimed at reducing the contraction by using calcium channel blockers or nitrates such as nitroglycerin.

Which of the following is TRUE about eosinophilic esophagitis It is more common in women than men It is more common in the elderly population. It is often associated with asthma and other allergies All of the above The correct answer is C. Eosinophilic esophagitis is a condition that usually affects young men. It results in dysphagia associated with large numbers of eosinophils in the mucosa of the esophagus. It is treated with diet, allergy medications, and steroids. It relates strongly with asthma and a tend

The interstitial cells of Cajal: Are found in the smooth muscle of the GI tract Play an important role in the generation of slow wave electrical activity. Serve as pacemakers governing the frequency of the slow wave All of the above The correct answer is D. The interstitial cells of Cajal are located in the smooth muscle of the GI tract, where they generate slow waves and act as a pacemaker to determine their frequency.

The transition from colon to rectum is signified by: The end of the tenia coli The end of the mucosal layer Loss of longitudinal muscle Loss of circular muscle The correct answer is A. Anatomically, the rectum does not possess the tenia coli, a longitudinal muscle visible on the large bowel.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from which nerve roots? T12-L2 L2, 3, 4 L4, 5, S1, 2, 3 S1, 2, 3 S2, 3, 4 The correct answer is E. The S2, S3, and S4 splanchnic nerves that supply parasympathetic innervation are important nerve roots to remember. “S-two, three, four keeps the pee and poo off the floor” is an easy way to remember their important function. That is, parasympathetic stimulation is responsib

What of the following is the least common origin of GI bleeds? Stomach Colon Jejunum 1st part of the duodenum Cecum The correct answer is C. Rationally evaluating this list can save you from unnecessary memorization. We can eliminate stomach (A) and the first stage duodenum (D) as these are the common sites of peptic ulcers, which are a common problem (not to mention gastric varices and many other causes). Likewi

Regarding esophageal neoplasms, which of the following is TRUE? Adenocarcinoma represents 90% of esophageal neoplasms worldwide Squamous cell carcinoma incidence is rapidly increasing in North America Squamous cell carcinoma is most common in the middle third of the esophagus 99% of esophageal adenocarcinomas are in the proximal esophagus. The correct answer is C. (A) is true of SCC. (B) is true of adenocarcinoma, which also usually presents in the distal esophagus.

Concerning gastric cancer, which of the following are true Has prominent symptoms early on Has pain relieved by eating Is commonly caused by H. Pylori All of the above The correct answer is C. Due to the large amount of space in the stomach, by the time symptoms occur, most patients have advanced disease, so (A) is false. Pain is also not relieved by eating with gastric cancer.

A 55 year old patient presents to your clinic with dysphagia. They state they experience difficulty with swallowing a few seconds after initiating swallowing. The patient only reports this only occurs when swallowing solid foods and reports mild heartburn. Which of the following conditions is at the top of your differential diagnosis? Carcinoma Peptic Stricture Jackhammer Esophagus Achalasia The correct answer is B. This patient presents with esophageal dysphagia. Since this patient has difficulty only swallowing solid foods a mechanical cause for the dysphagia is more likely. A peptic stricture is a common mechanical condition that usually results from acid reflux and can be accompanie

Which of the following are red flags to take note of when a patient presents with dyspepsia like symptoms? Age of onset <12 Vomiting Nausea Heart burn & belching Upper Abdominal Pain The correct answer is B. From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. Before calling dyspepsia functional, the lecture has you check for red flags: dysphagia, vomiting , nocturnal pain, GI bleeding or anemia, an abdominal mass, weight loss, and onset after age 40 . B. Vomiting is on the list, because persist

What is a possible complication of a choledochal cyst? Infection Stricture Malignancy All of the above None of the above The correct answer is D. A choledochal cyst is a congenital dilation of the common bile duct. The dilation predisposes the duct to bile stasis allowing for infection to occur. Infection can cause stricture formation, stone formation (bacteria deconjugate the bile acids), as well as cause metaplasia,

What is the pathogenesis of the development of carcinoma from a choledochal cyst? Bile stasis → deconjugated bile acids → bacteria overgrowth → metaplasia → dysplasia →cancer Bile stasis→bacteria overgrowth→deconjugated bile acids→metaplasia→dysplasia→cancer Bile stasis→conjugated bile acids→bacterial overgrowth→metaplasia→dysplasia→cancer Bile stasis→bacteria overgrowth→conjugated bile acids→metaplasia→dysplasia→cancer The correct answer is B. Dilation of the bile duct predisposes to the duct to bile stasis. Bile stasis permits bacteria growth within the duct and as the bacteria proliferate they deconjugate the bile acids. Deconjugated bile within the duct system, along with infection and inflammation, lead to met

Which of the following is not an anatomic constriction of the esophagus? Cervical Aortic Thoracic Diaphragmatic The correct answer is B. The three esophageal constrictions are the cervical which is created by the cricopharyngeal muscle, the thoracic created by the crossing of the left main bronchus and aortic arch, and the diaphragmatic made by its passage through the diaphragm.

What cell type is responsible for the creation of the spontaneous electrical rhythm needed for muscle contraction in the GI tract? Enterochromaffin like cells Parietal Cells Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs) Goblet Cells The correct answer is C. Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs) are the pacemaker cells that are interposed between SMCs that contribute to the creation of the spontaneous electrical rhythm of motility in the GI tract.

What statement is true concerning the ENS and the walls of the esophagus? Meissner’s plexus controls gastrointestinal motility. Meissner’s plexus is in between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers. Meissner’s plexus controls local secretion, absorption, and contraction of the submucosal muscle. Meissner’s and Auerbach’s plexuses are independent and do not require communication for proper function. The correct answer is C. Auerbach’s plexus controls gastrointestinal motility, and is located between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers of the esophagus. Communication between Auerbach’s and Meissner’s plexuses is crucial to function and both are interconnected.

What motility pattern is responsible for the mixing of food and GI juices? Peristalsis Tonic Segmentation Retrograde The correct answer is C. Segmentation is the rhythmic contraction pattern that allows for the mixing of food with the GI juices by both ends of the bowel contracting with a third contraction occurring in the middle. Peristalsis is a wave-like muscle contraction that moves food forward, tonic contrac

What hormone or peptide mediates contraction of the smooth muscle cells during fasting? Gastrin Motilin CCK Secretin VIP The correct answer is B. Motilin is the correct choice. Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion, CCK inhibits gastric emptying, secretin stimulates pancreatic secretion, VIP stimulates vasodilation.

What is not a possible symptom of GERD? Regurgitation Constipation Chronic cough Retrosternal burning pain The correct answer is B. Constipation is not a symptom of GERD. Regurgitation, heartburn (retrosternal burning pain- pyrosis), atypical chest pain, and extra esophageal presentations (chronic cough, asthma, dental erosions) are key symptoms of GERD.

Symptomatic GERD may lead to Barrett’s esophageal changes, in what part of the esophagus does this occur? Gastroesophageal junction Lower esophageal sphincter Upper esophageal sphincter Thoracic inlet The correct answer is A. Barrett’s esophagus is the replacement of normal squamous mucosa by columnar epithelium containing goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), this occurs at the gastroesophageal junction.

Which one of the following is false regarding Serotonin Receptor Antagonists? SRAs are only indicated for short-term use They are well-absorbed and metabolized by CYPS Their mechanism of action involve upregulating the action of 5-HT3 receptors Side effects are usually mild and easily manageable It is possible for them to increase the QT-interval. The correct answer is C. SRAs mechanism of action is to INHIBIT the 5-HT3 receptors in the CTZ and vomiting center. As well as those in the GI tract.

Where would fluid accumulate in the abdominal cavity if a patient is lying supine? Epiploic foramen Paracolic gutters Hepatorenal recess (Morrison’s Pouch) Lesser omentum Greater omentum C) Hepatorenal Recess (Morrison's Pouch). The epiploic foramen is the connection between the greater and lesser sacs -- fluid from infection or inflammation can accumulate here. The paracolic gutters limit the absorption of toxins in the lower pelvis. The hepatorenal recess would collect fluid due t

Which structure would bleed if cut in surgery? Median umbilical fold Medial umbilical fold Lateral umbilical fold Superior umbilical fold C) Lateral umbilical fold. The median umbilical fold is the obliterated urachus (the urachus is a remnant of the allantois which sends waste to the placenta during the first 7 weeks gestation. Once the cloaca ruptures and starts dumping waste into the amniotic fluid, there is no need for the allanto

Which of the following is NOT true about indirect inguinal hernias? A predisposing factor is having a patent processus vaginalis They are more common than direct inguinal hernias The hernia travels within the inguinal canal, within the processus vaginalis inside the spermatic cord The hernia enters the canal through the superficial inguinal ring medial to the inferior epigastric vessels The hernia exits through the superficial inguinal ring (often passing into the scrotum/labium majus) D) An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring which is LATERAL to the inferior epigastric vessels. All other answers are true.

Which of the following mechanisms are protective against GERD? Incompetent lower esophageal sphincter Abnormal peristalsis Mucosal integrity Irregular gastric emptying C) Mucosal integrity of the esophagus is protective against GERD, as is a competent lower esophageal sphincter, normal peristalsis and normal gastric emptying.

Which parts of the duodenum are retroperitoneal? 1st and 2nd 2nd and 3rd 3rd and 4th 1st and 4th The correct answer is B. Technically, the midgut portion of the duodenum is retroperitoneal. Most texts consider this to be the 2nd and 3rd stages of the duodenum, although some texts include the 4th part.

What portion of the pancreas lies posterior to the superior mesenteric artery? Head Neck Body Tail Uncinate process The correct answer is E. The uncus is the portion of the pancreas that hooks under the superior mesenteric artery and lies superior to the 3rd and 4th stages of the duodenum. For clarification, review the cadaveric images in the anatomy lectures, or refer to an anatomy atlas.

What are the small collections of lymphatic tissue found throughout the small intestine called? Kupffer cells Langerhans cells Dust cells Peyer’s patches The correct answer is D. Peyer’s patches are lymphoid tissue located in the small intestine (ileum). Kupffer cells are macrophages which can be found in the liver. Langerhans cells are immune cells located in the skin and mucosa. Dust cells are macrophages located in the alveoli.

Which of the following is FALSE about slow wave electrical activity in the GI tract? It is dependent on innervation from the enteric nervous system It is propagated aborally It coordinates contractions Slow wave refers to the spontaneous variation at rest of the muscle fibre The correct answer is A. Slow waves are not dependent on innervation by the enteric nervous system, so A is false. This is because the slow waves are spontaneous variations in the membrane potential of the smooth muscle fibres at rest (D). These spontaneous variations of muscle are therefore indepen

The proximal 2/3rds of the transverse colon is supplied by the: Splenic artery Ileocolic artery Middle colic artery Right colic artery The correct answer is C. The proximal ⅔ (majority) of the transverse colon is derived embryologically from the midgut, and is thus supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. More specifically, the middle colic artery is a branch off of the superior mesenteric, which supplies the proximal ⅔ of the t

The arterial supply of the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon originates from the: IMA (inferior mesenteric artery) SMA (superior mesenteric artery) Celiac trunk Renal artery Abdominal Aorta The correct answer is B. The blood supply is derived from the superior mesenteric artery, as explained in the previous answer (#25).

Which of the following does not aid in parasympathetic innervation of the gut? Pelvic splanchnic nerves Inferior hypogastric plexus Inferior mesenteric plexus Vagus nerve Greater splanchnic nerves The correct answer is E. Essentially, this question is asking which of the answers is non-parasympathetic (i.e. sympathetic) in innervation.

The most common cause of acute lower GI bleeding is: Crohn’s Disease Colorectal Cancer Post-polypectomy Diverticulosis The correct answer is D. As in the previous question, it may be valuable to remember the first few items on the differential list for LGI bleed. This includes diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, and hemorrhoids.

Which of the following is not a possible pathophysiology of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)? Altered GI motility Psychopathology Inflammatory response Visceral hyperalgesia The correct answer is C. An inflammatory response is not a characteristic of IBS. IBS is a functional disorder; this means that no true organic etiology can be found. Inflammation of the bowel would be more in keeping with an organic disease such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) rather than IBS.

Which is not a common pathogen causing Traveler’s diarrhea? E. coli Campylobacter jejuni Salmonella Clostridium difficile Shigella The correct answer is D. C. difficile, although a cause of diarrhea, is mainly implicated in hospital-acquired infections, not traveller’s diarrhea. Pathogens responsible for traveller’s diarrhea include: E. coli, Shigella, Campylobacter jejunii and salmonella (non-typhoidal).

A mother mentions that her youngest daughter, an older infant, drinks large amounts of juice and milk but eats little solid food. You tell the mother that this puts her daughter at highest risk for: Vitamin D deficiency Constipation Iron deficiency Chronic diarrhea The correct answer is C. Milk is fortified with Vitamin D, although it is best to also obtain it from other sources such as sunlight. This diet should not cause constipation. Children who just drink juice and milk, with little solid food are at high risk for iron deficiency, due to the low amount of

Regarding colorectal cancer etiology, which of the following is true? 80% arise from adenomatous polyps 20% arise from sessile serrated adenomas It is the most common cause of cancer-related death in non-smokers All of the above The correct answer is D. All of the above answers are true. Polyps, whether sessile or pedunculated, are the origin of colon cancer. Pedunculated or adenomatous polyps are the most common, accounting for 80%, while sessile polyps account for 20%. Colon cancer is the most common cause of cancer-relat

In colorectal cancer: Even if detected early on, patients generally have a very poor prognosis Left sided cancers present with obvious bleeding or obstruction FOB screening is recommended annually for all individuals 70 years and older In most cases, there is a short interval between polyp development and cancer The correct answer is B. If detected early on, these patients have a very good prognosis. Whereas right sided cancers typically present with non-GI symptoms such as weight loss and anemia, left-sided cancers generally present with more typical GI symptoms, largely due to the smaller lumen of the lef

Which of the following is a recommended strategy for colorectal cancer screening for a person with no risk factors? FIT test every 2 years between ages 50-74 (follow up positive cases with colonoscopy Colonoscopy at 50 years old, every 10 years FIT test every 5 years between ages 50+ Colonoscopy at 60 years old A and B C and D The correct answer is E. The appropriate screening regimen is a FIT test every 2 years between ages 50-74 (with follow up of positive cases with colonoscopy) OR a Colonoscopy every 10 years starting at age 50.

Which of the following is incorrect regarding functional gastrointestinal disorders? Visceral hypersensitivity is characterized by pain due to normal stretch as a result of increased signalling. IBS is the most common chronic GI disorder and affects up to 20% of women and 10% of men. Use of antibiotics can increase the risk of developing IBS. IBS symptoms can be alleviated in most patients through the elimination of a single food group. IBS symptoms are related to the impaired absorption of carbohydrates. The correct answer is D. is incorrect as in IBS no one food group is the absolute cause of the IBS

What is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children? Tylenol induced fulminant liver failure Reyes syndrome Extrahepatic biliary atresia Cystic fibrosis The correct answer is C. While there are many conditions that can lead to liver transplantation in children, the leading cause is extrahepatic biliary atresia. It can be congential or acquired. In the congenital form, it is a birth defect where the bile duct is blocked or absent. With the acquired f

Which of the following statements is correct? The superior mesenteric artery supplies the distal duodenum, the remainder of the small intestine and 2/3rd of the large intestine up to the hepatic flexure. The intestines are completely intraperitoneal Lymphatic drainage from the anal canal below the pectinate line drains into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes Parasympathetic innervation to the intestines comes from thoracic, lumbar, sacral splanchnic nerves The correct answer is C. From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Below the pectinate line, the anal canal comes from proctodeum ectoderm. It is lined by squamous epithelium, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes . Above the line, lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. So C is

The developing respiratory tract and esophagus are derived from the… Foregut Midgut Hindgut None of the above The correct answer is A. The developing respiratory tract and esophagus are both derived from the foregut. During the 4th -10th week of development the proximal aspect of the foregut develops a small diverticulum called the tracheobronchial diverticulum which eventually separates into the esophagus

Which is not part of the definition of constipation? 12 weeks in the last year of hard stools Less than 3 defecations per week Manual maneuvers may be required to facilitate defecation Sensation of incomplete evacuation Loose stools are not present The correct answer is A. Answer A is incorrect because according to Rome IV criteria, constipation is based on the past 6 months, not the past year.

What is the most definitive test for a diagnosis of celiac disease? IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) IgG anti deaminated gliadin peptide (DGP) Biopsy HLA Typing The correct answer is D. 95% of celiac patients are HLA DQ2, and 5% are HLA DQ8. False negatives can occur with the other options if they are already gluten free.

Which of the following is considered a red flag in a case of fever in a returned traveller? High stool frequency (>6/day, longer than 5 days) High Fever Blood in Stool Two of the above All of the above The correct answer is E. Red flags for the fever in a returned travellers are: - High stool frequency (>6/day, longer than 5 days) - High fever - Bloody stools - Stools with mucous - Diarrhea persisting for weeks to months

Patient present with recent abdominal pain (LLQ) and diarrhea for over a month, they have never had anything like this before. After appropriate preliminary triage, you sent patient for a blood test. The results show elevated leukocyte count. What is the most likely diagnosis? Food poisoning Diverticulitis Diverticulosis Ulcerative Colitis None of the above The correct answer is B. Food poisoning would be quite acute. Diverticulosis is a condition in which small sacs (diverticula) form in the walls of an organ like the stomach or colon. Diverticulitis is the inflammation and or infection of these sacs, leading to nausea/vomiting, chills, diarrhea, abdo

Your parent just got diagnosed with Irritable Bowel Syndrome, what is your treatment plans and next steps in management? (Choose 5 answers) Counsel patient as there is no cure Refer patient to surgery Dietary modification with immediate introduction of large amount of dietary fiber Dietary modification with low FODMAP diet Physical activity and regular sleep schedule Defecation coaching Symptom relief medication if necessary Refer to GI specialist right away Further imaging with biopsy Ultrasound Chest X-ray The correct answer is A, D, E, F, G. A: There is no cure, only management. B: No surgery will help. C: Dietary fiber must be introduced slow in these patients to avoid increase bloating. D: Low FODMAP will help. E & F: both are helpful therapeutic coaching options. G: yes, symptom relief might be ne

Which of the following is not part of the regular Colorectal Cancer Screening? FIT Test every 2 years, starting at age 50 Colonoscopy every 10 years Start Colonoscopy at the age of 45 If high risk, start screening at the age of 40 Sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, starting at age 50 The correct answer is C. In a normal screen Colonoscopy is every 10 years starting at the age of 50, unless have a first degree relative Dx with CRC under 60, then we screen at age of 40.

Which of the following is false regarding the Lipid digestion and absorption? Fat digestion mostly occurs in the small intestine, starting in the duodenum Lipases are produced by the Gastric Cells in the stomach Bile, secreted by the Gallbladder/Liver, emulsifies fats Generated Bile Salts are mostly excreted The correct answer is D. Bile Salts are usually recycled via reabsorption in the terminal ileum

A 5-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. On examination, the child appears pale and dehydrated. Laboratory tests reveal hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, consistent with a diagnosis of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). What is the appropriate management for this patient? Select all that apply. Fluid resuscitation Antibiotics Blood transfusion Dialysis Antidiarrheals Platelet transfusion The correct options are A), C), and D). Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a potentially life-threatening condition characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. It is most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infection, which is often asso

Which of the following would NOT aid in the classification of chronic diarrhea? >3 bowel movements/day increased stool liquidity duration of < 4 weeks stool weight > 200 g/day likely a noninfectious etiology C) In order to classify diarrhea as chronic the symptoms must have occurred for > 4 weeks. All other answers are true from chronic diarrhea

Which of the following is selective for Ulcerative Colitis but not Crohn’s? No inflammatory process in the GI tract There is an increased risk of colon cancer The depth of inflammation is transmural (all layers of the bowel wall are affected) There are no skip lesions, just continuous colonic involvement of inflammation beginning in rectum D) UC inflammatory changes are continuous and begin at the rectum, Crohn's disease if from "gum to bum" with a patchy appearance and lesions that 'skip' over different parts of the GI tract. A) is wrong such UC and Crohn's are both types of Inflammatory Bowel Disease. B) there is a risk of colon can

Anteriorly the 1st part of the duodenum is in contact with: The pancreas The right kidney The superior mesenteric artery The gall bladder The correct answer is D. The first part of the duodenum has the following relations: Anterior - gallbladder, quadrate lobe of liver; Posterior: bile duct, gastroduodenal artery, portal vein, IVC, pancreas; Superior: gallbladder, hepatoduodenal ligament; Inferior: pancreas, greater omentum.

Which of the following is not found on the transpyloric plane? Pylorus Renal and splenic hila SMA Pancreas 1st part of the duodenum Jejunum Gallbladder The correct answer is F. The jejunum is NOT in the transpyloric plane. This is easy to visualize in an anatomy atlas (or in your head) once you appreciate the relationships of the structures listed. The jejunum is below (inferior to) the transpyloric plane.

The most common cause of acute upper GI bleeding is: Mallory-Weiss tears Malignancy Peptic ulcer disease Varices The correct answer is C. It may be valuable to remember the first 3-4 items in the differential list for UGI bleed. That is, peptic ulcer disease (ulcers in the stomach or duodenum commonly bleed, especially if they penetrate/perforate a blood vessel), esophagitis (irritation of the esophagus, eithe

Which of the following is not a component of the refeeding syndrome? Hyperglycemia Hyperphosphatemia Fluid retention Cardiac arrest The correct answer is B. Hypophosphatemia is seen in the refeeding syndrome, as the high carbohydrate load leads to high phosphate demand resulting in low levels in the blood.

Benefits of breast-feeding a child include Fewer GI, respiratory and ear infections Better intellectual development Protection against food allergies All of the above The correct answer is D. Breastfeeding has a number of benefits, including all of those listed here. Review the lecture on nutrition throughout the life cycle for more information.

Which of the following is true of biliary colic It causes severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain It is provoked by ingestion of fatty foods Is often best diagnosed by a HIDA scan All of the above The correct answer is D. Biliary colic is another term for acute episodes of gallbladder or bile duct pain, such as cholelithiasis or choledocholithiasis. Since it relates to the gallbladder, right upper quadrant pain is a common feature (A) although epigastric pain may occur in its place. Often, th

Which of the following is NOT true of ascending cholangitis Pain, fever and jaundice are common symptoms Septic shock can result ERCP is rarely helpful in treating it It can result from choledocholithiasis The correct answer is C. ERCP is a primary treatment for unblocking the bile duct.

The first line diagnostic procedure of choice for imaging inflammation, obstruction, stones, or other pathology of the gallbladder and/biliary tree Ultrasound ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) HIDA (hepatobiliary imino-diacetic acid) scan MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography) Abdominal x-ray The correct answer is A. A patient reports rectal bleeding. On exam, hemorrhoids prolapse during defecation but reduce spontaneously. What grade are these hemorrhoids? Grade I Grade II Grade III Grade IV The correct answer is B. Deck and Anorectal Disease lecture agree: grade I = no prolapse; grade II = prolapse with spontaneous reduction; grade III = manual reduction; grade IV = irreducible.

A 35-year-old presents with acute severe anal pain after lifting heavy weight yesterday. Exam shows a tender, bluish perianal mass. What is the most appropriate treatment? Rubber band ligation Sitz Bath Excisional thrombectomy Sclerotherapy Colonoscopy The correct answer is C. Deck: painful thrombosed external hemorrhoid → excision within 72 hours; beyond 72 hours, conservative care and sitz baths; banding and sclerotherapy are internal-hemorrhoid treatments. The Anorectal Disease lecture gives the same 72-hour split.

A 68-year-old presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Bowel habits are unchanged and there has been no rectal bleeding. Hb is 92 g/L with a low ferritin, and he has lost 5 kg. Where is a colorectal cancer most likely to be? Rectum Sigmoid colon Descending colon Ascending colon Anal canal The correct answer is D. Right-sided (ascending/cecal) cancers usually present with non-GI signs – iron-deficiency anemia and weight loss ; left-sided and rectal cancers give GI signs (rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, mass on DRE). Anal canal tumours are usually squamous and bleed or hurt.

A 71-year-old on naproxen for knee osteoarthritis has epigastric pain that is worse with meals. Endoscopy shows an ulcer on the lesser curvature of the stomach. What is the most likely cause of this ulcer? H. pylori infection NSAID use Gastrinoma Bile reflux Smoking The correct answer is B. The lecture’s summary: duodenal ulcers are most often caused by H. pylori, gastric ulcers more often by NSAIDs . Management: stop the NSAID, test and treat H. pylori, PPI for 4–8 weeks, and biopsy a gastric ulcer to rule out malignancy.

A 66-year-old passes a large volume of maroon blood per rectum. HR is 124, BP 84/50. After two large-bore IVs, fluids and transfusion, he remains hypotensive. What is the most appropriate next investigation? Colonoscopy after bowel prep Upper endoscopy Tagged RBC scan CT colonography Flexible sigmoidoscopy The correct answer is B. Resuscitate first, then decide by stability: a stable lower bleed → colonoscopy; an unstable one → upper endoscopy (a brisk upper bleed can present as hematochezia) ± angiography and surgical consult. A tagged RBC scan is for a source not found at endoscopy.

A 70-year-old smoker has painless jaundice and 9 kg weight loss. CT shows a 3 cm mass in the head of the pancreas. What is the preferred way to obtain tissue? ERCP with biliary brushings CT-guided percutaneous liver biopsy Serum CA 19-9 level Exploratory laparotomy Endoscopic ultrasound FNA The correct answer is E. The lecture compares the two: ERCP biliary brushings are convenient but low yield (duct cells only, reactive changes); EUS-FNA targets the mass itself with higher yield. CA 19-9 monitors, it does not diagnose. Resectable head tumours go to a Whipple.

A 63-year-old has been in the ICU for 10 days after major trauma surgery and is on vasopressors. He develops fever and RUQ tenderness. Gallstone ileus Gallbladder adenocarcinoma Choledocholithiasis Gangrene and perforation Biliary colic The correct answer is D. Acute acalculous cholecystitis (~10%) occurs in the critically ill or after major surgery (stasis, hypoperfusion) and is more serious than calculous disease – ↑ gangrene and perforation , ↑ morbidity and mortality. A 74-year-old has 5 days of progressive constipation, then no stool or flatus, and distension. AXR shows a colon dilated to 8 cm with a 10 cm cecum and little small-bowel gas. NG tube and observe 48 hours Gastrografin challenge Surgery Colonoscopic decompression Laxatives and enema The correct answer is C. Large bowel obstruction (> 6 cm colon, > 9 cm cecum; #1 cause neoplasm) with a competent ileocecal valve behaves as a closed loop – it cannot decompress back through the small bowel, so surgery is indicated once LBO is diagnosed. An 80-year-old in hospital with pneumonia and hypotension develops crampy left-sided pain and passes bloody stools. There is no peritonitis. Which test will most often establish the diagnosis? Colonoscopy CT angiography Mesenteric angiography Serum lactate Tagged RBC scan The correct answer is A. Low-flow ischemia of the colonic watershed (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) = ischemic colitis : elderly, hospitalized, bloody bowel movements . A 22-year-old man with asthma and seasonal allergies presents with a meat bolus stuck in his esophagus, his third episode of solid-food dysphagia this year. Endoscopy shows vertical furrows and stacked rings. Which finding on biopsy confirms the diagnosis? Candida hyphae Columnar cells with goblet cells > 15 eosinophils per HPF Absent ganglion cells Viral inclusion bodies The correct answer is C. Eosinophilic esophagitis : young males, atopy, food bolus impaction, furrows and rings. Dx = > 15 eosinophils/HPF in the mid esophagus ; treat with PPI, swallowed topical steroids, dilation and food elimination. Goblet-cell metaplasia = Barrett esophagus.

A 64-year-old has LLQ pain and fever for 4 days. CT shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 7 cm pericolic abscess. He is hemodynamically stable with no free air. What is the most appropriate management? Oral antibiotics as an outpatient NSAIDs and follow-up in clinic IV antibiotics and a CT drain Urgent sigmoid resection Urgent colonoscopy and biopsy The correct answer is C. Leeper’s algorithm: uncomplicated → outpatient ; complicated with abscess < 5 cm → admit + IV ABX ; > 5 cm → admit, IV ABX + percutaneous drain ; perforation, shock or failure to resolve → urgent operation. Colonoscopy is not done in the acute attack.

Physiologic jaundice (low UGT1A1 at birth) peaks days 2–5. Jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks needs total and conjugated bilirubin without delay: conjugated hyperbilirubinemia → prompt referral for biliary atresia , where timely Kasai surgery matters. Serum lipase level Plain abdominal x-ray HbA1c and fasting glucose Serum amylase level Endoscopic ultrasound The correct answer is E. Chronic pancreatitis is diagnosed by imaging – there are no good blood tests (lipase/amylase are often normal). CT/MRI is most commonly used; endoscopic ultrasound is the most sensitive. A 58-year-old with compensated cirrhosis has a screening endoscopy showing large esophageal varices that have never bled. What is the most appropriate management? Repeat endoscopy in 1–2 years TIPS placement Octreotide infusion for 5 days Balloon tamponade Beta-blocker or band ligation The correct answer is E. Primary prophylaxis by screening EGD: no varices → repeat in 2–3 years ; small varices → repeat in 1–2 years (NSBB if high risk); large varices → NSBB or endoscopic variceal ligation . Octreotide, tamponade and TIPS are for acute bleeding.

Reabsorption and Secretion Schulich Reviews RBF ~25% of CO ; ~20% of RPF filtered PCT reabsorbs 50–60% of solute + water; Na-coupled glucose/amino acids/phosphate Fanconi = proximal RTA + glucosuria + phosphaturia + aminoaciduria; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors → NaHCO₃ loss TAL: Na-K-2Cl (loop diuretics, Bartter ); K⁺ back-leak → lumen + → paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; loops → urinary Ca loss DCT: Na-Cl (thiazides, Gitelman) ; major site of active Ca reabsorption; thiazides ↓ urinary Ca → Ca stones CD: amiloride/triamterene block principal-cell Na channel; spironolactone = aldosterone antagonist (blood side) Principal cell fails (↓ aldo, K-sparing) → ↑K⁺ + RTA; α-intercalated only → ↓K⁺ + RTA

Sodium Handling by the Kidney Schulich Reviews House's law : ECF volume disorders = Na problems; serum [Na] disorders = water problems RAAS fires in true ECF contraction (hemorrhage, diuretics) and "imagined" (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic) Aldosterone → Na retention, K⁺ secretion, alkalosis; mimics: Conn's, Cushing's, licorice ANP/BNP block CD Na channel → natriuresis; NSAIDs block PGs → Na retention, HTN, renal failure

Hyponatremia and Hypernatremia Schulich Reviews Hypernatremia (Na >144) = water deficit; correct ≤10 mmol/L per day (cerebral edema); oral water or D5W Hyponatremia (Na osm ; normal/high = pseudohyponatremia (glucose, mannitol) Symptomatic → 3% saline first; asymptomatic → fluid restrict, ≤8–10 mmol/L/day SIADH: 0.9% saline can lower Na further (hypotonic to a concentrated urine)

The kidneys purify blood by filtering it and reabsorbing nutrients. Beginning in the glomerulus, what is the correct pathway of ultrafiltrate within the nephron? (note: not all substructures are listed) Glomerulus -> distal tubule -> proximal tubule -> loop of Henle -> collecting duct Glomerulus -> proximal tubule -> distal tubule -> loop of Henle -> collecting duct Glomerulus -> loop of Henle -> distal tubule -> proximal tubule -> collecting duct Glomerulus -> distal tubule -> loop of Henle -> proximal tubule -> collecting duct Glomerulus -> loop of Henle -> proximal tubule -> distal tubule -> collecting duct Glomerulus -> proximal tubule -> loop of Henle -> distal tubule -> collecting duct The correct answer is F. Which of the following changes/hormones would lead to a decreased glomerular filtration rate? Noradrenaline Angiotensin II Prostaglandin secretion Increased heart rate The correct answer is A. Angiotensin II secretion leads to vasoconstriction of the efferent arteriole which increases the GFR. Prostaglandin secretion leads to afferent arteriole dilation and an increase in GFR. Increasing the HR increases the hydrostatic pressure of the blood and contributes to inc

Which of the following statements are correct? Juxtaglomerular cells can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasoconstrict to reduce GFR Juxtaglomerular cells can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasodilate to increase GFR The macula densa can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasoconstrict to reduce GFR The macula densa can detect increased osmolarity of the filtrate and will signal the afferent arteriole to vasodilate to increase GFR The correct answer is C. When the osmolarity of the filtrate is increased, the macula densa (located in the thick ascending loop of Henle) detects this change and signals the afferent arteriole to vasoconstrict to reduce GFR. This feedback mechanism is called the “Tubulo-Glomerular Feedback”.

Which statement below on the RAAS system is true? Aldosterone primarily binds to cells within the juxtaglomerular apparatus Renin reduces blood pressure by ultimately reducing the amount of aldosterone in the blood Aldosterone secretion leads to reabsorption of sodium and water in the kidney, and vasoconstriction Granular cells in the afferent arteriole sense ionic strength of the blood and the macula densa secretes renin The correct answer is C. Granular cells secrete renin, which activates the RAAS pathway leading ultimately to increased aldosterone in the blood. Aldosterone predominantly acts on cells in the collecting duct, by increasing the reabsorption of sodium and water. Aldosterone is also a vasoconstrictor.

The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is affected by several hormones. Which relationship below is true? Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and increase the GFR Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and decreases the GFR Noradrenaline constricts the afferent arteriole and increases the GFR Angiotensin II-receptor antagonists dilate the efferent arteriole and increase the GFR The correct answer is A. Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and increases the GFR. Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) constricts the afferent arteriole and decreases the GFR. Angiotensin II blockade dilates the efferent arteriole and decreases the GFR.

Which of the following regions of the nephron are implicated in excessive calcium excretion in the urine, and what agent can be used to resolve this? Liddle syndrome is a genetic condition that affects the principal cells of the kidney. In patients with Liddle syndrome, the protein channel that allows for the reabsorption of sodium by principal cells is unable to leave the apical membrane, leading to increased sodium reabsorption. What complication is expected in a patient with Liddle syndrome? Hypotension Hyponatremia Volume contraction Hypokalemia The correct answer is D. Increased sodium reabsorption leads to hypernatremia, and consequently hypertension and increased water retention. However, reabsorption of sodium leads to an increased secretion of potassium, which could lead to hypokalemia.

Which of the following options correctly lists the structures the surgeon would need to dissect to access the kidneys using a posterior surgical approach, from most superficial to most deep? Pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, renal capsule Perirenal fat, peritoneum, pararenal fat, renal capsule Pararenal fat, renal capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia Perirenal fat, pararenal fat, peritoneum, renal capsule The correct answer is A. The pararenal fat lies superficial to the renal fascia. The renal fascia encapsulates the kidneys, suprarenal glands and perirenal fat. The renal capsule is the fibrous capsule which sheathes the kidneys.

A patient presents to your office with lateral back pain at the T11 level. After taking a thorough history and performing a physical exam, you suspect this patient may have ureteric stones. Given the region of the radiating pain, which of the following locations would the ureteric stones likely be constricted in? Crossing over the pelvic brim Passing into the wall of the bladder At the renal pelvis In the urethra The correct answer is C. Ureteric pain is characterized by sharp pain in T11-L2 region (loin to groin), and as the stones pass through the ureter the level of pain radiates accordingly given the location in the Ureter. Which statement below is a correct difference between the left and right kidneys? The arteries supplying the left kidney are shorter than those supplying the right kidney The left kidney is more inferior than the right kidney The right renal vein receives deoxygenated blood from the right gonadal vein; the left renal vein does not receive deoxygenated blood from the left gonadal vein The right renal artery runs anterior to the inferior vena cava, whereas the left renal artery runs posterior to the descending aorta The correct answer is A. The aorta sits on the patient’s left side, and the inferior vena cava sits on the patient’s right side. This means that the left renal artery is shorter than the right renal artery, and that the left renal vein is longer than the right renal vein.

Which location is NOT one of the most common sites for a kidney stone to obstruct the ureter? Where the major calyx meets with the minor calyx At the junction of the renal pelvis and the ureter Where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim At the ureteric orifice in the bladder The correct answer is A. There are three natural constrictions in the ureters where kidney stones are likely to obstruct. These are: the junction of the renal pelvis and the ureter, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, and at the ureteric orifice in the bladder.

Outline the correct order of structures that urine passes through from the collecting duct to the bladder. (note: not all substructures are listed.) Collecting duct -> renal pelvis -> major calyx -> ureter -> bladder Collecting duct -> minor calyx -> renal pelvis -> ureter -> bladder Collecting duct -> major calyx -> ureter -> renal -> pelvis -> bladder Collecting duct -> renal column -> renal pelvis -> ureter -> bladder Collecting duct -> minor calyx -> major calyx -> renal column -> bladder The correct answer is B. Urine leaves the renal pyramid and enters the minor calyx. It is then fed into the major calyx, to the renal pelvis, to the ureter. Finally, the ureter connects to the bladder.

Taylor is a 55-year-old female patient presenting to your clinic in a distressed tachypneic state. A physical exam reveals pitting edema to the level of the kneecap. Which of the following statements is likely correct? The patient likely has low serum sodium The patient likely has high serum sodium The patient likely has high interstitial levels of sodium The patient likely has low interstitial levels of sodium. The correct answer is C. The pitting edema of the shin reveals ECF overload which is due to elevated total body sodium. Hyponatremia and Hypernatremia indicate water handling issues and suggest that the patient needs to consume less or more water, respectively.

Use the following options to answer the next FOUR questions. These chemicals inhibit a Na/Cl cotransporter channel in the distal convoluted tubule. Thiazide diuretics Loop diuretics K-sparing diuretics Prostaglandins The correct answer is A. Thiazide diuretics act in the distal convoluted tube and inhibit the Na/Cl cotransporter.

These chemicals inhibit Na/K-ATPase and result in natriuresis Thiazide diuretics Loop diuretics K-sparing diuretics Prostaglandins The correct answer is D.
