A patient with type II diabetes and renal insufficiency is experiencing edema. They are also currently on an ACEi. Which of the following diuretics would be appropriate for them? spironolactone chlorthalidone furosemide amiloride The correct answer is C. Furosemide is a loop diuretic that also increases renal blood flow, which can help with renal insufficiency in this case. Spironolactone and amiloride are K sparing diuretics and aldosterone antagonists, respectively, which could worsen hyperkalemia when used with ACEi. Chlo

A patient had undergone a kidney transplant and experienced a gradual decline in his renal function over 10 years. His creatinine has been steadily rising and the biopsy showed marked interstitial fibrosis. What is appropriate management for this patient i. Pulse with high dose steroids and gradually taper down to maintenance dose ii. Control underlying hypertension and hypercholesterolemia (if present) iii. Switch CNI to sirolimus iv. Initiate thymoglobulin i, ii, iii i, iii ii, iii all of the above The correct answer is A. Underlying HTN, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia worsens interstitial fibrosis, thus it’s important to manage in chronic transplant rejection. CNIs are nephrotoxic and induce fibrosis, so switching to sirolimus (weaker) would decrease scarring. Steroid pulse are used to tr

Which one of the following is FALSE; tacrolimus is more tolerated and effective compared to cyclosporin immunosuppression increases cancer risks Pregnant patients on immunosuppression should replace azathioprine with MMF. 95% of kidney rejections are cell mediated. The correct answer is C. Pregnant patients on immunosuppression should use azathioprine instead of MMF.

Pete is a 42 year old male who presents to your clinic with at 3 day history of nausea, vomiting, edema and muddy brown casts in his urine. He was recently prescribed Cox inhibitors for his chronic back pain. What is at the top of your differential? Nephritic Syndrome Acute interstitial Nephritis due to drug sensitivity Acute glomerulonephritis Acute Tubular Necrosis due to ischemic cause Acute Tubular Necrosis due to a toxic cause The correct answer is D. Given the presence of muddy brown casts in his urine, this patient is most likely presenting with acute tubular necrosis. As COX inhibitors can compromise blood flow, this is an ischemic cause rather than a toxic cause. Common toxic causes include chemotherapy and antibiotic

Which of the following is not an indication for dialysis for a patient with an acute kidney injury? Acidosis Fluid Overload Uremia Hypotension Ingestion of Drugs The correct answer is D. The acute indications for dialysis are Acidosis, Electrolytes (Hyperkalemia), Ingestion of drugs/Ischemia, overload & uremia (AEIOU)

Which of the following is the most common etiology of acute kidney injury in a hospital setting? Prerenal Causes Renal Causes Postrenal Causes The correct answer is B. Renal causes are most common, comprising 45% of AKI hospital admission. 21% of AKI causes are prerenal and 10% are postrenal.

Brian is a 22 year old international student from Taiwan. He presents with a 2 day history of edema, nausea & fatigue. Urinalysis finds 2.3 g of protein in his urine over 24 hours as well as red blood casts. What is at the top of your differential? Good pasture's Syndrome Wegner's granulomatosis Cryoglobulinemia IgA Nephropathy Churg-Strauss Disease Microscopic Polyangitis The correct answer is D. IgA nephropathy. This is the world-wide most common cause of glomerulonephritis & is most common in Asians.

The case. Brian is a 22 year old international student from Taiwan. He presents with a 2 day history of edema, nausea & fatigue. Urinalysis finds 2.3 g of protein in his urine over 24 hours as well as red blood casts. [Continued] Which of the following investigations are key to making this diagnosis? Select all that apply. IgA Levels C-ANCA ASOT IgG levels Biopsy The correct answer is E, A. IgA levels and biopsy are indicated in the diagnosis of IgA nephropathy in an adult.

Which of the following is not a key target to slow down renal disease progression in patients with chronic kidney disease? Blood pressure < 130/80 Dietary protein restriction in a patient with a high protein diet Hyperlipidemia: LDL < 4 Glycemic control: HgB A1C: <7 The correct answer is C. The target LDL level is <2. From 06 - Diabetic Nephropathy and 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease. The lipid target is LDL <2 , so an LDL of 4 is not a goal; it is hyperlipidemia left untreated. A : 130/80 is the BP target in diabetic patients (<140/80 in non-diabetics), usually wi

What is the most common indication for renal replacement therapy in chronic kidney disease? Uremia Refractory hyperkalemia Refractory metabolic acidosis Volume overload Pericarditis The correct answer is A. From 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease and 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The CKD lecture gives the indications for dialysis as AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia) or encephalopathy, "itis" (uremic pericarditis), Overload, Uremia . In CKD the decline is slow, and hyper

Gertrude is a 1st year medical student managing type 1 diabetes. Her LDL is 1.8, her blood pressure is 140/90 and her HgB A1C is 8.1. A 24 hour urine collection finds 90 mg of albumin in her urine and her urine dipstick is negative. Which of the following is not a viable treatment to prescribe? ARB ACE-I Statins SGLT2 inhibitors The correct answer is D. SGLT2 inhibitors should only be prescribed for patients with type 2 Diabetic nephropathy as SGLT2 inhibitors can induce ketoacidosis.

In the natural history of diabetic nephropathy, which of the following is typically the most immediate occurrence following hyperglycemia? Microalbuminuria GFR Decline GFR Elevation Hypoglycemia Proteinuria The correct answer is C. Following hyperglycemia, hormones are released which cause arteriole vasodilation. This causes more blood to enter the glomerulus, resulting in an increased GFR and pressure elevation that damages the glomerular basement membrane. Eventually microalbuminuria and proteinuria

Which of the following structures is not part of the retroperitoneum? 2/3 duodenum Pancreas Ascending colon Descending colon Sigmoid colon The correct answer is E. From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum and Summary Notes - Anatomy (duodenum). The lecture's GI retroperitoneal list is the duodenum, pancreas , ascending colon , descending colon and rectum. The sigmoid colon is not on it: it hangs on its own mesentery (the sigmoid mesoco

Which of the following correctly matches the diaphragmatic aperture with one of the structures that pass through it? Caval Opening: vagal trunks Esophageal Hiatus: right phrenic nerve Aortic Hiatus: thoracic duct The correct answer is C. From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The lecture's three apertures and their contents: the caval opening (T8) carries the IVC and the right phrenic nerve ; the esophageal hiatus (T10) carries the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks ; the aortic hiatus

A 53 year old female presents to the ER with generalized edema. A urinalysis reveals 3+ protein and hypoalbuminemia. You suspect nephrotic syndrome. How would you classify the pattern and type of proteinuria, respectively. Transient, Overflow Orthostatic, Glomerular Persistent, Tubular Persistent, Glomerular The correct answer is D. Persistent proteinuria indicates there is an underlying systemic disease, in this case nephrotic syndrome. This would also be considered glomerular proteinuria because albumin is inappropriately being filtered and excreted.

A 60 year old arrives at the ER with edema and decreased urine output. You measure her BP as 180/90. You order a urinalysis which reports 1+ proteinuria. Urine microscopy also reveals RBC casts. You order an urgent kidney biopsy which reports cresenteric glomerulonephritis. What treatment would you give to this patient? Select all that apply Supportive therapy is all that is needed Prednisone IV cyclophosphamide Dialysis The correct answer is B, C. This patient has rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. This is treated with prednisone, IV cyclophosphamide, and plasmapheresis if there is pulmonary hemorrhage from Goodpastures disease to remove antibodies

Which of the following are nonrenal factors that increase BUN? GI bleeding Corticosteroids Congestive Heart Failure Protein malnutrition Cirrhosis The correct answer is A, B, C. From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. BUN depends on how much urea is made and how much is reabsorbed , not just on GFR. The lecture's BUN:Cr table puts GI bleeding (a protein load digested from blood) and heart failure (hypoperfusion; a sodium-avid kidney reabsorbs

Which of the following is a contraindication to a renal biopsy? Select all that apply. Solitary kidney Transplanted kidney End stage renal failure Hyperkalemia The correct answer is A, C. From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. The lecture's contraindications include a solitary kidney (a bleed could cost the only kidney) and end-stage renal disease (small scarred kidneys; the diagnosis no longer changes management). The others on the list are an uncoopera

Which of the following is NOT a predisposing factor for testicular cancer: Cryptorchidism Atrophic testes Testicular trauma History of testicular cancer The correct answer is C. Trauma does not contribute to the development of testicular cancer.

Anh comes to your clinic complaining a gradual onset of pain in his scrotal area, which appears swollen and feels firm on palpation. A scrotal ultrasound shows increased blood flow to the area. What is your top differential diagnosis? Testicular torsion Orchitis Hydrocele Spermatocele The correct answer is B. Orchitis, or infection/inflammation of the testes presents with all of the mentioned symptoms. Testicular torsion generally has acute onset with decreased blood flow. Hydrocele presents with tense or fluctuant scrotum, and spermatocele is generally asymptomatic and feels lik

What is the correct first step for approaching Stage 1 hypertension in children? Rule out white coat hypertension Rule out secondary etiologies Decide on intervention Treat with medication The correct answer is A. Ruling out white coat hypertension is done first by doing a home BP measurement. Ruling out secondary etiologies is next by conducting additional investigations (eg. TSH, serum creatinine). The choice of intervention will come after the first two have been done.

How can you distinguish between post-infectious glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, and C3 glomerulopathy? Post-infectious GN is recurrent while the other two aren’t Post-infectious GN is not recurrent while the other two are Post-infectious GN and IgA nephropathy are recurrent while C3 glomerulopathy isn’t Post-infectious GN and IgA nephropathy are not recurrent while C3 glomerulopathy is The correct answer is B. C3 glomerulopathy also can recur even after transplant.

Which of the following is NOT an indication to circumcise in a patient with phimosis: Recurrent balanitis Failed medical therapy Prolonged phimosis Phimosis caused by trauma The correct answer is D. Trauma is a potential cause of phimosis but is not in itself a reason to circumcise.

What is a potential treatment for nocturnal enuresis associated with heavy sleepers? Nighttime alarm Anticholinergic ddAVP Surgery The correct answer is A. While heavy sleep-associated enuresis is very difficult to treat, behavioural modifications and night time alarms is the recommended approach.

Which of the following statements about pelvic vasculature is FALSE? The rectum blood supply drains into both the systemic circulation and the portal circulation The testicular/ovarian arteries are branches off the anterior division of the internal iliac artery The medial umbilical ligament is occluded after birth The internal pudendal artery exits through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle The pelvic venous plexuses are valveless, which allows metastases to spread in many different directions The correct answer is B. The testicular/ovarian arteries are the gonadal arteries. These arteries branch off the abdominal aorta, not the internal iliac arteries. This is because the gonads develop higher up in retroperitoneum and later descend into the scrotum or pelvis.

Which of the following structures does NOT exit through the greater sciatic foramen? Sciatic nerve Superior gluteal nerve External iliac artery Inferior gluteal nerve Internal pudendal artery The correct answer is C. The external iliac artery exits the pelvis anteriorly and enters the lower limb posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament. All of the other structures listed exit the pelvis posteriorly through the greater sciatic foramen.

During childbirth the mother must pass a baby (or babies, as well as the placenta(s)) through her cervix. The pain associated with childbirth is almost comparable to when a man has a man-cold. Through which of the following pathways would the mother experience cervical pain? Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with sympathetics to lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with sympathetics to sacral spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes Somatic sensory afferents travel directly from the cervix to the spinal cord, and pain is perceived exactly where it is felt Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with parasympathetics to lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes Visceral sensory afferents from the cervix travel retrograde with parasympathetics to sacral spinal levels, and the pain is referred to these dermatomes The correct answer is E. The cervix falls below the pelvic pain line. Visceral sensory afferents from structures below the pelvic pain line are unique in that they travel retrograde with parasympathetics to the sacral spinal cord. When the painful stimulus reaches the brain, it is perceived as comin

Which of the following statements about sexual development is FALSE? The paramesonephric duct persists in females and becomes the uterus and part of the vagina The testis-determining factors is the product of the SRY gene and is responsible for differentiation of the gonads into the testes The mesonephric duct degenerates in males The gonads are derived from the gonadal ridge, which itself is derived from intermediate mesoderm In females, the labioscrotal swellings remain unfused during development and become the labia majora The correct answer is C. The mesonephric duct persists in males as part of the genital tract.

Which of the following statements regarding urinary tract infections (UTIs) is FALSE? UTIs are one of the most common reasons for patients presenting to primary care Common causative organisms include E. coli and S. saprophyticus UTIs are common infections in the elderly, particularly those living in long-term care homes Examples of first line antibiotic choices include nitrofurantoin and TMP/SMX Urine culture is important in the workup for a young female patient presenting with typical UTI symptoms The correct answer is E. Urine culture is unnecessary in typical simple UTIs. The causative agent is likely to be susceptible to a first-line antibiotic, so it is standard to immediately begin treatment with antibiotics. Urine culture will delay treatment and also increase unnecessary costs. If a UT

Which of the following statements regarding antibiotic use in UTIs is TRUE? Septra (TMP/SMX) is the best option for UTIs because of low antimicrobial resistance Asymptomatic bacteriuria is a benign condition that never requires treatment Patients who experience recurrent UTIs can be given antibiotics prophylactically Antibiotics are first line treatment for a patient with delirium Male patients should always automatically receive IV antibiotics The correct answer is C. Prophylactic antibiotics are helpful for patients who have recurrent UTIs, which is defined as 2 or more uncomplicated UTIs within 6 months or 3 positive urine cultures within 12 months. Septra (TMP/SMX) is not as effective as some other antibiotics for treating UTIs because

Which of the following is NOT a cause of urinary retention? Prostate cancer Neurogenic bladder BPH Kidney stones Urethral strictures The correct answer is D. Urinary retention is the inability to void urine. Kidney stones do not cause urinary retention because they do not block the passage of urine from the bladder out through the urethra.

Which clinical or laboratory finding is NOT associated with bladder outlet obstruction? Oliguria/anuria Flank pain Proteinuria Elevated serum BUN and creatinine Urinary tract infection The correct answer is C. Proteinuria indicates a problem with the glomerulus and is not associated with urinary outflow obstruction.

Which of the following statements about benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is FALSE? Important points on patient history include dysuria, frequency, and nocturia Digital rectal exam should be performed to assess for prostate size and nodularity Patient quality of life due to urinary symptoms should be considered when assessing their need for BPH treatment BPH is very common and affects over 50% of men over age 60 PSA is not helpful in the assessment of BPH The correct answer is E. PSA can be used as a surrogate marker of prostate size; larger prostates produce more PSA, which can be measured as elevated serum PSA levels. Serum PSA can be measured and compared over time to track prostate enlargement.

Which of the following statements regarding the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is correct? A man with a small prostate and mild lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) should be given 5-α reductase inhibitors A man with a large prostate and severe LUTS that significantly impair his life should undergo radical prostatectomy A man with a small prostate and severe LUTS that significantly impair his life should be given the option of α-blockers or surgery A man with a large prostate and severe LUTS that do not cause him significant impairment should undergo surgery A man with a small prostate and severe LUTS that do not cause him significant impairment should be given 5-α reductase inhibitors The correct answer is C. Refer to the CUA Guidelines for the Management of BPH Therapeutic Algorithm.

Which of the following statements regarding prostate cancer screening is FALSE? PSA screening should be discussed with all men over 50 years old The role of PSA screening is controversial; North American and European guidelines differ All men over the age of 70 should be offered a DRE and PSA screening Prostate cancer screening does not require any imaging PSA and DRE are used for screening; prostate cancer can only be definitively diagnosed with a prostate biopsy The correct answer is C. Men over the age of 70 are not offered routine screening for prostate cancer. This is because a diagnosis of prostate cancer would not change their management. By a similar line of thought, men with less than 10 years of life expectancy are not offered PSA screening.

A 51M patient undergoes active surveillance for his low-risk prostate cancer. Unfortunately, his PSA doubling time has increased, suggesting that the tumor volume is progressing. The patient has ulcerative colitis and Lupus and refuses to have open surgery. Given this information, which of the following is the best management strategy? Watchful waiting; do not initiate treatment Insist that an open radical prostatectomy is the most appropriate management option Help the patient decide between brachytherapy and laparoscopic prostatectomy Help the patient decide between laparoscopic prostatectomy and external beam radiation Help the patient decide between brachytherapy, laparoscopic prostatectomy, and external beam radiation The correct answer is C. This is a challenging question. An open radical prostatectomy does not align with the patient’s desire to avoid surgery. External beam radiation is not appropriate for patients with IBD or Lupus (or in this case, both!), as it can cause proctitis. Laparoscopic prostatectomy

You are a radiologist. It is a lovely spring day and you are in a dark room reviewing a variety of images of renal masses. Which of the following radiological findings is most suggestive of renal cell carcinoma? A single mass with smooth borders and solid elements A small, exophytic solid mass that is strongly enhancing with contrast administration A small, non-invasive fatty mass A mildly enhancing, blood-filled mass with smooth borders and septa The correct answer is B. Options A and D are descriptions of renal cysts, which can be hyperdense (i.e. filled with blood or protein). Option C is an angiomyolipoma. Option B is most likely a renal cell carcinoma because it enhances brightly with contrast. However, this is not true in all cases.

Harry Styles presents with a localized renal cell carcinoma. After a brief period of active surveillance, he decides that he opts for surgical removal of the mass. Which of the following is NOT a minimally invasive surgical option? Radical nephrectomy and ipsilateral adrenal gland removal Laparoscopic partial nephrectomy Cryoablation Radiofrequency ablation The correct answer is A. A radical nephrectomy involves removing the kidney outside of Gerota’s fascia. This is a open surgery, and therefore, is not minimally invasive.

You are a clinical clerk shadowing a urologist. Which of the following patients’ presentations is the most concerning for urinary tract cancer? A 55F teacher with a 1-week history of lower urinary tract symptoms A 22M mechanic with left flank pain, microscopic hematuria, and nausea and vomiting A 71F hairdresser with gross, painless hematuria with stringy clots and back pain A 74M truck driver with gross hematuria and BPH who takes anticoagulants for his atrial fibrillation The correct answer is C. Gross hematuria with stringy clots is a common finding in upper urinary tract cancer. Although males are at a slightly higher risk than females, the final patients presentation is more in keeping with his use of anticoagulation and previous diagnosis of BPH. This patient’s o

On the second day of your family medicine rotation, you see a patient with gross hematuria. After a thorough history and physical exam, bladder cancer is at the top of your top differential diagnosis. What are your next steps? (Select all that apply) Urine microscopy Urine culture Ureteroscopy Refer to urology Cystoscopy Urine cytology Pelvic MRI Core needle biopsy of local lymph nodes Bloodwork for a CBC, creatinine and electrolytes Renal ultrasound The correct answer is A, B, D, F, I, J. All of these investigations are part of the initial work up for suspected bladder cancer. Referral to a urologist is key; they will rule out benign causes and characterize malignant disease. A ureteroscopy, cystoscopy and core needle biopsy may be ordered by a

Which of the following are not voiding symptoms? Weak stream Incontinence Straining to void Hesitancy The correct answer is B. Incontinence is a storage symptom. Voiding symptoms include: Weak stream, Intermittent voiding, Straining to void, Hesitancy, Emptying incompletely, Double voiding (WISHED). Storage symptoms include: Frequency, Urgency, Nocturia, and Incontinence.

Which of the following are not really effective for stress incontinence? Pelvic floor muscle therapy Behavioral modification (fluid restriction) Medical therapy Surgical therapy The correct answer is C. Medical treatment is not really effective for stress incontinence. Surgical therapy is the mainstay of treatment if conservative therapy is ineffective. Surgical therapy commonly done is midurethral sling .

55 year old Judy was recently diagnosed with urgency incontinence. What type of pharmacotherapy is recommended for urgency incontinence? a-blocker 5-a Reductase Inhibitor Anticholinergics Beta blocker The correct answer is C. For urgency incontinence, anti-cholinergics such as oxybutynin can be prescribed to block the muscarinic receptors in the bladder.

The case. 55 year old Judy was recently diagnosed with urgency incontinence. (Continuation of question 3) What type of side effects can be experienced with the drug prescribed for Judy? Dry mouth Dry eyes Constipation GI upset All of the above The correct answer is E. Anti-cholinergics are associated with side effects including: dry mouth, dry eyes, constipation, GI upset (think of SLUDGE!).

What is a gold standard imaging used to rule-in/out renal or urinary stones? Ultrasound CT KUB IVP MRI The correct answer is B. Non-contrast CT KUB (Kidneys, Ureters, Bladder) is the gold standard imaging technique to rule in/out renal stones.

Tyler is an 18-year-old male, who was incidentally found to have 2 mm ureteric stone. He is asymptomatic. As his doctor, how would you proceed? Surgical intervention Percutaneous nephrolithotomy Encourage fluid intake and reassure him that it is likely going to pass Shock wave lithotripsy Ureteroscopy The correct answer is C. Stones <4mm will pass 90% of the times without intervention.

The case. Tyler is an 18-year-old male, who was incidentally found to have 2 mm ureteric stone. He is asymptomatic. (Continuation of question 6) What if Tyler was presenting with fever and/or symptoms of UTI? Surgical intervention Shock wave lithotripsy Ureteroscopy Conservative therapy The correct answer is A. Fever/UTI is an indication for surgical intervention as it can lead to sepsis.

True or False: Thiazides commonly causes hypercalcemia. True False The correct answer is B. False. Although thiazide diuretics can be helpful in reabsorbing Ca2+ from urine back into bloodstream, it’s not a common cause of hypercalcemia. Which type of stones form in high urine pH? Calcium oxalate Calcium phosphate Uric acid calculi Cystine Stones The correct answer is B. Calcium phosphate stones precipitate in high urine pH. Uric stones and Cystine stones form in low urine pH – and thus therapeutic approach for uric and cystine stones include urinary alkalinization (raise urine pH!).

What is false about hemodialysis? Fistula is optimal. From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The AV fistula is the optimal access. Finish the sentence: Peritoneal dialysis... Is more expensive than hemodialysis Uses the deepest layer of abdominal skin as dialyzer Decreases patient autonomy Involves cardiovascular disease as its main complication The correct answer is D. From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. As with hemodialysis, most patients on peritoneal dialysis eventually die of cardiovascular disease . That is the sense in which it is the "main" complication: peritonitis is the commoner acute one. A : PD is less expensive than hemodia

True or False: Transplantation involves putting the patient on complete immunosuppression to prevent organ rejection. True False The correct answer is B. It’s not complete immunosuppression, there is a balance.

True or False: Transplantation can lead to many complications, such as diabetes and cancers. True False The correct answer is A. From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. True. The lecture's transplant complications are rejection, surgical anastomotic problems, infection (CMV, herpes), cancer from immunosuppression (lymphoma, skin cancer), cardiovascular disease, and drug side effects. Autoimmune diseases often affect the glomerulus. Where in the kidney should a biopsy be done in order to observe glomeruli? The capsule The medulla The cortex The ureter Answer C. In terms of gross kidney anatomy, the kidney consists of the capsule, the medulla, and the cortex. The glomeruli are situated in the cortex while the tubules and calices are found within the medulla. For more information, see the lecture “The Functional Anatomy of the Kidney”

Which of the following is part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus? The macula densa of the afferent arteriole The extraglomerularmesangial cells The renin producing granular cells of the efferent arteriole The macula densa of the thin descending limb Answer B. The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) consists of: the macula densa of the thick ascending limb, the extraglomerularmesangial cells, and the granular cells of the afferent arteriole. For more information, see the lecture “The Functional Anatomy of the Kidney”

For more information, see the lectures “The Functional Anatomy of the Kidney” and “Histology of the Kidney”

This set of kidneys become the “permanent” kidneys in humans and is functional by 12 weeks of fetal development. They develop from the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesoderm. What is the antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning? Activated charcoal Sodium bicarbonate Flumazenil Fomepizole Answer D. Fomepizole is given in cases of methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning. Activated charcoal is not very effective at absorbing alcohols so it is usually not indicated. Francis, a 65-year-old man, was brought to the emergency room by his son who discovered him passed out in the garage. The following blood values were obtained: pH: 7.30 PCO2: 28 Na+: 141 K+: 4.6 HCO3-: 12 Cl-: 102 Osmolarity: 330 Glucose: 5 BUN: 7.1 What acid-base disorder does Francis have? Respiratory acidosis Respiratory alkalosis Metabolic acidosis Metabolic alkalosis Answer C. First, look at the pH given. It’s below normal (7.4) so we know it is an acidosis. In acidosis either PCO2 is high (greater than 40 mmHg—respiratory acidosis) or HCO3- is low (less than 24 mEq/L—metabolic acidosis). In metabolic acidosis, acid gain or bicarbonate loss should result in a 1:1 equivalent reduction in PCO2 in healthy people with no other acid-base abnormalities. The formula for anion gap is:= [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) AG = (141) – ((102) + (12))\ = 27 For more information, see the lecture “Acid-Base Physiology”.

The case. Francis, a 65-year-old man, was brought to the emergency room by his son who discovered him passed out in the garage. The following blood values were obtained: pH: 7.30 PCO2: 28 Na+: 141 K+: 4.6 HCO3-: 12 Cl-: 102 Osmolarity: 330 Glucose: 5 BUN: 7.1 What is Francis’ osmolar gap? A) 36 B) 34 C) 42 D) 40 Answer A. The formula to calculate the expected osmolality of blood is: Osmolality = 2(Na+) + BUN + glucose = 2(141) + 7.1 + 5 = 294 The difference between the expected (294, given in the question) and his actual osmolality (330) is 36. For more information, see the lecture “Acid-Base Physiology”.

Renal artery stenosis Dehydration Conn syndrome Hydrochlorothiazide use Malignant hypertension The correct answer is C. The patient has hypokalemia and hypernatremia along with metabolic alkalosis. The key is in the aldosterone: renin ratio. A high ratio indicates an increase in aldosterone that’s not due to activation of the RAAS system. Therefore, Conn syndrome or primary hyperaldosteronism

A 53-year-old woman comes into the ER due to severe diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. She recently was on a cruise to the Caribbean. Her medications include: ramipril and spironolactone for her hypertension, crestor for her hypercholesterolemia, ibuprofen for her chronic back pain, and prophylactic heparin to prevent DVT (she has a positive history for recurrent DVTs). On investigation, her creatinine is 90, Na 143, K 2.0, Cl 111, HCO3 20, albumin 38. Which of the following contributed to her hypokalemia? ACEI Ibuprofen Spironolactone Diarrhea Crestor The correct answer is D. Diarrhea caused volume contraction leading to aldosterone secretion which led to acute K+ loss. ACEI/Spironolactone/NSAIDs all prevent K+ excretion (might lead to hyperkalemia). Cristor (a statin) has no significant effect on K+. In this case the acute and severe diarrhea PL

Addison’s disease Undiagnosed diabetes Beta blocker use Pseudohyperkalemia Digoxin use The correct answer is D. Since investigations are all normal, it is slightly odd to have such a high potassium level without changes in other values. From 13 - IV Fluids. The lecture sorts IV fluids by what is dissolved in the water. Which of the following is correct? The kidneys not only filter waste, they are also responsible for bone metabolism, erythropoiesis, and blood pressure control Cirrhosis can increase the blood urea nitrogen Vigorous exercise decreases creatinine As soon as GFR decreases, you will see a change in the creatinine BUN/Cr ratio of >60 indicates volume contraction The correct answer is A. Cirrhosis decreases BUN, vigorous exercise increases creatinine, GFR has to decrease ~50% before you’ll see a change in creatinine, BUN/Cr ratio of >80 indicates volume contraction.

True or false: the number one cause of renal failure is diabetes. True. From 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease. True. The lecture ranks the major causes of CKD as #1 diabetes (diabetic nephropathy), #2 essential hypertension, #3 glomerulonephritis, with polycystic kidney disease the commonest genetic cause of ESRD. It is important to image his kidneys to see if there is an obstruction and if so, where is the obstruction. Renal US, intravenous pyelogram, retrograde pyelogram, and Lasix renogram are all possible imaging modalities to use.

The case. An 82 yo man presents to the ER with suprapubic pain. He’s experienced anuria for 18 hours. After insertion of the Foley catheter, you notice the patient’s urine output is 8L in 12 hours. This makes you concerned for: central diabetes insipidus Excess water intake UTI Post obstructive diuresis Electrolyte abnormalities The correct answer is D. When someone has urinary retention for prolonged period of time and it is suddenly relieved, diuresis of the excess urea and water occurs. In which of the following part of the nephron do osmotic diuretics exert their greatest effect? Distal Convoluted Tubule Proximal Convoluted Tubule Ascending Loop of Henle Collecting Ducts Bowman’s capsule Answer B. Osmotic diuretics act by promoting the movement of water into the collecting system via osmosis. They exert their major function in the PCT (B) but also act on the descending Loop of Henle.

Camilla is 6 years old. Camilla’s mother brings her to the family doctor’s office because she has been having “accidents”. She was successfully toilet trained at age 2 ½ years but for the past 4 months she has been having trouble controlling her bladder when she is distracted such as when she is playing with friends or if she is in an unfamiliar environment. What type of enuresis does Camilla have? Primary nocturnal enuresis Primary diurnal enuresis Secondary nocturnal enuresis Secondary diurnal enuresis The correct answer is D. Secondary diurnal enuresis – Nocturnal enuresis occurs solely at night while diurnal has adaytime component. Primary enuresis occurs if a child has never had a period without enuresis while secondary enuresis occurs after a 6 month dry period. Thus, Camilla has secondary diu

Which of the following are options in the management of nocturnal enuresis? Bedwetting alarms Desmopressin Watchful waiting All of the above Answer D. All of the above – A bedwetting alarm sounds when it senses moisture and is effective within 6 weeks of initiation, desmopressin is synthetic antidiuretic hormone which causes urinary retention, and since the majority of children will outgrow bedwetting, treatment is often delayed unless t

Which of the following factors, if present during pregnancy, reduces the number of nephrons that the fetus develops? Prematurity Insulin resistance Obesity Intrauterine growth restriction All of the above Answer E. All of the factors listed reduce the number of nephrons that the fetus develops. Other factors include maternal ACEI or glucocorticoid use, or intrauterine hypoxia. Most nephrons are produced in the third trimester.

Which of the following problems during pregnancy can lead to fetal compression syndrome? Maternal diabetes Renal agenesis Infection during pregnancy Esophageal atresia Anencephaly Answer B. Renal agenesis leads to oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid) which in turn can cause fetal compression syndrome. Maternal diabetes, infection, esophageal atresia, and anencephaly can all lead to polyhydramnios.

On an ECG, peaked T waves that are greater than 2/3 the height of the QRS complex suggest that the patient is hyperkalemic. For more information, see the lecture “Introduction and Case of the Week.”

A 64-year-old male comes into your nephrology clinic referred by their family doctor. On a routine checkup, the family doc found 3+ proteinuria in the patient’s urine as well as hypoalbuminemia. An 80-year-old patient presents with acute kidney injury. Her BUN is 7 and Cr is 200. Urinalysis shows WBCs. Which of the following is considered the gold standard for detecting proteinuria? 24-Hour Urine Collection Urinalysis Protein/Creatinine Ratio Urine Protein Electrophoresis Excessively frothy urine Answer A. 24 hour urine collection is the most accurate measure because it takes into account GFR changes and other factors that can cause protein excretion to fluctuate during the day or in a single sample. Which of the following is NOT a criteria for the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome? Proteinuria >3.5 g/day Generalized Edema Hypoalbuminemia Hypolipidemia Answer D. In response to low protein levels, the liver increases the production of lipoproteins, resulting in hyperlipidemia. Which of the following is NOT a primary nephrotic syndrome? Minimal Change Disease Amyloidosis Membranous Nephropathy Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis Answer B. Amyloidosis, along with diabetes, is a secondary cause of nephrotic syndrome.

Which of the following diuretics would you give to a patient with hyperkalemia. Spironolactone Furosemide Triamterene Amiloride Isosorbide The correct answer is B. Furosemide is a loop diuretic that can cause potassium wasting which can be helpful in a patient with hyperkalemia. Spironolactone is potassium sparing (leading to hyperkalemia).

You are assessing a patient with a 25 year history of diabetes and 10 year history of poorly managed hypertension. Which of the following tests is most important to diagnose diabetic nephropathy? Which of the following is NOT a feature of diabetic nephropathy? Persistent proteinuria Progressive decline in GFR Hypertension History of poorly managed diabetes Occasional hematuria Answer E. Hematuria is not found in diabetic nephropathy, the pathologic changes cause proteinuria and decline in GFR. Which of the following is incorrect regarding proteinuria detection and quantification? The gold standard test for quantification is a 24 hour urine collection. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio can be multiplied by 15 to calculate the amount of protein in the urine. The correct answer is B. is incorrect as urinalysis is only semiquantitative as it only detects proteinuria of > 300 mg/day and it is also heavily influenced by urinary concentration.

Which of the following statements about microscopic hematuria is FALSE? It may have benign causes like menstruation, vigorous exercise, sexual activity, viral illness or urinary tract infections. An individual with microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts, dysmorphia and elevated serum creatinine should be evaluated for primary renal disease. If no benign causes for microscopic hematuria are found and the patient has a normal urinalysis and renal function then the patient does not need further investigation. Certain medications like aminoglycosides, cyclophosphamide, and diuretics can cause microscopic hematuria. Microscopic hematuria is defined as ≥ 2 RBC/hpf on 2 separate urinalyses without recent exercise, menses, sexual activity or instrumentation. Answer C. The patient described here should have a referral to urology to further examine the cause of their hematuria. All other statements are true.

Which of the following is a common cause of glomerular microscopic hematuria? IgA nephropathy Nephrolithiasis Pyelonephritis Papillary necrosis Prostatitis Answer A. This is the only listed cause that leads to bleeding at the glomerulus. The other causes are non-glomerular in the upper and lower urinary tract.

Which of the following statements is true about kidney disease in children. Compared to adults, children have a much lower incidence of chronic kidney disease. The incidence of chronic kidney disease in children is falling. Answer A. Children have a lower incidence of chronic kidney disease, a lower incidence of acquired kidney disease and a higher incidence of abnormalities of the urinary tract when compared to adults. When diagnosing nephrotic syndrome in children, when is a biopsy performed? After 28 days if the symptoms haven’t resolved. Upon presentation before treatment is initiated. Upon presentation, immediately before starting the child on corticosteroids and then changing or eliminating the corticosteroids if needed. If there is no response after treatment with corticosteroids for 28 days. You do not need to perform a biopsy in children, nephrotic syndrome is always due to minimal change disease which responds well to corticosteroids. Answer D. Minimal change disease is so common (70-90%) and exquisitely steroid sensitive that you treat with corticosteroids for 28 days before doing a biopsy. 28 days is based on the maximal sensitivity and specificity of time to remission.

Henry has an eGFR of 42, which stage of chronic kidney failure does her fall into? CKD is classified as 5 stages: I – GFR >90 II – GFR is 60-89 III – GFR is 30-59 IV – GFR is 15-29 V – GFR <15 Once at stage 3, the patient is at risk for irreversible progression of their renal impairment.

A 42-year-old man presents to the ER with severe flank pain and oliguria. What is a good screening test to narrow down your differential diagnosis? Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for prostate cancer? Family history Presence of androgens Advancing age African ancestry Smoking History The correct answer is E. family history, androgens, advanced age, and African ancestry are all risk factors for prostate cancer.

A 55-year-old man presents with obstructive urinary symptoms for 3 months. He has a family history of prostate cancer in his father and father’s brother. Androgen deprivation Chemotherapy (taxotere) Radical prostatectomy Radiotherapy Transrectal ultrasound biopsy of the prostate Answer E. A biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis and grade the tumor with a Gleason score.

A 76-year-old male presents to his GP with obstructive urinary symptoms. CT scan is needed to assess local spread. It would be important to visualize local lymph nodes and organs for any metastases that may be present. Which of the following is an acute side effect of radiation for locally advanced prostate cancer? Avascular necrosis Increased risk of hip fracture Hematuria Infertility Vascular based impotence Answer C. Hematuria is the only acute side effect listed, all the rest are potential late side effects of radiation.

Paul Ekins is a 64-year-old man that recently underwent radical prostatectomy for his prostate cancer (Gleason score= 7). What is the most appropriate management for this patient? This patient is eligible for radiation salvage therapy as he is likely to recover and has no evidence of systemic metastases from his cancer. Surgery is rarely repeated and hormone therapy is primarily used when there is metastatic recurrence.

Where does transitional cell carcinoma most commonly occur? Bladder Renal pelvis Ureters Urethra Prostate Answer A. Transitional cell carcinoma infrequently metastasizes to bone. Anaplasia found in situ often becomes invasive and metastatic. It is most likely to be diagnosed at a lower stage. Transitional cell carcinoma has a variable prognosis. Answer D. Transitional cell carcinoma is more likely to be diagnosed at a higher stage (more invasion). Visible urethral cancer is usually transitional cell carcinoma. Answer E. The histology found depends on the location of the cancer and can be transitional cell, squamous cell or adenocarcinoma.

A 19-year-old male presents to the emergency room with sudden onset of severe pain in his left testicle. On exam the left testicle is hard and extremely tender to palpation. A long-term care nurse calls about a 92-year-old woman with dementia who has been more agitated and confused for a week. She has no dysuria, no frequency, no fever and is incontinent at baseline. Bacteriuria is common in this population, and bacteriuria should not be treated in long-term care patients without urinary symptoms ; there is no evidence that treating it improves delirium or confusion, and reflex testing drives unnecessary antibiotics and resistance. An elderly man with acute urinary retention is catheterised and several litres of urine are drained. Over the next 24 hours his urine output is 12 L. What is the most likely explanation? Post-obstructive diuresis follows relief of complete bilateral ureteral or bladder outlet obstruction and is characterised by a large-volume diuresis. It is usually mild and self-limiting but occasionally life-threatening, so monitor fluids and electrolytes.

Urinary retention is a BPH-related complication and an indication for surgery , as are bladder calculi, recurrent UTI, recurrent hematuria from the prostate, upper-tract damage and failed or intolerable medical therapy. TURP is the gold-standard surgical therapy.

Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Both types are diagnosed by the same glucose thresholds — what separates them is the mechanism producing the hyperglycemia : absolute autoimmune insulin deficiency in type 1 vs. a spectrum of insulin resistance and relative deficiency in type 2. The lecture takes type 1 first, then the diagnostic cut-offs, then type 2 and its eight defects. ⭐ the alpha cells are spared in T1DM — the lesion is beta-cell specific. Autoantibody count, not presence, is what carries risk (1 = background risk, 3 = 40% in five years). Glutamic acid decarboxylase is the specific marker. Monozygotic concordance is higher in T2DM (90%) than T1DM (50%) — the counterintuitive fact worth remembering. And the octet explains why T2DM needs combination therapy : each drug class corrects a different defect. 1. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM): the mechanism Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) = immune-mediated destruction of islet beta cells → absolute insulin deficiency glucagon -producing alpha cells are SPARED Consequence of ↓ insulin ① glucose cannot be used → stays in blood ② body senses "starvation" → glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis release more glucose Genetics mostly polygenic ; genes both within and outside the major histocompatibility complex risk with family: 50% monozygotic twin · 5% non-identical sibling · 0.4% no family history 2. Autoantibodies in type 1 Present in up to 85% insulin/proinsulin (often appears after starting exogenous insulin) glutamic acid decarboxylase — most specific marker , in 70% insulinoma-associated protein 2 · zinc transporter 8 Risk depends on the count, not the presence 1 antibody alone does NOT ↑ risk above baseline (~0.4%) ; 2 = 25% in 5 years, 3 = 40% 3. Diagnosing prediabetes and diabetes The same thresholds for both types; prediabetes is the grey zone between normal and diabetes. Test Normal Prediabetes ( dysglycemia ) Diabetes Fasting plasma glucose 6.1–6.9 = impaired fasting glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 7.8–11.0 = impaired glucose tolerance ≥ 11.1 mmol/L Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) 6.0–6.4% ≥ 6.5% (adults) Random plasma glucose — — ≥ 11.1 mmol/L Fasting = no caloric intake for at least 8 hours · random = any time of day, regardless of the last meal HbA1c is not used to diagnose suspected type 1 diabetes 4. Stages of type 1 diabetes Staged, all with beta-cell autoimmunity: the number of working beta cells falls across the stages Stage 1 normoglycemia, pre-symptomatic Stage 2 dysglycemia , pre-symptomatic Stage 3 dysglycemia , symptomatic e.g. a child with anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase + anti-insulin antibodies and a fasting glucose of 6.5 mmol/L = stage 2 Stages 1 to 3 of type 1 diabetes: functional beta-cell mass falls long before symptoms appear 5. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) = a spectrum: predominant insulin resistance with relative deficiency ↔ predominant secretory defect with resistance no autoimmunity · no autoantibodies indolent prodrome of dysglycemia lasting years parallels the obesity epidemic (1980 → 2045: 108 million → 700 million) Genetics : mostly polygenic 90% monozygotic twin · 40% have an affected parent · 5–10% ↑ lifetime risk with a 1st-degree relative Type 1 Type 2 Mechanism Autoimmune beta-cell destruction → absolute deficiency Insulin resistance + relative deficiency Autoantibodies Up to 85% None — no autoimmunity Monozygotic twin concordance 50% 90% Course Stages 1 → 3 Years of dysglycemia Result Hyperglycemia from the starvation response Same net hyperglycemia, produced by the eight defects below 6. The "Ominous Octet" The "Ominous Octet" — eight defects driving T2DM hyperglycemia . Each is a drug target , which is why it is worth memorising in this direction. 02 Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes

Approach to New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes The whole diagnosis turns on one question: are symptoms present? If yes, a single abnormal glucose is sufficient — do not delay treatment for a confirmatory test. The lecture runs symptoms → diagnosis → the four education pillars → why control matters → hypoglycemia. ⭐ symptoms present → one abnormal glucose diagnoses diabetes ; no symptoms → two are needed. The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial logic underlies everything here — intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia , a trade-off now partly offset by pumps and continuous glucose monitors . Glucose gel works through buccal mucosa , so it can be given when swallowing is unsafe. 1. Symptoms of new-onset diabetes History three classic early symptoms nearly every patient has : polyuria (including nocturia / new bed-wetting ), excessive thirst , weight loss despite unchanged appetite then screen for late/severe features: vomiting · abdominal pain · dehydration · hypovolemic shock · hyperventilation (acidosis) · drowsiness · coma Physical exam : hydration status · weight loss · level of consciousness · Kussmaul breathing · acetone breath Lack of insulin: high glucose causes thirst and frequent urination, fat and protein breakdown cause weight loss, and ketone build-up causes acidosis, fast breathing and nausea 2. Diagnosis Symptoms present → one abnormal glucose is enough ; no symptoms → two abnormal measurements are needed Test Diagnostic result fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test ≥ 11.1 mmol/L Random plasma glucose + symptoms ≥ 11.1 mmol/L ← the one that matters acutely HbA1c is not one of the type 1 diagnostic criteria — the deck lists only random (with symptoms), fasting and 2-hour glucose Investigations random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 · urine dipstick for glucose and ketones (glycosuria + ketonuria) serum C-peptide (is she making any insulin?) arterial blood gas if diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is suspected ⚠ fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and glycated hemoglobin (A1c) are usually unnecessary here — the diagnosis is already clear 3. Management: the four education pillars Management — the four education pillars , delivered by a multidisciplinary team : dietician · social worker · diabetes nurse educator Treatment : insulin + structured education · treat DKA emergently if present Pillar Content Targets / numbers Blood glucose monitoring 4× per day (before meals + bedtime) · every 2–3 hours during illness · occasional nocturnal values · whenever hypoglycemic symptoms occur Method: fingerprick meter or continuous glucose monitor : FPG 4–8 , post-prandial 5–10 , A1c Non-diabetic: FPG 3–6, A1c 4–6% Severe/excessive hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness → pre-prandial target 6–10 mmol/L and a higher A1c Insulin administration Bolus (short/rapid-acting) + basal (intermediate/long-acting); sliding scale dosed to blood glucose and carbohydrate load 3 injections/day = NPH + fast-acting · 4 injections/day = long-acting (glargine/detemir/degludec) + fast-acting · or a pump Dose is age-dependent : onset · pre-puberty 0.7–1.0 · puberty 1.0–2.0 units/kg/day Dietary counselling Carbohydrate counting to match bolus dosing — Optimizing metabolic control Pumps (continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion, basal + bolus): better control, more reliable absorption, precise dosing, ↓ hypoglycemia risk , ↓ long-term complications, flexibility with food, shift work and time zones Continuous glucose monitor : interstitial glucose every 5 minutes · alerts when out of range or expected to be within 20 minutes Time in range = 3.9–10 mmol/L : the same A1c of 7% can hide 19% or 71% time in range Basal-bolus insulin copies the normal pancreas: a mealtime bolus at breakfast, lunch and supper, plus a steady basal dose given at bedtime Schulich Reviews Adjusting multiple daily injection doses: fix the insulin given BEFORE the abnormal reading — low at lunch → ↓ breakfast rapid-acting · high at bedtime → ↑ supper rapid-acting Follow-up : annual urinalysis for albuminuria ( diabetic nephropathy screening) 4. Why control matters: the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial Intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia A1c held at ~7% intensive vs ~9% conventional over ~9 years the trade-off is now partly offset by pumps and continuous glucose monitors 5. Acute complication: hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia symptoms come in two waves, and the order is the point Early = adrenergic Late = neuroglycopenic Mechanism Counter-regulatory catecholamine surge Brain is not getting enough glucose Features Shakiness, sweating, anxiety, hunger, pallor Hunger, drowsiness, confusion, convulsions, coma Action Treat promptly at this stage Assistance required — this is severe hypoglycemia Treatment give ~15 g of fast-acting sugar glucose tablet or juice · glucose gel (absorbed rapidly across buccal mucosa) · glucagon (intramuscular, subcutaneous or intranasal) · intravenous dextrose Prevention : treat early symptoms promptly · monitor regularly · adjust insulin before and after exercise · adhere to the meal plan

Insulin Preparations Choose a preparation based on what the insulin is covering — a meal (bolus) or the fasting state (basal). Every preparation works the same way once it reaches the receptor; they differ only in how fast they get there. The lecture runs structure → uses → the preparations → mechanism → adverse effects → practical points. ⭐ Analogues are NOT more effective at lowering HbA1c than human insulin — they are safer and more convenient (faster onset, better postprandial match, lower variability, less early-night hypoglycemia). Only regular insulin can be given intravenously. Basal insulins must never be used in pumps , and most basal insulins must not be mixed with another insulin before injection. Insulin does not interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other drugs — but drugs that alter glucose metabolism (e.g. steroids ↑ hepatic glucose production) change how well it works. Exogenous insulin is imperfect because physiological secretion is glucose-dependent , and that fine-tuning is lost. The preparations by what they cover: bolus (rapid-acting, fast-acting and regular human), basal (NPH, long- and ultra-long-acting analogues) and premixed, each with the modification that sets its kinetics, onset, peak and duration, and pump and intravenous rules 1. Structure sets the kinetics Insulin = two peptide chains (A and B) linked by disulphide bridges · made by beta cells as preproinsulin → proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide molecules pair into dimers and then hexamers (a trimer of dimers) · insulin binds its receptor only as a monomer Onset and duration are set by one thing: how fast monomers dissociate from the hexamer anything that stabilizes the hexamer (zinc, protamine, self-aggregation, albumin binding) → slower onset, longer duration bolus insulins are built to release monomers faster · basal insulins to release them slower Textbook figure of each insulin preparation in the vial, after injection under the skin and in the capillaries, with absorption rate and duration 2. Clinical uses Diabetes · hyperkalemia · hyperglycemic crisis ( diabetic ketoacidosis ) · diagnostic testing 3. Approach to a Suspected Endocrine Problem Every endocrine problem sorts into one of two kinds: structural (a mass) or functional (too much or too little hormone) — and both can be present at once . The sorting question determines the entire workup. The lecture orients you to hormones, sorts the problem, then works through masses, hormone problems and the dynamic tests. ⭐ the suppression/stimulation pairing is the single most testable idea here — excess is tested by trying to turn it off, deficiency by trying to turn it on . Primary adrenal insufficiency loses both cortisol AND aldosterone , which is what separates it from central causes. A benign mass can still be clinically important through pure mass effect. And always ask whether an exogenous hormone explains the picture before working up the gland. 1. Hormones: what they do and how they reach their target Four jobs reproduction ( estradiol , testosterone , prolactin ) growth and development ( growth hormone , sex steroids) maintaining the internal environment ( triiodothyronine , antidiuretic hormone , parathyroid hormone ) making, storing and using energy ( insulin , glucagon , cortisol ) By distance to target : autocrine = the cell itself · paracrine = a nearby cell · endocrine = distant, reached via the bloodstream 2. Structural or functional? The sorting question 3. Is the problem in the gland itself (primary) or somewhere else (secondary / tertiary / central)? Diagnosing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and the Grey Zone Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and T2DM share identical diagnostic thresholds — so the diagnostic work is (1) crossing the threshold, (2) deciding how many measurements you need, and (3) working out which type you are looking at. The lecture then turns to what else comes with T2DM, why it happens, who gets it, and how common it is. ⭐ the thresholds mark where retinopathy risk rises, not cardiovascular risk. Symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. Do not diagnose during acute illness (myocardial infarction, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery. C-peptide and anti-GAD move in opposite directions between the two types: low C-peptide + high anti-GAD = T1DM . >90% of all diabetes is Type 2 ; 589 million adults live with diabetes worldwide ( ~1 in 9 ), ~43% of them undiagnosed , and ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes. Finally — a T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent : weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range, though it can recur, so keep re-checking periodically . 1. Diagnostic criteria and the grey zone How many measurements symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. · a repeat confirmatory test is done on another day do not diagnose during acute illness (myocardial infarction, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery Test Normal Grey zone = prediabetes Diabetes Fasting plasma glucose 6.1–6.9 mmol/L = impaired fasting glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 7.8–11.0 mmol/L = impaired glucose tolerance ≥ 11.1 mmol/L Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) 6.0–6.4% ≥ 6.5% Random plasma glucose — — ≥ 11.1 mmol/L Why these particular numbers? The cut-points were not chosen arbitrarily and they are not the level at which cardiovascular risk rises they mark the glycemic level at which the risk of diabetic retinopathy rises sharply Retinopathy prevalence stays flat across glucose and A1c levels, then jumps at the diabetic cut-points ⚠ The grey zone is the target population for T2DM prevention — see 12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes 2. More than hyperglycemia: non-glycemic features and metabolic syndrome T2DM is not only a disease of hyperglycemia abnormal lipids ( hypertriglyceridemia , low high-density lipoprotein, small dense low-density lipoprotein ) ↑ systemic and vascular inflammation · ↑ free fatty acids · hypertension · sleep apnea metabolic syndrome — some or all of Why it matters essential hypertension · low high-density lipoprotein · hypertriglyceridemia · ↑ waist-to-hip ratio (visceral fat) · dysglycemia or T2DM Flags ↑ risk of cardiovascular disease and T2DM. In a patient who already has T2DM, metabolic syndrome raises cardiovascular risk further still 4. Pathophysiology: insulin resistance and insulin deficiency Two problems, and by diagnosis both are present Insulin resistance Insulin deficiency Definition Needs more insulin than normal to move glucose into liver, adipose and skeletal muscle Not enough insulin for the body's needs T1DM = absolute · T2DM = relative Causes Genetics · high fat / refined carb diet · lack of muscle activity · excess adipose tissue and fatty liver · systemic inflammation (adipocytokines) · abnormal mitochondria Genetics · surgery ( pancreatectomy ) · excess glucose (glucose toxicity feedback loop) · excess free fatty acids from visceral fat lipolysis Sequence if primary resistance → ↑ demand on pancreas → pancreas cannot keep up → diabetic glucose deficiency → glucose rises → glucose toxicity → further pancreatic stress → diabetic glucose Natural history of type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance rises early, insulin production compensates then fails, and glucose climbs 5. Risk factors Genetic : mostly polygenic 90% monozygotic twin concordance · 40% have an affected parent · 5–10% ↑ lifetime risk with a 1st-degree relative Environmental : obesogenic foods (low fibre, high fat, high refined sugars) · "portion creep" · inactivity · obesity · lower socio-economic status Intrauterine : birth-weight extremes (both under- and overweight) · in-utero exposure to high glucose · prematurity Populations at particular risk: Asian, South Asian, Hispanic, Indigenous, African American / African-descent, and women with previous gestational diabetes 6. Prevalence >90% of all diabetes is Type 2 ; 589 million adults live with diabetes worldwide ( ~1 in 9 ) ~43% of them undiagnosed ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes 7. Lowering blood glucose: the diagnosis is not always permanent A T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent : weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range it can recur, so keep re-checking glucose / A1c periodically But not always reversible : with significant insulin deficiency, glucose stays high despite excellent lifestyle change — not all T2DM is due to being overweight and underactive
06 Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes

Complications of Diabetes The acute emergencies separate on one variable: is there enough insulin to suppress lipolysis? Enough → no ketones → hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) . Not enough → ketogenesis → diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) . The lecture covers the two emergencies, their treatment and prevention, then the chronic small- and large-vessel complications and why they happen. ⭐ abdominal pain and vomiting = DKA, not HHS. Hours = DKA, days = HHS. T1DM = DKA, older T2DM = HHS. SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate DKA — and appear again in the sick-day rules as a drug to stop . Potassium falls with treatment, not before it. Proprioception goes early in peripheral neuropathy, and feet are affected before hands because of nerve length . 1. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) = no insulin at all → unopposed lipolysis → ketone production → anion gap metabolic acidosis Causes : absolute insulin deficiency → type 1 diabetes (T1DM) illness — anything ① dehydrating or ② physically stressful ( gastroenteritis , myocardial infarction , stroke , sepsis , pancreatitis ) lack of insulin — 1st diagnosis of T1DM, forgetting / withholding / rationing insulin , insulin pump malfunction medications — steroids , sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors , cocaine Presents as : ⏰ evolves over HOURS polyuria · polydipsia · weight loss · nausea, VOMITING, ABDOMINAL PAIN progresses to lethargy and coma if untreated Physical exam : toxic appearance · hypotension + tachycardia (shock) · dehydration (dry membranes, poor skin turgor) · acetone smell on breath · Kussmal's breathing Investigations ↑ blood glucose (often > 15) · ↑ serum and urine ketones ↑ anion gap — follow it during treatment · ↓ serum pH ( acidosis ) · ↓ serum bicarbonate (consumed; pH may be ~7.0) · plasma osmolality mildly ↑ Na⁺ ↑ or ↓ — high sugars falsely lower Na⁺, so correct for glucose K⁺ normal or ↓ — total body K⁺ is depleted even when serum looks normal ↑ creatinine (dehydration) 2. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) = enough insulin to inhibit adipose breakdown into ketones, but not enough to prevent hyperglycemia → profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without significant acidosis Causes : relative insulin deficiency → type 2 diabetes (T2DM) , usually older patients illness — dehydrating or physically stressful · lack of insulin — rationing, missed doses · drug effects — steroids worsen insulin resistance Presents as : ⏰ evolves over DAYS polyuria · polydipsia · lethargy → obtundation (rarely coma) NO abdominal pain and NO vomiting Investigations : same panel, but the discriminating pattern is very high glucose · ↑↑ plasma osmolality · minimal or absent ketones · pH and serum bicarbonate near normal — no significant anion gap The biochemical line between them — memorize this table. DKA HHS pH ≤ 7.3 > 7.3 Plasma glucose > 15 mmol/L > 30 mmol/L Serum bicarbonate > 15 mEq/L Plasma / urine ketones positive negative or trace Anion gap > 12 Serum osmolarity variable > 320 mOsm/kg (HIGH) Water deficit ~6 L ~9 L 3. Treating a hyperglycemic emergency Both require emergent treatment; fluid deficits are very large — even larger in HHS ① ABCs — airway, breathing, circulation ② Fluids — normal saline first , often many litres · add dextrose once glucose reaches ~12–14 mmol/L (5% dextrose in water with normal saline) so the insulin infusion can continue without causing hypoglycemia — normal glucose is not the immediate goal ③ Insulin — ALWAYS required in DKA , almost always in HHS ④ Monitoring every 1–2 hours — level of consciousness · Na⁺, K⁺, pH · glucose hourly on an insulin drip · volume status ( especially elderly — watch for heart failure ) HHS: same protocol — these patients are older, so monitor volume status especially closely The two traps that kill ① Potassium. Total body K⁺ is depleted even when the initial serum potassium looks normal — in DKA, low insulin has driven K⁺ extracellularly . Once you give fluid and insulin, K⁺ shifts back intracellularly and falls sharply , causing arrhythmias and death . K⁺ replacement is often required during treatment. ② Glucose falling too fast. Intravenous fluids and insulin will drop glucose. Add dextrose to the fluids so insulin can keep running until the dehydration — and in DKA the acidosis — is corrected. Then look for the cause — both emergencies should spark a search for the precipitant 4. Prevention: sick-day rules Type 1 : continue SOME insulin even when not eating (lower-dose basal) · monitor glucose and urine ketones frequently Type 2 : monitor glucose frequently STOP dehydrating medications during gastrointestinal upset — SGLT2 inhibitors , diuretics , metformin the stress of illness raises sugars, so taking some insulin is appropriate Always ask why — common themes: withholding insulin to control weight (DKA) · withholding medication for financial reasons · uncertainty about sick-day rules · new medications, especially steroids · big body stresses (infection, myocardial infarction, stroke) 5. Chronic complications: microvascular vs macrovascular Never used to frighten patients into compliance — they can occur despite excellent self-management Microvascular (small vessels) Macrovascular (large vessels) Conditions Retinopathy · nephropathy · neuropathy myocardial infarction · stroke · peripheral vascular disease Mechanism Capillary basement membrane thickening; matrix accumulation in the glomerulus → fibrosis → ↓ filtration surface ↑ free fatty acids → atherosclerosis → plaque in coronary and cranial arteries 6. Glucose-Lowering Drugs in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) Choose an agent based on which step of glucose metabolism is being manipulated , then narrow by hypoglycemia risk, effect on weight, and organ function. The lecture takes the drug groups in turn — sensitizers, secretagogues, then drugs that change absorption or excretion — and ends on choosing a second-line agent. ⭐ GLP-1RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors are the agents with proven cardiovascular benefit — pick one in a patient with CV disease. The incretin agents are secretagogues too, but only the glucose-independent secretagogues (SUs, meglitinides) carry meaningful hypoglycemia risk , because they release insulin independent of glucose level; the incretins do not, because their secretion is glucose-dependent . Weight gain: TZDs, SUs, meglitinides. Weight loss: GLP-1RAs, SGLT2 inhibitors, (metformin). Renal function matters twice: metformin is excreted unchanged in urine (lactic acidosis if it accumulates), and SGLT2 inhibitors lose efficacy as renal function falls. The drug classes by where they act: insulin sensitizers, insulin secretagogues (glucose-independent and incretins) and absorption or excretion, each with mechanism, HbA1c drop, hypoglycemia and weight effects, cost and what to avoid 1. Where the drugs act Therapeutic goals in T2DM : control symptoms · individualized glycemic control · avoid hypoglycemia · minimize acute and chronic complications · control associated risk factors Lifestyle first : more exercise · less food — add a drug when that is not enough Ways to lower glucose : ↓ gastric emptying · delay carbohydrate digestion · ↓ glucose release and gluconeogenesis · ↑ renal glucose excretion · ↑ insulin sensitivity · ↑ insulin secretion · ↓ glucagon release · give exogenous insulin Where each glucose-lowering drug class acts: gut, beta cell, liver, muscle, fat and kidney 2.
