08 Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes

Glycemic Goals of Care The target is never a single number — it is a negotiation between preventing long-term complications and avoiding hypoglycemia now . Tight control buys microvascular benefit; severe hypoglycemia carries ↑ mortality . The lecture runs why targets matter → how glucose is measured → reading it from symptoms → setting the target. ⭐ severity of hypoglycemia is defined by whether the patient can treat it themselves — not by the glucose number. A1c is the best-validated marker of control but lags , so it never replaces glucose readings when you are actively changing therapy. CGM measures interstitial, not blood, glucose. Tight control helps microvascular outcomes most; macrovascular benefit is probably yes in T1DM, probably not in T2DM . 1. Why the target matters It changes both outcomes and your prescribing Short-term (acute metabolic) Long-term (chronic structural) What good control avoids Symptomatic hyperglycemia · diabetic ketoacidosis / hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state · hypoglycemia Microvascular — retinopathy , nephropathy , neuropathy Macrovascular — stroke , myocardial infarction , peripheral vascular disease Evidence A1c > 7% is associated with ↑ micro- and macrovascular risk ; both fasting and post-prandial glucose correlate directly with complication risk Tight control improves microvascular outcomes across multiple trials Decisions it drives Whether to start glucose-lowering drugs — and which ( insulin , orals, or both) · doses and timing · intensity of monitoring ( continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) vs. fingerstick) Tight control helps microvascular outcomes most; macrovascular benefit: type 1 probably yes, type 2 probably not — the cardiovascular benefit of empagliflozin or liraglutide in type 2 is not clearly mediated by better glycemia But tight control (A1c ~6.0%) ↑ severe hypoglycemia, which is linked to ↑ mortality — not ideal for older/frail patients, long diabetes duration, advanced coronary artery disease or prior severe hypoglycemia Risk curves against glycated hemoglobin: retinopathy rises and severe hypoglycemia falls as A1c climbs 2. Monitoring tools: each measures something different Tool What it measures Window Pitfalls Self-monitoring (fingerstick) Capillary whole blood glucose This moment Frequency must be individualized CGM or flash glucose monitoring Interstitial fluid glucose — not blood Continuous, worn on body Gives pre-/post-meal and overnight data unavailable to fingersticks HbA1c Mean plasma glucose over the past 8–12 weeks , ~50% of the value from the last 30 days ~3 months Lags behind real-time changes ; distorted by the conditions below What falsely distorts an HbA1c Falsely ↑ : B12 / iron deficiency (↓ erythropoiesis) · chronic renal failure (altered glycation) · splenectomy · hyperbilirubinemia , alcohol, chronic opiates (assay) Falsely ↓ : erythropoietin / iron / B12 therapy, reticulocytosis, chronic liver disease · hemolysis — hemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis, some drugs · hypertriglyceridemia (assay) Variable : fetal hemoglobin, hemoglobinopathies ( sickle cell disease , thalassemias ), methemoglobin A1c is the best-validated marker of control but lags , so it never replaces glucose readings when you are actively changing therapy How often to check depends on type of diabetes — type 1 needs 4+/day, before each insulin dose , and often benefits from continuous glucose monitoring type of therapy — sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia → check more changes to therapy · adequacy of control · literacy and numeracy · propensity for and awareness of hypoglycemia · occupational requirements · acute illness Conversion chart from glycated hemoglobin to average blood glucose in mmol/L 3. Reading glucose from symptoms Patients can also read their own glucose from symptoms severity of hypoglycemia is defined by whether the patient can treat it themselves — not by the glucose number HYPERGLYCEMIA HYPOGLYCEMIA Glucose in the "double digit range" Glucose ≤ 4.0 mmol/L (on insulin or a secretagogue) polyuria , nocturia , polydipsia May be asymptomatic — consider hypoglycemic unawareness Weight loss, fatigue Hunger, sweating, dizziness, tachycardia , confusion, seizure, coma Metabolic decompensation → diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state Mild = autonomic, self-treatable · Moderate = autonomic and neuroglycopenic, still self-treatable · Severe = ASSISTANCE REQUIRED (bystander, family, emergency medical services, emergency department) 4. Setting the target Target Who Why HbA1c ≤ 7.0% Most people with T1DM or T2DM The validated default. > 50% of patients will not reach it — but any reduction is beneficial A1c ≤ 6.5% 🙍‍♂️ T2DM at low risk of hypoglycemia Further ↓ risk of chronic kidney disease and retinopathy A1c 7.1–8.5% 👵🏻 Recurrent severe hypoglycemia / unawareness · limited life expectancy · frail elderly or dementia (functionally dependent: 7.1–8.0% ) Hypoglycemia is more dangerous than hyperglycemia here (falls) No A1c End of life Just avoid symptomatic hyperglycemia and any hypoglycemia Fasting 4.0–7.0 mmol/L · 2-hour post-meal 5.0–10.0 mmol/L Self-monitoring targets — ≤ 130/80 mmHg blood pressure · low-density lipoprotein Alongside glycemia See 10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes

Obesity — Assessment and Management Obesity is a complex, progressive, relapsing chronic disease — abnormal or excessive body fat that impairs health . The lecture defines it, explains why it happens, then walks the 5 A's and the treatment ladder. BMI alone does not predict adiposity-related complications ; stage the impact , not just the number. ⭐ The most serious post-bariatric deficiency is thiamine — give it before any glucose or you precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy . tirzepatide (dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) beats semaglutide beats naltrexone-bupropion for weight loss. The BMI cut-off drops to 25 for South and East Asian patients. EOSS stages the functional impact , which is what determines bariatric referral — not BMI alone. Ghrelin is the only fasting/hunger hormone here; everything else in the list promotes satiety. The pharmacotherapy stopping rule is 5% at 12 weeks . Gastric banding is explicitly not recommended. And 20% of Canadians have obesity , with the socioeconomic gradient running opposite ways by sex — ↓ socioeconomic status means ↑ obesity in women, ↓ in men. 1. Definition — thresholds are ethnicity-specific Obesity = BMI ≥ 30 (≥ 25 in South and East Asian patients), plus waist circumference (WC) , because BMI alone is insufficient South and East Asian: overweight = 23.0–24.9 , obesity ≥ 25.0 kg/m² Thresholds move because BMI and WC do not account for body frame, musculature, or propensity for visceral adiposity BMI WC — men WC — women European ≥ 30.0 kg/m² South Asian ≥ 25.0 kg/m² East Asian ≥ 25.0 kg/m² < 80 cm ⚠ South and East Asian individuals develop visceral adiposity and obesity-related disease at a lower BMI — this is why the cut-off moves 2. Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS) Stages the functional and health impact of obesity, not the body size — and it is what is used when referring to the bariatric program Edmonton Obesity Staging System: stage 0 has no obesity-related problems, stage 2 an established comorbidity needing treatment, stage 4 severe end-stage disease; stage by health impact, not by body mass index 3. Complications — the 4 M's Use this as the assessment checklist, not a list to memorise loosely. Mental Mechanical Metabolic Monetary Cognition · depression · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder · addiction · psychosis · eating disorders · trauma · insomnia sleep apnea · osteoarthritis · chronic pain · gastroesophageal reflux disease · incontinence · venous thromboembolism · intertrigo · plantar fasciitis type 2 diabetes (T2DM) · dyslipidemia · essential hypertension · gout · fatty liver · gallstones · polycystic ovarian syndrome · cancer Education · employment · income · insurance · benefits · disability · weight loss programs · bariatric supplies 4. Prevalence 20% of Canadians have obesity Socioeconomic status runs opposite ways by sex : ↓ socioeconomic status means ↑ obesity in women, ↓ in men 5. Pathophysiology — far more than energy in vs. energy out Genetics : 60–70% of BMI is genetically determined. Early-life events : maternal starvation in pregnancy predisposes offspring to obesity intrauterine growth restriction → energy hoarding → later obesity Other contributors : iatrogenic (steroids, antidepressants/antipsychotics) · gut microbiome and circadian rhythm (shift workers) · social determinants of health (food/income insecurity, housing instability) · environment and culture Brain drivers of food-seeking hypothalamus (homeostasis) · mesolimbic system (pleasure) · frontal lobe (executive control) dopamine = wanting food, opioids = liking food Hormones of hunger and satiety FASTING state FED state — all promote satiety ghrelin — made in the stomach , ↑ hunger and food intake insulin , amylin — pancreas glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) , glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP), cholecystokinin , peptide YY — intestines leptin , adiponectin — adipose tissue After weight loss, these hormones shift to drive the return to the usual weight setpoint — why obesity relapses Hunger and satiety hormones: ghrelin from the stomach in the fasting state, and insulin, amylin, peptide YY, GLP-1, cholecystokinin, leptin and adiponectin in the fed state, all acting on the hypothalamus 6. Assessment — bias, stigma and the 5 A's Bias and stigma 56% have attempted weight loss between 2 and 20 times — assume effort, not inaction 95% of patients with severe obesity want to lose weight chairs, exam tables, bathrooms and scales must accommodate the patient place the scale in a private area, and do not announce weight unless they ask to hear it ASK — ask permission to discuss weight be non-judgemental · explore readiness for change · use motivational interviewing ASSESS — stage the disease and find root causes EOSS stage · BMI + WC if BMI ≥ 25 · the 4 M's History: weight history · contributors · rule out hypothyroidism , Cushing syndrome , medications, genetic disorders · cultural and family factors · diet and exercise history Physical exam: BMI · WC · blood pressure · acanthosis , hirsutism , Cushingoid features Labs: glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) · lipid panel · serum thyroid-stimulating hormone · alanine aminotransferase ADVISE — risks, benefits, options The goal is health and wellness, not a number. first goal may simply be stabilising weight · behavioural change yields 3–5% AGREE — realistic expectations and SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) 0.5–1.0 kg (1–2 lb) per week ; 5–10% total loss over 6–12 months ASSIST — barriers, resources, follow-up referrals (e.g. cardiology before an exercise plan) · contingency plans for travel · financial reality — dieticians are often out of pocket 7. Management — two foundations Medical nutrition therapy — for all Canadians, regardless of body size personalized · refer to a registered dietician , especially with celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease Physical activity — for all 30–60 min most days, moderate–vigorous + resistance training small weig

Preventing the Complications of Diabetes Three numbers drive prevention — glycated hemoglobin (A1c), blood pressure, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) — and each has its own first-line drug and its own set of complications it prevents. Glycemic control alone is not enough: it barely moves macrovascular risk. ⭐ Glycemic control prevents microvascular disease; blood pressure control is what prevents macrovascular disease in T2DM. ACEi/ARB are given for nephropathy even in patients without hypertension (see 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes ). Feet are examined daily at home and at every clinic visit — the monofilament test detects the loss of protective sensation before ulceration. The > 15 years of diabetes clause matters: a 35-year-old diagnosed at 18 qualifies for a statin. 1. What the trials showed The two trials : Diabetes Control and Complications Trial 1993 for type 1 diabetes (T1DM) · UK Prospective Diabetes Study 1998 for type 2 diabetes (T2DM) Better glycemic control and more intensive regimens produced microvascular complications: ✅ ↓ risk of developing or worsening macrovascular complications: NO effect from glycemic control — but ↓ blood pressure ↓ cardiovascular disease risk in T2DM hypoglycemia : ↑ risk — the cost of intensive control Diabetes Control and Complications Trial design: 1441 people with type 1 diabetes, conventional versus intensive insulin for 6.5 years Risk of retinopathy against risk of severe hypoglycemia across glycated hemoglobin: the trade-off intensive control makes 2. Lifestyle interventions Home monitoring of glucose AND blood pressure Smoking cessation — ↓ risk of myocardial infarction , stroke , peripheral arterial disease , and possibly retinopathy Activity + weight loss if ↑ BMI — ↓ blood pressure and blood glucose Annual ophthalmology screening — for diabetic retinopathy Examine feet DAILY for open wounds if vision impaired — ask a family member, or refer to chiropody · ensure comfortable shoes 3. In-clinic monitoring — feet, blood pressure, LDL Foot exam, every visit — Inspect for calluses and ulcers · assess pedal pulses · monofilament exam Monofilament test: press until the filament buckles, at the sites that best detect loss of protective sensation The three targets Target Value First-line drug What it prevents HbA1c ≤ 7% (see 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes ) metformin ± others Microvascular only — retinopathy , nephropathy , neuropathy blood pressure ≤ 130/80 mmHg angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) (or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) ) Cardiovascular outcomes, renal impairment, and retinopathy LDL statins Cardiovascular outcomes, possibly retinopathy 4. Drugs that protect beyond glucose Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors (e.g. empagliflozin) → cardiovascular AND renal protection. Incretin analogues (e.g. liraglutide) → cardiovascular protection. Coronary artery disease prevention — the age and duration triggers are the testable part Primary prevention (no known coronary artery disease (CAD) ) Secondary prevention (known CAD) Statin > 30 years AND diabetes > 15 years → statin ≥ 40 years → statin Statin — LDL target ACEi / ARB ≥ 55 years AND another CAD risk factor ( proteinuria , retinopathy , left ventricular hypertrophy ) → ACEi or ARB IN ADDITION to a statin renal disease → ACEi or ARB ACEi or ARB — blood pressure target Antiplatelet — acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg ± clopidogrel Coronary artery disease prevention by age: known CAD gets statin + ACEi/ARB + ASA; without it, 30-40 needs diabetes over 15 years for a statin, 40-55 gets a statin, and 55+ adds an ACEi/ARB if there is another risk factor 5. At diagnosis — refer early, pick the first drug Refer early dietician — dietary change to ↓ complication risk diabetes nurse educator — sugar testing, what to do when low or sick optometrist — yearly First medication Insulin — all T1DM , and T2DM patients who are very symptomatic (polydipsia, polyuria, yeast infections, weight loss, malaise) metformin — T2DM without many symptoms and no liver or renal concerns

Diabetes in Pregnancy The single discriminating question is when the hyperglycemia starts. Pre-existing diabetes mellitus (DM) is present during organogenesis (weeks 3–16) → congenital malformations. Gestational diabetes (GDM) appears at 24–28 weeks, after organogenesis → NO congenital malformations , but the same fetal morbidities. ⭐ GDM does not cause congenital malformations; pre-existing DM does — because of when the hyperglycemia occurs relative to organogenesis. Insulin needs FALL in trimester 1 and after delivery, and RISE steeply in trimester 3. Glyburide crosses the placenta; insulin does not. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated — use beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. Retinopathy that worsens in pregnancy usually settles after delivery without permanent damage , but screen pre-conception, during, and within the first postpartum year . Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern. 1. Pre-existing diabetes before pregnancy Pre-conception diabetes ( type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes (T2DM) ) is present from conception, throughout organogenesis (weeks 3–16+), often before pregnancy is even known Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern Congenital malformations : YES — depends on glycated hemoglobin (A1c) at conception 1.7–9.4% vs. 2–4% background (major malformations) tight control before conception ↓ anomalies by ~70% Pre-conception care Target A1c ≤ 7%, ideally ≤ 6.5%, BEFORE conception prescribe folic acid · screen for diabetic retinopathy Absolute risk of a congenital anomaly climbs steadily with periconceptional A1c 2. Congenital malformations and other infant morbidities Congenital malformations (pre-existing DM only) — grouped by system, which is how they are recalled Critical periods of development: most major structural defects arise in weeks 3 to 8, often before pregnancy is known Neurological Cardiovascular Gastrointestinal Genitourinary neural tube defects — spina bifida , anencephaly cauda equina regression (skeletal) transposition of the great vessels · coarctation of the aorta · truncus arteriosus · atrial septal defect · pulmonary stenosis · dextrocardia duodenal atresia · imperforate anus · anorectal atresia · situs inversus totalis double ureters · renal agenesis · hydronephrosis Other infant morbidities — these occur in BOTH groups: cesarean section (32–45%) · prematurity (15% before week 34) · fetal distress (9–28%) · macrosomia > 4 kg (9–28%) small for date (2–8%) if the mother has vascular disease (inadequate placental flow) ↓ calcium · ↑ red blood cell volume · hyperbilirubinemia neonatal hypoglycemia — the baby made ↑ insulin in utero. 3. Insulin requirements across pregnancy The bigger the placenta, the higher the hormones and the higher the insulin need. Preventing Type 2 Diabetes The target population is the grey zone — prediabetes , impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance (see 05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology ). The lecture walks three approaches in order: lifestyle → medication → surgery . No medication is approved in Canada for preventing diabetes — everything below is evidence, not indication. ⭐ Lifestyle beats metformin, 58% vs 31% — the single most testable number in this lecture. Thiazolidinediones have the biggest drug effect (62–72%) but the side effect profile that stops you using them. Acarbose's benefit disappears on discontinuation , unlike the durable effect of weight loss. Bariatric surgery is the most effective and still not first line — effectiveness and appropriateness are different questions. And nothing here is actually approved for prevention in Canada. 1. Lifestyle and diet Intensive lifestyle : Low-fat, low-calorie diet + 150 min activity per week risk reduction: 58% — the most effective non-surgical option Even 5% weight loss has benefit Healthy dietary patterns — Mediterranean, Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, Alternative Healthy Eating Index risk reduction ~20% · a pattern, not a single nutrient Diabetes Prevention Program: lifestyle cut diabetes incidence by 58% and metformin by 31% compared with placebo 2. Medications None is approved for prevention in Canada; these are the drugs with trial evidence. Drug Risk reduction Best in / caveats metformin 31% — roughly half the benefit of lifestyle More effective in the younger ( , the obese (BMI > 35) , and women with previous gestational diabetes thiazolidinediones 62% (rosiglitazone) – 72% (pioglitazone) — the largest drug effect Limited by adverse effects: peripheral edema , heart failure , osteoporosis and ↑ fractures acarbose ~25–36% (by oral glucose tolerance test ) Effect did NOT persist after discontinuation Orlistat ( tetrahydrolipstatin ) ~37% Assessed within obesity effectiveness studies; approved for weight loss, not prevention glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists Evidence exists liraglutide and semaglutide 3. Bariatric surgery Bariatric surgery : Most effective of all approaches Swedish Obese Subjects study: incident T2DM hazard ratio 0.22 vs usual care over 15 years NOT first line for prevention — cost and procedural risk The two most common in Canada : Roux-en-Y gastric bypass ( restrictive AND malabsorptive ) · sleeve gastrectomy ( restrictive only ) both 30–35% weight loss · mortality 1 in 500 · covered by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan Bariatric procedures: adjustable gastric band, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy and biliopancreatic diversion

Choosing an Antihyperglycemic — Case Analysis Every case runs the same four-part analysis : effectiveness → safety → additional benefits → suitability . The drug is chosen by the patient's characteristics, not the glycated hemoglobin (A1c) alone. The session sets out the framework, then four cases that each teach one mechanism, then dosing in kidney disease. ⭐ Sulfonylurea secondary failure means the next drug must not be another secretagogue. Linagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor that needs no renal adjustment. SGLT2 inhibitors cause genitourinary infections and volume depletion — and cause DKA at normal glucose. AGIs are contraindicated in IBS and inflammatory bowel disease . When insulin requirements exceed anything plausible, stop escalating and look for a receptor-level cause. 1. The framework Efficacy at lowering HbA1c — how much do I need to drop? high : insulin · metformin · GLP-1 analogues · sulfonylureas (SUs) · thiazolidinediones (TZDs) moderate : DPP-4 inhibitors · SGLT2 inhibitors · alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (AGIs) Effect on weight — does the patient need to lose weight, or are they already cachectic? loss: glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) · gain: SU, TZD, insulin Risk of hypoglycemia — do they live alone, drive, eat irregularly, or fear hypoglycemia? Only the secretagogues carry real risk Cardiovascular / renal benefit — established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease , heart failure , or chronic kidney disease (CKD) ? SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs Special populations — renal or hepatic impairment? See section 6 Practical factors — cost · injection vs oral · dosing frequency · adherence — often the deciding factor Where each antihyperglycemic class acts: beta cell secretagogues, sensitizers at muscle, fat and liver, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors in the gut, and incretin agents on gastric emptying and glucagon 2. Case 1 — hyperglycemia refractory to insulin Patient : 46-year-old woman · BMI 45.6 → 16.9 · A1c 14% · insulin > 50 units/kg/day Key factors cachexia with extreme insulin requirement acromegaly-like facies, extensive acanthosis nigricans , skin tags, vitiligo urinary tract infection on empagliflozin · H. pylori triple therapy Mechanism tested : Severe insulin resistance syndrome — when escalating insulin fails, the problem is at the receptor , not the dose What to do ask what explains resistance this extreme note SGLT2 inhibitors → glucosuria → genitourinary infection and that SU + TZD + insulin stack weight gain and hypoglycemia 3. Case 2 — Samuel: adherence and weight Patient : 47-year-old man · A1c 8.3% · dyslipidemia · +12 lb · travels constantly · irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) Key factors : forgets twice-daily metformin · needs weight loss · eats at consistent times Mechanism tested : matching dosing frequency to lifestyle What to do favour once-weekly GLP-1RAs or once-daily agents with weight loss ⛔ AGIs are contraindicated in IBS · and are taken three times daily 4. Case 3 — Nancy: secondary failure and fear of hypoglycemia Patient : 62-year-old woman · A1c 7.1% → 7.9% on max metformin + gliclazide · +5 lb · unemployed · refuses needles · fears hypoglycemia · eats irregularly She wants : glycemic control · weight loss · low hypoglycemia risk · affordable · oral Mechanism tested : Sulfonylurea secondary failure — the K⁺/ATP channel mechanism desensitizes over time What to do do not swap to another secretagogue (glyburide or repaglinide share the mechanism) needs an agent with no hypoglycemia risk , oral, affordable Sulfonylureas and meglitinides close the beta-cell K-ATP channel, depolarising the cell and releasing insulin 5. Case 4 — Albert: SGLT2 inhibitor, kidney injury and shock Patient : 72-year-old man in intensive care with acute kidney injury and shock on canagliflozin + hydrochlorothiazide + valsartan — a triple volume-depleting combination 18 months of falls from postural hypotension · foot swelling, ↓ urine output, nausea, shortness of breath Mechanism tested SGLT2i → glucosuria → osmotic diuresis → volume depletion → prerenal acute kidney injury plus euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) What to do recognise that the falls were the warning sign hold the SGLT2 inhibitor and diuretic · check ketones regardless of glucose Euglycemic DKA — the SGLT2 inhibitor trap DKA can occur with a near-normal blood glucose , because urinary glucose loss blunts the hyperglycemia you would normally use as your trigger to test. Suspect it in any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor and check ketones regardless of the glucose reading. 6. Antihyperglycemics and kidney function (Shah BR et al. Thyroid Hormone Synthesis & Calcium Homeostasis Two axes, one shape: a gland reacting to a single sensed variable. For the thyroid that is circulating triiodothyronine (T3) / thyroxine (T4), read by the hypothalamus and pituitary , and the exam turns on iodination coming FIRST, then coupling . For the parathyroid it is ionized Ca2+, read directly by the chief cell's calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) , and the exam turns on there being no parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor in the gut . The lecture covers the thyroid first, then calcium. ⭐ There is no PTH receptor in the gut — PTH raises absorbed calcium only indirectly , through calcitriol . Iodination precedes coupling , and iodide entry is active transport (NIS, then pendrin), never passive diffusion . The goitre of iodine deficiency is not the gland "trying harder" — it is loss of negative feedback → sustained TSH-receptor drive → follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia , and maternal deficiency is the #1 cause of preventable intellectual disability worldwide . somatostatin inhibits TSH ONLY, not PTH. Calcium is the single discriminator between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism , and hypocalciuria is what separates FHH from primary. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is anti-TPO , blocking iodination of thyroglobulin, treated with levothyroxine ; Graves disease is an activating anti-TSH-receptor antibody with exophthalmos . 99% of body calcium sits in bone as calcium phosphate , and of the 1% in blood 50% is free/ionized — that is the only fraction the CaSR reads and the only fraction that acts. 1. Drugs Affecting Calcium & Bone Mineral Homeostasis The lecture starts with vitamin D, then walks the bone drugs: antiresorptives first, then bone-forming. Choosing between the bone drugs turns on three questions: are you stopping bone loss (antiresorptive) or building bone (anabolic)? · what is the creatinine clearance (CrCl) , since bisphosphonates and teriparatide are both out below 30 mL/min while denosumab is not · and which way does the drug push serum calcium . ⭐ Every antiresorptive causes hypocalcemia and the one anabolic PTH drug causes hypercalcemia . denosumab is the drug of choice when renal function is poor — it does not depend on the kidney for elimination, unlike the bisphosphonates, which are excreted unchanged and accumulate . Denosumab's effects on bone turnover and bone mineral density are reversible ; bisphosphonates stay bound in bone , so their benefit and their ONJ risk persist long after stopping — denosumab carries the higher ONJ risk but that risk falls when the drug stops , and the bisphosphonate risk does not. teriparatide is not associated with ONJ and may even treat it. Every antiresorptive drives calcium down, so every patient on one needs adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D . romosozumab is the one drug in both classes at once , and the one whose contraindication list is short but whose cardiovascular signal is the reason to hesitate. The drugs by class: vitamin D and analogues, antiresorptives (bisphosphonates, denosumab) and anabolics (teriparatide, romosozumab), each with mechanism, calcium direction, route, adverse effects and what to avoid 1. Approach to Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis The whole evaluation runs on one test in one direction , then one question splits thyrotoxicosis into its causes: is the gland making hormone, or leaking it? — which is what radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake answers. The lecture goes: presentation → thyroid function tests → thyrotoxicosis → hypothyroidism. ⭐ TSH case-finds, free hormone confirms — and the only reason to break that order is suspected central disease , where TSH and FT4 go together and TSH moves WITH the hormone . RAI uptake answers why , not whether . High uptake = the gland is synthesizing; low uptake = hormone is leaking out of it or coming from a bottle , and low-uptake disease is treated supportively while you watch for the hypothyroid phase . Goiter symmetry is a free discriminator: symmetric points to Graves, asymmetric to nodular disease, and thyroiditis can have no goiter at all. Methimazole is first line for Graves and RAI is first line for nodular disease , because only Graves remits. Levothyroxine's 1-week half-life is why TSH is rechecked at 4 to 6 weeks and not sooner. anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, and ultrasound are the tests to leave alone in straightforward hypothyroidism. 1. The pathway — TSH first Serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) to case-find, free hormone only to confirm and grade. TSH works because primary disease, at the gland, is by far the most common kind , and there TSH moves opposite to the hormone ⚠ that logic inverts in central disease , where pituitary TSH is the broken part and moves with the hormone some labs add free thyroxine (FT4) (and free triiodothyronine, FT3) reflexively when TSH comes back abnormal , so the confirmatory step may already be done for you Every TSH and free T4/T3 pattern mapped to its diagnosis and treatment: central, subclinical and primary disease on each side, with thyroid storm and myxedema coma at the bottom 2. Hyperparathyroidism, Hypoparathyroidism & the Calcium Panel You do not diagnose these from the calcium alone - you read the pattern across four tests at once: parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcium, phosphate, vitamin D. Correct for albumin, then always send a PTH: those two steps decide the entire workup. The lecture runs calcium → hypercalcaemia → hyperparathyroidism → hypocalcaemia → hypoparathyroidism. ⭐ Correct for albumin, then always send PTH. Phosphate separates primary from tertiary when calcium cannot - primary drops it because PTH makes the kidney waste phosphate, tertiary raises it because the failing kidney cannot excrete it. PTH direction separates true hypoparathyroidism from the pseudo forms , and pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is the trap: Albright's phenotype with a completely normal panel . Vitamin D deficiency is the commonest cause of hypocalcaemia, and it is the one where phosphate is LOW rather than high. 1. Serum calcium and the albumin correction Only the free (ionized) calcium is active, and much of the total rides on albumin - so correct the total for albumin first corrected calcium = measured calcium + 0.02(40 − measured albumin) Calcium regulation: low calcium raises PTH, which acts on bone and kidney, and calcitriol from the kidney raises gut absorption Calcium, then PTH, then phosphate: the low side splits into hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and pseudohypoparathyroidism; the high side into malignancy, FHH, primary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism by fractional calcium excretion 2. Hypercalcaemia Causes - over 90% of all hypercalcaemia is hyperparathyroidism or malignancy PTH high or inappropriately normal → PTH-mediated : primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism · familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) PTH suppressed → PTH-independent : malignancy : metastases - breast · humoral PTH-related protein - lung, kidney, adult T-cell leukaemia · lymphokines - myeloma vitamin D related : exogenous, or granulomatous sarcoid and tuberculosis immobilisation on a background of Paget's, thyrotoxicosis or adrenal insufficiency thiazides · milk-alkali syndrome · acromegaly · phaeochromocytoma · parenteral nutrition Presents as Stones, bones, groans, moans, thrones, muscle tone, psychiatric overtones · often asymptomatic, found on a routine panel short QT , Osborn wave, bradycardia, atrioventricular block · weakness and hyporeflexia · nephrolithiasis · pancreatitis · confusion and apathy Hypercalcaemia on ECG: a short QT interval and an Osborn wave (arrows), both gone once the same patient's calcium is normalized Investigations 1. Corrected calcium , then PTH - always, and it is what decides the whole workup 2. 24-hour urine calcium + creatinine → fractional excretion of calcium (FE_Ca) if PTH is not suppressed 3. dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (bone density scan) · renal ultrasound · vitamin D Treatment - admit if corrected calcium is over 3 mmol/L 1. Volume repletion, assume a 4-6 L deficit , normal saline 2. Anaplastic carcinoma is what a well-differentiated cancer becomes , and it is the one that will not take up iodine. Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Risk and Treatment You can diagnose osteoporosis three ways, and only one of them involves a bone density scan. Once diagnosed, treatment choice turns on which fracture site you need to prevent and whether the patient has already failed or been harmed by an antiresorptive (a drug that slows bone breakdown). ⭐ A fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis on its own - but skull, hands, feet and ankles do not count , and neither does a genuinely traumatic fracture. T-score compares to a young adult, Z-score to age-matched peers ; only the T-score diagnoses. raloxifene and teriparatide have no hip fracture data - reach for a bisphosphonate, denosumab , or estrogen when the hip is the concern. Every anabolic course must be followed by an antiresorptive , at 1 year for romosozumab and 2 for teriparatide. Osteonecrosis of the jaw has a definition with a clock in it: exposed bone unhealed at 8 weeks , and dental work goes first . Groin or thigh pain in a patient on a bisphosphonate is an impending atypical femoral fracture , not arthritis. 1. Why it matters: the treatment gap A fragility fracture is the diagnosis - yet only 15% of patients are treated after a fragility fracture, against 80% who get a beta blocker after a heart attack. Ask: "Would a healthy young adult's bone likely break in this situation?" Metabolic Bone Disease: Osteomalacia, Paget's & Osteogenesis Imperfecta Three diseases of bone that are not osteoporosis, and the lab panel separates all three before any imaging. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect, Paget's is disordered remodelling, and osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen gene defect - the lecture takes them in that order. ⭐ ALP is the thread through all three: very high in Paget's, high in osteomalacia, normal in osteogenesis imperfecta. Calcium and phosphate are BOTH low in osteomalacia and BOTH normal in Paget's - that pair alone separates them. Urine calcium is LOW in osteomalacia , which is the opposite of what a stone-former's panel looks like. Proximal myopathy is the osteomalacia feature that osteoporosis never has , and it is what causes the falls. Bone-forming drugs are contraindicated in Paget's - you do not encourage a formation process that is already disordered, which makes zoledronate the answer and teriparatide the trap. Increased hat size and warmth over a bone are Paget's , and blue sclerae with fractures from birth are osteogenesis imperfecta . A young adult with celiac disease , falls, weakness and pseudofractures has osteomalacia, not osteoporosis. 1. The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis The axis is three tissues - hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, gonads - and one non-negotiable requirement: gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) must arrive in PULSES. A continuous GnRH signal does not amplify the axis, it shuts it down , which is exactly how a GnRH agonist becomes a chemical castration. ⭐ Pulsatility is the whole axis. Continuous GnRH suppresses, which is why an agonist ends up doing the same job as an antagonist but with a dangerous surge first . kisspeptin is the strongest positive input to the pulse generator , and steroids never touch the GnRH neuron directly - they work through interneurons. LH → theca and Leydig; FSH → granulosa and Sertoli , and inhibin brakes FSH alone . The shared α subunit is why the β subunit is what gets measured. Cholesterol to pregnenolone, in the mitochondrion, is the rate-limiting step. Estradiol and progesterone act without further metabolism; testosterone usually does not. Estradiol induces the progesterone receptor , so the order of the cycle is built into the receptors themselves. 1. The three levels and the two kinds of hypothalamic neuron The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis hypothalamus makes GnRH made by endocrine and non-endocrine cells , with endocrine, paracrine, autocrine and juxtacrine effects GnRH-I is the mammalian form · GnRH-II , first found in chicken hypothalamus, is also present in humans and differs by three amino acid shifts at positions 5, 7 and 8 anterior pituitary makes luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) - both named for their action in the ovary gonads make estrogen , progesterone , testosterone , plus activin and inhibin - inhibin and activin are the FSH-specific feedback arm Neuron type Axon goes Releases into Hormones Magnocellular (neurohypophyseal) across the median eminence into the POSTERIOR pituitary via the pituitary stalk directly into the general circulation oxytocin and vasopressin Parvicellular (hypophysiotrophic) into the median eminence only the portal circulation to the ANTERIOR pituitary GnRH , corticotropin-releasing hormone , thyrotropin-releasing hormone , growth hormone-releasing hormone , somatostatin 2. The hypophysial portal system and the median eminence The portal route, in order peptides released into the median eminence → primary plexus capillaries (fed by the carotid artery ) → hypophysial portal veins in the pituitary stalk ( long parallel veins connecting two capillary beds ) → secondary plexus supplying the anterior pituitary → hormones act on receptors there (e.g. the GnRH receptor) → LH and FSH enter the same capillaries into the general circulation The median eminence is one of only seven brain regions without a blood-brain barrier - so hypothalamic peptides can leave the brain it is where both halves of the hypothalamus are joined The hypothalamus also regulates food energy expenditure, body weight, fluid intake and balance, blood pressure, thirst, temperature and the sleep cycle , organised into nuclei from the preoptic area to the mammillary nucleus Hypophyseal portal system: hypothalamic neurons release peptides at the median eminence, portal veins carry them to the anterior pituitary, while other neurons run straight to the posterior pituitary 3. The GnRH pulse generator GnRH neurons spontaneously depolarize in a coordinated fashion , releasing GnRH pulsatile ly, which drives pulsatile LH and FSH the capacity is INTRINSIC : cultured GnRH neurons show the same coordinated release in vitro , so the rhythm is not imposed from outside Positive regulators : glutamate , neuropeptide Y , norepinephrine - and kisspeptin is the STRONGEST positive regulator Negative regulators : gamma-aminobutyric acid and endogenous opioid peptides Steroids act INDIRECTLY : estradiol and progesterone do NOT act on the GnRH neuron itself - they change the activity of other neurons that synapse onto it 4. The Menstrual Cycle One hormone does something no other hormone in the body does: estradiol switches its own feedback from negative to positive. That single switch divides the cycle in two: the follicular phase is built by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and dismantled by the estradiol it produces; the luteal phase runs on progesterone and lasts a fixed two weeks unless an embryo arrives. ⭐ Estradiol is the only hormone here that reverses the sign of its own feedback , and it needs both a level (300–500 pg/mL) and a duration (~48 hours) to do it. Getting one of those two right and the other wrong is the classic distractor. FSH falls during the follicular phase - counter-intuitively, because the follicle it grew is now making the oestrogen that suppresses it. The luteal phase is the fixed half of the cycle ; when a cycle is short or long, it is the follicular phase that varies. The corpus luteum regresses after two weeks unless an embryo rescues it , and that regression is menstruation. Testicular and Ovarian Function The two gonads are the same machine with different settings. What differs is the output: spermatogenesis makes 4 haploid gametes continuously from a self-renewing stem cell; oogenesis makes 1 from a reservoir that was finished before birth. That single asymmetry explains menopause, polar bodies, and why the two arrest points exist at all. ⭐ Map the four cells onto two hormones and you have the lecture: LH → Leydig and theca (androgen); FSH → Sertoli and granulosa (inhibin, and aromatase in the ovary). 4 gametes from spermatogenesis, 1 from oogenesis , and the female reservoir is fixed before birth. The oocyte is arrested twice: prophase I until recruitment, meiosis II until fertilization - fertilization is a trigger, not just a fusion. The blood-testis barrier exists because sperm are genetically foreign to their own host. Most FSH receptors wins the dominant-follicle competition, and assisted reproductive technology simply removes the competition by flooding the system. The granulosa cell trades FSH receptors for LH receptors as ovulation approaches - the same cell, answering to a different hormone. 5-α reductase makes DHT for hair, glands and external genitalia; aromatase makes estradiol and closes the growth plates. Only 5% of testosterone is free, and only that 5% works. 1. 01 Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease

Adrenal Gland Disease Every adrenal problem is one zone making too much, or the whole cortex making too little — and each product has exactly one screening test , which is what turns the incidentaloma workup into a fixed list of three. four products, four screening tests — and an incidentaloma gets three of them. Weight gain is the weakest Cushing sign; bruising, fracture and proximal weakness the strongest. Cushing needs two positive screens before the ACTH question is asked at all. ⭐ Primary insufficiency loses aldosterone as well as cortisol — so K⁺ is high, ACTH is high, and fludrocortisone is required; secondary spares all three. Alpha before beta, always. Cut-offs vary between labs: know the principle, not the number. Gold standards: adrenal vein sampling for lateralising Conn, insulin tolerance test for secondary insufficiency. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis: the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), the anterior pituitary releases adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), the adrenal cortex releases cortisol, and cortisol feeds back to switch off CRH and ACTH Every adrenal disease on one chart: the whole cortex making too little (Addison) or one zone making too much (Cushing syndrome, Conn, pheochromocytoma). A low or normal ACTH with low cortisol is secondary - that, and the pituitary side of Cushing, are on the pituitary chart. Open full size to enlarge. 1. Pituitary Gland Disease Every pituitary lesion is asked in two halves — what the mass is doing, and what the gland is making — and a macroadenoma answers both at once. mass effect and hormone status are two separate questions. Dopamine inhibits prolactin, so antagonists raise it. IGF-1 screens acromegaly because GH is pulsatile, and the OGTT confirms by failure to suppress . ⭐ The prolactinoma is the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first — it shrinks on a tablet, so a visual field defect is not an indication for surgery. Acromegaly does not make you taller. Steroid before thyroxine, always. A normal TSH beside a low free T4 is central hypothyroidism, not reassurance. 03 Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty

Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty Puberty is not switched on — the axis is built before birth, suppressed in infancy, and then DISINHIBITED. The menstrual cycle that follows runs on one hormone that reverses its own feedback. puberty is disinhibition, not activation. ⭐ The earliest measurable change is a NOCTURNAL rise in LH — before puberty LH is flat across 24 hours, and only in late puberty is it raised awake as well. Adrenarche is adrenal and separate from gonadarche, which is why pubic hair can appear with no gonadal activity. Most FSH receptors wins the dominant follicle. Ovulation is 36 hours after the surge. The follicular phase varies; the luteal phase does not. Boys end up taller because they start later, not because they grow faster. 1. Puberty: the words and the order The vocabulary is not interchangeable gonadarche (gonads activated by luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)) · adrenarche (adrenal androgens, a separate axis ) thelarche (breast, from ovarian estradiol) · pubarche (pubic hair, from adrenal androgen) · menarche · spermarche Sequence in girls: gonadarche → adrenarche → thelarche → growth spurt → menarche, over 4-5 years (this year's slide order; standard teaching puts adrenarche first) abnormal if it occurs 16 y (delayed) Genetics accounts for 50-75% of the variation in pubertal timing Boys end up taller because they start later, not because they grow faster History : age at each milestone and the order they came in · family history of pubertal timing · nutrition, weight change, exercise load · anosmia Physical exam : Tanner staging of breast AND pubic hair separately (they run on different axes) · height, weight and plotted growth velocity · thyroid, visual fields, dysmorphism ⚠ No investigation at all is needed for a normally timed, normally ordered puberty — reassurance and explanation where timing is normal Follow-up : re-plot growth velocity and re-stage at interval 2. Disorders of Growth One question splits the differential before any test: did the weight fall before the height, or is the child short and relatively chubby? Illness starves growth; endocrine disease arrests it. ⭐ Weight falls first in chronic illness; height falls first in endocrine disease, leaving a short chubby child. Bone age separates familial (on time) from constitutional delay (behind). Disproportionate short stature means skeletal dysplasia, not an endocrine cause. A random GH is worthless because GH is pulsatile. Congenital GH deficiency has a normal birth size and declares itself with neonatal hypoglycaemia. 1. Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum Two lines organise the whole lecture: the pelvic pain line , which decides where pain is felt and which block reaches it, and the nodal watershed , which decides where a cancer spreads. ⭐ Above the pain line pain refers to flank and back along sympathetics; below it to buttock and thigh along parasympathetics — and that single line predicts both the presentation and the block. Ovarian artery from the aorta, uterine from the internal iliac, and their anastomosis is what lets the ovaries be spared at hysterectomy. Fundus drains para-aortic while cervix drains iliac — one organ, two basins. Clitoris drains to deep inguinal, labial skin to superficial . 1. The reproductive tract Uterus — anteverted (relative to the vagina) and anteflexed (relative to the cervix) ; rests on the empty bladder body:cervix tracks hormone exposure: neonate 2:1 (maternal hormones) · childhood 1:1 · post-pubertal 2:1 · multiparous 3:1 · postmenopausal 1:1 Vagina — between urethra and rectum; posterior fornix is deepest rectouterine pouch is the lowest point when upright Uterine tubes — within the mesosalpinx · fertilization in the AMPULLA , which is also the commonest ectopic site Ovary — never enters the inguinal canal , unlike the testis Physical exam abdominal exam by quadrant · bimanual to size the uterus and assess mobility and adnexae · speculum for the cervix through the thin vaginal wall you can palpate the cervix, ischial spines, sacral promontory, uterine artery pulsation and ovarian irregularity 2. Seeing the tract Investigations beta-human chorionic gonadotropin first in any woman of reproductive age pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal) hysterosalpingography (HSG) for tubal patency — contrast should spill into the peritoneum culdocentesis via the posterior fornix for free fluid, since the rectouterine pouch is the lowest point when upright 3. Support and the pelvic floor Uterine ligaments cardinal ligament carries the uterine vessels ; uterosacral prevents prolapse broad ligament = mesometrium, mesosalpinx, mesovarium ovary: suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels · ligament of the ovary anchors it to the uterus Perineal body — central, midway between the ischial tuberosities, the final support of the pelvic viscera Pelvic diaphragm — levator ani (puborectalis medially, pubococcygeus intermediately, iliococcygeus posterolaterally) and coccygeus A transverse line between the ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into the urogenital and anal triangles 4. Blood supply Uterus : uterine artery — from the INTERNAL ILIAC , runs in the cardinal ligament "Water under the bridge" — the ureter passes UNDER the uterine artery ; identify it at hysterectomy Ovary : ovarian artery — from the AORTA the ovarian collateral (its anastomosis with the uterine) lets the ovaries be spared at hysterectomy Uterine tubes : tubal branches of uterine and ovarian Vagina : vaginal artery (middle) · internal pudendal (inferior) Perineum : internal pudendal — out the greater sciatic foramen, behind the sacrospinous ligament, back in via the lesser Arterial supply of the uterus and vagina: the ureter passes under the uterine artery, water under the bridge 5. Lymphatic drainage: the nodal watershed From Drains to Uterus Fundus → LUMBAR (para-aortic) Body and cervix → internal and external iliac Uterine tubes, ovary Lumbar Vagina Upper → iliac · inferior → sacral Perineum Skin → superficial inguinal Clitoris and vestibular bulb → DEEP inguinal Investigations : staging imaging is directed by the nodal basin — ⚠ fundus drains to para-aortic nodes, cervix to iliac, clitoris to DEEP inguinal, labial skin to SUPERFICIAL inguinal 6. Nerves and the pelvic pain line Fundus and body ABOVE the pain line — sympathetic to T11/12-L2 (tubes and ovaries too) → pain referred to mid-trunk, back, flank Cervix and vagina BELOW the line — parasympathetic to S2-S4 → pain referred to gluteal region, thigh, leg Perineum: pudendal nerve (S2-S4) , felt in the perineum directly · dorsal nerve of the clitoris is the primary sensory nerve History WHERE is the pain referred? Flank, back and mid-trunk point above the line; buttock, thigh and leg point below it then: cycle relationship, dyspareunia (superficial vs deep), bowel and bladder symptoms, obstetric and surgical history, trauma or straddle injury Anaesthesia, chosen by the pain line lumbar epidural or low spinal (L3/4) anaesthetises everything below the waist caudal (saddle) epidural reaches S2-S4 only and does not block the uterine fundus , so the mother still feels contractions and knows when to bear down pudendal block at the ischial spine covers the perineum and inferior quarter of the vagina but does not reach the cervix or superior vagina ⚠ Contractions are hormonal, not neural — no block stops labour The pelvic pain line: pain from organs above it (fundus, body, tubes, ovaries) travels with sympathetic nerves to T11-L2; from below it (cervix, upper vagina) with parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves to S2-S4; the perineum is somatic 7. The perineum, its fascia and episiotomy Perineal fascia and where fluid goes a ruptured urethra fills the superficial perineal pouch ( Colles fascia ↔ perineal membrane ) it cannot reach the thigh (Colles binds to the fascia lata) and cannot reach the anal triangle (Colles stops at the urogenital triangle) so it tracks up the anterior abdominal wall , deep to Camper's and Scarpa's but superficial to external oblique the deep pouch holds the voluntary external urethral sphincter , through which both the vagina and urethra pass in the female Physical exam : perineal body integrity , scars, swelling and where it does and does not track Episiotomy — median episiotomy divides the perineal body and directs tearing toward the anus ; mediolateral is safer mediolateral over median : the median cut brings more severe laceration, incontinence and fistula Perineal pouches in female and male: the deep pouch above the perineal membrane
07 Development of the Female Reproductive System

Development of the Female Reproductive System Female is the default : no testis-determining factor makes the ovary, no anti-Müllerian hormone keeps the Müllerian ducts, no testosterone dissolves the Wolffian ducts. Every anomaly below is one failed step in the fusion-and-canalisation sequence. Wolffian and Müllerian are reciprocal — one survives in each sex. Didelphys and bicornuate are failed FUSION; septate is failed RESORPTION; unicornuate is one duct that never formed. The vagina has two origins, upper third from the ducts and lower two-thirds from the bulbs. Absent vagina usually means absent uterus. ⭐ Always image the renal tract when a Müllerian anomaly is found — both systems arise from intermediate mesoderm, and urinary development precedes genital by about 10 days. 1. Sex determination: the default pathway SRY gene present → testis-determining factor → testis · absent → ovary No anti-Müllerian hormone → paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts develop · no testosterone → mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts degenerate Wolffian and Müllerian are reciprocal — one survives in each sex. 2. The indifferent gonad Primordial germ cells migrate from the yolk sac ( weeks 4-6, ~T10 ) to the gonadal ridge — no migration, no gonad Sexes are indifferent weeks 4-7 and distinct by week 12 By week 7 both duct systems sit side by side 3. The ovary and the oocyte reserve Primitive sex cords degenerate, cortical cords form, oogonia become primary oocytes arrested in prophase I ~400,000 at birth, and no oogonia form postnatally — the reserve is fixed before birth 4. Mesonephric (Wolffian) remnants All in the broad ligament epoöphoron (mesovarium) · paroöphoron (near the uterus) Gartner's duct (lateral uterine and vaginal wall ), which is the one that becomes a cyst A Gartner's duct cyst in the lateral vaginal wall is a mesonephric remnant and needs no workup beyond recognition Mesonephric (Wolffian) duct remnants in the female: the epoöphoron beside the ovary, the paroöphoron nearer the uterus, and Gartner's duct running down the lateral uterine and vaginal wall, the one that forms a cyst 5. Paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts and the vagina's two origins Paramesonephric ducts open cranially as the tubes and fimbriae and fuse caudally into the uterovaginal primordium → uterus, cervix, upper 1/3 vagina this induces the sinovaginal bulbs , which fuse into the vaginal plate and canalise into the lower 2/3 The vagina has two origins: upper third from the ducts, lower two-thirds from the bulbs The hymen ruptures perinatally Development of the uterus and vagina: sinovaginal bulbs form the vaginal plate, which canalises into the lower vagina 6. Müllerian anomalies Didelphys and bicornuate are failed FUSION; septate is failed RESORPTION; unicornuate is one duct that never formed. The four Müllerian anomalies side by side: unicornuate (one duct never formed), bicornuate (fusion of the upper body failed), septate (the septum was never resorbed) and didelphys (fusion failed all the way down, two cervices) Uterus didelphys Bicornuate uterus Septate uterus Unicornuate uterus Vaginal agenesis Vaginal atresia Failed step Fusion of the inferior paramesonephric ducts Fusion of the ducts forming the superior uterine body Resorption of the septum after fusion One duct never developed Sinovaginal bulbs never formed the vaginal plate Canalisation of the vaginal plate Anatomy Two separate uteri and cervices; double or single vagina One cervix, two horns, a shared lower body One cavity externally, divided internally by a septum One horn, one tube ; the other side absent No vagina — and the uterus is usually absent too , since it induces the bulbs Vagina present but not patent Presentation Often incidental; dyspareunia Often incidental Often incidental Often incidental Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics Primary amenorrhoea with cyclical pain — obstructed outflow Investigations Pelvic ultrasound, then MRI ⚠ Renal tract imaging in every case Pelvic ultrasound, then MRI ⚠ Renal tract imaging MRI — it is what distinguishes septate from bicornuate, and that is the distinction that changes management Hysteroscopy Pelvic ultrasound, then MRI ⚠ Renal tract imaging Examination · MRI · karyotype · hormones to confirm ovarian function ⚠ Renal tract imaging Examination · MRI Treatment Usually expectant Usually expectant The one most amenable to hysteroscopic resection Expectant Dilation or surgical reconstruction Surgical correction Prognosis Fertile, but increased premature delivery As didelphys Improves with resection Increased obstetric risk 1:5000 ; fertility depends on whether a uterus exists Good once relieved Absent vagina usually means absent uterus. History : primary amenorrhoea with or without normal secondary sexual characteristics · cyclical pain without bleeding (obstruction) · recurrent miscarriage or preterm delivery (fusion anomaly) · dyspareunia or an inability to use tampons · always ask about known RENAL anomalies Physical exam : external genitalia and whether the structures fused · patency and length of the vagina · presence of a cervix · bimanual for a uterus · Tanner staging (normal breasts with absent uterus points elsewhere than gonadal failure) Investigations : pelvic ultrasound first , then MRI for uterine morphology · karyotype · hormones to confirm ovarian function ⚠ imaging the RENAL tract is mandatory, not optional, whenever a Müllerian anomaly is found — urinary and genital defects travel together, because both arise from intermediate mesoderm Follow-up : counsel that many of these women are fertile but carry an increased rate of premature delivery , so pregnancies are followed as high risk 7. Introduction to Transgender Medicine Four words that are not synonyms, and a treatment ladder ordered by one thing: reversibility. dysphoria is the distress, not the incongruence. Blockers fully reversible, hormones partially, surgery not — and hormones wait until puberty has started. Fertility is discussed before hormones, not after. Comorbidity must be reasonably well-controlled, not cured . Testosterone effects are not fully reversible, and oral testosterone cannot be monitored at all. ⭐ Family support moves suicide attempt risk from 60% to 4%. 1. Definitions Sex is biological Gender is psychological Gender identity is the person's own articulation Sexual orientation is a separate axis entirely 2. Gender dysphoria Diagnosis — gender dysphoria is the DISTRESS , not the incongruence marked and persistent incongruence, a desire to transition and be accepted as the experienced gender a strong dislike of one's sexual anatomy or of anticipated pubertal changes Assessment — summarised as insistence · persistence · consistence (insistence: how firm, "I am" not "I wish"; persistence: how long; consistence: the same across settings) History : "Some young people feel they were born in the wrong body; have you ever felt like that?" · how puberty affected their identity · source of distress · social transition and who knows · fertility intentions ⚠ family support, which is the single largest modifier of suicide risk (60% → 4%) Physical exam : Tanner stage (it decides whether blockers or hormones are even on the table) · height, weight, blood pressure · baseline for the effects being monitored Epidemiology — 1 in 300 Canadians aged 15+ , two-thirds under 35 · 1.2-4.1% of adolescents · prevalence is rising, not falling Most PRE-pubertal children who identify as transgender do not persist; most ADOLESCENTS do — which is why puberty is where the ladder begins Mental health outcomes suicidality is 2-3× more frequent · 47% of trans youth in Ontario had considered suicide, 19% attempted youth managed with hormones, surgery where indicated and a multidisciplinary team including mental health clinicians had outcomes similar to the general population 3. Types of treatment: the reversibility ladder puberty blockers (fully reversible) → gender-affirming hormones (partially reversible) → surgery (irreversible) ⚠ Hormones do not start until puberty has started. Disorders of Sexual Differentiation A disorder of sexual differentiation (DSD) is a discrepancy between karyotype, gonad, internal genitalia and external genitalia — so the karyotype is the first test , because it decides which half of the differential you are in. The lecture builds the normal pathway, examines and investigates the newborn, splits the causes by karyotype, then manages the baby and the commonest cause, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) . karyotype first. 5α-reductase deficiency virilises at puberty (incompletely) because testosterone is normal; incomplete androgen insensitivity virilises only incompletely and adds gynaecomastia and azoospermia . T:DHT after hCG for the enzyme, DNA for the receptor. DHT builds the external genitalia, testosterone the internal ducts. ⭐ The 46,XX CAH infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY CAH infant looks normal and presents in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks. Sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery. 1. How sex develops, and what a DSD is Male path : the SRY gene makes testis-determining factor (TDF) → testes Sertoli cells: anti-Mullerian hormone (Mullerian-inhibiting factor, MIF) → the Mullerian duct regresses Leydig cells: testosterone → keeps the Wolffian duct → internal male genitalia 5-alpha-reductase turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT) → external male genitalia Female path is the default without SRY — but a 46,XX karyotype is needed for normal ovarian development DHT builds the external genitalia, testosterone the internal ducts Sexual differentiation: SRY makes testis-determining factor (TDF) and testes; Sertoli cells make anti-Mullerian hormone (MIF) to regress the Mullerian duct, Leydig testosterone keeps the Wolffian duct, and 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT for male external genitalia; without SRY, the female path is the default What this lecture is explicitly NOT about ⚠ Gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation are stated on their own slide as out of scope. A DSD is an anatomical and biochemical finding. ⚠ DSDs are not always associated with ambiguous genitalia — some present instead as abnormal pubertal development . 2. Examining the newborn History family history of ambiguous genitalia, virilisation, infertility or unexplained neonatal death · consanguinity pregnancy: maternal medications, maternal virilisation, maternal health neonatal crisis — vomiting, poor feeding, collapse at 1-3 weeks Physical exam PALPATE FOR GONADS — a palpable gonad is almost always a testis, which immediately narrows the differential phallus length and width · labioscrotal folds: fused or open, rugated, hyperpigmented · number and position of urogenital openings describe it with a drawn diagram , not prose general exam for dysmorphism and for hyperpigmentation (excess adrenocorticotropic hormone, ACTH) Use neutral terms: gonads, phallus, labio-scrotal folds. 3. Investigations: the karyotype splits the differential First line, every case : karyotype · pelvic and abdominal ultrasound Then other labs based on your differential 17-hydroxyprogesterone (markedly raised in 21-hydroxylase deficiency) · electrolytes and glucose — sodium↓, potassium↑, acidosis, low blood sugar testosterone:DHT (T:DHT) ratio after human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) stimulation for 5-alpha-reductase deficiency DNA analysis for androgen insensitivity Two further karyotype groups : ovotesticular DSD (chromosomes variable, gonads mixed) · mixed gonadal dysgenesis (45,X/46,XY) 4. 46,XY DSD: an under-virilised male Testes are present, but the external genitalia are incompletely virilised. Causes testis failed: gonadal dysgenesis (complete or partial) · testes regression cannot make androgen: Leydig cell hypoplasia (luteinizing hormone (LH) deficiency or LH receptor defect) · testosterone biosynthesis defects (non-virilising CAH: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD), 17,20-lyase, 17β-HSD) · deficient anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) synthesis or action cannot make DHT: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (autosomal recessive) receptor broken: androgen insensitivity ( X-linked recessive androgen receptor defect) 5. 46,XX DSD: a virilised female Ovaries are present, but a source of androgen has virilised the external genitalia. Causes CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency — the commonest androgen-secreting tumour transplacental maternal androgen or drugs Prader stages I to V of virilisation of the female infant, between normal female and normal male external genitalia, with the internal ducts above 6. Managing ambiguous genitalia at birth Refer to a tertiary centre — endocrinology, neonatology, genetics, gynaecology, urology, social work, psychology Delay assignment of sex of rearing, do not assign a name, do not register the birth until investigations are complete warn that a final diagnosis may take several weeks Sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery — evidence for the operations is lacking and only expert surgeons should be involved 7. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) Cause : Autosomal recessive, CYP21A2 on chromosome 6 ; 95% of all CAH is 21-hydroxylase deficiency Pathology : cortisol blocked → ACTH ↑ → adrenal hyperplasia → precursors shunted to androgen; aldosterone lost in 75% Shares of CAH : 21-hydroxylase ≈95% · 11β-hydroxylase 5% · 3β-HSD 1%; incidence 1 in 10,000 births Severity is set by residual enzyme activity 1-5% = simple virilising : cortisol deficiency and androgen excess without significant salt loss mild mutation = non-classic : premature pubarche, then hirsutism, acne and oligomenorrhoea — a polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome-like picture Presents as Girls: virilised — clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion, single urogenital opening · Boys: LOOK NORMAL — penile enlargement, scrotal pigmentation salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks Investigations : 17-hydroxyprogesterone markedly raised — the diagnostic marker (case: 400, normal sodium↓ potassium↑ , acidosis, low blood sugar Treatment lifelong hydrocortisone 1

Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) Renamed from polycystic ovary syndrome in 2026 because both halves of the old name were wrong. The diagnosis is a triad that needs no ultrasound , made by excluding the mimics of each limb separately — hyperandrogenism has its own list of them, ovulatory dysfunction has another. The lecture then works each limb (history, exam, labs), the insulin resistance behind the risk, the myths, and treatment. the follicles are arrested antral follicles and the ovary is a target, not the source — which is why the name changed. ⭐ Hyperandrogenism plus oligomenorrhoea plus clean exclusions is diagnostic without ever scanning her; ultrasound is an alternative route into the second limb, not a criterion of its own. Cystic ovaries are also not specific — they occur early after menarche and in normally cycling women , so the scan is neither required for the diagnosis nor sufficient for it. Testosterone only reads against its two ranges — female normal — so 2.1-2.5 is fractionally over and fits, while 10 is a male level and means a tumour; and a normal testosterone does not exclude PMOS, because clinical hyperandrogenism satisfies that limb by itself. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is what separates non-classic CAH from PMOS when the picture is otherwise identical. Acanthosis is the insulin sign; striae would mean Cushing's. Hirsutism is defined by distress, not by a score — the modified Ferriman-Gallwey grades it but ignores ethnicity and hair removal. Of the five treatments offered, only topical testosterone is wrong. Reassure that she can conceive — and advise contraception in the same breath. 1. The name, and what PMOS is Old name, two errors "polycystic": the follicles are arrested antral follicles, not cysts "ovary syndrome": the ovary is a target, not the source How common : over 170 million women, up to 20% of reproductive age Cause : multisystem; no single cause identified hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian dysregulation · luteinizing hormone↑ follicle-stimulating hormone↓ insulin resistance adipose converts adrenal androgen to testosterone PCOS pathophysiology: insulin resistance lowers sex hormone-binding globulin and raises free estradiol and LH, driving ovarian hyperandrogenism, while raised P450c17 activity adds ovarian and adrenal androgen 2. Diagnosis: the triad All three needed ① hyperandrogenism — on exam or on labs ② ovulatory dysfunction — oligomenorrhoea or cystic ovaries on ultrasound ③ exclusion of other disorders There is no gold-standard test — the diagnosis IS the clinical triad , and no ultrasound is required 3. Excluding the mimics First-line panel : 1. Exclusion panel first: beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) · prolactin · thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) · total testosterone beta-hCG → pregnancy · prolactin (normal The lecture's own exclusion list is seven — pregnancy · hyperprolactinaemia · exogenous testosterone · tumour producing testosterone · congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) · hyperthyroidism · early menarche or menopause Three of the seven are found by history, not by a disease work-up (so they have no column below) exogenous androgen : taking testosterone, or skin contact with a partner's topical testosterone — found only on a thorough medication and social history pregnancy : suspected on history, settled by beta-hCG early menarche or menopause : a thorough menstrual history , and no test beyond it Rate of onset is the other history discriminator : PMOS hirsutism creeps over years, a tumour's arrives fast Cushing syndrome keeps a column here but is not on the list of seven : the deck names adrenal Cushing's only as a source of an androgen-secreting tumour, while the lecture's case still argues against Cushing's explicitly, on absent striae and a normal fasting glucose PMOS Androgen-secreting tumour Non-classic CAH Cushing syndrome Hyperprolactinaemia Thyroid disease Causes Multisystem; Everything below 12 weeks can go medical or surgical; above it the options narrow and the complication profile changes. 98% of abortions are uncomplicated. ⭐ the 70-day / 10-week / 14-week / 25-week ladder is the spine of this lecture. Ovulation returns 2 weeks after a 1st-trimester abortion , so contraception starts the same day. Legal termination carries a lower maternal death rate (0.567 per 100,000) than live birth (7.06). 1. Fertilization and Infertility Infertility is 50% female and 50% male, so both partners are investigated. The lecture runs from how fertilization happens, through who to work up and why couples are infertile, to a six-step work-up timed to the cycle, and ends on recurrent pregnancy loss. ⭐ primary infertility means she has never been PREGNANT — not that she has no children , and a partner's children from another relationship do not change it. AMH measures reserve and does NOT predict natural fertility. Male aging ↓ volume, motility and morphology but leaves sperm concentration stable, and is NOT associated with aneuploidy — that is the maternal-age effect. Recurrent pregnancy loss is ≥ 2 losses, consecutive or not, including biochemical , and ~50% stay unexplained ; the treatable one is antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (5-20%), treated with heparin + aspirin at the first positive test . 1. Contraception and drugs used in gynecology Two questions, in this order. First, which axis is this drug on — estrogen, progestin, or androgen — and is it disrupting the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, blocking a sex-hormone-dependent tissue, or replacing a missing hormone? The indication and the adverse effects both follow from that. Then, for contraception specifically, counsel from the TYPICAL-use column, never the perfect-use one . The contraception lecture ranks the methods, walks natural, barrier, permanent, hormonal and intrauterine methods, then emergency contraception and the CHOICE project. The pharmacology lecture covers the same hormones as drugs, then the estrogen and progesterone modulators, androgens, the non-hormonal drugs and the gonadotropin-releasing hormone modulators. ⭐ The progestin-only contraceptive's primary mechanism is LOCAL, not central — cervical mucus, tubal peristalsis and endometrium, with ovulation suppressed in only ~50% of cycles (the injection excepted), which is exactly why the mini-pill fails at 3 hours late while a combined pill forgives. Every contraindication in the combined column is an ESTROGEN contraindication — which is why the answer to “what can she have instead?” is almost always a progestin-only or intrauterine method. Combined methods are contraindicated over age 35 at more than 15 cigarettes per day , and a past deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism contraindicates them only when she is off anticoagulation AND at higher risk of recurrence . The patch and the ring bypass first-pass metabolism, and that — not the dose — is why they carry more VTE risk than the pill. Drospirenone is the anti-androgenic progestin (spironolactone-derived) — the one to reach for in hormonal acne, and the one that risks hyperkalemia . tamoxifen is the selective estrogen receptor modulator that raises endometrial cancer risk; raloxifene is not — both raise VTE . clomiphene raises gonadotropins by blocking central negative feedback , which is why an estrogen receptor antagonist induces ovulation. GnRH agonists flare before they suppress; antagonists never flare. Finasteride lowers dihydrotestosterone, it does not block the androgen receptor — which is why it shrinks a prostate and thins body hair without touching muscle mass. 1. Cervical Cancer Screening Screening works because the precursor lasts years. Most human papillomavirus (HPV) infections clear; some produce a squamous intraepithelial lesion; a few progress to carcinoma, usually after 10+ years . Treat the lesion and the cancer never happens — which is why cervical cancer is 16th in Canada and 4th worldwide. The lecture runs HPV → vaccines → the Pap test → primary HPV screening → self-sampling. ⭐ eligibility is any ASYMPTOMATIC person with a cervix who has EVER been sexually active, from about age 25 — screening is not for symptomatic people, and a never-sexually-active patient may defer. Vaccination does not replace screening. At least 75% of people are exposed to HPV in a lifetime and condoms are only partially protective , because transmission is skin-to-skin beyond what a condom covers. Ontario switched to primary HPV screening in March 2025: HPV negative returns to screening in 5 years, HPV 16/18 goes straight to colposcopy, and cytology is only the triage for other high-risk types. An LSIL alone does not tell you which strain caused it — which is why the strain matters more than the grade. 1. Public Health and STIs This lecture is about the population, not the patient. The clinical question is who has an infection ; the public-health question is what makes a disease reportable, and what does reporting buy . the list of risk factors is broad enough that most sexually active people meet at least one — which is the argument for offering testing rather than selecting for it. ⭐ Reportability is what makes contact tracing possible , so it is not an administrative detail but the mechanism by which a diagnosed infection stops spreading. Youth under 25 carry the most chlamydia and gonorrhea. 1. Sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections (STBBIs) STBBI = an infection spread by sexual contact and/or by blood grouped together because the risk factors are shared includes: HIV · hepatitis B · hepatitis C · chlamydia · gonorrhea · syphilis · human papillomavirus 2. Global burden Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) acquired daily , worldwide: more than 1 million New infections yearly with one of four STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, trichomoniasis): 376 million 3. Local epidemiology (London) chlamydia is the commonest STI in London gonorrhea and syphilis are rising HIV rates have been stable Sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections reported each year in Middlesex-London, 2005 to 2018 4. Gonorrhea and antibiotic resistance Gonococcal resistance has forced three changes of drug class penicillins and tetracyclines until resistance emerged in the 1980s → fluoroquinolones in the 1990s → 3rd generation cephalosporins since the mid-2000s 5. Risk factors Partner sexual contact with a known STI · a new partner, or more than two in the past year a serially monogamous pattern, since these individuals are less likely to be tested anonymous partnering (internet, bathhouse, rave) Age sexually active youth under 25 , in whom chlamydia and gonorrhea are especially concentrated Contraception none, or sole use of a non-barrier method: oral contraceptives , Depo Provera and the intrauterine device all count , because none is a barrier Substances injection drug use · alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy, crystal meth, especially when associated with sex Practices unprotected oral, genital or anal sex · sex with blood exchange , including sadomasochism · sharing sex toys Circumstance sex workers and clients · "survival sex" , exchanging sex for money, drugs, shelter or food · street involvement and homelessness · victims of sexual assault or abuse History a previous STI 6. Reportable diseases Reportable disease = a disease that specified individuals are required by legislation to report to public health places obligations on clinicians, laboratories, institutions, public health authorities and governments Reportable STBBIs: chlamydia · gonorrhea · HIV · syphilis · hepatitis B · hepatitis C Benefits of reportability Surveillance : incidence and risk in the community, and risk-factor information Public health action : individual-level information enabling contact tracing , and it triggers the legislative authority of the Medical Officer of Health International obligation : fulfils Canada's duties under the International Health Regulations 7.
