Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) PID — the mechanism is a barrier failure. The endocervical canal normally separates the sterile upper tract from the polymicrobial lower tract ; a sexually transmitted infection breaches it, and symptoms can appear anywhere along the ascending route . How common : 100,000 cases a year in Canada · 10-15% of reproductive-age women have at least one Organisms Polymicrobial — chlamydia and gonorrhea are commonest, but also anaerobes · G. vaginalis · H. influenzae · enteric gram-negative rods · Streptococcus agalactiae → broad-spectrum cover is required Presents as pelvic pain · dyspareunia · discharge · fever · cervical motion tenderness — the "chandelier sign" · pelvic mass Admit if cannot exclude a surgical emergency · failed oral therapy · severe illness · tubo-ovarian abscess · immunodeficient · pregnant · youth or adolescent Treatment outpatient regimen A: ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscular once + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days with or without metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 14 days inpatient regimen A: cefoxitin 2 g intravenous every 6 hours + doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours , stepping down at 24 hours of improvement surgery only for medical failure or tubo-ovarian abscess — ⚠ PID is NOT easily treated surgically while preserving fertility Complications Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome = perihepatic adhesions after PID Pelvic inflammatory disease: infection ascends from the cervix through the uterus and tube to the ovary and pelvis 5. 09 Early Pregnancy Complications - Spontaneous Abortion and Ectopic

Early Pregnancy Complications Two questions run this lecture: is the pregnancy inside the uterus, and is it viable? A positive beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) with pain or bleeding is an ectopic pregnancy until the ultrasound says otherwise, and the ultrasound is only interpretable against the β-hCG level. IUD + positive β-hCG = ectopic until proven otherwise. ⭐ Rh-negative + positive β-hCG + vaginal bleeding = Rh immunoglobulin , whether the pregnancy is a miscarriage or an ectopic. β-hCG is the most important predictor of methotrexate failure — 92% success below 5000, and 4x the failure rate above it. Half of miscarriages have a normal karyotype; of the abnormal half, trisomy 16 is commonest and always lethal, and XO is the commonest isolated aneuploidy. Cerclage is elective at 12-16 weeks and rescue below 23 weeks. 1. Endometriosis The disease does not behave the way its extent predicts. The lecture defines it, explains why the pain and the findings mislead, then treats it two ways depending on whether she is trying to conceive. ⭐ most women with endometriosis do NOT experience infertility , despite it being the headline complication. Disease severity does not predict pain, and a normal examination does not rule it out. Pain begins about 2 days BEFORE menses — which is what separates it from primary dysmenorrhea , where pain comes with the bleeding. Many patients have had YEARS without a diagnosis , told repeatedly that painful periods are normal in the teenage years. 1. What endometriosis is Endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity Prevalence 1-7% of the population · 7% of first-degree relatives · 5-33% of infertile women Etiology — unknown retrograde menstruation (most cited — but most women have some degree of it ) coelomic metaplasia · haematogenous / lymphatic spread Sites, in order ovaries → uterine ligaments → rectovaginal septum → pelvic peritoneum · can be anywhere in the body Endometriosis sites in order of frequency: ovaries (where an endometrioma forms), uterine ligaments, rectovaginal septum and cul-de-sac, then pelvic peritoneum; it can occur anywhere in the body 2. Pain, and why the diagnosis is late Pain mechanism : inflammation , incompletely understood The severity of disease does not correlate with the degree of pain Pain begins about 2 days BEFORE menses — primary dysmenorrhea hurts with the bleeding Many patients have had YEARS without a diagnosis , told repeatedly that painful periods are normal in the teenage years 3. Asking about dyspareunia Ask, because she will not raise it "Have you ever had penetrative sexual activity? If yes, do you experience pain with it?" maintain a non-judgmental, normalizing approach Where the pain is tells you the cause superficial pain on penetration → vulvodynia · atrophy · vulvar skin conditions · vaginismus deep pain points to endometriosis , masses, adhesions or musculoskeletal causes 4. Physical examination Examination finding Note Nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments / cul-de-sac The most specific Fixed, immobile uterus From fibrosis and adhesions Adnexal mass An endometrioma Often NOTHING A normal examination does not rule it out ⚠ A normal examination does not rule it out — which is why it takes years to diagnose 5. Treatment Not trying to conceive Trying to conceive Principle Suppress ovulation + pain control ( non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ) — the disease is estrogen sensitive Suppression is not an option First line combined oral contraceptive · progestin-only pill · Visanne · progestin intrauterine device · implant · Depo-Provera Stage I-II: laparoscopic ablation or excision — improves spontaneous pregnancy for up to 9 months post-surgery Second line Orilissa or Lupron — a chemical menopause Stage III-IV: in-vitro fertilization , which bypasses the toxic pelvic environment , though implantation stays reduced Surgery Excision or ablation at laparoscopy — reserved for diagnosis, infertility optimization, or refractory disease when fertility is wanted ; do NOT repeat it — surgical risk Endometrioma surgery is avoided where fertility is wanted — it costs ovarian reserve Definitive hysterectomy with or without oophorectomy — not first line Not an option Two ways to suppress ovulation, and the split is the discriminator Pseudopregnancy — flood it with progestin: oral contraceptive pill · NuvaRing · Evra patch · Depo Provera · hormonal intrauterine system · Visanne Pseudomenopause — withdraw the estrogen: danazol , a testosterone derivative · Lupron or Zoladex, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists ⚠ Endometrioma surgery costs ovarian reserve — avoid it where fertility is wanted 7. 11 Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain

Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain One test sorts the differential, and it is the beta human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) . Everything that can kill her quickly is either pregnant or bleeding, and the β-hCG tells you which branch you are on before the ultrasound arrives. ⭐ an intrauterine device does NOT increase the incidence of ectopic pregnancy — it increases the likelihood that a pregnancy IS ectopic, if one occurs. That is a denominator effect, not a risk. A ruptured cyst mimics a ruptured ectopic exactly, and only the β-hCG separates them. Significant haemorrhage from a ruptured cyst is uncommon — most bleed minimally, which is why instability is notable. 1. The pathway: vitals, then the β-hCG ⚠ Identify the life- and limb-threatening causes first — that is what the β-hCG and the haemoglobin are for 2. Differential diagnosis by system Differential by system: gynecologic — pregnancy and its complications · dysmenorrhea · endometritis · neoplasm · salpingitis gastrointestinal — appendicitis · obstruction · diverticulitis · intussusception · Crohn's disease urologic — cystitis · pyelonephritis · nephrolithiasis musculoskeletal — hernia · trauma · muscle strain vascular — ischaemic bowel · sickle crisis neurologic — herpes zoster · abdominal migraine respiratory — pneumonia 3. History, examination and investigations History onset · duration · quality · location · radiation · aggravating and relieving factors associated gastrointestinal, genitourinary, fever, discharge, bleeding past medical, surgical, medication, gynecologic and family history the social history matters enormously in pelvic pain Physical exam vitals · general appearance · abdomen (inspection, auscultation, palpation) · pelvic (inspection, palpation) Investigations complete blood count · quantitative beta hCG · urinalysis and culture · vaginal and cervical cultures · ultrasound · group and screen 4. The four emergencies side by side Ectopic Pelvic inflammatory disease Ovarian torsion Ruptured ovarian cyst beta hCG POSITIVE Negative Negative NEGATIVE Onset Sudden, with bleeding Subacute, unwell for days Sudden, during vigorous activity — golf, intercourse, exercise Sudden, often after intercourse Timing Amenorrhea then bleeding Any Any 2-3 weeks from the last menstrual period — at ovulation Fever / WBC — Fever, WBC high Normal or near-normal — Haemoglobin Falling Normal Stable — she hurts, she is not bleeding Falling Key sign Shoulder pain, tenesmus , orthostatic drop cervical motion tenderness — chandelier sign , discharge A palpable, tender adnexal mass Shoulder pain, tenesmus, postural hypotension Mechanism of pain Visceral — stretching of the hollow tube ; shoulder pain is from blood on the diaphragm, so it is a RUPTURE sign Ascending infection through a breached endocervical barrier Infundibulopelvic ligament compressed → venous outflow blocked while arterial inflow continues → oedema → further compression → ischaemia Bleeding into the peritoneum Treatment Salpingectomy or salpingostomy, or methotrexate if stable, Antibiotics; admit if pregnant, adolescent, severe or failing oral antibiotics Surgical emergency — untwist and judge viability , then investigate the mass Usually self-limited ; surgery or interventional radiology if bleeding continues; prevent recurrence with ovulatory suppression Ectopic pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound: a gestational sac outside the uterus, between the uterus and the left ovary 5. Ectopic pregnancy and the intrauterine device Presents as pelvic pain, amenorrhea and vaginal bleeding ; confirmed with a positive β-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound Risk factors on this deck: pelvic infection · previous ectopic · smoking · adhesions · multiple sexual partners · intrauterine device in situ An intrauterine device does NOT increase the incidence of ectopic pregnancy it increases the likelihood that a pregnancy IS ectopic, if one occurs — a denominator effect, not a risk 6. Ovarian torsion: which ovaries tort A normal ovary can, but rarely Enlarged ovaries behave like a weighted pendulum — so torsion is usually a symptom of an underlying mass, benign or malignant Ovarian and adnexal torsion: the ovary, often with the tube, twists on its ligaments and cuts off its own blood supply; the tube rarely twists alone 7. Ruptured ovarian cyst Mimics a ruptured ectopic — only the β-hCG separates them Significant haemorrhage is uncommon — most bleed minimally, which is why instability is notable
12 Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain

Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain Chronic pain serves no purpose, and it rarely matches the damage. The lecture defines it, maps where it can come from, then walks five causes that are told apart by when the pain comes and what the uterus feels like . ⭐ up to 50% of women with chronic pelvic pain have experienced some kind of abuse or trauma — take the history. Boggy distinguishes adenomyosis from the firm irregular uterus of fibroids. Pain with no cyclic pattern and a normal structural examination is myofascial , and the honest goal there is pain reduction and improved function, not cure . 1. What chronic pelvic pain is Pain below the umbilicus for at least 6 months, severe enough to cause functional disability or require treatment. Acute pain is protective; chronic pain serves no physiologic purpose the intensity is often not proportional to the tissue damage — which is why the examination so often finds less than the story predicts How common : 10% of outpatient gynecology referrals · 40% of laparoscopies · 20% of hysterectomies for benign disease History : up to 50% have experienced abuse or trauma — take the history 2. Where the pain can come from Where the pain can come from: pelvic viscera (uterus, ovaries, bladder, urethra, rectum, sigmoid) somatic structures (skin, vulva, clitoris, vagina) musculoskeletal and ligamentous structures gastrointestinal and urologic referred pain 3. The five causes side by side Primary dysmenorrhea Endometriosis Adenomyosis Fibroids Myofascial pain Who Late teens and 20s, then declines 1-7%; 5-33% of infertile women Parous, 4th-5th decades ; incidence 5-70% ~50% of women over 40 on imaging ; 25% clinically apparent Any age; often years of pain Timing of pain WITH menses , worst days 1-2 ~2 days BEFORE menses With menses, sometimes Pressure rather than cyclic pain NOT related to the cycle at all Bleeding Normal Not usually menorrhagia Abnormal uterine bleeding — commonest with submucosal Normal Examination Normal — no lab or physical findings Uterosacral nodularity · fixed uterus · endometrioma · often NOTHING Tender, enlarged, BOGGY uterus Enlarged, firm, irregular, mobile uterus Globally tender pelvis, normal uterus, no masses Pathology Prostaglandin-driven ischaemia Endometrium outside the uterus Endometrial glands and stroma DEEP IN the myometrium — a histological definition; 15-30% of resected uteri (pathology deck) Benign MONOCLONAL smooth muscle tumours High resting tone in levator ani and piriformis Diagnosis Clinical Laparoscopy + biopsy (2 of 3: glands, stroma, hemosiderin) Mostly a clinical diagnosis — history and examination ; ultrasound and MRI sometimes help; NOT by biopsy — the glands are too deep , often incidental at hysterectomy Ultrasound Clinical Treatment Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and ovulatory suppression Ovulatory suppression + NSAIDs; surgery selectively Suppression · danazol · gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists · uterine artery embolization (UAE) · hysterectomy is the gold standard Suppression; submucosal → hysteroscopic resection ; large or pedunculated → myomectomy or hysterectomy Multidisciplinary ; manual soft tissue release is essential ; trigger-point local anaesthetic; amitriptyline , gabapentin ⚠ Adenomyosis is NOT diagnosed by biopsy — the glands are too deep — so although it is defined histologically, it is mostly a clinical diagnosis 4. Primary dysmenorrhea: why NSAIDs are first line Menses is a generalized inflammatory state prostaglandins from endometrial sloughing induce contractions → uterine pressure exceeds arterial pressure → uterine ischaemia → anaerobic metabolites accumulate → stimulate type C pain neurons Any hormonal method that reduces menstrual flow improves it, because there is less endometrium to slough 5. Adenomyosis Boggy distinguishes adenomyosis from the firm irregular uterus of fibroids Adenomyosis on MRI: the arrows mark the thickened myometrium dotted with bright foci, with the endometrium (E) and bladder (Bl) labelled 6. Uterine fibroids: location decides everything Risk factors more common in African American , obese, early menarche and hereditary cases smoking is associated with LESS risk Location → treatment submucosal → bleeding and hysteroscopic resection intramural, subserosal and submucosal → may respond to uterine artery embolization pedunculated → risk of torsion , and myomectomy or hysterectomy Reproductive dysfunction only occurs with fibroids that distort the cavity ⚠ Pregnancy after uterine artery embolization is NOT advised — case reports only , which is what separates UAE from myomectomy for a patient who still wants to conceive Fibroid locations, which decide both the symptoms and the operation: submucosal fibroids bulge into the cavity and bleed, intramural sit in the wall, subserosal and pedunculated push outward and cause mass effect; cervical and broad ligament fibroids are less common Uterine artery embolization: a catheter passed from the femoral artery into the uterine artery releases particles that cut off the fibroid's blood supply, with angiography images of the procedure 7. Myofascial pelvic pain Pain with no cyclic pattern and a normal structural examination is myofascial Goal : pain reduction and improved function, not cure
13 Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain

Approach to the Pathology of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding and Pelvic Pain Exclude the structural causes first, then use age, common reasons and clues to narrow what is left. The differential is ABCDEHIN (Anatomic, Baby, Coagulopathy, dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB), Endocrine, Hormones, Infectious, Neoplasia), and one visible finding can delete five of the eight letters. ⭐ of the four lesions here, endometriosis, polyps and leiomyomas cause infertility — adenomyosis does NOT. Fibroids are not pre-malignant and are not a precursor to malignancy. A mass at the os narrows the differential to the structural letters and away from the functional ones , which is the entire method of this lecture. 1. The pathway: structural causes first A mass at the os narrows the differential to the structural letters and away from the functional ones a mass at the os points to Anatomic · Baby · Neoplasia structural = Anatomic / Neoplasia / Infectious (benign PALE + malignancy) and Baby · functional = Coagulopathy · DUB · Endocrine · Hormones 2. Endometrial polyp A benign overgrowth of the lining, in the uterine cavity Two microscopic types those resembling the background endometrium hyperplastic ones, which carry an association with endometrial hyperplasia Rarely a polyp harbours malignancy, so always send the ENTIRE polyp What to tell the patient : not a tumour, a benign growth of the lining, sent to pathology to confirm Endometrial polyps grow from the lining into the uterine cavity, either broad-based (sessile) or on a stalk (pedunculated), and a pedunculated one can protrude through the cervical os 3. Leiomyoma (fibroid) A benign smooth muscle neoplasm — not pre-malignant, and not a precursor to malignancy ⚠ Rapid growth + a SINGLE mass + an older patient = consider leiomyosarcoma , not a fibroid What to tell the patient : a benign tumour of uterine muscle Where leiomyomas sit - submucosal, intramural, subserosal, pedunculated, cervical, broad ligament 4. Adenomyosis Why it bleeds : more endometrial tissue, plus entrapped blood in cystic areas that rupture Why it hurts : the myometrium contracting because blood irritates it , plus the same rupture ⚠ NOT diagnosed by biopsy — the tissue is too deep What to tell the patient : not a tumour, not pre-malignant, the lining sitting deeper in the wall than usual Adenomyosis on a cut uterus: the myometrium is thick and trabeculated, and a dark cystic pocket of entrapped blood sits deep in the wall, well below the endometrium 5. Endometriosis Endometrial tissue outside the uterus What to tell the patient : the lining occurring outside the uterus, going through the cycle just as it does inside 6. Vulvar Lesions and Vulvar Cancer The vulva is skin, and three questions separate the three lichens: does it scar, does it involve the vagina, and how much does it itch? Get those right and most of the rest is pattern recognition against a biopsy threshold that is deliberately low. ⭐ 50% of women with vulvar cancer are ASYMPTOMATIC , and where there are symptoms pruritus is the commonest complaint — the same symptom as every benign condition above it. Lichen sclerosus is the commonest cause of chronic vulvar disease and is premalignant, which is why treatment is lifelong. LP is the only lichen in the vagina and mouth — so a normal vulva does not end the examination. 1. Approach to Abnormal Uterine Bleeding Develop an approach rather than memorizing definitions, and divide by age first. Anovulation is the major underlying cause of abnormal uterine bleeding , so the workup walks down the axis asking two questions at each level: is the feedback working , and did the structure form and is it functioning . ⭐ Anovulation is the major cause of abnormal uterine bleeding - and the ventricular fibrillation arrest with a hemoglobin of 38 was diagnosed only because someone finally asked about her cycles. Nobody had asked. Dysfunctional uterine bleeding cannot be reached while a structural cause is unexplained , because it is a diagnosis of exclusion. The pituitary makes TSH and PRL too, so either can stop ovulation. Every patient over 40 with abnormal uterine bleeding gets an endometrial biopsy. 1. Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada Primary prevention happens before conception; secondary prevention happens after it. Every couple has a 2-3% chance of a baby with some congenital anomaly regardless of screening — that baseline never reaches zero, and every result is interpreted against it. ⭐ In Ontario NIPT is NOT a first-line screen for low-risk women , despite being the best performer - it is kept for the funded indications. A screen gives a risk; only CVS or amniocentesis gives an answer , and only for the assay ordered on it. Noonan has a normal karyotype; Turner does not. Maternal serum screening does not cover trisomy 13. Carrier screening starts with the mother. 1. Primary prevention: the family history Before conception : counselling, a personal and family history, and referral in time to test before pregnancy folic acid from 3 months before pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects Take 3 generations · ask about ethnic background on both sides and any past carrier screening Red flags in the family history — the referral triggers Consanguinity and neonatal deaths · developmental delay or autism · birth defects and congenital anomalies 3 miscarriages, recurrent loss and infertility male infertility — congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, associated with mutations in the cystic fibrosis gene (CFTR) an existing genetic diagnosis anywhere in the family · early-onset heart disease or sudden death · ethnic backgrounds on either side 2. Example: fragile X Three triggers to refer a personal or family history ovarian insufficiency with elevated follicle-stimulating hormone before 40, of unknown cause male relatives with isolated cerebellar ataxia and tremor Genetics : an X-linked CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 — over 200 = the syndrome · 50-200 = premutation the premutation causes fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (often misdiagnosed as Parkinsonism) or primary ovarian insufficiency — see FMR1 disorders 3. Always start with the mother — Ashkenazi Jewish Tay-Sachs disease · Canavan disease · familial dysautonomia 1/30 · 1/37 · 1/32 (the SickKids panel on the next slide prints 1/29 · 1/57 · 1/30; check with the lecturer) French Canadian — Bas-St-Laurent, Gaspésie, New Brunswick Tay-Sachs disease 1 in 14 Anabaptist Separate Amish and Old Order Mennonite panels — 4. Secondary prevention: screen or diagnose? After conception , every test is either a screen (gives a risk) or a diagnostic test (gives an answer) A positive screen always needs a diagnostic test. 5. Invasive diagnosis These return an ANSWER, because they put fetal DNA in your hands: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) Amniocentesis Gestational age 11-13 weeks 15-20 weeks Miscarriage risk 1/400, ~1% (as printed; 1/400 is 0.25%, so the two figures disagree - check with the lecturer) 1/800, ~0.5% (as printed; 1/800 is about 0.13% - check with the lecturer) Other risks Maternal cell contamination · confined placental mosaicism — Chorionic villus sampling - a suction tube guided by ultrasound takes chorionic villi for chromosome analysis Amniocentesis - an ultrasound-guided needle through the abdomen draws amniotic fluid Both are only as good as the assay ordered on them : karyotype · microarray · targeted single-gene testing when the family's mutation is already known a karyotype or microarray on that same sample would still miss a 1 base pair variant a mutation already known in the family is answered only by fetal DNA — CVS or amniocentesis — with the mutation-specific test ordered on it Which test sees which size of abnormality - karyotype, microarray, single-gene testing Timelines are the real constraint, against a 24-week limit on termination NIPT ~10 days · CVS microarray ~2 weeks · single gene test ~3 weeks minimum ⚠ "Lethal" does not necessarily mean the baby dies immediately after birth — technology can sustain life for indefinite periods 7. Early pregnancy counselling Most of what a pregnant patient asks about is safer than she fears. The counselling job is to say what is actually safe, name the few things that do carry risk , and in each case explain why. ⭐ Toxoplasmosis risk comes from undercooked meat far more than from cats , and it presents as chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications . The lecture sets two numbers: 18-23 weeks' gestational age for travel and 300 mg of caffeine a day. Zero alcohol is the advice, but low-level exposure is not likely to harm the baby , so a patient who drank before she knew she was pregnant can be reassured. ⚠ The one drug caveat the lecture names is that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may slightly increase postpartum hemorrhage . They do not cause birth defects. From the full deck: ⭐ NVP becomes hyperemesis gravidarum when it causes hypovolemia or weight loss . ⭐ Any headache after 20 weeks means excluding preeclampsia , and acetaminophen, not NSAIDs , treats it. Heartburn steps up from lifestyle to antacids to an H2-blocker or proton pump inhibitor. Abdominal pain worries you differently by trimester : spontaneous abortion and ectopic in the 1st, abruption, HELLP/preeclampsia and acute fatty liver later. Spotting is normal if it needs only a liner , and placenta previa changes everything (investigate any spotting, abstain from intercourse). Every pregnancy is screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria , because untreated it causes preterm birth. 1. Prenatal care providers Midwives, family physicians and obstetricians (see 08 - OB Care Providers ) 2. Alcohol Zero alcohol is safest (the general consensus) But low levels are not likely to be harmful · use is common worldwide and usually does not lead to fetal alcohol syndrome so a patient who drank before she knew she was pregnant can be reassured 3. Weight gain and exercise Weight gain : lower BMI → gain more · higher BMI → gain less many factors drive it, and it may be a sensitive topic , so discuss it respectfully Exercise (uncomplicated pregnancy): aerobic + strength conditioning, regularly , whatever her previous activity level screening tool: the Physical Activity Readiness Medical Examination for Pregnancy (PARmed-X for Pregnancy) 4. Travel 18-23 weeks' gestational age is the safest window Some vaccines and antimalarials are safe Most travel insurance does not cover the baby · refer most questions to travel medicine 5. Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) Very common: 70-80% of pregnant people Onset as early as 4 weeks, peaks at 9 weeks the summary slide says it resolves around the end of the 1st trimester , the full deck says it usually lasts until 14-16 weeks' gestational age and 90% resolve by 22 weeks Treatment non-drug: lifestyle and eating changes · ginger · acupressure drugs: doxylamine-pyridoxine is the most common first-line drug · dimenhydrinate ⚠ Hyperemesis gravidarum = severe vomiting causing hypovolemia or weight loss infrequent · typically resolves by mid-pregnancy hospitalise if it does not respond to outpatient therapy 6. Tobacco, cannabis and drugs Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada: ask all pregnant women periodically about alcohol, tobacco, prescription and illicit drugs Tobacco and cannabis smoking are linked to adverse pregnancy and childhood outcomes → offer cessation counselling 7. Medications Likely safe : antihistamines · antiemetics · puffers · antidepressants · many common antibiotics Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors no link to birth defects, preterm birth, preeclampsia or stillbirth ⚠ may slightly increase postpartum hemorrhage 8. Work Harmful jobs are rare ; most jobs are fine Minimise the risk with human resources / occupational health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 9. Food Risk extremely low : raw eggs · deli meats · soft cheeses · sushi · most fish, eaten regularly Avoid or limit raw / rare / undercooked meat → toxoplasmosis , a much higher risk than from cats top-predator fish , only rarely - they carry high mercury Congenital toxoplasmosis, classic triad : chorioretinitis · hydrocephalus · intracranial calcifications 10. Supplements and caffeine Folic acid prevents neural tube defects and preterm birth Caffeine ≤ 2 cups of coffee (300 mg) a day is safe Sections 11-20 are the full Common Concerns in Pregnancy deck (Lauren Columbus, registered midwife). For each complaint: what is normal, how to treat it, and what makes it abnormal . 11. Fatigue, sleep and insomnia First trimester : extremely common fatigue, from the sleep-inducing effect of progesterone and less REM (rapid eye movement) sleep · made worse by NVP Anemia can also cause fatigue hemoglobin ≤ 110 g/L · about 40% of pregnancies worldwide · most often iron deficiency symptoms: fatigue · shortness of breath · restless legs re-check hemoglobin and ferritin in the 3rd trimester and start oral iron as needed Third trimester : nearly everyone sleeps badly (less REM sleep, more trips to urinate) · 2/3 report significant disturbance by the end of pregnancy non-drug options first (daytime naps, meditation, iron for restless legs) over-the-counter doxylamine or diphenhydramine if it is severely affecting her 12. Abdominal pain, cramping, round ligament pain and back pain Crampiness is common : the uterus grows fast and pushes organs aside Always assess in person : pain after trauma , or pain with hypertension , vaginal bleeding or fever History: severity · frequency · onset · duration The worry depends on gestational age Worrying causes Other causes 1st trimester cramping ± spotting → spontaneous abortion · severe cramping → ectopic pregnancy , especially with no ultrasound yet 2nd and 3rd trimester life-threatening: placental abruption · HELLP syndrome / preeclampsia · acute fatty liver fibroid degeneration · constipation · fetal movement · gastrointestinal infection Labour : rhythmic, regular tightenings in waves, 20-60 seconds with several minutes between , getting stronge

Hysterectomy approaches Choose the least invasive route the anatomy allows. Every approach is a "short stay" with same-day discharge except abdominal , and the lecture walks the routes down a ladder, each rung being what to use when the one above is blocked. ⭐ Abdominal is the only approach not planned as same-day discharge - it needs a 2-3 day hospital stay. Vaginal is the only approach without abdominal entry , and the one where tubes and ovaries are not as accessible . Shared limitation of every minimally invasive route is a large uterus ; the vaginal-route pair add narrow introitus/pelvis and poor uterine descent , and the laparoscopic pair add suturing skill and operative time . TLH and robotic replace abdominal, not vaginal/LAVH. 1. Choosing the route ⚠ When the indication is bleeding control, medical options come first - hysterectomy is for failed medical management and special circumstances The ladder: vaginal → laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (LAVH) → total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH) or robotic → abdominal The first four are minimally invasive · shared limitation of every minimally invasive route: a large uterus 2. Vaginal hysterectomy Minimally invasive · no abdominal incisions - the fewest incisions of any approach Short stay · same-day discharge Limitations prior pelvic surgery · extensive scarring · large uterus · narrow introitus/pelvis · poor uterine descent tubes/ovaries not as accessible 3. Laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (LAVH) Minimally invasive · requires entry into the abdomen · uterus removed via the vagina Short stay · same-day discharge Used in place of vaginal, when the pelvis needs assessing or the tubes and ovaries need removing What it adds assess the pelvis/scarring · bladder flap · remove tubes/ovaries · "second look" for hemostasis Limitations : large uterus · narrow introitus/pelvis · poor uterine descent 4. Total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH) Minimally invasive · requires entry into the abdomen · short stay, same-day discharge Used in place of abdominal - should NOT replace vaginal/LAVH Limitations : large uterus · laparoscopic suturing takes skill and more operative time 5. Robotic-assisted hysterectomy Minimally invasive · requires entry into the abdomen · short stay, same-day discharge Used in place of abdominal - should NOT replace vaginal/LAVH Excellent option for morbidly obese patients Limitations large uterus ( articulating instruments make it more manageable ) laparoscopic suturing takes skill and more operative time 6. Abdominal hysterectomy NOT minimally invasive · 2-3 day hospital stay Reserved for more complex cancers · patient factors not amenable to a minimally invasive approach · very large uterus · complications during a minimally invasive attempt 7. Types of hysterectomy Named by what comes out : Term What comes out What stays Total hysterectomy Uterus and cervix - Subtotal hysterectomy Uterus Cervix retained Salpingectomy Fallopian tubes Ovaries Salpingoopherectomy Fallopian tubes AND ovaries - "Partial" hysterectomy (lay term) Uterus, with or without cervix, with or without tubes Ovaries retained - no surgical menopause

Dilation and curettage One procedure, one objective: know what goes wrong and what you do about it. Every complication is a consequence of one step, so learn the complications by the step that causes them . ⭐ Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated for therapeutic abortion but NOT for a D&C done for missed abortion or pregnancy loss - the same procedure, two indications, one gets antibiotics. Repeat curettage is what drives Asherman's. Hematometra is re-evacuated immediately; retained products may wait for medical management - the two "something is still in the uterus" complications get opposite tempos. 1. What a dilation and curettage is Dilation and curettage (D&C) = vacuum aspiration of a pregnancy under 14 weeks through a rigid cannula on electric suction Indications (both under 14 weeks ) first-trimester pregnancy loss: incomplete, inevitable, missed abortion therapeutic abortion Not for : ectopic pregnancy (nothing in the cavity) · termination over 14 weeks · endometritis Sequence : cervical preparation → bimanual exam confirms gestation → paracervical block → mechanical dilation only if preparation was inadequate → suction curettage of all products 2. Cervical preparation May be unnecessary if the cervix is already open (incomplete or inevitable abortion): Cervical preparation Agent Timing Note Chemical misoprostol · oral, buccal or vaginal 1-12 hours before may be unnecessary if the cervix is already open (incomplete / inevitable abortion) Osmotic laminaria (seaweed) or Dilapan (synthetic) 24 hours before, placed in the internal os swells as it takes up fluid Osmotic dilators: laminaria (seaweed) and Dilapan swelling from 0 to 24 hours 3. Bimanual exam and anesthesia Bimanual exam confirms gestation and gestational age Paracervical block at this step Anesthesia overall : local (cervical block with or without conscious sedation) or general 4. Mechanical dilation and curettage Mechanical dilation with Hegar dilators , only if preparation was inadequate amount of dilatation = weeks of gestation skipping it lowers discomfort and infection Suction curettage of all products · sharp curettage is unnecessary in most cases 5. Complications The lecture's only objective - each belongs to a step: Complication Step that causes it What it looks like What you do Cervical shock paracervical block vasovagal reaction nothing: limited to a few minutes Uterine perforation dilatation or suction suspected during the procedure; visceral injury in rarer cases finish under ultrasound or laparoscopic guidance Infection instrumentation — prophylaxis for therapeutic abortion, NOT for missed abortion / pregnancy loss Cervical trauma tenaculum or instruments lacerations — Hemorrhage evacuation points to uterine atony , low implantation , or larger gestational age repeat curettage may be needed Hematometra (post abortal syndrome) post-procedure blood accumulating in the uterine cavity re-evacuate immediately Retained products of conception incomplete evacuation products remain after evacuation secondary D&C or misoprostol Asherman's syndrome curettage, above all repeat curettage adhesions in the endometrial cavity → secondary amenorrhea prevention: avoid repeat and sharp curettage Asherman's risk ⚠ Asherman's follows curettage in 8%, and repeat curettage (for retained products or retained placenta post partum) raises it to 30% by a third consecutive procedure (within 24 hours) (as the slide prints it; the commonly cited figures are about 16% after one curettage and about 32% after three or more, with no 24-hour window - check with the lecturer) so retained products are managed with misoprostol where possible, rather than a reflex second D&C

Clinical approach to menopause Every treatment decision splits on which symptom you are treating: vasomotor symptoms (VMS) are systemic and need systemic therapy; genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) is local and is treated locally. Estrogen is the gold standard for VMS and the second line for GSM, so the real question is whether she can have it systemically. ⭐ Estrogen is the gold standard for VMS, and a woman with a uterus must have progesterone with it ; estrogen alone only after hysterectomy. Vaginal estrogen treats GSM but not VMS , and systemic MHT can under-treat GSM, so some women need both. Transdermal estrogen skips first-pass metabolism and has the better clotting profile. A history of venous thromboembolism or stroke is enough to contraindicate estrogen - it need not be active. 1. Menopause and perimenopause The terms are set by age and by the last period: Term Definition Menopause Amenorrhea x 12 months · average age 51-52 in Canada Early menopause 40-45 years Premature ovarian insufficiency years Perimenopause The transition; symptoms begin, possibly years before the last menstrual period · cycles shorten, then lengthen, then cease After menopause estradiol and progesterone fall while follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone rise (loss of feedback) The dynamics of perimenopause: the follicle reserve runs out by about 51, so estradiol and progesterone fall and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) climbs; the final menstrual period marks menopause 2. Staging and premature ovarian insufficiency Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop (STRAW+10) staging - reproductive years, menopause transition and postmenopause, with menstrual and hormone criteria Premature ovarian insufficiency (under 40) = disordered menses ≥ 4 months + follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) > 25 IU/L 3. Why early menopause matters Under 45 : coronary heart disease events ↑ 50% · stroke ↑ 23% · cardiovascular mortality ↑ 19% · all-cause mortality ↑ 12% · cognition, quality of life, bone Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) started before 50 → ↓ all-cause mortality (Nurses' Health Study) 4. Approach to the patient Can she have systemic estrogen? no contraindications, younger than 60, and History menses: last menstrual period , regular, heavy, intermenstrual spotting symptoms: hot flashes, sleep, mood, GSM, libido contraindications to MHT: blood clot, breast cancer history Physical exam examine the vulva if she has GSM symptoms, to rule out skin conditions Investigations menopause is a clinical diagnosis (amenorrhea x 12 months) the deck asks whether she needs a Pap or an endometrial biopsy , and leaves it open Follow-up : review the risk-benefit profile annually · evaluate the endometrium for bleeding on MHT 6. 04 Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass

Ovarian neoplasms Every ovarian tumour is named by its lineage (epithelial, germ cell, sex cord/stromal) plus its behaviour (benign, borderline, malignant), and the age of the patient predicts the lineage : epithelial in adults, germ cell in the young . ⭐ Beware the bilateral atypical mucinous tumour: it is a metastasis until the appendix has been checked . Serous carcinoma is the #1 ovarian cancer and presents late , which is why mortality is high. Borderline vs carcinoma = invasion , not architecture. Mucinous carcinoma is the one carcinoma that is usually unilateral. Granulosa cell tumour recurs late (> 10 years) and ruptures ; its estrogen shows up in the endometrium first. 1. Approach to an ovarian mass Ovarian tumours by cell of origin - germinal epithelium, germ cell and gonadal stroma - each split into benign, borderline and malignant, with the layers of the follicle Most ovarian neoplasms are not malignant ; cancer is more likely post-menopausal Presents as pain ( rupture, torsion ) · distension ( ascites, mass effect ) · compression ( change in bladder / bowel habits ) systemic (weight loss, fever, anorexia) · endocrine ( estrogenic or androgenic ) often asymptomatic until late Investigations imaging finds the mass · in a young woman add germ cell serum markers (diagnosis and post-op monitoring) the diagnosis is histologic 2. Epithelial tumours Naming : cell subtype ( serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, transitional ) + architecture (cyst-, -fibroma) + behaviour serous cyst adenoma (benign) · serous cystadeno fibroma (cystic and fibrous, benign) · serous borderline tumour (pre-cancerous) · serous adenocarcinoma (malignant) What separates borderline from carcinoma is stromal invasion Tumour Lineage · who Gross / histology Behaviour Clue Serous cystadenoma Epithelial · adult Unilocular cyst, clear fluid , single bland layer Benign Serous = the most common epithelial subtype Mucinous cystadenoma Epithelial · adult Multilocular , jelly-like mucin , tall columnar mucin-filled cells; can be enormous Benign Increasing abdominal girth Serous borderline tumour Epithelial · adult Papillary excrescences , complex architecture, atypical cells, no frank invasion Pre-cancerous; excision, very good prognosis; can seed implants (serous only), adhere, recur, progress to low-grade carcinoma Only the serous subtype forms implants Serous carcinoma Epithelial · post-menopausal (younger if familial) Stromal invasion ; solid and cystic, haemorrhage and necrosis #1 ovarian cancer ; often advanced at presentation ; bilateral common Spreads across the peritoneum Mucinous carcinoma Epithelial · adult Invasive mucinous glands Bilaterality is the exception among carcinomas Bilateral + atypical mucinous = look for an appendix primary 3. Ovarian carcinoma: origin, spread, treatment Origins the ovary's own surface epithelium , dragged into the stroma at ovulation, forms epithelial inclusions that give rise to the epithelial tumours a second pathway runs from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) in the fimbria , which exfoliates onto the ovary and peritoneum Where it goes pelvic peritoneum · omentum · bowel serosa · liver serosa · diaphragm · stomach · pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes · lungs the uterus, tubes and broad ligament by direct extension Where ovarian carcinoma spreads - peritoneum, omentum, serosal surfaces, diaphragm, lymph nodes and lungs Treatment surgery first : uterus, ovaries, tubes, omentum, peritoneal biopsies, with or without lymph nodes chemotherapy for advanced stage Prognosis: confined = good; higher stage = poor 4. Post-menopausal bleeding The lecture walks the approach in the order you do it: define the bleed → work it up → list the causes → read the biopsy report → manage atrophy, hyperplasia or carcinoma. One rule runs through all of it: endometrial carcinoma must be excluded in every woman with post-menopausal bleeding , however benign the story. ⭐ Without atypia the management is medical; with atypia it is surgical - the atypia line is the whole biopsy-report question. Risk factors for hyperplasia and type 1 carcinoma are the same: unopposed estrogen . ⚠ Atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion - it must fit the other investigations. Endometrial cancer is the #1 gynecologic malignancy and the 4th most common cancer in women ; endometrial names the site, endometrioid names the (most common) type. 1. Definition Any bleeding after 12 months without menses is post-menopausal bleeding (PMB) How common : 11% over one year in a diary study (Astrup 2004); the in-class deck (2025) says it occurs in 5-25% of post-menopausal women The most common cause is atrophy; the most serious is carcinoma or hyperplasia. The investigation is the same for both: speculum exam, transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) , and endometrial biopsy 2. Diagnostic pathway History bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea · hormone replacement therapy (HRT) (63% bleed in the first six cycles) · tamoxifen risk factors for unopposed estrogen (obesity, polycystic ovarian syndrome, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause) · family history of colorectal or endometrial cancer ( Lynch ) in-class deck adds diabetes and age to the hyperplasia risk factors Physical exam general + abdominal + pelvic · uterus normal or enlarged speculum exam every time - an endometrial mass at the os or an ulcerated cervical mass is a different diagnosis in-class deck: inspect the vulva (lesions, atrophy, scratching) · human papillomavirus (HPV) test / cytology if not up to date · cervical biopsy if a lesion is seen · endometrial biopsy (Pipelle) Investigations TVUS (normal off HRT; the in-class hyperplasia slide says "typically normal while its own ultrasound slide says endometrial biopsy for > 5 mm, any PMB, or recurrent bleeding at (skipping the last group misses 4% of cancers) saline infusion sonohysterography for a thickened stripe (finds focal lesions, cannot tell benign from malignant ) · hysteroscopy for focal lesions and when office biopsy is impossible · dilation and curettage (D&C) when nothing else is available ⚠ a negative Pap does NOT end the workup Investigation Discriminator TVUS off HRT; Causes Most common in PMB : atrophy · exogenous hormones (HRT, tamoxifen) · endometrial hyperplasia · endometrial polyp · endometrial adenocarcinoma, which must be ruled out In-class differential : atrophic vaginitis · endometrial hyperplasia / adenocarcinoma · cervical cancer · cervical polyp · vulvar lesion · non-gynecologic bleeding ; structural lesions shown: endometrial polyp, submucosal fibroid , endocervical polyp Treatment follows the pathology report (sections 4-6) 4. Atrophy (genitourinary syndrome of menopause) Causes : hypoestrogenism → microerosion, inflammation, spotting; from the endometrium, vagina or vulva Pathology : scant fragments of atrophic endometrium; a diagnosis of exclusion that must fit the other investigations How common (in-class): vulvovaginal atrophy (VVA) affects 50-80% of post-menopausal women Presents as dryness · itching · burning · dyspareunia · postcoital bleeding loss of labial fullness · pallor of urethral and vaginal epithelium · narrow introitus · minimal moisture · loss of urethral meatal turgor · (in-class) loss of rugae and elasticity · yellow thin discharge · petechiae exclude lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, atopic or contact dermatitis, vulvar lesions Treatment atrophy → local estrogen (cream, pill / suppository, ring) or nothing if not troublesome · HRT · usually the family physician in-class adds: water-based lubricants , vaginal moisturizers (Replens), vaginal hyaluronic acid suppositories · vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) suppositories Prognosis : benign 5. Pathology of the breast Place the lesion by the tissue it arises from, then tell the lesions of that tissue apart by presentation. The lecture goes anatomy → benign lesions → their cancer risk → malignant lesions → prognosis. ⭐ inflammatory carcinoma is defined by the clinical appearance of diffuse acute mastitis; peau d'orange is neither necessary nor sufficient , and a skin punch biopsy confirms the cancer. ⚠ Breast cancer is the #1 cancer in Canadian women but the #2 cancer death, behind lung . ⚠ Two benign lesions mimic cancer clinically : fat necrosis (irregular mass, skin retraction) and a healed abscess (fixation by fibrosis). ⚠ Not every non-sporadic cancer is BRCA : 20% are non-sporadic but only 5-7% carry a high-penetrance mutation. 1. Approach to common breast problems Three presentations reach the family physician - a lump, a sore breast, nipple discharge - and every one is sorted the same way: the older the woman, the more likely the complaint is serious . The lecture takes them in turn (lumps in men first), then ends on risk factors and screening. ⭐ pre-menopausal with a benign history and exam: re-examine after the next menstrual cycle; post-menopausal or high risk: investigate immediately. Imaging splits at 35 - ultrasound below, mammogram above. Galactorrhea is bilateral, multiple ducts ; worrisome discharge is unilateral, single duct, spontaneous, bloody . Mammography misses 12-15% , and number needed to screen 721 per death prevented. 1. Breast lumps in males Pubertal swelling: 85-90% resolve within 2 years A mass reported as gynecomastia is benign - ask about meds 2. Breast lumps in females Most lumps are not cancer: cancer is ~10% of masses History age · location · how and when found · skin changes · change in size · change with menstrual cycle · other lumps in axilla · family history Physical exam offer a chaperone · inspect with hands pushing on hips nodes: central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral, infra- and supraclavicular supine, vertical strips (better than pie or spiral) , clavicle to inframammary fold, midsternal to posterior axillary line , pads of fingers 2-4, light/medium/deep · tail of Spence Clinical breast exam: patient supine, palpating in vertical strips over the lateral (top) and medial (bottom) breast Worrisome single · hard · immovable · irregular borders · > 2 cm ⚠ skin changes, peau d'orange and nipple retraction are late findings and rarely seen - their absence reassures nothing Benign : smooth · normal/fibroglandular tissue, cyst, fibroadenoma Follow-up : pre-menopausal, benign: re-examine after next cycle Investigations (tissue too dense, risk too low for mammography) · MRI if > 35 mammogram first +/- US 3. Nipple discharge History : spontaneous vs expressed · single vs multiple ducts · bloody or serous · mass Benign - galactorrhea : usually bilateral, multiple ducts , expressed on compression not related to pregnancy/lactation causes: stimulation · hyperprolactinemia · dopamine suppressors · chest wall injury · chronic kidney disease, hypothyroid, cirrhosis Worrisome - unilateral, single duct, spontaneous bloody or serous · mass · > 50 pathologic causes: papilloma (most common) · ectasia · fibrocystic · malignancy 5-10% Investigations : identify duct/quadrant · rule out Paget's · periareolar US, mammogram · galactogram · cytology Treatment : galactogram not diagnostic · must excise to be sure · surgical consult 5. Obstetrical care providers Three providers, one team, taken one at a time. For each, ask who can do what, and at which point a pregnancy leaves their scope : family medicine and midwives each carry a low-risk pregnancy from antenatal care to 6 weeks post partum , while the obstetrician is the consultant for anything complicated and the only one who operates. ⭐ Midwives provide informed choice rather than informed consent , which is why a client can choose outside the regular recommendations. ⚠ The obstetrician provides no care for the infant and has no lactation training ; the family physician follows the baby from birth onward and the midwife for 6 weeks. Fetal anomalies at any stage go to MFM , not a general OB. Preeclampsia is a consult trigger in all three phases , and the post partum list is short: postpartum hemorrhage, a 3rd or 4th degree tear, preeclampsia. Asking for help is not a failure. 1. Family medicine obstetrics Training : family medicine + 6-12 months of extra obstetrical training Cares for : low-risk pregnancies - their own patients plus referrals from other physicians; all routine antenatal, intrapartum and post partum care Delivery vaginal · many perform vacuum-assisted deliveries cesarean is a referral (rural exceptions) Oxytocin in labour : all manage it (induction / augmentation) Post partum the patient: many see her until 6 weeks , then ongoing if in their practice; primary-care knowledge throughout the infant: from birth onward , for years if their patient · some return the baby to the referring physician immediately Distinct advantage : continuity of care and the "whole patient" - recognises and treats depression , upper respiratory tract infection etc. during antenatal and post partum care 2. Midwifery Training : direct entry, 4 years · 7 programs in Canada · regulated by province ( unregulated only in Prince Edward Island and Yukon ) Cares for : low-risk pregnancy and birth, client-centred Delivery vaginal, low-risk · delivery at home, in a birthing centre or clinic, or in hospital Oxytocin in labour : variable - use without an obstetrician consult depends on location and training · some sites also need nursing support for an epidural (changing in London) Post partum the patient: 6 weeks post partum , including breastfeeding · home visits are commonplace the infant: cares for the infant for 6 weeks Distinct advantage informed choice, not informed consent (the client may choose outside the recommendations) 30-90 min appointments · prenatal and post partum home visits 3. Obstetrics Training : generalist obstetrician (OB) = 5-year obstetrics and gynecology residency · maternal fetal medicine (MFM) = the same + a 2-year fellowship Cares for : consultant to family medicine and midwives for complicated antenatal, intrapartum or post partum care · preconception counselling (MFM optimises the medically complex patient before conception) Delivery : all forms - operative vaginal and cesarean section · manages the complicated case and every operative delivery Oxytocin in labour : yes Post partum the patient: low-risk - often only a 6-week visit · not involved in most of the post partum transition · no lactation training (encourages breastfeeding from personal experience only) the infant: no care for the infant after delivery When to consult OB Antepartum Intrapartum Post partum Medically complicated patient ( diabetic , essential hypertension , prior preeclampsia , elevated BMI , systemic lupus erythematosus ) · fetal anomalies ( MFM ) · atypical or abnormal antepartum fetal surveillance · need for a planned cesarean Fetal anomalies ( MFM ) · atypical or abnormal fetal surveillance · labour dystocia , failure to descend , assessment and rotation of fetal position · considering operative vaginal delivery or cesarean · preeclampsia / eclampsia Significant postpartum hemorrhage · 3rd or 4th degree tear · preeclampsia Abbreviations the deck defines : OB obstetrician · OBGYN obstetrics and gynecology · MFM maternal fetal medicine · SLE lupus · BPP biophysical profile · NST non-stress test 4. The maternal health team Work together and communicate: each provider has their own strengths and skill sets Asking for help is not a failure

Pathology of first trimester bleeding Three "baby" causes of first trimester bleeding, told apart by where the products of conception are and what the trophoblast is doing. The lecture lists the causes of bleeding, then takes spontaneous abortion → ectopic pregnancy → gestational trophoblastic disease in turn. Every one is worked up the same way, and the tissue goes to pathology , because only the microscope proves where the gestation was. ⭐ complete = paternal only, diploid, no fetus, high hCG, big uterus; partial = triploid, fetus possible, low-normal hCG, small uterus. Choriocarcinoma has no villi ; a mole has too many swollen ones. hCG can be negative in an ectopic. Choriocarcinoma goes to the lung first (> 90%) but kills through liver or brain. 1. Causes of bleeding and the workup Causes of bleeding in a reproductive-age woman, ABCDEHIN A natomic ( PALE : polyp , adenomyosis , leiomyoma , endometritis ) B aby (spontaneous abortion, ectopic, gestational trophoblastic disease) C oagulopathy · D ysfunctional uterine bleeding · E ndocrine · H ormones (exogenous) · I nfectious · N eoplasia History amenorrhea or a light last period, bleeding, cramping, passage of clot or tissue Physical exam vitals ( shock = rupture ) · uterus large for dates = complete mole, small for dates = partial · adnexal mass · cervix open or closed Investigations serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin ( β-hCG ) + pelvic ultrasound are the two investigations that matter then every piece of tissue passed or sampled goes to pathology ⚠ an endometrial sample cannot diagnose an ectopic, it can only fail to find products of conception 2. Spontaneous abortion Definition : loss of a gestation before fetal extrauterine viability ( 15% of known pregnancies (underestimated) Causes mostly unknown · fetal chromosomal / congenital abnormality is #1 TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, other, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) · maternal: implantation, chronic disease, endocrine, infection Presents as : bleeding, cramping, clot or tissue Pathology Products of conception (villi, trophoblast, ± fetal parts) + gestational endometrium (glands, decidualized stroma ) Diagnosis clinical, or microscopy of curettage or passed tissue · must see products of conception to prove intrauterine gestation Prognosis : incomplete may need dilation and curettage Type of abortion Vaginal bleeding Products passed Note Threatened Yes No Inevitable Yes No Incomplete Yes Yes May need dilation and curettage for the remainder Complete Yes Yes Missed Yes or no No Recurrent ≥ 3 : investigate, refer to medical genetics Types of spontaneous abortion: the cervical os is closed in threatened, complete and missed, and open in inevitable and incomplete; only threatened keeps fetal cardiac activity for sure Follow-up : ≥ 3 spontaneous abortions = recurrent : work-up + medical genetics 3. Ectopic pregnancy Definition : implantation of products of conception at a site other than the endometrium 1-2% of gestations · #1 site: fallopian tube (90%) · others: ovary, abdominal cavity, cervix Causes pelvic inflammatory disease (commonest) · intrapelvic adhesions (surgery, appendicitis) · endometriosis · intrauterine device · previous ectopic Presents as triad: amenorrhea, pain, adnexal mass · shock if ruptured hCG normal, declining or negative Pathology Hematosalpinx , wall thinned or ruptured · villi, trophoblast, fetal parts in the tube endometrium decidualized but NO products of conception Diagnosis no sac in the uterus + adnexal mass on ultrasound · products of conception absent from endometrium, present at the ectopic site Prognosis : rupture and hemorrhage 4. Gestational trophoblastic disease Definition : abnormal trophoblast proliferation · three types: complete mole ( commonest ), partial mole, choriocarcinoma Complete mole Partial mole Choriocarcinoma Causes Empty ovum + 1 sperm that duplicates (90%) or 2 sperm (10%) · diploid 46 XX or XY, paternal only Ovum + 2 sperm (diandric) , or 1 that duplicates · triploid 69 XXX or XXY : 2 paternal + 1 maternal Any gestational event: 50% mole, 25% spontaneous abortion, 25% normal pregnancy , recent or years later Pathology Abundant swollen hydropic villi, no fetal tissue · diffuse hydropic change + trophoblastic proliferation Lower volume · two villous sizes (hydropic + small normal or fibrotic) · less trophoblastic proliferation · irregular-shaped villi with stromal inclusions · fetal tissue may be present Red hemorrhagic uterine mass, any size · no villi, malignant trophoblast, hemorrhage + necrosis Presentation 1/1000 USA, 1/500 Asia · bleeding · uterus large for dates · hyperemesis 25%, hypertension / pre-eclampsia 25%, hyperthyroidism · hCG markedly elevated Bleeding · uterus small for dates · the complete-mole symptoms are rare · hCG low to normal Abnormal bleeding · persistent, markedly elevated hCG Diagnosis "Snow storm" without fetus · caught early (8-12 wk) on routine ultrasound Focal cystic change with fetus formation · often under-recognized clinically Often presumptive on clinical findings · malignant trophoblast in the sample Prognosis 80% cured by curettage · 15% invade or persist · 2-3% become choriocarcinoma · serial hCG Most cured by curettage · 5-10% invade or persist · rarely choriocarcinoma · serial hCG > 90% lung metastases at diagnosis · 80% 5-year survival with chemotherapy · death from liver or brain metastases Follow-up : serial hCG to baseline after any mole

Teratogenesis A teratogen is judged by what it hits and when : the same exposure does nothing in weeks 1-2, produces a major structural anomaly during organogenesis (weeks 3-8) , and a functional or minor defect in the fetal period. The lecture then walks the four kinds of teratogen: physical → infectious → maternal condition → chemical . ⭐ Weeks 3-8 (organogenesis) is the window of greatest sensitivity; weeks 1-2 are usually not susceptible, and the fetal period is less sensitive - CNS, eyes and external genitalia stay sensitive to term. ⚠ FDA category C means no data, not safety ; the D/X split is benefit may outweigh risk vs. risk outweighs any benefit . Hyperthermia and maternal diabetes both cause neural tube defects and cardiovascular defects - hyperthermia adds abdominal wall defects and spontaneous abortion, diabetes adds CNS, spine and limb defects. 1. What a teratogen is, and when it matters 9 in 10 pregnant women take at least one medication , so the question is rarely whether she is exposed but how to counsel her Anomaly size major = affects life expectancy, health status, physical or social functioning minor = little or no impact on health or short- or long-term function The susceptibility timeline: embryonic period (organogenesis) vs. fetal period History every drug, supplement, herbal, recreational drug and occupational exposure timing against the last menstrual period (organogenesis or not) infections, fever ≥ 39°C, radiation · maternal diabetes and its control · rubella immunity 2. Physical teratogens radiation · hyperthermia (core ≥ 39°C, extreme or prolonged) Defects : spontaneous abortion, neural tube defects , cardiovascular defects, abdominal wall defects Radiation : fetal dose not to exceed 50 rads Heat : the hazard is extreme heat, not exercise ⚠ do NOT tell her to stop exercising or to fear a short sauna - core temperature does NOT exceed 39°C with exercise in pregnancy 3. Infectious teratogens TORCH : toxoplasmosis · other ( syphilis, zika, parvovirus , varicella zoster virus, Listeria) · rubella · cytomegalovirus · herpes simplex virus vertical transmission : in utero, at delivery, or after birth via breast milk Cytomegalovirus : #1 infectious cause of birth defects in North America · 40% transmission with a 1st maternal infection Herpes simplex virus : caught in the last 3 months: 30-50% transmission → cesarean section Rubella : vaccinate · check titres Toxoplasmosis : cat feces, uncooked meat · not routinely screened in Canada 4. Maternal conditions diabetes Defects : neural tube, central nervous system (CNS), spine, cardiovascular, and limb defects Prevention : glycemic control before conception and through pregnancy · folic acid before conception 5. Chemical teratogens medications · vitamins/minerals/herbal products · recreational drugs · toxins doxylamine-pyridoxine (Diclectin) is the only anti-nausea drug approved in pregnancy The deck's case: mycophenolate ~25% malformation, ~50% spontaneous abortion Risk graded by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) categories: FDA category The discriminator: which studies, and what they show Examples A controlled human studies show no risk doxylamine-pyridoxine · folic acid · levothyroxine B no human studies ; animal studies show no risk amoxicillin · loratadine · ondansetron C no controlled studies in animals OR humans fluconazole · metoprolol · sertraline D evidence of human risk exists ; benefits may outweigh risks in certain situations paroxetine · diazepam · lisinopril · phenytoin · lithium X both animal and human studies show fetal abnormalities ; risk outweighs any possible benefit methotrexate · simvastatin · warfarin Counselling by phase Pre-conception (the moment to counsel): optimize disease management · 1 mg folic acid daily for antiepileptics · minimize dose and number of therapeutics · consider switching to an alternative medication · counsel on potential teratogenesis Antenatal : potential dose increases Post-partum : dose adjustments · breastfeeding considerations · restarting medications · switching back to previous therapeutics Resources and referral FRAME Clinic ( Fetal Risk After Maternal Exposure , Western / Children's Hospital London Health Sciences Centre) · Reprotox · LactMed · MotherToBaby

First trimester ultrasound and hCG Two questions, one for each half of the lecture. For dating: which landmark is visible decides which measurement dates the pregnancy , and each landmark is retired the moment the next one appears. For a positive test with an empty uterus: a single human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) value never settles a pregnancy of unknown location; only the rate of change does , so the answer is almost always to repeat it. ⭐ Once an embryo is seen, MSD is never used again: CRL dates the pregnancy, best when > 10 mm (7 weeks), accurate to 3-8 days. A gestational sac is visible from 32 days, a yolk sac from 5 to 5+5 weeks, a heartbeat by 6+0. hCG level does not predict ectopic rupture , and a falling hCG does not exclude an ectopic: 8% of untreated ectopics fall at the same rate as a miscarriage (Silva 2006). MSD is also retired once it passes 14 mm , and CRL hands over to the BPD after 84 mm (14 weeks) , where the two are equally good at 12-14 weeks. 1. First trimester ultrasound: when and how All women should be offered a dating scan at 7-12 weeks ; it beats the last menstrual period and cuts inductions for post-dates Quality standard : transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) of uterus and adnexa · transabdominal only for a high mass or free fluid 2. Dating a pregnancy: why the last period is not enough Last menstrual period (LMP) dating assumes regular 28-day cycles, mid-cycle ovulation and fertilization, correct recall, off the oral contraceptive pill for months Even a correct LMP cannot fix implantation without assisted reproductive technology follicular waves · sperm survive 5-7 days · ovulation-to-implantation varies by up to 11 days 3. The rise of hCG: how the teaching changed Rate of rise in a viable intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) Study Consequence Doubling every 2 days Historical teaching Any deviation read as failing fetus, threatened miscarriage or ectopic ≥ 66% in 2 days Kadar 1990, 20 women Lower limit of an 85% confidence interval (CI), so 8% of viable IUPs rose slower ≥ 53% in 2 days (as low as 35%) Barnhart 2004, 287 patients 99% CI: The deck's normal range : rise ≥ 53% over 2 days (99% CI) , or a doubling time of 1.4-2.1 days ⚠ A "normal" rise does not exclude an ectopic : a non-viable IUP or an ectopic can rise like a viable IUP Horne 2004: 340 women with pain/bleeding 63 with a ≥ 66% rise, 10 (16%) had an ectopic Silva 2006: of 200 diagnosed ectopics, 60% had a rising hCG at diagnosis and 21% rose ≥ 53% over 2 days 6. The discriminatory zone the hCG above which TVUS should show a gestational sac in a normal IUP The old 1000-2000 cut-off ignored slow-rising and low-normal viable pregnancies and mislabelled them as failed or ectopic 2000-3000 keeps them in the pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) differential (the conclusion slide words it as raising the range from 1500 IU to 2000-3000 for stable patients) By the numbers in PUL ≥ 2000 : most likely a non-viable IUP (NVIUP) , 2x as likely as an ectopic 2000-3000 : ectopic 19x more likely than a viable IUP (38 NVIUP : 19 ectopic : 1 viable IUP, 2% chance ) ≥ 3000 : ectopic 70x more likely than a viable IUP (140 : 70 : 1, 0.5% chance ) 7. Pregnancy of unknown location and falling hCG Investigations serial hCG rather than one absolute value ⚠ a single hCG in the overlap zone does not distinguish viable IUP, non-viable IUP and ectopic Treatment stable + hCG 2000-3000 + no ectopic seen → repeat, do not act this spares inappropriate misoprostol , dilation and curettage and laparoscopy Rate of decline in a failing pregnancy (Barnhart 2004, 710 NVIUP managed expectantly): quadratic, and depends on the level ≥ 5000 mIU/mL: at least 35% over 48 h · 500: at least 24% · 50: 12% the conclusion slide says 12-32% over 2 da

Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy Every decision turns on two questions: when did the blood pressure (BP) rise relative to 20 weeks , and is the high BP the disease itself (chronic / gestational) or a symptom of it (pre-eclampsia / eclampsia)? The first sets the diagnosis; the second sets whether you treat the number or deliver the patient. The lecture goes normal BP → the disorders → their complications → management. ⭐ 20 weeks is the line: HTN diagnosed before it is chronic, after it (with normal BPs documented) is gestational; pre-eclampsia adds proteinuria. Mild is >140 / >90 , severe is >160 / >110 , always 2 readings >15 min apart . ⚠ HELLP can present with a completely normal BP. The primary maternal danger of severe HTN is stroke , so any neurological symptom means investigate for an intracranial event. Treat the number in chronic / gestational HTN; in pre-eclampsia the number is a symptom and complications drive delivery planning . 1. Normal blood pressure in pregnancy ↓ systemic vascular resistance outpaces ↑ blood volume, so BP falls from weeks 8-12 and returns to pre-pregnancy norms at 20-24 weeks In pre-eclampsia this normal 8-24 week dip fails (↑ systemic vascular resistance) 2. Second trimester ultrasound One screening scan with five jobs, walked in the order the lecture takes them: dating and growth → number of fetuses → placental location → anatomy screen → soft markers. The scan is a screen , so what it finds leads to more testing, not to a diagnosis. ⭐ Every pregnant person in Canada should have the screening anatomy scan between 18 and 22 weeks; no risk factor is required to earn it , so age, prior losses, a prior affected baby and a normal amniocentesis all get the same scan. ⚠ Fetal well-being (biophysical profile) is a 3rd trimester assessment and is not part of the 2nd trimester scan. ⚠ A soft marker is not a birth defect ; it changes a risk, not a diagnosis. Dating, fetal number and chorionicity are all done in the 2nd trimester only if the 1st trimester did not settle them . 1. Which trimester's scan does what Trimester Weeks What the ultrasound is for 1st to 13+6 Pregnancy dating (the most accurate time to do it) · genetic screening ( nuchal translucency ) 2nd 14+0 to 27+6 The screening anatomical scan at 18-22 weeks , with the five purposes below 3rd 28+0 on Fetal growth and well-being (the biophysical profile lives here, NOT in the 2nd trimester scan) The five purposes of the 2nd trimester scan 1. Dating and growth · 2. Number of fetuses · 3. Placental location · 4. Screen of fetal anatomy · 5. Soft markers for aneuploidy 2. Dating and fetal growth Fetal biometry = standardized measurements and formulas biparietal diameter (BPD) and occipital-frontal diameter (OFD) across the skull · head circumference (HC) around it · femur length (FL) end to end What it settles sonographic dating only if not already done in the 1st trimester · growth against gestational age Fetal biometry - BPD, OFD and HC across and around the skull, FL along the femur 3. Number of fetuses Count , then a full anatomical assessment of each fetus Confirm chorionicity (the type of multiple pregnancy) Confirms the multiple pregnancy; easier and more accurate in the 1st trimester 4. Placental location Wall : anterior or posterior Relationship to the cervix a placenta reaching the internal os is placenta previa Cord insertion : into the placenta and into the fetus Placental location - placenta, fetal head, cervix and internal os on ultrasound 5. Screen of fetal anatomy The main job : rule out major congenital anomalies birth defects affect 2-3% of all pregnancies , and many are diagnosed antenatally What is looked at , each reported normal or abnormal head (posterior fossa: cerebellum, vermis; thalami, fornices, choroid plexus) · facial profile · spine · 4-chamber heart with its axis · outflow tracts · abdomen · cord vessels · limbs What follows a birth defect : further genetic testing or more detailed imaging for prenatal diagnosis, especially when several combine Why look for anomalies at all (the lecture's own three reasons) counsel the parents on what to expect · direct further investigations antenatally or postnatally · decide the place of delivery and level of care the finding needs Anatomy screen views - cerebellar view of the head, facial profile, spine 6. Soft markers for aneuploidy Soft marker = an ultrasound finding tied to ↑ risk of trisomy 21 or 18 choroid plexus cysts · short femurs · intracardiac echogenic focus · echogenic bowel They are NOT birth defects ; if seen, further genetic screening/testing may be offered Birth defect (purpose 4) Soft marker (purpose 5) What it is A structural anomaly in the fetus A normal-variant finding that raises the odds of aneuploidy What follows Further genetic testing or more detailed imaging for prenatal diagnosis, especially when several combine An offer of further genetic screening or testing , not a diagnosis

Topics in antenatal care Three routine pieces of antenatal care, in lecture order, each with a when and a why: feed the pregnancy ( folate + iron ), vaccinate it ( inactivated only ), and screen the mother's blood. The antibody question turns on one thing: does she already have an antibody? ⭐ The only vaccine category not considered safe is live attenuated (measles-mumps-rubella, varicella, bacille Calmette-Guérin) , and the reason is a theoretical one, not an observed one. Tdap is timed (27-32 weeks) because the point is the baby's passive immunity; influenza is not timed because the point is the mother. RhIG is prophylaxis for the unsensitized : it clears fetal cells before the maternal immune system responds, so it does nothing once an antibody exists. ⚠ A titre of 1/8 or greater is the line for severe-anemia risk; below it, keep testing monthly. Sensitization needs a source : previous pregnancy, transfusion, or drug abuse, and the fetus is only at risk if it carries the antigen, hence the partner screen. 1. Vaccination Most vaccines are safe ; the ones with a potential risk are delayed until post-partum History: vaccines received or needed Live attenuated - AVOID Recommended in ALL pregnancies Inactivated, select scenarios Examples measles-mumps-rubella, varicella, bacille Calmette-Guérin tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) · influenza Hepatitis A and B · Haemophilus influenzae type b · meningococcus · rabies Why Theoretical risk of improper preparation → active infection (realistically very low) Safety established by decades of observational data ; clear benefit to mother and/or fetus Indicated by exposure or risk, not routine When Delay until post-partum ; may consider if risk/benefit favours vaccinating Tdap 27-32 weeks → maternal antibodies cross the placenta = passive immunity to the baby · Influenza any gestational age or post-partum, in flu season → ↓ maternal risk/severity As indicated 3. Antibody screening and Rh immunoglobulin Group & screen in the 1st trimester for all blood type + Rh status + any maternal antibodies Sources of sensitization (ask in the history): previous pregnancy, blood transfusion, drug abuse No antibody and Rh negative → Rh immunoglobulin (RhIG) to every Rh negative mother after 8-10 weeks with bleeding, an invasive procedure or trauma · routinely 28-30 weeks · post-partum if the baby is Rh positive it clears fetal cells before the maternal immune system responds, so RhIG prevents an antibody ; it does nothing once one exists 4. When an antibody is found If she has one, the titre decides whether the fetus is watched Investigations titre + find the source of sensitization + partner zygosity (the fetus is only at risk if it carries the antigen) ⚠ an antibody generally has to be present at the beginning of pregnancy to cause trouble under 1/8 → serial titres, monthly · 1/8 or more → middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity on ultrasound (correlates with fetal hemoglobin) Worsening anemia → polyhydramnios and fetal hydrops Treatment sensitized and stable → deliver 37-38 weeks severe anemia → deliver earlier ( 34-35 weeks on) · early gestation → intrauterine transfusion of antigen-negative blood, serially if needed
