Care for pregnancy in the first trimester Three jobs in the first 12 weeks, in the lecture's order: confirm the pregnancy, date it, and screen it - then count the obstetric history (GTPAL) and follow the uterus as it grows. Every question turns on a threshold or a counting rule. ⭐ EDB is fixed once set by the most reliable method - later discrepancies are growth, not dating. A gestational sac alone does not confirm a pregnancy ; the yolk sac is required, and location excludes ectopic. CRL after 14 weeks is not a dating tool. Herpes simplex virus and hepatitis C are not routine bloods. Symphysis-fundal height matches weeks only from 20 weeks . 1. Diagnosing and confirming pregnancy Presents as : missed menses with or without nausea / vomiting, urinary frequency, breast tenderness, bloating irregular cycles: symptoms matter more, amenorrhea is not apparent ⚠ Early symptoms should never be relied on exclusively ; some have none, some are misattributed (the flu) ⚠ bleeding in early pregnancy is mistaken for menses and delays diagnosis , especially at the extremes of age and on the oral contraceptive pill Common 1st-trimester symptoms : amenorrhea or menstrual irregularity (light spotting) · nausea/vomiting or food aversions · mood swings · fatigue · breast tenderness · frequent urination later in pregnancy instead: perception of fetal movements · heartburn · urinary frequency/incontinence History : last normal menstrual period (LNMP) and cycle regularity · prior ectopic / recurrent miscarriage (the reason to bother confirming with human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)) Serum hCG thresholds Serum hCG Meaning Negative 5-25 Very early pregnancy or assay error > 25 Diagnostic of pregnancy 1500 Intrauterine gestation visible on transvaginal ultrasound 5000 Intrauterine gestation visible on transabdominal ultrasound Ultrasound : a gestational sac alone does not confirm a pregnancy - the yolk sac is required , and location must be established to exclude ectopic Confirming a pregnancy at 8 weeks on transabdominal ultrasound: the gestational sac (yellow) holds the yolk sac (pink) and the embryo (green), which places the pregnancy inside the uterus 2. Dating the pregnancy The rule above the rest : once the estimated date of birth (EDB) is set by the most reliable method (in vitro fertilization (IVF) transfer date, or 1st-trimester ultrasound) it is FIXED a later scan that disagrees is reporting growth , not a new due date Dating method When Rule Caveat Naegele's rule Rough estimate at booking LNMP + 7 days - 3 months + 1 year (gestation ~ 280 days = 40 completed weeks ) Depends on a known, normal LNMP Pregnancy wheel / app Most common Same arithmetic Same limitation 1st-trimester ultrasound - crown-rump length (CRL) Most accurate : little biological variability; use the first scan with CRL ≥ 10 mm (~7 weeks) if several exist Unreliable after 14 weeks - flexion and orientation vary 2nd-trimester ultrasound - multiple parameters > 14 weeks head circumference, biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference, femur length combined Any ultrasound (Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada #303) IVF transfer date IVF pregnancies Overrides every ultrasound - Crown-rump length (CRL): the longest straight line from the top of the head to the rump of the embryo; the first scan with a CRL of 10 mm or more (about 7 weeks) sets the due date 3. Early pregnancy investigations Routine for ALL pregnancies complete blood count (hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, platelets) · group and screen (type, Rh , antibodies) · rubella immunity · hepatitis B, HIV, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test · gonorrhea/chlamydia · urine culture ( asymptomatic bacteriuria ) Enhanced first trimester screen (eFTS) , 11-14 weeks nuchal translucency ultrasound + 4 serum analytes · offered to all regardless of age or risk Selected populations only ⚠ herpes simplex virus, hepatitis C are NOT routine - high risk or exposure only thyroid-stimulating hormone (known thyroid disease, dose adjustment) · hemoglobinopathy screen (Mediterranean, Southeast Asian, African for sickle cell, or low mean corpuscular volume/hemoglobin) · non-invasive prenatal testing / chorionic villus sampling (known carrier: balanced translocation, muscular dystrophy) 4. GTPAL GTPAL (gravida, term, preterm, abortions, living) = the counting rule for the obstetric history GTPAL letter Counts Trap G Pregnancies, including the current one Twins = one G T Pregnancies to ≥ 37 weeks A neonatal death after a term delivery still counts as T P (preterm) Pregnancies 20-37 weeks A 32-week stillbirth counts here A Losses Miscarriage, ectopic, therapeutic L Living children Twins = two L; stillbirth and neonatal death = not L Para (G/P form) Pregnancies delivered > 20 weeks Hides term/preterm, multiples, deaths 5. Normal uterine growth Physical exam in the 1st trimester : uterus closed fist → small grapefruit by 12 weeks , fundus reaching the pelvic brim / symphysis ; not a dating tool in the first trimester Trimester Uterine size Landmark 1st (to 12 weeks) Fist → small grapefruit Fundus at pelvic brim / symphysis 2nd (14-20 weeks) Small/medium cantaloupe, now abdominal Fundus at umbilicus by 20 weeks ; from then symphysis-fundal height in cm = weeks 2nd (20-26 weeks) Fundus turns to anterior abdominal wall Organ displacement begins 3rd (28 weeks on) Watermelon at term Rectus diastasis; diaphragm displaced up - perceived dyspnea Fundal height by week: just above the pubic bone at 12 weeks, at the umbilicus by 20 weeks, under the sternum at 36-38 weeks, dropping again at term as the head engages

Approach to sexual health Two halves to this lecture: the physiology you contrast between cis-men and cis-women, and the interview you run so the patient can raise the problem they came in with. The whole conversation turns on one move: know your own biases, then ask permission, so the patient never has to raise it first. ⭐ The refractory period is the sex difference: males are physiologically incapable of another orgasm after the first; females have none and can have multiple orgasms. NO is the neurotransmitter of clitoral engorgement , and photoplethysmography is how VBV is measured. Orgasm is cerebral , not spinal. The interview separates on repetition as the tool that unpacks a euphemism, and on asking permission first . ⚠ Never assume orientation or monogamy in the wording: "How many partners in the past year?" , not "Are you monogamous?" ; say "partner" . 1. Step one: your own biases, and who has concerns Acknowledge your own implicit biases before you walk into the room , so they are not carried into the encounter Who has concerns 50-98% of women : interest · orgasm · lubrication · dyspareunia · body image · unmet needs · need for information · abuse/coercion 40% of men , mainly erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation · men are the ones most likely to feel ashamed asking for help 2. Models of the sexual response cycle Model Year Phases What it adds Masters & Johnson 1966 4 : excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution direct laboratory observation (>10,000 episodes; 382 women, 312 men) · criteria precise but arbitrary , vary dramatically between individuals Kaplan 1979 3 : sexual drive → excitement → orgasm puts desire first, drops plateau + resolution Basson 2001 circular most widely used · intimacy / motivations → variable desire → attention to stimuli → subjective arousal + autonomic nervous system response → arousal triggers desire → satisfaction feeds back The Masters & Johnson sexual response cycle, male vs female Basson circular model (2001): multiple motivations lead to attention to stimuli, then subjective arousal with an autonomic response that triggers desire; desire can arise at any point, and the rewards feed the next cycle 3. uterus fully elevated · clitoris withdraws under hood · labia minora darken ↑ circumference of coronal ridge · glans turns purplish · testes elevate further · Cowper's gland droplets at meatus Orgasm Taking the sexual history The interview, start to finish Making the patient comfortable assure complete confidentiality very early · nonjudgmental whatever the patient admits to Body language : hands/arms · pectoral flush · position in chair · postural echo (mirror-image sitting = harmony) Determining the problem terminology the patient knows ( "sex" , not "intercourse" ) · open questions , silence , repetition repetition unpacks a euphemism: "Checkup?" → "Performing?" → "Ashamed?" 5. A productive conversation and the 5 P's Ask permission to talk about sexual health, proactively, so the patient never has to raise it first ⚠ There is NO standard validated comprehensive sexual health assessment tool ⚠ Never assume orientation or monogamy in the wording: "How many partners in the past year?" , not "Are you monogamous?" ; say "partner" The 5 P's : Partners · Practices · Protection / Past sexually transmitted infection · Pregnancy plans · (optional) Pleasure 7. Physiologic changes in pregnancy Pregnancy rewrites the "normal" for almost every organ system, and the whole lecture is one question asked seven times: is this number physiologic (expected in pregnancy) or pathologic (disease) ? Part 1 walks the systems in the order the slides take them; Part 2 applies the question to the two findings that are almost universal, anemia and a low platelet count . ⭐ Platelets below 100,000 are not gestational thrombocytopenia until proven otherwise - gestational is 75% of cases, starts mid-to-late second trimester, rarely drops below 100,000 and needs nothing; ITP starts before or early in pregnancy, goes below 100,000, and does not normalize post partum . Anemia cut-offs are 110 in the first trimester and 105 after , dilution is the commonest cause and iron deficiency (ferritin under 30) the commonest disease . Creatinine in the 80s is abnormal in pregnancy even when the lab says normal. Resting heart rate above 110 is not "just pregnancy." Total T4 rises with TBG; free T4 holds; TSH dips with the hCG peak and is observed, not treated. D-dimer is up in every pregnancy, so a high one does not diagnose a pulmonary embolism - but the threshold to look for a clot is lower, not higher. Antepartum hemorrhage Bleeding in the 2nd/3rd trimester turns on two questions: is it painful, and whose blood is it? The lecture walks the sources, then each placental cause in turn, then the management that applies to all of them: assess mother and fetus together, continuously . ⭐ Painful bleeding + tender uterus = abruption; painless bleeding = previa; small bleed + fetal distress = vasa previa, and the blood is fetal. ⚠ Never examine the cervix of a bleeder until ultrasound has cleared the placenta. Kleihaur-Betke finds fetal blood in the mother ; Apt finds it in the vaginal blood - only Apt diagnoses vasa previa. Abruption is a diagnosis of exclusion ; previa is an ultrasound diagnosis. A previous C/S raises the risk of previa and accreta, not vasa previa ; vasa previa comes from a velamentous cord (type 1) or a succenturiate lobe (type 2) . 1. Where the bleeding comes from Non-obstetrical : hemorrhoids/varices · bladder infection/renal stones · rarely masses, lacerations → treat the cause, as in a non-pregnant patient Obstetrical : placental/uterine, cervical or fetal always assess for labour : cervical dilatation frequently causes bleeding ("show") a painful bleed with a tender uterus is an abruption · a painless bleed is a previa until the ultrasound says otherwise · a small bleed with a distressed fetus is fetal blood - a vasa previa 2. The four placental causes side by side Placental abruption Placenta previa Vasa previa Accreta / increta / percreta Definition Premature separation of the placental/maternal interface (1st trimester = subchorionic hemorrhage) Implantation over, or just adjacent to, the internal cervical os · marginal/partial = within 2 cm · complete = covering the os Unprotected umbilical vessels traverse the cervix / within 2 cm · Type 1 = velamentous cord insertion · Type 2 = succenturiate lobe / multilobed placenta Abnormal placental invasion into the uterus over a previous uterine incision lacking complete endometrial cover Incidence, timing 1/200-1/300 · mostly 35-38 weeks , any gestation ~1/300 at term · seen at the 18-20 week morphology scan , often resolves by 3rd trimester · sentinel bleed 26-28 weeks , then 30-40% rebleed ~1/2500 Risk rises with previous C/S / uterine surgery with or without previa Whose blood Maternal Maternal Fetal Maternal Presentation Painful active bleeding , mild to profuse · " unrelenting contractions " · tender, sometimes rigid uterus · mother and fetus usually stable unless severe · concealed (central) form: no bleeding, pain out of keeping, fetal distress Painless bleeding, mild or severe · fetus stable unless mother hemodynamically unstable Volume may be very small but fetal distress is frequent Often silent until delivery: bleeding the myometrium cannot contract to control Diagnosis Diagnosis of exclusion once other sources are ruled out (edge bleeds drain out, so ultrasound is often unrevealing) Ultrasound placental location Apt test on vaginal blood ; heightened suspicion with known velamentous cord Ultrasound, history of uterine surgery Treatment Blood irritates the myometrium, so it may progress to labour ; risk of rupture of membranes as membranes stretch over clot · deliver by maternal/fetal status Complete previa: cesarean section · marginal >1 cm from the os may allow vaginal birth in select cases · aggressive transfusion + clotting-factor replacement pre and post delivery Deck gives no specific management beyond the shared pathway (fetal distress drives delivery decisions) Almost always hysterectomy unless the invasion is very focal Why it bleeds badly / Prognosis Larger area affected in concealed abruption Any cervical change (dilatation, even thinning) disrupts the implantation · the cervix is not designed to shed and has no myometrium to clamp the vessels · hypovolemia/shock, consumptive coagulopathy , ↑ hysterectomy A tiny volume is a large share of the fetal blood volume Myometrium cannot contract over the invaded site 3. Placental abruption Two forms at the placental edge (most): active vaginal bleeding with cramping concealed (central): blood trapped behind the placenta - no bleeding, pain out of proportion, more fetal distress Risk factors hypertension · trauma · previous abruption · autoimmune condition · preterm prelabour rupture of membranes · smoking/cocaine · intrauterine infection Placental abruption: an edge separation drains as vaginal bleeding with cramping, while a central (concealed) separation traps the blood behind the placenta, giving no bleeding and pain out of proportion 4. Placenta previa Types : marginal or partial = within 2 cm of the cervix · complete = covering the cervical os Complications maternal hemorrhagic shock · disseminated intravascular coagulation · preterm birth · cesarean delivery · maternal transfusion not fetal hemorrhage (the blood is maternal) and not pre-eclampsia 5. Vasa previa The only cause where the blood is fetal , so a small bleed matters Type 1 : a velamentous cord insertion · Type 2 : vessels running between the lobes of a succenturiate (multi-lobed) placenta either way, exposed fetal vessels lie over the cervix Vasa previa: type 1 from a velamentous cord insertion, type 2 from vessels running between the lobes of a succenturiate (multi-lobed) placenta; either way, exposed fetal vessels lie over the cervix 6. Approach to the small fetus Three labels that sound alike and mean different things, then the hunt for the one that is pathological. Find the fetus with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) as early as possible , name the cause, then let the Doppler and the gestational age decide delivery . ⭐ SGA is a percentile ( SFH >2-3 cm less than weeks screens; ultrasound EFW confirms . A trisomy is the intrinsic cause ; smoking, hypertension and multiples restrict nutrient delivery . Placental insufficiency below the 3rd percentile shows absent EDF and ↓ amniotic fluid , not polyhydramnios. Delivery, not time, is the only way to feed the fetus better. 1. The approach at a glance 2. Small for gestational age, low birth weight and IUGR Small for gestational age (SGA) is a percentile, low birth weight (LBW) is a weight, IUGR is a pathological process , and the first two say nothing about the third Estimated fetal weight (EFW) by the Hadlock formulas: head circumference · abdominal circumference · biparietal diameter · femur length SGA IUGR LBW / very low birth weight / extremely low birth weight large for gestational age Defined by EFW for gestational age A pathological process impairing growth potential (↓ growth rate) Absolute birth weight: EFW >90th percentile for gestational age Depends on gestational age? Yes: the actual weight for the label varies with gestational age No cut-off at all: can still sit above the 10th percentile and be IUGR No: independent of gestational age Yes Implies Usually constitutionally small (normal intrinsic factors) Something is wrong: maternal, fetal or placental Risk of neonatal complications (a paediatric / neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) cut-off) May be normal for parental size Adverse-outcome flag Any Lower is worse n/a Birth weight against gestational age: low, very low and extremely low birth weight are fixed lines at 2500, 1500 and 1000 g, while small and large for gestational age follow the curving 10th and 90th percentiles 3. Investigations Find the cause : enhanced first trimester screen / non-invasive prenatal testing / amniocentesis; toxoplasmosis / cytomegalovirus Fetal well-being : UA Doppler, amniotic fluid volume, NST Follow-up : frequency set by severity and by NST / Doppler findings UA Doppler waveform Placental microvasculature What you see Normal Intact Continuous forward flow through the whole cycle ↓ EDF, ↑ resistive or pulsatility index Early damage Baseline EDF drops toward the zero line Absent EDF ~50% damaged Flow pauses at end-diastole Reversed EDF ~70% damaged Flow runs backward at end-diastole Umbilical artery Doppler waveforms in placental insufficiency 6. Management and delivery Treatment reverse the reversible (smoking, hypertension) to limit worsening ⚠ no catch-up growth in utero; delivery is the only true way to improve nutrient delivery if premature: steroids for lung maturation, transfer to NICU-level care Delivery by gestational age >37 weeks: deliver , even with no other risks 32-37 weeks: deliver if oligohydramnios or persistently abnormal Dopplers , even just resistive index >95th percentile (abnormal NST, absent or reversed EDF) Mode of delivery follows the usual obstetric indicators, but oligohydramnios or abnormal Dopplers raise the cesarean section risk

Approach to preterm labour Everything turns on where she sits on one line: threatened preterm labour → preterm labour → preterm birth, with membranes intact or ruptured. Each step adds the intervention that buys the next one time, and the lecture walks them in that order. ⚠ Antibiotics in PPROM INCREASE latency (the inherited note had it backwards). ⭐ Steroids are the one intervention given at every stage ; tocolysis needs contractions , magnesium needs an imminent birth , penicillin needs a delivery . Cerclage is for cervical insufficiency before 24 weeks, never for ruptured membranes. Dehydration and UTI mimic TPTL : hydrate and dip the urine before reaching for a tocolytic. 1. The preterm line: definitions Term Definition (all before 37 weeks ) Course Threatened preterm labour (TPTL) Signs or symptoms of labour , cervical change not required May resolve without delivery or progress Preterm labour Spontaneous labour contractions leading to cervical dilatation May still resolve, or lead to preterm birth Preterm birth Delivery, spontaneous or iatrogenic Morbidity is gestational-age dependent Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) Membrane rupture before 37 weeks , before labour ↑ preterm birth, chorioamnionitis, abruption, cord prolapse 2. Causes of preterm labour premature maternal or fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation · inflammation and infection · decidual hemorrhage · pathologic uterine distension · idiopathic (common) PPROM adds mechanical stress and bleeding weakening the membranes 3. Consequences of prematurity respiratory distress syndrome, apnea, bronchopulmonary dysplasia · intraventricular hemorrhage · glucose abnormalities · necrotizing enterocolitis · retinopathy · sepsis · prolonged neonatal intensive care unit stay 4. Risk factors previous spontaneous preterm birth · multifetal gestation · cervical surgery (cone > loop electrosurgical excision procedure) · short cervix · cervicitis (gonorrhea, chlamydia, bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas, ureaplasma, mycoplasma) non-Hispanic black race (?socioeconomic confounders) · age extremes · assisted reproductive technology · Mullerian anomalies, fibroids · chronic disease · Ehlers-Danlos · smoking/substances · no prenatal care 5. Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes Confirm it : a gush on history · speculum for pooling · nitrazine · ferning · low amniotic fluid on ultrasound Without intervention, under 32 weeks : 50% deliver within 48 hours, 75% within 7 days Treatment : antibiotics for latency (Mercer protocol) · complete the steroid course · watch for chorioamnionitis Confirming ruptured membranes: a history of a gush, pooling of fluid in the vaginal fornix, nitrazine paper turning from orange to dark blue, and a fern pattern when amniotic fluid dries on a slide 8. When preterm birth is imminent Magnesium sulfate : birth imminent and under 34 weeks → IV bolus + infusion for neuroprotection (↓ cerebral palsy) Penicillin : IV if GBS positive or status unknown and the birth is preterm

Process of labour and birth Each stage of labour asks the same two questions: what event ends it, and what am I measuring to know it is progressing. The 1st stage is measured on the cervix, the 2nd on the fetus, the 3rd on the placenta, the 4th on the mother - and the lecture walks them in that order. ⭐ true labour = regular contractions causing progressive cervical dilation; Braxton Hicks change nothing at the cervix. Station is measured from the ischial spines , dilation is complete at 10 cm . ⚠ The earliest sign of placental separation is the firm, globular uterus , not the gush of blood. ⚠ In the 4th stage the danger is postpartum hemorrhage on top of a 500 mL autotransfusion , so a cardiac patient needs watching for the ↑ cardiac work. 1. Labour and its four stages Labour = regular uterine contractions causing progressive cervical dilation Contraindications to labour : placenta previa · vasa previa · cord presentation · abnormal lie · prior classical cesarean section or significant uterine surgery · active genital herpes Friedman curve = a guideline, not a rule 1st stage 2nd stage 3rd stage 4th stage Definition onset of labour → full dilatation · latent 0-4 cm , active 4-10 cm full dilatation → delivery of the fetus ("pushing") delivery of fetus → expulsion of placenta first hour after birth Friedman timing primiparous 6-18 h , active phase 1.2 cm/h · multiparous 2-10 h , active 1.5 cm/h primiparous 30 min-3 h · multiparous 5-30 min 2-30 min 1 h Progress measured on the cervix the fetus (station) the placenta (signs of separation) the mother (vitals) The stages of labour on the Friedman curve The first three stages of labour: stage 1 initial (latent) phase with a closed cervix, then active phase with an effaced cervix; stage 2 crowning of the head; stage 3 delivery of the placenta along the clamped umbilical cord 2. Abnormal labour and birth The lecture walks the fixes in the order you reach for them when labour stalls: work out which of the 4 P's is the problem → induce or augment → help with an instrument → cesarean section. It ends on the two things that go wrong around birth: uterine rupture and postpartum hemorrhage . ⭐ Uterine atony is the #1 cause of PPH - so a firm uterus sends you looking for tears instead. Abnormal FHR is the #1 reason for forceps or vacuum, and the first sign of uterine rupture. Vacuum cannot rotate; forceps can. A previous C/S for dystocia lowers the odds of a VBAC; one for breech raises them. Bishop under 6 → ripen before you induce. Carboprost: not in asthma. Ergonovine: not in hypertension. 1. Labour dystocia and the 4 P's Labour dystocia = abnormally slow progress through labour slow cervical dilatation = failure to progress · slow descent = failure to descend the most common reason cited for a cesarean section (C/S) not the same as shoulder dystocia , which is an emergency (shoulder stuck behind the pubic bone) When labour is slow, go through the 4 P's and fix the ones you can: P What it is Can you change it? How Power Contractions + pushing Yes Weak contractions: artificial rupture of membranes (ARM), then IV oxytocin · weak pushing: oxytocin, coaching, pain relief Passage The bony pelvis No Cannot be changed without breaking bone · symphysiotomy only in theory (last resort in severe shoulder dystocia) Passenger Fetal presentation, position, size Presentation and position yes, size no Breech → external cephalic version (ECV), before labour · rotate (by hand or forceps) to occiput anterior · too big to fit → C/S for cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) Psyche Support + emotional wellbeing Yes Continuous support improves maternal and fetal outcomes · pain control as the patient wishes (not an epidural for everyone) 2. Induction of labour Indications - any condition that raises the risk to mother or fetus post dates · preeclampsia · diabetes · maternal disease (cardiac, renal, respiratory) · rupture of membranes (PROM; the slide expands it as "preterm rupture of membranes", though PROM usually means prelabour rupture of membranes - check with the lecturer) · fetal growth restriction · placental abruption or insufficiency · twins · oligohydramnios · cholestasis of pregnancy · fetal anemia from alloimmunization · fetal demise low risk at 39 weeks (ARRIVE trial): fewer cesareans, less preeclampsia, fewer stillbirths Contraindications (anything that rules out labour): placenta previa, vasa previa, cord presentation · transverse lie · prior classical C/S or major uterine surgery · active genital herpes · invasive cervical cancer Pre-induction assessment confirm the due date · fetal position · estimated fetal weight · cervical exam · consent cervix scored by the Bishop score : under 6 = unfavourable → ripen it first · over 6 = favourable (shorter induction, more vaginal births) also raise success: multiparity · ruptured membranes · lower BMI · taller height · smaller baby · no preeclampsia Method, in two steps ① Cervical ripening to about 2 cm: chemical = prostaglandins (Cervidil, Prostin gel, misoprostol) · mechanical = Foley catheter balloon ② ARM , which may start labour on its own · if not, IV oxytocin Bishop score: dilation, effacement, consistency, position and station each scored; under 6 needs ripening 3. Augmentation with oxytocin Indication : labour has started but is not progressing (dystocia) ARM, then an oxytocin infusion titrated to a good contraction pattern and cervical change oxytocin can start contractions, strengthen weak ones, and boost pushing contractions hard to measure → intrauterine pressure catheter on oxytocin → continuous fetal heart monitoring , with time between contractions for the fetus to recover 4. Operative vaginal delivery Forceps or vacuum to speed up the 2nd stage (pushing) Indications fetal: atypical or abnormal fetal heart rate (FHR) - the #1 reason · head turned the wrong way (occiput transverse or posterior) maternal: must avoid straining (cerebrovascular or cardiac disease) · exhaustion or ineffective pushing labour: prolonged 2nd stage Contraindications absolute: unengaged head · cervix not fully dilated · not head-first (or face, brow) · CPD · fetal bleeding or bone disorder · any reason not to deliver vaginally relative: poor head flexion · rotation over 45° (vacuum only) · head still mid-pelvis · prematurity Vacuum Forceps Can do Traction only - cannot rotate Traction, rotation, flexion, extension Stop if 3 contractions · 3 pop-offs · 20 min without progress Cannot apply them properly · no descent with traction · 20 min Typical harm Baby's scalp: cephalohematoma, subgaleal hemorrhage , jaundice Mother: more tears · baby: facial nerve palsy , eye injury Newborn scalp collections: subgaleal hemorrhage spreads (dangerous) · cephalohematoma is cut off at the suture lines · caput succedaneum = swelling with a poorly defined edge 5. Cesarean section Indications the big four, 70% of all C/S : dystocia · abnormal FHR · previous C/S · malpresentation (breech or transverse) others: abnormal placenta (previa, vasa previa, accreta) · blockage (fibroid, mass) · maternal infection (herpes, HIV) · twins or more · cervical cancer · fetal anomalies breech is more likely with: uterine anomalies · pelvic tumours · previa · hydrocephalus or anencephaly · oligohydramnios · a lax uterus (many births, polyhydramnios, multiples) · previous breech cord prolapse : overt (cord seen or felt) · occult (beside the head) · cord presentation (below the head, before the waters break) · most likely in transverse lie, least in head-first Incisions skin: Pfannenstiel (low transverse) is standard · vertical midline for a crash section, obesity, an old scar, a bleeding disorder uterus: low transverse is standard and allows a later trial of labour · a classical (vertical) or T-shaped scar does not Complications infection: endometritis 4-5% ( 35-40% without antibiotics

Hemorrhagic shock Shock is cellular hypoxia, and hemorrhagic shock is the hypovolemic kind: lost blood → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output. The lecture walks it in order: recognise shock → grade the loss from the vitals → remember why the obstetric patient fools you → resuscitate → prevent the lethal triad , because she is young, healthy and volume-expanded, so she compensates until she suddenly does not . ⭐ Blood pressure is normal through class II (up to 30% loss, ~1500 mL); it falls only in class III , so a normal BP does not exclude shock and tachycardia (> 100, class II) is the first vital to move . ⚠ Do not overlook the young healthy patient: she may surprise you with how much she has lost while still looking well. Bleeding is treated by stopping the bleeding ; fluids and blood buy time, and each unit given feeds the coagulopathy arm of the triad. 1. Shock and its features Shock = cellular and tissue hypoxia (↓ oxygen delivery, ↑ oxygen consumption, or poor oxygen use) hypovolemic shock = ↓ intravascular volume → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output two kinds: hemorrhagic (blood loss) · non-hemorrhagic (↓ circulating volume, e.g. extreme dehydration) Presents as - the 8 features of shock hypotension · tachycardia · oliguria · abnormal mental status · tachypnea · cool, clammy, cyanotic skin · metabolic acidosis · hyperlactatemia 2. Lactation Lactation needs three things: prolactin to make milk, oxytocin to eject it, and removal of milk by infant or pump, which must begin by day 3 . Nearly every breastfeeding problem is a failure of one of the three, so ask which one broke . ⭐ By day 3 control switches from endocrine to autocrine: milk removal, not hormone, now drives supply , which is why removal must start by day 3 and why poor extraction lowers production. Low supply is the most common reason to stop breastfeeding. Mastitis is treated by continuing to nurse , not by stopping; an abscess needs drainage . Breast size doesn't matter. Alcohol is not a contraindication; smoking and street drugs are to be avoided. 1. The four stages Schulich Reviews 4 stages: mammogenesis (breast preparation) → lactogenesis (synthesis from alveoli; stage 1 mid-pregnancy, stage 2 copious after delivery) → galactokinesis (ejection) → galactopoiesis (maintenance) 2. Breast anatomy Lobes : 15-20 per breast, split by fibrous septae · each drained by a lactiferous duct Lobules inside each lobe hold the terminal duct lobular units - the milk-making alveoli, wrapped in myoepithelial cells that contract to squeeze milk out Milk's path : terminal ducts → lactiferous ducts → lactiferous sinus → opening on the nipple Breast anatomy: lobules and alveoli drain through lactiferous ducts and sinuses to the nipple 3. Postpartum care The puerperium is a return to baseline on a fixed timetable , so the complication is whatever breaks the timetable: blues past 2 weeks , bright red bleeding returning after 24 h , fever on 2 of the first 10 days . ⭐ Blues that last more than 2 weeks, or are severe within the first 2 weeks, are postpartum depression. ⚠ EPDS item 10 scored 1-3 at any total is a self-harm risk needing immediate assessment. The puerperal-infection clock excludes the first 24 h , and delayed PPH starts after 24 h . Refer ALL antepartum and postpartum patients to pelvic floor physiotherapy. 1. Approach to Neonatal Care Every newborn is examined within 24 h and kept pink, warm and sweet; the extra care turns on which reserve this baby lacks : heat (no shivering), glucose (glycogen lasts 8-10 h , gluconeogenesis not normal until 2-4 days ), or bilirubin clearance. ⭐ Symptomatic hypoglycemia is a medical emergency: IV dextrose, not a feed (a jittery IDM who cannot latch, glucose 2.3). The GA curves run higher the more mature the baby , so the same TSB can need treatment at 35 weeks and not at 40. ⚠ Sepsis runs through all three : hypoglycemia can be a sign of it, it causes hyperbilirubinemia, and temperature instability is a jaundice risk factor, so consider it in any sick baby . 1. Approach to Amenorrhea Amenorrhea is a compartment problem — the block sits in the outflow tract, the ovary, the pituitary or the hypothalamus — and two numbers sort it : the beta hCG first, always , then follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) , which says whether the pituitary is shouting at a dead ovary (high FSH) or not shouting at all (low FSH) . ⭐ rule out pregnancy first, before any other test and whatever the story sounds like. High FSH means the ovary has failed; low FSH means the problem is above it - that one number splits the differential, and a normal FSH with normal prolactin and TSH points at anovulation, which is where PMOS lives. Turner is the commonest primary cause (27%); PMOS, the new name for PCOS, is the commonest secondary cause (28%) - and pregnancy is ruled out before either. A progesterone withdrawal bleed proves estrogen and a patent outflow tract. Pubarche and testosterone split MRKH (46,XX) from androgen insensitivity (46,XY). 1. Common concerns in pregnancy Most of these complaints are physiologic, and two things drive most of them: progesterone and hydration. The job is to use the trimester to frame the differential , then find the red flag that turns a normal symptom into one to investigate - infection, bleeding, hypertensive disease, thrombosis or preterm labour. ⭐ Hyperemesis gravidarum is nausea where food and liquids will not stay down - missed work or constant nausea alone does not make it - and it means admission and IV fluids . Good counselling is reassurance plus a clear safety net , and asking what she is most worried about. Bleeding is investigated at any gestational age (ultrasound + speculum), even when it is only on wiping. Third-trimester nausea is reflux, not hCG : treat the acid, not the nausea. Normal blood pressure does not excuse a headache from preeclampsia bloodwork. Cramping that settles with water is dehydration; cramping that does not is a trip to triage. ⚠ Yeast and BV are not just a nuisance - they are risk factors for preterm labour. 1. Drugs in Pregnancy and Lactation Most drugs reach the baby, and most of them are still safe : the placenta is not a barrier , and most drugs cross into milk in minute amounts . So the question is never "does it get there?" but how much, when, and can the baby clear it - and the risk of the drug is always weighed against the risk of the untreated disease . ⭐ An RID under 10% is generally considered safe; the milk/plasma ratio alone is not the risk - the dose the baby actually gets and how fast the baby clears it are. Atenolol is the beta-blocker to avoid in breastfeeding (RID about 20%, kidney-cleared, and a newborn's kidneys filter poorly in week 1). Weeks 1-2 are all-or-none, weeks 3-8 make major malformations, the fetal period makes functional defects. Drugs cause only about 1% of birth anomalies, and the baseline major-malformation risk is 2-4%. 1. Why the data are thin, and why we treat anyway Very few trials enrol pregnant or breastfeeding women , so fetal-risk data come from "accidents" (exposure before she knew she was pregnant, or a drug she could not stop) have enough data to judge fetal risk · > 90% of pregnant women take a medication (average 2.9 prescriptions) · Animal data do not transfer : > 1,200 drugs malformative in some animal model are known not to be in humans Untreated disease is a risk too (asthma, epilepsy, depression, psychosis, infection) · the question is "if a pregnant woman needs a medication, why is she denied it?" 2. The placenta, and how much risk there is to begin with No placental barrier : as a general rule, most drugs reach the fetal circulation to some extent Baseline risk of a major malformation = 2-4% · every pregnancy has about a 97% chance of a healthy baby Causes of birth anomalies : genetic 25% · environmental (infections, micronutrient and folic acid deficiency) · drugs or other substances only 1% · about half have no known cause a baby born with a malformation: > 99 in 100 times it is NOT a drug ⚠ Fear is a teratogen too : after Chernobyl about 2,500 pregnancies were terminated in Greece , an estimated 10,000-15,000 across Europe, out of unwarranted fear 3. Timing, dose and genes decide the effect Teratogenic effects by timing: all or none, major malformations, functional Exposure window Weeks Effect "All or none" (preimplantation) 1-2 ↑ spontaneous abortion , otherwise no effect Organogenesis (embryonic) 3-8 Major malformations , by timing and drug Fetal period 9-38 Functional effects (e.g. angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, immunosuppressants) · brain development is a continuum Also : dose (threshold, dose-response) · genetic susceptibility Drug effects on the fetus , one example each: spontaneous abortion ( misoprostol ) · growth restriction ( beta-blockers , cigarettes) · teratogenicity ( thalidomide , valproate ) · neonatal withdrawal (heroin) · neonatal toxicity ( lithium ) · long-term neurobehavioural (alcohol) · cancer (diethylstilbestrol) 4. SSRIs 1%? statins "probably a myth" Even a real teratogen harms only a fraction of exposed babies · ⚠ be most careful with newer drugs , whose fetal toxicity often surfaces years after release 5. How drugs get into breast milk Most drugs cross into milk, but in minute amounts Cross more when the drug has: high maternal plasma levels · low molecular weight · little protein binding · high lipid solubility , or a transporter (breast cancer resistance protein, BCRP) molecular weight > 500 daltons does not enter milk : insulin (> 6,000) and heparin (40,000) stay out; ethanol (200) gets in Then the baby has to absorb it : oral bioavailability in the baby's gut 6. Decreased risk of preterm labor Decreased risk of placental abruption Increased risk of fetal growth restriction Increased risk of preterm premature rupture of membranes The correct answer is C. This is pre-eclampsia — hypertension plus proteinuria developing after 20 weeks . One of the underlying mechanisms is thought to be abnormal remodeling of the uterine spiral arteries , which leads to inadequate blood flow to the placenta and therefore impaired fetal growth .

Which of the following describes normal variations in blood pressure throughout pregnancy? Blood pressure normally drops in the second trimester , because pregnant women are relatively vasodilated — but BP should return to normal at term . Option C is the trap: a rise to hypertension in T3 is pathological ( pre-eclampsia ), not a normal variation.

RhIG is prophylaxis only: it does nothing once an antibody already exists.

After delivery, Pam will be in a hypoestrogenic state, not hyperestrogenic, that will persist if she is breastfeeding.

Rachel has recently become a mother to a healthy baby girl, Emma. Although the pregnancy was unexpected, her partner Ross is ecstatic, despite the 3% chance of pregnancy with their contraceptive of choice. Ross insists that Emma be breastfed, although Rachel is unsure. Which of the follow statements regarding breastfeeding is FALSE and should not be used to help Rachel decide to breastfeed? Breastfeeding provides a host of long-term health benefits to both Emma and Rachel Breastmilk is a sustainable, waste-free, environmentally-friendly practice Breastmilk is the recommended exclusive nutrition for the first 6 months of life Breastfeeding is a reliable method of contraception Colostrum will provide Emma passive immunity to help prevent infections Breastfeeding can help accelerate Rachel’s recovery from childbirth The correct answer is D. Breastfeeding can prolong postpartum anovulation and provide some contraceptive benefit but should not be relied on. Contraception should be implemented 6 weeks postpartum or whenever sexual activity resumes.

A mother is tearful, irritable and sleeping poorly 4 days after birth, and still bonding well with her baby. Which feature would make postpartum depression, not blues, the diagnosis? Onset on day 3-5 Weepiness and mood lability Insomnia in the first week Symptoms lasting over 2 weeks Occurring in a first pregnancy The correct answer is D. Postpartum blues affect up to 85% of mothers, start in the first days and are self-limited, within about 2 weeks . Blues lasting over 2 weeks, or severe within the first 2 , point to postpartum depression. Screen with PHQ-2, then EPDS or PHQ-9.

Which of the following is part of the lethal triad of hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock (choose 3): Acidosis Coagulopathy Change in mental status Hypothermia Hyperlactatemia Oliguria The correct answer is A, B, D. A, B, D are the lethal triad! However, all of the above are indeed signs of hypovolemic shock. Treat the lethal triad by maintaining tissue perfusion (O2, IV fluid, transfusion), warming the patient, and limiting blood loss.

Which of the following should you NOT do for a patient in active hemorrhagic shock? Patient in hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock should be kept NPO instead. Answers B-D should all be done. Ensure to take vitals, maintain ABC, and consult gynecology urgently if the cause is gynecological. Inserting a foley catheter would be important for monitoring urine output.

Which of the following is the correct order for the progression of placental microvascular damage found on umbilical artery doppler? Reversed EDF →Decreased baseline EDF →absent EDF Decreased baseline EDF →absent EDF →reversed EDF Absent EDF →decreased baseline EDF →reversed EDF The correct answer is B. Reversed EDF occurs when 70% of microvasculature is damaged.

Management of neonatal sepsis includes all of the following except: Perform blood, urine, and CSF cultures to identify the causative agent Chest x-ray Broad-spectrum antibiotic use, including antivirals if HSV is suspected Provide hemodynamic and ventilation support as necessary Begin antibiotics once culture and sensitivity results are available The correct answer is E. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be initiated immediately if neonatal sepsis is suspected, and can be adjusted after culture and sensitivity results are available.

Introduction to MSK anatomy The vocabulary the rest of the musculoskeletal (MSK) block is built on, and the approach every MSK complaint gets: which structure is the pain coming from, what is wrong with it, and are there red flags? ⭐ Red flags? is the step you never skip. Degenerative = pain with activity, better with rest · inflammatory = pain at rest, morning stiffness, warm and swollen. Upper motor neuron = increased tone, brisk reflexes, Babinski positive · lower motor neuron = normal or low tone, reduced reflexes · MSK weakness has no objective sensory loss . Muscle and tendon hurt to contract AND to stretch; ligament hurts on passive movement. Concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens, isometric doesn't move. Hilton's law : the nerve to the muscle is the nerve to the joint. Joint pain comes from the capsule, ligaments and bone , not the cartilage. 1. The general approach to an MSK complaint Step 1 · know the anatomy : consider every structure in the area as a possible pain generator, plus pain referred in from elsewhere Step 2 · the clinical features of each structure (the history and exam below) Step 3 · red flags? No → treat in the usual fashion · Yes → investigate the red flag Anatomic localization (which structure) is not the differential diagnosis (what is wrong with it) History : OLDCARS - onset, location, duration, character, aggravating or alleviating, associated features, radiation, severity · works for pain, sensory symptoms and weakness Exam : the body part and the joint above and below (referred pain is real) Red flag category Clues Cancer Constitutional symptoms · history of cancer · site-specific Infection Fevers, chills · looks unwell · immunocompromised · IV drug use Trauma Recent trauma · osteoporosis · severe pain Visceral Depends on the site: flank or writhing pain · aortic aneurysm · kidney stones · GI or genitourinary symptoms Inflammatory Morning stiffness · rashes · marked joint swelling, redness Vascular The 5 P's · skin discolouration · aortic aneurysm · claudication Neurologic Urinary retention, bowel incontinence · saddle anesthesia · frank weakness or sensory loss · claudication Some of these clues are specific to one condition - give the ones that fit, not the whole list 2. ( normal bone, real trauma vs weak bone : osteoporosis, tumour, infection) · tumour (+ systemic features) · avascular necrosis · infection (+ systemic features) Joint ("arthritis") Pain around the joint , worse weight-bearing, may be swollen Degenerative (osteoarthritis) vs inflammatory (gout, rheumatoid, septic) Capsule, ligament Pain around the joint · instability , pain on PASSIVE movement Sprain (hurts in any direction) → rupture (frank instability: subluxation, dislocation) Muscle, tendon Pain with MOVEMENT · hurts to CONTRACT and to STRETCH Strain (hurts to use) vs rupture (looks weak) · tendin osis (overuse, not -itis) · inflammation, infection · tumour (soft-tissue mass) · compartment syndrome Peripheral nerve Sensory and strength changes Compression or stretch from any cause (nearby arthritis, abscess, inflamed tendon, tumour, sleeping on the arm) · intrinsic nerve damage (infection, inflammation, tumour invasion) Degenerative pattern Inflammatory pattern Pain with activity, better with rest · gradual onset · ± stiffness through the day · ± locking or instability · may be weak · swelling only secondary Pain at rest · morning stiffness · swelling, warmth, redness · ± rash · malaise · fever, weight loss (especially infection) · acute or subacute onset 3. Weakness: pain, muscle, or nerve? Weakness is very common when pain is present , because it hurts to move: is it weakness, pain, or both? Upper motor neurons live in the brain and spinal cord · the lower motor neuron starts at the anterior horn cell and runs out to the muscle MSK weakness (partial or complete tear) Lower motor neuron (peripheral nerve injury) Upper motor neuron (stroke, spinal cord injury) Pain Usually painful, may bruise Painful ("pinched nerve") or painless Often painless (stroke) · can be neuropathic Onset Acute (Achilles rupture) or chronic (rotator cuff degeneration) Acute or chronic Often acute Sensation No objective sensory loss Sensory loss in the same nerve's territory Sensory loss in the matching territory Weakness Only that muscle (others may look weak from pain) Any muscle that nerve supplies More diffuse (e.g. hemiplegia) Tone, reflexes Reflex lost only at the ruptured tendon Normal or low tone · reduced reflexes · Babinski negative Increased tone (spasticity) · brisk reflexes · Babinski positive Three dropped feet : same weakness, three sites - tendon rupture (no sensory loss, tender dorsum) · common peroneal nerve (lateral leg numb, tender at the fibular head) · L5 root (lateral leg and dorsal foot numb, pain from the back down) 4. Managing a non-red-flag MSK diagnosis Education first: what it is, what to expect ① Non-drug : relative rest, activity changes · RICE or POLICE (protection, optimal loading, ice, compression, elevation) · heat, cold, ultrasound, laser · acupuncture, yoga, massage · rehabilitation · gait aids · braces (orthoses) ② Drugs : topical (anti-inflammatory) → injected (local steroid) → systemic (oral NSAID such as ibuprofen, acetaminophen) ③ Interventional or surgical : only after the less invasive options fail Then follow-up · contributing factors (mood, fatigue) · treat the activity and participation limits, not just the impairment Red-flag conditions get their own treatment : cancer → surgery, chemotherapy, radiation · infection → antibiotics ± debridement · trauma → casting, surgery, rehab 5. Anatomy of the back and neck Every structure here is a possible pain generator in the mechanical back pain lecture. Learn what makes each region's vertebrae different, which ligament stops which movement, and which back muscles a strain hits. ⭐ Anterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperextension; the narrow posterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperflexion (which is why discs bulge out beside it). Cervical = transverse foramina + bifid spines · thoracic = costal facets + long downward spines · lumbar = big bodies. C1 nods "yes", C2 turns "no"; no disc between them. Trapezius = cranial nerve XI · deep back muscles = dorsal rami. Erector spinae → lifting strains · transversospinalis → rotation strains. 1. The vertebral column Jobs : protect the spinal cord · carry body weight · posture and movement (flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation) 33 vertebrae : 7 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral (fused into the sacrum) · 4 coccygeal (fused into the coccyx) Curves absorb stress and protect the back Primary curves Secondary curves Where Thoracic and sacral · concave anteriorly Cervical and lumbar · concave posteriorly When Fetal period (flexed fetal position), kept for life Early infancy, as the baby extends out of flexion Too much Kyphosis (thoracic): anterior vertebrae eroded or fractured, e.g. osteoporosis Lordosis (lumbar): pelvis tilts forward · weak trunk muscles, pregnancy Scoliosis = an increased sideways curve with rotation of the vertebrae (weak back muscles, posture, congenital vertebral defects, unequal leg length) 2. A typical vertebra Body (front): carries weight, gets bigger going down Arch (back) = pedicles (join arch to body) + laminae (close it behind) vertebral foramen = the hole for the cord, between body and arch spinous process (back) and transverse processes (sides) = muscle and ligament attachments 4 articular processes → facet ( zygapophyseal ) joints = plane synovial joints between neighbours The superior and inferior vertebral notches of neighbouring pedicles form the intervertebral foramen , where the spinal nerve exits Joints between vertebrae : each vertebra joins the ones above and below at the disc (bodies) and the facet joints · except C1 (joins the skull) and L5 (joins the sacrum) Rib joints (thoracic): the rib head meets the superior costal facet of its own vertebra, the inferior costal facet of the vertebra above, and the disc between · the rib tubercle meets the transverse process of its own vertebra (costotransverse joint) Laminectomy = removing spinous processes and laminae to take pressure off the cord or roots (tumour, herniated disc, bony overgrowth) Typical vertebra from above and from the side: body, pedicles, laminae, processes, vertebral foramen and intervertebral foramen 3. The intervertebral disc Between vertebral bodies: attaches neighbours, permits movement, absorbs shock joined to the bodies at the end plate (cartilage fused to the disc + a thin layer of porous bone) anulus fibrosus = outer rings of fibrocartilage · nucleus pulposus = inner gel, high water content About 25% of the column's height · thickest in cervical and lumbar spine · no disc between C1 and C2 Herniation : most posterolateral herniations are at L4/L5 or L5/S1 and hit the root just below (the L4 disc hits L5) 4. Regional differences Cervical Thoracic Lumbar Body Small Heart-shaped, costal facets for ribs Large , short heavy pedicles Vertebral foramen Large , especially C3-C7 (cervical enlargement of the cord) Small, circular Triangular, larger than thoracic Transverse process Short, with transverse foramina (vertebral artery C6 up to C1; only the vein at C7) Long, with facets for the rib tubercle Long and slender , no costal facets Spinous process Short, bifid · C7 long = vertebra prominens Long, slopes down over the next one Short and stout Facets face Superior facets up and back · inferior facets down and forward Superior facets back and slightly out · inferior forward and slightly in Superior facets back and in · inferior forward and out Main movement Flexion, extension Rotation , some lateral flexion · facet orientation blocks excessive flexion and extension Flexion, extension, some side bending, limited rotation Atypical cervical vertebrae C1 ( atlas ) : a ring - two lateral masses joined by an anterior arch (in place of a body) and a posterior arch (in place of laminae) · a groove for the vertebral artery on its upper surface · atlanto-occipital joints → "yes" nod (flexion, extension) C2 ( axis ) : the dens projects up from the C2 body and pivots against the back of C1's anterior arch → atlanto-axial pivot → "no" rotation Sacrum : 5 fused vertebrae · carries body weight to the ilium through the sacroiliac joints · front (pelvic) surface smooth and concave, back rough and convex · paired sacral foramina for the sacral nerves · sacral hiatus = site of a caudal epidural 5. Ligaments Ligament Where Resists Anterior longitudinal Broad, strong band on the front of bodies and discs, occiput to sacrum Hyperextension Posterior longitudinal Narrow , inside the canal on the back of the bodies Hyperflexion Ligamentum flavum Pale yellow, joins adjacent laminae — Supraspinous Tips of the spinous processes, C7 to sacrum — Ligamentum nuchae Continues the supraspinous above C7: very strong band from the external occipital protuberance to the cervical spinous processes, out to the skin · fills the neck curve Attachment for neck and upper back muscles Interspinous · intertransverse Between neighbouring spinous · transverse processes — Ligaments of the vertebral column on a sagittal section, with the same ligaments on MRI 6.
