02.2 Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain

Clinical approach to mechanical back and neck pain Most back and neck pain is "mechanical": axial pain that is worse with movement and better with rest. The work is to screen every patient for red flags and, with none, to treat conservatively without imaging, since an exact anatomical diagnosis is often unnecessary. ⭐ No red flags and under 6 weeks → no imaging. Disc pain is worse with flexion; facet pain is worse with extension. Mechanical pain is worse with movement, better with rest. Herniation = worse with cough or sneeze, sudden after lifting, younger patient. Whiplash: keep moving, no collar. Muscle pain has no diagnostic test . Nerve-root pain, stenosis and the red-flag conditions themselves are on the non-mechanical chart ; the vertebrae, ligaments and back muscles are in 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck . 1. The approach Possible pain generators : paraspinal muscle and soft tissue · intervertebral disc · facet ( zygapophyseal ) joint · nerves in the spine · sacroiliac joint History : OLDCARS (onset, location, duration, character, alleviating or aggravating, radiation, severity) plus red flags Exam : the spine itself · contributing lower-limb problems · a neurological exam · signs of red flags palpable landmarks: C7 (vertebra prominens) · acromion · spine and medial border of the scapula · ribs 6-12 · iliac crest · sacrum 2. Red flags Category Red flags Think of Neurological Progressive weakness or sensory change · saddle anesthesia · incontinence · erectile dysfunction · loss of hand dexterity · ataxic gait · abnormal reflexes Cord or cauda equina compression Inflammatory Morning stiffness · improves with exercise · pain in the 2nd half of the night · family history · rashes · eye symptoms Spondyloarthropathy Neoplastic Young age · severe night pain , no relief with rest · weight loss · night sweats · history of cancer · associated signs (e.g. blood in the urine) Tumour, metastasis Infectious Fever · sweats · IV drug use · immunosuppression Osteomyelitis, discitis, abscess Fracture (subacute or chronic) Fall or trauma · osteoporosis · previous fragility fracture Fracture Vascular Neck pain with dizziness on neck movement , cranial nerve signs, drop attacks · limb pain with activity, with or without neck or back pain (claudication) Vertebral artery insufficiency · distal claudication 3. Investigations: when (not) to image Most low back pain needs no imaging : soft tissue often doesn't show · it can't separate symptomatic from asymptomatic changes · it rarely changes management · but it is required to look for red flags With red flags, add targeted tests: blood work and cultures (infection) · abdominal or other imaging (cancer) · angiography (vascular) · electromyography (nerve) Who to image (Canadian Association of Radiologists) no red flags and under 6 weeks → NO imaging symptoms over 6 weeks despite good conservative care → an X-ray can be the starting point imaging indicated → MRI is best · CT only if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable · X-ray otherwise only to look for red-flag conditions (fracture, malignancy) suspected uncomplicated herniated disc or spinal stenosis → image only after a failed 4-6 week conservative trial red-flag indications for MRI : suspected cancer · infection · cauda equina syndrome · severe or progressive neurological deficit · suspected compression fracture · urgent if an epidural abscess or hematoma is a worry Test Best for X-ray ($) Cheap, quick screen of alignment and fractures CT ($$) Bony detail , trauma MRI ($$$) Best for non-bony structures · most expensive Bone scan Disease in many places · "hot" vs "cold" lesions CT myelogram Dye injected into the thecal sac · only if MRI is contraindicated Image-guided injection Diagnosis and treatment 4. Mechanical pain: what it looks like Definition : axial pain that is worse with movement and relieved by rest location : midline or just beside it, neck or back onset : anywhere from acute to chronic · usually built up by degeneration, then "tweaked" by stairs or a bad bend character : dull ache or sharp, stabbing red flags: none · imaging often normal (disc degeneration shows up in many adults with no back pain) 5. Muscle pain and whiplash Three muscle problems : acute strain or spasm · repetitive strain (repetitive tasks, forceful exertion, vibration, compression, awkward postures) · myofascial trigger points (hyperirritable spots, tender when pressed, can refer pain) No test diagnoses it : investigate only to rule other things out Treatment : rule out red flags → reassure (excellent prognosis) → relative rest → ice or heat → topicals · a short course of oral anti-inflammatories → physiotherapy for postural support Whiplash associated disorder : neck symptoms after an acceleration-deceleration injury (car crash) muscles most often (strains, partial tears) · less often facets > anterior longitudinal ligament > bone > cord under 5% still have severe symptoms at 2 years more than pain, stiffness and reduced range → X-ray if fracture is a worry · MRI if neurological signs · otherwise keep moving, no collar , heat or ice, acetaminophen or NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral or topical), modest physiotherapy (aggressive programs can worsen it) 6. Spondylosis: the degenerative cascade Spondylosis = degenerative disc disease + facet arthropathy ( degenerative disc disease , facet syndrome ) with loss of disc height and thickened ligaments The cascade : repeated axial loading → end-plate damage → tears in the anulus → nucleus pushes into the tears ( internal disc disruption ) → disc loses height → angles change, facets overloaded: synovial thickening, cartilage loss, osteophytes , lax capsule → slipping (degenerative spondylolisthesis) · thickened ligaments, bulging disc → lateral stenosis (roots in the foramina) and central canal stenosis Disc pain (internal disc disruption) Facet joint pain What Pain from the disc itself, not from it pressing on something · nucleus pushes out through radial or
03.1 Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord

Anatomy of the back and spinal cord The spinal cord is shorter than the spine, and almost every clinical rule in the non-mechanical back pain lecture follows from that: where it ends, which root a disc hits, where a needle can go safely, and why lumbar and cervical stenosis behave differently. ⭐ The cord ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris) but the dural sac runs to S2 - so a lumbar puncture or epidural goes in at L3/L4 or L4/L5, into the cauda equina, not the cord. C1-C7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7, everything after below. Epidural space and subarachnoid space are real; subdural is potential. Ventral root = motor, dorsal root = sensory. C7 = middle finger, triceps · L5 = big toe extension · S1 = lateral foot, Achilles. 1. The spinal cord Part of the central nervous system , continuous with the medulla · a reflex centre and the pathway between body and brain Runs from the foramen magnum to L1-L2 in adults Not uniform in width cervical enlargement (C4-T1 cord levels) → brachial plexus (upper limb) lumbosacral enlargement (L1-S3 cord levels) → lumbar and sacral plexuses (lower limb) The end of the cord conus medullaris = the tapered tip, at L1-L2, just below the lumbar enlargement filum terminale (internum) = a thread of pia from the tip to the coccyx, anchoring the cord cauda equina ("horse's tail") = the lower lumbar, sacral and coccygeal roots running down past the cord's end to their own foramina Why it is short : in the embryo the cord fills the whole canal, but the spine outgrows it, leaving the cord in the upper two-thirds of the canal The cord ends at L1-L2; cervical enlargement for the brachial plexus, lumbar enlargement for the lumbosacral plexus; 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal nerves 2. Spinal nerves and where they exit 31 pairs : 8 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral · 1 coccygeal Nerves Exit the spine Why it matters C1-C7 Above their own vertebra C8 Below C7 - 8 cervical nerves, only 7 cervical vertebrae The switch point T1 downward Below their own vertebra (under its pedicle) Lower lumbar, sacral, coccygeal Leave the cord high, travel down as the cauda equina , exit at their own foramen The gap between cord segment and foramen grows going down Making a spinal nerve ventral (anterior) rootlets = motor (+ presynaptic autonomic fibres; cell bodies in the anterior horn) · dorsal (posterior) rootlets = sensory (cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion) roots join in the intervertebral foramen as a mixed spinal nerve it splits into a dorsal ramus (skin and deep muscles of the back) and a ventral ramus (limbs and the rest of the trunk) L5 is the biggest lumbar nerve in the smallest lumbar foramen : the lower lumbar nerves are the most easily compressed Review the inside of the cord in 04 - Introduction to the Nervous System 3. Meninges and spaces Layer or space What it is Clinically Epidural space Real space outside the dura · fat + internal venous plexus Epidural anesthetic goes here Dura mater ("tough mother") Tough outer layer · forms the dural sac down to S2 · anchored to the coccyx (filum terminale externum) · continuous with the cranial dura Pierced by spinal nerves Subdural space Potential space — Arachnoid mater Delicate, no blood vessels · held against the dura by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure — Subarachnoid space Real space with CSF and the cord's vessels · enlarges below the cord as the lumbar cistern (L2 to S2) , holding the cauda equina Lumbar puncture , spinal block Pia mater Directly on the cord, roots and vessels · denticulate ligaments anchor the cord in the dural sac · continues as the filum terminale — 4. Epidural vs spinal block and lumbar puncture Both done at L3/L4 or L4/L5 - below the end of the cord , so the floating cauda equina roots move away from the needle Epidural : needle into the epidural space , around the dura · bathes the cauda equina roots after they leave the sac → numb below the level · widely used in labour Spinal block / lumbar puncture : needle into the subarachnoid space · drug straight into CSF or CSF sampled from the lumbar cistern patient on their side with the trunk flexed Epidural: needle stops in the epidural space; spinal block or lumbar puncture: needle enters the subarachnoid space and CSF 5. Dermatomes, myotomes and root lesions Dermatome = the skin supplied by one spinal nerve root · myotome = the muscles supplied by one root A root lesion gives sensory change in its dermatome, weakness in its myotome, and a reduced reflex Neighbouring dermatomes overlap a lot · overlap is minimal only at the ventral axial line , where non-sequential segments sit side by side Why the pattern is segmental : each somite keeps the nerve of its own segment, even when its muscle cells migrate down the limb epimere → epaxial back muscles (splenius, erector spinae, transversospinalis) · dorsal ramus hypomere → lateral and ventral trunk muscles and all limb muscles · ventral ramus most myotomes fuse, so most muscles get more than one segment (several nerves to one trunk muscle, or several nerves joined in the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses) Root Dermatome (sensation) Myotome (movement) Reflex C5 Lateral shoulder to lateral elbow Shoulder abduction , elbow flexion Biceps, brachioradialis (C5/6) C6 Lateral forearm, thumb and index finger Elbow flexion, wrist extension Biceps, brachioradialis (C5/6) C7 Middle finger Elbow extension Triceps L4 Medial lower leg, medial malleolus Ankle dorsiflexion Patellar L5 Dorsum of the foot (1st-3rd web spaces) Big toe extension Hamstrings (often absent normally - compare sides) S1 Lateral foot and heel Plantar flexion Achilles The cord tapers to the conus medullaris at L1-L2; the filum terminale anchors it; the cauda equina roots run on below
03.2 Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain

Clinical approach to non-mechanical back and neck pain Non-mechanical pain is either a squeezed nerve - at the side (radiculopathy) or in the centre (stenosis, cauda equina, myelopathy) - or "everything else" that the red flags find (inflammatory, fracture, visceral, infection, tumour). Without red flags, start the same conservative care as for mechanical pain. ⭐ Saddle anesthesia + urinary retention or fecal incontinence = cauda equina syndrome → urgent MRI and decompression within 48 hours. Lumbar stenosis squeezes roots (neurogenic claudication, eased by bending forward, no bladder change); cervical stenosis squeezes the cord (clumsy hands, upper motor neuron signs) → urgent consult. A disc hits the lower root: C4/5 → C5, L4/5 → L5. Radicular pain is eased by slackening the nerve . Inflammatory pain gets better with movement. Spondyl osis degenerates, spondyl olysis fractures, spondylo listhesis slips. The red-flag list and who to image for mechanical pain are on the mechanical chart ; the cord, its exits and the dermatome table are in 03.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord . Reading the spine on X-ray is in 04 - Axial Spine Radiology . 1. Triage: which group is this? Take the history and exam, and exclude non-spinal causes : hip disease · visceral (pancreatitis, endometriosis, kidney stone) · vascular (aortic aneurysm, claudication) · systemic (e.g. endocarditis) · viral syndromes Diagnostic triage (Traeger 2017, primary care) serious spinal disease, under 1% : vertebral fracture · metastasis · spinal infection · axial spondyloarthropathy · cauda equina radicular pain, radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, 5-10% non-specific low back pain, 90-95% : acute or persistent No red flags → advice and reassurance : good prognosis, no immediate imaging , consider non-drug treatment Group Non-drug Drug Radicular pain Exercise, physiotherapy Neuropathic agents · opioids for rescue Acute non-specific Stay active, no bed rest · physiotherapy NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · skeletal muscle relaxants · weak opioids Persistent non-specific Exercise · psychological therapies · multidisciplinary care · physiotherapy NSAIDs, with caution Nerve compression can come from ANYTHING that takes up space : disc, spondylosis, abscess, tumour, bleed, a slipped vertebra (spondylolisthesis) 2. Radiculopathy: compression at the side Definition : a spinal nerve root compressed or malfunctioning in or around the neural foramen , from any cause degenerative causes are by far the most common (disc herniation, spondylosis) others: tumour (primary, metastasis, carcinomatous meningitis) · infection (abscess, tuberculosis) · sarcoidosis · diabetic neuropathy of the root · trauma · arteriovenous malformation Presents as onset acute or insidious , depending on the cause limb > neck or back , in a dermatome burning, tingling, electrical eased by positions that slacken the nerve (arm overhead, legs curled) weakness and reduced reflexes in a myotome · sensory change Where : lumbar - under 1% non-degenerative , mostly the L5 and S1 roots · cervical - mostly C7 and C6 , from cervical spondylosis Which root does the disc hit? The lower one cervical : nerves exit above their vertebra → C4/5 disc → C5 · a C6/7 disc → C7 lumbar : the upper root has already left; a paracentral disc hits the traversing root → L4/5 disc → L5 · a far-lateral L4/5 disc catches L4 Treatment conservative first : education, excellent prognosis (most settle over months) · relative rest, ice or heat · topicals, oral anti-inflammatories, short course of opioids if severe · physiotherapy image if red flags, or the deficit is severe or progressing (e.g. marked arm weakness) · electromyography tests the root neck pain or arm pain from degeneration: MRI only with neurological signs or symptoms, or pain over 4 weeks of conservative care · CT only if MRI is contraindicated · X-ray not indicated (degenerative changes from early middle age, usually unrelated to symptoms) next: epidural steroid injection → surgical decompression (refractory symptoms · progressive or severe deficit · tumour, large abscess, trauma) A paracentral L4/5 disc hits L5 while a far-lateral one hits L4; a C6/7 disc hits C7 3. Central stenosis: lumbar roots vs cervical cord The cord ends at ~L1 → lumbar central stenosis squeezes roots , cervical central stenosis squeezes the cord - so they look and are treated entirely differently Lumbar central stenosis Cervical stenosis → myelopathy What is squeezed Nerve roots (cauda equina) Spinal cord Onset Typically insidious Picture of an atraumatic spinal cord injury Symptoms Legs > back · burning, tingling · distal worse Clumsy hands , wasted intrinsic hand muscles · arm tingling, distal worse · gait and balance problems · urinary incontinence (retention with overflow) · often a radiculopathy too Key sign Neurogenic claudication : worse walking a distance · relieved by bending forward (grocery cart, walking uphill) and by sitting (more slowly than vascular claudication) Upper motor neuron signs below the level Bladder, bowel No problems Urinary incontinence Imaging Mild to moderate claudication: none, or non-urgent MRI (especially a surgical candidate) MRI , the modality of choice Treatment Flexion-based activity and physiotherapy are the mainstay Urgent neurosurgical or spine consult for decompression 4. Cauda equina syndrome The severe end of lumbar central stenosis : heavy compression, worst at the lowest roots Red flags : weakness · saddle anesthesia · urinary retention · fecal incontinence Urgent MRI · a neurosurgical emergency - outcomes much better if decompressed within 48 hours of onset See cauda equina syndrome 5. "Everything else": the red flags Mechanical Inflammatory Movement Worse Better Rest, night Better with rest Night pain in the 2nd half of the night Morning stiffness — Significant Also — Sacroiliac joints · ask about eyes, rashes, family history, enthesopathy, other inflammatory joint pain Inflammatory → seronegative spon

Axial spine radiology Read every spine film the same way, ABCS, and then ask of each finding: which view shows it best, what is the sign, and does it change what happens next? Fracture (stable or unstable), spondylolysis (the Scottie dog's collar) and scoliosis (the Cobb angle) are the three the objectives name; the normal variants are the things not to call disease. ⭐ A fracture that reaches the posterior elements is unstable. Spondylolysis = collar on the Scottie dog (oblique view); isthmic spondylolisthesis adds the forward slip (lateral). Cobb angle over 10° is scoliosis, over 50° is surgical. Lateral C-spine: four smooth lines, atlantodental interval under 3 mm, prevertebral tissue under 7 mm at C2 and 22 mm at C6. Perched facets → MRI and urgent neurosurgery. A limbus vertebra is not a fracture. 1. The systematic approach: ABCS A lignment: cervical mild lordosis · thoracic kyphosis · lumbar lordosis , and each vertebra lined up with the next B ones: follow the cortices · vertebral body height · pedicles and transverse processes C artilage and joints: cartilage is invisible, so read the disc spaces (calcification, bony bridging) and the facet joints S oft tissues: prevertebral and paraspinal · then the whole image (lungs, heart shadow, kidney or gallstones, bowel, free air) Start with alignment : a break in it tells you where to look · then the vertebrae, the disc spaces and the soft tissues in turn Compare with previous imaging when you have it 2. Cervical spine Standard views : AP (anteroposterior) · lateral · right and left oblique · open-mouth (odontoid) acute trauma, especially in a collar: no oblique views (don't move the neck) · most acute trauma gets CT instead, because plain films miss subtle fractures flexion and extension views are not routine: only when subluxation or instability is suspected (the atlantodental interval can be measured on them) View What normal looks like Pathology it shows AP Count all seven: T1 meets the 1st rib , C7 above it · C1 is a ring, C2 has a body and the dens (the mandible may hide both, so they get the open-mouth view) · spinous processes in a straight line · facet joints parallel · uncinate processes at the sides (enlarge in osteoarthritis) · C7 transverse process over ~2-2.5 cm = cervical rib Spinous processes off the midline or unevenly spaced → facet dislocation Lateral - the single most important view C1-C7 and T1, counted down from C1-C2 or up from the prominent C7 spinous process (vertebra prominens) · 4 smooth lines : anterior vertebral · posterior vertebral · spinolaminar · spinous process · atlantodental interval under 3 mm adults, under 5 mm children · prevertebral soft tissue under 7 mm at C2, under 22 mm at C6 (or no wider than the vertebral body) · airway smooth and open: nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx, trachea Fractures, perched facets, spondylosis · prevertebral widening: retropharyngeal abscess, trauma, hematoma Oblique (right and left) The neural foramina open up (C2-C3 down to C6-C7, both sides), bordered above and below by the pedicles · spinous processes look foreshortened The neural foramina and the facets Open-mouth (odontoid) C1's lateral masses line up with C2 · joint spaces symmetric Misalignment = injury or instability · dens fracture 3. Thoracic spine Standard views : AP · lateral · swimmer's view (arm raised) for the upper thoracic spine hidden by soft tissue added when an upper thoracic abnormality is suspected, or when the radiographer finds the standard views don't show it · it also shows the lower cervical spine, and T1 is the vertebra below the prominent C7 spinous process AP : count from T1 (1st rib) to T12 (12th rib) · spinous processes teardrop-shaped over the bodies · endplates as sclerotic margins · pedicles oval with corticated margins · transverse processes and ribs · a mild curve can be positional when the patient is in pain, or come from osteoarthritis Lateral : the normal kyphosis · bodies, endplates, disc spaces · pedicles look elongated and border the oval neural foramina · facet joints easiest to see in the mid to lower thoracic spine · the ribs curve behind 4. Lumbar spine and sacrum Standard views : AP and lateral · oblique only when requested, for the pars interarticularis · sacrum and sacroiliac joints on dedicated views if asked AP : five lumbar vertebrae, L1 is the one below the 12th rib (4 or 6 lumbar-type vertebrae = transitional) · broader than thoracic, with more horizontal spinous and transverse processes · both pedicles visible on every level · sacroiliac joints and sacral foramina symmetric Lateral : bodies, endplates, disc spaces, pedicles, foramina · the pars interarticularis (between the superior and inferior articular processes) - its defect is a cause of low back pain Oblique: the Scottie dog - nose = transverse process · ear = superior articular facet · front leg = inferior articular facet · neck = pars interarticularis Sacrum and sacroiliac joints : sacral ala = the sides of S1 (beside the first sacral foramina) · lateral masses beside the S2-S4 foramina · coccyx of 4 or 5 segments · the sacroiliac joint runs obliquely, so the AP shows only parts of it · a dedicated sacral film centres lower than the lumbar AP (which centres near the umbilicus) Oblique lumbar views: the Scottie dog outline, and a pars defect forming its collar 5. Pathology Any bone, any body part: TIMS-C = Trauma and tumours · Infection, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), idiopathic · Metabolic and malignancy · Systemic disease (leukemia, lymphoma) and senile (osteoarthritis) · Congenital (look on an immature skeleton) Trauma : hyperflexion, hyperextension, compression , burst and distraction injuries Jefferson = C1 ring broken in several places · hangman's = both pars of C2 (traumatic slip of C2), unstable · extension teardrop = anteroinferior corner (C2), a hyperextension injury; rotation can injure the cord · flexion teardrop = front of the body, with cord, posterior colum
05.1 Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity

Anatomy of the proximal upper extremity The bones and joints of the shoulder girdle and arm, learned for what goes wrong with them: which landmark breaks, which nerve runs beside it, and what holds each joint together. The muscles, nerves and vessels are next week; what to do about a separated, arthritic, unstable or frozen shoulder is on the SHOULDER BONES AND JOINTS chart. ⭐ Surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve · shaft fracture → radial nerve (it lies in the radial groove). The glenohumeral joint trades stability for range - held by the labrum, rotator cuff and ligaments, and dislocates anteroinferiorly. The coracoclavicular ligament, not the acromioclavicular, carries the AC joint: tear both and it dislocates. The coracoacromial arch stops upward displacement, and the cuff tendons run underneath it. Sternoclavicular joint: the clavicle fractures before the joint dislocates. Supraglenoid = biceps, infraglenoid = triceps. 1. The pectoral girdle and its four joints Pectoral girdle = clavicle + scapula , with four joints Scapulohumeral rhythm : full shoulder movement needs the scapula to reposition the glenoid as the arm moves, so the muscles work from a stable origin Shoulder range of motion uses the glenohumeral joint plus the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints and the scapula gliding on the chest wall Joint Bones Type Held together by Clinically Sternoclavicular Medial (sternal) clavicle + manubrium Synovial Strong surrounding ligaments The only joint linking the arm to the axial skeleton · dislocation is rare - the clavicle breaks first Acromioclavicular (AC) Acromial end of the clavicle + acromion Plane synovial, uniaxial · wedge-shaped articular disc Acromioclavicular ligament : strengthens it superiorly · coracoclavicular ligament : the strong pair of bands to the coracoid that gives most of the stability and suspends the scapula and arm from the clavicle AC ligament alone torn = subluxation · AC + coracoclavicular torn = dislocation (clavicle up, acromion prominent) Scapulothoracic Deep surface of the scapula on the thoracic wall Conceptual, not a true joint Muscles Part of every shoulder movement Glenohumeral Large humeral head + shallow glenoid fossa Ball-and-socket , multiaxial Labrum · rotator cuff · ligaments (section 4) Most mobile joint in the body Clavicle, scapula and humerus with the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular, scapulothoracic and glenohumeral joints, and the same bones outlined on an X-ray 2. Clavicle and scapula Clavicle : S-shaped (medial half convex forward, lateral half concave forward) · enlarged triangular sternal end · flat acromial end Scapula : triangular flat bone, essential for overhead movement Landmark What it does Acromion Meets the clavicle → AC joint Coracoid process ("duck's beak") Large projection for muscle and ligament attachments Glenoid fossa Shallow socket for the humeral head Supraglenoid · infraglenoid tubercle Long head of biceps · long head of triceps Spine Splits the back into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae (homes of supraspinatus, infraspinatus) Subscapular fossa The front surface, for subscapularis Suprascapular notch Bridged by the transverse scapular ligament → a foramen for nerves and vessels Superior and inferior angles Attachments and landmarks On an AP shoulder X-ray (arm internally rotated) find: scapula · clavicle · coracoid process · glenoid fossa · acromion · humeral head · greater tubercle 3. Humerus and the elbow end Proximal humerus head (meets the glenoid) · anatomical neck (separates the head from the tubercles) greater (superolateral) and lesser (superoanterior) tubercles = insertions · between them the intertubercular (bicipital) groove for the long head of biceps surgical neck = the narrowing below the head and tubercles, a common fracture site deltoid tuberosity (mid-shaft) · radial (spiral) groove on the back of the shaft for the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery Distal humerus medial epicondyle : common flexor origin · ulnar nerve runs behind it lateral epicondyle : common extensor origin capitulum (lateral) ↔ radial head · trochlea (medial) ↔ trochlear notch of the ulna coronoid fossa takes the ulna's coronoid process in full flexion · olecranon fossa takes the olecranon in full extension Proximal forearm radius (lateral, shorter): head pivots in the annular ligament and meets the capitulum and the ulna's radial notch · neck (between head and tuberosity) · radial tuberosity (biceps) ulna (medial, longer): olecranon (triceps) · coronoid process (brachialis) · trochlear notch · radial notch Fracture At risk Surgical neck (low-energy fall onto the hand, elderly with osteoporosis) Axillary nerve Shaft, transverse (direct blow to the arm) Radial nerve ± deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery Distal humerus Median nerve Medial epicondyle Ulnar nerve Proximal humerus: head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular groove, deltoid tuberosity and radial groove 4. The glenohumeral joint Built for mobility : poor fit of a large head in a shallow glenoid · several bursae · lots of articular cartilage · lax capsule Stabilisers Glenoid labrum : fibrocartilage ring that deepens the socket and improves the fit rotator cuff tendons : supraspinatus · infraspinatus · teres minor · subscapularis ligaments Ligament Where Job Glenohumeral (superior, middle, inferior) Thickenings of the front of the capsule Strengthen it anteriorly Coracohumeral Base of the coracoid → front of the greater tubercle Strengthens the capsule superiorly Coracoacromial Acromion → coracoid = with the bones beneath, the coracoacromial arch Roof that stops the head moving up · so strong the humerus or clavicle breaks first Transverse humeral Greater → lesser tubercle Holds the biceps tendon in its groove The rotator cuff tendons pass under the arch ; the gap narrows in full abduction Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa between the acromion and the cuff · axillary recess : a loose pouch of the inf
05.2 Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity

Clinical approach to the bones and joints of the shoulder Two questions sort most of this lecture: is it the acromioclavicular (AC) joint or the glenohumeral joint, and is passive range of motion lost as well as active? Separation, arthritis, instability and frozen shoulder each answer them differently. Rotator cuff disease is on the ROTATOR CUFF DISEASE chart, biceps tendinopathy in 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm , and the ligaments behind each problem on the anatomy chart in 05.1 - Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity . ⭐ Passive range of motion splits deep shoulder pain: lost in noninflammatory arthritis (cuff strong, asymmetric joint space) and frozen shoulder (X-ray normal), kept in inflammatory arthritis (cuff weak, symmetric joint space, erosions). AC separation: types I-III nonoperative, IV-V surgery. Traumatic instability is unidirectional and "torn loose" (reduce, then labral repair if young or recurrent); atraumatic is multidirectional and "born loose" (rehab first). Frozen shoulder: 20% of diabetics, global loss of active and passive motion, normal X-ray. 1. AC joint problems Common, and easy to sort out : acute injury = AC instability ("separation") · gradual onset = AC osteoarthritis (wear and tear) AC joint separation a fall or blow onto the tip of the shoulder (the lecture's cyclist going over the handlebars) graded I to V by increasing displacement treatment : types I-III: education, sling, analgesics, local therapy (ice) and early exercises · types IV-V: surgery AC joint osteoarthritis treatment : education · activity modification · local treatment (ice, injections) · analgesics · surgery 2. Glenohumeral arthritis Progressive pain, reduced motion and loss of function · two clinical patterns, told apart by passive range and cuff strength Noninflammatory ( osteoarthritis , post-traumatic) Inflammatory (rheumatoid, psoriatic, crystalline) Pain Deep aching Deep aching Motion Active AND passive reduced Active reduced · passive often greater than active Rotator cuff strength Usually intact Usually poor X-ray Asymmetric joint space · osteophytes · cysts · subchondral sclerosis Symmetric joint space · bone deformity · erosions · osteopenia Treatment : nonoperative first (education · activity modification · medications · physiotherapy exercise program) · then operative (debridement or replacement) debridement : reserved for young patients · not curative , relieves "catching" replacement : anatomic or reverse · 85% good or excellent · 90% survive 10 years · joint replacement is effective · complications: infection, loosening, instability, fracture, progressive rotator cuff disease X-rays of a normal shoulder, an anatomic (standard) replacement and a reverse replacement 3. Instability Shoulder instability = the inability to keep the humeral head centred in the glenoid · a continuum: reduced → subluxated → dislocated Anatomic factors: ligaments and labrum matter most · then bones (a shallow glenoid: the golf ball on a tee) · rotator cuff and muscle forces · nerves ligaments can be torn or stretched · the labrum adds surface area and depth and acts as a bumper ligament laxity gives multidirectional instability (? connective tissue disorder, ? poor motor control) Name it by onset (traumatic or atraumatic), direction (anterior, posterior, inferior, combined) and degree (subluxation or dislocation) Traumatic Atraumatic Pattern Unidirectional, anterior >> posterior · " torn loose " AMBRI : A traumatic · M ultidirectional · B ilateral · motor control poor · " born loose " Treatment Reduce : safety first (monitors) · analgesia · manipulate to correct the deformity · re-examine neurovascular status · post-reduction X-ray · surgery often : young or recurrent dislocators → labral (capsule-labral) repair, 85% success Rehab (physiotherapy, muscle control) first · surgery uncommon: inferior capsular shift (open or arthroscopic), 70% success Degree of instability: reduced (head centred on the glenoid), subluxated (partly off), dislocated (fully off) 4. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) Shoulder stiffness has three kinds of cause: intra-articular (arthritis, post-traumatic joint deformity) · extra-articular (capsular, muscular, heterotopic bone) · combined Adhesive capsulitis = spontaneous, global restriction of active AND passive motion with no known intrinsic shoulder disorder 2% of adults · 20% of people with diabetes · onset in the 40s-50s · pathophysiology unknown associations: diabetes · most often idiopathic · cervical disc, thyroid and cardiac disease Stages : freezing (inflammatory) → frozen → thawing Diagnosis : arthritis and post-traumatic deformity are the differential, but the X-rays are normal and there was no trauma Treatment education · pain management · usually self-limited physiotherapy is controversial : no quality studies show a significant effect intra-articular steroid : better than physiotherapy, no difference at 1 year · hydrodistension (hydroplasty, "brisement" from the French briser , to break: liquid injected under pressure) surgery ( manipulation or arthroscopic capsulectomy ): faster return of motion, same as everything else at 2 years

Anatomy of the brachial plexus Five roots (C5-T1) regroup into five terminal nerves. The question the lecture turns on: from the muscles and skin that are lost, which part of the plexus is injured? Learn which roots feed each branch, and where along the plexus each branch leaves. ⭐ Superior trunk = C5 + C6, middle = C7, inferior = C8 + T1 - and the posterior cord takes all three posterior divisions, so the radial nerve, like the median, carries every root (C5-T1). The roots are ventral rami. Divisions give off no branches. Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → winged scapula. Axillary nerve (C5, C6): deltoid + teres minor. Ulnar nerve = C8, T1, from the medial cord. The median and ulnar nerves pass through the arm but supply nothing there . 1. The five segments The brachial plexus = the ventral rami of C5-T1 (the cervical enlargement of the spinal cord) · starts in the neck, ends in the axilla as the terminal branches · brachial = arm, plexus = braid In order: roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches (" R eally T hirsty? D rink C old B eer") The plexus "roots" are ventral rami, not the dorsal and ventral roots of a spinal nerve · each is already a mixed nerve (motor + sensory) Drawing it : " 3 Wise (Y) Men (M) go bowling. One got a strike (X); the other got a spare (\\) " - three Y's at the roots, the M of the terminal branches, the X where the superior and middle trunks' divisions cross, the \ where the inferior trunk's posterior division joins the posterior cord The whole plexus: roots C5-T1, superior, middle and inferior trunks, anterior and posterior divisions, lateral, posterior and medial cords, and the five terminal branches with their roots 2. Trunks, divisions and cords Trunks : superior = C5 + C6 · middle = C7 alone · inferior = C8 + T1 · only the superior trunk gives off a nerve (suprascapular); the middle and inferior trunks give off none Divisions : each trunk splits into an anterior (A) and a posterior (P) division (6 in all) no nerves branch off the divisions anterior divisions → nerves to the flexor (front) compartments · posterior divisions → nerves to the extensor (back) compartments Cords , named by where they sit around the axillary artery Cord Formed by Roots carried Lateral Anterior divisions of the superior + middle trunks C5-C7 Medial Anterior division of the inferior trunk, carrying on alone C8, T1 Posterior All three posterior divisions C5-T1 3. Branches before the terminal five Arises from Nerve Roots Supplies Clinical Root Dorsal scapular C5 Rhomboids · levator scapulae Pierces the middle scalene , then runs back to the rhomboids Roots Long thoracic C5, C6, C7 Serratus anterior (along its superficial surface) Damage → winged scapula Superior trunk Suprascapular C5, C6 Supraspinatus + infraspinatus — Lateral cord Lateral pectoral C5, C6, C7 Pectoralis major and minor Runs above and medial to pectoralis minor Medial cord Medial pectoral C8, T1 Pectoralis major and minor Pierces pectoralis minor on its way to pectoralis major Medial cord Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm T1 Skin of the medial arm and axilla · upper forearm Runs beside the ulnar nerve Medial cord Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm C8, T1 Skin of the medial and anterior forearm Runs beside the ulnar nerve Posterior cord Upper subscapular C5, C6 Upper subscapularis — Posterior cord Thoracodorsal C6, C7, C8 Latissimus dorsi Also called the middle subscapular nerve Posterior cord Lower subscapular C5, C6 Lower subscapularis + teres major — The nerve to the subclavius also comes off at trunk level (not examinable) 4. The five terminal branches The lateral and medial cords make an "M" : musculocutaneous (lateral) · median (one root from each cord) · ulnar (medial) · the posterior cord ends as the axillary and the radial nerves Root count: " 3 M usketeers A ssassinate: 5 M ice, 5 R ats and 2 U nicorns" - musculocutaneous 3 · median 5 · radial 5 · ulnar 2 · axillary C5, C6 Nerve Cord Roots Motor Sensory Musculocutaneous Lateral C5, C6, C7 All of the anterior arm : pierces coracobrachialis , then runs between biceps and brachialis Lateral forearm (ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) Median Lateral + medial C5-T1 Most forearm flexors + five hand muscles · nothing in the arm Part of the hand Ulnar Medial C8, T1 1.5 anterior forearm muscles + most hand muscles Medial hand Axillary Posterior C5, C6 Deltoid + teres minor Skin over the shoulder Radial Posterior C5-T1 Extensors of the back of the arm and forearm Back of the upper limb The lateral cord sends a lateral root and the medial cord a medial root ; the two join to form the median nerve Each nerve's course through the arm (median crossing the brachial artery, ulnar piercing the medial septum, radial in the radial groove) and the skin it supplies are on the neurovascular chart Which fracture threatens which nerve (surgical neck → axillary, shaft → radial) is on the chart in 05.1 - Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity The "M" of terminal branches: musculocutaneous (C5-7), median (C5-T1) and ulnar (C8, T1) in front; axillary (C5, 6) and radial (C5-T1) from the posterior cord
02.1 Anatomy of the Muscles of the Shoulder

Anatomy of the muscles of the shoulder Three groups of muscles move the shoulder: the pectoral muscles in front, the deltoid and teres major, and the four rotator cuff muscles that hold the humeral head in its socket. For each one, know where it attaches, which nerve supplies it and what it does . The superficial back muscles this lecture reviews (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) are on the chart in 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck ; the axillary artery is in 04 - Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity . ⭐ Supraspinatus starts abduction (the first 15°) and the deltoid's middle head carries it on. Infraspinatus and teres minor rotate laterally; subscapularis alone rotates medially and alone inserts on the lesser tubercle. Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → winged scapula. Axillary nerve = deltoid + teres minor. Teres major adducts and is not in the cuff. Pectoralis minor pulls the scapula down and forward; serratus anterior protracts it. 1. Pectoral region Muscle Origin Insertion Nerve Action Pectoralis major Medial clavicle · sternum · upper 6 ribs and their costal cartilages Lateral lip of the intertubercular groove Medial + lateral pectoral Adducts, flexes and medially rotates the humerus Pectoralis minor Ribs 3-5 (near the costal cartilages) Coracoid process Medial + lateral pectoral Stabilises the scapula by drawing it inferiorly and anteriorly against the chest wall Serratus anterior Ribs 1-8 Medial border of the scapula Long thoracic (C5, C6, C7) Protracts the scapula Long thoracic nerve lesion → winged scapula : serratus anterior can no longer hold the medial border of the scapula against the chest wall when the patient pushes with the arm 2. Deltoid and teres major Muscle Origin Insertion Nerve Action Deltoid Lateral ⅓ of the clavicle · acromion · spine of the scapula Deltoid tuberosity of the humerus Axillary (C5, C6) · myotome C5, C6 Anterior head: flex + medially rotate · middle head: abduct · posterior head: extend + laterally rotate Teres major Inferior angle of the scapula Medial lip of the intertubercular groove Lower subscapular Adducts + medially rotates the arm Teres major is not part of the rotator cuff · it sits below teres minor 3. Rotator cuff ("SITS") Muscle Origin Insertion Nerve Action Supraspinatus Supraspinous fossa Greater tubercle Suprascapular (C5, C6) First 15° of abduction · stabilises the glenohumeral joint Infraspinatus Infraspinous fossa Greater tubercle Suprascapular (C5, C6) Lateral rotation · stabilises Teres minor Lateral border of the scapula Greater tubercle Axillary (C5, C6) Lateral rotation · stabilises Subscapularis Subscapular fossa (front of the scapula) Lesser tubercle Upper + lower subscapular (C5, C6, C7) Medial rotation · stabilises All four stabilise the glenohumeral joint by holding the humeral head in the shallow socket · most of the cuff is myotome C5, C6 Three go to the greater tubercle; only subscapularis goes to the lesser tubercle Supraspinatus runs under the acromion, with the subdeltoid (subacromial) bursa between them : the tendon that gets pinched - see the ROTATOR CUFF DISEASE chart in 02.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder Rotator cuff from the front (subscapularis) and from behind (supraspinatus above the spine of the scapula, infraspinatus and teres minor below) Insertions: supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor on the greater tubercle, subscapularis alone on the lesser tubercle
02.2 Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder

Clinical approach to the muscles of the shoulder Rotator cuff disease is the most common shoulder disorder: stage it by how far the tendon has gone, and treat it nonoperatively unless pain persists, the shoulder is weak, or it followed an acute injury. The other painful shoulders (AC joint separation and arthritis, glenohumeral arthritis, instability, frozen shoulder) are on the SHOULDER BONES AND JOINTS chart in 05.2 - Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity ; the cuff muscles themselves are in 02.1 - Anatomy of the Muscles of the Shoulder ; biceps tendinopathy is in 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm . ⭐ Rotator cuff disease: active motion is less than passive, unlike frozen shoulder and noninflammatory arthritis where passive motion is lost too. Usually intrinsic (vascularity, tension overload, degeneration); acromion shape is the extrinsic factor. Stage I inflamed → physiotherapy or subacromial decompression · II partial → consider repair · III full → repair · arthropathy (head rides up to the acromion) → reverse replacement. Surgery only for persistent pain, weakness or an acute tear. 1. Rotator cuff disease Rotator cuff disease : the most common shoulder disorder · prevalence rises with age · onset in the 40s · progressive The cuff's two jobs : shoulder stabilisation and arm motion · four muscles: supraspinatus · infraspinatus · teres minor · subscapularis 2. Why the tendon fails Intrinsic (the usual cause): vascularity · tension overload · tendon degeneration Extrinsic : acromion morphology - the subacromial space volume or a combination 3. Presentation and examination Symptoms : restricted motion · pain · weakness Move : active motion (in frozen shoulder and noninflammatory arthritis passive motion is lost too) Impingement signs : Neer · Hawkins · painful arc Strength tests : supraspinatus · infraspinatus · subscapularis 4. Stages and treatment Stage The tendon Treatment if nonoperative care fails I Inflammation , tendon intact Physiotherapy · subacromial decompression II Partial-thickness defect Consider rotator cuff repair III Full-thickness defect Rotator cuff repair Rotator cuff arthropathy Massive defect · humerus migrates superiorly and abuts the acromion · arthritis results Reverse shoulder replacement Treatment, first for every stage : education · activity modification · pain management (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · physiotherapy (muscle reconditioning) · injections - nonsurgical in the majority Surgery when : pain persists · weakness · following an acute injury - "the best surgeons know when NOT to operate" Rotator cuff disease spectrum: impingement, partial-thickness tear, small and then massive full-thickness tear
03.1 Anatomy of the Muscles of the Arm

Anatomy of the muscles of the arm The arm (shoulder to elbow) is two compartments, each with one job and one nerve: the front flexes the shoulder and elbow and supinates; the back extends them . The detail worth knowing is which joints each muscle crosses , because that decides what it can move. ⭐ The biceps is a strong supinator; brachialis, not biceps, is the primary flexor of the forearm. Musculocutaneous = everything in front; radial = triceps behind. Biceps long head starts on the supraglenoid tubercle, triceps long head on the infraglenoid tubercle - both cross the shoulder. Coracobrachialis crosses only the shoulder; brachialis only the elbow. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis . 1. Two compartments Deep to the skin, the brachial fascia wraps the arm · the medial and lateral intermuscular septa run from it to the humerus and split the arm into front and back Compartment Muscles Nerve Actions Anterior Biceps brachii · coracobrachialis · brachialis Musculocutaneous Flex the shoulder · flex the elbow · supinate the forearm Posterior Triceps brachii (the only one) Radial Extend the shoulder · extend the elbow Cross-section of the arm: biceps and brachialis in front (musculocutaneous nerve), the three heads of triceps behind (radial nerve), split by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa 2. Anterior compartment Muscle Origin Insertion Crosses Actions Biceps brachii Long head: supraglenoid tubercle , then through the intertubercular groove · short head: coracoid process Radial tuberosity + bicipital aponeurosis Shoulder and elbow Strong supinator · flexes the elbow · weak shoulder flexor · resists shoulder dislocation Coracobrachialis Coracoid process Middle ⅓ of the medial humerus Shoulder only Flexes and adducts the shoulder · resists dislocation Brachialis Distal ½ of the anterior humerus Coronoid process of the ulna Elbow only Primary flexor of the forearm (more than the biceps) Biceps is the most superficial · coracobrachialis and brachialis lie deep to it The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis , then runs between biceps and brachialis 3. Posterior compartment Head of triceps brachii Origin Crosses Long infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula Shoulder and elbow Lateral Proximal ⅓ of the posterior humerus Elbow Medial Distal ⅓ of the posterior humerus Elbow All three heads insert on the olecranon of the ulna Actions : primary elbow extensor · the long head also extends the shoulder and resists shoulder dislocation Nerve : radial, which runs in the radial groove (its course is on the NEUROVASCULAR chart)
03.2 Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm

Clinical approach to the muscles of the arm Anterior shoulder pain: is it the long head of the biceps tendon, or something next to it? The tendon shares its space with the rotator cuff and its origin with the labrum, so the anatomy explains why it gets into trouble and the examination does most of the diagnosing . (The other shoulder conditions in the objectives are on the shoulder chart .) ⭐ Tenderness in the intertubercular groove, with pain on shoulder and elbow flexion with the forearm supinated, points to the long head of biceps; weakness plus a visible retracted-muscle defect means it has torn. The exam is the most useful test - ultrasound if unclear, MR arthrogram if you suspect a SLAP lesion . The tendon is hypovascular , and most cases settle with active physiotherapy . 1. Proximal biceps tendinopathy Proximal biceps tendinopathy = a common cause of shoulder pain "Tendinopathy", not "tendinitis" : a spectrum from overuse and degeneration (tendinosis) to acute inflammation to a partial or complete tear Who (it can affect anyone) younger: athletes, especially overhead throwing · inflammatory conditions older: overuse and degeneration (very common) 2. Why the long head is vulnerable: location, location, location Lives right next to the rotator cuff tendons → shares their trouble Weaves through the tight intertubercular groove → susceptible to impingement Starts on the supraglenoid tubercle AND the superior glenoid labrum → labral problems = biceps problems The proximal tendon is relatively hypovascular → heals poorly The long head of biceps tendon runs over the humeral head beside the rotator cuff tendon and attaches at the top of the glenoid 3. History and exam History : acute (tear or inflammation) or chronic (degenerative, overuse) onset · anterior shoulder pain Physical exam tender over the tendon in the intertubercular groove pain worse with shoulder flexion and elbow flexion, particularly with the forearm supinated a frank tear → weakness and a visible defect as the muscle retracts (the "Popeye" deformity) 4. Differential and investigations Clinical examination is often the most helpful Differential diagnosis neighbouring tendon or bursa: rotator cuff tendinopathy · subacromial bursitis joint: labral tear ( SLAP lesion ) · shoulder or acromioclavicular (AC) joint arthritis referred: cervical radiculopathy · facet joint ( facetogenic ) pain · a visceral cause presenting as shoulder pain a C8 radiculopathy gives pain or tingling in the hand , so it sits low on the list (C4 or C5 can give shoulder pain) Investigations ultrasound if unclear : assesses the rotator cuff tendons and the subacromial bursa at the same time MR arthrogram if you suspect a SLAP lesion 5. Management Education : prognosis depends on the injury · the vast majority are chronic and improve with conservative management Non-drug : physiotherapy is the mainstay - modalities may help acute pain, but active therapy is necessary · relative rest from overhead activity Drugs : analgesia as needed Intervention : surgery can be considered for refractory cases
04 Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity

Neurovascular supply of the proximal upper extremity Follow the main artery from the neck to the elbow, then the nerves that run beside it. The clinical payoff is which nerve or vessel sits where a fracture can reach it and which nerve supplies which patch of skin . ⭐ The radial nerve and profunda brachii lie together in the radial groove, so a mid-shaft humerus fracture threatens both; the brachial artery hugs the medial shaft and is at risk too. Median and ulnar nerves supply nothing in the arm. Axillary → brachial at the lower border of teres major; brachial → radial + ulnar in the cubital fossa. Median cubital vein = blood draws. Biceps reflex = C5, C6. 1. 05.1 Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity

Osteology of the distal upper extremity From the elbow to the fingertips: which bump fits into which socket, and what each joint lets you do. The landmarks matter because they are what you name on a plain X-ray and where the tendons and nerves attach. (What goes wrong at the elbow is on the elbow chart .) ⭐ Scaphoid = the most fractured carpal bone; lunate = the most dislocated, and it can press on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. Capitulum ↔ radial head, trochlea ↔ trochlear notch. Carrying angle over 15° = valgus, under 5° = varus. Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are pivots; the middle one is a syndesmosis. The ulnar collateral ligament's anterior band is the strongest. Distal humerus fracture → median nerve; medial epicondyle fracture → ulnar nerve. 1. Clinical approach to the elbow Elbow pain is sorted two ways: by where it hurts (front, inside, outside, back) and by which structure is at fault (bone, ligament or joint · muscle or tendon · something else). Overlay the anatomy, look for the pattern, rule out the red flags, and remember a fracture can sit anywhere. (The bones and ligaments themselves are on the osteology chart .) ⭐ A young child who will not use an arm after it was pulled has a radial head subluxation: reduce it by pronation and extension, no cast, and image only to rule out a fracture. An elbow dislocation after a FOOSH is a red flag: check the ulnar nerve and watch for compartment syndrome. A red olecranon swelling with systemic signs is infected: aspirate and give antibiotics. Medial pain with no end point on valgus stress in a pitcher = ulnar collateral ligament. 1. The approach History : look for patterns · OLDCARS · acute (traumatic, inflammatory) vs chronic (degenerative, overuse) · overlay the anatomy: which structures are medial, which lateral Physical exam : look (swollen? deformed?) · feel (where is it tender? hot?) · move (is range of motion restricted?) · specific tests for specific structures · don't forget the nerves Management approach : which investigations (if any) will help · no red flags → apply your pattern · then educate → non-drug → drug → interventional · your patient is a person 2. The differential Where Bone, ligament, joint Muscle, tendon Other structures Anterior Arthritis (degenerative, post-traumatic, inflammatory) Distal biceps tendinopathy — Medial Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) sprain or tear Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow) Ulnar neuritis or neuropathy Lateral — Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow) — Posterior Arthritis Triceps tendinopathy Olecranon bursitis Fracture can be anywhere · joint and ligament problems cost range of motion, stability and pain 3. Arthritis of the elbow Types : degenerative (osteoarthritis) · inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, gout, psoriatic arthritis; more in the rheumatology lectures) · post-traumatic (earlier osteoarthritis, possibly in a different pattern) Osteoarthritis presents as : a degenerative history, gradual onset · achy, sore pain with flares · mechanical symptoms: stiffness, loss of range of motion, locking · bony changes X-ray : loss of joint space · osteophytes · subchondral sclerosis or cysts Treatment education: a grumbling, long-term course with no cure non-drug: ice · physiotherapy to keep range of motion · occupational therapy to keep function drugs: topical anti-inflammatories · oral acetaminophen or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; mind the side effects) · steroid injection surgery only for an intolerable end stage : debridement or arthroplasty (joint replacement) Lateral X-ray of an osteoarthritic elbow: narrowed joint space with bony spurs 4. Dislocations: two joints, two different patients Elbow dislocation Radial head subluxation ("nursemaid's elbow") Joint Humero-ulnar (the elbow itself) Proximal radioulnar: the anular ligament is thinner and weaker distally in children , letting the radial head slip Who and how Fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) · posterior is the most common Child, rare after age 5 · girls and the left arm more often · a pull (longitudinal traction) along the arm Presents as Capsule and ligament rupture · skin breaks · nerve injury, especially the ulnar nerve · compartment syndrome Acute pain · refuses to use the arm, holds it flexed against the body Investigations A red flag : traumatic Imaging only to rule out something else (a fracture) Treatment Closed reduction + splint at 90° · may fail if soft tissue is interposed or it will not stay reduced → open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) Closed reduction by pronation and extension · no cast or orthosis Elbow dislocations by direction: posterior (the most common), anterior, lateral, medial and divergent 5. Ulnar collateral ligament injury The UCL stabilises the medial elbow · injured by chronic, repetitive overuse (baseball pitchers) Presents as : a pop over the medial elbow if it tears suddenly · pain on palpation of the medial elbow · no end point on valgus stress , excessive motion Investigations : probably needs an exam by sports medicine or orthopaedics · MRI may help Treatment education: ligaments heal slowly, if at all , depending on the tear non-drug: ice · physiotherapy to strengthen the dynamic elbow stabilisers, proprioceptive work · an orthosis for extra stability drugs: topical anti-inflammatories · oral acetaminophen or NSAIDs reconstruction (Tommy John surgery) only if needed for functional goals : a tendon graft ( palmaris longus, semitendinosus , others), then years of physiotherapy 6. Olecranon bursitis A bursa (over 150 in the body) is a thin, fluid-filled sac between bone and soft tissue that lets tissue glide; irritated, it fills with fluid → pain, tenderness, swelling when superficial The most common superficial bursitis Causes : a single hard blow (fall on the elbow) · sustained or repeated pressure (leaning on the elbow; develops over months) · infection through a skin break, seen or not Tell them apart : the history helps, and they look different "not scary" : often no investigations · X-ray if there was trauma · ultrasound or MRI if it does not behave normally "bad" = infected : erythema and systemic signs → aspirate and choose antibiotics (± incision and drainage) gout or an inflammatory arthropathy can swell the whole elbow and be mistaken for bursitis → treat the cause Treatment (red flags ruled out): benign and often self-limiting once the cause is removed · ice, rest, compression, elevation · modify the activity, pad the elbow · topical anti-inflammatories, NSAIDs · bursectomy if infected or chronic
06.1 Anatomy of the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity

Anatomy of the muscles of the distal upper extremity The forearm is two compartments with two nerves and two epicondyles: the front flexes and pronates, runs on the median nerve and starts at the medial epicondyle; the back extends and supinates, runs on the radial nerve and starts at the lateral epicondyle. The exceptions are what gets examined. ⭐ Flexor carpi ulnaris and the half of flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers are the 1½ anterior forearm muscles on the ulnar nerve; every other anterior muscle is median, and every posterior muscle is radial. Flexor digitorum profundus is the only muscle that bends the fingertip. Brachioradialis sits in the back but flexes the elbow. Side-to-side wrist movement pairs a flexor with an extensor. Mallet finger = splint; a complete avulsion fracture = surgery. The forearm in cross-section: anterior and posterior compartments 1. 06.2 Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity

Clinical approach to the muscles of the distal upper extremity Tendon problems around the elbow are sorted by where the pain sits and whether the tendon has ruptured. Most are a slow, degenerative tendinosis rather than an inflamed tendinitis , which is why the treatment is education, activity change and eccentric physiotherapy rather than anti-inflammatories alone. ⭐ Most elbow tendon pain is tendinosis: collagen degeneration without inflammation, treated with education, activity change and eccentric physiotherapy twice daily for 12 weeks rather than anti-inflammatories alone. Tennis elbow = extensor carpi radialis brevis, pain just distal to the lateral epicondyle, worse gripping and supinating. Golfer's elbow = common flexor origin, pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation. A distal biceps rupture (pop, bruise, changed contour, poor supination) needs orthopaedics urgently; a proximal one usually does not. 1. Approach to a muscle or tendon problem History : look for patterns · onset, location, duration, character, aggravating and relieving factors (OLDCARS) · acute (traumatic, inflammatory) vs chronic (degenerative, overuse) · overlay the anatomy (which structures are medial, which lateral) Physical : look (swollen? deformed?) · feel (where is it tender? hot?) · move (is range of motion restricted?) · specific tests for specific structures · don't forget the nerves Management : which investigations (if any) will help? · if no red flags, apply your pattern · educate · non-pharmacologic · pharmacologic · interventional · remember the patient is a person Muscle and tendon problems affect elbow pain and elbow strength ; the full elbow differential by structure and location is on 05.2 - Clinical Approach to the Elbow 2. Biceps tendinopathy and rupture Tendinitis / tendinosis Rupture Common clinical points Insidious onset · pain on resistance · pain on stretch · the usual treatments Trauma, or the end of long overuse · a "pop" heard or felt · pain (or none) · bruise · weakness · change in muscle contour Proximal (long or short head) Anterior shoulder pain Not uncommon (especially in the elderly) · often degenerative · usually still functional: typically non-operative Distal biceps Anterior elbow pain Rare but consequential: poor supination, weak flexion · call orthopaedics urgently: a limited time window for repair 6. Managing any tendinopathy Education : tell them what it is and what to expect · many improve quickly, some become quite chronic · address the offending movements and activities Non-pharmacologic modalities (ice), RICE modify the offending activity : rest by time or by task · adjust ergonomics and biomechanics (positioning, less excess force) orthoses and taping to support and realign forces · tennis elbow counterforce strap during the offending activity physiotherapy: eccentric strengthening twice daily for 12 weeks (stimulates collagen production and strength) massage, which may stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen Pharmacologic : anti-inflammatories can be considered, but may not help much in chronic tendinOSIS (topical preferred) Intervention or surgery : regenerative options such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) are uncertain · surgical referral if refractory Practice pointer: rather than "have you tried physio?", ask "show me what you've been doing in physio" Schulich Reviews All three review points for this lecture are carried above (bolded): lateral epicondylitis (extensor carpi radialis brevis; 30s-40s, occupational; pain distal to the lateral epicondyle with gripping, supination, resisted extension and passive stretch), medial epicondylitis (common flexor origin; resisted flexion + pronation, passive stretch) and distal biceps rupture (rare, urgent orthopaedic referral, poor supination, weak flexion).
07.1 Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity

Anatomy of the neurovascular supply of the distal upper extremity Know which nerve supplies which forearm muscle, where each nerve and artery runs and can be hurt, and which spinal root a movement or patch of skin tests. The cubital fossa is where most of it meets. ⭐ The median nerve and its anterior interosseous branch supply the whole anterior forearm except flexor carpi ulnaris and the ring-and-little-finger half of flexor digitorum profundus (ulnar); the radial nerve and its deep and posterior interosseous branches supply the whole posterior forearm. Cubital fossa, lateral to medial = biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve. The ulnar nerve is exposed behind the medial epicondyle; the median nerve is pinched between the heads of pronator teres and in the carpal tunnel; the radial deep branch pierces supinator. Radial pulse = between flexor carpi radialis and abductor pollicis longus. C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger; C8 bends the fingers, T1 spreads and closes them. 1. 07.2 Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity

Clinical approach to the neurovascular supply of the distal upper extremity With tingling or numbness around the elbow, first ask whether there is true sensory loss : tingling can come from any tissue or be referred, but true sensory loss is neurogenic . Then map it to one nerve and one site; the one this lecture works through is the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle . ⭐ Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow = medial elbow pain, numbness and tingling into the ring and little fingers and a positive Tinel sign at the elbow; treat it by educating (it is reversible), keeping pressure off the elbow and splinting against night-time hyperflexion, and go to EMG/NCS and surgery early only for significant or progressive weakness. True sensory loss is neurogenic; tingling alone can come from any tissue or be referred. The sensory loss of UNE is ulnar, sparing the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which is what separates it from a C8 problem. Pronator syndrome = median nerve between the heads of pronator teres: proximal anterior forearm pain plus the lateral 3½ fingers and palm. 1. Abnormal sensation: nerve or not? Tingling or abnormal sensation can come from lots of things: nerve, muscle, tendon, ligament, joint Don't forget referred pain: is it cardiac? True sensory LOSS is neurogenic Where the forearm nerves run and where each can be pinched is on 07.1 - Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity 2. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (UNE) Also called cubital tunnel syndrome · the ulnar nerve can also be compressed at the wrist, but that is less common (Wrist and Hand Part 2) Causes of nerve irritation direct trauma: hitting the "funny bone" · repeated pressure (leaning on a desk) elbow flexion puts the nerve under tension (during sleep) the nerve subluxing as the elbow flexes · ligament hypertrophy? · medial epicondylosis (bulk)? Clinical features pain at the medial elbow numbness and tingling from the medial forearm into the ring and little fingers · the fingers "fall asleep" positive Tinel sign at the entrapment site : light tapping over the nerve sends tingling ("pins and needles") into its distribution check for sensory loss · check for motor deficits Motor and sensory features sensory: ulnar territory (the medial hand and the ring and little fingers, palm and back), which is NOT the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and NOT C8 motor : may or may not be weak · if weak, the small muscles of the hand are usually most affected 3. Managing ulnar neuropathy at the elbow Rule out red flags : significant or progressive weakness may need more aggressive treatment at an earlier stage Electromyography (EMG) / nerve conduction study (NCS) : identifies the diagnosis and its severity · separates nerve irritation (neuritis) from nerve damage (neuropathy) Education is critical : neuritis is totally reversible , and so is mild neuropathy Non-pharmacologic : avoid external pressure (don't lean on it; ergonomics) · avoid hyperflexion of the elbow : a towel splint or elbow pad overnight Pharmacologic : not much Intervention / surgery : ulnar neurolysis or ulnar nerve transposition The ulnar nerve's sites at risk 4. Pronator syndrome What it is : the median nerve compressed between the two heads of pronator teres , usually from muscle bulk built by elbow overuse Presents as : pain and tenderness at the top of the front of the forearm · hyperesthesia over the palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers and the adjacent palm The median nerve's sites at risk Schulich Reviews Carried above (bolded): ulnar neuropathy (cubital tunnel): pain at the medial elbow, positive Tinel at the elbow, the nerve subluxes with flexion , causes including leaning, direct trauma and sustained flexion in sleep; management: reversible, towel splint against night-time hyperflexion, neurolysis or transposition . The review's sensory flag is settled from this year's slides: the symptoms run from the medial forearm into the ring and little fingers , while the sensory loss on exam is ulnar territory, not the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and not C8 .
08.1 Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1

Anatomy of the wrist and hand, part 1 Part 1 builds the hand from the joints up: what each joint allows, the fascial bands that hold the tendons down and roof the carpal tunnel, the four muscle compartments with their nerves, and the two arterial arches. The nerves of the hand and the carpal tunnel's clinical problems are Part 2; the wrist fractures are on the Clinical Approach chart. ⭐ The flexor retinaculum roofs the carpal tunnel, which carries 9 tendons (4 superficialis, 4 profundus, flexor pollicis longus) plus the median nerve; the ulnar nerve and artery pass on top of it. The thumb's CMC joint is a saddle, which is what lets the thumb oppose. Thenar muscles = recurrent branch of the median; hypothenar, adductor pollicis, interossei and the medial two lumbricals = ulnar. PAD and DAB: palmar interossei adduct, dorsal interossei abduct. Superficial arch = mostly ulnar; deep arch = mostly radial. 1. 08.2 Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 1

Clinical approach to the wrist and hand, part 1 Two fractures from a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) : the distal radius , judged on X-ray by three questions (crooked? short? smooth?) and reduced if it is not, and the scaphoid , which can hide on the first X-ray and loses its blood supply if missed. Treatment is dictated by age and activity level and by how displaced the fracture is . The chart also carries part 2, the numb hand (carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the wrist). ⭐ Snuffbox swelling and tenderness after a FOOSH with a normal X-ray is treated as a scaphoid fracture and imaged with CT or MRI: its blood flows retrograde, so a missed fracture can end in nonunion or osteonecrosis. Distal radius X-ray: crooked (normal ~12° palmar tilt), short (ulnar variance; compare sides), smooth (a step over 1 mm → arthrosis). Closed reduction = analgesia, traction, increase the deformity to unlock it, correct, 3-point mould; surgery if reduction is inadequate. Scaphoid: undisplaced or distal → cast; displaced or proximal → surgery. 1. Joints of the hand IP joints: hinge · MCP joints: condyloid · CMC joints: plane (fingers 2-5) and saddle (thumb, allowing opposition) · the anatomy is on 08.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1 2. Distal radius fracture Very common injury · FOOSH · localized pain · poor function if the anatomy is not restored Three X-ray questions Question What to look at Normal If left uncorrected 1. Is it crooked (bent)? The articular angle on the lateral view About 12° of palmar tilt (the lecture's fracture: 20° dorsal) Distal radio-ulnar joint motion is altered · forearm rotation becomes restricted 2. Is it short? Ulnar variance : greater than neutral = the radius is short · compare with the other side Neutral Ulnar impaction syndrome 3. Is it smooth? The joint surface Smooth A step over 1 mm → post-traumatic arthrosis : radiocarpal arthritis with pain and stiffness, treated by fusion Treatment principles ① age dependent : treatment is forgiving at the extremes of age ② closed reduction ③ surgical reduction if the reduction is inadequate (still crooked or not smooth): open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) or external fixation ④ rehabilitate Closed reduction, step by step adequate analgesia : hematoma block (1% lidocaine into the fracture hematoma) · regional anaesthesia · conscious sedation traction · then increase the deformity, which unlocks the fragments · then correct the deformity 3-point mould + cast · well moulded does not mean tight Plaster of Paris Fibreglass For Cheaper · easily moulded Lightweight yet strong · waterproof options · more radiolucent Against Poor resistance to water · heavy Expensive · harder to mould Padding: cotton (cheap, under plaster or fibreglass) or synthetic (waterproof) Volar (palmar) tilt on the lateral wrist X-ray 3. Scaphoid fracture The most common carpal bone fracture · young people · usually heals uneventfully, but sometimes difficult to diagnose , and delayed diagnosis brings complications Unique blood supply: retrograde flow (it enters distally and flows back) → nonunion and osteonecrosis Clinical exam : swelling and localized tenderness (the snuffbox) Imaging: be SUSPICIOUS · an X-ray is usually sufficient, but if the X-rays are normal, treat it as fractured and get CT or MRI Treatment : undisplaced or distal pole → cast until union · displaced or proximal pole → surgery (volar approach) Complications : nonunion · osteonecrosis · late arthrosis The lecture's cases : a scaphoid tubercle fracture · a 25-year-old man whose CT showed the fracture, casted and healed on CT at 8 weeks · a displaced proximal-pole fracture, fixed operatively 4. Soft tissues of the hand The fascia, compartments, intrinsic muscles, digital sheaths and arterial arches in this deck are charted on 08.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1 Schulich Reviews Carried above (bolded): distal radius fracture (FOOSH): X-ray for angulation, length against the ulna (compare the other side) and joint surface; an uneven joint surface → radiocarpal arthritis → fusion · forgiving at the extremes of age · closed reduction: traction → increase the deformity → correct → cast; ORIF or external fixation if alignment fails · scaphoid: FOOSH, young; X-ray can be normal → treat as fractured, then CT/MRI; retrograde blood supply → nonunion, osteonecrosis · undisplaced/distal → cast; displaced/proximal → surgery . Not carried: the review's casting rules ("weekly x-ray") are not on this year's slides; its ganglion cyst and mallet finger point is taught in 06.1 - Anatomy of the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity this year and is charted there.
01.1 Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 2

Anatomy of the wrist and hand, part 2 Part 2 is the hand's nerves: which nerve feels which skin, which nerve runs which small muscle, and what the hand looks like when one of them is cut. Part 1 covered the joints, the soft tissues and the blood supply. The syndromes themselves (carpal tunnel, ulnar neuropathy at the wrist) are on the CLINICAL APPROACH PART 2 chart. ⭐ Median nerve = LOAF (lumbricals 1-2, opponens pollicis, abductor and flexor pollicis brevis) and the palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers; the deep ulnar branch runs every other intrinsic muscle. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the carpal tunnel, so carpal tunnel compression spares the central palm. Opponens pollicis has no backup: lose the median, lose opposition. Nine tendons + the median nerve in the tunnel; the ulnar nerve and artery go through Guyon's canal instead. Proximal ulnar = claw hand with radial deviation; Guyon's canal = claw without it; proximal median = hand of benediction. 1.
