01.2 Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 2

Clinical approach to the wrist and hand, part 2 For a numb, tingling hand, ask which fingers. Thumb to half the ring finger is the median nerve, usually squeezed in the carpal tunnel ; the little finger and half the ring finger is the ulnar nerve, squeezed in Guyon's canal . Each has a nerve-root mimic in the neck (C6 and C8) , and electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies tell them apart. The nerve anatomy and the lesion-level hand signs are on the ANATOMY PART 2 chart; hand infections are on the MSK INFECTIONS chart. The chart also carries part 1, the distal radius and scaphoid fractures. ⭐ Carpal tunnel syndrome = numbness and tingling in the median territory, worse at night and with the wrist bent, with normal median function above the wrist; EMG and nerve conduction studies separate it from C6 radiculopathy, and treatment runs education → night orthosis → steroid injection → carpal tunnel release. Medial 1½ fingers + weak intrinsics = ulnar nerve; at the wrist think handlebars, and rule out C8 and the elbow. Both are reversible if caught early. 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) Definition : compression of the median nerve at the wrist, in the carpal tunnel · the "bread and butter" peripheral nerve diagnosis The tunnel : floor = carpal bones · roof = transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum) · contents = tendons of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus and superficialis + the median nerve · the ulnar nerve and artery and palmaris longus run superficial to it Causes extrinsic (less space) : fracture · flexor tenosynovitis (the finger flexor tendons share the space) · ganglia · inflammation (rheumatologic conditions) · pregnancy (edema) · acromegaly intrinsic (a more susceptible nerve) : diabetes · amyloidosis · alcohol and, very commonly, idiopathic Presents as numbness and tingling in the median nerve territory , often predominantly at night worse with the wrist flexed or extended (driving, holding a phone) potentially thumb weakness (abductor pollicis brevis) median function above the carpal tunnel is normal : the median-supplied forearm muscles are spared · maybe Tinel's and Phalen's signs Differential : C6 radiculopathy is the main one · tendinopathy · thumb-base (carpometacarpal) arthritis Investigations : electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies : nerve vs muscle or bone · CTS vs C6 · how severe the nerve damage is Treatment, in order education: a common problem · hand position · reversible if discovered early non-drug: a rigid wrist-hand orthosis worn overnight only · avoid aggravating positions and vibrating tools drug: corticosteroid injection of the carpal tunnel surgery: carpal tunnel release 2. Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist ( Guyon's canal syndrome ) Definition : the ulnar nerve compressed in Guyon's canal (carpals + an overlying ligament, carrying the ulnar nerve and artery) · the nerve's other site at risk is behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow Causes (extrinsic, less space): fracture · ganglia · inflammation (rheumatologic conditions) · compression: "handlebar neuropathy" Presents as : reduced feeling (hypoesthesia) in the medial 1½ digits · weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles Differential : C8 radiculopathy is the main one · ulnar nerve at the elbow · tendinopathy Investigations : EMG and nerve conduction studies : nerve vs muscle or bone · elbow vs wrist vs C8 · severity Treatment : education (hand position and pressure; reversible if discovered early) → relieve the pressure (specialized gloves, change the handlebars) → Guyon's release

Upper extremity radiology Read every film the same way, then use the one line or landmark each joint gives you. Skeleton mature or not → bone (cortex, medulla, density) → alignment → joints → soft tissues. At the shoulder the Y-view sets the direction of a dislocation, at the elbow the fat pads and two lines find a hidden fracture, and at the wrist the three Gilula arcs check the carpal alignment. ⭐ A visible posterior fat pad is always abnormal: supracondylar fracture in a child, radial head or neck fracture in an adult. The Y-view decides anterior (subcoracoid) vs posterior dislocation. The anterior humeral line and the radiocapitellar line both aim at the centre of the capitellum. Osteoarthritis = joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, marginal osteophytes. Three smooth Gilula arcs = carpal alignment kept, even when a bone is fractured. 1. The systematic read Skeletal maturity first : a visible, unfused physis (growth plate) = immature · fused, no visible plate = mature long bone: epiphysis (end, with a growth centre) · physis (lucent line in children) · metaphysis · diaphysis (shaft) · cortex (dense outer layer) · medullary cavity Then: bone integrity (cortex, medulla, density, generalized bone disease) → alignment (fracture, dislocation) → joints (inflammation, narrowing, degeneration) → muscles and soft tissues (can be abnormal when the bones look normal) Bone pathology: "TIMS-C" = T rauma, tumours · I nfection, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), idiopathic · M etabolic, malignancy · S ystemic (leukemia, lymphoma), senile (osteoarthritis) · C ongenital (mostly an immature skeleton) Osteoarthritis = 3 findings : joint space narrowing (cartilage is radiolucent, so lost cartilage narrows the gap) · subchondral sclerosis (denser, not stronger) · marginal osteophytes · graded mild, moderate or severe on the combination 2. Shoulder Standard series (trauma, osteoarthritis): AP (front-to-back) · Y-view · Grashey · special views (instability, a suspected dislocation) are not covered · the lecture also reads the axillary view AP : the anatomical neck (head-neck junction) and surgical neck (just below the articular surface) are reference lines, not visible structures · the labrum is fibrocartilage, so it does not show axillary : beam through the armpit · the coracoid and the lesser tuberosity are both anterior , which orients the film · the acromion + distal clavicle form the acromioclavicular (AC) joint · an os acromiale (unfused ossification centre) is not a fracture · the anatomical and surgical necks don't show here, so find the lesser tuberosity (and roughly where the greater one is) · some overlap is normal, but the joint space should not look widened Y-view : coracoid (anterior limb) · scapular spine + acromion (posterior limb) · scapular body (vertical limb) · the humeral head should sit centred over the glenoid Dislocation : anterior = humeral head subcoracoid (under the coracoid) · posterior = farther from the coracoid · the Y-view tells them apart · subluxation = partial contact, dislocation = complete loss Also seen: surgical neck fracture · osteoarthritis (the 3 findings) 3. Wrist AP and lateral views AP : distal radius and ulna at the distal radioulnar joint · radial and ulnar styloids · the radiocarpal joint · the TFCC (triangular fibrocartilage complex) is radiolucent , so calcification there hints at a TFCC problem carpal bones, radial to ulnar : proximal row scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform · distal row trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate · never reverse the order lateral : Lister's tubercle (dorsal radius, check it for fracture) · scaphoid and pisiform in front, triquetrum behind, trapezoid hidden behind the trapezium · carpal bones overlap, so the AP is essential for fractures Arcs of Gilula : 1 = proximal surfaces of the proximal row · 2 = distal surfaces of the proximal row · 3 = proximal surfaces of the distal row · any break, step-off or widening → carpal injury Fractures can keep the arcs intact : scaphoid (proximal pole) + triquetrum · distal radius + ulnar styloid base · look for cortical disruption or a lucent line in each bone Also seen: an expanded distal radius with a large lytic lesion and thin cortex reaching the

Anatomy of the hip joint The hip is the shoulder's opposite: it sacrifices some mobility for stability, and is the most stable joint in the body . The lecture builds it from the bones (pelvis, femur, and the tibia and fibula below), then the capsule and ligaments that hold it, then the arteries whose failure explains why a femoral neck fracture is so dangerous. The fracture itself (presentation, workup, surgery) is on the HIP FRACTURE chart. ⭐ The medial circumflex femoral artery carries most of the femoral head's blood, so a femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis; the artery of the ligament of the head is minor and often inadequate. Hip = stability over mobility (bony fit, ligaments, muscles); shoulder = mobility over stability. The iliofemoral (Y) ligament is the strongest in the body and limits extension; the pubofemoral limits abduction. The labrum deepens the socket; the ligament of the head adds no strength. Iliac crest = L4; ischial tuberosity = sitting bone and hamstring origin. Posterior dislocation = short, medially rotated leg and a sciatic nerve at risk. 1. 03.2 Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint

Clinical approach to the hip joint: hip fracture The lecture is one condition worked in order: is this a hip fracture, is the patient stable, why did they fall (and why did the bone break), what is the plan, and what happens after surgery. "Hip fracture" means a proximal femur fracture , and the fracture's level on the X-ray picks the operation . The hip's bones, ligaments and blood supply are on the HIP JOINT ANATOMY chart; osteoarthritis, labral tears and the tendon problems are on the HIP PAIN chart. ⭐ Hip fracture = an older person after a fall with groin pain and a short, externally rotated, abducted leg; suspect it even when the pain or the fall was small, X-ray the AP pelvis and hip, and CT if the X-ray is clear. Then ask why they fell (bloods, troponin, ECG, chest X-ray) and why the bone broke (tumour, osteoporosis). Surgery within 24-48 hours: displaced neck → arthroplasty; intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric → intramedullary nail. Afterwards: early mobilization, heparin for 14-30 days, falls and fracture prevention. 1. Is this a hip fracture? Who : the risk factors are whatever raises the risk of falls (previous falls · weakness: peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stroke · polypharmacy: sedatives, diuretics, psychotropics, antiarrhythmics · poor nutrition · poor eyesight · the environment) plus whatever raises the risk of osteoporosis the lecture's bone mineral density (BMD) testing list: everyone 65 and over · 50-64 with a fragility fracture, long-term glucocorticoids, a parental hip fracture, a vertebral fracture or osteopenia on X-ray, heavy alcohol, smoking, weight under 60 kg or loss of over 10% since age 25 , rheumatoid arthritis · under 50 with a fragility fracture, long-term glucocorticoids, hypogonadism or menopause before 45 , malabsorption, primary hyperparathyroidism History : sudden groin or lateral upper-thigh pain after a fall · sharp or deep ache · may radiate to the knee or leg · worse with movement and weight bearing , eased by staying still · ⚠ high suspicion in an older person even if the pain or the trauma was minimal Exam : look : leg shortened, externally rotated and abducted · cannot bear weight · feel : tender over the hip · move : painful range, log roll , straight leg raise Do not mistake a dislocation for a fracture : a posterior dislocation (the common one) leaves the leg shortened, internally rotated and adducted ; an anterior dislocation leaves it externally rotated, abducted and flexed . A fracture is shortened, externally rotated and abducted Posterior and anterior hip dislocation: the position of the leg and of the femoral head against the acetabulum Investigations : X-ray: AP pelvis and hip · negative but suspicion still high → CT Types : femoral neck (subcapital) · intertrochanteric · subtrochanteric Types of hip fracture along the proximal femur: subcapital and transcervical neck fractures, intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric, and greater or lesser trochanter fractures 2. Stable? Then why? Stable? airway, breathing, circulation (especially a young patient after high-velocity trauma ) · pelvic fracture? · check distal pulses and nerve function, especially the sciatic nerve Why did they fall? recent illness (nutrition, dehydration) · syncope or presyncope · cardiac symptoms → complete blood count, electrolytes, troponin · ECG (atrial fibrillation?) · chest X-ray (pneumonia) Why did it break? a pathologic fracture (less trauma than it should take, e.g. a bone tumour)? · a fragility fracture automatically qualifies as osteoporosis → start the osteoporosis workup 3. Plan and after Surgery for the vast majority, within 24-48 hours (standard of care) : quicker return to weight bearing, fewer complications of immobility femoral neck, displaced → arthroplasty (hemi = femoral head · total = head + acetabulum), required to preserve the head's blood supply femoral neck, non-displaced → maybe non-operative (only if very non-displaced in a poor surgical candidate) · maybe screws across the fracture · arthroplasty, the surgeon's choice intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric → intramedullary nail (essentially all surgical) After surgery : complications all come from immobility · venous thromboembolism → low-molecular-weight heparin for 14-30 days · pneumonia (a common cause of death) · muscle atrophy · infection (urinary) · delirium · bedsores Early mobilization with interdisciplinary rehab · falls prevention (comorbidities, environment, occupational therapy and physiotherapy, gait aids) · fracture prevention (vitamin D, calcium, secondary osteoporosis workup, antiresorptive) Schulich Reviews 147 hip fractures per 100,000 people aged 40 and over · women are 2× more likely to fracture a hip; men are 1.3× more likely to die afterwards , and about 25% die of any cause within a year
04 Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh

Anatomy of the gluteal region and thigh Two organising ideas carry the whole lecture. In the buttock, piriformis is the landmark : only the superior gluteal vessels and nerve leave the pelvis above it, everything else below. In the thigh, three compartments each have one job and one nerve - front: femoral, inside: obturator, back: sciatic. ⭐ Piriformis is the landmark: only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels leave above it; the sciatic, inferior gluteal and pudendal nerves leave below, and an injured superior gluteal nerve (hip replacement) gives the Trendelenburg sign. The pelvis drops on the unsupported side, so a right hip drop on right swing = a weak LEFT gluteus medius. Front = femoral, inner = obturator, back = sciatic - except the hamstring part of adductor magnus (tibial) and the short head of biceps (common fibular). NAVEL from lateral to medial; the femoral nerve sits outside the sheath. Injections go in the upper outer quadrant, away from the sciatic nerve. The saphenous nerve is at risk when the great saphenous vein is harvested. 1. Passageways out of the pelvis The sacrotuberous (sacrum → ischial tuberosity) and sacrospinous (sacrum → ischial spine) ligaments turn the sciatic notches into two foramina Greater sciatic foramen Lesser sciatic foramen Connects Pelvis → gluteal region Gluteal region → perineum Above piriformis Superior gluteal artery, vein and nerve — Through it Piriformis Tendon of obturator internus Below piriformis Inferior gluteal vessels and nerve · sciatic nerve · posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh · nerves to quadratus femoris and to obturator internus · pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels , turning back in to reach the perineum 2. Clinical approach to hip pain First ask where the patient means by "hip". True (intra-articular) hip pain is usually anterior, in the groin ; patients often point to the lateral buttock , and sometimes to the buttock itself, and each place has its own short list. The hip fracture is on the HIP FRACTURE chart. ⭐ Point first: groin = inside the joint (OA, labral tear, avascular necrosis), lateral = the greater trochanter, buttock = piriformis. Hip OA is a clinical diagnosis: groin pain, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, internal rotation lost first; an X-ray confirms it, no MRI needed. Can't put socks on → hip OA; tender trochanter, can't lie on that side, socks fine → GTPS. Clicking and locking → labral tear; MR arthrogram is the study of choice. Buttock pain worse sitting, ± sciatica → piriformis syndrome. 1. Anterior hip and groin pain: usually inside the joint Differential : arthritis (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, septic) · labral tear · avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) · iliopsoas tendinopathy Hip osteoarthritis (OA) : degenerative, often age-related "wear and tear" · primary (idiopathic, elderly) or secondary (post-traumatic, younger) presents as : anterior hip or groin pain , the "C" sign · gradual or sudden onset · worse with prolonged activity · night pain · morning stiffness under 30 min , and stiffness after prolonged sitting · crepitus, locking or sticking · decreased range of motion (getting in and out of a car, bending) · antalgic gait exam : leg length discrepancy? · internal rotation is reduced first · FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation) · Stinchfield · FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) investigations : a clinical diagnosis · X-ray confirms it (and can monitor progression), but X-ray changes do not always match symptoms · CT or MRI generally not needed (secondary causes, surgical planning) start with an X-ray : MRI adds nothing to the diagnosis and has a long wait · CT shows bone well but gives much more radiation · ultrasound is poor for a deep joint like the hip treatment : non-drug first ( education, exercise and physiotherapy , functional supports, weight management , tai chi, a cane) · drugs ( oral NSAIDs , Tylenol, duloxetine) · image-guided intra-articular injection (steroid, hyaluronic acid or platelet-rich plasma) · hip replacement : hemiarthroplasty (femoral head and neck replaced, acetabulum spared) · total (head, neck and acetabulum) · resurfacing (head and acetabulum, neck spared) Labral tear : all ages, commonly active females · vague groin pain with clicking, catching, snapping, locking · FABER and FADIR positive · X-ray only to exclude other pathology · MR arthrogram is the imaging study of choice · general hip pain treatment → arthroscopic labral debridement or repair Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) : disrupted blood flow to bone, commonly the femoral head · causes: trauma · steroids (oral or intramuscular) · alcohol · lupus · sickle cell disease · radiation 2. Lateral hip pain Greater trochanter bursitis : a very common cause of lateral hip pain · chronic friction of the iliotibial band over the greater trochanter irritates the bursa · female > male a clinical diagnosis : pain over the greater trochanter with point tenderness (highly sensitive) · worse with weight bearing · can't lie on that side · ± radiates into the buttock or down the thigh to the knee · no swelling, redness or skin changes imaging not often needed · ask about a recent increase in activity · positive Ober's test treatment : physio ( stretch the iliotibial band, strengthen the hip abductors ) · PRICE (protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation) · NSAIDs · corticosteroid injection Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) : bursitis is only half the story : overuse and chronic tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus (which insert on the greater trochanter), with flares of bursitis and/or tendinitis similar presentation, but more chronic and recalcitrant · single leg stance test · insidious, or a sudden flare after unaccustomed exercise, a fall, prolonged weight bearing or sporting overuse imaging: X-ray, ?ultrasound, ?MRI · treatment : physio (stretch the iliotibial band, strengthen the hip abductors) · load management · weight management · NSAIDs, injections · weak-evidence adjuncts (shock-wave therapy, ultrasound) · ?surgery Can you put your socks on? Hip OA can present laterally and is easily confused with GTPS. Seated sock-putting needs hip flexion and external rotation (basically FABER), so it is hard in hip OA and fine in GTPS (standing on one leg to do it hurts in GTPS) Lateral hip pain GTPS Hip OA History Pain on activity · pain lying on that side disrupts sleep Morning stiffness · associated groin pain · progressive Exam Tender greater trochanter · pain on single leg stance for 30 s Difficulty putting on socks · reduced range · pain on internal and external rotation 3. Posterior hip (buttock) pain Piriformis syndrome : a muscle strain and/or tendinopathy with buttock pain · may impinge the sciatic nerve → radicular symptoms down the leg causes: trauma to the buttock · prolonged sitting (sedentary jobs) · anatomic anomalies · ?piriformis hypertrophy worse getting out of bed, with prolonged sitting and with hip movements · tender over piriformis · Pace (resisted abduction and external rotation) · Beatty (side-lying, hold the flexed knee off the table) · FAIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) · Freiberg (forceful internal rotation of the extended thigh) electromyography (EMG) only if the nerve is involved · treatment : physio (stretch piriformis, range of motion, deep massage) · NSAIDs · ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection · ?surgery Snapping hip syndrome : very common · can be deep (inside the joint), anterior, lateral or posterior · if it isn't painful, don't worry about it ; if it is, treat the structures in that area (muscle: stretch and strengthen · bone: strengthen, ?inject, ?surgery · ligament: strengthen, ?inject)

Anatomy of the knee, part 1 The knee's bones barely fit together, so it is held by soft tissue: muscles (above all the quadriceps femoris) give most of the stability, and four cardinal ligaments plus two menisci add passive support. Knowing which structure resists which movement is what lets you name the injury on the acute knee injury chart. ⭐ Valgus stresses the MCL (which drags the medial meniscus with it); varus stresses the LCL (which has no meniscus attached). ACL: weaker, taut in extension, stops the tibia sliding forward, tested by Lachman. PCL: strongest, taut in flexion, stops the tibia sliding back. Dashboard injury = PCL; MCL injuries outnumber LCL injuries. The fibula is not in the knee joint. Peripheral meniscal tears heal; central ones don't. Skyline view = patellofemoral joint; tunnel view = loose bodies. Popliteus unlocks the knee. 1. Osteology and the knee on X-ray patella = a sesamoid bone inside the quadriceps tendon Femoral condyles (lateral, medial) sit on the tibial condyles (together the tibial plateau) · medial and lateral femoral epicondyles above them Tibial tuberosity = anterior bump where the patellar ligament inserts Intercondylar eminence of the tibia = attachment area for the cruciate ligaments and menisci · intercondylar fossa (notch) of the femur behind it The fibula is NOT part of the knee joint - it does not touch the femur Plain radiograph views View Shows Front-to-back (AP) Both condyles, the joint line, the intercondylar eminence Lateral Patella, femoral and tibial condyles, tibial tuberosity Skyline (axial) The patellofemoral joint and patellar fractures Tunnel The intercondylar notch: a loose body or bone fragment in the joint 2. The knee joint Hinge synovial joint , with some gliding and rotation about the long axis 3 articulations : lateral femoral + lateral tibial condyle · medial femoral + medial tibial condyle · femur + patella Largest joint in the body , with the largest capsule and an extensive synovial membrane Capsule reinforcement Side Reinforced by Anterior Quadriceps tendon / patellar ligament (replaces the fibrous capsule here) · medial and lateral patellar retinacula (from vastus medialis and lateralis) Medial Tibial (medial) collateral ligament · pes anserinus, semimembranosus, medial head of gastrocnemius Lateral Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament · biceps femoris · iliotibial band Posterior Oblique popliteal ligament (from semimembranosus) · arcuate popliteal ligament (from the fibular head, over popliteus) Inside the capsule Cruciate ligaments and menisci · ⚠ the cruciates are not enclosed by the synovial membrane Knee flexed, anterior view: the two collateral ligaments outside, the two cruciates crossing in the notch, and the menisci on the tibial plateau 3. The four cardinal ligaments Ligament Runs from → to Shape, strength Stops Taut in Tested by Tibial (medial) collateral (MCL) Medial femoral epicondyle → medial tibia Strong, long, broad · deep fibres fixed to the medial meniscus Valgus (leg forced outward) Extension Valgus stress on the flexed knee Fibular (lateral) collateral (LCL) Lateral femoral epicondyle → head of the fibula Strong, thin, cord-like · not attached to the meniscus Varus (leg forced inward) Extension Varus stress on the flexed knee Anterior cruciate (ACL) Medial side of the lateral femoral condyle → tibial intercondylar area, just in front of the eminence Thinner, weaker Tibia sliding forward under the femur (foot free) · femur sliding back on the tibia (foot planted) · hyperextension · excess medial rotation Extension Lachman (knee ~30°, the gold standard ) · anterior drawer (hip 45°, knee 90°, hamstrings relaxed) Posterior cruciate (PCL) Lateral side of the medial femoral condyle → back of the tibial intercondylar area Broader, strongest Tibia sliding back under the femur (foot free) · femur sliding forward on the tibia (foot planted) Flexion Posterior drawer Cruciates are named for where they attach on the tibia Crossed-fingers trick : cross your fingers over the same-side knee - the middle finger is the ACL, the index finger the PCL The MCL holds the medial meniscus, so damage to one puts the other at risk How each one is injured MCL injuries are more common than LCL injuries : a valgus force on an extended knee, or excessive twisting of the flexed knee · LCL: a strong varus force on the medial side of the knee ACL: a forceful blow to the thigh with the foot fixed drives the tibia forward · or rotation plus valgus on a flexed knee → the unhappy triad (ACL + MCL + medial meniscus) PCL: the "dashboard" injury - something strikes the front of the tibia with the knee flexed and forces the tibia back · the patellar ligament may avulse from the tibial tuberosity ACL taut in extension, PCL taut in flexion 4. The menisci C-shaped fibrocartilage wedges, thick at the rim and thin in the middle: deepen and stabilize the joint and absorb shock Blood supply : the periphery is richly vascularized, the centre is avascular (fed by synovial fluid) → peripheral tears can heal, central ones cannot Medial meniscus Lateral meniscus Shape C-shaped, broader at the back Nearly circular, smaller Mobility Firmly fixed to the tibial collateral ligament , so little movement Freely movable (popliteus pulls it back in flexion) Injury Torn more often (with the MCL, in the valgus-twist "unhappy triad") Not as susceptible Tibial plateau from above: medial meniscus (C-shaped, joined to the MCL), lateral meniscus (rounder), ACL in front, PCL behind 5. Locking and unlocking: the screw-home mechanism Locking : in the final 15-20° of extension the shapes of the condyles and menisci make the femur rotate medially on the tibia → the ligaments tighten maximally → the knee is stable for "quiet standing" with little muscle work Unlocking : popliteus rotates the femur laterally (~5°) to start flexion, and pulls the lateral meniscus back out of the way
06.2 Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 1

Clinical approach to the knee, part 1 An acute knee injury is named from three things: the mechanism, how fast it swelled, and which test is positive. A pivot with a pop and immediate swelling is the ACL; a blow to the front of the flexed tibia is the PCL; a valgus or varus collision is a collateral; a twist on a planted foot with delayed swelling and locking is a meniscus. ⭐ Pop + immediate swelling (hemarthrosis) after a pivot = ACL; the other ligament injuries swell little, and a meniscal tear swells late. Lachman, anterior drawer and pivot shift for the ACL; posterior drawer, sag sign and reverse Lachman for the PCL. Dashboard knee = PCL. Valgus → MCL (± medial meniscus, ± ACL = unhappy triad); varus → LCL (look for a PCL injury). Locking or catching = meniscus. Red-zone tears are repaired, white-zone tears resected. The structures themselves (where each ligament runs, why the medial meniscus is fixed, the red and white zones) are on the knee anatomy part 1 chart; knee pain without an injury, and the swelling timeline, are on the part 2 chart. 1. Ligament injuries ACL tear PCL tear MCL injury LCL injury How common Female 4.5 : 1 · pivoting sports · anatomic and biomechanical factors Less common than ACL tears Very common Uncommon in isolation Mechanism Non-contact 60-80% : cutting or pivoting while slowing down · contact 30%: a direct blow causing hyperextension or valgus Direct blow to the anterior tibia with the knee flexed ("dashboard") · hyperextension Valgus force, almost always a collision High-energy varus force, almost always a collision Presents as "Pop" · immediate swelling (hemarthrosis) · "instability" or "giving out" · lateral knee pain from a bone bruise Poorly defined pain, sometimes posterior · minimal swelling Medial pain · minimal to no swelling No swelling in isolation Goes with — Meniscal and chondral injuries Medial meniscal tear (sometimes) · ACL tear if completely torn PCL injury Exam Lachman · anterior drawer · pivot shift Posterior drawer · sag sign · reverse Lachman Valgus stress on the flexed knee Varus stress on the flexed knee Imaging X-ray to rule out a fracture (usually normal) · MRI if the exam cannot decide X-ray and stress X-ray (grading) · MRI if a posterolateral corner injury is suspected — — Treatment Rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE) · weight bearing as tolerated · crutches as needed · physiotherapy · orthopedic referral for ACL reconstruction Physiotherapy generally enough · PCL bracing · surgery only for rotatory instability or a posterolateral corner injury Early range of motion · bracing Bracing · surgical repair if other injuries and/or instability Return to play 9-12 months after surgery · 3-6% re-injury 50% return to the same or a higher level — — MCL and LCL injuries each range from a sprain to a complete tear 2. Meniscal tears Meniscal tear : mechanism varies with age and degeneration · rotation or twisting with the foot planted Presents as : medial or lateral joint-line pain after the injury (or delayed) · delayed or intermittent swelling · ± mechanical symptoms: locking and catching Exam : joint effusion · joint-line tenderness · McMurray's test · Thessaly's test Imaging : X-ray usually normal (but shows how much knee osteoarthritis ) · MRI if conservative care fails or a large tear is suspected Blood supply zones : red-red (vascular rim) · red-white · white-white (avascular centre) Tear patterns : longitudinal · degenerative · flap · radial · bucket handle · horizontal cleavage Tear Treatment Degenerative Physiotherapy (range of motion, strengthen quadriceps and hamstrings) · oral over-the-counter drugs, intra-articular corticosteroid · accommodative bracing or activity changes · surgery depends on how much osteoarthritis there is : arthroscopic repair vs debridement · arthroplasty as a last resort Traumatic, in the young Physiotherapy first · meniscal repair : red or red-white zone , larger tears, bucket-handle , meniscal root tears, younger patients · meniscal resection : white zone , chronic degenerative · options: partial meniscectomy, meniscal repair, meniscal transplantation Return to play: 6 weeks to 3 months, depending on repair or meniscectomy Meniscal zones: red (vascular rim) can heal and is repaired; white (avascular centre) cannot and is resected 3. The unhappy triad Unhappy triad = MCL + medial meniscus + ACL , from a forced valgus (lateral) blow ① forced valgus stretches the MCL and it tears · ② the medial meniscus, attached to the MCL, takes a bucket-handle tear · ③ forced abduction, external rotation and slight flexion tear the ACL Unhappy triad: a valgus blow from the outside tears the MCL, the medial meniscus and the ACL

Anatomy of the knee, part 2 The patella always wants to slide laterally, and the knee spends structures stopping it. The angle of the femur (the Q-angle) pulls it out; the vastus medialis and a buttress of bone on the femur hold it in. Around it sit the bursae that become knee bursitis, and the nerves and arteries that cross the joint. ⭐ The Q-angle makes the quadriceps pull the patella laterally; vastus medialis and the bony buttress on the lateral femur hold it in. Wider Q-angle in females → more lateral subluxation and patellofemoral pain. Genu valgum raises the Q-angle and loads the lateral condyles; genu varum lowers it and loads the medial. Housemaid's knee = prepatellar; clergyman's knee = superficial infrapatellar. 1. The extensor mechanism and patellar stability Quadriceps femoris → quadriceps tendon → patella → patellar ligament → tibial tuberosity the patella sits inside this tendon (a sesamoid bone), so the quadriceps are its main stabilizer The pull is not straight : because of the Q-angle the quadriceps pull the patella superolaterally , while the patellar tendon pulls straight down the resultant force tends to sublux the patella laterally during knee extension Two things resist the lateral pull ① vastus medialis pulls the patella medially ② an extra buttress of bone on the lateral patellar surface of the femur (seen on a skyline X-ray) abnormal bony shape of the patella or distal femur predisposes to patellar dislocation Quadriceps (Q) and patellar tendon (P) pulls add up to a lateral resultant (R); vastus medialis pulls back medially 2. The Q-angle and knee alignment Q-angle = angle between a line from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the patella and a line from the patella to the tibial tuberosity A normal Q-angle spreads weight evenly between the medial and lateral femoral and tibial condyles Wider in females (wider hips) → more lateral pull → more lateral patellar subluxation and patellofemoral pain syndrome Alignment Femur angle Q-angle Load falls on Normal Diagonal in the thigh Normal Shared between medial and lateral condyles Genu varum (bow-legged) More vertical Smaller Medial condyles Genu valgum (knock-kneed) Steeper angle Larger Lateral condyles The Q-angle is wider in females than in males 3. Bursae around the knee Fluid sacs that stop tendons and skin rubbing on bone; irritation from chronic friction = bursitis Bursa Where Note Suprapatellar Deep to the quadriceps tendon Attached to articularis genu and the synovial membrane; articularis genu pulls it tight when the knee extends Prepatellar Over the patella, under the skin "Housemaid's knee" : friction between skin and patella, working on the knees Infrapatellar (superficial and deep) In front of and behind the patellar ligament Superficial: "clergyman's knee" : friction over the tibial tuberosity, sitting on the knees on hard surfaces Pes anserinus Under the pes anserinus tendons on the medial tibia pes anserinus bursitis 4. Nerves and blood supply Nerves ( Hilton's law : a joint is supplied by the nerves to the muscles that act on it): femoral and sciatic nerves · articular branches of the obturator and saphenous nerves Arteries : the genicular anastomosis - superior and inferior, medial and lateral genicular branches of the popliteal artery · collateral flow from the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery Popliteus : adds little posterior stability, but unlocks the knee (laterally rotates the femur to start flexion from full extension) and pulls the lateral meniscus back during flexion
07.2 Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 2

Clinical approach to the knee, part 2 Part 2 is the knee pain that builds up rather than happens: after any trauma, how fast it swelled sorts the injury; without trauma, where it hurts and whether there is a lump tells the overuse and swelling problems apart. Then the four injections, compared on onset, how long they last, cost and evidence. ⭐ Anterior knee pain worse after activity and prolonged sitting, with no swelling, in a young woman = patellofemoral pain syndrome: a clinical diagnosis, treated with physiotherapy to balance vastus medialis. Swelling within 6 hours of trauma = ACL tear, fracture or patellar dislocation. Lateral knee ache while running downhill (less with sprinting) = iliotibial band. A swelling behind the knee: ultrasound it, and don't miss a DVT or aneurysm; 6 weeks of conservative care unless vessels or nerves are compromised. Steroid: fast, cheap, short. Hyaluronic acid: long-lasting, expensive. 1. Anatomy of the leg The leg is four sealed compartments, each with one job and one nerve: anterior dorsiflexes (deep fibular), lateral everts (superficial fibular), and both posterior compartments plantarflex (tibial). Learn that grid and nerve injuries, compartment syndrome and foot drop follow from it. ⭐ Anterior = dorsiflexion = deep fibular; lateral = eversion = superficial fibular; both posterior = plantarflexion = tibial. Common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula → foot drop with a numb dorsum; deep fibular alone → numb first web space only. Tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior both invert. Tarsal tunnel: Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry. Standing calf raise = gastrocnemius; seated = soleus. The fibula breaks just above the lateral malleolus in extreme inversion. 1. 01.1 Anatomy of the Ankle and Foot

Anatomy of the ankle and foot The foot is built to hold its arches up and stay stable on uneven ground. Know which way the ankle is weakest (plantarflexed), which ligament gives first (the anterior talofibular), and which tendons and ligaments hold each arch up - sprains, flat feet and pulses all follow from it. The leg's compartments, the tarsal tunnel and the bones on X-ray are on the leg chart. ⭐ The ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion and least stable in plantarflexion, so the plantarflexed, inverted ankle tears the anterior talofibular ligament first. The deltoid ligament is thick and strong and stabilizes eversion. Inversion and eversion happen at the subtalar joint, not the ankle. The talus head and spring ligament are the keystone of the medial arch ; tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and fibularis longus hold the arches - lose tibialis posterior and the foot goes flat. Posterior tibial pulse between the medial malleolus and the Achilles, foot inverted; always compare both sides. Deep fibular = the first web space; medial plantar = medial 3½ toes. 1. Dorsum and sole of the foot Extensor retinacula = thickened fascia over the anterior compartment tendons · stop them bowstringing when the ankle dorsiflexes superior: tibia to fibula · inferior: Y-shaped , stem from the calcaneus Flexor retinaculum holds the deep posterior tendons as they pass behind the medial malleolus Tendons on the dorsum : tibialis anterior (broad attachment on the medial foot) · extensor digitorum longus (splits into 4, works with extensor digitorum brevis) · extensor hallucis longus (to the big toe, works with extensor hallucis brevis) Plantar fascia : continuous with the deep fascia of the leg · thick central part = plantar aponeurosis protects the sole · supports the longitudinal arches · holds everything together Intrinsic muscles of the sole : like the palm of the hand, but they work as a group to support stance and keep the arches up , most active at toe-off 4 layers: ① abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi · ② quadratus plantae, lumbricals · ③ flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis · ④ plantar (3) and dorsal (4) interossei or by compartment: medial (abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis) · intermediate (flexor digitorum brevis, quadratus plantae, lumbricals, adductor hallucis) · lateral (flexor and abductor digiti minimi) · interosseous (= the 4th layer) Long tendons in the sole : tibialis posterior · flexor digitorum longus · flexor hallucis longus, which runs under the sustentaculum tali 2. Ankle (talocrural) joint Hinge synovial joint : distal tibia and fibula grip the top (trochlea) of the talus · the lateral malleolus reaches ~2 cm lower than the medial dorsiflexion : tibialis anterior, fibularis tertius, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus · plantarflexion : gastrocnemius and soleus through the Achilles tendon Stability depends on position : the trochlea is wider in front dorsiflexion = highest congruency, most stable ("digging in your heels") plantarflexion = lowest congruency, least stable → some wobble allowed, and most injuries happen plantarflexed Capsule thin front and back, reinforced at the sides by the collateral ligaments 3. Ankle ligaments Ligament Parts Runs What it does Clinical Lateral collateral (relatively weak) Anterior talofibular (ATFL) · calcaneofibular (CFL) · posterior talofibular (PTFL) Fibula → talus and calcaneus Minor protection against inversion ATFL = the most vulnerable , torn in inversion sprains · sprains are more often lateral because the ankle tends to invert Medial collateral = deltoid ligament (thick, strong) 4 bands: anterior and posterior tibiotalar · tibiocalcaneal · tibionavicular Medial malleolus → talus, calcaneus, navicular Stabilizes the ankle in eversion Severe inversion or eversion can avulse bone instead Spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) — Sustentaculum tali → navicular, below the deltoid Holds up the head of the talus : with it, the "keystone" of the medial arch Stretched or torn → talar head drops between calcaneus and navicular, medial arch flattens , forefoot abducts and everts Lateral collateral ligaments: anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular and posterior talofibular Medial side: the deltoid ligament from the medial malleolus, with the spring ligament below it 4. Arches of the foot Weight goes tibia → talus → back to the calcaneus and forward to the metatarsal heads; the arches flatten and spring back between those points. 01.2 Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot

Clinical approach to the ankle and foot Two questions run the lecture: after a twisted ankle, does this patient need an X-ray (the Ottawa rules); and for a sore foot without injury, where exactly does it hurt? Almost every one of these gets better slowly with education, footwear and physiotherapy - surgery is the exception. ⭐ Ottawa rules: X-ray the ankle only for bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight immediately and in the emergency department; X-ray the foot only for tenderness at the navicular or base of the 5th metatarsal, or the same weight-bearing test. Lateral sprain = plantarflexion + inversion, ATFL first; treat with early mobilization. Plantar fasciitis = anteromedial heel pain on the first morning steps; Achilles tendinopathy = posterior heel, worse with passive dorsiflexion. Tibialis posterior dysfunction: medial ankle pain, then a flexible then rigid flat foot ("too many toes"). Morton's neuroma burns, sits between the 3rd and 4th metatarsals, and never weakens. The ligaments, arches and pulses themselves are on the ankle and foot anatomy chart. 1. Ankle sprain "Sprain" = a ligament injury , from a partial to a full tear of any or all three lateral ligaments · dislocation when all three are fully torn Lateral sprain - up to 85% mechanism: foot plantarflexed and inverted at the "twist" (landing from a jump, stepping in a hole) order of injury: anterior talofibular (ATFL) > calcaneofibular (CFL) > posterior talofibular (PTFL) Medial sprain : similar, but the deltoid ligament (foot caught on turf during a kick) Exam : swelling · bruising (ecchymosis) · pain on palpation over the ligament(s) · anterior drawer test (ATFL) Treatment education: most improve · how to avoid recurrence rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE) · brief immobilization only if needed · early mobilization · strengthening and proprioception · bracing or taping has pros and cons NSAIDs or analgesics as needed ligament reconstruction only for ongoing instability despite conservative care 2. Who needs an X-ray: the Ottawa foot and ankle rules Ankle X-ray series Foot X-ray series Pain in The malleolar zone The midfoot zone Plus ANY of Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus (back 6 cm) · or of the medial malleolus · cannot bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the emergency department Bone tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal · or the navicular · cannot bear weight both immediately and in the emergency department Ottawa foot and ankle rules: malleolar zone (back 6 cm of each malleolus) and midfoot zone (navicular, base of the 5th metatarsal), plus inability to bear weight When a sprain isn't just a sprain (reading and managing the fracture is on the FRACTURE charts): unimalleolar (may be non-operative, decided by the stability of the talus) · bimalleolar (usually forceful eversion , both malleoli, usually surgical) · trimalleolar (unstable, surgical) · Maisonneuve (forceful external rotation , interosseous ligament torn, with a medial malleolus avulsion or deltoid rupture and an ATFL injury; usually surgical) 3. Overuse problems: where does it hurt? Condition Where it hurts, and who Key features Management Achilles tendinopathy Posterior heel , just above or right at the calcaneal insertion · runners, especially after a rise in training Tender · worse with passive dorsiflexion Education: a long, slow improvement · activity changes · footwear that does not press on the tendon · heel wedge used cautiously · physio: stretching, eccentric strengthening , friction massage, shock-wave therapy · topical or oral NSAIDs, ?topical nitrites · intervention or surgery rare Achilles rupture Active people in their 30s-40s (and older, as people stay active) — Surgical repair vs casting or an air-cast boot : surgery may re-rupture slightly less, but brings infection, wound problems, scarring and sural nerve injury · involve the patient in the decision Plantar fasciitis Anteromedial calcaneus , on the first morning steps and with ongoing activity · age 40-60, F > M Chronic insertional inflammation of an overworked fascia · tender · worse with passive dorsiflexion · often a tight Achilles (less dorsiflexion) · an overuse injury (running, aerobics), often with improper footwear · pain also rises with extension of the big toe Education: long, slow improvement · cushioned heel pad · heel lift (careful long-term) · shoes with arch support · weight loss · physio: stretch the fascia, strengthen tibialis posterior and the intrinsics · night splints · oral NSAIDs (rarely by injection) · surgical release very, very rarely Tibialis posterior dysfunction Medial ankle pain ± swelling Tendon hypovascular distal to the medial malleolus · risks: trauma, steroid use, inflammatory arthritis, obesity, diabetes · a spectrum: mild → significant weakness → flexible flat foot → rigid flat foot · "too many toes" sign Education on risk factors · RICE · physiotherapy (strengthen tibialis posterior and the other arch stabilizers) · orthosis (foot or ankle-foot; corrective or accommodative) · NSAIDs if needed · surgery by severity Bunion (hallux valgus) Medial first metatarsophalangeal joint · tops of the toes in a tight shoe box Footwear (why more common in women) · metatarsus varus · secondary toe deformities · the big toe is out of position for toe-off, so the other toes work harder Treat early and often to avoid surgery · positioning only if flexible · wider toe box · nothing much pharmacologic (?topical NSAID) · surgical correction or realignment Morton's neuroma Usually between the 3rd and 4th metatarsals · middle-aged, F > M Perineural fibrosis of a common digital nerve · burning dysesthesia · provoked and relieved mechanically (high heels, narrow toe box) · squeeze or palpation reproduces it · possibly sensory findings, no motor Education, so they own the fix · lower heels, wider and taller toe box · metatarsal pad in an orthosis · neuropathic pain

Lower extremity radiology Each joint has a standard pair of views plus an extra one for a specific question, and the lecture uses each joint to show one classic finding: osteoarthritis at the hip and knee, and fractures graded by where they sit at the ankle. ⭐ Weber type is set by the fibular fracture's level against the syndesmosis: A below (usually stable, boot), B at (depends on the medial side), C above (unstable, surgery). The mortise view is the one that shows the syndesmosis. Order an AP pelvis with a hip X-ray to compare sides. Osteoarthritis looks the same at every joint: lost joint space, osteophytes, subchondral cysts and sclerosis. Three malleoli broken = a dislocated ankle. 1. Knee Views : AP and lateral are standard · add a tunnel , skyline or standing view when the differential needs it Osteoarthritis : the same four signs - lost joint space, osteophytes, subchondral cysts, subchondral sclerosis 3. Ankle views AP · lateral · mortise Mortise view = the one that opens up the tibiofibular syndesmosis (on the AP the tibia and fibula overlap there) 4. Ankle fractures Lateral malleolus fracture : graded by the Weber classification - the level of the fibular break relative to the tibiofibular syndesmosis Weber type Fibular fracture is... Stability Treatment A Below the syndesmosis Usually stable if the medial malleolus is intact Walking boot and crutches for 6 weeks , weight-bear as tolerated B At the syndesmosis Variable - depends on the medial malleolus and deltoid ligament Surgery (open reduction and internal fixation) if unstable C Above the syndesmosis Unstable · often with a bimalleolar fracture or deltoid injury Usually open reduction and internal fixation A Maisonneuve fracture (high fibula) counts as Weber C Weber A, B and C: the fibular fracture below, at, and above the tibiofibular syndesmosis Medial malleolus fracture (sources differ on the mechanism: this note says forced inversion, the ankle sprain note says forced eversion - check the slides) chip fracture = an avulsion : the deltoid ligament pulls off a flake of bone as it ruptures transverse · vertical comminuted = several pieces, usually high-energy trauma Bimalleolar : lateral and medial malleolus Trimalleolar : both malleoli + the back of the distal tibia → no stable bony link between leg and foot, so the ankle dislocates Trimalleolar fracture on the AP, mortise and lateral views

Nerve injury Every nerve injury asks four questions: is it a nerve injury? where is it? how bad is it? what now? The pattern of numbness and weakness says where (root or named nerve); the layer that was cut says how bad , and that predicts recovery. Electrodiagnostic studies confirm both. ⭐ Neurapraxia (myelin only, compression) recovers in weeks; axonotmesis (axon cut, epineurium intact) regrows on its own at 1 mm a day (1 inch a month); neurotmesis (epineurium cut) cannot recover spontaneously. Radiculopathy = dermatome with fuzzy borders, myotome weakness and radiating neck or back pain; mononeuropathy = sharp-bordered patch and weakness confined to one nerve's muscles. Numb thumb: lateral forearm numbness or weak biceps → C6; weak abductor pollicis brevis → carpal tunnel. Nerve conduction size reflects the axon, speed reflects myelin. An axonal injury cannot be called axonotmesis or neurotmesis until you see whether it recovers. 1. The peripheral nerve Somatic peripheral nervous system : sensory (afferent) fibres carry signals from skin, muscle and joints to the central nervous system · motor (efferent) fibres carry them out to skeletal muscle Wrappings , inside out: endoneurium around each axon (a protective tube) · perineurium around each fascicle (holds a bundle of axons) · epineurium around the whole nerve (holds a bundle of fascicles) One nerve = many axons , not a single wire · the layered wrappings keep it working, and which layers are torn decides how well it heals Myelin lets the signal jump node to node, so it is faster and insulated 2. How bad: the Seddon classification Grade Damaged Still intact Typical cause Recovery Neurapraxia Myelin only → conduction slowed or blocked (the signal cannot reach the target at all) Axon and all three wrappings Compression (Saturday night palsy) Temporary: resolves within weeks (6-12) once the cause is removed Axonotmesis Axon , with varying damage to its supporting tissues (endoneurial tube, perineurium) and fascicles deranged Epineurium - a tube to keep regrowing fibres in line Crush, stretch Spontaneous but SLOW: 1 mm a day = 1 inch a month Neurotmesis Epineurium - the nerve is discontinuous Nothing Cut No spontaneous recovery - no track for the axons to follow Seddon classification: neurapraxia (myelin damaged), axonotmesis (axon cut, epineurium intact), neurotmesis (axon and epineurium cut) After an axon injury : Wallerian degeneration of the axon beyond the injury (cytoskeleton breaks down, membrane integrity is lost, macrophages clear the debris) → Schwann cells multiply, release cytokines and growth factors and clear debris too, the cell body releases trophic factors, the axon regrows - much better with an endoneurial tube to follow, very poorly with no epineurium to guide it 3. Where: localizing the lesion Levels : motor neuronopathy (anterior horn cell) · radiculopathy (spinal root) · plexopathy (brachial or lumbosacral plexus) · mononeuropathy (one named nerve) · polyneuropathy (diffuse) First make sure it is a nerve: weakness may be a tendon and numbness may be poor blood flow · true sensory loss is always neurogenic , but central or peripheral? · pain with or without weakness can be hard to sort out clinically Dermatome : skin supplied by one spinal root · dermatomes overlap , so the edges are fuzzy · e.g. C6: lateral arm, forearm and thumb Myotome : the muscles one spinal root supplies, whatever peripheral nerve carries the fibres · e.g. C6: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus, latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior, pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis One nerve carries several roots : the radial nerve's muscles run from C5 to T1 (brachioradialis C5-C6, triceps C7-C8, extensor indicis C8-T1) · root charts come from surgically seen roots matched to the muscles abnormal on electromyography (EMG) Radiculopathy Mononeuropathy Lesion Spinal nerve root · compressed in the intervertebral foramen ("pinched nerve") One named nerve · compressed at a common site (carpal tunnel) Onset Sudden or insidious · usually a clear time of onset Depends on the mechanism: chronic compression = insidious (more common) · traumatic cut = sudden Pain Neck or back pain radiating down the arm or leg · aching or sharp, then electric, burning or zinging along the dermatome Numbness, tingling, sometimes neuropathic burning or electric pain Sensory map Dermatome, fuzzy borders Well-circumscribed area of that nerve · may radiate: complaints outside the territory, but usually no objective signs there Weakness Myotome + myotomal reflex loss Only that nerve's muscles - not other muscles from the same root supplied by another nerve Worse with / better with Positions that stretch the root (neck extension) / taking tension off (arm overhead) Pressing on the nerve (leaning on the elbow, driving, typing) / position and rest Duration · severity Months · can be severe Variable Sensory maps: C6, C7, C8 dermatomes (radiculopathy) vs radial, median and ulnar nerve territories (mononeuropathy) "Numb thumb" (frequent tingling, less feeling over the thumb): the median nerve territory and the C6 dermatome overlap at the thumb, so test what they do not share carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve): thumb sensation + motor to abductor pollicis brevis (a C8 root muscle) C6 radiculopathy : C6 dermatome (lateral arm, forearm, thumb) + what C6 sends through the musculocutaneous nerve: lateral forearm sensation (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) and biceps power Foot drop after trauma: dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion 0/5, sharp-bordered numbness over the dorsum of the foot, reflexes intact → electromyography abnormal in peroneus longus, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum brevis only, paraspinals normal → common peroneal axonopathy at the fibular head · if gluteus medius, semimembranosus, tibialis posterior and the L5 paraspinals are abnormal too (one root, several nerves) → L5 radiculopathy 4. Fracture radiology Describe every fracture x-ray in the same order, so the person on the phone can picture it without seeing it. Detect it first ( trace the cortex, look for secondary signs ), then describe it systematically : views → location → type → descriptors → joint surface → other findings → bone quality , then what healing looks like. More than one descriptor for each fracture. Mnemonic OLD ACIDS : Open or closed · Location · Degree (complete or incomplete) · Articular surface · Comminution and type · Intrinsic bone quality · Displacement · Soft tissue injury. ⭐ Trace the cortex and look for secondary signs: a fat-fluid level or effusion means an intra-articular fracture even when no line is seen · an oblique fracture shows on one view, a spiral needs several · describe the distal fragment relative to the proximal (not for the clavicle) · intra-articular reductions must be anatomic · a transverse fracture with trivial trauma suggests pathological bone · the line widens at 10-14 days because it is healing · delayed union is twice the expected time, non-union no healing in 6-9 months. 1. Get the right films Standard views : anteroposterior (AP, front-to-back) · lateral · oblique · the body is described in anatomic position Special views for particular sites: mortise view - ankle (shown beside the AP in the lecture) scaphoid views - wrist in ulnar deviation, and the clenched-fist view Y-view - shoulder More than one view : an oblique fracture shows on one view, a spiral needs multiple views 2. Location Right or left · which bone · which part: epiphysis (end) · physis (growth plate - immature skeleton only) · metaphysis · diaphysis (shaft) · apophysis (non-articular bump where muscles or tendons attach, under traction) A growth plate fracture is a Salter-Harris injury: see 08 - Pediatric Orthopedics 3. Type Complete (all the way through) or incomplete (bowing, buckle, greenstick, Salter-Harris - immature skeleton) · others: avulsion , open Pattern Fracture line Clue Transverse Straight across, perpendicular to the shaft Pathological fractures are usually transverse Oblique Diagonal, seen on one view Check a second view to tell from spiral Spiral Winds around the shaft Twisting injury · needs multiple views · can resemble oblique, with a butterfly fragment Comminuted More than two fragments Segmental , or a triangular butterfly fragment Longitudinal / linear Along the long axis — Transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted and butterfly-fragment fractures on x-ray 4. Descriptors (displacement) Describe the distal fragment relative to the proximal one - except the clavicle , where the proximal fragment is described relative to the distal (neck muscles pull it up) Four components: angulation · translation · rotation · distraction Translation (displacement) - movement of the ends away from each other, loss of alignment along the long axis, in shaft widths · more than a full width = "off-ended" Angulation - by the direction of the apex: varus = apex lateral (distal fragment directed laterally, as the slide puts it) · valgus = apex medial (distal fragment pointing medially) Rotation - distal fragment turned internally or externally; hard to read, so look at the joints above and below Length : distraction (pulled apart) · impaction (driven in, "telescoped") · override (fragments overlap) - both of the last two foreshorten Translation is measured in shaft widths: half-shaft width versus off-ended 5. Joint surface involvement Extra-articular : joint spared · reduction can be relatively anatomic · the bone remodels, particularly with weight-bearing Intra-articular : risk of secondary osteoarthritis · reduction must be anatomic · longer to heal step-off or depression - an abrupt break in the joint's cortical line; trace the cortex fracture not appreciable? look for the secondary signs: hemarthrosis (effusion) and a fat-fluid level ( lipohemarthrosis ) subluxation or dislocation Extra-articular fracture spares the joint surface; intra-articular runs into it 6. Other findings Open (compound) - through the skin (the lecture's case: upper and mid third of the tibia and fibula) Foreign body or hardware · periprosthetic fracture around an implant Avulsion - a tendon or ligament pulls off a fragment (e.g. an intra-articular, dorsally displaced triangular fragment at the extensor tendon attachment on the distal phalanx) Diastasis - a widened or incongruent joint with or without fracture: pubic symphysis, acromioclavicular joint Amputation 7. Bone quality Weakened bone → pathological ( fragility ) fracture : usually transverse , spontaneous or with trivial trauma 8. Healing on x-ray Mostly secondary (spontaneous) healing : inflammatory, then reparative ( callus ), then remodelling phases; complete remodelling takes years · primary (contact) healing when the bone surfaces are directly apposed, as in internal fixation: no callus (Kirschner wires (K-wires) in the lecture) Healing is a clinical diagnosis : no tenderness, no motion at the fracture site, weight-bearing possible On x-ray : the fracture line widens at 10-14 days (resorption, not displacement) · callus at 2 weeks · union = mature bridging callus with the medullary space restored Upper limb 3-10 weeks (distal humerus longest, 8-10) · lower limb 6-12 weeks (femoral neck and shaft longest) Delayed union = healing takes twice as long as expected · non-union = no healing in 6-9 months · malunion = non-anatomic healing · management: see 05 - Fracture Management

Fracture management Every fracture follows the same sequence: resuscitate → reduce → hold the reduction → check it on x-ray → rehabilitate. The lecture then covers the two situations that change the plan - open fractures and the complications , of which compartment syndrome is the emergency. ⭐ Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch = compartment syndrome, a clinical diagnosis - remove the cast, call orthopedics, fasciotomy; do not wait for the pulse to go · any fracture with a wound is open: early antibiotics, tetanus, early debridement and stabilisation · non-union = not healed in twice the expected time; hypertrophic means not enough stability · femoral head, talus and scaphoid are the avascular necrosis sites · heterotopic ossification hides from x-ray early. 1. Goals and steps Goals : restore anatomy ( length, alignment, rotation, translation ) · allow early motion · avoid complications of immobility and of poor healing · improve function ① Resuscitate - bones bleed, and sharp edges can injure vessels ② Reduce (not needed if non-displaced) - choice depends on fracture type and site, displacement, open or closed, and whether the patient can have surgery (other injuries may be more life-threatening) closed (no direct view): analgesia and sedation → longitudinal traction, exaggerating the deformity → keeping traction, reverse it open : in the operating room under anesthesia, seeing the fragments ③ Maintain the reduction cast or splint external fixation - screws held by an external fixator internal fixation - plates, screws, pins, nails · with open reduction = open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) ④ Post-reduction x-ray - is the reduction adequate (orthopedics has criteria), and is the chosen fixation maintaining it? ⑤ Rehabilitation - as much movement as is safe, as early as possible · protect weight-bearing as directed · physiotherapy and occupational therapy for basic and functional mobility · prevent contractures 2. Open fractures Fractured bone or hematoma exposed through a traumatic break in soft tissue and skin · any fracture with a wound, even distant, is open until proven otherwise More complications : infection , non-union and delayed union, incomplete recovery - worse with more energy (contamination, soft tissue trauma, dead bone) Goal : turn an unstable, contaminated wound into a stable, clean one that lets the fracture heal The lecture's case : open, spiral fracture of the distal third of the tibial shaft · mildly displaced: shortened, posterior translation, apex lateral angulation early antibiotics (the lecture's case: 2 g intravenous cefazolin) · tetanus prophylaxis (given in the emergency department) · closed reduction and splint while waiting for orthopedics early surgery : remove all dead tissue including bone fragments · gently irrigate with sterile saline · stabilise (the case: intramedullary nail) early closure of the soft tissue: minimal contamination and little tissue removed → direct closure at the open reduction and internal fixation · a worse injury may need a plastic surgery flap 3. Compartment syndrome Pressure in a closed fascio-osseous space rises beyond what the structures inside can tolerate · lower leg (tibial fracture) and forearm most often Muscle and nerve are metabolically active → injury within 2 hours of ischemia → cell death → leaky capillaries → more swelling → more pressure Causes : external - tight cast , direct pressure, circumferential burn eschar · internal - hematoma, fluid leak (extensive burns, reperfusion after a vascular repair, crush) A clinical diagnosis - urgent call to orthopedics pain out of proportion to the injury · pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles (a tibial fracture with rising narcotic needs, terrible pain, and pain on dorsiflexion for the anterior compartment or plantarflexion for the posterior) paresthesia (midterm) → paralysis (very late) pulselessness is not typical - by then it has been missed No test is needed when the clinical picture is there · measure pressure only when the patient cannot communicate (uncooperative, sedated, child): diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure under 20 mmHg , or compartment pressure over 30 mmHg Management : call orthopedics · remove casts and compressive dressings · elevate · cool · monitor · definitive: fasciotomy 4. Other complications Complication What it is Key points Venous thromboembolism Clots from Virchow's triad : endothelial injury, stasis, hypercoagulability Describes most orthopedic trauma patients · higher risk: multiple injuries · spinal cord or head injury · lower limb or pelvic fracture · older age · long surgery or long wait · prevent mechanically (intermittent pneumatic compression; an inferior vena cava filter stops emboli, not clot) or with drugs (acetylsalicylic acid, low-molecular-weight heparin), chosen for the patient (e.g. polytrauma with a bleed in the head) Non-union Not healed in twice the expected time Atrophic - no significant bone, impaired healing · hypertrophic - lots of bone but not stable enough · infected · fix with stabilisation (especially if hypertrophic), biology (nutrition, metabolic, stop smoking, bone graft), clearing infection (irrigation, debridement, antibiotics), reconstruction Malunion Healed in an abnormal position Assess every plane: shortening, angulation, rotation, translation · osteotomy (a surgical break, ± removing bone, to realign and stabilise) if it affects comfort or function now or later Avascular necrosis Bone cell death from lost blood supply Femoral head, talus, scaphoid - all have a retrograde blood supply · pain · surgical Post-traumatic arthritis Arthritis after a peri-articular fracture Uncommon in hip and knee, over 50% after ankle fractures , the most common cause of ankle arthritis · pain on weight-bearing, less motion · managed like osteoarthritis: pain control, physiotherapy to keep mobility, surgery if all else fails Heterotopic ossification Excessive ectopic bone, often afte

Understanding and managing chronic pain Most chronic pain is no longer a tissue problem but a processing problem: the nervous system has been turned up (central sensitization, "wind-up"), so the plan aims at managing pain and function, not cure : education, active therapy and a multimodal drug plan, with adjuvant drugs before opioids and opioids only under the START principle. ⭐ Chronic pain is mostly sensitized (neuropathic) pain that outlasts the injury, so "hurt does not equal harm" and the treatment with good evidence is individualized, supervised exercise, not passive therapy. Massage helps only alongside exercise and education. SSRIs do little for pain; tricyclics and SNRIs (norepinephrine) do. Gabapentin and pregabalin are for neuropathic pain; their main side effect is sedation. NSAIDs: a 2-3 week trial. Adjuvants before opioids; watchful opioid dose 90 mg morphine equivalent per day; strong recommendation against opioids after addiction. 1. How pain normally travels and is turned up or down Nociceptive pain : transduction → conduction → transmission → perception · the stimulus is well localized , with a clear duration, intensity and quality Fibres Fibre Myelin Speed Carries Feels A-beta (large, "non-nociceptor") Myelinated 30-70 m/s Touch, pressure, vibration Sharp, well localized A-delta (small, nociceptor) Thin myelin 12-30 m/s Pinprick pain · cold threshold Sharp, well localized C (small, nociceptor) Unmyelinated 0.5-2 m/s Pain (heat, cold, pressure) · heat threshold Dull, poorly localized, persistent Dorsal (posterior) horn : the nociceptive fibre releases glutamate (onto AMPA, NMDA and metabotropic glutamate receptors), substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) · the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor is normally blocked by magnesium Central sensitization ("wind-up") : repeated input releases the magnesium block → NMDA activation → more calcium inside the cell → more sodium channels, potassium channels blocked → the same stimulus gives a bigger signal Ascending pathways (anterolateral system) medial system (intralaminar thalamus → anterior cingulate cortex, insula, amygdala, hypothalamus): the emotional "suffering" lateral system (ventral posterolateral thalamus → primary somatosensory cortex): where it hurts Three ways pain is dampened gate control : A-beta input switches on the inhibitory interneuron, while A-delta and C input switches it off · so rubbing a sore spot helps endogenous opioids (enkephalins, endorphins, dynorphins; mu, delta and kappa receptors, most in the medial system): before the synapse less calcium enters, so less glutamate is released · after the synapse more potassium leaves, so the neuron responds less descending inhibition from the brainstem (periaqueductal gray, locus coeruleus for norepinephrine, raphe nuclei for serotonin) · more norepinephrine and serotonin = more pain inhibition Gate control: A-beta touch fibres switch on the inhibitory interneuron; C fibres switch it off 2. Types of pain and how long it lasts Acute Subacute Chronic Lasts Seconds , at the same time as the cause Hours to days Over 3 months Matches the cause? Proportional to the cause Primary or secondary hyperalgesia , allodynia , spontaneous pain Can outlast tissue healing · a long-term disease · big emotional component Mechanism Nociceptive Mostly nociceptive, some neuropathic Mostly neuropathic , some nociceptive Neuropathic pain = from a lesion (inflammation) or dysfunction (ectopic firing) of the nervous system itself shows as spontaneous pain or hypersensitivity · can feel like nociceptive pain but usually described as burning, electric, pins and needles, numbness Neuropathic vs nociceptive pain: how each is described and behaves 3. Chronic pain: two kinds, and what it does to the person Chronic nociceptive (the minority): nociceptors are chronically activated, e.g. chronic inflammatory disease, osteoarthritis · treat by preventing further nociceptive activation Chronic neuropathic (the majority): the injury has healed but processing is increasingly abnormal wind-up · peripheral sensitization drives central over-activation through more glutamate receptors · less descending serotonin and norepinephrine · pain-avoidant behaviour ("fear of harm") classified as peripheral or central pain syndromes, complex pain disorders and mixed pain syndromes Mood : comorbid depression in 5-87% · somatic symptoms are common (appetite, sleep, energy, weight change) predictors of depression: pain intensity · number of painful areas · frequency of severe pain · other psychosocial factors anxiety is one of the most disabling parts · activity avoidance → deconditioning, social isolation "It hurts when I move" : avoidance is driven by fear of harm and spreads to anything that might hurt operant conditioning: pain lifting at work → avoid work = less pain → work avoidance and absenteeism instead of activity modification and treatment · classical conditioning also plays a part Effects on the patient : physical (mobility, sleep, fatigue, appetite) · social (relationships, sexual function, recreation) · mood (depression, anxiety, anger, irritability) · society (health care use, disability, lost work, substance use) 4. The team Team approach : drug, non-drug and interventional options · rehabilitation in individual and group sessions · psychology support Refer to a multidisciplinary chronic pain clinic when: not responding to standard analgesics · to review management to date and find options · activity, mood and social isolation are getting worse because of pain Clinic roles physicians (anesthesia, neurology, physical medicine and rehabilitation, internal medicine, psychiatry): review investigations, trial drugs, give interventions, assess mood and activity, refer on · build a long-term plan for the family physician to follow nurses : support medical management and interventions, documentation, triage psychologists : group and individual therapy for depression and anxiety · cognitive b

Psychological factors in managing chronic pain Pain is a sensory and emotional experience, shaped by the mind: assess the pain and its effect on function, recognize when distress points to a somatic symptom and related disorder (or factitious disorder or malingering), and manage chronic pain biologically, psychologically and through rehabilitation : managed, not cured. ⭐ Factitious disorder: behaviour conscious, gain unconscious (the sick role); malingering: conscious, for external gain; somatic symptom disorders: unconscious inner gain. Somatic symptom disorder = distressing symptoms + excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours, over 6 months. Conversion disorder needs findings incompatible with known disease. Medically unexplained symptoms reach over 60% in neurology. CBT for pain targets mental filter, catastrophizing and emotional reasoning; avoid progressive muscle relaxation. Intervene before 12 weeks. 1. Assessing chronic pain History and physical exam duration and nature of the pain associated symptoms, physical and psychological, including suicidal thoughts past health care contacts and treatments: alternative therapies, medications, home remedies · what worked and what did not effect on function Investigations : review all past investigations · new ones only as clinically indicated Charting the pain : descriptive words · 0-10 numeric score · face scales · visual analogue scale · multidimensional tools (McGill Pain Questionnaire) · a pain assessment form with a body diagram Pain diary : when · the situation · the sensation (described, rated 1-10) · the distress (described, rated 1-10, separately) · action taken Pain scales: verbal, visual analogue, 0-10 numeric and faces 2. Pain is shaped by the mind Pain = "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage" Shaped bottom-up and top-down by: prior experiences · attention and expectation · mood (anxiety, depression) · nerve chemistry and structural changes · genetics · peripheral and central sensitization Dimensions of pain : physiological (onset, duration, cause) · sensory (intensity, quality) · affective (mood, anxiety, depression, well-being) · cognitive (meaning of pain, view of self, coping, beliefs) · behavioural (communication, activity, pain behaviours, medications) · sociocultural (family, work, recreation, social influences) Subjective , but objective markers track it: pain behaviours · physiological measures · change in function Stimulus → attention → interpretation → coping strategy → behaviour , with learning from the consequences, inside the limits set by culture and family Fear-avoidance model : pain experience → catastrophizing (fed by negative mood and threatening illness information) → pain-related fear → avoidance → disuse, depression, disability → more pain no fear → confrontation → recovery Work : workplace factors (loads, organization, psychosocial context) poorly matched to the individual → discomfort, pain and tissue damage Fear-avoidance model: catastrophizing and fear lead to avoidance and disability; confrontation leads to recovery 3.
