Pediatric orthopedics Children's bones are not small adult bones: they bend, they have a growth plate that breaks first, and they remodel. The lecture is an approach to pediatric musculoskeletal (MSK) problems in two halves: injuries (fracture patterns, growth plate, apophysis) and the developmental problems you screen for (hip dysplasia, clubfoot, leg shape, scoliosis). The limping child has its own chart: 09 - Child with a Limp . ⭐ A child's growth plate fails before the ligament - a "sprain" in a child may be a Salter-Harris I fracture , and every growth plate injury needs follow-up for 1-2 years · type II is the most common · Barlow pushes out, Ortolani slips in, both useless after 3-6 months · Pavlik harness up to 6 months · Ponseti casting then boots and bar for clubfoot · bow legs normal to 2, knock knees 3-7 · scoliosis rarely hurts, and surgery aims to stop progression. 1. How children's bones differ More porous and pliable → different fracture patterns Periosteum (outer bone-forming layer) is thicker and more active → adds width and drives healing Physis (growth plate) = cartilage at the ends of long bones a site of relative weakness : the growth plate is more likely to fail than a ligament, so children fracture rather than sprain or dislocate injury can cause growth arrest Long bones grow by endochondral ossification : a hyaline cartilage model is replaced by bone at primary (diaphysis) and secondary (epiphysis) ossification centres; the physis is replaced last Apophyses = tendon insertion sites: where avulsions and overuse injuries happen 2. Pediatric fractures Mechanisms : falls from low height · sport · pedestrian struck · vehicle operator · non-accidental injury in infants and toddlers Most are single-limb and minor Fracture What happens Typical site Buckle Cortex buckles on itself under compression - the most common Distal radius metaphysis after a fall on an outstretched hand Greenstick Bone bends and breaks on one side only Mid-shaft Plastic deformation Bone bows with no visible fracture line — Avulsion A burst of muscle contraction pulls the apophysis off a fast-growing bone · any apophysis Pelvis (the lecture's case: a 14-year-old boy with sudden anterior hip pain and an antalgic limp in a 100 m dash) · 5th metatarsal · medial epicondyle · treatment often non-surgical Three fractures only children get: buckle, greenstick and plastic deformation Healing is seldom the problem - getting the alignment right early is ("as long as the two bone ends are in the same room they will heal together") · alignment criteria depend on the child's age Remodelling (the skeleton restoring its own alignment) helps: at least 2 years of growth left · metaphyseal fracture · defect in the plane of the joint does not help: displaced intra-articular fractures · mid-shaft fractures with significant angulation or rotation · defect out of the joint's plane Closed reduction : get everything ready first · hematoma block or conscious sedation (most control) → splint or cast (duration by site and type) → always post-reduction and post-casting films to check the reduction → timely follow-up casting is an active treatment that takes skill and experience reductions fail when not pre-planned on the X-ray and the deformed arm · when details are missed (direction and size of the force, translation AND angulation, hand position while moulding) · or the cast has excess padding or is too short 3. Growth plate injuries: Salter-Harris Type Fracture line Notes I - Slipped Straight through the physis Often misdiagnosed as a sprain (sprains are rare in kids) · excellent prognosis · stable with closed reduction II - Above Through the physis and up into the metaphysis Most common · distal radius · prognosis usually good · usually stable with closed reduction III - Lower Through the physis and down into the epiphysis Intra-articular · needs an anatomic reduction · prognosis usually good IV - Through Metaphysis, physis and epiphysis Intra-articular · danger of a bony bridge between metaphysis and epiphysis · lateral condyle of the humerus, distal tibia · needs anatomic reduction V - Rammed Compression of the physis Often missed · diagnosed late, by the growth arrest · refer to orthopedics for follow-up Major complication: growth arrest → leg length discrepancy or angular deformity · about 10% develop a growth disturbance risk factors: age · severity · type (IV and V) · method of reduction · vascularity of the growth plate · open versus closed injury treatment depends on the growth remaining Every growth plate injury is serious, whatever the type or site : follow at least 1 year (preferably 2) and warn the family about complications Salter-Harris types I to V: through the physis, into the metaphysis, into the epiphysis, through all three, and a compression 4. Elbow and overuse injuries The elbow is a confusing area of pediatric trauma : ossification centres vary in appearance, the very young have none at all, and the exam is often limited Elbow ossification centres should appear in this order and by these ages , CRITOE , at about 1 · 3 · 5 · 7 · 9 · 11 years : capitellum · radial head · internal (medial) epicondyle · trochlea · olecranon · external (lateral) epicondyle Swelling = suspect a more serious bony injury. Call pediatric orthopedics for: a significantly swollen elbow (especially before ossification) · instability · a displaced fracture · an incongruously reduced dislocation Apophysitis = overuse traction injury at a tendon insertion, in adolescents Osgood-Schlatter disease (tibial tuberosity: microavulsions from repeated traction partly separate it; girls 8-14, boys 10-15 ; localized pain, swelling, tenderness, usually gradual) · Sinding-Larsen disease (distal patella) · Sever's disease (calcaneus) clinical diagnosis · benign and self-limiting, settles within 2 years , excellent prognosis · RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) when acute · activity as tolerated (often modified) · anti-inflammatories as nee

The child with a limp A limping child's age narrows the list, and one question comes first: is this a septic joint? After infection is ruled out, three hip conditions own the lecture - transient synovitis (young, after a virus, settles), Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (school-age, the femoral head dies), and slipped capital femoral epiphysis (overweight teenager, an emergency). ⭐ An overweight teenager with a limp and knee pain has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis until the hip x-ray says otherwise - stop weight-bearing and call orthopedics · fever, high markers and refusal to bear weight point to a septic joint, not transient synovitis · transient synovitis: 3-10, after a virus, afebrile, normal tests, gone in 7-10 days · Perthes: 4-8, painless limp, avascular femoral head, keep the motion. 1. Approach Abbreviations: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) · juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) · slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) · non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) Kocher criteria (septic arthritis vs transient synovitis of the hip): temperature over 38.5 °C · white cell count over 12 × 10⁹/L · ESR over 40 mm/h · cannot walk on it · (C-reactive protein was added later) Uncommon but serious at every age : leukemia · tumours (neuroblastoma metastases and eosinophilic granuloma under 4; Ewing sarcoma 4-16; osteoid osteoma and osteosarcoma in teens) Other causes : missed developmental dysplasia of the hip (painless waddle, leg length difference) · clubfoot · overuse injury · trauma · neuromuscular disease · inflammatory arthritis Warning signs in any abnormal gait : asymmetry · getting worse · leg length difference · pain · deformity · an associated condition 2. The three hip conditions Transient synovitis Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease Slipped capital femoral epiphysis What Non-infectious inflammation of the hip lining after a viral infection Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head Fracture through the growth plate: the head ends up posterior and inferior on the neck - done to rule out septic arthritis X-ray AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral (flattening, fragmentation) · bone scan, MRI X-ray AP and frog-leg : earliest sign a wide, irregular physis · Klein's line along the top of the neck misses the head (Trethowan sign) · MRI if unclear Treatment NSAID and reassurance · self-limiting in 7-10 days Refer orthopedics · keep range of motion with physiotherapy (better motion, better outcome) · take weight off (crutches, brace, swimming, cycling) · NSAIDs, acetaminophen · surgery (osteotomy) for some Stop weight-bearing at once · emergency orthopedics · pin it where it lies ( do not force a reduction ): stable → one screw in situ · unstable → open reduction and internal fixation Outcome Full recovery Early osteoarthritis if poorly treated Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (about 25%) · arthritis · the fixed physis stops growing (little growth left) Abbreviations in the table: C-reactive protein (CRP) · anteroposterior (AP) Perthes can look like transient synovitis early on (Kai) SCFE outside the usual age or weight → look for an endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency) SCFE on a hip diagram: the growth plate widens first, then a line along the top of the femoral neck no longer cuts the femoral head Perthes disease: a normal femoral head beside one collapsed by avascular necrosis

Physical activity prescription Physical activity works like a drug, so prescribe it like one: check it is safe, then write a dose with F.I.T.T., then tailor it. The biggest gain comes from getting inactive people to do some , and a doctor's advice alone raises activity. ⭐ 150 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity plus strength training twice a week - and the biggest gain is from none to some · talk test: sing = light, talk = moderate, no conversation = vigorous · blood pressure over 180/100 is an absolute contraindication until controlled · raised blood pressure without symptoms → start at low to moderate intensity · F.I.T.T. = 5 times a week, moderate, 30 minutes, aerobic · beta-blockers blunt heart rate, so cap intensity. 1. Why prescribe it Low fitness is an independent risk factor for all-cause mortality , as important as smoking, hypertension and high cholesterol → helping patients move more matters as much as helping them stop smoking or lower blood pressure and cholesterol Risk reductions : all-cause mortality 30% · cognitive decline 40% · type 2 diabetes 35% · hypertension 33% · depression 48% · bone fractures 66% · breast cancer 20% · coronary heart disease and stroke 25% · colorectal cancer 19% Bones and muscles : regular activity cuts hip fractures 55% , through fewer falls (strength, proprioception, coordination, gait, reaction time) · small rise in bone density (1-3%) with regular high-impact training (strengthening, jogging) Heart and blood : ↑ oxygen uptake and use · ↑ endothelial function · ↑ plasma volume, ↓ viscosity · ↑ contractility, coronary flow and stroke volume · ↓ oxygen demand, heart rate and blood pressure In coronary heart disease, stroke and heart disease, exercise compares with drug treatment for mortality Evidence as "medicine" in over 30 conditions, among them depression, anxiety, dementia, type 1 and 2 diabetes, hypertension, lipids, obesity, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic back pain, cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, stroke How much regular physical activity cuts the risk of eight conditions and of death overall 2. How much: the guidelines and the talk test At least 150 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic activity (Canadian guidelines, adults 18-64: in bouts of 10 minutes or more) plus muscle and bone strengthening at least 2 days a week · vigorous only: 75 minutes a week · build strength, sit less, improve balance More is better (dose-response), but the largest benefit is going from none to some → target the sedentary · even 5 minutes has real benefits Intensity How it feels Talk test Examples Light Little change Can sing — Moderate ↑ breathing and heart rate, warmer, may sweat if hot or humid Can talk, not sing Brisk walking, stairs, cycling, dancing, swimming Vigorous ↑↑ breathing and heart rate Cannot hold a conversation Sports, running, aerobics, cardio machines Strengthening Heavy enough that only 10-15 repetitions are possible — Standing from sitting, stairs, heavy gardening or shopping, weights, bands, push-ups, sit-ups 3. Is it safe? Screening and risk Death during vigorous exercise is rare (about 47 per 100,000 a year, vs 190 for motorcycle accidents and 260 for cancer) → sedentary patients start low, go slow Any patient with unstable or uncontrolled symptoms must be reviewed before starting Absolute contraindications : new or uncontrolled arrhythmia · resting or uncontrolled tachycardia · resting blood pressure over 180/100 · symptomatic hypotension · unstable or crescendo angina · acute or unstable heart failure · unstable diabetes · acute febrile illness Cardiovascular risk Screening and advice Asymptomatic, low risk Self-directed activity Asymptomatic, low risk but significant risk factors (e.g. ↑ blood pressure) Begin with low to moderate intensity Asymptomatic, high risk Possible cardiovascular investigations (ECG) first Symptomatic cardiovascular disease Supervision at first, or referral to an exercise specialist Pre-participation screening (American College of Sports Medicine) : regular exerciser? → signs or symptoms? → known disease? · symptoms → medical clearance (a regular exerciser stops ) · known disease without symptoms → clearance if inactive, moderate intensity if already active · none → light-to-moderate if inactive, moderate-to-vigorous if active signs and symptoms: chest, neck, jaw or arm pain · breathless at rest or mild exertion · dizziness or syncope · orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea · ankle edema · palpitations · claudication · known murmur · unusual fatigue · stop and evaluate if any occur during exercise 4. Writing the prescription History : current activity · intentions · past activity and enjoyment (school, job, leisure, everyday) · preferences (alone, team, group, indoors or out) and barriers · is it safe (symptoms, past history) Goals are personal - playing with grandchildren, less breathless on stairs, lower disease risk (often after an event such as a myocardial infarction or cancer), looking good (not everyone is moved by health) The lecture's case : a 68-year-old woman, sedentary (used to walk her dog on trails), worried about falling · new, untreated hypertension (140/85) · father died after a myocardial infarction at 70, mother broke a hip at 73 The 3 A's : Ask (current activity, do they know the benefits) · Advise (on the benefits) · Act (signpost on to help and support) F.I.T.T. Means Typical prescription Frequency How often 5 times a week (aerobic) Intensity How hard Moderate - can talk but not sing Time How long 30 minutes Type What kind Aerobic: walking, cycling, dancing, swimming, jogging Adjust if there is severe pain during exercise, pain that does not settle afterwards, more night pain, or more joint swelling 5. Hypertension and its medications Hypertension : control blood pressure over 180/100 with medication first · warm-up 15 min and cool-down 10 min

MSK oncology: the soft tissue mass Almost every lump is benign, but the one that is a sarcoma must not be shelled out like a lipoma. The lecture turns on which features make a mass suspicious , and what to do before anyone cuts: image and core biopsy, not excise. ⭐ Over 5 cm, deep, fixed, growing or painful → image (MRI) and core biopsy before anyone excises it - under 5 cm with no suspicious feature can be excised · no fine needle aspiration for primary diagnosis · sarcomas are usually painless and spread to the lung (stage with CT chest) · wide resection plus mostly pre-operative radiation · adjuvant chemotherapy is not standard. 1. Soft tissue and its tumours Soft tissue = non-epithelial, extraskeletal tissue (muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, vessels, nerves), excluding the reticuloendothelial system, glia and the supporting tissue of organs · from mesoderm ("mesenchymal") Benign tumours are about 100× more common than malignant (about 300 vs 2 per 100,000) · sarcoma = a malignant tumour of soft tissue or bone · rare Incidence rises with age , except the pediatric sarcomas : neuroblastoma · rhabdomyosarcoma · Ewing sarcoma · equal distribution around the world Soft tissues under the microscope: skeletal muscle, vessels, nerve, smooth muscle, fat and fibrous tissue 2. Causes and classification About 99% have no known cause · trauma: myositis ossificans Known links environmental: asbestos → mesothelioma · vinyl chloride → angiosarcoma · herbicides, dioxin, radiation, foreign material → undifferentiated sarcoma virus: human herpesvirus 8 → Kaposi sarcoma immunodeficiency: chronic lymphedema → angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves) genetic: Li–Fraumeni syndrome (p53) · retinoblastoma (Rb) · neurofibromatosis (neurofibromin) Named by the adult tissue they resemble : Tissue Benign Malignant Fat Lipoma Liposarcoma Skeletal muscle Rhabdomyoma Rhabdomyosarcoma Smooth muscle Leiomyoma Leiomyosarcoma Fibrous tissue Fibroma Fibrosarcoma Peripheral nerve Neurofibroma Neurofibrosarcoma Behaviour : benign - limited growth, may recur, no spread · intermediate - locally aggressive, no or rare (5-10%) metastasis · malignant - locally aggressive, metastasises often well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumour) recurs locally but does not spread · it can progress to dedifferentiated liposarcoma , which recurs and metastasises Diagnosis is histological: routine histology first (it sets the differential and picks the extra tests), then histochemistry, immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics, molecular tests, electron microscopy 3. History and exam History - pin the timeline down : when first noticed, how big then and now (compare to fruit or nuts) → has it grown? trauma · pain or numbness ( sarcomas are usually painless ; significant symptoms → think metastases , and document them before you do anything) · recurrence (what was it called before?) · other lumps (multiple lipomas are common) · family history of lumps (lipomas and sarcomas can run in families) Exam : location, size, skin changes · consistency · superficial (subcutaneous) or deep (muscle) · mobile, tethered or fixed · regional nodes (uncommonly involved) Reassuring Suspicious Limited growth · minimal symptoms · superficial Rapid growth · pain · recurrent · deep · fixed · difficult location 4. What to do next Under 5 cm, no suspicious features → excise Over 5 cm, or under 5 cm with any suspicious feature → imaging (MRI preferred, CT, rarely ultrasound) or a surgical expert BEFORE biopsy Why not just cut it out? The common presentation: a lump thought benign, sarcoma never on the differential, excised with little or no margin, and the pathology says sarcoma ("whoops") · errors in biopsy or excision can reduce the chance of cure and lead to amputation Biopsy , by a physician experienced in sarcoma, disturbing the mass as little as possible core needle - the best compromise: less invasive, adequate tissue, good diagnosis · incisional - more tissue, more invasive · excisional - not ideal if it is a sarcoma fine needle aspiration is cheap, easy, fast and atraumatic but not used for primary diagnosis : poor cell yield, hard to tell tumour types apart, too little tissue for extra tests then expert pathology review with ancillary tests Lipoma or well-differentiated liposarcoma? Immunohistochemistry: MDM2 negative and CD34 positive → lipoma 5. Treatment and prognosis Staging first (CT chest) · all possible sarcomas go to a multidisciplinary team Surgery : wide resection (a cuff of normal tissue) is preferred · marginal resection is the "whoops" · a wide resection with a 1-2 cm margin is rare; one with a positive or close margin is common, hence the radiation Radiation : added to surgery it cuts local recurrence from 30% to 10% · mostly pre-operative : better long-term function, because only the tumour is radiated and the surgery removes most of the radiated tissue · in the lecture's cases: 6 weeks of radiation, then surgery 6-8 weeks later Chemotherapy : uncommon (select subtypes, trials) · adjuvant chemotherapy is not standard (no survival benefit) · very curable with chemotherapy plus radiation or surgery: osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma in young adults Leiomyosarcoma and liposarcoma: often curable with surgery plus radiation Not curable → palliative care can still greatly improve quality of life Follow-up (the lecture's case 2): clinic at 6 months, chest X-ray yearly, discharged with no recurrence at 5 years Prognosis tools: nomograms such as Memorial Sloan Kettering's

MSK infections First decide how deep the infection goes - skin, a closed space in the hand, a joint, or bone - because depth decides the treatment. Skin infections get antibiotics; pus in a closed space, a joint or dead bone needs drainage or debridement too : antibiotics alone will not save you . ⭐ Depth decides treatment: cellulitis (dorsal hand, irregular edge) gets antibiotics; a closed-space hand infection, an infected joint or dead bone needs drainage or debridement too - antibiotics alone will not save you. Kanavel's 4 signs = flexor tenosynovitis. Cat bite → Pasteurella; human bite → Eikenella. Several infected joints → think endocarditis. MRI is the most sensitive test for osteomyelitis; vertebral osteomyelitis = blood cultures + MRI spine, 6 weeks of IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone. A diabetic foot wound is not always infected, and a swab always grows something. 1. An acutely swollen joint or soft tissue Musculoskeletal infections can sit in : joint · bone · tendon sheath (tenosynovitis) · bursa (bursitis) · muscle (pyomyositis, myositis) · skin and soft tissue (cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis) Differential of an acute monoarthritis : infectious (bacterial, viral, mycobacterial, fungal) · crystal (gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD)) · inflammatory (reactive arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoid) · trauma · blood (hemarthrosis) · malignant History : onset · which joints · fever, rash · exposures (intravenous (IV) drug use, sexual contact, travel) · past medical and social history, past procedures · immune-compromising conditions, inflammatory joint disease (rheumatoid arthritis) Exam : vital signs · effusion, redness, old scar, rash · warmth, a subtler effusion felt, compare with the other side · range of motion and function limited by pain · red flags for infection: fever, pain, a big loss of range of motion Septic arthritis of one joint (also on the acute monoarthritis chart, 08 - Acute Monoarthritis ) How : blood-borne seeding or direct inoculation · risk : immune compromise, type 2 diabetes, alcohol, age over 80 , IV drug use, rheumatoid arthritis · the joint is a "synovial Petri dish": inflammation → joint damage Organisms : adults - S. aureus (methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant (MRSA)) · streptococci (group A, also B, C, G) · rarely gram-negative bacilli · children - S. aureus, streptococci Investigations : blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, C-reactive protein · blood cultures · joint aspirate (cell count, cut-offs over 20 000 and over 50 000 · microscopy for crystals · Gram stain) · ± imaging · keep the differential open: coagulopathy, HIV, travel Treatment = surgery (incision and drainage) + antibiotics : joint decompression · irrigation (removes the organisms and the proteolytic and lysosomal enzymes) · debridement of dead soft tissue · goal: keep the synovium as an immune-competent natural barrier Empiric : cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours vs vancomycin 15 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours · course 2-4 weeks by the references, in practice S. aureus 4-6 weeks Older patient, septic or gout? both may be febrile · septic: high white count, positive culture or Gram stain · gout: joint fluid 20 000-50 000, monosodium urate crystals on microscopy 2. Approach to polyarthritis Several sore joints: is it inflammatory or degenerative, acute or chronic, and which joints in what pattern? Every inflammatory arthritis is a clinical diagnosis : the history (timing, pattern, risk factors) and the extra-articular clues get you there; tests narrow it down. Don't reflexively order an antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) on every patient with joint pain - consider your differential first. ⭐ Symmetric small + large joint polyarthritis sparing the DIPs is rheumatoid arthritis; asymmetric with DIPs, dactylitis and psoriasis is psoriatic; axial with large peripheral joints is a spondyloarthropathy; symmetric weight-bearing is OA. Acute is 6 weeks or less. Red joint → aspirate. A negative ANA rules out connective tissue disease; a positive one rules nothing in. RF and anti-CCP are for diagnosis and prognosis, never for follow-up; anti-CCP is the specific one. Lupus and Sjögren's do not erode. Gout crystals are negative needles; pseudogout crystals are positive rhomboids. 1. Classifying arthritis Type : inflammatory (an immune response attacks the joint: autoimmune · infectious · crystalline ) vs non-inflammatory (degenerative = primary osteoarthritis (OA) , or secondary OA, e.g. after inflammatory arthritis · cartilage breakdown from recurrent structural trauma · trauma · avascular necrosis · neuropathic (Charcot) · recurrent hemarthrosis · hemochromatosis) Duration : acute 6 weeks or less · chronic over 6 weeks · Number : mono 1 joint · oligo 2-3 · poly 4 or more Synovitis (inflamed synovium) = more fluid ( swelling ) · warmth · pain · stiffness · redness only with infection or crystals 2. Causes of inflammatory polyarthritis Acute (under 6 weeks) Chronic (over 6 weeks) Polyarticular gout · infectious and post-infectious, including viral · rheumatic fever · drug reaction ( serum sickness ) · early rheumatoid, connective tissue disease, vasculitis or seronegative arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis · connective tissue disease (lupus, myositis, Sjögren's, scleroderma, mixed) · reactive arthritis · seronegative spondyloarthropathy (psoriatic, enteropathic) · palindromic rheumatism · systemic vasculitis · polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis · adult-onset Still's · sarcoidosis · drug reactions Many acute polyarthritides become chronic if the basis is autoimmune Acute differential: mainly inflammatory ( infectious · early autoimmune · crystalline ) · chronic : mainly established seropositive and seronegative autoimmune disease Viral arthritis : during or weeks after the infection · self-limited , supportive care; if severe, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and a short prednisone course (the viruses: see 01 - MSK Infections ) 3. History: timing, pattern, risk factors Onset : acute (hours to days) → crystal, infectious · insidious (weeks to months) → rheumatoid, connective tissue disease, degenerative Course : episodic (comes and goes, usually acute, lasting days) → crystal · migratory → palindromic rheumatism, rheumatic fever, early gonococcal arthritis · progressive and additive → rheumatoid, connective tissue disease, degenerative Pattern (small: metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal and distal interphalangeal (PIP, DIP), metatarsophalangeal (MTP), interphalangeal (IP) · medium/large: shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, ankle · axial: spine, sacroiliac) Pattern Think Symmetric, small + large joints Rheumatoid arthritis (other symmetric: lupus, connective tissue disease) Asymmetric, small + large joints Psoriatic arthritis (other asymmetric: gout, reactive) Primarily axial , with peripheral large joints Axial spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis) Symmetric, mainly weight-bearing Osteoarthritis Joint clues : axial → ankylosing spondylitis · 1st carpometacarpal (thumb base) → OA · 1st MTP → gout, OA · DIPs → OA, psoriatic arthritis; spared in rheumatoid and other connective tissue diseases · MCPs → rheumatoid, calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) · wrists, shoulders, elbows, ankles → rheumatoid, CPPD, psoriatic Other musculoskeletal findings : synovitis · tenosynovitis · dactylitis (sausage digit) · enthesitis (tendon insertion) · bursitis · deformities (nodules, Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, swan-neck, boutonnière, ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation) Risk factors : age, sex, ethnicity · family history (autoimmune disease · psoriasis · inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)) · triggers (infection, medication, injury, diet for gout) · comorbidities (psoriasis, IBD, chronic kidney disease) Age : degenerative rare to start young , rises with age · inflammatory: rheumatoid arthritis and most connective tissue diseases peak around age 40 , a second, later peak = elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetric small joints of the hands and feet plus large joints, with the distal interphalangeal joints spared Osteoarthritis: distal and proximal interphalangeal joints, thumb base, big toe, and the weight-bearing hips, knees and spine 4. Extra-articular manifestations Disease Look for Rheumatoid arthritis Ulnar deviation and MCP subluxation · rheumatoid nodules · pulmonary nodules · episcleritis Psoriatic arthritis Skin psoriasis · nail pitting , nail psoriasis · enthesitis · dactylitis · uveitis Reactive arthritis Conjunctivitis · urethritis · arthritis ("can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree") · vesicopustular skin lesions Gout Tophi · podagra · olecranon bursitis Osteoarthritis Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes Lupus Malar rash · discoid lupus · oral ulcers · subacute lupus rash Dermatomyositis Heliotrope · Gottron's sign and papules · shawl, V and holster signs · mechanic's hands Scleroderma Sclerodactyly · Raynaud's · calcinosis · nail-fold capillary changes By organ system : eyes (uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis, dry eyes (sicca)) · mouth (aphthous ulcers) · skin (malar rash, diffuse photosensitive rash, Gottron's, vasculitic rash, erythema nodosum, livedo reticularis, Raynaud's, tophi, nodules, keratoderm

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis A child with a joint swollen for more than 6 weeks and no other cause: which of the seven subtypes is it? The subtype, set by fever and rash, or how many joints in the first 6 months , decides the uveitis screening and the treatment . What makes children different from adults is growth and silent uveitis . ⭐ A young ANA-positive girl with oligoarticular JIA has the highest risk of silent uveitis, so she needs slit lamp screening every 3 months whatever her joints are doing. Oligoarticular = 4 or fewer joints, a painless limp, almost never the hip. Systemic = daily spiking fever + salmon rash, mistaken for infection or leukemia, risk of macrophage activation syndrome, interleukin-1 or -6 blockers. Enthesitis-related = boys over 10, HLA-B27, painful red eye, 30% become ankylosing spondylitis. ANA prognosticates, it does not diagnose. 1. Definition and presentation Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) : onset under 16 · 1 or more joints · lasting over 6 weeks · other causes excluded (a diagnosis of exclusion) the diagnosis is clinical : bloodwork and imaging are adjuncts The most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood (about 1 in 1000 Canadian children), rarer than adult inflammatory arthritis (1%) · most subtypes more common in girls · rare before 6 months Presents as : joint pain with inflammatory features: morning stiffness, better with movement, responds to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · usually subacute or chronic · altered weight-bearing, functional loss parents notice · may have extra-articular features Red flags (think of something else) : constitutional symptoms · acute onset · severe pain · can't walk · night pain waking the child · severe tenderness or redness of the joint 2. The seven subtypes Subtype Share Who Joints and features Labs and eyes Oligoarticular 35%, the most common Girls 4:1 · under 6 (usually 1-3, peak 2-4) 4 or fewer joints , 1-2 at first: knee , ankle, wrist, elbow · warm, swollen, not very tender → "painless limp" · almost never the hip Antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive → highest uveitis risk Polyarticular, rheumatoid factor (RF) negative 15% Girls 3:1 · younger (2-5) 5 or more joints in the first 6 months, slow onset · fewer joints, asymmetric · stiff 60+ min after inactivity · fatigue RF negative Polyarticular, RF positive 5% (3-5%) Girls · older (10-14, late teens) Many joints · like adult rheumatoid arthritis RF positive Systemic (Still's disease) 10% Boys = girls · any age Spiking fevers ≥ 39 °C once or twice daily , late afternoon, well between · evanescent salmon rash with the fever · aches without swelling early , effusions later · unwell during the fever, better when it settles · big liver and spleen, nodes, serositis · lethargy, weight loss, growth disturbance · often thought to be infection or leukemia White cells and platelets high, anemia · the most serious subtype Enthesitis-related 10% Boys · over 10 Enthesitis · sacroiliitis · dactylitis · may have peripheral joints · family history of ankylosing spondylitis, bowel disease, psoriasis, uveitis, reactive arthritis HLA-B27 in 50% · uveitis symptomatic (pain, photophobia, decreased vision), often recurrent, may be both eyes · often a good prognosis, but 30% develop ankylosing spondylitis Psoriatic 10% Girls · two peaks (young and preteen) Family history of psoriasis · nail pitting, onycholysis (nail lifting) · dactylitis - Undifferentiated 15% Any age Fits none of the categories, or 2 or more (e.g. oligoarthritis + family history of psoriasis + HLA-B27) - Oligoarticular prognosis is usually good, in thirds : ⅓ no other joints, may remit for good · ⅓ 1-2 more joints but 4 or fewer in total · ⅓ extend to many joints ("extended course") The "twins" (enthesitis-related and psoriatic) are the childhood forms of the adult seronegative spondyloarthropathies 3. Complications: a growing skeleton Untreated synovitis over time → muscle atrophy · joint contracture · joint damage and deformity · leg length discrepancy Growth : general growth slows during active disease · local: shortening or lengthening of a limb · micrognathia (small jaw) the inflamed joint first shows advanced maturation (early ossification: carpal bones, patella), then growth arrest early epiphyseal closure → short limb or small mandible · inflamed during adolescence → delayed closure → long limb X-ray: soft tissue swelling, effusion, periarticular osteopenia · joint space loss and erosion uncommon · ankylosis of the neck and wrist possible Morbidity : uveitis → blindness · functional disability · rarely joint replacement · growth disturbance · lower rates of finishing school and reaching work goals · macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA A big impact on growth and development and on the physical, social and emotional functioning of the child and family · early detection and referral prevent morbidity Accelerated ossification: more carpal bones have appeared in the inflamed right wrist than the left in a 2-year-old 4. Uveitis Anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature · mostly in the first 4 years of JIA Typically asymptomatic (except in enthesitis-related) and does not track the arthritis , so regular slit lamp screening · untreated → synechiae, glaucoma, cataract , band keratopathy, cystoid macular edema, blindness Risk factors: ANA positive · girl · young · recent onset Screening interval by subtype, age at onset, disease duration and ANA ANA-positive oligo- or polyarticular, onset at 6 or under → every 3 months for the first 4 years , then 6 months for the next 3 every other oligo- or polyarticular child → every 6 months (7 years if onset at 6 or under · 4 years if onset over 6) then yearly · systemic → yearly throughout Treatment : steroid drops → oral steroids → methotrexate → biologics (infliximab, adalimumab) · uveitis can drive treatment on its own Anterior, intermediate and posterior uveitis; JIA mostly causes the anterior form 5. Osteoarthritis A chronic single joint that hurts with use is osteoarthritis (OA) until a red flag says otherwise. It is a clinical diagnosis : the X-ray stages it, it does not make it. Then ask the four questions: what stage? which biomechanical factors can be fixed? is there a role for medicines? do they need surgery? No treatment yet preserves the joint; every one aims to improve life with it. ⭐ Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis - activity-related pain, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, a cool joint, no red flags - and the X-ray only stages it. A warm joint is not OA. OA is not wear and tear: it is a whole "sick joint" that fails to heal. Only active, exercise-based therapy works; passive therapies do not. No drug preserves the joint. Joint replacement is for end-stage disease only; arthroscopy is not recommended. 1. Chronic monoarthritis: the differential 1. Osteoarthritis · 2. osteoarthritis · 3. osteoarthritis · 4. chronic crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition, CPPD), basic calcium phosphate) First tell it apart from mechanical or sports causes of chronic knee pain (no arthritis) Less commonly: inflammatory (autoimmune) arthritis (rheumatoid, seronegative, juvenile idiopathic arthritis) · neuropathic (Charcot) joint (diabetes, syphilis) · chronic infection (atypical mycobacteria, with immunosuppression) · neoplasm (pigmented villonodular synovitis, synovial chondromatosis) · avascular necrosis or spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee 2. Diagnosis and staging Presentation of chronic OA monoarthritis one joint: knee >> hip; ankle; shoulder >> big toe (1st metatarsophalangeal joint) · thumb base and hand joints usually come with a polyarthritis pain, aching or stiffness brought on or worsened by activity · not chronic widespread pain (think something else) morning stiffness under 30 minutes (usually under 5) exam: joint tenderness · cool or similar-temperature effusion (not warm or hot) · joint thickening · crepitus Diagnosis = must have + must not have must have : joint pain, stiffness or aching on most days, chronic (over 6 weeks) , worse with activity must not have (red flags): infection · autoimmune disease (rheumatoid, seronegative spondyloarthritis) · malignancy · injury (fracture) · avascular necrosis · or crystal disease, tendinopathy X-ray : changes alone do NOT diagnose OA, but they are specific → use it to stage (early, established, late or end-stage) · also the classification criteria for OA research studies what it shows: joint space narrowing and osteophytes · end stage: severe joint space narrowing, bone on bone ⚠ MRI or bone scan: almost never - expensive; only to rule out other problems when the diagnosis of OA is in doubt Kellgren-Lawrence grades on knee X-rays: grades 1-2 early OA, grades 3-4 late to end-stage OA Kellgren-Lawrence (K/L) grade : 1-2 = early OA · 3-4 = late to end-stage OA 3. OA as a disease Epidemiology : 1 in 7 Canadian adults over age 20 · the most common joint disorder worldwide · symptomatic hip and knee OA is the 11th-leading cause of disability worldwide · most symptomatic knee OA starts at 35-55 disability = loss of mobility = poor quality of life symptomatic knee OA prevalence rises exponentially in the 4th and 5th decades Primary OA (the majority) : risk factors but no clear cause - obesity and metabolic syndrome · ageing and senescence (cartilage thins, making the tissues more susceptible; age raises the risk but does not cause OA) · mechanical factors : joint trauma, alignment · polygenic genetic risk (family history) · female sex 1.4× · muscle weakness · occupation Secondary OA : caused by an underlying disease or injury - post-traumatic (after an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or meniscus tear) · metabolic or endocrine (acromegaly, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis) · rare monogenic (Stickler, Marshall syndromes, skeletal and chondral dysplasias) · joints damaged by inflammatory autoimmune arthritis (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis) post-traumatic OA is never "too young" : anterior cruciate ligament tear at 23 → knee OA by 36 · over 50% risk of needing a knee replacement by 55 , likely higher without goal-directed, evidence-based management Pathophysiology : a "sick joint" - every joint tissue is affected · OA is NOT caused by wear and tear or age ; risk factors make the tissues susceptible · chronic metabolic and physiologic stress → inflammation, pain, breakdown · joint failure (like heart failure) = failure of the tissues to heal → remove what impairs healing (obesity, inactivity) 4. Treatment The approach, four questions what stage? early · late · end-stage which biomechanical factors can be treated? alignment · overuse or repetitive injury · weakness · gait disturbance is there a role for medical treatment? to improve pain, function, quality of life do they need surgery (joint replacement)? only end-stage disease with unacceptable symptoms and impact on quality of life Goals : non-drug and drug treatments improve symptoms (less pain, better function, less disability, better quality of life) · limited by cost, time and access Non-drug (hip and knee) : lose 5% of body weight · 150 minutes of activity a week (walk, swim, bike) · neuromuscular control (Tai-Chi, GLA:D) · walking aids, insoles, shoes, unloader brace · joint protection education · cognitive behavioural therapy · topical heat physiotherapy means ACTIVE therapy : it must involve exercise, preferably neuromuscular for balance and strength · ✘ passive therapies (ultrasound, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), laser, acupuncture) are not recommended education, usually by occupational therapy: protect the joint from what aggravates it · avoid risky movements Drugs (hip and knee) : topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (diclofenac two or three times daily) · acetaminophen (clinically meaningful effect?) · oral NSAIDs if no contraindications · duloxetine (a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, SNRI) · int

Seronegative arthritides A family of inflammatory arthritides that are rheumatoid factor negative and HLA-B27 linked: spine and sacroiliac joints, entheses, sausage digits and uveitis. Ankylosing spondylitis is the prototype; the others are told apart by what comes with the joints: psoriasis, a recent infection, or bowel disease . ⭐ Back pain that starts under 40, creeps in over months, stiffens for over an hour in the morning, wakes them at night and gets better with exercise is inflammatory: think ankylosing spondylitis and image the sacroiliac joints. Seronegative = rheumatoid factor negative, HLA-B27 linked. Psoriatic arthritis: asymmetric, distal interphalangeal joints, dactylitis, nail changes; avoid hydroxychloroquine. Reactive arthritis: young man, gut or genital infection 1-3 weeks before, can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree. Conventional DMARDs don't help spinal disease; TNF and IL-17 inhibitors do. 1. The family Spondyloarthritis (SpA) = inflammation of the spine and spinal joints, but it can be purely peripheral with no back symptoms Enthesitis = inflammation where a ligament, tendon or joint capsule inserts into bone, ending in new bone or fibrosis "Seronegative" because rheumatoid factor is absent · linked to HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27) Members : ankylosing spondylitis (the prototype) · psoriatic arthritis · reactive arthritis · arthritis with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis · acute anterior uveitis · undifferentiated · juvenile ( enthesitis-related ) What points to SpA symptoms: inflammatory back pain · peripheral arthritis · enthesitis (heel) · anterior uveitis imaging: sacroiliitis on X-ray or MRI labs: raised ESR and CRP (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) · HLA-B27 · family history predisposing diseases: infection ( Chlamydia ) · psoriasis · Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis history: good response to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) 2. Inflammatory vs mechanical back pain Inflammatory (spondyloarthritis) Mechanical Age at onset Under 40 Any Onset, duration Insidious, over 3 months Acute, under 4 weeks Morning stiffness Over 60 minutes Under 30 minutes Night pain Yes No Activity Improves it Worsens it Exam Sacroiliac tenderness · lost mobility in all planes · reduced chest expansion No sacroiliac tenderness · abnormal flexion · normal chest expansion Neurologic deficits Unlikely Possible 3. Comparing the three main diseases Ankylosing spondylitis Psoriatic arthritis Reactive arthritis Who 0.1-1.4% of people 5-7% of people with psoriasis (psoriasis: 1.2% of people) · first-degree relatives 50× more likely to get arthritis Young men, 20-40 · formerly "Reiter's syndrome", a name not to use Trigger Genetic (HLA-B27) Psoriasis first in ⅔, arthritis first or together in ⅓ Gut or genitourinary infection 1-3 weeks earlier (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter; Chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections) · not an infected joint Spine Starts at the sacroiliac joints (both sides, symmetric) and climbs → new bone fuses it into a rigid column ("bamboo spine") Axial in 20-40%: asymmetric sacroiliitis, large non-marginal "jug-handle" syndesmophytes Sacroiliitis Peripheral joints Usually a lower-limb oligoarthritis ; can come before the back pain Asymmetric oligoarthritis (over 50%) · rheumatoid-like (15-25%) · distal interphalangeal joints (5-10%) · arthritis mutilans (5%) Large-joint oligoarthritis · enthesitis Signature extras Anterior uveitis (25-30%) · aortitis, aortic insufficiency, conduction problems · upper-lobe lung fibrosis Nail changes (80% , vs 30% in psoriasis alone) · dactylitis (sausage digit) · conjunctivitis 20%, uveitis 7% (uveitis more with axial disease) "Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree" : conjunctivitis or uveitis + urethritis or cervicitis + arthritis · keratoderma blennorrhagicum · circinate balanitis HLA-B27 Over 90% of white patients (50-80% others) · but 8% of the white general population carries it · 50-100× the risk Some (also B38, B39, DR4) Linked Course Progressive fusion Variable Self-limiting, chronic or progressive · chronic arthritis or sacroiliitis in 15-30% Treatment Physiotherapy for all (posture, chest expansion, fewer deformities) · NSAIDs (indomethacin best) : mild-moderate symptoms, watch for gut side effects · conventional DMARDs don't work in the spine (peripheral disease only) · TNF or IL-17 inhibitors (symptoms, range of motion, fatigue) Methotrexate (skin + joints) , sulfasalazine, leflunomide · apremilast · TNF inhibitors (skin, joints, spine, nails) · IL-12/23 (not the spine), IL-17, IL-23, JAK inhibitors · avoid hydroxychloroquine (psoriasis flares) · conventional DMARDs: little proof they stop X-ray progression · apremilast = phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor, skin + joints, slows X-ray progression, weaker than biologics · TNF inhibitors also treat enthesitis and dactylitis and slow X-ray progression · IL-17: skin, spine and joints By symptoms DMARDs = disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs · TNF = tumour necrosis factor · IL = interleukin · JAK = Janus kinase Ankylosing spondylitis: bony bridges fuse the vertebrae into a "bamboo spine" 4. Ankylosing spondylitis in more detail Genetics : twins 60% concordant if identical, 20-25% if non-identical and HLA-B27 positive Sacroiliitis on a pelvic X-ray : usually bilateral and symmetric, the synovial-lined lower ⅔ first · earliest erosion on the iliac side (thinner cartilage; "pseudowidening") → sclerosis → complete fusion Classification : modified New York criteria (radiographic sacroiliitis, grade 2 or more on both sides or grade 3-4 on one , + at least 1 clinical criterion) · ASAS (Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society) axial SpA: ≥ 3 months of back pain, onset under 45, then sacroiliitis on imaging + at least 1 SpA feature, or HLA-B27 + at least 2 other features · imaging = active inflammation on MRI or definite sacroiliitis on X-ray Non-radiographic axial SpA : no diagnostic sacroiliac change on X-ray

Connective tissue disorders Connective tissue is in every organ, so these autoimmune diseases are multi-system, more common in women, usually antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive, often with Raynaud's. The lecture's five: SLE, Sjögren's, systemic sclerosis, inflammatory myositis and mixed connective tissue disease . Tell them apart by the signature feature and the specific antibody , then treat by which organ is involved and how badly . ⭐ A negative ANA makes lupus highly unlikely; a positive ANA proves nothing, so order anti-DNA only when the ANA is positive. Hydroxychloroquine is the anchor drug for every lupus patient. The malar rash spares the nasolabial folds; the discoid rash scars. Anti-DNA and anti-Smith point to lupus, anti-Ro/La to Sjögren's, anti-Jo-1 to myositis with lung disease, anticentromere to limited and anti-Scl-70 to diffuse scleroderma. Dermatomyositis in an older adult can be paraneoplastic. Scleroderma renal crisis → ACE inhibitor. APS with fetal loss → ASA + heparin, not warfarin. 1. Telling them apart Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) Sjögren's syndrome Inflammatory myositis ( dermato- , polymyositis ) Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) How common 1 in 1000 · women 9:1 , young (the most common) Half of cases with SLE · in 10-20% of SLE 2 in 10,000 1 in 100,000 1 in 10,000 Signature Rash in the sun · oral ulcers · non-erosive arthritis · serositis · kidney · counts down Recurrent clots (arteries or veins) or recurrent pregnancy loss · livedo reticularis · low platelets Dry eyes + dry mouth (sicca) · parotid swelling · dental caries Proximal weakness (shoulders, hips, neck), high creatine kinase (CK) · dermato: heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules , mechanic's hands · poly: no rash Tight skin (sclerodactyly) · Raynaud's in nearly all · dysphagia, reflux · fingertip ulcers Key antibodies ANA (over 95%) · anti-double-stranded DNA · anti-Smith · antiphospholipid · low C3, C4 Anticardiolipin · lupus anticoagulant · false-positive Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) syphilis test · must be persistent ANA 80-90% · rheumatoid factor (RF) 90% · anti-Ro and anti-La ANA 80% · anti-Jo-1 (very specific; lung disease, bad prognosis ) ANA over 95% · limited: anticentromere · diffuse: anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I; lung fibrosis), anti-nucleolar, anti-RNA polymerase (renal crisis) Danger Kidney · brain (seizure, psychosis) · cardiovascular events from early atherosclerosis · infection Catastrophic APS ("thrombotic storm") B-cell lymphoma (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, MALT) Cancer (dermatomyositis, older adults) · swallowing and aspiration · heart rhythm · interstitial lung disease Highest mortality of all : lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, heart, renal crisis Mainstay of treatment Hydroxychloroquine for everyone + steroids by severity Anticoagulation by situation (below) - High-dose steroids → steroid-sparing drug Treat the organ involved Choose the best disease (the lecture's own drill): proximal weakness + high CK → polymyositis · the same + new Raynaud's + rash over the knuckles → dermatomyositis · dry eyes and mouth → Sjögren's · rash in the sun + oral ulcers → SLE · dysphagia, Raynaud's, fingertip ulcers, sclerodactyly → systemic sclerosis · repeated clots + livedo → APS · not specific: interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's, a positive ANA the lecture's cases: sun rash, mouth and nose sores, ANA + anti-DNA, blood and protein in the urine → SLE · dry eyes and mouth with new repeated cavities, parotid swelling, anti-Ro, anti-La, purpura on the shins → Sjögren's · retrosternal dysphagia, tight skin of hands, arms and face, crackles at the lung bases, nucleolar ANA, anti-Scl-70 → systemic sclerosis 2. Lupus: what to look for Classification criteria, not diagnostic criteria (made to standardise research groups) 1982 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) : at least 4 of 11, for over 6 weeks (below) · many still use it · a second set from the SLE International Co-operating Clinics (SLICC) 2019 EULAR/ACR (European and American rheumatology bodies): ANA ≥ 1:80 required + 10 or more points , at least one clinical domain, highest item per domain, "ever had" counts, nothing with another explanation Lupus can be systemic (SLE) or skin only (cutaneous) · subacute cutaneous lupus : widespread, non-scarring, photosensitive rash (upper back, shoulders, arms, neck; face often spared), usually anti-Ro positive , in either form Lupus loves rashes : besides the three in the criteria, livedo reticularis and vasculitis (small vessel = leukocytoclastic · larger vessel = the digital arteries) Criterion What sets it apart 1. Malar rash (butterfly) Fixed redness over the cheeks and nose, spares the nasolabial folds · photosensitive · presenting feature in under ⅓ · not rosacea , which has dilated vessels, isn't autoimmune and doesn't spare the folds 2. Discoid rash Raised patches with adherent scale and follicular plugging · head, neck, arms, hands · heals with scarring 3. Photosensitivity Rash in any sun-exposed area 4. Oral or nasal ulcers Often several, sometimes painless, witnessed, no other cause 5. Arthritis Inflammatory, prominent morning stiffness, non-erosive 6. Serositis Pleuritis (worse breathing in, effusion) · pericarditis (worse lying down, effusion, ECG changes) 7. Kidney Glomerulonephritis : protein + blood in urine, a rising creatinine is bad · World Health Organization classes: 1 normal or minimal change · 2 mesangial · 3 focal proliferative · 4 diffuse proliferative (the worst) · 5 membranous 8. Neurologic Seizures or psychosis with no drug or metabolic cause (uremia, ketoacidosis, electrolytes) 9. Blood Hemolytic anemia (Coombs positive, reticulocytes, large mean corpuscular volume) · white cells under 4.0 or lymphocytes under 1.55, on 2 or more occasions · platelets under 100,000 with no offending drug · antibodies break the cells apart 10.
