Vasculitis Vasculitis is inflammation of the blood vessel wall, and the patient feels sick all over. The lecture asks two things: when to suspect it in a vague multi-system illness, and how to tell the types apart by the size of vessel they hit , with giant cell arteritis as the emergency you cannot miss. ⭐ Suspected giant cell arteritis (over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR and CRP) → draw the blood, then prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg) now; biopsy after. Rule out infection before immunosuppressing. Normal ESR and CRP make giant cell arteritis highly unlikely; a negative temporal artery biopsy does not rule it out. Large = giant cell and Takayasu, medium = polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki, small = the ANCA trio, cutaneous leukocytoclastic and Henoch-Schönlein purpura. Order ANCA only when small vessel vasculitis is suspected; a negative one does not rule it out. 1. What inflamed vessels do Mechanism : immune cells infiltrate the vessel wall wall thickens → less blood downstream → can block completely → ischemia and clots damaged wall can balloon out → aneurysm Presents as : systemically unwell (fevers, weight loss, fatigue, fast pulse, diffuse aches) · almost any organ, so examine head to toe · some types are uniformly fatal if untreated A normal artery, then narrowing from inflammation, total occlusion, and an aneurysm with clot 2. Primary vs secondary Primary = no known cause, over 20 disorders, sorted by vessel size Secondary = an identifiable cause, so look for it first : infection : hepatitis B and C, HIV, other viral, bacterial, fungal toxins and drugs : allergic reaction, cocaine cancer : blood cancers, paraneoplastic connective tissue disease : lupus , rheumatoid arthritis , Sjogren's syndrome Infection matters most to exclude : rule it out before making a diagnosis , because steroids make an infection worse 3. Classification by vessel size Vessel size Examples From the lecture Large giant cell arteritis · Takayasu arteritis Giant cell arteritis is the most common vasculitis Medium Classic polyarteritis nodosa · Kawasaki disease · Behcet's disease Kawasaki disease: one of the two most common in children Small, ANCA-associated granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's) · microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) · eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss) The most common systemic small vessel vasculitides Small, others Cryoglobulinemia · cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis · Henoch-Schönlein purpura Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis can stand alone or be part of another type (the lecture's case: painful non-blanching purpura on the legs, ankle pain and swelling, unwell for 6 weeks · differential: coagulopathy or vasculitis) · Henoch-Schönlein purpura: the other most common in children 4. When to suspect it, and the workup Suspect primary vasculitis in someone: chronically unwell with fevers, chills or weight loss · several organ systems · purpura · very sick with multi-organ failure · lung hemorrhage plus renal dysfunction · and no infection or cancer found Diagnosis is hard: rare, many types, variable and vague symptoms that can take years, many organs, mimics common diseases, can be caused by other diseases · yet diagnose it in time to prevent complications History and exam are critical ; tests confirm. Biopsy of an involved tissue clinches it , but is not always possible Every patient : head-to-toe history and exam · rule out infection · age-appropriate cancer screening up to date · complete blood count, creatinine, liver enzymes, ESR and CRP (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein), urinalysis · chest X-ray · urgent rheumatology referral , other services by organ inflammation (non-specific) : normocytic anemia · reactive thrombocytosis · high ESR and CRP · low albumin (chronic) silent organ damage : kidneys and lungs may give no symptoms → creatinine · blood and protein in the urine · chest X-ray (nodules in GPA) rule out infection : white cells · blood, urine, sputum cultures (fungal, acid-fast) · liver enzymes · hepatitis B and C (cryoglobulins, low complement) · HIV · syphilis (VDRL) rule out cancer : age-appropriate screening · serum protein electrophoresis What vasculitis can do to each organ, from stroke and vision loss to purpura and glomerulonephritis 5. Giant cell arteritis Who : only over 50 (most over 70) · lifetime risk 1% women, 0.5% men · Northern European descent Which vessels : a large vessel vasculitis with a predilection for cranial arteries, especially the temporal artery (temporal arteritis) Presents as : new headache · temporal and scalp tenderness · jaw claudication · tongue claudication · diplopia · vision loss · stroke · plus fatigue, fever, weight loss, limb claudication, Raynaud's, chest pain, arthritis · polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (limb girdle pain and stiffness, worse in the morning): see 03 - Body Pain Exam : tender temples · swollen, rope-like temporal artery · optic disc swelling · pulselessness, bruits, blood pressure difference Vision loss in 15-20% : may be transient ( amaurosis fugax ); untreated, total loss follows in the same and the other eye within days to months · acute painless loss is permanent Differential of the cranial picture : sinusitis · cranial neuropathy · dental infection · intracranial tumour · temporomandibular arthritis · severe hypertension · acute angle-closure glaucoma · migraine or cluster headache · meningitis or encephalitis · neck pain Investigations ESR and CRP immediately : if neither is raised, GCA is highly unlikely (under 2% are negative for both) temporal artery biopsy within 1-2 weeks : transmural inflammation + giant cells is 100% specific , but 50-70% are negative (skip lesions) , so a negative biopsy cannot rule it out temporal artery Doppler ultrasound in specialised centres: halo sign (wall edema), specificity over 85%, absent in ~30%, unreliable outside specialty centres Management draw ESR and CRP, then start prednisone 1 mg/

Acute monoarthritis A hot, red, swollen joint is infected until the fluid says otherwise. Acute monoarthritis = one inflamed joint for less than 6 weeks (oligo = 2-3 joints, poly = 4 or more), and its differential is infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout (and, rarely, reactive or psoriatic arthritis). The three look alike at the bedside, so the needle, not the exam, decides . ⭐ Any red, hot, swollen joint gets aspirated for the 3 C's - cell count, culture with Gram stain, crystals - because septic arthritis is an emergency that gout and pseudogout imitate exactly. Gout = needle-shaped, negatively birefringent, big toe; pseudogout = rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent, knee of an older person with osteoarthritis. Septic arthritis = admit, urgent I&D, empiric IV cefazolin (or vancomycin + ceftriaxone), 4-6 weeks. Uric acid can be normal during an attack, and high uric acid alone is not gout. Never start allopurinol during an attack. Cell counts are inflammatory in all three: the Gram stain, culture and crystals decide. 1. Approach: if the joint is red, aspirate it What it is: an intense inflammatory response to a foreign organism or substance in a joint · must rule out infection · crystals of uric acid or calcium pyrophosphate can do it too Aspirate ( joint aspiration ) and send the 3 C's : cell count (a couple of hours) · culture and sensitivity with Gram stain (24-48 hours) · crystals (a couple of hours) "To inject is human, to aspirate divine" - never inject a steroid before infection is excluded Fluid in the three lecture cases: septic ankle 59 · gout 15 · pseudogout 18 (× 10⁹ cells/L as the slides print it, all inflammatory ) · so the cell count does not separate them: Gram stain and culture find the infection (Gram-positive cocci in clusters); crystals tell gout from pseudogout (detailed fluid interpretation: 01 - Rheumatology Investigations ) 2. Septic arthritis - a medical emergency Septic arthritis : without rapid detection and treatment → fulminant joint damage Organisms : gram-positive cocci 80% - Staphylococcus 60%+ , Streptococcus 20% · gram-negatives 15% (immunocompromised, elderly, neonates, intravenous (IV) drug users) · anaerobes (adults: S. aureus, including methicillin-resistant (MRSA), and group A, C, G streptococci) How it gets in : through the blood from a remote site (#1) · direct inoculation (penetrating trauma, recent surgery) · spread from infected bone next door Risk factors systemic: immunosuppressed - diabetes, cancer, methotrexate, leflunomide, prednisone, anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and other biologics · very young or old · alcohol excess, IV drugs · recent infection local: prosthetic joint · recent joint surgery · existing joint disease (arthritis) · penetrating trauma · skin infection Workup : aspirate (3 C's) · blood cultures · blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, C-reactive protein · ± imaging Treatment : admit · urgent incision and drainage (I&D) - an infected joint is a closed space - repeated until the joint is clean · empiric IV antibiotics : cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours , or vancomycin 15 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours (MRSA risk) · 4-6 weeks in all the lecture's case: sent urgently to the emergency department · orthopedic surgery consulted · to the operating room that evening · started on IV cefotaxime · analgesia and rest 3. Gout vs pseudogout Gout Pseudogout Crystal Uric acid (monosodium urate) Calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) Under polarized light Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent Rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent Typical joint Lower limb · 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe) in 50% Lower limb · knee most common Who Men 35-50 · women after menopause (estrogen helps excrete uric acid) Older people, often with osteoarthritis Risk factors Impaired kidney function · diuretics (furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide) · alcohol · family history · male · with obesity, hypertension, diabetes, high lipids — Onset Over a few hours, very intense · can't stand the bedsheets touching it · may have fever Less intense, slower to peak · may have fever Untreated About 7-10 days Several days to a few weeks Bloods Blood count (white cells, platelets may rise) · creatinine · uric acid (may be normal during an attack) · fasting glucose, lipids — Acute treatment Rest, ice, elevation · steroid injected into the joint · oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor (COXIB): indomethacin 50 mg by mouth three times daily · colchicine 0.6 mg every 8 hours · prednisone 30 mg daily × 2 days, then down 5 mg every 2 days Rest, ice, elevation, hydration · steroid injected into the joint · oral NSAID or COXIB: indomethacin 50 mg three times daily · the same prednisone taper (no colchicine on the lecture's list) Prevention Allopurinol (below) · diet, less alcohol, hydration — Polarized microscopy: needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent urate crystals (gout) vs rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals (pseudogout) 4. Gout in more detail "The disease of kings": acute inflammatory arthritis from uric acid crystals deposited in the joint Hyperuricemia : production > excretion · under-excretion is the commonest reason · ⚠ many people with high uric acid never get gout → hyperuricemia CANNOT diagnose gout, and isolated hyperuricemia is not treated Uric acid rises with age : steadily in men · in women only after menopause Order of treatment (the overflowing sink): mop up first = treat the attack · then lower the level = treat the hyperuricemia if needed Triggers (SMARTS) : S urgery · M echanical injury · A lcohol · R ecent illness · T ravel or dehydration · S tarting or stopping allopurinol Diagnosis : aspirate and find urate crystals - the only proof Diet : meat and seafood are bad · vegetables and low-fat dairy are good · less alcohol · good hydration Recurrence : 60% in 1 year · 80% in 2 · 90% in 5 - one attack makes another likely Allopurinol (blocks xan

Rheumatology investigations No rheumatic disease is diagnosed by a blood test alone - there must be clinical features too (the one exception is gout , proven by uric acid crystals in joint fluid). For a suspected connective tissue disease (CTD) the antinuclear antibody (ANA) is the screen and comes first ; anti-DNA only follows a positive ANA , the extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) panel names the antibody, and complement is a specialist's test . ⭐ Order the ANA only when you suspect a connective tissue disease - a positive rules nothing in, a negative makes most CTDs less likely - and never follow a negative one with anti-DNA, or repeat it · anti-DNA is very specific but only ~50% sensitive, and tracks renal lupus · anti-Sm is the fairly specific ENA; Ro goes with photosensitive lupus and congenital heart block · complement is a specialist's test · rheumatoid factor is non-specific; anti-CCP is the specific one · ANCA only when vasculitis is suspected. 1. ANA: what it is and when to order it What it is : autoantibodies that bind to antigens in the nucleus of cells - the immune system should make antibodies to foreign proteins, not human ones Order it only when you suspect an autoimmune connective tissue disease - otherwise it is a waste of money about 1 in 3 women are ANA positive , but lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) is 1 in 1,000 → many false positives yes : weight loss, a new rash in the sun, high creatine kinase and new weakness · new oral ulcers, hair loss, low white cells and platelets · new glomerulonephritis of unknown cause (yes/maybe) no : a low white count explained by myelodysplastic syndrome with no lupus features · fatigue and widespread pain (fibromyalgia) Reading it : a titre - the stronger the positive, the larger the dilution: 1/1280 is a strong positive · the pattern can change with the dilution (1/80 speckled and homogeneous, 1/640 homogeneous) Do not repeat it : not a negative from a year ago with no new symptoms, and no utility in following the titre - a positive at any time can count in the criteria for SLE A positive ANA does not rule in disease ; a negative ANA makes most CTDs less likely CTDs are heterogeneous · many have characteristic clinical and lab features that make the diagnosis · treatment depends on the organ involved and the severity, and should involve a specialist 2. Anti-DNA An autoantibody against the DNA in the nucleus → the ANA should be positive Order only with a positive ANA, when you are expecting SLE - a young woman with low white cells, low platelets, a malar rash and hair loss gets the ANA first , not anti-DNA Very specific for SLE but very insensitive: positive in only about 50% Correlates with renal SLE and disease activity - high in active disease, may turn negative after treatment Pitfall: outside labs often use a kit that also detects single-stranded DNA , which is neither sensitive nor specific 3. ENA panel The lab screens positive or negative, then runs more assays for which antibody Antibody Goes with Anti-Ro (SSA) SLE with photosensitivity and rash · babies of positive mothers: congenital heart block , neonatal lupus Anti-La (SSB) Ro and La together → Sjögren's syndrome Anti-Sm (Smith) Fairly specific for SLE Anti-RNP Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) and SLE Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase 1) Scleroderma, especially with interstitial lung disease Anti-PM-Scl Dermatomyositis-scleroderma overlap Anti-Jo1 Polymyositis with interstitial lung disease Anti-RNA polymerase 3 Scleroderma renal crisis 4. Complement (C3, C4) Low in active lupus, especially lupus nephritis - complement is used up when antibodies bind healthy tissue · or an inherent deficiency of one or more alleles Specialist test - a waste of money for a family physician to order 5. Other rheumatology blood tests Pick the test from the clinical picture : acute hot single joint → aspirate (cell count, culture, crystals) · symmetric small-joint polyarthritis → rheumatoid factor + anti-CCP + ESR and CRP · inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, uveitis → HLA-B27 + ESR and CRP + sacroiliac imaging · suspected vasculitis → ANCA Abbreviations: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) · C-reactive protein (CRP) · anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) · human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) · anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) Many tests are also done for safety - which organs are involved, and is it safe to start a drug (blood count, creatinine, liver enzymes, hepatitis B and C) Rheumatoid factor Anti-CCP What it is Antibody (usually IgM) against the Fc end of IgG Antibody against citrullinated proteins Specificity Poor : 5-20% of healthy people · Sjögren's, lupus, myositis, MCTD · hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis, syphilis, endocarditis · lung fibrosis, sarcoidosis · lymphoma High (95%) - separates rheumatoid arthritis from other causes of a positive rheumatoid factor Use Prognosis : positive → more severe disease (erosions, extra-articular features) Can appear years before arthritis · not covered by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) - only if rheumatoid arthritis is suspected; better to refer ESR and CRP : non-specific - raised in any inflammation, never diagnostic · very high in giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica HLA-B27 : in over 90% of white people with ankylosing spondylitis , but 8% of the general white population carry it → a gene is not a disease · order when the picture fits (inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, uveitis) ANCA : only if you suspect systemic vasculitis - not covered by OHIP c-ANCA (anti-proteinase 3) → granulomatosis with polyangiitis · more likely to mean real vasculitis p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase) → microscopic polyangiitis , eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis · more false positives both positive → think cocaine cut with levamisole · levels follow disease activity only loosely c-ANCA stains granules across the neutrophil's cytoplasm; p-ANCA stains around the nucleus

Rheumatology treatments Two kinds of drug: ones that relieve symptoms fast (steroids, NSAIDs, acetaminophen) and ones that change the disease (DMARDs, then biologics). In rheumatoid arthritis joint damage happens early, so start a disease-modifying drug early and aggressively , and use prednisone short term, as a bridge . ⭐ Methotrexate (weekly, teratogenic, liver, marrow and lung toxicity, monthly bloodwork, folic acid) is the first DMARD, started within 3 months - and triple therapy beats one drug · NSAIDs and steroids relieve symptoms but do not stop joint damage · high-dose prednisone only for organ- or life-threatening disease; gout and polymyalgia rheumatica need medium doses · hydroxychloroquine: yearly eye exam, no bloodwork, safe in pregnancy · leflunomide → hypertension · no TNF inhibitor with infection, heart failure class III-IV, cancer or multiple sclerosis · aspirate an acute hot joint before anything is injected. The four drug groups: steroids by dose and route, NSAIDs and analgesics, conventional DMARDs and biologics, each with when to choose it, what to avoid and what to watch 1. Steroids Prednisone : non-specific - blocks pro-inflammatory proteins, ↓ neutrophil migration, inhibits cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), ↓ prostaglandins and leukotrienes · most useful in the ACUTE setting because it works rapidly · ↓ pain, swelling, stiffness and physical disability · good short term, not long term : used short term or as a bridge until steroid-sparing drugs start Dose depends on the condition High (~1 mg/kg of ideal body weight) - life- or organ-threatening: ANCA-associated vasculitis · lupus nephritis · inflammatory myositis · giant cell arteritis · intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone 1 g daily × 3 days ("pulse") in an emergency, to jumpstart it before high-dose oral prednisone, e.g. giant cell arteritis with vision involvement Medium - flares without major organ involvement: rheumatoid arthritis flare 20-40 mg, tapered as the DMARD starts · polymyalgia rheumatica 15-20 mg daily × 4 weeks, a quick taper to 10 mg daily, then down 1 mg every 4 weeks until off · self-limited, lasts 6 months to 2 years · with giant cell arteritis (~15%) → high dose , to lower the risk of blindness · acute gout 25-30 mg × 3 days, then down 5 mg every 3 days (NSAIDs or colchicine work too) · self-limited, so no high dose · lower doses with relative contraindications such as diabetes or cardiovascular disease Low (5 mg or less) - chronic use when nothing else works or is tolerated (the adrenals make the equivalent of ~7 mg a day) Routes : by mouth (easy to taper) · intramuscular (lasts 3-4 weeks; poor adherence) · intravenous (rapid, then switch to oral) · intra-articular when only a few joints or weight-bearing joints are involved, with fewer systemic effects · for inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis, rotator cuff tendinitis Side effects of chronic use : appetite and weight gain · gastritis · mood change, psychosis · infection · Cushing's syndrome · acne · osteoporosis · avascular necrosis · hypertension · hyperglycemia · cataracts and glaucoma · proximal myopathy · slow wound healing · thin skin Relative contraindications → a steroid-sparing drug: diabetes · cardiovascular disease · osteoporosis · recurrent infections · glaucoma or cataract 2. NSAIDs, acetaminophen, opioids Non-selective NSAIDs COX-2 selective Acetaminophen Opioids Examples Ibuprofen 600-800 mg three times daily · naproxen 500 mg twice daily · meloxicam 15 mg daily · diclofenac 75 mg twice daily · indomethacin 50 mg three times daily Celecoxib 200 mg daily Up to 3 g a day in divided doses (e.g. 2 extra strength tablets three times a day) — Action Reversibly block COX-1 and COX-2 → ↓ prostaglandins Block COX-2 only → spare the stomach-protecting prostaglandins Analgesic, NOT anti-inflammatory Do not treat inflammation Use Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, pseudogout · efficacy similar, try another if one fails As NSAIDs, with less GI toxicity Osteoarthritis, mechanical back pain, regional pain Hardly ever used - the goal is to treat the inflammation, which eases the pain · a possible role in chronic pain, but other options preferred (misuse) Watch Hypertension, myocardial infarction, stroke · gastritis, peptic ulcer · renal insufficiency · caution in cardiovascular, GI and renal disease · interactions (anticoagulants) · 3rd trimester: premature closure of the ductus arteriosus · screening CBC, ALT, creatinine Otherwise the same risks Minimal: no stomach, constipation, blood pressure or cognitive effects · liver disease: max 2 g a day Impaired cognition, constipation, dependence and withdrawal NSAIDs are NOT disease-modifying : they ease pain and swelling in new rheumatoid arthritis or flares but do not prevent disease activity or delay erosions Abbreviations: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) · cyclooxygenase (COX) · gastrointestinal (GI) · complete blood count (CBC) · alanine aminotransferase (ALT) · erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) · C-reactive protein (CRP) Arachidonic acid feeds COX-1 (stomach, kidney, platelets) and COX-2 (inflammation, pain, fever); non-selective NSAIDs block both, coxibs only COX-2 3. Conventional DMARDs Why early : joint damage is early - 90% of the joints are affected in the first year, erosions in >90% within 2 years (X-ray progression fastest in the first 2 years), disability is early and half are work-disabled at 10 years, and severe disease raises mortality → a window of opportunity before any erosions Principles : treat early (within 3 months of symptoms) · treat aggressively ( triple therapy beats one drug in early rheumatoid arthritis) · treat to target (remission: no swollen or tender joints) · adjust every 3-6 months if the target is not met Starting : discuss side effects, interactions, contraindications · baseline bloodwork · most need monthly bloodwork Drug Dose · onset Key toxicities Monitoring Notes Methotrexate 20-25 mg

Body pain Pain all over without swollen joints: what kind of pain is it, and is it inflammatory? An older patient with stiff shoulders and hips and raised inflammatory markers has polymyalgia rheumatica , which melts on low-dose prednisone. Diffuse, migratory pain with fatigue, poor sleep and fog is central pain - fibromyalgia - and that is a positive diagnosis, not a leftover. ⭐ Polymyalgia rheumatica = over 50, shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, raised ESR/CRP, no weakness, and a dramatic response to low-dose prednisone within days - no response means the wrong diagnosis. Fibromyalgia has normal inflammatory markers, is a positive diagnosis (2010 criteria), and often sits alongside another disease. Myositis is weakness with a high creatine kinase; PMR is pain without weakness. Fibromyalgia: exercise and education first; duloxetine, pregabalin or low-dose amitriptyline; never opioids. Prednisone over 7.5 mg for over 3 months needs bone protection. 1. The approach ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate · CRP = C-reactive protein · PMR = polymyalgia rheumatica 2. Three kinds of pain Nociceptive Neuropathic Central Cause Inflammation or mechanical damage in the tissue Damage to peripheral nerves Faulty pain processing in the brain and cord → hyperalgesia (pain "turned up") Sounds like Local pain Burning, tingling, electric, numb Diffuse or multifocal, waxes and wanes, migrates · can sound neuropathic · touch and tight clothing hurt Responds to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), opioids, local injections Peripheral and central drugs (NSAIDs, gabapentin ) Drugs that change pain neurotransmitters Examples Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, cancer Diabetic neuropathy , post-herpetic neuralgia Fibromyalgia , irritable bowel syndrome, jaw (temporomandibular) pain, tension headache Any mix can coexist - fibromyalgia alongside rheumatoid arthritis or diabetic neuropathy - and treating the peripheral pain can ease the central pain 3. Pain pathways Ascending (facilitatory) pathway : carries pain up · glutamate on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (plus substance P) · turned up in central pain Descending (inhibitory) pathway : damps the signal · norepinephrine, serotonin, endogenous opioids · turned down in central pain → hypersensitivity In fibromyalgia both are abnormal : less norepinephrine and serotonin breakdown products in spinal fluid, more substance P and glutamate · so any drug that raises norepinephrine and serotonin helps Ascending pain pathway (red) carrying pain up the spinothalamic tract; descending modulation (blue) from the periaqueductal grey and brainstem nuclei 4. Fibromyalgia Definition : widespread pain for 3 months or more with other somatic symptoms, not explained by anything else · about 1 in 100 , mostly women · can follow emotional or physical trauma What patients say central pain: "I hurt everywhere" · "it hurts to be hugged" · light, noise, smells bother them severity: exhausted , cut back work and family · "fog" , forgetful · unrefreshed after 8 hours' sleep · boom-and-bust days somatic, often seen by other specialists first: headaches · jaw pain the dentist can't explain · abdominal pain (irritable bowel) · always feels like a bladder infection (overactive bladder) · non-cardiac chest pain · "stiff hands but the rheumatologist says my joints aren't swollen" 2010 Fibromyalgia Classification Criteria - all three ① widespread pain index 7+ and symptom severity 5+ , or pain index 3-6 and severity 9+ ② symptoms at a similar level for 3 months or more ③ no other disorder explains the pain the 1990 version (3+ painful regions, 11 of 18 tender points) has been replaced - nice to know ⚠ Not a diagnosis of exclusion : it is common to diagnose fibromyalgia plus something else · risk is higher with any rheumatologic or psychiatric disease , IBD (inflammatory bowel disease), multiple sclerosis, hepatitis B and C, Lyme, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus · treating the other disease alone won't fix the fibromyalgia Targeted tests only : muscle pain → creatine kinase · neuropathic symptoms → diabetes workup · joint complaints → examine for swelling · fatigue → complete blood count, ferritin or iron studies, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), CRP, liver enzymes, creatinine, albumin, sleep study Mostly diagnosed and managed by family doctors Treatment Detail Education Family doctor, group programs, the Arthritis Society Exercise Best evidence · weight-bearing or not · Tai Chi, yoga, warm pool · graded, explained, ideally physiotherapy-guided Cognitive behavioural therapy Sleep hygiene · pacing · mindfulness · mood Treat other inputs Nociceptive pain (physio for mechanical back pain, joint injections for osteoarthritis) · sleep apnea · psychiatric illness · rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, endometriosis SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) duloxetine (best evidence) , venlafaxine · work with or without depression · ✘ don't help sleep Gabapentinoids pregabalin , gabapentin · act on the facilitatory pathway · ✔ help sleep Tricyclics, low dose amitriptyline , nortriptyline, cyclobenzaprine · help pain, fatigue and sleep · ✘ no effect on mood ⚠ Opioids Do not use - no better for pain, and sleep, disability and pain interference are better without them Prescribing : emphasise non-drug therapy ( as effective as drugs ) · one drug, lowest dose, titrate slowly · see them regularly · combine if needed · set expectations: half of patients get a 30% improvement 5. Polymyalgia rheumatica Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) = insidious pain and stiffness of the neck, shoulders, upper arms and hips · profound morning stiffness · fatigue · weight loss · mild fever, night sweats Who : over 50 · women, Northern European descent · linked to giant cell arteritis A misnomer : the muscles are normal - no weakness , normal biopsy · the inflammation is in joints and the tissues around them (bursae, tendons, capsules) · exam is normal apart from pain Labs : raised ESR and CRP · anemia · high platelets M

Introduction to neurology Each neurology patient is a logic puzzle: describe the problem, localize the lesion , then use the localization and the history to build the differential diagnosis and plan the tests. The first fork is always central nervous system (upper motor neuron signs) or peripheral nervous system (lower motor neuron signs) . ⭐ Localize first: upper motor neuron = spasticity, hyperactive reflexes, Babinski, no atrophy; lower motor neuron = normal tone, reduced reflexes, atrophy, fasciculations. Lesions at L1 and above are upper motor neuron, below L1 lower. Cerebellum and basal ganglia lesions do not cause weakness. -plegia is paralysis, -paresis is weakness. Middle cerebral artery stroke: face and arm worse than leg. Weak eyes and swallowing point to the neuromuscular junction; generalized proximal weakness to muscle. 1. Why it matters About 10% of patients seen in a family doctor's office come with a neurological symptom Neurology touches everyone: a headache that might be worrying, a parent's stroke to prevent, a patient's first seizure Course order: about 1.5 weeks of neuroanatomy and neurophysiology first, then clinical neurology and neurosurgery, the eye and the ear 2. The vocabulary Term Means -plegia Paralysis , essentially no voluntary movement -paresis Weakness · paraparesis = both legs · quadriparesis = all four limbs · hemiparesis = one side Dysarthria Trouble articulating Aphasia Trouble producing or understanding language · expressive (producing) · receptive (understanding) Dysphagia Trouble swallowing Ataxia Trouble with motor coordination Dysmetria Trouble reaching a specific target Obtunded Reduced level of awareness, cannot be fully roused Dominant hemisphere = where language is housed · usually left in right-handed people Middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke = contralateral weakness of face and arm more than leg , because of where they sit on the homunculus Motor (precentral) and sensory (postcentral) homunculus: face and hand lateral, leg medial 3. How the nervous system is organized Neuron : cell body (holds the nucleus) · dendrites (projections out from the cell body) · axon (long projection that carries action potentials to other neurons or to muscle, through the axon terminal and synapse) · most axons are covered in myelin , which insulates and contains the action potential Central nervous system (CNS) = brain and spinal cord · peripheral nervous system (PNS) = cranial nerves, nerve roots, plexus, nerves, neuromuscular junction, muscle, sensory receptors Grey matter = neuron cell bodies (cortex folded into gyri; basal ganglia and thalamus deep to it; nuclei in the brainstem) · white matter = myelinated axon tracts linking one part of the CNS to another Lobe Functions Frontal Motor · speech production · executive function (planning, problem solving) Parietal Sensation · orienting attention in time and space Temporal Auditory processing · language understanding · memory Occipital Vision Basal ganglia : deep nuclei that combine cortical activity into one movement · speed of movement is a big part of their job Thalamus : relay centre, most sensory input passes through it Limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate and others): emotion regulation and memory Cerebellum : coordinates and fine-tunes movement of limbs, gait, speech and swallowing Brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla): holds all the cranial nerve nuclei and the sensory tracts in and motor tracts out Spinal cord : cervical (C1 to C8), thoracic (T1 to T12), lumbosacral segments · white matter outside (sensory tracts ascend, motor tracts descend), grey matter inside (cell bodies) · ends at about the L1 vertebral body , below which lie the lumbar roots ( cauda equina ) Planes : coronal · axial · sagittal Coronal, axial and sagittal planes of the brain 4. The three pathways Motor : motor cortex (plans movement, contralateral to the action) → white matter tracts → brainstem → crosses in the medulla → spinal cord → anterior horn cell → nerve root → peripheral nerve → neuromuscular junction → muscle Refinement loops back to the motor cortex: the cerebellum improves accuracy, the basal ganglia control timing and integration cerebellar lesion: no weakness , but poor coordination basal ganglia lesion: no weakness , but either slow, hard-to-start, rigid movement ( parkinsonism ) or excess movement (chorea, dystonia, athetosis, hemiballismus) Sensory : peripheral nerve → root → spinal cord → brainstem → thalamus → white matter → primary sensory cortex Dorsal column (vibration, proprioception): runs on the same side until it crosses in the medulla Spinothalamic (pain, temperature): crosses on entering the spinal cord , runs up the lateral cord Visual : the image lands inverted and flipped on the retina → optic nerves → optic chiasm , where the left half of the visual field from both eyes goes to the right optic tract (and vice versa) → occipital pole 5. Upper or lower motor neuron Upper motor neuron (brain or spinal cord) Lower motor neuron (anterior horn cell, root, plexus, nerve, neuromuscular junction, muscle) Tone Spasticity Normal tone Tendon reflexes Hyperactive Reduced or absent Plantar response Extensor (Babinski) Flexor or absent Atrophy No significant atrophy Muscle atrophy Fasciculations None May be present 6. The clinical approach - Four steps : describe the problem (summarize symptoms and signs) → localize the lesion → differential diagnosis → plan investigations and management - How to localize 1. CNS or PNS? Upper motor neuron features point to the CNS, lower motor neuron features to the PNS 2. Narrow it down: signs of cortex (language, neglect)? sensation affected or spared? painful or painless? distribution? bladder symptoms? - Why localize : it decides what to image, or whether it can be imaged at all (no computed tomography (CT) of the head for a spinal cord problem) - Spinal cord ends at about L1 : lesions at L1 and above give an upper motor neuron pattern, below L1 a lower motor neuro

Introduction to neuroanatomy A map to hang the rest of neuro on: where things are (the brain's parts, the lobes, the brainstem and its cranial nerve nuclei, the spinal cord tracts, the ventricles and vessels) and what each one does, so that a sign or symptom can be traced back to a place. ⭐ Brainstem nuclei go 2-4-4: midbrain III-IV, pons V-VIII, medulla IX-XII (CN XI nuclei in the rostral spinal cord). FLAIR has no CSF signal, so it shows white matter abnormalities; T2 makes CSF bright. Central sulcus = frontal from parietal; insula = taste. Middle meningeal artery rupture → epidural hematoma. Astrocyte foot processes are part of the blood-brain barrier. 1. Basic organization Grey matter = nerve cell bodies · white matter = axons, no neuronal cell bodies Central nervous system (CNS) = brain + spinal cord · peripheral nervous system (PNS) = spinal nerves, cranial nerves , ganglia, sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves CNS: integrates and coordinates incoming and outgoing signals · housed in the skull and vertebral canal · protected by the meninges (pia, arachnoid, dura mater) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Functional division : sensory input (afferent, toward the CNS) → integration (interprets, decides) → motor output (efferent, away from the CNS, to muscles and glands) Simple vs complex function : a pain reflex from stepping on something sharp never needs the brain (fast, for survival) · planning universal health care does The brain's four parts : brainstem (medulla + pons + midbrain) · cerebellum · diencephalon · cerebrum (2 hemispheres) grey matter sits inside, around the hollow ventricles, with white matter outside it · the cerebrum and cerebellum add an outer sheet of grey matter, a cortex (not present in the spinal cord) · the rest of the brain's grey matter is in clusters called nuclei 2. Orientation and imaging Directions: rostral-caudal · dorsal-ventral · superior-inferior · anterior-posterior · rostral-caudal and dorsal-ventral follow the bend between brain and spinal cord Planes: coronal (cut from dorsal to ventral) · horizontal / axial (parallel to the horizon) · sagittal (cut from anterior to posterior) Method What it shows X-ray (radiograph) Bony abnormalities · nervous tissue is invisible CT Sectional images at 2 mm resolution · lesions differ in density (brightness) from normal brain MRI T1 Separates central nervous tissue from other fluids and tissues · some grey-white difference MRI T2 Emphasizes CSF · less grey-white contrast MRI FLAIR No CSF signal → detects white matter abnormalities 3. Forebrain: cerebrum and diencephalon Forebrain = telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres + deep structures) + diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, subthalamus) Cerebrum : most rostral and largest part, 80% of brain mass · 5 lobes per hemisphere Fissures split the hemispheres: longitudinal (right from left) · transverse cerebral (cerebrum from cerebellum) · sulci = shallow grooves · gyri = twisted ridges Sulci between lobes : central (frontal from parietal) · lateral (temporal from frontal and parietal) · parieto-occipital (parietal from occipital) Lobe Functions Frontal (anterior cranial fossa) Voluntary movement ( primary motor cortex , precentral gyrus) · planning movement · eye movement · speech production Parietal Processes sensory stimuli ( primary somatosensory cortex , postcentral gyrus) · spatial awareness · understanding speech Temporal (middle cranial fossa) Auditory cortex · olfactory cortex · recognizing objects, words, faces Occipital Visual cortex Insula (covered by frontal, parietal and temporal lobes) General visceral sensation · taste Limbic (medial surface) Cingulate gyrus · parahippocampal gyrus Forebrain (telencephalon, diencephalon) on a sagittal brain 4. Deep structures and diencephalon Basal ganglia : deep forebrain nuclei that integrate cortical activity into one motor output · striatum (caudate nucleus, putamen) · substantia nigra of the midbrain motor control: regulate the intensity of movement, control rhythmic repetitive tasks, help learn habits basal forebrain nuclei make acetylcholine (arousal, learning, memory, motor control) · their degeneration is linked to Alzheimer's disease Thalamus : primary relay and processing centre for sensory information · sensory nuclei for every conscious sense except smell · everything reaching the cortex relays through it connections: limbic system (memory, emotion) · basal ganglia (motor coordination) · primary sensory areas (auditory, visual) Hypothalamus : main visceral control centre · autonomic nervous system (heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, secretion) · emotion and motivation · temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep · endocrine control Epithalamus : pineal gland → melatonin (sleep at night) Cerebellum : posterior to the brainstem, joined by the cerebellar peduncles · pontine nuclei relay between cerebrum and cerebellum to coordinate voluntary movement 5. Brainstem and cranial nerve nuclei Most caudal part of the brain, in the posterior cranial fossa · passageway for tracts between cerebrum and spinal cord · 10 of the 12 cranial nerves attach here · automatic survival behaviours Segment (rostral → caudal) Cranial nerve (CN) nuclei Anterior Posterior Midbrain : motor control, visual and auditory reflexes III, IV Cerebral peduncles · mammillary bodies · optic nerve Superior colliculus (visual reflexes) · inferior colliculus (reflexes to sound) Pons : relay between brain areas, movement and facial expression V, VI, VII, VIII The pons Superior, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles Medulla oblongata : vital autonomic control (breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, digestion) IX-XII (CN XI nuclei sit in the rostral spinal cord ) Pyramids · olives Fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis · obex Pyramids = descending voluntary motor tracts · most cross in the caudal medulla ( decussation of the pyramids ), so each hemisphere moves the opposite side of the body Medullary centres: cardiac · vasomotor (blood pressure) · respiratory

Cranial nerve anatomy and function Twelve nerves, one question each time: what does this nerve carry, how do I test it, and what does a lesion look like? The cranial nerve nuclei and the nerves themselves are the lower motor neuron part of the pathway, so the trick is telling a nerve lesion from an upper motor neuron (cortical, subcortical or brainstem) cause. ⭐ Forehead spared and eye closes weakly = upper motor neuron (central) facial palsy; forehead involved and eye will not close = lower motor neuron (Bell's palsy). Double vision is never from a lesion above the brainstem. Third nerve compression: think posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Corneal reflex = V1 in, VII out. The tongue points to the weak side. Do not test smell with a noxious stimulus. 1. The ground rules Cranial nerves (CN) = bundles of nerve fibres that exit the cranial cavity · 12 pairs · numbered I to XII from front (rostral) to back (caudal) by where they leave the brain Fibres are sensory, motor, or both ; some also carry autonomic fibres names: " O h O h O h T o T ouch A nd F eel V ery G ood V elvet AH " fibre type: " S ome S ay M arry M oney B ut M y B rother S ays B ig B rains M atter M ore" (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both) Sympathetic fibres do not start in a cranial nerve : they reach the head on the internal carotid plexus and hitch a ride on cranial nerves (V1 to the pupil dilator; VII to the lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands) Localizing : voluntary movement runs cerebral cortex → subcortical white matter → brainstem (all central nervous system, upper motor neuron ) → cranial nerve nucleus → cranial nerve ( peripheral nervous system, lower motor neuron ) The 12 cranial nerves leaving the base of the brain, with their targets 2. Facial anatomy The face has two nerves that are easy to mix up: the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) moves the face , the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) feels it and chews . Learn the structures by layer (bone and foramina, muscles, parotid, vessels, nerves) and each finding traces back to one of them. ⭐ The facial nerve (VII) moves the face; the trigeminal nerve (V) feels it, and V3 also works the chewing muscles. The angle of the jaw is not trigeminal: it is the great auricular nerve (C2-C3). Supraorbital, infraorbital and mental foramina = V1, V2, V3. Orbicularis oculi closes the eye; frontalis raises the brow. The facial nerve branches inside the parotid gland. Masseter protrudes the jaw; temporalis retracts it. 1. Bones and foramina Facial skeleton (viscerocranium) : the jaws, the nose and part of the orbit nasal bones · maxilla · zygomatic bone · mandible · the frontal bone is not technically a facial bone but makes up the forehead Foramina (windows or holes) in the facial skeleton transmit nerves and blood vessels ; the trigeminal sensory branches come out through them: Foramen Nerve through it Division Supraorbital (foramen or notch) Supraorbital (from the frontal nerve) V1 Infraorbital Infraorbital V2 Mental Mental V3 2. Introduction to neurophysiology Symptoms follow from how neurons signal: an all-or-none action potential, sped up by myelin, handed across a chemical synapse as excitation or inhibition, inside a cortex where each area has its own job. Break one step (strip the myelin, damage one language area) and you can predict what the patient shows. ⭐ The action potential is all-or-none: strength is coded by firing frequency, never by size. It starts at the axon hillock when depolarization reaches about −55 mV from rest at about −65 mV. Myelin gives saltatory conduction; multiple sclerosis strips it and slows conduction. Ionotropic = fast and local; metabotropic = second messenger, widespread, longer-lasting. Glutamate excites and GABA inhibits in the brain; glycine inhibits in the spinal cord; acetylcholine excites at the neuromuscular junction. Wernicke's: fluent nonsense, cannot understand, unaware; Broca's: effortful, understands, aware. 1. The brain as a network Neurons sit in a thin, heavily folded sheet, the grey matter · about 100 billion neurons and 10 times as many glial cells · each neuron contacts about 1000 others , and those connections hold our memories Axons in fibre tracts (millions of miles in total) form the white matter Signalling is expensive: the brain is 1 to 3% of body mass but uses about 20% of the body's energy , so only a small share of neurons is active at once Grey matter needs more oxygen than white matter , and blood goes preferentially to the grey matter in use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) detects this → shows which cortex is active in a task diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) → shows the axon tracts (white matter) The dense interconnection lets a focus of abnormal activity spread to other areas → why the cortex is prone to epilepsy (a seizure) 2. The neuron The neuron is the functional unit of the nervous system · neurons and muscle cells are excitable (they generate and respond to electrical signals) Part Job Dendrites Collect and integrate incoming signals Soma Cell body Axon hillock Junction of soma and axon · where the action potential starts Axon Carries action potentials over long distances Synapse Contact with other neurons · site of many drugs and toxins A neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, myelinated axon with nodes of Ranvier, axon terminal 3. Membrane potential and the action potential Resting potential about −65 millivolts (mV) , more negative inside · depolarization = less negative · hyperpolarization = more negative A depolarizing stimulus that reaches threshold (about −55 mV) at the axon hillock starts an action potential , which then runs the whole axon to its terminal by activating each segment in turn In health it is all-or-none : every action potential is the same size Frequency coding : information is carried by the pattern of action potentials, not their size · for a touch: how hard = firing frequency on one axon, and how many axons fire how long = how long the firing lasts where = which axons fire (each comes from a different body part) what = which receptors those axons attach to (heat, cold, pain, light or heavy touch) Labelled line coding : each sense has its own dedicated pathway, and the brain reads any signal on that line as that sense (action potentials on the optic nerve are read as vision) Myelin is an insulator that greatly speeds conduction: the action potential skips from node to node ( saltatory conduction ) demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis makes conduction slow and unreliable Ion movements at rest, during depolarization, repolarization and the return to rest 4. The chemical synapse Action potential reaches the axon terminal → calcium-triggered release of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft → binds receptors on the next cell → removed by diffusing away , reuptake or enzyme breakdown Receptor How it works Effect Examples Ionotropic Binding opens an ion channel Fast, local Excitatory (excitatory postsynaptic potential, a brief depolarization) : glutamate , main excitatory transmitter in the brain · acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction · Inhibitory (inhibitory postsynaptic potential, a brief hyperpolarization) : GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), main inhibitory transmitter in the brain, target of many sedating drugs · glycine in the spinal cord Metabotropic Acts through a second messenger (for example G-protein coupled receptors) More widespread, longer-lasting Dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine receptors Synaptic plasticity : N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptors can be modified, so a synapse strengthens or weakens over time · the basis of learning and memory Neuropharmacology : many drugs (treatments and drugs of abuse) are receptor agonists or antagonists , or change reuptake or enzyme breakdown More than 50 neurotransmitters, in 3 classes: amino acids (GABA, glutamate, glycine) · amines (acetylcholine, dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin) · peptides (substance P for pain and inflammation, dynorphin an opioid) GABA-A receptor : ionotropic, fast hyperpolarization · many binding sites that affect each other, so benzodiazepines act more strongly with alcohol · many drugs act at more than one receptor (alcohol also blocks glutamate receptors) 5. Circuits and cortex Divergence (one neuron onto many): motor control , coordinating actions and controlling reflexes Convergence (many neurons onto one): sensation , comparing inputs to extract features Cortex has 6 layers layer 4 = input (from the thalamus and other cortex) · thickest in primary sensory areas · primary visual cortex is called striate cortex because its layer 4 is so thick layers 3 and 5 = output (to other cortex, thalamus, brainstem, spinal cord) · thickest in primary motor cortex Brodmann divided the cortex into 43 areas by structure · each area has its own function ( functional localization ), so a lesion can remove one function and leave the rest intact 6. Aphasia: functional localization in a patient Wernicke's aphas

Orbital anatomy Every orbital symptom points to a structure: know which walls break, where the eye's fluid is made and drained, which nerve moves each muscle and where the orbit's veins lead. Then a blowout, a high-pressure eye, a droopy lid, a wandering eye or a spreading facial infection tells you what is damaged. ⭐ "(LR6 SO4)3": an oculomotor palsy leaves the eye down and out with ptosis, a trochlear palsy up and in, and an abducens palsy cannot look outward (head turn). The thin floor and medial wall break in a blowout fracture (teardrop sign); the lateral wall is strongest. Ciliary body makes aqueous humor, the canal of Schlemm drains it; poor drainage is glaucoma. Pupil constrictor = parasympathetic (III); dilator = sympathetic. Horner syndrome: miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis. Central retinal artery occlusion: instant, complete blindness. Superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus: the route for facial infection. 1. The bony orbit A pyramid of seven bones (frontal, ethmoid, lacrimal, maxilla, zygomatic, sphenoid, palatine). The eye is largely held in place by fat in the orbit, helped by the muscles. Neurophysiology of vision The lens and pupil focus light, the retina turns it into signals and starts finding edges, and the pathway sorts those signals by visual field on the way to the occipital cortex, where ever more complex features are pulled out. Because each level is laid out so precisely, the shape of a visual loss tells you where the lesion is. ⭐ Nasal retinal fibres (temporal field) cross at the chiasm: a chiasm lesion gives bitemporal hemianopia; an optic tract lesion gives a homonymous hemianopia on the opposite side. Near vision = ciliary muscles contract, lens rounds. Fovea = cones only, sharpest and colour, blind in very dim light; periphery = rods, sensitive to light, low acuity. Only ganglion cells fire action potentials in the retina. Glaucoma takes the periphery first, macular degeneration the centre. Dorsal stream = where/action (optic ataxia); ventral = what (agnosia, prosopagnosia). 1. The eye and focusing the image We see only light of 400 to 700 nanometres wavelength, a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum Pupil = the hole in the centre · iris = the coloured part, sets pupil size · sclera = the white · cornea = clear sheet in front of the pupil and iris · retina = holds the photoreceptors · fovea = region of sharpest vision Light passes through the cornea, pupil and lens · the focus on the retina is set by lens shape and pupil diameter Looking at Ciliary muscles Lens Something near Contract Rounder (accommodated) Something far Relax Flat (unaccommodated) Ageing : the lens loses its elasticity and stays too flat for near objects even with the ciliary muscles fully contracted → near objects blur → reading glasses ( presbyopia ) · a short-sighted person who ages needs bifocals When the lens cannot change shape enough (for example because of the eyeball's shape): myopia (focuses near, not far) → concave lens · hyperopia (focuses far, not near) → convex lens Accommodation: a rounder lens focuses a near target, a flatter lens a far one 2. Pupillary light reflex Bright light → iris constricts the pupil → keeps the photoreceptors from being saturated A smaller pupil also sharpens the image (less blur on the retina, greater depth of focus, as with a camera aperture) Light in one eye should constrict both pupils : a simple test of cranial nerves · in through the optic nerve (cranial nerve II) → Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain → out through the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) The pupillary light reflex: retina and optic nerve to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, back out via nerve III to both pupils 3. the only retinal cells that fire action potentials ) · sideways flow through horizontal and amacrine cells Rods Cones Light sensitivity High (larger outer segment) · essential for night vision Low Colour None Three types (trichromatic) Where Mostly the periphery (120 million per eye) Only cones in the fovea Acuity Low: many widely spaced photoreceptors converge on one ganglion cell (large receptive field, about 3 degrees) High : few, closely packed photoreceptors per ganglion cell (small receptive field, about 0.03 degrees) · the fovea is also a pit, so light scatters less Dim stars show in the periphery but vanish when you look straight at them · in very dim light the fovea is basically blind and the brain fills in the gap The fovea covers the central 2 degrees (about 1%) of the visual field but its ganglion cells make up about 50% of the optic nerve Optic disc = blind spot : no photoreceptors where the axons leave the eye · lies nasal to the fovea, so the blind spot is in the temporal half of each eye's field · two eyes and filling-in hide it Tests : a letter chart tests acuity at the fovea · a visual field test (look straight ahead, respond to each flash) finds scotomas (blind spots) Retinal ganglion cell Size and speed Receptive field Share Input and job P (parvocellular) Smaller, slower Smaller 90% Colour , mainly from cones M (magnocellular) Larger, faster Larger 5 to 10% No colour, mainly from rods · flashing or moving stimuli Centre-surround receptive fields (built by bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells): on-centre = how much brighter than the background · off-centre = how much darker · they accentuate edges (first step in feature detection) and give constancy by measuring change across an edge rather than absolute light Colour blindness : about 8% of males (about 2% lack the red or green pigment, red-green dichromats; about 6% have a green pigment shifted toward red, anomalous trichromats) vs about 0.5% of females · usually inherited on the X chromosome 4. Neuroanatomy of the cortex Function is mapped onto the cortex, so a deficit points to a place: learn each area as where it is → what it does → what a lesion looks like , then the white matter that links the areas and the limbic circuit that makes memory. ⭐ Broca's aphasia: non-fluent, comprehension intact; Wernicke's aphasia: fluent but incoherent, comprehension impaired; arcuate fasciculus: understands but cannot respond properly. Motor cortex is precentral (BA 4), sensory postcentral (BA 1, 2, 3), and both serve the opposite side. Left parietal damage = Gerstmann syndrome. Bilateral hippocampal damage = anterograde amnesia; mammillary body necrosis = Wernicke-Korsakoff. Association fibres stay in one hemisphere; commissural fibres cross; projection fibres run up and down. 1. 01 Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon

Neuroanatomy of the brainstem, basal ganglia and diencephalon Four deep structures, each with one job to learn: the basal ganglia choose which movement goes ahead , the diencephalon relays and regulates , the brainstem carries the tracts and the cranial nerve nuclei (III to XII) , and the cerebellum coordinates the same side of the body . For the brainstem, the question is always which level, and which part of that level , because that decides what a lesion takes out. ⭐ Direct pathway (D1) releases the thalamus = GO; indirect pathway (D2, through the GPe and subthalamic nucleus) inhibits it = STOP. Lose nigral dopamine → Parkinson bradykinesia; lose the striatum → Huntington chorea. The subthalamic nucleus is the only excitatory basal ganglia nucleus. Ventral medulla lesion → contralateral hemiparesis; lateral medulla → ipsilateral face pain and temperature loss. Motor nuclei medial, sensory lateral to the sulcus limitans. CN IV leaves the back of the midbrain. A midline (vermis) cerebellar lesion gives truncal ataxia; the cerebellum works on the same side. 1. Basal ganglia: the parts Deep forebrain nuclei inside the cerebral white matter that integrate cortical activity into one motor output (also roles in cognition, learning and emotion). Formed from : caudate nucleus (arches over the thalamus ) · putamen · globus pallidus · amygdala · the substantia nigra of the midbrain also influences them Striatum = caudate + putamen = the input (receives excitatory glutamate from the cortex) putamen = mostly movement (from sensory and motor cortex) · caudate = more cognitive (from association cortex) nucleus accumbens = the ventral striatum Lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus · the internal capsule separates them from the caudate and thalamus Globus pallidus external (GPe) = relay of the indirect pathway · globus pallidus internal (GPi) = the output to the thalamus Subthalamic nucleus (STN) = the only excitatory (glutamate) nucleus · every other basal ganglia projection is GABA (inhibitory) Substantia nigra pars compacta (midbrain) sends dopamine to the striatum (mostly the putamen) and tunes both pathways 2. Direct vs indirect pathway The thalamus is under constant inhibition from the GPi. Release-inhibition model: the direct pathway releases the thalamus (inhibits the inhibitor) → more cortical output; the indirect pathway adds inhibition → less cortical output. Direct pathway ("GO") Indirect pathway ("STOP") Dopamine receptor D1 - dopamine excites it D2 - dopamine inhibits it Chain Cortex → striatum ⊣ GPi ⊣ thalamus → cortex ( bypasses the STN ) Cortex → striatum ⊣ GPe ⊣ STN → GPi ⊣ thalamus → cortex Thalamus Released (ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei → supplementary motor and premotor cortex) Inhibited more Feedback on the cortex Positive Negative Result Starts target-oriented movement Blocks competing movements Disease Parkinson disease : substantia nigra dopamine lost → direct pathway hypoactive (and the indirect one released) → GPi overactive → thalamus over-inhibited → bradykinesia , akinesia Huntington disease : caudate and putamen degenerate → indirect pathway lost → STN and GPi under-active → involuntary movements ( chorea ) (→ excites · ⊣ inhibits) · The opposite imbalance (STN and GPi too inhibited, thalamus too free) causes the hyperkinetic disorders and drug-induced dyskinesias in Parkinson disease. Direct pathway: the striatum inhibits the internal globus pallidus, releasing the thalamus to drive the motor cortex Indirect pathway: through the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, ending in more inhibition of the thalamus 3. Diencephalon The centre core of the forebrain , surrounded by the cerebral hemispheres · paired, mostly grey matter · borders the third ventricle . Part Where What it does Thalamus Middle of the brain · 80% of the diencephalon · ~a dozen nuclei The relay ("gateway") to the cortex : every part of the brain that talks to the cerebral cortex relays through a thalamic nucleus · sensory nuclei for every conscious sense except smell · organizes, amplifies or tones down signals Hypothalamus Between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies · pituitary hangs below · ~a dozen nuclei Main visceral control centre ("the master gland's master"): autonomic system · emotion · temperature · hunger, thirst · behaviour · sleep-wake · endocrine control · memory Epithalamus ( pineal gland ) Roof of the third ventricle Secretes melatonin (under the hypothalamus) → circadian rhythm , sleep at night Subthalamus Below the thalamus Holds the subthalamic nucleus Thalamic nuclei on the slide : anterior · medial · pulvinar · lateral geniculate (vision) · medial geniculate (hearing) · ventral posterolateral (body sensation) · ventral posteromedial (face sensation) · ventral lateral · ventral anterior (motor loops) Hypothalamus, by function (homeostasis): hunger · satiety · cooling + parasympathetic · heating + sympathetic · circadian rhythm · makes ADH and oxytocin · thermoregulation, sexual behaviour, releases GnRH 4. Brainstem: surfaces and levels Rostral → caudal: midbrain → pons → medulla , in the posterior cranial fossa. Three jobs: a passageway for the tracts between cerebrum and cord · 10 of the 12 cranial nerves attach (face and neck) · automatic survival behaviours . The fourth ventricle lies between the pons and cerebellum; the cord's central canal opens into it at the obex . 02 Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum

Neuroanatomy of the spinal tracts and cerebellum Every tract question comes down to two facts: what it carries, and where it crosses. Put those together and a lesion's level and side tell you which modalities go, and on which side, which is how the tracts localize lesions in the cord, brainstem and cortex. ⭐ Dorsal columns cross in the medulla, spinothalamic fibres cross in the cord where they enter, and the lateral corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramids, so a one-sided cord lesion takes vibration, position sense and power on its own side but pain and temperature on the other. Gracilis = medial = below T6; cuneatus = lateral = above T6. Spinocerebellar tracts end on the same side. Lateral system = contralateral, distal limbs, skilled; medial system = bilateral, axial, posture. Sensory = 3 neurons through the thalamus; motor = 2 neurons, UMN and LMN. 1. How the pathways are built Afferent = toward the central nervous system (CNS) (ascending, sensory) · efferent = away from it (descending, motor) · in the CNS cell bodies sit in nuclei and axons run in tracts ; in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) they sit in ganglia (e.g. the dorsal root ganglion) and run in nerves A pathway is a chain of neurons · bilateral (one each side) · named origin → destination (spinothalamic = spinal cord → thalamus) · most decussate (cross the midline): ipsilateral = same side, contralateral = opposite side Spinal cord : 31 pairs of spinal nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal) · the cord ends at the L1/L2 vertebra · ascending tracts mostly in the dorsal (back) compartment and the edge of the cord, descending tracts in the lateral and ventral white matter Sensory chain = 3 neurons 1st order : pseudounipolar, cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (PNS), axon into the CNS 2nd order : cell body in the dorsal horn or a brainstem nucleus ; its axon crosses and synapses in the opposite thalamus 3rd order : cell body in the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus → internal capsule (posterior limb) → primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) Motor chain = 2 neurons : upper motor neuron (UMN) , cell body in the cerebral hemispheres or brainstem , axon usually crosses → lower motor neuron (LMN) , cell body in a cranial nerve motor nucleus (face) or the ventral horn (body) → cranial or spinal nerve → skeletal muscle Spinal cord cross-section: ascending tracts (blue) and descending tracts (red) 2. The three ascending pathways Pathway Carries 1st-order synapse Crosses Ends in One-sided cord lesion Dorsal column-medial lemniscus Fine touch, vibration, pressure, conscious proprioception Nucleus gracilis + cuneatus (medulla) Brainstem (caudal medulla) : internal arcuate fibres → medial lemniscus Primary somatosensory cortex Lost on the same side , below the lesion Spinothalamic (anterior + lateral) Pain, temperature, crude touch Dorsal horn Spinal cord, at the level of entry ( anterior white commissure ) Primary somatosensory cortex + cingulate and insular cortex Lost on the opposite side , below the lesion Spinocerebellar (anterior + posterior) Subconscious proprioception Dorsal horn Posterior: never → inferior cerebellar peduncle · anterior: not at all, or twice (cord + superior cerebellar peduncle) Cerebellum (same side) Same side Dorsal columns : fasciculus gracilis is medial = below T6 (lower limb and trunk) · fasciculus cuneatus is lateral = above T6 (upper limb and neck) · first-order axons climb the same side to the caudal medulla, the second-order axons cross as the internal arcuate fibres and climb as the medial lemniscus to the ventral posterior lateral (VPL) thalamus Spinothalamic : the first-order neuron synapses straight away in the dorsal horn ; the second-order axon crosses immediately in the anterior white commissure and climbs the opposite side to the thalamus Somatosensory cortex = postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe, mapped as a homunculus (lips, tongue, hand large) The medulla: nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send fibres across the midline to form the medial lemniscus 3. Lower motor neurons: where they sit Face : cell bodies in cranial nerve nuclei of the brainstem → axons in cranial nerves Body : cell bodies in the ventral horn → ventral root → spinal nerve → peripheral nerve Medial motor column : every spinal level · axial muscles (posture, balance) · lateral motor column : cervical and lumbosacral cord only · limb muscles (skilled movement) · both act on the same side The LMN is the final common pathway : it integrates every descending tract (cortex, red nucleus, reticular formation, vestibular nuclei) and sensory input into one signal to the muscle 4.
