Cerebellum: the connections Peduncles

Neurophysiology of sensation Each skin receptor reports one kind of touch down its own "labelled line", and two pathways carry sensation to the cortex: one crossing in the medulla, one in the cord. That split is what lets you predict the side of a deficit after a one-sided cord lesion . ⭐ Touch and proprioception cross in the medulla; pain and temperature cross in the cord where they enter, so a cord hemisection loses touch and position sense on the lesion's side and pain and temperature on the other. Pacinian = vibration (rapid, large), Meissner = fine texture (rapid, small), Merkel = edges (slow, small), Ruffini = stretch and finger position (slow, large). Test pain or temperature, not touch, to map a dermatome. Burning and freezing are felt by nociceptors. Cuneate = arm, gracile = leg. 1. Receptors in the skin Skin mechanoreceptors respond to physical distortion (bending, stretching) and differ by depth in the skin , structure and rate of adaptation Touch is needed for fine motor control : a nerve block of the fingertips (which spares the muscle receptors) makes delicate tasks clumsy Receptor Depth Adapts Receptive field Senses best Meissner corpuscle (stacked flat cells, mainly hairless skin) Shallow Rapidly Small Very fine texture Merkel disc Shallow (dermis-epidermis border) Slowly Small Edges, roundness, fine surface detail Pacinian corpuscle (largest, onion-like capsule) Deep Rapidly Large Diffuse vibration (holding a power saw) Ruffini ending (branched fibre in a capsule) Deep Slowly Large Skin stretch → position of the fingers Deep receptors have larger receptive fields because skin compression over a wide area reaches them Hair follicle receptors (free nerve endings wrapped around follicles, very sensitive): localized flutter , a bug landing on the skin Nociceptors (pain), two kinds of free nerve ending on a myelinated axon: fast → early, localized, intense pain that can start a withdrawal reflex on an unmyelinated axon: slow → later, diffuse, long-lasting pain (dull, throbbing) Thermoreceptors : heat-sensitive (hot, not burning) · cold-sensitive (cold, not freezing) · burning or freezing stimuli activate nociceptors Skin receptors by depth: Merkel disc and Meissner corpuscle near the surface, Pacinian corpuscle and Ruffini ending deep in the dermis 2. How a stimulus is coded Mechanotransduction (Pacinian corpuscle) : pressure deforms the capsule → mechanically sensitive ion channels open → receptor potential → an action potential if it reaches threshold Frequency coding : a stronger, longer stimulus → a higher-rate train of action potentials that lasts longer Every receptor responds quickly at onset; they differ in how fast they adapt to continued pressure Labelled line coding : each receptor has its own "private line", so the brain knows which receptor type an axon carries · perception depends on which axon fires, not on how it was stimulated · banging the funny bone fires the ulnar nerve at the elbow and the fingers tingle 3. The two pathways Dorsal column-medial lemniscus Anterolateral (spinothalamic) Carries Touch receptors + muscle proprioceptors Pain + temperature receptors First axon Large dorsal root axons climb the same side in the dorsal columns → cuneate nucleus ( arm ) or gracile nucleus ( leg ) in the medulla Small dorsal root axons synapse in the spinal grey matter at the level of entry Crosses Medulla (second-order axon, then the medial lemniscus ) Spinal cord , straight away Thalamus Ventral posterior nucleus Intralaminar + ventral posterior nuclei Ends in Primary somatosensory cortex (S1) Primary somatosensory cortex (S1) Somatotopy in the dorsal columns : new afferents join laterally as the cord ascends, so at high cervical levels leg fibres are medial, trunk in the middle, arm lateral At the dorsal column nuclei (the first synapse), convergence and centre-surround inhibition reshape the signal: a stimulus in the centre of the field excites the neuron and one in the surround inhibits it through an interneuron, sharpening edges (as in the retina) · many afferents converging on one neuron = a large field and poor acuity (two-point discrimination on the back vs the fingertip) Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (crossing in the medulla) beside the spinothalamic tract (crossing in the spinal cord) 4. Clinical use Cord hemisection ( Brown-Sequard syndrome ): the two pathways climb in different columns and cross at different levels , so a right hemisection cuts fine touch and proprioception from lower segments on the right (same side) pain and temperature from lower segments on the left (opposite side) Dermatome = the skin supplied by one spinal nerve · neighbours overlap, more for touch than for pain and temperature → test pain or temperature to find the level of a segmental nerve injury 5. Primary somatosensory cortex S1 = areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2 on the postcentral gyrus , each with its own distorted body map (the sensory homunculus ) · fingers and lips are over-represented , like the fovea in vision · the posterior parietal cortex (areas 5, 7) lies behind it Each area extracts a different feature Area Input Extracts 3a Muscle proprioceptors Limb position 3b Touch afferents Touch (feeds areas 1 and 2) 1 Rapidly adapting afferents (from 3b) Texture · preferred-orientation cells 2 Slowly adapting afferents (from 3b) Size and shape of objects · preferred-direction cells Higher somatosensory areas represent increasingly complex features, as in vision
04 Neurophysiology of the Cerebellum and Basal Ganglia

Neurophysiology of the cerebellum and basal ganglia Two side loops tune movement without commanding it: the cerebellum corrects errors and teaches motor skills, the basal ganglia release the wanted movement and suppress the rest. Damage gives movement disorders with normal power , and the tremor, the tone and the course tell a cerebellar lesion from Parkinson disease . ⭐ Cerebellar disease = can start but inaccurate, intention tremor, low tone, same-side signs, stable or improving; Parkinson disease = can't start, rest tremor, rigidity, progressive; and neither is an upper motor neuron disorder. Vestibulocerebellum = balance and nystagmus · spinocerebellum = gait and tone · cerebrocerebellum = dysmetria and intention tremor. Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex, and they inhibit. Climbing fibres teach. Dopamine turns the direct pathway up and the indirect down; Huntington disease loses the indirect pathway; too much L-dopa over-drives the direct pathway; both give chorea. 1. Side loops in the motor system Both take input from wide areas of the cerebral cortex and send output through the thalamus back to the sensorimotor cortex ; both also project to the brainstem They do not contribute directly to the descending tracts, so they have no upper motor neurons → not upper motor neuron (UMN) disorders 2. Cerebellum: what it does Corrects errors in movement commands and imparts motor skills · in: motor, somatosensory and parietal association cortex, plus sensory input from the brainstem and cord · out: corrections to motor cortex (through the ventral lateral thalamus), brainstem and cord Cortex folded into folia and deep fissures , which hold half of all the neurons in the brain Subdivision Anatomy In → out Tunes Damage Vestibulocerebellum Flocculonodular lobe Vestibular organs → vestibular nuclei → eye, limb, trunk muscles Balance, stance, gait , the vestibulo-ocular reflex Wide-based ataxic gait (looks drunk) · Romberg sign : imbalance worse with eyes closed · nystagmus Spinocerebellum Vermis + intermediate cerebellum Vision, hearing, skin and muscle afferents → fastigial (vermis) or interposed (intermediate) nucleus → spinal cord Ongoing movement and muscle tone Ataxic gait (poor leg control) · falls walking heel-to-toe ("drunk-driver test") · hypotonia Cerebrocerebellum Lateral cerebellum Copy of the cortex's motor command → dentate nucleus → motor and premotor cortex Skill and coordination Ataxia in skilled movement · dysmetria (inaccurate) · dyssynergia (segments poorly coordinated) · intention tremor · fails finger-to-nose Cerebrocerebellar deficits present on the SAME (ipsilateral) side (often one-sided, depending on the lesion) · intention tremor comes near the end of a movement, from over-responses of the long-loop reflex through the motor cortex Cerebellum from behind: vermis, intermediate and lateral zones; anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes 3. The cerebellar circuit and motor learning The basic circuit is the same everywhere in the cerebellum, with three parts: 1. Direct path : sensory input → deep cerebellar nuclei (or vestibular nucleus) → motor systems 2. Mossy fibres → granule cells → parallel fibres → Purkinje cells : a weak, widely broadcast signal (~200,000 parallel fibres reach one Purkinje cell) 3. Climbing fibres → Purkinje cells : the error signal ("something needs to change") · one climbing fibre per Purkinje cell, many synapses · it modifies the parallel-fibre connection Purkinje cells INHIBIT the deep cerebellar (or vestibular) nuclei, and that is the only output of the cerebellar cortex Climbing fibre = the teacher, parallel fibre = the student: that is motor learning Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) : turning the head turns the eyes equally the other way (a 3-neuron reflex: semicircular canal → vestibular nucleus → eye muscle). When the image slips on the retina (ageing, new glasses), climbing fibres report it and change the Purkinje output onto the vestibular nucleus, re-tuning the reflex's gain ; they stop firing once there is no slip Prism goggles : healthy subjects adapt their dart throws and show an after-effect when the prisms come off · cerebellar patients show no adaptation and no after-effect The "repair shop" : it masks motor disorders from lesions elsewhere , so cerebellar lesions themselves cause longer-lasting disorders 4. Basal ganglia: release and suppress Release appropriate movements and suppress inappropriate ones from the premotor and motor cortex · damage contributes to Tourette syndrome (inappropriate utterances released) In : frontal, parietal and temporal cortex converge on the striatum (caudate + putamen) · out : the globus pallidus (external and internal segments) → ventral anterior / ventral lateral thalamus → motor cortex Modulators : the subthalamic nucleus (reciprocally connected with the globus pallidus) and substantia nigra pars compacta (dopamine to the striatum) · the substantia nigra pars reticulata projects to the superior colliculus for eye movements Disinhibition is the core idea : at rest the globus pallidus fires steadily and inhibits the thalamus Direct pathway Indirect pathway Route Cortex → striatum ⊣ globus pallidus ⊣ thalamus The same, plus an extra inhibitory synapse in the globus pallidus and a side loop through the subthalamic nucleus Effect Striatum inhibits the globus pallidus → disinhibits the thalamus → excites UMNs in motor cortex → releases the movement Inhibits the thalamus Dopamine (pars compacta) Up-regulated Down-regulated 5. Basal ganglia disorders Parkinson disease Too much L-dopa ( levodopa ) Huntington disease What goes wrong Pars compacta dopamine neurons degenerate Excess activity in the direct pathway Indirect pathway selectively degraded Thalamus Too much inhibition → too little drive back to premotor and motor cortex Too little inhibition Too little inhibition Type Hypokinetic Hyperkinetic Hyperkinetic Shows as Can't start voluntary movement Spontaneous movements ( chore

Neurophysiology of reflexes Motor control is a hierarchy, from the motor unit up to the prefrontal cortex: how force is graded, how the muscle's own sensors drive the spinal reflexes, how the motor cortex sets those reflexes, and why a lesion of the upper or the lower motor neuron looks so different at the bedside . ⭐ UMN lesion = flaccid at first, then spastic, hypertonic, hyperreflexic with clonus and an upgoing big toe, no fasciculations and no severe atrophy; LMN lesion = flaccid, hypo- or areflexic, fasciculations, fibrillations, severe atrophy. Spindle = in parallel, length, Ia, monosynaptic stretch reflex; Golgi tendon organ = in series, force, Ib, inhibits its own muscle. Small motor neurons are recruited first. Fibrillation = one fibre (EMG only); fasciculation = a whole motor unit (visible); spasm = a whole muscle (descending control). Supplementary motor area lesion → apraxia on both sides. 1. Lower motor neurons and motor units Lower motor neuron (LMN) = innervates muscle fibres directly · cell body in the ventral horn (cervical enlargement C3-T1 for the arm, lumbar L1-S3 for the leg) or the brainstem alpha motor neurons → force · gamma motor neurons → fusimotor drive to the muscle spindle Motor unit = one alpha motor neuron + all the muscle fibres it innervates (the smallest unit of motor control) · motor neuron pool = all the alpha motor neurons to one muscle Innervation ratio (fibres per motor unit): leg muscles > 1000 · eye or finger muscles · smaller ratios allow finer gradations of force 2. Grading muscle force Action potentials are all-or-none, so force is graded two ways: Fire faster : at higher frequencies one fibre's twitches fuse Recruit more motor units (the size principle) : smaller motor neurons have lower thresholds and are recruited first , and their units are fatigue-resistant · larger motor neurons join only for large, brief forces (walk → run → gallop → jump) Size principle: slow fatigue-resistant units carry standing and walking; fast fatigable units are added for running and jumping 3. Neuromuscular junction and spontaneous firing Neuromuscular junction : one of the largest synapses in the body · in health one action potential releases enough acetylcholine to contract the motor unit (one-to-one fidelity) · target of poisons ( botulinum toxin , curare ) and disease ( myasthenia gravis ) Sign What fires on its own Visible? Points to Fibrillation One muscle fibre No , only on electromyography (EMG) Changed excitability of the fibre: denervation or motor neuron death Fasciculation A whole motor unit Yes , a large visible contraction Hypersensitive motor neuron , or injury to the axon before it enters the muscle Spasm The whole muscle or a group of muscles Yes, moves the body Many causes, typically pathology in descending motor control 4. Muscles are sensory organs too Muscle spindle Golgi tendon organ Lies In parallel with the muscle fibres (its length changes with the muscle) In series with the muscle fibres, in the tendon Signals Muscle length and velocity Muscle force (contraction stretches the tendon and squeezes it) Axon Ia (the fastest conducting in the body) · plus gamma motor neurons to set the spindle's length Ib 5. Spinal reflexes Reflex Trigger Circuit Result Monosynaptic stretch Muscle stretch → spindle fires Ia axon synapses on every alpha motor neuron in that muscle's pool and on synergists · and on an inhibitory interneuron to the antagonist Agonists contract, antagonists relax, countering the stretch · tested clinically by the tendon tap Reverse myotatic Rising force → Golgi tendon organ fires Ib axon → interneuron that INHIBITS the same muscle's alpha motor neuron Keeps tension constant (a steady grip on a paper cup) Flexion-crossed extension Painful stimulus (skin nociceptors, Aδ fibres) A more complex circuit across the cord Stimulated leg flexes (withdrawal), the opposite leg extends (balance) Central pattern generators : walking is hardwired in the spinal cord · people with a severed cord can be trained to step on a moving platform · they simplify the job of descending control The spinal reflexes are governed by descending motor control Monosynaptic stretch reflex: a passive stretch excites the spindle, Ia afferents fire the same muscle and inhibit its antagonist 6. Motor cortex and the lateral corticospinal tract Primary motor cortex (M1) = area 4 (precentral gyrus), lowest stimulation thresholds · a motor homunculus , with the face and hand (fine control) over-represented M1 maps movements, not muscles : one M1 neuron drives several muscles · a column drives a synergy (muscles acting together) · the same muscle can be driven by different columns Lateral corticospinal tract : the longest tract in the central nervous system (so vulnerable) and one of the largest (~1 million axons) · not fully developed at birth from ⅓ area 4 (primary motor) · ⅓ area 6 (premotor + supplementary motor) · ⅓ primary somatosensory cortex crosses at the pyramidal decussation (medulla-cord junction) → lateral motor neurons → monosynaptic connections onto motor neurons of distal muscles (fingers) → finely controlled finger movement Anterior (ventral) corticospinal tract : from area 4 + area 6 only (no sensory cortex) · fewer axons · stays uncrossed until the spinal cord , then makes bilateral, polysynaptic connections onto medial motor neurons of proximal and axial muscles → posture Two jobs for M1 corticospinal neurons Starting a movement : planning activity in premotor cortex (area 6) can lead the movement by up to 800 ms, then M1 fires · the command goes to alpha and gamma motor neurons together (alpha-gamma co-activation) · M1 firing rate sets the force Shaping the stretch reflex : stretch also triggers a cortical long-loop response , which is voluntary and context-dependent (catching a ball: resist the stretch or give way) 7. Upper vs lower motor neuron lesions Upper motor neuron (UMN) = any neuron with a descending projection that controls lower motor neuro

Spinal cord Find the level, then the pattern: upper vs lower motor neuron signs say cord or root, the lowest sensory level approximates the cord level , and which modalities are lost, and on which side, names the cord syndrome , which in turn points to the cause. ⭐ Anterior cord loses movement and pain but spares vibration and position; posterior cord loses vibration and position but spares movement; central cord hits the hands hardest; Brown-Séquard loses power and position on the lesion's side and pain and temperature on the other. Complete injury = no rectal tone and no perianal sensation. Cervical cord lesion = UMN signs in arms and legs; cervical root = LMN signs in one arm. Bilateral leg pain, saddle anesthesia and bowel or bladder loss = cauda equina, an emergency. A cervical disc hits the lower root; a lumbar disc catches the traversing root. 1. Anatomy that decides the pattern The cord runs from the foramen magnum to about L1/L2 ; beyond the conus the nerve roots run on as the cauda equina Three pathways to consider Pathway Carries Crosses A one-sided cord lesion loses it on the Lateral corticospinal (cell bodies in the cortex) Motor Medullary pyramids ; synapses in the ventral horn Same side Spinothalamic (anterolateral) Pain, temperature In the cord , at entry Opposite side Dorsal columns Proprioception, vibration Medulla (medial lemniscus) Same side Blood supply : one anterior spinal artery + two posterior spinal arteries · the central area supplied only by the anterior spinal artery is mostly motor 2. Assessing the cord Sensory : dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration) · spinothalamic (pain, temperature) · light touch uses both · look for a sensory level dermatome = the skin supplied by a single spinal root Motor : bulk, tone, power, reflexes myotome = the muscles one root supplies · not easy to test on a screen, so test movement at a joint (elbow flexion = C5, C6) key movements on the International Standards (ISNCSCI, ASIA) chart: elbow flexors C5 · wrist extensors C6 · elbow extensors C7 · finger flexors C8 · finger abductors T1 · hip flexors L2 · knee extensors L3 · ankle dorsiflexors L4 · long toe extensors L5 · ankle plantar flexors S1 · plus voluntary anal contraction and deep anal pressure Three possible motor results Normal Lower motor neuron (LMN) Upper motor neuron (UMN) No abnormal findings Wasting , low tone , decreased strength, diminished or absent reflexes Subtle loss of bulk, increased tone , decreased strength, hyperreflexia , upgoing toe UMN = brain or spinal cord · LMN = spinal nerve roots or peripheral nerve 3. Cord (myelopathy) vs root (radiculopathy), by level Level ==Cord lesion (myelopathy) = UMN Root lesion (radiculopathy) = LMN== Cervical Arms and legs One arm Thoracic Most likely : both legs ± bowel and bladder — Lumbar — Most likely : one leg · but beware cauda equina syndrome Cord dysfunction gives UMN findings and presents as a syndrome ; root compromise gives an LMN pattern with more isolated signs 4. Spinal cord injury: complete vs incomplete Complete : no sensory or motor function below the clinical level , including loss of rectal tone and perianal sensation Incomplete : the level separates normal function from partial impairment below it · grouped by the part of the cord hit: Syndrome Motor below the lesion Pain, temperature Vibration, position Causes Anterior cord Complete paralysis (corticospinal) Lost at and below the level Intact (with 2-point discrimination) anterior spinal artery occlusion : atherosclerosis · aortic aneurysm, thrombosis, dissection, surgery · compression (disc, tumour, posterior osteophyte, kyphoscoliosis) · stab injury Posterior cord Normal (corticospinal weakness only if posterior compression is severe) Intact Lost vitamin B12 deficiency · syphilis · posterior extrinsic mass · spinal cord tumour surgery Central cord Hands profoundly affected , strength returns going up the arm Lost , "suspended" or cape-like Usually spared (light touch too: dissociated sensory loss) Commonest pattern in elderly trauma (hyperextension) · syrinx · intrinsic tumour · multiple sclerosis Brown-Séquard Same side paralysis (opposite side strong) Opposite side Same side Rare · trauma or a process inside the cord · usually incomplete The four incomplete cord syndromes: which part of the cord is damaged and where motor and sensory function is lost Anterior cord also brings autonomic dysfunction : orthostatic hypotension , and bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction depending on the level Cauda equina syndrome (roots, not the cord): bilateral leg pain or paresthesia , LMN paraparesis , saddle anesthesia , impaired bowel or bladder control · an EMERGENCY 5. Causes: not just trauma or tumour Think through every category: Vascular : stroke, arteriovenous malformation, fistula Infectious : epidural abscess, viral, syphilis (tabes dorsalis) Trauma : fracture, stab, disc, radiation Autoimmune : lupus Metabolic : subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12) Inflammatory : multiple sclerosis Neoplastic : metastatic, extradural, intrinsic Congenital : achondroplasia, "trisomy 23" (as printed in the source; there is no trisomy 23, probably trisomy 21 is meant) Degenerative : disc herniation, arthritis, motor neuron disease ( ALS ) Grouped another way: compressive (bone lesion, disc herniation, epidural hemorrhage, abscess, tumours, arteriovenous malformation, syringomyelia) vs non-compressive (transverse myelitis, demyelination such as multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica, spinal artery thrombosis and vasculitis, toxins and radiation, degenerative disease, B12 and vitamin E deficiency, paraneoplastic). 6. Nerve roots (radiculopathy) Radicular pain · paresthesia or numbness in a dermatome · LMN weakness in a myotome Which root a disc hits : in the neck , a herniation compresses the lower root (a C5-6 disc → the C6 root , which runs in the C5-6 foramen over that disc) · in the lumbar spine it catches the traversing root (an L5-S1 disc → the S1 roo

Neuro-ophthalmology Visual symptoms that do not come from the eyeball itself: double vision, eyes that will not hold still, unequal or sluggish pupils, and a missing part of the visual field. Each one points to a place along the nerves and brain pathways , so the lecture is really about localizing. ⭐ Anisocoria worse in the light = the big pupil cannot constrict (parasympathetic); worse in the dark = the small pupil cannot dilate (sympathetic, Horner, rule out carotid dissection). A third nerve palsy with a blown pupil is compressive (aneurysm); pupil-sparing is microvascular. Fourth = head tilt, often congenital; sixth = cannot abduct, think raised intracranial pressure. Gaze-evoked nystagmus beats toward the gaze and comes from the cerebellum, brainstem or a toxin. RAPD = that optic nerve. Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasm; temporal lobe = superior defect, parietal = inferior. 1. Double vision (diplopia) Diplopia arises when the two eyes are not aligned : one eye looks at the target and its image falls on the fovea (the actual image , in the centre) · the other looks elsewhere and its image falls off the fovea (the false image , off-centre) Which nerve moves which muscle : lateral rectus = VI, superior oblique = IV, all the rest = III (medial, superior and inferior rectus, inferior oblique) Nerve The eye The point to remember Third nerve palsy (oculomotor) Down and out , ptosis It can spare the pupil or involve it : a "blown pupil" (large, not reactive to light) is bad , because it means compression (aneurysm) of the parasympathetic fibres on the nerve's surface · a pupil-sparing palsy is microvascular (the nerve's deep vessels) Fourth nerve palsy (trochlear, superior oblique) Vertical double vision Head tilt · often congenital Sixth nerve palsy (abducens, lateral rectus) Cannot abduct , turned in · head turned toward the weak side Ask: underlying raised intracranial pressure ? (look for papilledema; the nerve runs a long course from the pons) 2. Nystagmus Nystagmus = an eye movement disorder: a slow drift of the eyes away from the target pendular : the eyes drift back, so they seem to wobble jerk : they snap back quickly · most nystagmus is jerk · it "beats" in the direction of the fast (snapping) phase Gaze-evoked nystagmus , the most common form : trouble holding eccentric gaze , so it beats toward the gaze (left-beating on left gaze, right on right, up on upgaze, down on downgaze) Why : the circuit that holds eccentric gaze is in the brainstem and cerebellum ; a lesion lets the eyes drift back to the midline (slow phase), then they saccade back to the target (fast phase) · an "ataxia of the eyes" Causes structural lesion in the cerebellum (or brainstem) : stroke · bleed · tumour · demyelination · degeneration (e.g. alcohol) inherited : hereditary ataxia syndromes toxins : alcohol · phenytoin (Dilantin) and other antiseizure drugs · lithium 3. The pupil Pupil size = parasympathetic tone (constricts) vs sympathetic tone (dilates) Parasympathetic: constriction Sympathetic: dilation Pathway Optic nerve (the afferent) → pretectal nucleus (midbrain) → both Edinger-Westphal nuclei → third nerve → ciliary ganglion → pupil sphincter 1st neuron : hypothalamus → ciliospinal centre (C8-T1) · 2nd : over the lung, past the subclavian artery → superior cervical ganglion · 3rd : along the internal carotid → long ciliary nerves → pupil dilator (and Müller's muscle of the lid) Bilateral link Each pretectal nucleus feeds both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so both pupils constrict to light in one eye — Pupillary light reflex: optic nerve to the pretectal area, then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, cranial nerve III and the ciliary ganglion to each constrictor Anisocoria (unequal pupils): first ask is one pupil big, or the other small? (a parasympathetic paresis on one side, or a sympathetic paresis on the other) → compare them in bright light and in the dark difference worse in bright light → the big pupil cannot constrict → parasympathetic (e.g. a compressive third nerve palsy) difference worse in the dark → the small pupil cannot dilate → sympathetic : Horner syndrome → rule out internal carotid artery dissection 4. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) RAPD = a defect of one optic nerve , the afferent arm of the light reflex Found with the swinging flashlight test : light in the good eye → both pupils constrict · swing to the bad eye → both pupils dilate , because less light is "seen" · the efferent (third nerve) side is intact, which is why it is relative 5. Visual field defects Fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross at the chiasm ; temporal fibres do not, so each side of the brain sees the opposite visual field Pathway: optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations (temporal and parietal lobes) → occipital cortex Lesion (left side) Field defect Optic nerve Decreased vision in that eye Back of the optic nerve (at the chiasm) That eye blind + a junctional scotoma (upper temporal) in the other eye Optic chiasm Bitemporal hemianopia (e.g. a pituitary macroadenoma pressing from below) Optic tract Right homonymous hemianopia Lateral geniculate nucleus Right homonymous sectoranopias (wedges) Temporal lobe (lower radiation) Right homonymous superior defect Parietal lobe (upper radiation) Right homonymous inferior defect Occipital lobe, upper bank Right homonymous inferior quadrantanopia Occipital lobe, lower bank Right homonymous superior quadrantanopia Occipital lobe Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing Tip of the occipital lobe Right homonymous scotomas (central) Visual pathway lesions and the field defect each one causes Schulich Reviews An RAPD is often from optic neuritis , which can be a sign of multiple sclerosis .

Cortical syndromes Some deficits can only come from the cortex, so finding one tells you where the lesion is. Language problems point to the dominant hemisphere; neglect points to the non-dominant one. Knowing them also stops an aphasic patient being written off as "confused" or delirious. ⭐ Aphasia = dominant hemisphere; neglect = non-dominant hemisphere. Broca's (inferior frontal) = halting speech, understanding intact; Wernicke's (posterior temporal) = fluent nonsense, understanding lost; global = full MCA territory. Any cortical sign rules out a pure subcortical or brainstem lesion. Cortical sensory signs only count if primary sensation is intact. Test comprehension with motor , not verbal, commands. 1. Why cortical signs matter They help localize the lesion (for example, a stroke), explain the presentation , and show that pathology is present ⚠ They stop a patient with aphasia being mistaken for confused or delirious Where a sign points: Level Signs Key point Cortex Aphasia · neglect · apraxia · cortical sensory signs · usually homonymous hemianopia ( especially if isolated ) Any one of these = cortex Subcortex (white matter tracts) Pure motor weakness of one side · pure sensory change of one side (face, arm, leg) · ataxic hemiparesis (mild ataxia + mild weakness) No cortical signs Brainstem vertigo plus another symptom · diplopia plus another symptom · crossed sensory symptoms (face one side, body the other) No cortical signs 2. The dominant hemisphere Dominant = the hemisphere where language is located right-handed people: typically the left left-handed people: left in 60% · right in 19% · both (bilateral language) in 20% A dominant-hemisphere middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke usually disturbs language 3. Aphasia Aphasia = impairment of language (communicating and/or understanding it), from the dominant hemisphere not the same as dysarthria , which is impairment of articulation Broca's area, Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus joining them Type Lesion Speech Understanding Broca's (expressive) - a motor impairment Inferior frontal lobe Slow, halting (speaking or writing) · none if severe · paraphasic errors (combined sounds, wrong word) Intact Wernicke's (receptive) - a sensory impairment Posterior temporal lobe Fluent but makes no sense · sounds like a foreign language if severe · real words that do not cohere if mild Impaired Global Full MCA territory No verbal output None Naming and repetition are reduced in all three ; the keeners' three ( conduction , transcortical motor , transcortical sensory ) are in the chart above How to test language : naming · comprehension · fluency · repetition · reading · writing (start simple, get harder) Test How Major deficit Minor deficit Naming Name pictures or items, simple → complex (cup → button → stethoscope) Cannot name a watch or pen Names the item, not its parts (face of the watch) Comprehension Follow instructions, simple → complex · the command must be motor, not verbal Cannot follow a 1-step command Follows 1-2 steps, not 3 Fluency Open-ended question, or describe a picture · sounds that make no sense still count as fluent No vocalizations Some hesitation finding words Repetition Repeat a phrase ("no ifs, ands or buts") Cannot repeat even single words Repeats simple phrases, not complex sentences 4. The non-dominant hemisphere: neglect Neglect syndromes go with the non-dominant hemisphere visual neglect : does not attend to visual stimuli on one side, but may still blink to a threat there sensory neglect : does not attend to sensory stimulation on one side asomatognosia : does not recognize their own body parts (thinks their arm is the examiner's) anosognosia : does not recognize that they have a neurological deficit difficulty putting clothes on ( dressing apraxia ) 5. Apraxia Apraxia = cannot carry out a motor task despite having the power to do it A cortical syndrome, typically from a parietal or frontal lobe lesion Recognize it from examples: cannot pretend to use a hammer · cannot form a finger or hand posture · cannot get dressed · cannot whistle · cannot draw you need to understand and recognize apraxia, not the names of the subtypes 6. Cortical sensory signs and extinction Cortical sensory signs localize to the sensory association cortex , but only if primary sensation is intact Graphesthesia lost: cannot read a number or letter traced on the skin Stereognosis lost: cannot identify an object by touch alone position sensation : cannot tell the direction a stimulus is moving ⚠ A loss of primary sensation (pin, temperature, pressure, vibration, light touch) cannot be pinned to the cortex : the lesion could be anywhere on the sensory pathway Extinction : detects a stimulus on either side alone, but when both sides are stimulated at once , misses the affected side sensory extinction (simultaneous light touch) → parietal lobe · visual extinction (simultaneous visual cues) → occipital lobe Schulich Reviews Face + arm weaker than the leg = middle cerebral artery (MCA); leg weaker than face + arm = anterior cerebral artery (ACA): on the WEAKNESS chart

Approach to weakness Weakness can come from anywhere between the cerebrum and the muscle fibre. The key localizing clues are the type of weakness (upper or lower motor neuron), the signs and symptoms that come with it, and where the weakness falls. ⭐ No sensory loss narrows LMN weakness to the anterior horn cell (segmental), neuromuscular junction (fluctuating, eyes first) or muscle (proximal, symmetric). UMN = spastic, hyperreflexic, upgoing toe, pyramidal (arm extensors and leg flexors weak); LMN = atrophy, fasciculations, reflexes normal or reduced, tone normal. A sensory level means spinal cord; crossed face and body means brainstem. Polyneuropathy is distal; myopathy is proximal. 1. Weakness, and what mimics it Weakness = loss of voluntary movement from interruption of the motor pathway at any point from cerebrum to muscle fibre ⚠ Mimics (function lost for another reason): incoordination (cerebellar disease) · apraxia (cerebral cortical lesions) · severe sensory loss (proprioceptive failure) 2. Upper vs lower motor neuron Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion = disruption of the corticospinal pathway (cortex · subcortical white matter · internal capsule · brainstem · spinal cord) corticospinal input normally suppresses spinal reflexes , so losing it → hyperreflexia and spasticity Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion = interruption from the anterior horn cell out to the muscle (anterior horn cell · root · plexus · nerve · neuromuscular junction · muscle) Feature UMN (brain or spinal cord) LMN (anterior horn cell to muscle) Bulk No atrophy Atrophy (the nerve no longer brings neurotrophic factors) Fasciculations None Possible , especially anterior horn cell and nerve (a motor unit firing on its own) Reflexes Hyperreflexia Normal, hyporeflexia or areflexia Tone Spasticity Normal Plantar response Upgoing (positive Babinski ) Downgoing Distribution Pyramidal : brain → one side · spinal cord → both sides below the lesion Fits the level : root → myotomal · anterior horn cell, nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle each have their own pattern Pyramidal weakness (UMN; the corticospinal tract runs through the medullary pyramids): arms: extensors weaker than flexors (triceps legs: flexors weaker than extensors (knee flexion suspect mild pyramidal weakness → examine arm extensors and leg flexors , which go first likely evolutionary: upright humans keep strong arm flexors (feeding) and leg extensors (walking) Where the weakness falls for a hemispheric, brainstem, spinal cord, root, nerve, polyneuropathy and muscle lesion 3. Where it localizes Level Type Pattern Clues Causes Brain UMN Hemiparesis, pyramidal · face + arm > leg = middle cerebral artery (MCA) · leg > face + arm = anterior cerebral artery (ACA) · face = arm = leg = internal capsule Aphasia, neglect , headache, seizures Stroke · brain tumour · multiple sclerosis (MS) Brainstem UMN Hemiparesis (less often quadriparesis), pyramidal Cranial nerve symptoms (diplopia, vertigo) · cerebellar findings · crossed (ipsilateral face, contralateral body) Stroke · MS · tumour Spinal cord UMN Paraplegia or quadriplegia , pyramidal Sensory level · neck or back pain · urinary symptoms Trauma · disc herniation · tumour · epidural hemorrhage · MS Anterior horn cell LMN Segmental , no sensory loss - Polio and polio-like illness · ALS (also has UMN signs, from the cortical motor neurons) Root LMN Myotomal · reflex of that root reduced Neck or back pain radiating into a limb · dermatomal sensory loss Disc herniation · foraminal stenosis Multiple roots LMN Many muscles over more than one root level, sometimes both sides Usually painful , with sensory symptoms Cauda equina compression · infectious polyradiculitis · leptomeningeal carcinomatosis Plexus LMN One limb, more muscles than one nerve or one root - Trauma · tumour · inflammatory Single nerve LMN Muscles of that nerve - Ulnar, radial, common peroneal, sciatic palsies Polyneuropathy LMN Length-dependent : symmetric, distal > proximal , feet first · or mononeuritis multiplex Sensory prominent - Neuromuscular junction LMN Fluctuating · descending : eyes first (ptosis, diplopia), then speech and swallowing Sensation normal · reflexes usually normal Myasthenia gravis Muscle LMN Symmetric, proximal (trunk, shoulder and hip girdle) No sensory involvement · reflexes often normal Inflammatory myopathies ( polymyositis , dermatomyositis ) · muscular dystrophies 4. History and exam History : where (one limb, one side, both sides) · how (abrupt, or gradual and progressive) · functional impact (what is hard) · other symptoms (sensory change · speech, language or swallowing · pain · bowel or bladder ) Exam confirms the location, extent and character · know what normal is, so you catch mild weakness and side-to-side differences Medical Research Council (MRC) scale : 0 none · 1 flicker · 2 moves with gravity eliminated · 3 full antigravity power · 4 some power against resistance (4-, 4, 4+) · 5 full power The lecture's cases, one line each: 2 weeks of trouble with stairs and dressing · neck flexors and extensors, deltoids, triceps, hip flexors weak · reflexes, tone and sensation normal → muscle 2 months of trouble walking, numb feet · weak ankles · absent ankle reflexes · pinprick lost to the knee → peripheral nerve weak legs · brisk knees and ankles, upgoing toes · pinprick lost up to the inferior scapula → spinal cord Schulich Reviews Acute weakness: an ischemic stroke follows a vascular territory ; a hemorrhage may not, and more often brings a headache; migraine weakness "marches" and comes and goes over minutes; Todd's paresis improves over hours; psychogenic weakness is inconsistent and better when distracted

Approach to localization Use the same approach for every neurological problem: describe it, localize the lesion, then build the differential from the description and the localization . Localizing helps you plan the right investigations ; the time course tells you what kind of lesion it is. ⭐ Any cortical sign puts the lesion in the cortex; vertigo or diplopia plus something else, or crossed face-body sensory symptoms, puts it in the brainstem; pure motor, pure sensory or ataxic hemiparesis without cortical signs puts it in the subcortex. Hyperacute = stroke or hemorrhage; subacute = inflammation, infection or tumour. MCA = face and arm >> leg. Dysarthria spares language; aphasia does not. Bilateral leg weakness can be cortex (parasagittal) all the way to muscle. 1. The approach 1. Describe the problem - onset : acute · subacute · chronic - course : progressive · intermittent · stable - deficits : cognitive · motor · sensory · coordination 2. Localize the "lesion" with your neuroanatomy 3. Offer a differential diagnosis , taking the description and the localization into account The tempo predicts the type of lesion : Tempo Lesion Hyperacute Ischemic stroke · hemorrhage Acute Trauma Subacute Inflammation · infection · tumour Subacute to chronic Tumour 2. Is it the brain, the cord or the periphery? Upper motor neuron (UMN) vs lower motor neuron (LMN) signs, and the pattern of weakness, are on the Approach to weakness chart Bilateral leg weakness can come from : a parasagittal cortical lesion (for example a parasagittal meningioma) · the spinal cord · anterior horn cell disease · multilevel lumbosacral radiculopathies (for example spinal stenosis) · polyneuropathies · myopathy UMN signs in the legs (brisk reflexes, upgoing toes) → spinal cord : look for a sensory level , which tells imaging where to look 3. Where in the brain: the localization pearls Level Look for Key point Cortex Aphasia · neglect syndromes · homonymous hemianopsia Any one = cortex Subcortex (white matter tracts) Pure motor hemiparesis or pure sensory hemibody (face, arm, leg) · ataxic hemiparesis (mild ataxia + mild hemiparesis) No cortical signs Brainstem (intrinsic) vertigo plus another symptom · diplopia plus another symptom · crossed sensory symptoms (face vs body) No cortical signs Middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke : the MCA supplies the mid and lower homunculus , so face and arm >> leg frontal lobe only → mostly motor · mostly parietal → mostly sensory · internal capsule → motor and sensory dominant -hemisphere MCA stroke usually disturbs language (aphasia types: on the Cortical syndromes chart) Case: sudden right face and arm (> leg) weakness, no verbal output but follows commands, no neglect → expressive aphasia → left frontal lobe, left MCA territory 4. Difficulty speaking: dysarthria or aphasia? Two main neurological causes: dysarthria (articulation) and dysphasia / aphasia (language) Slurred speech with normal comprehension, naming, repetition and fluency = dysarthria Any lesion along the speech production pathway can cause dysarthria : central : cortex (mouth area) · subcortex · thalamus · brainstem · cerebellum and its pathways peripheral : nerve (for example the recurrent laryngeal nerve ) · neuromuscular junction (for example myasthenia gravis ) · muscle (myopathy) Tell the sites apart by what comes with it : findings only a cranial nerve explains · UMN vs LMN findings · weakness · ataxia · sensory symptoms 5. The cerebellar system It coordinates all movement : eyes, articulation, swallowing, the arms and gait (think of someone drunk; alcohol is a cerebellar toxin) nystagmus · dysarthria · dysphagia · finger-to-nose ataxia · dysdiadochokinesia (rapid alternating movements) · heel-to-shin ataxia · gait ataxia · impaired tandem walking Case: slurred speech plus slight right finger-to-nose ataxia → the cerebellar system (here a right cerebellar hemorrhage) Schulich Reviews Localization is the most tested skill: work through the lecture's cases

Neuroembryology The nervous system comes from ectoderm: the neural tube becomes the central nervous system , and every later structure is a dilation or a layer of that tube. Most of the pathology is a step that failed: a neuropore that did not close, or neurons that did not migrate . ⭐ Cranial neuropore fails = anencephaly; failure along the spine = spina bifida - and 400 mcg of folic acid helps prevent both. Myelomeningocele has cord outside; meningocele has only meninges; occulta is skin-covered. High AFP suggests spina bifida. Neuronal migration disorders present with drug-resistant epilepsy: smooth brain (lissencephaly), too many small gyri (polymicrogyria), absent corpus callosum. Alar plate = dorsal, sensory; basal plate = ventral, motor. Myelination runs caudal to rostral, mostly after birth. 1. Gastrulation and neurulation - Gastrulation (from about day 16, started by the primitive streak ) = formation of the 3 germ layers · sets up the body plan (bilateral symmetry, 3 axes) and makes the first neuroepithelium - the notochord (from the notochordal plate, a mesodermal derivative) tells nearby ectoderm to become neural tissue and sets the axes through gradients of sonic hedgehog - the neural plate forms first at the cranial end - Neurulation : 1. dorsal ectoderm forms the neural plate (neuroectoderm), which folds into neural folds and a neural groove ( day 18 ) 2. the folds meet in the midline and fuse cranially and caudally, starting from the cervical region 3. cranial (anterior) neuropore closes on day 24-25 4. caudal (posterior) neuropore closes on day 26-28 5. throughout, neural crest cells "pinch off" and start to migrate - End product: a continuous neural tube (neuroectoderm lining a fluid-filled centre) along the dorsal embryo, with an enlarged cranial end that dilates and flexes into the early brain Ectoderm part Becomes Neural tube Central nervous system (brain, spinal cord) Neural crest cells Peripheral and enteric (gut) neurons · glia · pigment cells (melanocytes) · cartilage and bone of the face and skull · smooth muscle Surface ectoderm Epidermis · hair · nails · sebaceous glands · olfactory and mouth lining · eyes 2. Brain vesicles The three primary vesicles: prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), rhombencephalon (hindbrain) Primary vesicle Secondary vesicle (by week 5) Becomes Cavity Prosencephalon (forebrain) Telencephalon (two lateral vesicles) Cerebral hemispheres Lateral ventricles Diencephalon (midline vesicle) Thalamus and hypothalamus · eyes (retina, via the optic cups) · part of the pituitary Third ventricle Mesencephalon (midbrain) Does not divide Midbrain (its alar plates form the colliculi) Cerebral aqueduct Rhombencephalon (hindbrain) Metencephalon (rostral half) Pons and cerebellum Fourth ventricle Myelencephalon (caudal half) Medulla Fourth ventricle Cranial nerve nuclei (by week 4): CN I from the telencephalon · CN II from the diencephalon (it continues the optic cup) · CN III mesencephalon · CN IV-VIII metencephalon · CN IX-XII myelencephalon 3. Timeline of brain development The processes run in parallel , not one after another: neurogenesis : neurons multiply from the ventricular lining of the tube, symmetrically at first, then exponentially · first neurons (about week 4) are motor neurons of the cervical ventral horn · 6 cortical layers by about week 18 · gyri visible by about week 24 gliogenesis : follows neurogenesis, peaks around birth , continues after · different glia come from different parts of the telencephalon migration : new neurons form transient structures and the CNS expands fast · genetically controlled , so genetic syndromes can disrupt it synaptogenesis : needs astrocytes , region-dependent · in the cortex from about weeks 24-27 , continuing into early adulthood myelination : caudal to rostral (spinal cord and brainstem first), largely after birth · myelin inhibits synaptogenesis and plasticity · corticospinal tract done by 2 years , corpus callosum by late adolescence Brain development from neural tube to adulthood: neurulation, migration and neurogenesis early; synaptogenesis, gliogenesis and myelination late 4. Spinal cord development The caudal two-thirds of the tube → spinal cord ; its cavity → the central canal The wall splits into a mantle layer (deep → grey matter ) and a marginal layer (superficial → white matter , white once its fibres myelinate) the mantle layer forms a floor plate , a roof plate and a lateral mass on each side Alar and basal plates : the roof plate induces the alar plate , the floor plate induces the basal plate Plate Becomes Alar plate (dorsal) Dorsal horn (sensory) · also the sensory nuclei of CN V, VII, VIII, IX and X Basal plate (ventral) Ventral horn (motor) Intermediate plate (mid-portion of the lateral mass) Intermediate horn Developing spinal cord: alar plate becomes the sensory dorsal horn, basal plate the motor ventral horn The spine outgrows the cord : early on the cord runs the length of the embryo · the vertebral column and dura grow faster, so the cord's end rises (making the filum terminale and cauda equina ) · it ends at L3 at birth and about L2-L3 in adults 5. Neural tube defects Anencephaly Spina bifida What failed The upper (cranial) part of the neural tube does not close all the way The neural tube does not close all the way anywhere along the spine , so the backbone over the cord does not form Picture Born without parts of the brain and skull (the forebrain) · what remains is often not covered by bone or skin · about 1 in 4,500 Damage to the spinal cord and nerves · physical and intellectual disability, mild to severe , by the size and level of the opening and whether cord and nerves are involved Outcome No cure or standard treatment ; almost all die shortly after birth By type, below Spina bifida types, most to least severe : Myelomeningocele (most severe): meninges and spinal cord protrude · motor and sensory loss below the level · often needs surgery Meningocele (mod

Autonomic nervous system The autonomic nervous system is the visceral motor supply to the viscera, smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands, in two divisions that mostly pull in opposite directions. The clinical payoff is recognizing a cut sympathetic supply to one side of the face (Horner syndrome) and telling it from a third nerve palsy. ⭐ Horner = small pupil + milder ptosis + flushing + no sweating, same side, eye directed normally; CN III palsy = dilated pupil + paralysed levator + eye down and out + no accommodation. Sympathetic = thoracolumbar, short pre- and long post-synaptic fibres, synapse in the chain; parasympathetic = cranio-sacral, long pre- and short post-synaptic, synapse near the target. Sympathetics to the head synapse in the superior cervical ganglion and ride the carotid arteries. Parasympathetic empties the bladder; sympathetic holds it. 1. Organization: two divisions Sympathetic Parasympathetic Job Fight or flight Rest and digest Leaves the central nervous system at Thoracolumbar cord · cell body in the intermediolateral horn Cranio-sacral : cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, and the vagus) · sacral cord Pre-synaptic fibre Short Long Synapse In the sympathetic chain In ganglia close to the target Post-synaptic fibre Long Short Does Dilates the pupil · ↑ heart rate and force · dilates bronchioles · dilates vessels to skeletal muscle · constricts vessels to the gut · ↓ peristalsis · activates sweating Tears (lacrimation) · salivation · urination · digestion · defecation · sexual arousal Parasympathetic (left) and sympathetic (right) effects on each organ, with the cranial-sacral and thoracolumbar outflows 2. Sympathetic pathways To the limbs : the pre-synaptic fibre enters the chain through the white ramus communicans at its own level, runs up or down the chain, and synapses at another level lower limb → L2-S3 ganglia · upper limb → cervical ganglia · head → superior cervical ganglion the post-synaptic fibre leaves through the grey ramus communicans and travels with somatic nerves To the head : pre-synaptic fibres from about T1-T3 climb the chain without synapsing → synapse in the superior cervical ganglion → post-synaptic fibres leave through the grey ramus and ride the carotid arteries and their branches , then hitch a ride on trigeminal nerve branches near their targets 3. Head and neck: the four parasympathetic ganglia Pre-synaptic fibres from nuclei of CN III, VII and IX (the vagus is the exception) → synapse in one of four ganglia → post-synaptic fibres travel with branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) to smooth muscle and glands Sympathetics to each ganglion's targets all come from the superior cervical ganglion Ganglion Parasympathetic: nucleus → nerve Does Sympathetic route → does Ciliary Edinger-Westphal (accessory oculomotor) → inferior branch of CN III → short ciliary nerves Ciliary muscle (accommodation) · sphincter pupillae (constricts) Internal carotid plexus through the cavernous sinus → dilator pupillae and superior tarsal muscle Pterygopalatine Superior salivatory → CN VII → greater petrosal → nerve of the pterygoid canal Tears (post-synaptic fibres ride V2 to the lacrimal gland) · nasal, palate and pharynx mucosa Internal carotid plexus → deep petrosal → nerve of the pterygoid canal → ↓ tears · nasal, palate and pharynx vessels and mucosa Submandibular Superior salivatory → CN VII → chorda tympani, joining the lingual nerve ( V3 ) Submandibular and sublingual saliva Facial and lingual arteries → vasoconstriction of those glands' vessels Otic Inferior salivatory → CN IX → tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal → auriculotemporal (V3) Parotid saliva External carotid branches → vasoconstriction of parotid vessels Corneal sensation (the afferent side): cornea → short and long ciliary nerves → nasociliary nerve → trigeminal ganglion → trigeminal nuclei 4. Horner syndrome Horner syndrome = interruption of the cervical sympathetic supply to one side of the face · signs on the same side : miosis , ptosis , vasodilation , anhidrosis : miosis (small pupil) ptosis , often less severe than a third nerve palsy (the levator, on CN III, still works) vasodilation (flushing) anhidrosis (no sweating) Where the lesion can be : anywhere on the head's sympathetic route - the T1-T3 cord outflow · the cervical sympathetic chain · the superior cervical ganglion · the internal carotid plexus through the cavernous sinus into the orbit The three-neuron sympathetic path to the eye: hypothalamus to C8-T1, over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion, then along the carotid to the pupil dilator and eyelid Horner syndrome (loss of sympathetics) CN III palsy (loss of parasympathetics and motor) Pupil Constricted Dilated Eye directed Normally Down and out (intorsion) Ptosis Often less severe Levator palpebrae superioris paralysed Other Flushing (vasodilation) · anhidrosis No accommodation (blurry vision) 5. The bladder Supply Pre-synaptic → synapse Does Parasympathetic Pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4) → inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus Motor to the detrusor (empties) · inhibits the internal urethral sphincter Sympathetic Lumbar splanchnics (L1-L2) → inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus Contracts the internal urethral sphincter (holds) Somatic Pudendal nerve External urethral sphincter · pelvic and perineal muscles Visceral afferents Inferior bladder (below the pelvic pain line) → with the parasympathetics (voiding reflex) · superior bladder (above it) → with the sympathetics

Neuroradiology Different objects need to be looked at different ways: pick the modality that best resolves the object of interest . Each one trades three kinds of resolution against cost, availability, invasiveness and radiation; on MRI you also pick the sequence. ⭐ Fluid is dark on T1, white on T2, and white on FLAIR except for CSF - so FLAIR makes edema stand out. Radiography has the best spatial resolution, fluoroscopy and ultrasound the best temporal, MRI the best contrast. CT: widely available, but radiation; ultrasound: no radiation; MRI: expensive, limited, long. DWI measures restricted water diffusion (cellularity); SWI shows blood products. 1. Three kinds of resolution Spatial : can you resolve more than one nearby object ? (the detail) Contrast : can you resolve objects of similar density ? (the range of greys) Temporal : can you resolve objects over time ? (as in a video) 2. The modalities Modality How it works Spatial Contrast Temporal For Against Radiography (plain X-ray) Differential attenuation of X-rays by tissues +++ + None Inexpensive · instant · universally available - Fluoroscopy Pulsed X-rays (0.5-16 frames a second) · real-time · digital subtraction removes the baseline image so only new things (contrast, air) show ++ + +++ Real-time Limited availability · invasive ( angiography ) CT (computed tomography) X-ray attenuation, built into slices · contrast improves contrast resolution · multi-phase scanning adds temporal resolution ++ ++ None or + (depends on protocol) Widespread availability Moderate expense · radiation dose Ultrasound Grayscale : speed of sound and time to echo in different media · Doppler : frequency shift off a moving reflector + ++ +++ Widely available · inexpensive · no radiation - MRI Differential energy states of protons in a changing magnetic and radiofrequency field ++ +++ 0 / + - Expensive · limited availability · long scan 3. MRI sequences Sequence Type Fluid Shows T1 "Anatomic" Dark (hypointense) Structural abnormality · enhancement (with contrast) T2 "Pathologic" White ("water is white in T2") Edema FLAIR "Pathologic" White except CSF (inversion recovery suppresses the CSF signal) Makes edema more conspicuous DWI / ADC (diffusion-weighted imaging, apparent diffusion coefficient map) A T2-weighted sequence - Restricted diffusion of water · a measure of cellularity SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) "Pathologic" - Hemoglobin in its different oxidation states, including hemosiderin · accentuates an artifact first met on gradient echo (GRE) T2 and FLAIR are the "pathologic" sequences: they suppress "noise" and make pathology stand out Advanced imaging: MR angiography · MR perfusion · MR spectroscopy · functional MRI The same five sequences: T1 (CSF dark), T2 (CSF white), FLAIR (CSF dark, edema bright), DWI and SWI (dark spots of blood) 4. Putting it to work The lecture's case runs the stroke imaging in order: plain CT → CT angiography (CTA) → CT perfusion (CTP) → catheter angiography (fluoroscopy) → clot pulled out by thrombectomy → DWI afterwards

Approach to head injuries Every head injury is a trauma patient first : run the primary survey with the cervical spine protected, then grade the brain injury with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) . A severe injury is a race against rising intracranial pressure and herniation, settled by a STAT CT and often the operating room; a concussion is a clinical diagnosis, managed by removal from play, brief rest and a graded return. ⭐ A lucid interval after a contact injury is an epidural hematoma until the CT says otherwise - and a symptomatic epidural goes to the operating room. Uncal herniation: same-side blown pupil, opposite-side weakness; Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, apnea) means the medulla is being compressed. Subdural: bridging veins, falls, the elderly; operate within 4 hours. Diffuse axonal injury: unconscious at the scene and stays in a coma, with a CT that can look nearly normal. Severe = GCS 3-8. Concussion is clinical: most never lose consciousness, no impact is needed, and a helmet does not prevent it. Rest 24-48 hours, then return to learn before return to play. 1. A trauma patient first Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) : primary survey and initial resuscitation, then secondary survey and definitive treatment A - airway: cervical spine (C-spine) precautions , intubation with manual in-line C-spine traction if needed B - breathing · C - circulation: large-bore IV, bloodwork to look for coagulopathy D - disability: neurological exam and GCS · E - expose: other injuries A falling level of consciousness or a blown pupil : intubate with C-spine precautions · head of the bed up · IV mannitol or 3% saline for osmotic diuresis · STAT CT scan The module adds : hyperventilation (PaCO2 below 34) to reduce brain swelling · no lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is possible · no corticosteroids - they reduce vasogenic edema and have no role in traumatic brain injury Who : 20 per 100,000 a year · peak age 15-24 · young → motor vehicle crashes · older → falls Schulich Reviews Intubate if the GCS is below 8 (the lecture says intubate as needed, with in-line C-spine traction) 2. Grading severity with the Glasgow Coma Scale Three parts, maximum 15 : eye opening (4 spontaneously · 3 to speech · 2 to pain · 1 none) · verbal response (5 oriented · 4 confused · 3 inappropriate · 2 incomprehensible · 1 none) · motor response (6 obeys commands · 5 localises to pain · 4 withdraws from pain · 3 flexion to pain · 2 extension to pain · 1 none) Easy to determine · objective · reproducible · predicts outcome Severity GCS Minor 15 Mild 13-14 Moderate 9-12 Severe 3-8 Mortality in severe injury GCS on admission: above 8 → 12% · 5-7 → 27% · below 5 → 78% coma over 1 day → 30-50% · intracranial pressure over 20 (normal under 15) → 50% Epidural 10-25% vs subdural 45-70% 3. Types of head injury Skull fractures : linear · depressed · basilar · open or closed Basilar (base of the skull): raccoon eyes · Battle sign · cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaking from the ear or nose · blood behind the eardrum (hemotympanum) · may not show on CT · risk of meningitis Focal injuries : contusions (coup, contrecoup) · hematomas (epidural, subdural, intracerebral) · penetrating injury (knife, missile, gunshot) Diffuse injuries : concussion and shock-wave injury (blasts, sports) · diffuse axonal injury · traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage 4. bleed, frontal or temporal in 80-90% , found in 25% of closed head injuries · blood dissects the brain beside it, which is otherwise normal CT: well-defined, homogeneous, hyperdense · large with shift, ↓ consciousness and focal deficits → surgery · mortality 25-72% Diffuse axonal injury : an acceleration injury (shaken baby syndrome) · 50% of all severe brain injuries · unconscious at the scene, then persistent coma · co-exists with other injuries · high morbidity and mortality petechial hemorrhages at the grey-white junction · corpus callosum · dorsolateral pons · cervicomedullary junction - difficult to see on CT Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage : same acceleration mechanism and same picture (unconscious at the scene, persistent coma) · pial vessels rupture 5.
