Multiple sclerosis Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed by dissemination in space and time - lesions in different parts of the central nervous system at different times, on MRI with cerebrospinal fluid support - once a better explanation is ruled out . A relapse is new neurological dysfunction lasting 24 hours or more with no other cause , and treatment is chosen by category of disease-modifying drug, not drug by drug. ⭐ MS needs dissemination in space (2 typical regions) and time (a new or an enhancing-plus-non-enhancing lesion), and oligoclonal bands can stand in for time - but only once a better explanation is ruled out. A relapse is new, lasts 24 hours or more, and has no other cause. Myelitis ~50%, optic neuritis ~25% (pain on moving the eye), brainstem or cerebellar ~15%. Relapsing-remitting is 85% at onset; primary progressive worsens from the start without relapses. EBV is the leading risk factor: 32-fold, likely necessary but not sufficient. 1. What MS is, and who gets it An immune-mediated attack (B and T cells) on oligodendrocytes (myelin) in the central nervous system → axonal damage, and eventually axonal loss · slowed conduction from the brain and cord to the body Where the lesions sit : cortical or juxtacortical · periventricular · brainstem · cerebellum · spinal cord Who : the most common disabling disease of the central nervous system in Canada (of young adults) · prevalence 240 per 100,000 (Ontario 230) · female 3:1 · age 20-40 · most often white or Northern European Why : genes, environment and lifestyle genes: all known genetic variants explain only 20-30% of MS heritability environment: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) : infection raises MS risk 32-fold (2022) - likely necessary but not sufficient · adolescent obesity · smoking · vitamin D deficiency · low sunlight · shift work · infectious mononucleosis · passive smoking · (oral tobacco, coffee and alcohol go the other way) lifestyle: smoking · obesity · diet · shift work 2. Disease courses Course Pattern Clinically isolated syndrome A first attack (a relapsing form) Relapsing-remitting 85% of all MS at onset · attacks, then recovery · disability builds in steps Secondary progressive Relapsing-remitting that turns into steady worsening Primary progressive Gradual worsening from the start , without relapses Each is also labelled active or not active , and with or without progression (Lublin 2014) Prognosis : 50% have minor disability at 6-8 years · 21% need help walking at 15 years · median time to needing help walking 27.9 years (about age 59) Disability is scored on the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) : 1-2 minimal disability → 6 assistance needed to walk → 10 death from MS Courses of multiple sclerosis: disability over time 3. Relapses: how MS presents A relapse : an episode of new symptoms of neurological dysfunction · acute or subacute onset · lasting 24 hours or more · not attributable to another cause · not a pseudo-relapse (the lecture names pseudo-relapse without describing it) Typical relapse Share at onset Presents as Myelitis (spinal cord lesion) ~50% Sensory changes · weakness · bladder and bowel dysfunction Optic neuritis ~25% Vision loss · pain with eye movement Brainstem or cerebellar syndrome ~15% Double vision · vertigo · ataxia · dysarthria Other features : sensory disturbances · fatigue · Lhermitte's sign (an electric-shock sensation on bending the neck) Schulich Reviews Charcot's triad : dysarthria, nystagmus, intention tremor 4. Diagnosis: the 2017 McDonald criteria Diagnosis = evidence of dissemination , with clinical attacks and MRI or cerebrospinal fluid findings combined in space : lesions in 2 or more typical regions - periventricular · cortical or juxtacortical · infratentorial · spinal cord in time : new lesions on a follow-up MRI , or enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at the same time CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time MRI is central ; a lumbar puncture looks for oligoclonal bands Always rule out a better explanation : neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMO) · myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease (MOGAD) · vascular · infection · metabolic MS lesions: bright periventricular spots on T2/FLAIR (left), dark holes on T1 (right) Differential (VITAMIN) vascular : headaches and migraine · stroke · CADASIL infection : HIV · syphilis · Lyme disease · West Nile virus toxins : cocaine and its additives autoimmune : of the brain (neuromyelitis optica, MOGAD) · systemic (Sjögren syndrome, Behçet disease) metabolic : vitamin B12 · inflammatory : sarcoidosis · neoplastic : lymphoma the mimics seen most often: neuromyelitis optica, MOGAD, sarcoidosis, lymphoma or other tumour, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), rheumatologic disease 5. Treatment Disease-modifying therapy (DMT): learn the categories, not every drug (the lecture's summary names three: injectables, orals, infusions) Category Examples Notes Injectables ("platforms") Interferons · glatiramer acetate (Copaxone) Long-term safety data · poor adherence Standard orals Dimethyl fumarate · teriflunomide · fingolimod Easier to take than injectables Induction Cladribine An oral drug with long-lasting effects (about 4 years) High efficacy Natalizumab · B-cell therapies (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, rituximab) B-cell therapies are now very widely used Symptomatic therapy Symptom Treatment Spasticity baclofen · tizanidine · stretching · physiotherapy Pain, paresthesias amitriptyline · gabapentin · duloxetine (Cymbalta) · cannabidiol (CBD) Urinary symptoms Parasympatholytics (solifenacin) · urology referral Erectile dysfunction sildenafil Depression Antidepressants Fatigue Amantadine · modafinil Walking speed fampridine (Fampyra) Coming : a vaccine against EBV is in a phase 1 trial (2025) Early diagnosis and treatment can improve long-term outcomes

Approach to stroke Time is brain: localize, then a non-contrast CT rules out hemorrhage before clot-busting with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, up to 4.5 hours) and clot retrieval (thrombectomy) for a proximal large-vessel occlusion. Once the patient is stable, the cause sets secondary prevention: a clot from the heart → anticoagulant; everything else → antiplatelet. ⭐ Non-contrast CT comes first, because any hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to tPA. tPA up to 4.5 hours; thrombectomy for a proximal large vessel occlusion with a perfusion mismatch, even when tPA cannot be given. tPA exclusions: BP over 185/110, INR over 1.4, platelets under 100,000, a factor Xa inhibitor in 24-48 hours. Neglect or aphasia = cortex (MCA), not a lacune. Heart clot → anticoagulate; everything else → antiplatelet. Endarterectomy only for symptomatic stenosis over 70%. TIA: CT, ASA (add clopidogrel for 21 days if already on it), TIA clinic. Hypertensive bleeds are deep; amyloid bleeds are lobar. 1. Definitions and causes Stroke = sudden onset of a neurological deficit caused by a problem with the brain's blood supply Ischemic = a blocked vessel: a large vessel (e.g. the middle cerebral artery (MCA) or a branch) or a small vessel ( lacunar ) Hemorrhagic = a ruptured vessel bleeding into or around the brain Transient ischemic attack (TIA) = a brief episode of neurological dysfunction from focal brain or retinal ischemia, symptoms usually under an hour , and no acute infarction Infarction = tissue death from lack of oxygen · penumbra = stunned but still viable brain around the infarcted core Ischemic core and penumbra on CT Ischemic causes : ① artery-to-artery embolus (carotid, intracranial stenosis, aorta) · ② cardioembolic · ③ lacunar (small vessel) · ④ artery dissection (vertebral, carotid) · ⑤ low perfusion → watershed infarcts between territories (can cause laminar necrosis of the cortical ribbon) · ⑥ cryptogenic 2. Is it a stroke? Mimics of acute weakness Ischemic stroke : follows a specific vascular territory Intracerebral hemorrhage : may not follow a territory · more often with a headache migraine : weakness "marches" , slow onset and offset · may cross territories · minutes, rarely hours · more often young women Todd's paresis : after a (maybe unwitnessed) seizure · improves gradually over hours Psychogenic : inconsistent, especially when distracted · no vascular territory hypoglycemia can cause focal symptoms (especially over old strokes): check the glucose 3. Stroke syndromes Territory Classic presentation Left MCA Aphasia + right face and arm > leg weakness Right MCA Neglect of the left side · anosognosia + left face and arm > leg weakness Anterior cerebral artery (ACA) Opposite leg weakness Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) Opposite homonymous hemianopsia Lacunar ① clumsy hand-dysarthria · ② pure motor (face, arm, leg equally) · ③ pure sensory · ④ ataxic hemiparesis · ⑤ sensorimotor Basilar Eye-movement weakness (ophthalmoparesis) · crossed sensory findings · vertigo 4. Hyperacute management - Paramedics activate the stroke protocol ; the stroke team (neurologist, resident, stroke nurse) waits in the resuscitation room - On arrival : vitals · cardiac monitor · 2 IV lines (one for tPA) · labs ( INR, creatinine, CBC ) · point-of-care glucose · past history and medications (they bear on the cause and the tPA risk) - NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS): level of consciousness · gaze · visual fields · face · arm and leg · limb ataxia · sensation · language · dysarthria · extinction and inattention → is it a stroke, where, and how severe - Localize before you look at the scan : you know where to look for subtle early ischemic change and which vessels to study - suspected basilar thrombosis → always a CT angiogram (a normal plain CT has missed basilar clots that ended in locked-in syndrome) - and you will not be misled by incidental findings or old infarcts - Goals : door to imaging under 25 minutes · door to needle under 60 minutes - Imaging, in order 1. Non-contrast CT head : rule out hemorrhage (an absolute contraindication to tPA) · look for early ischemic change = infarcted, unsalvageable brain · the more early ischemic change, the higher the bleeding rate with tPA 2. CT angiogram (CTA) : a large vessel occlusion? 3. CT perfusion (CTP) : a perfusion mismatch = the best measure of salvageable brain Early ischemic change on CT: an acute infarct beside normal brain 5. tPA and thrombectomy tPA up to 4.5 hours after onset - the earlier the better 0.9 mg/kg: 10% as a bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 1 hour risk of significant hemorrhage: 6% - vessels downstream of the clot were ischemic and leaky, and leak or burst when flow returns more patients have minimal or no disability at 3 months (+13%, number needed to treat 7.7) Exclusion criteria for tPA intracerebral hemorrhage on CT, or ever · significant early ischemic change (may not treat if over 1/3 of the MCA territory ) symptoms suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage , or a seizure at onset BP over 185/110 despite treatment stroke or serious head trauma under 3 months · major surgery under 14 days · gastrointestinal or urinary bleed under 21 days · arterial puncture at a non-compressible site, or a lumbar puncture, under 7 days platelets under 100,000 · INR over 1.4 · PTT over 40 s · a factor Xa inhibitor in the last 24-48 hours glucose under 3 or over 22 · caution in pregnancy, pericarditis, endocarditis Thrombectomy : a proximal large vessel occlusion with a perfusion mismatch → formal angiogram and clot extraction (stent retriever), under sedation or general anesthetic Only 10-20% are tPA candidates (too late, unwitnessed onset, anticoagulated, too mild, hemorrhagic) and under 5% thrombectomy candidates · not a tPA candidate can still be a thrombectomy candidate (on anticoagulants, over 4.5 hours) Thrombectomy: a stent retriever pulls the clot out and restores flow 6. Stroke unit and finding the cause Admission orders : careful BP monitoring for 24 hours

Approach to sensory symptoms Localize first: is the numbness central or peripheral, and where along the path? A truncal sensory level with brisk reflexes is the spinal cord; a symmetric, distal, burning picture that develops over years is a length-dependent polyneuropathy (diabetes); weakness ascending over days with lost reflexes is Guillain-Barré syndrome . ⭐ A truncal sensory level (with brisk reflexes below it) is the spinal cord, not a neuropathy. Guillain-Barré: weakness ascending over days after an infection, with lost reflexes - watch the breathing; IVIG shortens it. Diabetic neuropathy: distal, symmetric, burning, with autonomic symptoms; shooting pain down one leg is a root. S1 root: little toe and sole numb, ankle reflex gone. Nocturnal hand tingling relieved by shaking is carpal tunnel: splint, don't image. Demyelination recovers in up to 12 weeks; axons regrow 1-2 mm a day. 1. Localizing sensory symptoms Central or peripheral? central : brain cortex · subcortical · brainstem · spinal cord peripheral : dorsal root ganglion · root · one nerve (mononeuropathy) · many nerves (polyneuropathy: length-dependent , or mononeuritis multiplex ) A truncal sensory level is what best separates an acute spinal cord lesion from an acute peripheral nerve lesion - bladder urgency, back pain, absent reflexes and symmetric weakness do not A thalamic lesion (e.g. a hemorrhage) → as it recovers, a clumsy hand and burning pain on the opposite side - not neglect (cortex), not muscle atrophy (nerve) A root (e.g. S1 after lifting a heavy patient): back pain radiating down the leg · loss of pinprick and temperature over the little toe and sole · an absent Achilles (ankle) reflex 2. How peripheral nerves are damaged Type What happens Examples Recovery Functional block Channels that keep the resting potential or fire the action potential fail briefly · no gross damage lidocaine (a sodium channel blocker) · hypothermia · brief compression Transient, reversible Axonopathy: Wallerian degeneration The axon breaks down beyond a focal injury in an otherwise healthy nerve Crush, laceration, injection · severe ischemia (vasculitis) · severe metabolic or toxic insult Sprouts grow 1-2 mm a day : months to years · depends on the endoneurium, Schwann cells and reaching the right target Axonopathy: distal dying back The far end of the axon degenerates first, then further back Metabolic: diabetes , kidney failure · drugs: vincristine , cisplatin , metronidazole · lead, arsenic, mercury, acrylamide · hereditary Possible if the cause is removed, but slow and often incomplete Demyelination Myelin breaks down over one to several internodes → conduction fails Immune: Guillain-Barré syndrome , chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) · diphtheria toxin · hereditary Schwann cells remyelinate: up to 12 weeks Neuronopathy The cell body dies (anterior horn or dorsal root ganglion) Motor: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis , polio, West Nile · sensory: paraneoplastic, Sjögren, vitamin B6 toxicity, cisplatin — Nerve injury after trauma neurapraxia : functional block and demyelination, axon intact (compression, brief ischemia) → complete recovery in weeks to 3 months axonotmesis : Wallerian degeneration with Schwann cells and endoneurium preserved (many crush injuries) → 3-12 months , may be incomplete over long distances neurotmesis : axon and connective tissue cut, complete loss of function → limited regrowth, surgical repair often needed Where neuropathy causes act: systemic causes everywhere, root and plexus causes proximally, compression and trauma distally 3. Characterizing a peripheral neuropathy Which fibres : sensory · motor · autonomic - sensory only, sensorimotor, or sensory and autonomic? Time course : acute (days to 6 weeks) · subacute (6 weeks to 6 months) · chronic (over 6 months) Pattern (once a root or plexus is excluded): length-dependent polyneuropathy · mononeuropathy · mononeuritis multiplex Axonal or demyelinating : best shown on EMG 4. Three patterns to tell apart Length-dependent polyneuropathy Guillain-Barré syndrome Spinal cord lesion (e.g. MS) Tempo Chronic (years) Days , often after an infection Days to weeks, may settle Main problem Sensory: painful, burning feet Weakness >>> sensory loss Sensory ± weakness, bladder urgency Pattern Distal, symmetric (stocking-glove) Ascending : toes → knees, then fingertips Everything below a level on the trunk Reflexes Reduced in the legs Lost or reduced (areflexia) Brisk below the level · Babinski signs Also Autonomic: postural light-headedness, urinary hesitancy, constipation Can reach the cranial nerves and breathing muscles → respiratory failure, sometimes intubation A positive Romberg sign Test — EMG: usually demyelinating (axonal forms exist) MRI of the brain and spinal cord (suspicious for MS) Treatment Treat the pain : an analgesic or an antidepressant IVIG shortens the course · slow recovery over weeks to months · best treated by a neurologist As for MS Diabetes is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in Canada : axonal (large and small fibres) · distal (stocking-glove) · symmetric · sensorimotor · often painful shooting pain down one leg is a root, not the diabetic neuropathy (he also has degenerative disc disease) other causes: infection (HIV, leprosy) · drugs · metabolic (uremia, thyroid) · autoimmune · hereditary · idiopathic Guillain-Barré syndrome = acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP): autoimmune, antibody-mediated , often after an infection (antigen mimicry) Hands numb at night, relieved by shaking, normal exam → carpal tunnel, not MS: no imaging; nocturnal wrist splints help MS in brief : the most common acquired demyelinating disease of the central nervous system · patchy plaques in the brain and cord · dissemination in time and space · 85% relapsing-remitting (some become secondary progressive), 15% primary progressive (see 02 - Multiple Sclerosis ) Stocking-and-glove distribution of a length-dependent polyne

Neuropathic pain Neuropathic pain comes from a damaged or malfunctioning nervous system, not from injured tissue, so it is treated differently from ordinary (nociceptive) pain. Recognize it by its symptoms , find the cause, then choose one agent to fit what else the patient has and titrate it slowly to the maximum dose. ⭐ Allodynia = pain from a non-painful touch; hyperpathia = too much pain from a painful one; dysesthesia = uncomfortable sensations such as burning. Neuropathic pain is not treated like nociceptive pain: acetaminophen and NSAIDs are for tissue pain. Poor sleep or cost → amitriptyline; depression → duloxetine; trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine; narcotics last. One drug at a time, titrated to the maximum - change it for side effects first, or no effect after a month at the top dose. CRPS: more pain, for longer, than the injury explains, with swelling, temperature, colour and skin changes. 1. Two kinds of pain Nociceptive Neuropathic Source Tissue injury, inflammation, temperature, pressure or stretch A neurological cause Types Somatic or visceral Peripheral or central nervous system injury or dysfunction Treatment Acetaminophen · NSAIDs · opioids Its own drugs (section 4) 2. Symptoms Allodynia = pain from a non-painful touch (sheets brushing across the feet) Hyperpathia = a painful stimulus provokes an exaggerated amount of pain (pinprick testing is extremely painful) Dysesthesia = uncomfortable sensations (burning pain) Descriptors patients use : electrical · shooting · burning, hot or cold · pins and needles 3. Causes Peripheral Central Length-dependent neuropathy : diabetic · small fibre sensory · chemotherapy-induced Lesions of the thalamus · brainstem · spinal cord Radiculopathy · postherpetic neuralgia · trigeminal neuralgia · nerve injury Phantom limb pain likely has a central part Small fibre neuropathy (toes "on fire" at night, a length-dependent small fibre neuropathy): diabetes is the most common cause ; without diabetes most are idiopathic, and some are genetic (from the module) If neuropathic pain is present : evaluate the cause and examine - is there an important neurological diagnosis? Some causes are reversible , and classic syndromes respond to specific drugs ( trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine ) Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS): an uncommon chronic pain syndrome after a focal tissue or nerve injury, with inflammatory and autonomic features · pain greater than the injury explains, lasting longer than healing should take · the limb: severe pain and allodynia, swelling, temperature and colour changes, skin and hair changes · peripheral and central sensitization · treatment is hard and multidisciplinary Background, nice to know : after nerve damage, ↑ sodium and ↓ potassium channels make neurons hyperexcitable , firing on their own (spontaneous, paroxysmal pain) · injury can cause central sensitization in the spinal cord, which early treatment can avoid · norepinephrine and serotonin drive the descending pain-inhibiting pathways, so raising them increases inhibition 4. Treatment Class Examples Choose it when Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) amitriptyline · nortriptyline Poor sleep · cost (amitriptyline is the cheapest) Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) duloxetine · venlafaxine Depression Anticonvulsants gabapentin · pregabalin · in specific situations a sodium-channel drug, carbamazepine Trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine Topical agents Capsaicin · lidocaine gel or patch — Other Cannabinoids · narcotics ( opioids ) Narcotics only as a last resort Trial and error : trial one agent and titrate it up slowly to the maximum dose significant side effects before an appropriate effect → change the drug no effect after 1 month at the highest dose → change the drug

Approach to headache Rule out a secondary headache - rare, but potentially life-threatening - while you decide whether there is a primary headache disorder , which can also badly affect quality of life and may need treatment. The SNOOP4 red flags point to the secondary causes; with none, the features of the attack name the primary headache: migraine, tension-type or cluster. ⭐ Screen every headache with SNOOP4 first: a thunderclap headache is a subarachnoid hemorrhage until an urgent CT - and a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if the CT is negative - says otherwise. Over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication → ESR, CRP and high-dose steroids today, before the biopsy. Fever and a stiff neck → antibiotics before any scan or lumbar puncture. Obese, worse lying down, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema → MRI and MR venogram before the lumbar puncture. Tension-type: both sides, pressing, no nausea; migraine: one side, pulsating, worse with activity; cluster: strictly one side at the eye, restless, with same-side autonomic signs. Triptans at onset, never with coronary disease; acute drugs on under 2-3 days a week. First preventive: beta-blocker or amitriptyline; high BMI → topiramate. 1. History and examination History : the pain in detail ( NILDOCAAFIAT : N ature (quality) · I ntensity (0-10) · L ocation · D uration · O nset (acute or gradual) · C ontributing triggers · A ggravating · A lleviating · F requency · I mpact on function · A ttribute (what they think causes it) · T reatment tried) + the features of a secondary headache (SNOOP4, below) Examination, and why vital signs : high BP can itself cause headache · infection changes the vitals · some headache drugs change BP and heart rate fundoscopy : papilledema raises concern for raised intracranial pressure pupils, light responses, eye movements, visual fields · neurological exam : a neuro-ophthalmological or focal deficit suggests a secondary headache body habitus : obesity → idiopathic intracranial hypertension; a large neck and obesity → obstructive sleep apnea neck : marked stiffness → meningeal irritation (meningitis) · neck muscle pain can present as headache scalp : tenderness → giant cell arteritis · temporomandibular joint : its disorders can present as headache 2. Red flags: SNOOP4 Red flag Need to exclude S Systemic symptoms: fever, chills, weight loss Metastasis, infection N Neurological symptoms or deficits (especially focal) Stroke, mass, encephalitis O Older age at onset ( over 50 ) Temporal arteritis , glaucoma, mass O Onset sudden: thunderclap Bleed P Papilledema Raised intracranial pressure P Positional Worse lying down → mass or raised pressure · worse upright → low pressure (intracranial hypotension) P Precipitated by Valsalva Raised intracranial pressure P Progressive , or a substantial change in pattern Any secondary cause Secondary causes vascular : ischemic stroke · intracerebral hemorrhage · subarachnoid hemorrhage · cerebral venous thrombosis · posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) · reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) · cranio-cervical artery dissection · vasculitis idiopathic or inflammatory : giant cell (temporal) arteritis · idiopathic intracranial hypertension trauma : after a dural puncture · concussion · drugs and toxins : medication overuse headache neoplastic : meningioma · vestibular schwannoma · pituitary adenoma (apoplexy) · choriocarcinoma · infectious : meningitis, encephalitis · systemic infection 3. Secondary headaches not to miss Presents as First test Treatment Subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal) Thunderclap: worst ever, peaks within seconds · nausea, vomiting, photophobia · neck stiffness Urgent non-contrast CT (sensitivity 98% day 0 · 76% day 2 · 50% at 1 week · 30% at 2 weeks ) → negative: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia Secure the aneurysm ( 03 - Approach to Stroke ) · untreated, re-bleeds 15% in 24 hours, 40% within a month Bacterial meningitis Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status · Kernig and Brudzinski signs Blood cultures · lumbar puncture if safe (image first if signs of raised pressure) IV ceftriaxone + vancomycin at once (± ampicillin if elderly or immunocompromised, ± acyclovir if herpes simplex encephalitis is possible) · never delayed for imaging or lumbar puncture Giant cell arteritis (the most common vasculitis; over 50) New headache · scalp tenderness · visual disturbance (amaurosis fugax, blurring, double vision) · jaw claudication · constitutional and polymyalgic symptoms · limb claudication ESR and CRP · temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound · can be normal: the disease is patchy High-dose glucocorticoids started at once, without waiting for confirmation , then tapered · untreated → permanent vision loss Brain tumour Steady, persistent, often worse in the morning · nausea or vomiting · worse with coughing, exercise or position · does not respond to usual remedies · personality change, seizure, focal deficit Urgent MRI with contrast (CT if no MRI) · papilledema = raised pressure · CT chest, abdomen and pelvis: primary or metastasis? — Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Worse lying down · pulsatile tinnitus · horizontal double vision ( sixth nerve palsy ) · transient visual obscurations · visual defects · risk: obesity, steroids, vitamin A, tetracycline MRI with MR venography before the lumbar puncture (empty sella, flattened posterior globe, venous sinus stenosis) · opening pressure over 250 mm H2O Weight loss · acetazolamide , topiramate · shunt or optic nerve sheath fenestration · close eye follow-up 4. Primary headaches: migraine, tension-type, cluster Migraine Tension-type Cluster Who 3rd most prevalent, 7th most disabling condition worldwide The most prevalent (38% a year) 0.1% · onset ~30 · men 3:1 · 85% smokers · alcohol triggers Duration 4-72 hours 30 minutes to 7 days 15-180 minutes , every other day to 8 a day Side One side (can be both) Both sides (always) Strictly one side : around and above the
07 Approach to Altered Level of Consciousness

Approach to altered level of consciousness Consciousness has two parts: alertness (being awake: wakefulness, vigilance, responding to stimuli) and awareness (the content: everything the cortex does) . First find what is treatable, then let the exam - brainstem reflexes, breathing, the motor response, eye opening, any sign of awareness - place the patient on the spectrum from brain death to minimally conscious. ⭐ Vegetative state is awake but not aware; locked-in syndrome is aware but cannot move - only upward gaze and eye opening are left. Look for the treatable causes (glucose, shock, drugs, meningitis, encephalitis, hematoma) before labelling a coma. Coma needs both hemispheres, both thalami, or the brainstem above the mid-pons. Decorticate = arms flex, above the red nucleus; decerebrate = all extend, below it; triple flexion is spinal. Minimally conscious minus vs plus = command following. The FOUR score works in an intubated patient; the GCS verbal score does not. GCS ≤ 8 = severe. Brain death = no brainstem reflexes + no breathing on apnea test + no confounders. 1. What keeps us conscious Alertness (arousal) is the volume; awareness (content) is the tuning: you can be alert without being aware, but not aware without being alert Both are kept up by the ascending reticular activating system : the reticular formation in the upper pons and midbrain projecting widely to the cerebral cortex , through the thalamus (intralaminar nuclei) and through the hypothalamus and basal forebrain Ascending reticular activating system: reticular formation in the upper pons and midbrain projecting through both thalami to the cortex 2. Causes of coma, and what else to consider Coma = loss of both alertness and awareness · the system has to fail in one of three places : both hemispheres (global cortical dysfunction) : metabolic, toxic, hypoxic-ischemic injury , trauma, large bilateral destructive lesions both thalami or the hypothalamus : stroke ( "tip of the basilar" syndrome ), destructive lesions (hemorrhage, tumour) the brainstem above the mid-pons : trauma, stroke, herniation (central, uncal, falcine, midline shift) · consciousness falls with the degree and rate of shift, not its direction Treatable causes to find first : shock or low blood pressure · low blood glucose · diabetic ketoacidosis · hypertensive encephalopathy · drug intoxication · bacterial or fungal meningitis · herpes simplex encephalitis · brain abscess · epidural or subdural hematoma Other causes of an altered level of consciousness : syncope · seizure · the post-ictal state · encephalopathy or delirium Coma mimics (aware, but cannot show it): locked-in syndrome · severe neuromuscular disease ( Guillain-Barré syndrome , myasthenia gravis ) · neuromuscular blockade (iatrogenic) · akinetic mutism · psychogenic unresponsiveness 3. Examining the unconscious patient Observe : how much stimulation it takes to get a response · agitation · any communication · breathing pattern and ventilator needs · spontaneous or asymmetric movement · automatisms (yawning, sneezing, coughing, swallowing, hiccoughing) · fundoscopy Cranial nerve reflexes Reflex In Out What to know Pupillary light II III (Edinger-Westphal → ciliary ganglion → iris sphincter) Size, shape, reactivity · a "blown" (Hutchinson) pupil = uncal herniation · a small pupil with ptosis = sympathetic loss ( Horner's syndrome ) Oculocephalic (doll's eyes) VIII III, IV, VI Only if there is no cervical spine concern · localizes supranuclear, internuclear, nuclear or nerve lesions Caloric ( vestibulo-ocular ) VIII III, IV, VI COWS is for awake patients only · in coma, an intact reflex = slow deviation toward the cold ear, no fast phase Corneal V VII Lift both lids, touch each cornea with a cotton wisp (or tissue, eye drops); watch for closure Gag / cough IX X Gag often absent in the ICU · suction catheter down the breathing tube for a deep cough · cough is often the last reflex lost Motor : tone · spontaneous movement and command following ( is it reproducible , not just a reflex?) · pain: central (sternum, trapezius, supraorbital ridge, mandible) or peripheral (nail bed) → grimace, localizing, withdrawal · tendon reflexes and plantar responses Decorticate (flexor) : arms flex, legs extend → lesion above the red nucleus (midbrain or above) Decerebrate (extensor) : arms and legs extend → lesion below the red nucleus (lower brainstem) Triple flexion (hip, knee, ankle) = a spinal reflex , needs no brainstem Coma scales Glasgow Coma Scale FOUR score Parts Eyes 1-4 · verbal 1-5 · motor 1-6 Eyes · motor · brainstem reflexes · respiration , each 0-4 Range 3-15 · ≤ 8 = severe brain injury 0-16 Intubated? Verbal cannot be scored : E2 VT M4 = 6T No verbal part, so it works Weakness Built for head trauma · does not assess the brainstem well Newer 4. Disorders of consciousness, and brain death Five syndromes : coma · vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness syndrome) · minimally conscious minus · minimally conscious plus · emergence · locked-in syndrome is compared with them but is not a disorder of consciousness Vegetative state : awake (sleep-wake cycles, autonomic function kept) but not aware · reflexive only: grimace, yawn, roving eyes, flexion withdrawal, decorticate posturing, brief unsustained pursuit · no language, no purposeful response, incontinent Minimally conscious : limited but definite awareness · minus = visual pursuit, localizes pain, smiles or cries to stimuli, no commands · plus = follows commands · emerged = functional communication and object use Functional MRI can show awareness the bedside misses (imagining tennis lights the motor areas as in healthy people) Brain death (Canadian criteria), all of : a known cause and no reversible mimic · deep unresponsive coma , no motor response (spinal reflexes allowed) · no brainstem reflexes : gag, cough, and on both sides corneal, pupillary (pupils mid-size or larger) , vestibulo-ocular · no breathing effort on the apnea test · no confounder

Approach to seizures After a first seizure the questions come in order: was it a seizure, was it provoked, and how likely is another? The workup exists to estimate that last number: a recurrence risk of 60% or more is the threshold for treatment , and the lesion on MRI or the discharges on EEG are what push it there. ⭐ A single unprovoked seizure with a normal MRI and EEG → discuss treatment; a structural lesion, epileptiform discharges or a second unprovoked seizure over 24 hours apart makes it epilepsy (recurrence ≥ 60%) → recommend treatment. Provoked seizure (immediate post-traumatic, fever, glucose, sodium, alcohol) → treat the cause, no drug. Remote stroke or old trauma = unprovoked, not provoked. Onset not seen = unknown onset. Every first seizure gets an MRI and an EEG. Drug-resistant = 2 appropriate, tolerated drugs failed → refer to a comprehensive epilepsy centre (a third drug can be tried alongside the referral). 1. Seizure, and how seizures are classified Epileptic seizure = a transient occurrence of signs or symptoms from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain Classified by where it starts (International League Against Epilepsy, 2017) Focal onset Generalized onset Unknown onset Starts in One area of the brain Both sides from the start Not seen (unwitnessed) Awareness Aware or impaired awareness — — Motor Motor onset (automatisms, clonic, tonic, epileptic spasms) Motor (tonic-clonic, myoclonic, epileptic spasms) Tonic-clonic, epileptic spasms Non-motor Non-motor onset (behaviour arrest, sensory, autonomic) Non-motor = absence (3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave on EEG) Behaviour arrest Spread Can become focal to bilateral tonic-clonic — — A seizure that cannot be placed is unclassified Focal, generalized and unknown onset seizures, with their secondary classifications 2. The first seizure: was it one, and was it provoked? History is the key : details of the event · speak with witnesses , review ambulance records · anything that needs urgent evaluation (fever, trauma) Seizure risk factors : febrile seizures or childhood epilepsy · significant head trauma · past meningitis or encephalitis · family history of seizures or epilepsy Physical exam is often normal · tongue biting , musculoskeletal injuries · ⚠ enduring confusion, a low level of consciousness or a persistent focal deficit → urgent evaluation Provoked Unprovoked Definition A transient factor acting on an otherwise normal brain temporarily lowers the threshold No temporary or reversible factor · an enduring epileptogenic abnormality Examples Immediate post-traumatic · fever · glucose, sodium · alcohol Genetic conditions · remote structural lesions : brain tumour, old stroke, old brain trauma Treat? No - treat the underlying cause Depends on the recurrence risk (below) 3. Investigations: estimating the risk of another seizure Bloodwork as the history needs · electrolytes, including extended electrolytes CT often done acutely in the emergency department · rules out a clear structural cause (hemorrhage, tumour) MRI is required in every first-seizure workup · epilepsy protocol, with a dedicated look at the temporal lobes · a structural abnormality raises the recurrence risk EEG is required · epileptiform activity raises the recurrence risk · childhood absence epilepsy: abrupt 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave with staring 4. To treat or not to treat Situation What to do Non-epileptic event · provoked seizure Do not treat - treat the underlying cause Single unprovoked seizure Discuss the options with the patient Recurrent unprovoked seizures / epilepsy (recurrence risk ≥ 60% ) Recommend treatment Status epilepticus Treat as a neurologic emergency Epilepsy (operational definition), any one of : 2 unprovoked (or reflex) seizures more than 24 hours apart 1 unprovoked seizure + a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years (as after two seizures: a lesion on MRI, discharges on EEG) an epilepsy syndrome Classifying an epilepsy : seizure type → epilepsy type (focal, generalized, combined generalized and focal , unknown) → epilepsy syndrome · etiology at every level : structural (stroke, trauma, tumour, mesial temporal sclerosis ) · genetic (inherited, de novo or mosaic, polygenic) · infectious ( viral encephalitis , bacterial meningitis , neurocysticercosis ) · metabolic (inborn errors) · immune (autoimmune or paraneoplastic: anti-NMDA receptor, anti-LGI1, anti-Hu, anti-GAD65) · unknown Syndromes (by age): childhood absence epilepsy · juvenile myoclonic epilepsy · benign Rolandic epilepsy · West syndrome · Dravet syndrome · Lennox-Gastaut syndrome Comorbidities : non-epileptic seizures · depression , anxiety , attention deficit hyperactivity disorder · migraine · cognitive impairment · sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) 5. Chronic management of epilepsy Choosing a drug : one drug or several · treats a comorbidity too (headache, mood) · side effects · dose range · adherence · blood levels · titration, cross-titration, weaning · drug interactions · cost and coverage · age · pregnancy: teratogenicity Antiseizure drug target Examples Sodium channel phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide SV2A (vesicle release) levetiracetam T-type calcium channel ethosuximide GABA-A receptor benzodiazepines, barbiturates Several mechanisms valproate, topiramate Drug-resistant epilepsy = 2 tolerated, appropriately chosen and used drugs (alone or combined) have failed to give sustained seizure freedom (3 times the prior gap between seizures, or 1 year, whichever is longer) first drug → second drug (switch or combine) → refer to a comprehensive epilepsy centre , trying a third drug alongside the referral : confirm it is epilepsy · rule out non-epileptic seizures and pseudoresistance (wrong diagnosis, wrong dose, nonadherence) · ketogenic diet, behavioural therapy presurgical evaluation : MRI, PET, ictal SPECT, functional MRI · long-term video-EEG · neuropsychological testing · Wada test →

Recovery in the nervous system A cut axon always loses its far end; whether it grows back depends on where it is. Peripheral axons can regrow along the empty Schwann cell tube when the stumps meet; central axons are held back by their surroundings, not by an inability to grow, and the brain recovers mainly by plasticity. ⭐ Central axons regrow inside a peripheral nerve graft (Aguayo) - so it is the central environment, not the neuron, that blocks regeneration. Peripheral regrowth needs stump-to-stump contact and the empty Schwann cell tube, helped by laminin and nerve growth factor. Crush injury → poorer regeneration and traumatic neuroma. Facial nerve regrowth gone wrong → synkinesis, including tears while eating. After axotomy: Wallerian degeneration distally, central chromatolysis in the cell body. 1. From axotomy to reconnection Both stumps swell , the proximal and the distal Beyond the cut (distal) : Wallerian degeneration - myelin breaks into myelin ovoids · the segment cut off from the cell body degenerates and is cleared · the muscle it supplied atrophies The cell body : central chromatolysis (the Nissl substance disperses) Across synapses : trans-synaptic degeneration can spread upstream or downstream Regrowth : sprouts with growth cones extend from the proximal stump in search of a target , steered by trophic factors and extracellular matrix molecules - not at random → reconnection with a target Not the same as segmental demyelination (myelin lost, axon intact) or axonal degeneration (the axon dying back from its far end) After a cut: Wallerian degeneration of the distal axon, debris cleared, then the axon regrows and is remyelinated 2. Peripheral vs central regeneration Peripheral nervous system Central nervous system Regrowth Sprouts grow from the proximal stump along the empty distal Schwann cell tube Sprout extension is inhibited Needs Stump-to-stump contact · laminin, nerve growth factor and other factors — The proof — Albert Aguayo : central axons regrew into a peripheral nerve graft → the central environment, not the neuron, blocks it How it recovers Regrowth to the target Plasticity : ongoing remodelling of dendrites and dendritic spines Conditions for peripheral regeneration : close stumps · an intact Schwann cell tube to follow · a clean cut rather than a crush or maceration (a crush makes regeneration less likely) 3. When regeneration goes wrong Misguided, haphazard sprouting reaches the wrong target Synkinesis : after a facial nerve injury, fibres reinnervate the wrong target · orbicularis oculi instead of orbicularis oris · the lacrimal gland instead of a salivary gland (tears while eating) · it shows that regeneration happened Traumatic neuroma : a tangle of regrowing axons · more likely after a crush or macerating injury than a clean cut · can cause chronic pain

Neurosurgical emergencies Headache, coma, a new neurological deficit or trauma bring a patient to neurosurgery, and the cause is almost always PRESSURE inside a closed skull: hemorrhage, tumour or trauma. The decision is what is taking up the space, because emergency neurosurgery is decompression , and blood, a tumour's edema and trapped cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are each removed or shrunk a different way. Head injury grading and the herniation types are in 01 - Approach to Head Injuries . ⭐ Mannitol shrinks brain that still has an intact blood-brain barrier; dexamethasone shrinks a tumour's vasogenic edema by restoring a broken one. Epidural: lens-shaped, arterial, lucid interval, blown pupil on the same side - early decompression does predictably well. Acute subdural: crescent, bridging veins, outcome unpredictable. Ruptured aneurysm: re-rupture 6% day 1, 20% at 2 weeks, 50% at 6 months - repair early. Hydrocephalus: external ventricular drain now, shunt later; untreated it kills by herniation. Intubate for GCS 1. The neurosurgical exam: localize, don't just reassure Level of consciousness : Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS): eyes /4, verbal /5, motor /6 · ⚠ intubate for GCS to protect the airway Cranial nerves : II acuity, fields, fundus · III pupillary response and eye movements · V facial sensation, chewing muscles, corneal reflex · VII facial droop · VIII hearing · IX and X gag · XI shrug · XII tongue Motor : pronator drift · bulk, tone, power, reflexes · hands, arms, legs, feet · compare the sides Sensory : light touch, pinprick, proprioception · find the sensory level on the trunk · cerebellar exam ⚠ " GCS 15, moving x 4 " can hide a patient with 1/5 hand intrinsics and 0/5 legs: a T1 spinal cord injury 2. The bleeds: which space, and what to do Epidural Acute subdural Subarachnoid Source Middle meningeal artery , between dura and skull Bridging veins to the dural sinuses, under the dura Ruptured aneurysm , in the subarachnoid space Story Blow to the side of the head · stunned · lucid interval (played on with a headache) · then cannot be woken High-energy trauma (rollover, intoxicated, on ASA) · comatose Explosive headache unlike any other · vomiting · photophobia · stiff neck · retinal hemorrhage · can be GCS 15 Signs Blown pupil on the side of the clot (third nerve) · the opposite side weaker Fixed dilated pupil · posturing Normal exam possible CT Lens-shaped (convex) Crescent (concave) Blood in the subarachnoid space · lumbar puncture: blood in the CSF Treatment EARLY decompression → predictably good results Evacuate · outcome unpredictable , set by the brain injury underneath Early aneurysm repair · protects against the next bleed only Why a ruptured aneurysm is an emergency : a single hemorrhage brings 50% death and 75% disability · re-rupture: 6% on day 1, 20% by 2 weeks, 50% by 6 months · outcome depends on the neurological status at presentation CT: epidural hematoma is lens-shaped (convex), subdural hematoma is a crescent 3. Lowering the pressure: medical decompression Dexamethasone (Decadron) Mannitol Use Tumour with vasogenic edema Make room for a mass or swollen, damaged brain How Restores the blood-brain barrier in leaky tumour vessels → the edema and the "effective" tumour size shrink Osmotic shrinkage of brain with an intact blood-brain barrier Dose in the lecture 10 mg IV 300 cc of 20% IV push Brain tumour : weeks of progressive deficit (word-finding difficulty, slurred speech, a clumsy hand) then a rapid fall in consciousness → intubate if GCS dexamethasone + mannitol → resect once stable (72 hours later in the lecture's case) 4. Hydrocephalus Hydrocephalus : CSF trapped in the ventricles squeezes the brain from inside · e.g. after bacterial meningitis : a febrile teenager who cannot be roused , dysconjugate gaze, cloudy CSF Untreated hydrocephalus can kill : death and disability come from brain herniation Divert the CSF : short term an external ventricular drain (placed in the emergency department) · long term a ventriculoperitoneal shunt · treat the cause (antibiotics) Schulich Reviews Epidural hematoma: a contact injury (a fall onto cement), skull fracture in about 80%; torn dural vessels, the middle meningeal artery in about 50%; brief loss of consciousness → lucid interval → coma ; operate if symptomatic or an acute clot is 1 cm or more; mortality about 25% Subdural hematoma: acceleration-deceleration (car accident); elderly and people with alcohol use disorder ; slow, progressive fall in consciousness; goes with diffuse axonal injury; mortality about 30%, worse with a lower GCS Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: torn pial vessels ; blood is patchy or lobar , where an aneurysmal bleed sits near the cisterns and the middle, anterior and posterior cerebral arteries; CT angiography next; complications include intraventricular hemorrhage and hydrocephalus Traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage: a well-defined, homogeneous, hyperdense bleed on non-contrast CT, in the frontal and temporal lobes; control the blood pressure, reverse any coagulopathy ; half die within a month Lowering intracranial pressure: head of the bed up 30° , neck midline, collar loosened · intubate, sedate, cool, drain CSF, paralyze, temporary hyperventilation · adequate blood pressure · mannitol or hypertonic saline (23.4% bolus, 3% longer term) Hydrocephalus is common in children ; a child weeks after meningitis with headache, an abnormal gait, raised pressure and no fever = hydrocephalus

Neuroinfections Suspected meningitis is a race: culture the blood, then start empiric treatment at once - never held back for the CT or the lumbar puncture. The CT comes first only with focal signs or a decreased level of consciousness; the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) then tells bacterial from viral, and cortical signs (language trouble, focal seizures) point to herpes simplex encephalitis. ⭐ Blood culture, then empiric treatment at once (ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone with the first dose, + acyclovir; + ampicillin if over 50 or immunocompromised); CT first only with focal signs or a decreased level of consciousness. Neutrophils + low glucose (ratio Language trouble, focal seizures and no stiff neck → herpes simplex encephalitis: mesial temporal MRI, CSF HSV PCR, IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h. Listeria: over 50 or immunocompromised. Neonates: E. coli and group B strep. Gram-negative diplococci = N. meningitidis. 1. Infections of the central nervous system Four kinds of organism : bacterial ( bacterial meningitis , abscess) · viral ( viral meningitis , viral encephalitis ) · fungal ( cryptococcal ) · protozoal ( neurocysticercosis ) Where it sits : meningitis (the meninges) · encephalitis (the brain tissue) · abscess (walled off) Meningitis, encephalitis, meningoencephalitis and abscess: where in the brain each infection sits 2. Meningitis vs encephalitis: how they present Bacterial meningitis Viral (herpes simplex) encephalitis Age Any age Older Fever · decreased awareness Yes · yes Yes · yes Nuchal rigidity Yes (Kernig's, Brudzinski's) No Rash Can be No Language disturbance No Yes (word salad), confusion Other cortical signs — Focal seizures · impaired memory · aphasia · focal deficits Emergency? Yes Yes Classic triad of meningitis : fever · altered mental status · nuchal rigidity Aseptic (viral) meningitis : no organism isolated · headache, fever, mild meningeal signs, photophobia, rash · not very sick 3.
