Empiric treatment of bacterial meningitis in adults (all IV) Drug Dose Covers Give Ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 h H. influenzae · N. meningitidis · penicillin-susceptible S. pneumoniae · MSSA Everyone Vancomycin 1 g every 8 h Ceftriaxone-resistant S. pneumoniae · MRSA Everyone Ampicillin 2 g every 4 h Listeria Over 50 or immunocompromised Acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h Herpes simplex In the lecture's empiric order for a healthy adult Dexamethasone 10 mg with the first antibiotic dose , then every 6 h for 4 days ↓ illness and death, most for S. pneumoniae Complications : sepsis · hydrocephalus · cranial nerve palsies · vasculitis → stroke · cerebritis · abscess · seizures · coma · death Aseptic meningitis : supportive, rehydration 6. Herpes simplex encephalitis The most common and important viral encephalitis · headache, fever, language disturbance , confusion, decreased awareness Confirm the diagnosis : CT/MRI of the mesial temporal lobe · CSF HSV PCR · EEG (temporal spikes) · biopsy Treat: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h, dosed on ideal body weight (700 mg for a 70 kg patient) MRI in herpes simplex encephalitis: bright signal in the temporal lobes Schulich Reviews Bacterial meningitis = " sick "; viral meningitis = " lousy " (headache, stiff neck, fever) → an NSAID and reassurance Kernig's sign = knee extension resisted with the hip flexed · Brudzinski's sign = neck flexion makes the hips flex · jolt accentuation of the headache Empiric bacterial meningitis treatment as " CAAV + D ": ceftriaxone, acyclovir, ampicillin (elderly or immunocompromised), vancomycin + dexamethasone; give antibiotics and the steroid early (less death and hearing loss); dexamethasone can stop if it is not bacterial S. aureus after head trauma or neurosurgery; neonates (E. coli, group B strep) → ampicillin + gentamicin A brain abscess is an organized infection

Multidisciplinary care in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has no cure and only two modestly effective drugs, so the most important treatment is the team. Recognise the mixed upper and lower motor neuron picture , then know who handles what as the weakness spreads. ⭐ ALS = UMN and LMN signs together in two or more regions, with no prominent non-motor involvement. Riluzole (glutamate antagonist) and edaravone (antioxidant) are the only drugs, both modest; BiPAP also extends life. Death is from respiratory muscle failure or aspiration pneumonia, on average 3 years from onset. Swallowing and speech = speech-language pathologist; cough, breathing, ankle-foot orthoses = physiotherapist; hand splints and home changes = occupational therapist; tube-feeding teaching = dietitian; prescribing BiPAP = physician. 1. What ALS is Definition : a neurodegenerative disease causing upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) weakness motor neurons are lost in the motor cortex and the spinal cord (anterior horn cells) How common : 2-3 per 100,000 Cause : 5-10% hereditary (autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive patterns) · the rest sporadic, the cause uncertain: probably genetic predisposition + environmental exposures + chance Presents as : hand weakness · foot drop · slurred speech (dysarthria) · trouble swallowing (dysphagia) · shortness of breath (dyspnea) → progressive weakness that spreads to most of the body Course : average survival 3 years from onset · death usually from respiratory muscle failure or aspiration pneumonia ALS symptoms by region: bulbar (speech, saliva, swallowing), respiratory, upper body (hand weakness, dressing, handwriting) and lower body (tripping, stairs, weak feet) 2. Diagnosis History : progressive, relatively isolated motor symptoms Exam : LMN signs (atrophy, fasciculations) + UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity) in at least two regions , without prominent extra-motor involvement Investigations only to rule out other explanations, as appropriate: nerve conduction studies · cerebrospinal fluid · MRI · metabolic tests 3. Treatment No cure Only two approved drugs , both modestly effective : Riluzole : glutamate antagonist , reduces excitotoxicity Edaravone : antioxidant Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) can extend life once symptoms of breathing insufficiency appear Most important treatment = managing symptoms and function through multidisciplinary care · seen in the clinic every 3-6 months to maximize function and minimize symptoms 4. The multidisciplinary team Member What they handle Speech-language pathologist Communication : dysarthria ( spastic, flaccid or both ) → compensatory strategies for patient and family · augmentative and alternative communication devices, high- or low-tech · strategies for language and cognition · Swallowing (food, drink and saliva) : bedside clinical assessment, modified barium swallow , fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing · texture changes (minced, puree, thickened liquids) · discusses feeding tubes Physiotherapist Breathing : shortness of breath on exertion and orthopnea (balancing activity, raising the head of the bed ) · signs and prevention of chest infection · keeping the airways clear · cough and secretion clearance (deep breathing and coughing, manually assisted cough , breath stacking , chest percussion, mainly oral suction at home) · Limbs : range-of-motion exercises (prevent frozen shoulder) · protect the shoulders from strain · stretching for spasticity · gait aids: ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop , canes, walkers Occupational therapist Keeps independence and participation : activities of daily living , environment and accessibility, work and leisure · compensatory techniques, equipment ( hand splints ), resources, home and vehicle modifications Social worker First visit: psychosocial assessment (family and community supports, work, income and insurance, wills and powers of attorney ) · later: care needs, disability financial options , adjustment to disability and mood Dietitian Eating routine, swallowing limits, nutritional adequacy , other conditions, drug-supplement interactions, bowels, fluids, skin · weight monitoring · supplements, high-protein high-energy diet, texture changes · enteral (tube) feeding : whether it is needed, supplies, teaching Nurse Explains the team, the contact between visits (troubleshoots with patient and local caregivers) · coordinates team meetings, follow-up and clinical trials · advance care planning Physician Confirms the diagnosis · drugs for drooling (sialorrhea), spasticity, pain, constipation, depression, pseudobulbar affect · starts and monitors BiPAP with a respirologist · end-of-life discussions · trial recruitment Schulich Reviews ALS is a diagnosis of exclusion : also rule out Lyme disease and heavy metals Baclofen for spasticity

Brain tumours A brain tumour shows itself by raised intracranial pressure , a focal deficit, a change in the person or a seizure, and the red flag tying them together is that the symptoms keep progressing . Metastases are more common than primary tumours ; among primaries gliomas lead, and contrast enhancement (grade) decides how fast to treat. ⭐ Progressive symptoms are the red flag for a brain tumour: weeks to months suggests a highly malignant tumour, months or longer a benign or slow-growing one. Raised-ICP headache is worse lying down, in the morning and with coughing or Valsalva; papilledema comes late. Uncal herniation = same-side third nerve palsy and dilated pupil with opposite-side weakness. Metastases outnumber primaries (lung, breast, melanoma, renal cell); gliomas are the commonest primary. Contrast MRI is the test; enhancement means a high-grade glioma; tissue is still needed. Glioblastoma = maximal safe resection, then radiation with temozolomide; a low-grade glioma with only controlled seizures is watched with serial MRI. Primary CNS lymphoma: B-cell, in the immunosuppressed and HIV. 1. Intracranial pressure (ICP) Normal : adults 5-15 mmHg (7.5-20 cm of water) · young children 3-7 · infants 1.5-6 Monro-Kellie hypothesis : the skull is a rigid box of constant volume, so brain + cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) + blood + any mass must share it → the brain compensates by pushing out venous blood and CSF , up to a point · past it, pressure rises Measuring it lumbar puncture , lying on the side with the legs extended · ⚠ caution with a space-occupying lesion ( PUNISH ) intracranial monitor , with or without a ventricular drain (advantage: it can drain CSF) What raises it (mass effect) focal : tumour · hemorrhage (spontaneous or traumatic) · infection (brain abscess) · brain infarction generalized : hydrocephalus · meningitis or encephalitis · brain edema (trauma, hypoxia, drowning, after CPR) Symptoms of raised ICP (after compensation fails) decreased level of consciousness (reticular activating system) headache, nausea and vomiting · vomiting from irritation of the vomiting centre and chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema of the medulla Cushing response : hypertension with reflex bradycardia papilledema , only LATE herniation : brain shifts from one compartment to another → cranial nerve palsy (third most common, also fourth and sixth) · posterior cerebral artery compression and infarction · decreased consciousness and death Raised-ICP headache , a red flag in any headache history: holocephalic or localized · persistent, progressive, positional (worse lying down) · worse in the morning, wakes the patient · worse with coughing or Valsalva (lying down lowers central venous return; Valsalva raises central venous resistance) Herniation What it does Subfalcine under the falx Uncal (transtentorial) same-side third nerve palsy · same-side dilated pupil · opposite-side weakness Central (transtentorial) decreased consciousness Transcalvarial out through a skull defect Tonsillar fatal : compresses the medulla (cardiorespiratory compromise) Descending herniation : cranial nerve palsies (third, fourth, sixth) · brainstem compression · posterior and anterior cerebral artery strokes · vessel shearing ( Duret hemorrhage ) · Cushing's triad : hypertension, bradycardia, apnea Types of brain herniation: subfalcine, uncal, central, transcalvarial and tonsillar 2. When to suspect a brain tumour Headache : persistent · progressive · positional, worse lying down · often worse in the morning · wakes the patient · with nausea and vomiting · worse with coughing and Valsalva Focal symptoms : weakness · sensory loss · trouble speaking (dysphasia) · gait or visual disturbance · begin insidiously and progress Mental status change : apathy, withdrawal · personality change · confusion · altered consciousness · may be mistaken for depression or dementia Seizures , especially focal Key red flag = progressive symptoms · duration helps : weeks to a few months → highly malignant · months or longer → benign or slow-growing Diagnosis : history → exam → confirmatory imaging → tissue from biopsy or resection Imaging (primary and secondary alike): contrast-enhanced MRI with gadolinium = test of choice · contrast-enhanced CT otherwise 3. Primary vs secondary Secondary (metastasis) Primary How common More common: the most common CNS tumours · 15% of people dying of cancer have them at autopsy · 15-20% of cancers first show up as a brain metastasis Gliomas most common · meningiomas · CNS lymphoma · nerve sheath tumours (schwannoma, neurofibroma) · sellar tumours (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma) · germ cell tumours Where from Lung (16%; small cell and adenocarcinoma) · breast · melanoma · renal cell · rarely prostate, gastrointestinal, bladder, gynecologic Classified by benign vs malignant · cell of origin · grade · molecular markers Diagnosis Contrast MRI ; a CT must have contrast · tissue still required Contrast MRI ; enhancement = high grade (3 or 4) Treatment Resect if accessible and causing symptoms (biopsy only if difficult) → whole-brain radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery · treat the primary · choice depends on clinical status and prognosis Varies with type and grade : surgery, radiation and chemotherapy all play a role, but cure is rare Contrast MRI: a low-grade glioma does not enhance, an anaplastic oligodendroglioma enhances, a glioblastoma enhances around a necrotic centre 4. Gliomas Most common primary brain tumours · vary in histology, aggressiveness, response to treatment and prognosis By cell of origin : astrocytoma · oligodendroglioma · ependymoma WHO grade Name Behaviour I Pilocytic astrocytoma Not malignant; surgically curable II Low-grade glioma (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma) Slower-growing, but malignant III Anaplastic glioma (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma) Malignant, high grade IV Glioblastoma multiforme Malignant, high grade WHO 2016 integrated diagnosis =

Movement disorders Movement disorders give too much movement (hyperkinetic) or too little (hypokinetic). The clinical work is telling essential tremor from parkinsonism , then Parkinson's disease from the other causes of parkinsonism , and treating Parkinson's disease only once it limits function. ⭐ Parkinson's tremor is at rest and asymmetric, with slowness and rigidity and small handwriting; essential tremor comes with posture or action, is symmetric, involves head and voice, gives large handwriting and gets better with alcohol. Parkinsonism is a syndrome: ask about antipsychotics and antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide) before calling it Parkinson's disease. Treat only when it limits function; levodopa (with carbidopa) helps bradykinesia and rigidity most and must never be stopped suddenly. Rigidity is velocity independent; spasticity is velocity dependent. Vertical gaze palsy + early falls = PSP; autonomic failure + parkinsonism or cerebellar signs = MSA. 1. Hyperkinetic vs hypokinetic Hyperkinetic (too much movement) Hypokinetic (too little movement) Ballismus · chorea · athetosis · tremor · dystonia · tics Parkinsonism : bradykinesia (slow movement) · akinesia (trouble starting movement) 2. Parkinson's disease What it is : a neurodegenerative disease from degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra How common : 1% of people over 60 · average onset age 60 · mostly sporadic , rarely hereditary Features: T.R.A.P. T - tremor : usually asymmetric , often only at rest early · hands or feet · "pill-rolling" R - rigidity : the same at any speed (velocity independent), unlike spasticity, which is velocity dependent · often increases with augmentation (opening and closing the other hand) A - akinesia / bradykinesia : akinesia = trouble starting (getting out of a chair, starting to walk) · bradykinesia = slowness (finger tapping, fist open-close, miming turning a doorknob, foot tapping) P - postural instability : trouble with balance Common findings, top to bottom : less blinking · less facial expression (hypomimia) · soft, mumbling voice · asymmetric features · resting tremor (an action tremor too if severe) · rigid, not spastic tone · bradykinesia of the arms or legs · small handwriting (micrographia) · less arm swing · stooped posture · turning "en bloc" · postural instability Prognosis : slowly worsens · dyskinesias develop (chorea and dystonia) · depression often · dementia · death usually from aspiration pneumonia Midbrain: the normal substantia nigra contains pigmented cells (left); in Parkinson's disease the pigmented cells are lost (right) 3. Treating Parkinson's disease No treatment needed if the symptoms do not limit function · once they do, dopamine replacement Dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier Treatment How it works Key points Levodopa Dopamine precursor that DOES cross the blood-brain barrier · given with a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor : carbidopa (Sinemet) or benserazide (Prolopa), or it would all become dopamine outside the brain Most effective · bradykinesia and rigidity benefit most, tremor variably · start low, titrate slowly · ⚠ never stop suddenly : withdrawal suddenly worsens symptoms MAO-B inhibitors Reduce dopamine metabolism Early disease Dopamine agonists Stimulate dopamine receptors pramipexole · ropinirole Anticholinergics — Tremor-specific Deep brain stimulation Stimulates regions of the basal ganglia Severe disease Complications of levodopa : motor fluctuations ("on-off", wearing off) · dyskinesias (abnormal involuntary movements: chorea or dystonia) in 50% of those treated 5 years or longer Other symptomatic therapies · no proven neuroprotective drug yet 4. Parkinson's disease vs parkinsonism Parkinsonism = a clinical syndrome of tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and postural instability , in any combination · Parkinson's disease is one specific cause, not the only one Other causes basal ganglia disease : stroke, bleed, tumour, infection drugs : antipsychotics and antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide ) repeated head trauma other neurodegenerative syndromes : multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, diffuse Lewy body disease toxins : carbon monoxide , cyanide 5. Essential tremor vs Parkinson's tremor Essential tremor Parkinson's disease When With posture or action At rest Side Symmetric Asymmetric Where Arms most, also head and voice Hands or feet Writing Large and shaky Small (micrographia) Alcohol Improves it — Course May be hereditary · worsens over time Slowly worsens Treatment None if mild · beta-blocker or primidone · other anticonvulsants · deep brain stimulation if refractory Levodopa and the rest 6. Progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple system atrophy Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) Multiple system atrophy (MSA) Defining feature Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy : impaired vertical eye movements · "supranuclear" = the pursuit and saccade problems can be overcome by vestibular input (vestibulo-ocular reflexes) Autonomic nervous system dysfunction Plus Early falls and major balance trouble · axial tone increased more than limb tone · parkinsonism One of: parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar dysfunction (MSA-C) Prognosis — Death within 6-9 years of symptom onset Schulich Reviews Rigidity is cogwheel ; test postural instability with the pull test PSP also brings dementia

Non-Mendelian genetics Two ways inheritance breaks Mendel's rules: mitochondrial DNA comes almost only from the mother and is shared out unevenly between cells , and a triple nucleotide repeat grows as it is passed on . That is why mitochondrial disease varies by tissue and worsens with time, and why repeat disorders start earlier and hit harder in each generation (anticipation). ⭐ Mitochondrial DNA comes almost only from the mother, and heteroplasmy (a random mix of normal and mutant copies) with a tissue threshold explains why the same mutation looks different in each tissue and worsens over time. Point mutations are maternal; deletions and duplications are sporadic; nuclear-gene mitochondrial disease is Mendelian. Suspect mitochondrial disease when 2 or more systems are involved; lactate is raised in blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Anticipation = the repeat grows each generation, so onset is earlier and disease worse. Huntington: CAG in HTT, 40 or more repeats = will develop HD, 36-39 = may not; juvenile HD is rigid, not choreic. Myotonic dystrophy: CTG in DMPK, cannot let go of a grip; over 1,000 repeats = congenital. Pre-symptomatic HD testing only after counselling by a geneticist or genetic counsellor. 1. Mitochondria and their DNA Mitochondria = the cell's "power houses": oxidative phosphorylation by the 5 complexes of the respiratory chain makes ATP · they also import proteins from the cytosol and assemble their own 100s to 1000s per cell · four compartments: outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane folded into cristae (holds the respiratory chain) , matrix (holds 1-10 identical mitochondrial DNA molecules) Mitochondrial disorders include : pyruvate dehydrogenase complex defects · Krebs cycle defects · respiratory chain defects · disorders of mitochondrial DNA replication, maintenance and repair → ↓ ATP production Dual control by nuclear and mitochondrial genes Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) : circular, 37 genes (13 respiratory chain proteins, 2 rRNAs, 22 tRNAs), 1-10 copies per mitochondrion Nuclear DNA : over 300 genes for respiratory chain proteins, mtDNA replication, expression and repair, antioxidant defence, iron homeostasis, import machinery 2. Mitochondrial DNA disease: heteroplasmy, threshold, maternal inheritance Homoplasmy = every copy of mtDNA identical (healthy) · heteroplasmy = a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA (disease) Point mutations: maternal inheritance · deletions and duplications: sporadic Why it progresses : in dividing cells mitochondria are shared out at random , so cells get different numbers of mutant and healthy ones · in non-dividing cells (neurons, muscle) mitochondria replicate with metabolic demand and exercise → mutant mtDNA accumulates in affected tissues → symptoms worsen over time Threshold effect : a tissue fails only once its non-functioning mitochondria pass a threshold , which differs between tissues · any organ can be affected, but high-energy tissues suffer first: brain, retina, skeletal muscle, heart Maternal inheritance : the egg has many mitochondria, the sperm only a few, so mtDNA passes almost only through the mother Genetic bottleneck : a germ cell carrying mutant mtDNA makes eggs with high, intermediate or low mutant loads → affected, mildly affected or unaffected children Replication and random segregation of mutant mtDNA: from homoplasmy through heteroplasmy, with the mutant phenotype appearing once a threshold is crossed 3. Nuclear-gene mitochondrial disease Nuclear DNA mitochondrial diseases follow Mendelian inheritance : autosomal recessive, X-linked, autosomal dominant Mitochondrial depletion syndromes : nuclear gene mutations in mitochondrial nucleotide synthesis or mtDNA replication → too little mtDNA for the key respiratory chain subunits → too little energy 4. When to suspect a mitochondrial disorder Consider it when 2 or more suggestive findings are present: System Findings Brain and nerves hypotonia · ataxia · intellectual disability · seizures · migraines · dementia · sensorineural hearing loss Eyes retinitis pigmentosa · optic atrophy · nystagmus · ophthalmoplegia (eye muscle paralysis) Muscle Weakness · exercise intolerance Heart hypertrophic cardiomyopathy · arrhythmias · heart block Blood Macrocytic anemia · pancytopenia Endocrine diabetes mellitus · diabetes insipidus · exocrine pancreatic dysfunction · short stature Gut, liver and kidney Gut dysfunction, intestinal pseudo-obstruction · liver dysfunction or failure · renal tubular acidosis · Fanconi syndrome 5. Investigations and treatment ↑ lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid · MRI or magnetic resonance spectroscopy: lactate peak , basal ganglia changes, leukodystrophy, atrophy Muscle biopsy : immunohistochemistry and respiratory chain enzyme analysis · gene panels : mtDNA and nuclear mitochondrial genes No effective treatment · a "mitochondrial cocktail" of respiratory chain cofactors: riboflavin , coenzyme Q10, thiamine 6. Triple nucleotide repeat disorders and anticipation Anticipation : the expanded repeat is unstable and tends to grow as it is passed to each generation , so offspring of an affected person can have earlier and more severe disease · the larger the repeat, the earlier the onset and the worse the disease All are autosomal dominant · treatment is supportive · genetic counselling , family planning, prenatal and preimplantation genetic diagnosis Huntington disease Myotonic dystrophy Repeat CAG in the HTT gene → expanded polyglutamine tract in huntingtin → the protein aggregates in neurons → selected neurons degenerate CTG in the DMPK gene Inheritance Autosomal dominant Autosomal dominant Presents as Mean onset 35-44 years · 2/3 neurologic, 1/3 psychiatric · early: clumsiness, minor involuntary movements, personality change, psychiatric symptoms, may keep working · middle: prominent chorea , dysarthria, dysphagia, weight loss, cognitive decline, cannot work, still independent in basic daily activities · late: completely dependent , mute

Pediatric neurology: the floppy infant, the seizing child, the ataxic child Three presentations, one habit: an unstable child gets ABCDE (and a glucose) before anything else. Then the exam sorts it: a floppy infant is central (brain) or peripheral (motor neuron, junction, muscle) ; a febrile seizure is simple or complex, and any seizure past 5 minutes is status epilepticus ; an ataxic child has one of three common causes or one of three can't-miss ones. ⭐ Floppy + weak + absent reflexes = peripheral (spinal muscular atrophy, junction, muscle: check creatine kinase); floppy + strong + brisk reflexes + global delay = central (infection, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, chromosomal, metabolic). Hypotonia right after birth → hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy or chromosomal; after day 1 → metabolic. Simple febrile = generalized, 15 minutes or a repeat in 24 hours = complex. A seizure past 5 minutes is status: benzodiazepine (2-3 doses), then levetiracetam (phenobarbital under 30 days), then intensive care. Check glucose in every seizing or floppy child. Ataxia: intoxication, postinfectious and tumour are the common three; stroke, meningitis and tumour can't be missed; image for any other neurologic sign, a subacute course or trauma, not for a simple ingestion. Tumour with hydrocephalus → neurosurgery now. Part 1: the infant with hypotonia 1. What hypotonia is Hypotonia = decreased muscle tone : less resistance of the muscles to passive stretch · these infants are called "floppy" Not the same as weakness (decreased power or strength): not every hypotonic infant is weak 2. The unstable infant with acute hypotonia Acute causes : infection (sepsis, meningitis) - the most common · central nervous system (stroke, seizure) · endocrine ( hypoglycemia , electrolytes, thyroid, congenital adrenal hyperplasia) · surgical (volvulus, necrotizing enterocolitis) · toxin ingestion · metabolic (urea cycle defects) · non-accidental trauma : always on the list when the history does not fit the infant or keeps changing ABCDE first , as for any unstable child Airway : patent? Breathing : rate, oxygen saturation · oxygen, assist breathing if needed Circulation : heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, central pulses ( femoral is best in infants) · isotonic fluid (normal saline) if circulation is poor · consider inotropes (epinephrine) Disability / Dextrose : check the blood sugar and treat hypoglycemia immediately · level of consciousness Expose : signs of injury or bleeding Stable : history and exam pinpoint the diagnosis in about 50% 3. Central vs peripheral Central hypotonia Peripheral hypotonia Where Any systemic disease affecting the brain · the most common cause in newborns Motor neuron · neuromuscular junction · muscle Causes Infection (sepsis, meningitis, herpes simplex virus, TORCH) · hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy · chromosomal ( trisomy 21 , Prader-Willi syndrome ) · metabolic disorders Spinal muscular atrophy (motor neuron) · congenital myasthenic syndromes (junction) · infant botulism ( Clostridium botulinum ) · drug toxicity (aminoglycosides) · congenital muscular dystrophy (muscle) Alertness ↓ level of consciousness Alert Development Global developmental delay (more than one area) Normal speech and cognition, delayed gross and fine motor Strength Normal (moves limbs against gravity) Weak (cannot lift limbs against gravity) · facial weakness , feeding and breathing difficulty Reflexes Normal or exaggerated , primitive reflexes persist, may have clonus Decreased or absent Other Dysmorphic features → a syndrome (trisomy 21) — Timing of onset narrows it : right after birth → central nervous system ( hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy , chromosomal) · after the first day of life → metabolic 4. History and exam History : onset · how motor development was noticed (missed motor milestones?), better, worse or the same, any lost skills (→ degenerative, e.g. metabolic) · prenatal and perinatal : maternal drugs and infections, pregnancy complications, gestational age, delivery, APGAR scores, NICU stay · overall development (fine motor, gross motor, verbal, social) · family history of hypotonia, delay, metabolic or chromosomal disease · medications, allergies, immunizations General look : normal tone = arms and legs slightly flexed , good head control · hypotonic = limbs hang loosely , poor head control · respiratory distress (indrawing, grunting, tracheal tug) · dysmorphic features · plot weight, length and head circumference Tone manoeuvres Vertical suspension (held under the arms): normal = shoulders press down on your hands · hypotonic = slips through your hands Horizontal suspension : normal = lifts head, keeps trunk extended for a while · hypotonic = flops over your arm in a "U" Pull to sit : normal = flexes neck and helps with the arms (head lag is normal in newborns and gone between 2 and 6 months ) · hypotonic = significant head lag , no help from the arms, cannot stabilize the trunk Full exam : heart failure → muscle disease or mitochondrial disorder · enlarged liver and spleen → lysosomal or glycogen storage disorder 5. Investigations and management Brain : CT or MRI if a central cause is suspected · blood : electrolytes, extended electrolytes, TSH, ammonia (metabolic screen), specialized metabolic tests, karyotype , genetic tests · creatine kinase : raised in most muscle disorders · electromyography (muscle and motor neuron health) · muscle biopsy Management depends on the cause : early referral to pediatric neurology (and metabolics and genetics) · supportive care: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, nutrition, psychology, speech-language pathology Part 2: the child with a seizure 6. What a seizure is Seizure = abnormal, excessive, synchronous neuronal discharge in the brain Types : focal (one side or one limb) · generalized (whole body) · atonic (loss of tone) · clonic · tonic-clonic Most seizures stop on their own within 5 minutes · convulsive status epilepticus is most common under age 2 Convul

Monocular vision impairment Vision loss in one eye puts the problem in front of the optic chiasm; loss in both eyes puts it behind. Then sort by pain and tempo : sudden painless loss is sorted by the pupil and the fundus, and three of the five causes need emergency measures and ophthalmology now. Gradual loss is sorted by which part of vision goes: the periphery (glaucoma), everything hazy (cataract) or the centre (macular degeneration). ⭐ A white retina with a cherry-red spot and an RAPD is a central retinal artery occlusion: massage the eye now, refer emergently, then find the embolus's source. Swollen disc with an RAPD: older with headache, jaw claudication and scalp tenderness is giant cell arteritis (ESR, CRP, steroids, biopsy); a healthy young woman is optic neuritis (look for multiple sclerosis). Flashes, floaters and a curtain = retinal detachment. Glaucoma is silent and takes the periphery first; only lowering the pressure treats it. Cataract = leading reversible cause of blindness; macular degeneration = leading irreversible cause over 50. 1. History and exam History : pain? · transient, persistent or progressive? · one eye or both? · all or part of the field? · timeline (abrupt, hours, days, weeks) · baseline acuity past medical history: diabetes , cardiovascular disease, autoimmune disease, hypertension past eye history: diabetic retinopathy , glaucoma , eye surgery, contact lenses Exam visual acuity · confrontation visual fields swinging flashlight test : a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) (Marcus Gunn pupil) - moving the light from the normal eye to the abnormal one, the pupil dilates instead of constricting = a significant lesion of the retina or optic nerve of that eye · the key sign in monocular loss red reflex : dull = a media opacity (cloudy cornea, lens or vitreous) · ophthalmoscopy pressure (tonometry) 2. Sudden painless vision loss Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) Giant cell arteritis (GCA) Optic neuritis Retinal detachment Vitreous hemorrhage Who Older, hypertension Older · inflammation of large and medium vessels (cranial arteries, proximal aorta) Healthy young woman Healthy, middle-aged Long-standing diabetes Clues Sudden, severe (hand motion) New headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness , tender thick temporal artery, weight loss, fever, malaise · polymyalgia rheumatica Sudden, reduced acuity Flashes, new floaters, a "curtain" , peripheral field loss · acuity may be normal Acuity down to hand motion Exam RAPD · white opacified retina + cherry-red macular spot RAPD · swollen disc + flame-shaped hemorrhages RAPD · swollen disc · clear media Dark mobile spots in the red reflex · usually not seen with a direct ophthalmoscope Proliferative retinopathy : fragile new vessels bleed Do Ocular massage (heel of the hand, 10 s press, 10 s release, for 5 min) · emergent referral · find the source (carotid atheroma, heart valves) ESR + CRP now (ESR usually > 60) · visual symptoms → IV methylprednisolone 1 g × 3 days ; none → prednisone 40-60 mg daily · emergent referral for temporal artery biopsy Neuro-ophthalmology · MRI, possible IV corticosteroids · neurology to rule out multiple sclerosis Refer promptly Pan-retinal laser photocoagulation by a retina specialist Central retinal artery occlusion beside a normal fundus: pale retina with a cherry-red macula Emergency measures and referral : CRAO · ischemic optic neuropathy · giant cell arteritis High-dose steroids in GCA protect the other eye and prevent occlusions elsewhere (stroke, aortic arch syndrome) 3. Glaucoma (primary open-angle) Progressive, irreversible optic neuropathy with typical disc and field changes · 3.5% of the world · raised eye pressure is the main risk factor, not the definition ( normal tension glaucoma ) Presents as : nothing at first · peripheral vision goes first · acuity falls very late Risk factors : open angle = family history, older age, Black , raised pressure, myopia , past eye trauma, steroids, vasospasm (Raynaud's, migraine) · angle closure = family history, older age, Asian , female , hyperopia The angle = where the cornea and iris meet, the eye's drainage system Pressure : normal 10-21 mmHg · Goldmann applanation, Tono-Pen, air puff Disc : normal cup-to-disc ratio , usually symmetric (a difference > 0.2 is suspicious) · Field : arcuate defect, nasal step Refer : pressure > 21 or a suspicious disc · timely, not same-day unless the pressure has spiked > 30 Treatment : lowering the pressure is the only treatment : drops, laser, surgery Optic disc in glaucoma: the cup enlarges as the nerve is lost 4. Cataract Opacity or discolouration of the lens · leading cause of reversible blindness Risk factors : age, genetics, trauma, steroids , eye inflammation, metabolic disease (diabetes), radiation, prior eye surgery, UV exposure Presents as : reduced acuity · glare, starbursts or halos · trouble driving at night · " second sight " (lens myopia improves near vision) · varies with where the opacity sits Exam : acuity down · hazy view on ophthalmoscopy · a dense cataract dulls the red reflex or whitens the pupil · pressure normal · types: nuclear sclerosis, posterior subcapsular, cortical Treatment : non-urgent referral · visually significant or hiding the retina → extraction with an intraocular lens 5. Age-related macular degeneration Leading cause of irreversible blindness over 50 (North America) · central acuity ↓ + distortion ( metamorphopsia ) · Amsler grid Refer if any : central acuity ↓ · new distortion · drusen or blood at the macula Wet (neovascular) Dry (atrophic) Share ~20% ~80% What happens Choroidal neovascular membrane : leaky vessels break through to the retina, bleed, leave exudates Retinal atrophy (geographic atrophy) Macula Drusen + subretinal hemorrhage Drusen + pigment changes Course Can drop suddenly and severely Slow Treatment Anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) injections into the eye (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept) Slow it : AREDS2 formula vita

Red eye and ocular trauma Most red eyes are harmless; the job is to catch the few that threaten sight. The red flags do it: severe pain, photophobia, haloes or reduced vision, and on exam a ciliary flush, a cloudy cornea, an abnormal pupil, a shallow chamber or a high pressure. With none, it is the lids, the conjunctiva, a burst vessel or a scratch. With any, it is keratitis, iritis or angle closure, and urgent referral to ophthalmology . In trauma, look for an open globe first. ⭐ Pain, photophobia, haloes or reduced vision turn a red eye into keratitis, uveitis or acute angle closure glaucoma, and an urgent referral. Conjunctivitis by discharge: watery after a cold = viral (no antibiotics); lids glued with yellow-white pus = bacterial (fluoroquinolone); pus within 12-24 hours = gonococcal (ceftriaxone + azithromycin, refer); itch = allergic. An abrasion stains but the cornea stays clear; keratitis is a white infiltrate in a hazy cornea. Uveitis has a low or normal pressure; angle closure is rock hard with a shallow chamber. Never prescribe anesthetic drops, and leave steroid drops to the ophthalmologist. Trauma: a peaked pupil or positive Seidel means an open globe - shield and refer. 1. History and exam of a red eye History : onset (sudden or progressive) and timeline · one eye, both, or a sector · pain or photosensitivity · discharge (serous or mucopurulent, how much) · itch · vision change · recent cold · family members with a red eye · contact lenses: the 3 S's (swim, sleep, shower in them?) · recent trauma or eye surgery past eye history · autoimmune disease · eye drops (over the counter or prescribed) · other medications · family eye history · occupation, recreational drugs Exam visual acuity with glasses, one eye at a time - reduced vision is a red flag pupils : shape, size, light reaction (direct, consensual, swinging flashlight, accommodation) · eye movements in all directions head and neck: lymph node in front of the ear , a dermatomal rash (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) · proptosis, bruising, bony step-off lids : edema, lesions (stye, chalazion), scaling at the lash base ( blepharitis ) · evert the lid for a foreign body · discharge amount and character conjunctiva : hemorrhage · diffuse conjunctival hyperemia vs ciliary flush · chemosis (edema) cornea : haze, edema, opacities · fluorescein with cobalt blue light shows a broken epithelium · foreign body (slit lamp, or penlight and magnifier) anterior chamber : blood ( hyphema ) or pus ( hypopyon ) · shallow chamber → think acute angle closure glaucoma Red flags : blurred vision (if it clears with blinking it is discharge) · severe pain (keratitis, ulcer, iritis, scleritis, acute glaucoma) · photophobia (iritis) · coloured halos (corneal edema, often from high pressure) · ↓ acuity · ciliary flush · corneal opacity · pupil abnormality · shallow chamber · raised pressure · proptosis Not vision threatening : blepharitis · stye or chalazion · conjunctivitis · dry eye · corneal abrasion · subconjunctival hemorrhage · Vision threatening : scleritis · corneal ulcer or keratitis · uveitis · acute angle closure glaucoma · trauma · orbital cellulitis 2. Pediatric ophthalmology Anything that blurs, blocks or misaligns one eye while a child's vision is developing can leave that eye permanently weak (amblyopia), so the lecture is about catching it early. Three checks do it: acuity in each eye, alignment, and the red reflex - and a white reflex is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise . ⭐ A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise - refer immediately. Amblyopia = reduced acuity with no eye disease; refer immediately and patch the good eye, the earlier the better. In the Brückner test the brighter reflex is the turned eye; a dimmer one means refractive error or an opacity. Concomitant squint keeps the same angle in every gaze (childhood); an angle that changes with gaze means a nerve palsy, blowout fracture or thyroid eye disease. Refer a constant turn at any age, an occasional one beyond 3-4 months, and any nystagmus. 1. Amblyopia Amblyopia : reduced visual acuity with no detectable organic disease , from a disruption of normal visual development · usually one eye, can be both Type Cause Strabismic The turned eye is ignored (suppressed) by the brain, so its visual cortex does not develop · in adults a squint causes double vision instead Refractive A difference in refractive error between the eyes : the eye with the smaller error gives the clearer image, and the other becomes amblyopic Form deprivation and occlusion Something clouds the view (cataract, corneal scar) or blocks it ( ptosis ) Testing : acuity in each eye separately newborns : acuity is hard to measure → light reflexes, pupils, fundus infants to age 2 : cover each eye in turn - the child objects when the good eye is covered ages 2-5 : eye charts (HOTV, tumbling E, picture cards after age 2) Management : immediate referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist for any suspected amblyopia · early treatment · patch the good eye · plus treat the cause: glasses for unequal refraction, surgery for cataract or strabismus Amblyopia: one eye sends a clear image and the other a blurred one, so the brain comes to favour the clear eye 2. Strabismus Strabismus = misalignment of the two eyes · esotropia (in) · exotropia (out) · hypertropia (up) · hypotropia (down) Concomitant (non-paralytic) Incomitant (paralytic or restrictive) Angle of turn About the same in every direction of gaze Changes with the direction of gaze Muscles Work normally, the eyes are just not aimed at the same thing One or more muscles or nerves not working, or mechanically restricted Typical Onset in childhood 3rd, 4th or 6th nerve palsy · orbital blowout fracture · restrictive thyroid eye disease ( Graves orbitopathy ) Testing : acuity · obvious deviation? · nystagmus · the cardinal positions of gaze · corneal light reflexes · cover test (no equipment, from 6-7 months) · red reflex prominent epicanthal folds give pseudostrabismus Treatment : patching, glasses, both, or surgery · no role for vision training or exercises Refer : occasional deviation beyond 3-4 months · constant deviation at any age · any child with nystagmus · abnormal red reflex, especially a white one (immediate) 3. The red reflex Red light reflex : light reflected back from the retina, a reddish-orange glow that varies with fundus pigment (the red eye of night-time flash photos) · the most important test in pediatric ophthalmology : contactless, no dilating drops, a few seconds, and it finds several problems at once Brückner test : both eyes at once, from 1/3 m or more , in dim light (big pupils), child looking into the distance · compare brightness, colour, alignment, symmetry · direct ophthalmoscope, retinoscope, or a flash photo; parents may notice the asymmetry ⚠ Disease in both eyes is easy to miss if the two reflexes match The reflex is It means Examples Dimmer or different in one eye , or a visible opacity Refractive error or something along the visual axis Myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism (the eye with the larger error is dimmer) · keratoconus ("oil droplet") · cataract (not always white) · corneal abrasion · hyphema · vitreous hemorrhage · retinal pigment changes Brighter in one eye Strabismus: the brighter eye is the turned eye Its pupil looks slightly larger · detects turns as small as 3 prism dioptres · check the corneal light reflexes too White ( leukocoria ) Something destroys, detaches or discolours the retina in line with the pupil, or a dense opacity in front of it Retinoblastoma first · retinopathy of prematurity · congenital cataract (dense or white) · Coats' disease · persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous · inflammation (toxocariasis, congenital CMV) · coloboma · familial exudative vitreoretinopathy · retinal detachment Physiologic white reflex : light ~15° off axis catches the optic nerve head · common, but not dismissed without referral and a full eye exam Retinoblastoma : the most important and dangerous cause, rule it out first · uncommon, about 1 in 180,000 births · from embryonic retinal cells, so mostly under age 4 · late diagnosis → up to 70% die ; optimal therapy → over 95% cured (3-year survival ~96%) · 90% have no family history and are one-sided (15% of one-sided still carry a germline RB1 mutation) · both eyes → ~100% positive family history · treated by enucleation, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, laser ± cryotherapy · germline carriers die more often of a second cancer than of the retinoblastoma Your role with an abnormal reflex : timely referral (amblyopia, life-threatening causes) · stress attending without needless worry · take a family history of eye disease · ask the family to bring old photographs Bruckner test: the red reflex is brighter in the misaligned eye

Hearing loss Every hearing-loss question turns on one split: is sound failing to reach the inner ear (conductive), or is the inner ear or its nerve failing (sensorineural)? The tuning forks make that split at the bedside, and a sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency where a sudden conductive one is not. ⭐ Weber goes to the bad ear in a conductive loss and to the good ear in a sensorineural loss; the Rinne (bone louder than air) confirms the conductive side, so always do both. Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency: ENT, audiogram, MRI, and steroids within 10 days. Conductive loss leaves an air-bone gap; sensorineural does not. Presbycusis takes the high pitches symmetrically; noise makes a 4,000 Hz notch. One-sided sensorineural loss with tinnitus and imbalance: acoustic neuroma until the MRI says otherwise. With a perforated drum use only non-ototoxic drops (ciprofloxacin + dexamethasone). 1. Sound and the ear Sound = variations in air pressure · frequency (pitch) in hertz (Hz), heard from 20 to 20,000 Hz · intensity (loudness) in decibels (dB), a log scale : every 10 dB is 10 times the intensity, and is heard as about twice as loud 0 dB = the softest sound a normal ear hears · conversation 60 dB · lawnmower 90 · rock concert 120 · gunshot 140 · jet takeoff 150 we hear best at 2,000-4,000 Hz, the range of speech Outer ear : auricle (pinna) + a 3 cm canal that protects the drum and resonates at 2,000-4,000 Hz Middle ear : air-filled · tympanic membrane · ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) : sound in air cannot move fluid, so the ossicles turn air pressure changes into mechanical force on the oval window · Eustachian tube to the pharynx equalizes pressure Inner ear : the cochlea (2¾ turns, 3.5 cm unrolled), three fluid chambers: scala vestibuli and tympani (perilymph) · scala media ( endolymph ) organ of Corti on the basilar membrane: moving the membrane shears the hair cells against the tectorial membrane · inner hair cells transduce, outer hair cells amplify oval window pushed by the stapes · the wave runs scala vestibuli → helicotrema → scala tympani → round window , which bulges out tonotopic : base stiff → high pitch · apex floppy → low pitch · hair cells → spiral ganglion → the cochlear part of cranial nerve VIII pathway: brainstem → medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus → primary auditory cortex in the superior temporal gyrus , tonotopic all the way 2. History and examination History : character ( loudness or clarity ) · duration · onset (sudden or insidious) · rate of progression · one or both ears · ear pain · discharge · pressure or fullness · tinnitus · vertigo · facial and trigeminal symptoms · symptoms specific to the differential Exam : otoscopy · pneumatic otoscopy shows whether the drum moves (fluid behind it does not) Tuning forks (512 Hz) : the office or emergency tool that separates a sudden conductive loss (infection, effusion) from a sudden sensorineural loss (an emergency) ; always do both Weber : fork pressed hard on the midline (forehead, nasal bone, front tooth) · where is it loudest? (detects a 5 dB difference) · loudest in the affected ear = conductive · loudest in the normal ear = sensorineural Rinne : fork on the mastoid (bone conduction, straight to the inner ear), then beside the ear (air conduction, through drum and ossicles) · normal: air > bone · conductive: bone > air · sensorineural: air > bone worked example : Weber goes to the RIGHT = right conductive OR left sensorineural → Rinne on the right: air > bone = left sensorineural ; bone > air = right conductive Weber test Rinne test 3. Vertigo "Dizzy" can mean anything, so the history does the work (80% of it): first, is it true vertigo (an illusion of rotary movement)? Then how long does each attack last, and is hearing affected? That pair names the peripheral causes. ⭐ Attack length and hearing name the cause: seconds = BPPV, 24 minutes to 24 hours with fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus and fullness = Ménière's, days without hearing loss = vestibular neuronitis, with hearing loss = labyrinthitis. BPPV: Dix-Hallpike (latency, torsional, fatiguing nystagmus) to diagnose, particle repositioning to cure (80% after one). COWS: cold opposite, warm same (fast phase). Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo with autophony = superior canal dehiscence. Vestibular neuronitis: oral steroids within 72 hours, no antivirals. Aminoglycoside toxicity: stop the drug; the loss is usually permanent. 1. Vestibular physiology The vestibular apparatus sits in the inner ear beside the cochlea, shares the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII) , and uses the same hair cells (mechanoreceptors): bending toward the tallest hair (the kinocilium) opens potassium channels and depolarizes the cell Two kinds of sensor Semicircular canals Otolith organs ( utricle , saccule ) Detects Rotation (angular acceleration) Linear movement and head position relative to gravity How Endolymph lags behind (inertia) and bends the cupula Ear stones (otoconia) weigh down a gel membrane over the macula ; tilt or straight-line movement slides it and bends the hairs Arrangement Three canals at right angles in each ear: one horizontal , two vertical-oblique · each paired with one on the other side The two organs lie perpendicular to each other Drives "Image stabilization": the vestibulo-ocular reflex Posture control Baseline firing (~100 action potentials a second) lets a hair cell signal both ways : bending toward it → more firing, away → less Canals work in pairs (push-pull) : turning right raises the right horizontal canal's firing and lowers the left · the brain reads the difference So a problem in one ear reads as head rotation even when the head is still → vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia, nausea and vomiting 2. Nystagmus and the vestibular reflexes Vestibulo-ocular reflex : keeps the image still on the retina as the head moves · as few as 3 neurons , compensating within 10-15 ms , far faster than vision could Nystagmus : rhythmic to-and-fro eye movement with a slow phase (the vestibular drift) and a quick phase (a reset saccade) · named by the fast phase Physiologic Pathologic Rotation-induced · caloric-induced (COWS) · optokinetic · end-point Spontaneous vestibular : direction fixed , mostly horizontal , suppressed by visual fixation · positional · gaze-paretic · rebound · congenital · dissociated Caloric test (lying down, so the horizontal canal is nearly vertical): water in the ear canal makes the endolymph flow cold lowers firing, as if the head turned away → fast phase to the opposite side · warm raises it → fast phase to the same side: COWS = Cold Opposite, Warm Same in an unconscious patient it tests the brainstem: the eyes should move together · only one eye moves = medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion (conjugate gaze lost) · no movement = low brainstem lesion Caloric test 3. The dizzy patient Balance = inputs ( vestibular · vision · proprioception ; 2 of 3 are usually enough) → processing (central, cerebellum ) → outputs ( eye muscles , flexors and extensors ) History is the most important 80% of the workup · anxiety is often the cause or the effect · then exam, and imaging (CT, MRI) Vestibular (true vertigo) Other "dizziness" Feels like Spinning Lightheaded , unsteady, disoriented Time course Limited duration, episodic Chronic disequilibrium With it Hearing (cochlear) symptoms · vagal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, sweating, moving the bowels) · worse with head movement Cardiac or neurological symptoms · loss of consciousness Causes Inner ear and vestibular nerve Organic : presyncope and vasodepressor syncope , arrhythmia, orthostatic hypotension , hyperventilation, anemia, peripheral neuropathy, poor vision, musculoskeletal, drugs · psychiatric : depression, anxiety, panic disorder , phobic dizziness, somatization 4. The peripheral vertigo syndromes BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo): the most common vestibular end-organ disorder brief vertigo (10-30 s) set off by specific head movements (looking up, rolling over in bed) · motion sensitivity when severe · hearing normal cause: idiopathic (degenerative) · head trauma (also iatrogenic; the commonest cause of bilateral BPPV) · mechanism: free-floating particles (otoconia from the utricle) in the posterior canal (canalithiasis); lateral canal variants, superior canal very rare Dix-Hallpike : latency , then direction-specific torsional nystagmus (left ear clockwise, right counterclockwise), limited duration , reverses on sitting up , fatigues with repeats particle repositioning (Epley or Semont) : 80% cured after one session, 95% after three · persistent or atypical cases are rare · intractable → posterior canal occlusion Ménière's disease : episodic vertigo, 24 min to 24 h · fluctuating, low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss · tinnitus · aural fullness 2nd most common vestibular disorder (10% of dizzy-clinic visits) · 50-100 per 100,000 · both ears in 25-30% , usually within 5 years · familial endolymphatic hydrops (less endolymph resorbed, more made) is its histological correlate, though not every hydropic ear has Ménière's · Ménière's syndrome = a secondary cause: syphilis, trauma, labyrinthitis treatment ladder : ① everyone, for 3-6 months: low salt

Integration of medicine and neurology The nervous system is often where a disease of another system shows itself. The lecture works four cases (cancer, breathlessness, nutrition, the heart), and each one asks the same two things: where is the lesion, and how did the illness get there? ⭐ Acute, stepwise deficits in several territories = cardioembolic strokes until proven otherwise; look for endocarditis, take two sets of blood cultures and give no tPA. Wernicke triad: ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, confusion; refeeding without thiamine triggers it, so give thiamine before glucose. Dyspnea worse lying down with a normal heart and chest = bilateral phrenic nerve palsies. Checkpoint inhibitors cause myasthenia gravis and myositis: stop the drug and/or give steroids, with oncology. B6 harms by excess; copper deficiency after bariatric surgery mimics B12's cord damage. 1. Cancer: how it reaches the nervous system Mechanism What happens Examples Direct effect: compression Primary tumour or metastasis presses on a structure Spinal cord → myelopathy · nerve root → radiculopathy · peripheral nerve → mononeuropathy Direct effect: invasion Tumour grows into the nerve, plexus, brain or spinal cord Metastases to the central nervous system (commonly breast and lung ) Immune-mediated, indirect (paraneoplastic) The tumour induces an antibody-mediated effect on a non-tumour organ Limbic encephalitis · dermatomyositis · myasthenia gravis · cerebellitis Toxic effect of treatment Chemotherapy · radiation ( immediate or delayed ) · resective surgery Chemotherapy neuropathy · radiation encephalopathy · post-mastectomy pain syndrome Immune checkpoint inhibitor autoimmunity The drug blocks PD-L1 (a brake tumours carry in large amounts), freeing T cells against the tumour and against self Hepatitis · colitis · myasthenia gravis · inflammatory myopathies Case 1 : a man on ipilimumab and nivolumab for metastatic melanoma has 3 weeks of progressive ptosis, neck flexion and proximal weakness , a head drop and a Trendelenburg gait, with normal reflexes and sensation → lower motor neuron, junction or muscle investigations (module): CK (muscle) · acetylcholine receptor antibody (junction) · EMG / nerve conduction studies to tell them apart Management of checkpoint inhibitor autoimmunity : discuss with oncology stopping the inhibitor and/or starting steroids · steroids may reduce how well the tumour treatment works 2. Breathlessness: the neurological causes Causes of dyspnea : cardiac (heart failure, ischemia, outflow restriction) · pulmonary (obstructive, restrictive, infiltrative, shunting) · hematologic (anemia) · neurological Neurological dyspnea = respiratory muscle weakness , approached like any other weakness, level by level Level Cause of respiratory muscle weakness Muscle Hereditary and inflammatory myopathies Neuromuscular junction Myasthenia gravis Peripheral nerve Phrenic nerve palsy · Guillain-Barré syndrome Root Multilevel cervical radiculopathy ( C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive) Anterior horn cell ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) Spinal cord High cervical myelopathy Case 2: bilateral phrenic nerve palsies - dyspnea worse lying down (she sleeps in a recliner), with a normal heart, chest and neurological exam lying down, the diaphragm does most of the work (it pushes the abdomen down) · upright, the intercostals do investigations : chest X-ray · diaphragm fluoroscopy during inspiration and expiration · lung function seated vs supine · phrenic nerve conduction studies · imaging of the neck and mediastinum 3. Nutrition: deficiencies and excesses Nutrient Neurological picture Key point Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency Wernicke's encephalopathy : classic triad of ataxia + ophthalmoplegia + encephalopathy (confusion) · beriberi = sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy · wet beriberi adds a cardiomyopathy Refeeding without thiamine can trigger it · treatable with thiamine · preventable: give thiamine BEFORE glucose whenever nutrition is in doubt Vitamin B12 deficiency Subacute combined degeneration : dorsal column dysfunction , peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy The deficiency classically tied to neurological symptoms Copper deficiency ( hypocupremia ) Myelopathy Impaired gastric absorption, e.g. after bariatric surgery Vitamin B6 toxicity Sensory neuropathy Too much, not too little Refeeding syndrome Electrolytes shift into cells: ↓ sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate → first encephalopathy (confusion, unsteadiness) → then muscle weakness → if severe seizures · arrhythmias After prolonged starvation (e.g. anorexia), refeed very slowly and check electrolytes often Case 3 : a 9-year-old eating almost nothing for weeks gets a nasogastric tube; within a day she has diplopia (both 6th nerves), confusion and severe ataxia → cannot be localized to one place: generalized dysfunction with strong pons involvement → Wernicke encephalopathy , triggered by refeeding 4. In-class: approach to seizures ⭐ Seizure over syncope: unconscious for more than a minute, eyes turned to one side, side-of-tongue biting, and confusion lasting minutes to hours; a faint lasts under a minute with only brief confusion. Focal slowing or spikes on EEG mean MRI. Valproate is the worst teratogen; levetiracetam and lamotrigine are the safer choices, with folic acid. Never stop antiseizure drugs because of pregnancy. A posterior shoulder dislocation should make you think of a seizure. A case session built on the first-seizure approach (see the Week 14 approach to seizures chart for the workup and when to treat). What it adds: telling a seizure from a faint, reading the EEG report, and choosing a drug for a young woman. 1. Seizure or syncope? Differential of a brief loss of consciousness : syncope (low brain perfusion, cardiac or blood pressure) · seizure · psychogenic · sudden raised intracranial pressure (acute hydrocephalus) · brainstem transient ischemic attack (rare) Syncope Seizure Warning Lightheaded, nauseated, palpitations Aura possible Length of unconsciousness 10-60 seconds 1 minute to several minutes Eyes Open, may roll up Open, may turn to one side Limb movements None, tonic or clonic None, tonic or clonic · may be asymmetric Afterwards Brief confusion, up to 5 minutes Confusion for minutes to hours · possible Todd's paresis Incontinence Rare More common Tongue biting None Possible (side of the tongue) Movements: clonic = shaking · tonic = stiff · myoclonic = jerks 2. History clues Earlier seizures → more likely a seizure Aura · asymmetric onset · deficit afterwards → focal seizure Triggers (sleep loss, drugs or medications, head injury, illness, fever) → provoked vs unprovoked Adults rarely present with a first generalized seizure - they present with focal ones · first generalized seizures are common in children Adult first seizure : electrolytes and CT head now, EEG and MRI as an outpatient (full workup in the Week 14 chart) 3. EEG and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy Focal slowing or focal spikes on the electroencephalogram (EEG) = a focal lesion → MRI is required to look for cortical dysplasia, mesial temporal sclerosis , tumour or old infarct Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy : easily controlled - lifestyle (sleep, food, fluids) and low-dose drugs · a sleep-deprived EEG brings out the abnormality 4. Antiseizure drugs in young women Older antiseizure drugs weaken oral contraceptives → check interactions Teratogens : always add folic acid · avoid the worst drugs in anyone who could become pregnant Worst Better options Valproate (highest malformation risk) · phenytoin · several drugs together Levetiracetam · Lamotrigine · carbamazepine ⚠ Do not stop antiseizure drugs for pregnancy : seizures risk fetal hypoxic injury , maternal status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) 5. Complications of a seizure Posterior shoulder dislocation · injuries from falls · aspiration · status epilepticus (permanent brain injury) · SUDEP

The dying patient and medical assistance in dying (MAiD) Two questions run through the lecture: who decides when the patient cannot ( capacity → substitute decision maker ), and, when the patient can and asks to die, are they eligible for MAiD, and which stream's safeguards apply? Around both sits palliative care : comfort for the patient and support for the family. ⭐ Stream 2 (natural death not reasonably foreseeable) adds an expert assessor, a 90-day wait, and forbids the waiver of final consent. Capacity = understand + appreciate; it is decision-specific and can fluctuate, and the clinician offering the treatment assesses it. Advance care planning wishes are not consent; code status is not goals of care. The SDM order starts with a court guardian and a Power of Attorney for Personal Care, then spouse, child, parent, sibling. Turning the patient and symptom medications do not hasten death. A conscientious objector must still make an effective referral. 1. Capacity and the substitute decision maker Capacity (Health Care Consent Act) has two parts ① the ability to understand the information relevant to the decision ② the ability to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding (or not deciding) not global: specific to the decision (may be capable about meals but not about treatment) · can fluctuate over time Who assesses it : the health practitioner offering the treatment must determine capacity before treating (this can be delegated) Substitute decision maker (SDM) : gives or refuses consent for an incapable patient, taken in this order ① court-ordered guardian of the person · ② attorney under a Power of Attorney for Personal Care (not the one for property) · ③ representative appointed by the Consent and Capacity Board ④ spouse or partner · ⑤ child (16 or older) or parent with right of custody (or the Children's Aid Society) · ⑥ parent with right of access · ⑦ siblings · ⑧ any other relative · ⑨ the Public Guardian and Trustee 2. Code status, goals of care, advance care planning What it is Key point Code status Which resuscitation (if any) to give if the heart stops or breathing stops Needs informed consent from the patient or the SDM Goals of care Discussions that prepare for consent: who the patient is, how their values shape their goals, and how those fit the clinical picture and the treatments on offer Code status is not the same as goals of care Advance care planning Wishes voiced ahead of time to guide a future SDM Wishes, not decisions: not "advance consent" (the future is speculation) · still prepares the person and the SDM 3. Palliative care Definition (World Health Organization): an approach that improves quality of life for patients and families facing life-threatening illness, preventing and relieving suffering by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, physical, psychosocial or spiritual a team approach : practical needs · bereavement counselling · a support system so patients live as actively as possible until death most people would prefer to die at home , so it must be available in the community Symptom management : drug and non-drug measures for pain, respiratory distress, delirium, agitation , knowing their indications, adverse effects and complications Tools Palliative Performance Scale (version 2): disease burden and progress toward the end of life (the most used) Edmonton Symptom Assessment System : screens for symptoms palliative care can manage Routes in : the patient declines or stops treatment · the physician judges treatment futile or likely to cause suffering and suggests it · alongside active treatment for hard-to-control symptoms · after a severe irreversible disability the classic exam example: a severe stroke whose best outcome is full dependence in a nursing home; if that is unacceptable to the patient, focus on comfort and start no tube feeding or intravenous fluids 4. Supporting the patient and family through dying Patient- and family-centred : dignity and respect for the patient, family and significant others · speak to the patient even if comatose · look after the family's needs (rest, self-care) · answer questions honestly Uncertainty : outcomes fall on a spectrum; a family told to expect the worst may be angry when the patient does better ("you broke my heart for no reason") Temporary improvement for hours to days after stopping feeds, medications or fluids is common : reassure, use the time together, re-evaluate only if it lasts many days Moral distress when a family's choice clashes with your values: "it's not my journey" · trust the SDM or attorney to choose as the patient would · choose your own SDM and tell them what you would NOT want Myths to answer not starving to death : the organs shut down together, with no hunger or thirst · offer sips and tastes; the patient is in control turning does not hasten death : it relieves pressure and gives staff a brief exam every 4 hours ( mottling of the extremities → call the family) · symptom medications do not hasten death either patients often die as they lived (alone, or once the family has gathered) · give the family permission to step away from the bedside 5. Autopsy review Two questions decide everything after a death: who has the authority (the coroner under the Coroner's Act, or the family through informed authorization), and what actually caused it , written as a chain of diseases, not as the way the body stopped. ⭐ A medicolegal autopsy falls under the Coroner's Act, so the family cannot refuse it; a hospital autopsy needs informed authorization (estate trustee first, then spouse and adult children, parents, siblings), and the family may restrict it. Part I runs backwards: each line is caused by the one below it; Part II holds contributors outside the chain. Never write a mechanism ("cardiac arrest", "multisystem organ failure", "sepsis") as the cause. Sudden and unexpected deaths are signed by the coroner, expected natural ones by the doctor. A suspected genetic disease found at autopsy matters to living relatives. 1. Two kinds of autopsy An autopsy (also necropsy, post-mortem examination) is done by a pathologist · the two kinds are not procedurally different ; their focus and emphasis are Hospital autopsy Medicolegal autopsy Done by Hospital pathologist Usually a forensic pathologist Investigation Medical Medicolegal death investigation ± police Where the death happened In hospital (a controlled environment) May come from hospital ( the majority do not ) Kind of death Natural (family requests, genetics, education, research, quality assurance) Falls under the jurisdiction of the Coroner's Act Authority Informed authorization from the estate trustee or next of kin The Coroner's Act: the family does not authorize it When to contact the coroner (any one): family concerns about care · sudden, unexpected death (no clinical history of a potentially fatal illness) · any "unnatural" death (accident, suicide, homicide) · death on a psychiatry ward · maternal death · seizure disorder · Children's Aid Society involvement in a child's death 2. The hospital autopsy Informed authorization: has the appropriate person authorized it? In descending order ① the deceased's estate trustee (no will, or not known: whoever is applying to the court to become trustee, if the family agrees; if they dispute it, go down this list) ② spouse (married, or living together in a conjugal relationship for at least a year or as parents of a child) and adult children · ③ parents · ④ siblings · ⑤ any other next of kin who is mentally capable for the decision The approach mirrors the physician-patient interaction : the same duties of consent, professionalism and confidentiality (the CanMEDS roles) Organ retention and restrictions : some organs need further examination (most often the brain and heart ) · the family may restrict the autopsy, typically to a limited internal exam or no organ retention What it is for (its value) diagnose disease · the accuracy of the clinical diagnosis, tests and imaging · unresolved clinical issues · the effects of treatment · the extent of disease suspected genetic disease : findings that protect the health of living relatives assuage grief · research · teaching · it informs the death certificate Steps ① clinical history : medical records, ambulance call report, verbal report from the clinician, pathology consultation form ② external exam : nutrition and development, hair, tattoos, scars , all body surfaces, disease, congenital anomalies, injuries, resuscitation ③ internal exam : Y-shaped incision , organs removed as a block, weighed and examined · scalp retracted, calvarium sawn, brain removed · special dissections → a provisional anatomical diagnosis (gross findings ± pending tests) not routinely examined unless indicated: eyes · bowel lumen · limb bones · joints · tendons · back of the neck · back and limb muscles · spinal cord · pelvic and shoulder girdles · parathyroids · middle and inner ear ④ additional tests and consultations (histology, genetics, blood) ⑤ opinion : an integration of everything, read in the context of the case · findings rarely stand alone (the misconception: "all is revealed when one opens the body") 3. The death certificate A permanent record of what natural disease, injury, event or combination led to the death · used for statistics (International Classification of Diseases coding uses the underlying cause ), surveillance, public health and research funding, and as a legal document (proof of death, family, insurance) Certifies identification · cause of death · manner of death · asks about an autopsy · not used for stillbirths Who signs : sudden and unexpected → coroner or medical examiner · expected natural → doctor or certain nurses 4. Cause of death: the WHO format Cause of death = the disease and/or injury that ends life · stated by the WHO method, the common-sense causal chain Part I : the sequence of events, working backwards from the final condition - each condition causes the one above it : (a) immediate ← (b) intermediate ← (c) underlying Part II : other significant conditions that contributed but are not in the chain (often risk factors) Causal chain = cause of death statement · initiating event = manner of death Example 1 Example 2 Example 3 I (a) Hemopericardium Upper gastrointestinal bleed Right pulmonary squamous cell carcinoma I (b) Ruptured myocardial infarct Ruptured esophageal varix — I (c) Coronary atherosclerosis and thrombosis Alcoholic liver cirrhosis — Part II Diabetes mellitus Hemophilia Tobacco smoking Be specific infection : the disease and/or organism, and the site (COVID-19 pneumonia · Haemophilus influenzae meningoencephalitis) cancer : site of origin, metastatic site and type (pulmonary metastasis of colonic adenocarcinoma) Leave out the mechanism of death (the physiological or biochemical process by which death came about): it only attests to the fact of death and adds nothing about the cause - cardiac arrest · arrhythmia · exsanguination · respiratory arrest · multisystem organ failure · sepsis

A 70-year-old right-handed woman has sudden left face and arm weakness, worse than the leg. She ignores the left side of the room and insists nothing is wrong with her. Which artery is most likely occluded? Left MCA Right ACA Right MCA Right PCA Basilar artery The correct answer is C. Neglect and anosognosia are non-dominant (right) hemisphere cortical signs, and face + arm > leg is the MCA pattern. A left MCA stroke would give aphasia with right-sided weakness. The ACA favours the leg, and the PCA gives a homonymous hemianopia.

A 60-year-old has sudden vertigo and double vision, with reduced pain sensation on the left side of the face and on the right arm and leg. Where is the lesion? Left cerebral cortex Right internal capsule Cerebellar hemisphere Cervical spinal cord Brainstem The correct answer is E. Brainstem signs are vertigo plus something else, diplopia plus something else, and crossed sensory findings (one side of the face, the opposite side of the body). A hemispheric lesion affects the face and body on the same side.

A patient has intention tremor and dysmetria of the left arm and left leg, with normal strength. Where is the lesion most likely? Left cerebellar hemisphere Right cerebellar hemisphere Right internal capsule Left motor cortex Right thalamus The correct answer is A. Cerebellar lesions affect the same side of the body: the cerebellum talks to the opposite motor cortex, which drives the opposite side of the body, so the two crossings cancel.

A 75-year-old with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hyperextends his neck. He has weakness that is much worse in both arms than in both legs. What is the most likely syndrome? Anterior cord syndrome Brown-Sequard syndrome Posterior cord syndrome Cauda equina syndrome Central cord syndrome The correct answer is E. Central cord syndrome affects the upper limbs more than the lower, because the arm fibres of the lateral corticospinal tract lie most medially. The review's classic setting is a hyperextension injury in an older patient with cervical disease.
