A 15-year-old hockey player still has headaches and poor concentration 5 weeks after a concussion. What does this meet criteria for? Chronic traumatic encephalopathy Second-impact syndrome Post-traumatic epilepsy Diffuse axonal injury Post-concussion syndrome The correct answer is E. Post-concussion syndrome is symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks in adults or more than 4 weeks in youth. A first concussion usually recovers fully in 1-4 weeks. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is a degenerative picture years after repeated concussions.

A patient with a large metastatic brain tumour has headache and drowsiness. MRI shows extensive vasogenic edema around the lesion. Which drug reduces this edema by restoring the blood-brain barrier in the tumour vessels? Dexamethasone Mannitol Acetazolamide Hypertonic saline Levetiracetam The correct answer is A. Dexamethasone restores the BBB in leaky tumour vessels, shrinking the surrounding vasogenic edema and the effective tumour size. Mannitol and hypertonic saline work osmotically and need an intact BBB.

A child with acute hydrocephalus has rising intracranial pressure, and CSF must be diverted today. What is the usual short-term option? Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt External ventricular drain Serial lumbar punctures Oral acetazolamide Decompressive craniectomy The correct answer is B. Short term: an external ventricular drain. Long term: a VP (cerebral) shunt. Untreated, hydrocephalus can herniate the brain, which is fatal.

A 66-year-old has sudden weakness of the right leg, much worse than the right arm and face. Speech and language are normal. Which artery is most likely occluded? Left MCA Right ACA Left PCA Left ACA Basilar artery The correct answer is D. Leg > face and arm is the ACA pattern, contralateral to the lesion ("when you see an ANT you lift your LEG"). The MCA pattern is face + arm > leg.

A 45-year-old has the sudden "worst headache of my life". A non-contrast CT head, done 14 hours after onset, is normal. What is the next step? MRI with contrast Lumbar puncture Repeat CT in 24 hours Discharge on a triptan EEG The correct answer is B. A thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise. CT is most sensitive early, and its sensitivity falls each day. If CT is negative, do an LP for xanthochromia (yellow CSF from hemoglobin breakdown).

A 68-year-old on warfarin has a deep intracerebral hemorrhage from hypertensive arteriopathy. Warfarin is held and BP is being lowered below 160/110. What DVT prophylaxis is appropriate on admission? Low-molecular-weight heparin Unfractionated heparin Mechanical compression Continue warfarin ASA 81 mg The correct answer is C. In ICH: control BP (< 160/110), hold all antiplatelets and anticoagulants, and use mechanical DVT prophylaxis. The review adds a repeat CT at 24 h, starting LMWH prophylaxis only if the clot has not expanded.

A 30-year-old has bilateral, pressing headaches of mild intensity lasting a few hours. They are not worse when she climbs stairs, and she has no nausea. Which diagnosis fits best? Migraine without aura Cluster headache Medication overuse headache Tension-type headache Idiopathic intracranial hypertension The correct answer is D. Tension-type: bilateral, pressing (non-pulsating), mild-moderate, 30 min to 7 days, not worse with activity, no nausea, and at most one of photophobia or phonophobia. Migraine is unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, worse with activity, and has nausea.

A 25-year-old with typical migraine and no cardiovascular disease asks what to take for an attack. What is the best acute plan? Opioid at peak of pain Amitriptyline at onset Verapamil at onset Daily codeine combination Early triptan plus NSAID The correct answer is E. Treat migraine early and in combination: an abortive triptan ± NSAID ± antiemetic. Triptans work best taken at onset. Amitriptyline is a preventive, verapamil is the cluster preventive, and regular analgesic use risks medication overuse headache.

A 35-year-old man has attacks of severe right periorbital pain with right-sided tearing and nasal congestion, several times a day for weeks at a time. Which drug is the usual preventive? Verapamil Propranolol Amitriptyline Topiramate Sumatriptan The correct answer is A. Cluster headache (a TAC): side-locked V1 pain with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms. The preventive of choice is verapamil. Attacks are aborted with SC sumatriptan, inhaled zolmitriptan or 100% O 2 .

A 72-year-old has a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing and blurred vision. ESR and CRP are high. What should be done first? Temporal artery biopsy first High-dose prednisone Oral sumatriptan MRI brain first Acetazolamide The correct answer is B. Giant cell arteritis is an emergency because of the risk of vision loss. Start high-dose glucocorticoids early (with a later taper) and refer to ophthalmology; the temporal artery biopsy should not delay treatment.

After a neck injury, a 40-year-old develops a unilateral headache radiating to the neck and face, with a mild ptosis and a small pupil on the same side. What is the most likely diagnosis? Cluster headache Giant cell arteritis Cervical artery dissection Subarachnoid hemorrhage Posterior communicating aneurysm The correct answer is C. Cervical artery dissection (spontaneous or after trauma): headache radiating to the neck and face with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. It can cause an ischemic stroke. A PComm aneurysm gives a blown pupil, not a small one.

A 26-year-old woman with obesity has daily headaches that are worse lying down, with pulsatile tinnitus and papilledema. MRI shows no mass. Which drug is used to treat this? IV dexamethasone Sumatriptan Verapamil Acetazolamide Mannitol The correct answer is D. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: raised ICP with no cause found, linked to obesity. The review's features are headache worse supine, pulsatile tinnitus and diplopia. Treat risk factors and give acetazolamide; a shunt is the surgical option.

A 78-year-old with fever, neck stiffness and confusion is started on empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis. Ampicillin is added because of her age. Which organism does it cover? Streptococcus pneumoniae Neisseria meningitidis Haemophilus influenzae Staphylococcus aureus Listeria monocytogenes The correct answer is E. Empiric regimen "CAAV + D": ceftriaxone, acyclovir, ampicillin (elderly or immunocompromised), vancomycin, plus dexamethasone. Ampicillin covers Listeria. Ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae and S. aureus, and vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcu

A febrile patient's lumbar puncture shows a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 0.2, with many neutrophils. Which diagnosis is most likely? Bacterial meningitis Viral meningitis HSV encephalitis Normal CSF Subarachnoid hemorrhage The correct answer is A. A normal CSF:serum glucose ratio is > 0.6. A low ratio (< 0.3) indicates bacterial meningitis, which also shows a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis. Take the samples before antibiotics.

A 55-year-old has fever, confusion, word-finding difficulty and a focal seizure. CT head is unremarkable. Which test confirms the most likely diagnosis? CSF Gram stain CSF HSV PCR Blood culture Serum ESR EEG The correct answer is B. Cortical features (focal seizures, aphasia, memory loss) point to encephalitis, most often HSV. CSF HSV PCR is the only way to confirm it. Start IV acyclovir before the result returns.

A 28-year-old woman had optic neuritis last year and now has numbness in both legs. Which finding is needed to diagnose multiple sclerosis? Oligoclonal bands on lumbar puncture A positive family history of MS Lesions separated in time and space Enhancing lesions on a single MRI Low vitamin D level in serum The correct answer is C. MS is diagnosed by dissemination in time (separate events) and space (different sites), once other diseases are excluded. Oligoclonal bands are sensitive but not specific, and low vitamin D is a risk factor, not a criterion.

A 30-year-old has a first unprovoked seizure. The EEG shows epileptiform discharges, putting his recurrence risk at 60% or more over 10 years. Which statement is correct? Not epilepsy until a second seizure Provoked seizure; no diagnosis Not epilepsy unless MRI is abnormal Epilepsy, given the ≥60% risk Epilepsy only if it lasted over 5 min The correct answer is D. Epilepsy is any of: 2 unprovoked seizures more than 24 h apart; 1 unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of 60% or more over 10 years (such as epileptiform EEG or a structural MRI lesion); or an epilepsy syndrome.

A 50-year-old with severe hyponatremia (Na 118) has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. His brain MRI is normal. How is this seizure classified? Unprovoked seizure Epilepsy Status epilepticus Febrile seizure Provoked seizure The correct answer is E. A provoked seizure is a transient factor (fever, glucose, Na, alcohol) acting on an otherwise normal brain. Without the trigger it would not have happened. An unprovoked seizure has an enduring cause such as a tumour, old stroke or trauma.

A patient with postherpetic neuralgia says even the touch of her bedsheets on the area is painful. What is this called? Hyperpathia Allodynia Dysesthesia Paresthesia The correct answer is B. Allodynia = pain from a stimulus that is not normally painful (sheets, clothes). Hyperpathia = an exaggerated response to a painful stimulus (pinprick). Dysesthesia = an unpleasant abnormal sensation such as burning.

A 60-year-old has brief electric-shock pains in the right cheek, triggered by chewing and touching the face. Which drug is first choice? Gabapentin Carbamazepine Duloxetine Oxycodone Capsaicin cream The correct answer is B. Trigeminal neuralgia classically responds to carbamazepine. Postherpetic neuralgia classically responds to gabapentin. Opioids are a last resort in neuropathic pain.

A patient with painful diabetic neuropathy also has major depression. Which agent is the best choice to treat both? Pregabalin Gabapentin Duloxetine Lidocaine patch Carbamazepine The correct answer is C. Duloxetine (an SNRI) treats neuropathic pain and helps depression. Amitriptyline is the cheap choice that helps sleep. Titrate one agent up and change it only after 1 month at a high dose with no effect.

Six weeks after a wrist fracture, a woman has burning hand pain far worse than expected for the injury, with swelling and colour and temperature changes. What is the most likely diagnosis? Postherpetic neuralgia Cervical radiculopathy Small fibre neuropathy Complex regional pain syndrome Chemotherapy-induced neuropathy The correct answer is D. In CRPS, a focal tissue or nerve injury leads to chronic pain with inflammatory and autonomic features (swelling, colour, temperature, skin and hair changes). The pain is greater and lasts longer than the injury would explain. It is hard to treat.

In a patient with an acute ischemic stroke, the non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage. Which scan comes next to look for a large vessel occlusion amenable to thrombectomy? CT angiogram CT perfusion Carotid Doppler MRI brain Echocardiogram The correct answer is A. The stroke protocol images in order: non-contrast CT (bleed, early ischemic change), then a CT angiogram (large vessel occlusion, for thrombectomy), then CT perfusion (mismatch = salvageable brain). Doppler and echo belong to the later etiology workup.

A 76-yr old male was brought into the ER after he fell from a ladder height of 17 feet. He landed on his occiput on the concrete driveway. He was comatose at the scene. EMS intubated him and brought him to the emergency department where you are the on-duty physician. On examination, his eyes are not open to voice or pain; he is intubated; his best motor response is bilateral flexion posture to painful stimulation. What are the components of his Glasgow Coma Scale? (Please check all that apply) Eye Opening -0 Eye Opening -1 Eye Opening -2 Speech - 0 Speech -1 Speech - 2 Motor - 0 Motor - 1 Motor - 2 Motor - 3 The correct answers are B, E, and J.

Steve was checked into the board. His helmeted head struck the board hard. He staggered back to the bench. There was no loss of consciousness. He immediately complained of headache, dizziness, and "seeing stars". He did not have any neurological deficits. You were his hockey team physician. What would be the appropriate management in the arena? Please choose all that apply. Ice it and send him back out to play Get him to the emergency room immediately if he becomes drowsy Let him rest in the dressing room alone Get him to the emergency room if he complains of arm/leg tingling Remove him from play, rest him in the sideline, and frequently check on him Get him to the emergency room immediately for a head CT Give him some Advil You agree with his coach that there is no concussion since he was wearing a helmet and since there was no loss of consciousness You agree with his coach that he keeps playing since your team is losing Get him to the emergency room if he complains of severe neck pain The correct answers are B, D, E, and J. This question examines the management of concussion in the field. It is important to recognise that concussion can occur without loss of consciousness and with helmet (Wrong-8). A 55-year-old man had had MS for 5 years. He tells you over that time she has not had any "attacks", but has noticed a slow worsening of gait and balance. What type of MS does he most likely have? Relapsing remitting MS (RRMS) Secondary progressive MS (SPMS) Primary progressive MS (PPMS) Inflammatory MS The correct answer is C. He likely has PPMS. He has had a slow worsening of symtposm over 5 years without any relapses. This is how PPMS presents.

The case. Case 1. A 72 year old man has the acute onset of left face, arm, and leg "numbness" while watching TV at 7pm. He is concerned, so he calls his son. His son, appropriately, tell him to call 911. His past medical history is significant for hypertension and hypothyroidism. His only medications are amlodipine and levothyroxine. EMS takes him to the ER and a stroke protocol is activated. In the ER at 7:45pm, he is found to be alert, not aphasic, has normal gaze and full visual fields. He has a subtle left facial droop, moderate left arm weakness, and moderate left leg weakness. There is no ataxia, but testing is difficult secondary to weakness on the left. There is no significant sensory deficit, including no neglect. Where does this localize? Right MCA Right ACA Right subcortical The correct answer is C. There are no cortical findings present, such as neglect. Also, isolated motor symptoms spanning face, arm and leg would also be consistent with a subcortical localization.

Small arteriole occlusions which cause lacunar stroke are not accessible for an embolectomy.

The case. Case 2. A 69 year old woman has an episode of difficulty talking and using her right hand while she is shopping with her daughter. The symptoms last 10 minutes and completely resolve. She believes it was because she was late eating lunch and was hungry. She sees her family physician the next day and tells her about this event. Her medical history is remarkable for being a current smoker, previous cholestectomy, and previous breast cancer (cancer free for 15 years). She is on no medications at this time. Her family physician finds that her blood pressure is 110/78 and her heart rate is irregularly irregular. Her neurological examination is entirely normal. What should the family doctor do? Order a CTA head and neck Order an EKG Order an MRI Refer to the TIA clinic Start ASA 81mg Start a DOAC The correct answers are A, B, D, and E. This sounds classic for a TIA. Its best to refer these patients to the TIA clinic for a rapid assessment. While she is waiting for the TIA clinic, it would be reasonable for her to be started on aspirin. Her past medical history is remarkable for a prior intracerebral hemorrhage 2 years ago which caused her to have left sided weakness and she has been using a walker since that time. She has a history of atrial fibrillation, diabetes and hypertension. Her medications include ASA 81mg od, metformin 500mg bid, and hydrochlorothiazide 25mg od. On arrival in the ER, she is awake and alert. She cannot name the images on the stroke card. She is unable to follow 1 step commands. She is able to speak, but it sounds like she is speaking a foreign language (despite English being her first language). There seems to be a right superior quadrantanopia. She has a right facial droop affecting the lower right face. There is a very slight right pronator drift and there is no leg weakness. Sensory testing is challenging due to language, but there is no obvious deficit. Where does this localize to? (fill in the blank) Left temporal lobe. The case. A 29 yo administrative assistant complains of numbness and tingling of the hands for the past six months. Her cousin has multiple sclerosis. She has "googled" her symptoms and is very worried that she may have multiple sclerosis as well. Her symptoms are intermittent, nocturnal and relieved by shaking her hands. Her exam is normal. The MOST appropriate action is to: Reassure her that this is not MS and investigation not required Reassure her that with a normal exam there is no problem with the nervous system. Agree that MS is a possibility and discuss a plan of investigation Inform her that sensory symptoms are common and rarely life threatening but offer an MRI if she would find this reassuring Reassure her that this is not MS, imaging is not necessary but nocturnal wrist splinting might be helpful. The correct answer is E.

The case. A 26 year old female presents to the ER with a 3 day history of tingling in the toes and soles of her feet. Over 48 hrs the sensory symptoms progressed to the knees and started in the fingertips. Today her legs gave out and she fell to the ground. She had a cold 3 weeks ago but is otherwise healthy. Exam was remarkable for proximal and distal weakness of all 4 limbs, areflexia, down going toes and mildly impaired vibration sensation at fingers and toes with normal pinprick appreciation. Which of the following statements regarding localization is the MOST accurate? The prominent weakness suggests the lesion localizes to muscle The pattern of weakness (quadriparesis) makes the cervical cord the most likely localization The paresthesias and absent reflexes make peripheral nerve the most likely localization In a 26 year old woman, the possibility of multiple sclerosis and a central localization needs consideration The acuteness of the presentation makes peripheral neuropathy an unlikely localization. The correct answer is C.

He also complains of shooting pain down the posterior right leg. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin , hypothyroidism on l-thyroxine. He has known degenerative disc disease and chronic low back pain. Which symptom is LEAST likely to be explained by a diabetic peripheral neuropathy? Postural lightheadedness Painful burning feet Urinary hesitancy Shooting pain in the posterior right leg Constipation The correct answer is D.

Only prescribe an analgesic if its for neuropathic pain. Only prescribe an antidepressant if it is a TCA or an SNRI with recognized benefit for neuropathic pain

Apart from mild urinary urgency, she noticed no other neurologic symptoms. Two years earlier, she experienced numbness of left arm and face lasting 2 months. She did not seek medical attention at that time as symptoms occurred during a stressful period at work. Symptoms resolved as she settled into her new job, reinforcing this. Which of the following examination findings would be most surprising in this scenario? A normal neurological examination Hyperactive but symmetrical reflexes in the limbs with bilateral Babinski signs A sensory level at T6 A positive Romberg sign A stocking distribution of sensory loss with reduced reflexes in the legs The correct answer is E.

A 78 year old man has suffered a hemorrhage affecting his left thalamus. Problems he might expect to contend with as he recovers include: Clumsiness of his right hand and burning pain on the right side of his body Neglect of his right arm and leg, making rehabilitation efforts challenging Atrophy of the muscles of his right arm and leg Impaired position and vibratory sensation on his left side and impaired pain and temperature sensation on his right side Impaired right sided sensation, apathy and impaired judgement The correct answer is A.

A 52 year old nurse complains of pain in his lower back radiating down his left leg beginning after he transferred a heavy and uncooperative patient. His sensory exam reveals loss of pinprick and temperature over the small toe and the plantar surface of his foot. What other finding would be common in this clinical situation? A positive Romberg test An absent Achilles reflex An absent quadriceps reflex Difficulty standing on his heels Weakness of great toe extension The correct answer is B.

The case. Case 1. Your 65 year old patient tells you she is having difficulties falling asleep because she feels her toes are "on fire" as she's trying to get to sleep. Diagnosis in psychiatry ⭐ There is no lesion, test or scan in psychiatry: the diagnosis is made by matching the interview to operational criteria (symptoms, number, duration, exclusions, specifiers). Clinically significant distress or impairment is required for almost every diagnosis. An expected response to loss or stress is not a disorder. Other specified gives the reason criteria are not met; unspecified does not. The five axes were abandoned in DSM-5 ; the biopsychosocial formulation answers "why this person, today?" Psychiatry has no lesion to find, so how do you make a diagnosis that holds up? You match what the interview gives you against operational criteria (the DSM-5), then put the person back around the checklist with a formulation. 1. Why psychiatric diagnosis is different Psychiatry = the biopsychosocial study of disorders of cognition, perception, emotion and behaviour Unlike neurology, there is no identifiable lesion : no physical sign, blood test, biopsy or scan makes the diagnosis the diagnosis rests on the clinical interview and observation a diagnosis names a cluster of symptoms and signs thought to share a pathological process A good diagnosis is valid (accurate) and reliable (stable) validity, three kinds: conceptual (the criteria pick out the right people) · construct (separates conditions with different causes) · predictive (patients follow the same course over time) the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5) exists to make diagnoses more valid and reliable Almost every diagnosis requires clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other functioning 2. What a diagnosis is not An expected or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss Socially deviant behaviour (political, religious, sexual) or a conflict between the person and society, unless it comes from a dysfunction in the person 3. Types of psychiatric disorder, by what is impaired Impaired Examples Cognition Dementia · psychotic disorders · major depression and bipolar disorder · obsessive-compulsive disorder · anxiety · dissociative disorders · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder Behaviour Conduct disorder · oppositional defiant disorder · anxiety · personality disorders · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder Perception Somatic symptom (somatoform) disorders · psychotic disorders Basic functions Sleep · eating · sexual disorders Emotions Mood disorders · schizoaffective disorder · anxiety 4. Using the DSM-5: operational criteria Operational criteria = a set of conditions the patient must meet to receive the diagnosis; they improve reliability Match the interview against each part: key symptoms · threshold number of symptoms · duration · key exclusions (better explained by a substance, a medical condition or another disorder) · specifiers (severity, remission, features, subtypes) Pitfalls normal reactions to stress are not accounted for → false positives symptoms too mild to be a disorder symptoms over-endorsed or fabricated · symptoms fluctuate and depend on the patient's account "check-the-box" interviewing that loses the patient's narrative (not patient-centred) 5. Putting the person back in: formulations Multi-axial formulation - dropped as a formal structure in DSM-5 , still a useful reference: Axis Covers I Clinical disorders (major mental disorders, learning disorders) II Personality disorders and intellectual disability (lifelong, shape Axis I) III Acute medical conditions and physical disorders IV Psychosocial and environmental factors V Level of functioning (clinical judgement, severity measures) Biopsychosocial formulation - the more holistic picture DSM-5 favours: answers "why this person, with this presentation, on this day?" 6. False negatives, and when criteria are not met False negatives happen even with a standard approach patients minimize symptoms or present atypically → handled by interviewing skill real dysfunction, but full criteria are not met When criteria are not met: Other specified = you state the reason the criteria are not met Unspecified = no reason given (e.g. not enough information, as in the emergency room)

The psychiatric interview ⭐ Balance content (information, symptoms) with process (rapport, empathy) - without the relationship the patient will not share the content. The history of presenting illness takes at least half the interview , funnels open → closed , and needs a reference point ("When were you last well?") . Screen safety every time, including thoughts of harming others. The mental status exam is gathered during the interview, not after it. Ask about diabetes and lipids in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder . The interview is the psychiatric investigation: it has to gather the content (information, symptoms) while building the process (rapport, empathy) that lets the patient share it. The sections below follow the order of the interview. 1. Two components, held in balance Component What it is Why it matters Content Information · symptoms Builds the diagnostic hypothesis Process Rapport · empathy The therapeutic relationship that makes the patient trust you with sensitive information 2. Introduction and identification Introduce yourself and your role · put the patient at ease · show respect and interest · attend to comfort Identifying data: name · gender (ask pronouns if not obvious) · age ("what is your age?") · marital status · parental status (who is caring for the children now?) · occupation and finances · cultural background 3. History of presenting illness At least half the interview Funnel strategy : open-ended questions first ("What brought you in today?") → closed, verifying questions ("Do you isolate yourself when depressed?") Reference point - define what "present" means: "When were you last well?" · "When were you content with how you were functioning?" separates the present episode from the past psychiatric history Precipitants : relationship difficulties · stopping treatment or a medication change · substance use · medical illness or new medical drugs 4. Psychiatric screening (before the past history) Screen for The question turns on Depression Down or less interested most of the day, nearly every day, for 2 weeks or more → then sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, guilt, slowing or restlessness, suicide Mania or hypomania A period "up", "high" or persistently irritable, not when intoxicated → grandiosity, less need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, risky pleasure-seeking Panic disorder Sudden rush of symptoms peaking within 10 minutes , some out of the blue , then 1 month or more of fear of another attack or changed behaviour Agoraphobia Avoiding places in case of an attack · fear of being unable to escape or get help Specific phobia Fear of a specific thing (heights, blood, flying) causing avoidance, distress or interference Obsessions / compulsions Intrusive thoughts, images or urges that keep coming back · driven, repeated actions (washing, checking, counting) Generalized anxiety Excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday things with physical effects Post-traumatic stress A very upsetting event → nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance, gaps in memory, loss of enjoyment Social anxiety Fear of being watched, the focus of attention, or humiliated, with avoidance Psychosis Beliefs others find odd · being spied on, mind read, thoughts inserted, special messages · voices or visions · only when sad, high or irritable? Substance use Use despite harm, danger or legal trouble · 3+ drinks in 3 hours on 3+ occasions · tolerance · failed attempts to stop · withdrawal · over 2 hours a day spent on it Safety - always : thoughts of killing yourself or not waking up · self-harm · thoughts of hurting others · unsafe driving · unprotected sex · arrests older adults: the 3 F's - fire, flood, falls 5. Past psychiatric history Goals: the longitudinal course · severity · predisposing, precipitating and protective factors The illness: age of onset · first symptoms and triggers · functioning before and after · number and length of hospitalizations Its impact: "How is your life different?" · "How do you cope?" · "What opportunities were lost?" Treatments : biological (medications - names, doses, durations ) · physical ( electroconvulsive therapy , transcranial magnetic stimulation, bright light) · psychosocial ( cognitive behavioral therapy , skills training) · "Has anything made a difference?" 6. Mental status exam Gathered mostly by observation during the interview , not as a separate step - components by ABC STAMP LICKER 7. Medical history, chosen by disorder Disorder Ask about Mood disorders Weight loss (melancholic depression) · obesity (carbohydrate craving in seasonal depression) Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder Diabetes · high lipids Substance use Skin lesions (crystal methamphetamine) · abscesses · HIV, hepatitis B and C (injection drug use) · alcoholic pancreatitis Obsessive-compulsive disorder Skin picking, excoriation, maceration from handwashing 8. Family and personal history Family history - in biological relatives: mental illness · alcohol or drugs · eccentric behaviour · suicide attempts or deaths · estrangement non-biological relatives still matter (an alcoholic step-parent shapes the environment, not the genes) Personal history - go chronologically from childhood , once rapport exists, with the hypothesis in mind development (pregnancy and birth briefly, home situation, attachment, clear rules) · childhood adversity (violence, punishment out of proportion, sexual abuse) · school · childhood personality · relationships and supports · sexual history · legal history · occupational history 9. Ending the interview and the plan Don't finish on a sensitive topic · thank the patient · acknowledge their commitment · ask what you missed and how they feel now · discuss the plan Treatment plan: most urgent next steps · safety issues · inpatient or outpatient · treatment approach · psychological supports
03 Phenomenology and the Mental Status Exam

Phenomenology and the mental status exam ⭐ Affect is what you observe in the moment; mood is what the patient reports over time - and you comment on whether they are congruent . Circumstantial gets to the point; tangential never does. Flight of ideas → mania; loosening of associations → psychosis. Hallucination = no stimulus; illusion = real stimulus misread. Ego-syntonic suicidal thoughts are the higher-risk kind. The mental status exam is gathered during the interview, in every encounter. Phenomenology asks how the patient experiences a symptom, not just which symptom it is; the mental status exam (MSE) is the objective record of what you observed. The exam is the "physical exam" of psychiatry, laid out by ABC STAMP LICKER. 1. Phenomenology Two meanings: Phenomenological psychopathology = objective description of the signs and symptoms (the "what" ) Karl Jaspers = empathic, neutral description of the subjective experience - the one the lecture focuses on, as part of the art of medicine The skill: elicit the symptom and understand how the patient lives it "auditory hallucinations" does not tell you what it is like to hear voices physicians treat "who's", not "what's" 2. The mental status exam: what it is The objective part of the assessment · the "physical exam" of psychiatry Not a separate part of the interview - assessed on the fly as you talk · is a separate heading in a case presentation Done in every encounter, in every field , not only with mental illness 3. The components: ABC STAMP LICKER Letter Component What you record A Appearance Grooming, dress for the setting and weather, oddities, tattoos, track marks B Behaviour Calm or restless, slowed, pacing · abnormal movements (tremor, tics) C Cooperation Willing, guarded, evasive, argumentative, over-familiar, eye contact · accessibility (willing and able to share?) S Speech Rate, rhythm, tone, volume , latency, articulation, amount · errors: mutism, fast speech (tachylalia), cluttering, repeating own words (palilalia), apraxia, dysarthria · pressured speech points to a thought disorder T Thought Form (process) - how it flows (§4) · Content - delusions, obsessions, preoccupations, safety A Affect Observed, in the moment : dysphoric, euthymic, euphoric, irritable, labile · range (restricted, blunted, flat) · appropriate to content? congruent with stated mood? M Mood Patient's own description, over time ("1 to 10, 5 is your normal") P Perception Hallucinations · illusions (§5) L Level of consciousness Alert, awake, oriented · dissociation I Insight (and judgement) Insight = understands the illness and what drives it · judgement = appreciates the consequences of choices C Cognition Orientation, attention, memory, executive function, abstraction · not formally tested unless there is a concern (then the Mini-Mental State Examination or Montreal Cognitive Assessment) K Knowledge base Knowledge = what you know · intelligence = what you do with it E Endings Suicidal and homicidal thoughts (§6) R Reliability Consistent with other data and within the interview? gaps? logical history? Judgement sits under Insight in the upper-year notes and under Knowledge base in the lecture note (sources differ - check the slides) A poor choice is not a mental illness : people have the right to make unwise decisions 4. Thought form: getting from A to B Form Path from question (A) to answer (B) Typical of Goal-directed Straight from A to B Normal Circumstantial Detours through irrelevant detail, but gets to B — Tangential Drifts off and never reaches B — Flight of ideas Rapid jumps from tangent to tangent, links barely visible Bipolar disorder (mania) Loosening of associations No logical connection between thoughts - the most severe Psychotic disorders Derailing : the upper-year notes treat it as the same as loosening of associations; the lecture note lists it separately as abruptly losing the train of thought (sources differ - check the slides) Also: illogical, perseverative 5. Thought content and perception Delusion = a fixed, false belief out of keeping with the patient's cultural norms themes: persecutory, grandiose, jealousy, somatic, erotomanic, nihilistic, religious, control, reference bizarre (impossible) vs non-bizarre (possible) · mood-congruent , incongruent or neutral overvalued ideas also go here (e.g. misreading things as being about you) Perception: Stimulus present? Note Hallucination No - perception without a stimulus Any sense; auditory commonest ( commanding vs commenting); not always pathological Pseudohallucination No Experienced through an "inner sense", not truly through the senses Illusion Yes - misperception of a real stimulus Can be normal or abnormal 6. Endings: safety Suicidal thoughts : passive (thinking about it) vs active (planning or acting) · self-injury ego-syntonic (not distressing to the patient) = higher risk - a red flag · ego-dystonic = distressing Homicidal thoughts : assessed the same way

Organ donation ⭐ The family can refuse donation in both opt-in and opt-out systems, even when the patient registered. Neurologic death = no consciousness + no brainstem reflexes + apnea, whole brain, known cause, no confounders. Circulatory death = arterial pressure under 5 mmHg, then 5 minutes hands-off, declared by 2 physicians. Nova Scotia is Canada's only opt-out province. Organs need donation close to death; tissue can wait - and every death is referred for tissue. Normothermic regional perfusion grew the donor pool by 30-50%. Organs must be taken very close to the time of death; tissues can be taken after it. The lecture turns on the two routes to deceased organ donation - death by neurologic criteria and death by circulatory criteria - and on what makes families say yes. 1. The Canadian framework Level Who Responsible for National Canadian Blood Services Sharing organs across provincial borders (equitable access) · monitoring performance · national policies and guidelines · national campaigns · legal and ethical challenges Provincial Provincial organizations (Ontario: Trillium Gift of Life Network ) Their own policies and regulations within the national framework · choosing opt-in or opt-out Trillium: patient-facing, 24/7 , coordinates sharing across Canada and the United States 2. Opt-in vs opt-out consent Opt-out (presumed) consent - aims to close the gap between supply and demand used in many countries, including Spain (the world's highest donor rate) Nova Scotia, 2021 - the only Canadian province; all others are opt-in families of all medically suitable donors are approached · donors rose afterwards (other changes may have contributed) In both models, the family can still refuse - even if the patient registered as a donor · rare, because most families follow the patient's wishes 3. Pathways to donation The brain dies when starved of oxygen, three ways: ① injury and swelling cut off its blood flow · ② the heart stops · ③ breathing stops Refer to Trillium when a GIFT trigger is present: G rave prognosis (Glasgow Coma Scale under 3, as written in the note - check the threshold on the slides) · I njured brain with no recovery expected · F amily raises donation · T herapy being limited 4. Death by neurologic vs circulatory criteria Neurologic criteria Circulatory criteria Situation Brain death (irreversible coma) Decision to withdraw life-sustaining treatment · medical assistance in dying (MAiD) · unsuccessful resuscitation Defined by Complete absence of consciousness + absent brainstem reflexes Cessation of circulation Requirements Known cause · no confounding factors · absent brainstem reflexes · absent breathing effort on the apnea test · whole-brain (not just brainstem) death · absent cerebral blood flow (blood-flow test or cerebral angiogram) Withdrawal as usual · continuous arterial line · pressure under 5 mmHg · 5 minutes hands-off (no return of circulation, so death is permanent) · 2 physicians declare death (time of death = end of the 5 minutes) 5. Optimizing the donor and the organs What is good for the patient is good for the organs : blood pressure with fluids and pressors · lung protection (steroids) · nutrition · hormone replacement (e.g. levothyroxine) · hypothermia for kidney donors Circulatory-death donors: direct procurement perfusion · machine perfusion · normothermic regional perfusion - new, ↑ the donor pool by 30-50% and improves transplant volume and outcomes Tissue donation : every patient who dies is referred ; if suitable, the family is approached 6. What makes families say yes Families may refuse because of: perceived quality of care (a gap in their loved one's care) not understanding brain death timing - feeling rushed, asked straight after the prognosis talk setting - asked somewhere public rather than a private room not enough information, or an untrained approach Building the relationship communication: right place · often · clear language · several formats trust: emotional support · physical needs · dignity and respect · enough information time : to talk with staff, to decide, to be with their loved one Culture and faith : many faiths actively support donation as a good deed at the end of life · faith leaders want to help explain their faith's position to their communities

Depressive disorders ⭐ Major depression = 5 of 9 symptoms for 2 weeks, one of them low mood or anhedonia, and never a manic or hypomanic episode. Persistent depressive disorder = the rule of 2's: 2 years, 2 symptoms, never 2 months well. DMDD: outbursts 3 times a week for 12 months, onset before 10, diagnosed only from 6 to 18. Atypical = mood reactivity, hypersomnia, weight gain, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity; melancholic = no reactivity, worse mornings, early waking. SSRIs first line, 4-6 weeks to respond; ECT first line when treatment is urgent or there are psychotic or catatonic features - 80-90% response. Light therapy first line for seasonal depression. No antidepressants in bipolar disorder. Every depressive disorder shares sad, empty or irritable mood with somatic and cognitive changes that impair function; they are told apart by symptom count, duration, age, timing and cause. Then: why depression happens (biological, psychological, social) and how it is treated. 1. The depressive disorders Major depressive disorder (MDD) · persistent depressive disorder (PDD, dysthymia) · disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) · premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) · substance-induced depressive disorder · depressive disorder due to another medical condition · other specified and unspecified An expected, culturally approved response to a stressor or loss is not a disorder 2. Major depressive disorder The commonest depressive disorder · single episode or recurrent (2 or more) recurrence risk climbs: 50-60% after the first episode · 75% after the second · 90% after the third A major depressive episode = criteria A-C A: 5 or more of 9 symptoms, in the same 2 weeks, a change from before - at least 1 must be depressed mood or loss of interest (anhedonia) (mnemonic SIGECAPS ) depressed mood · loss of interest or pleasure · weight or appetite change (more than 5% of body weight in a month) · insomnia or hypersomnia · psychomotor agitation or slowing (seen by others) · fatigue · worthlessness or excessive guilt · poor concentration or indecision · recurrent thoughts of death or suicide "nearly every day", most of the day B : clinically significant distress or impairment C : not due to a substance or another medical condition D : not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder E : never a manic or hypomanic episode (otherwise it is bipolar) 3. Specifiers (what kind of episode) Severity (mild · moderate · severe) · remission ( full = no significant symptoms for 2 months ) · early or late onset Specifier Requirement Note Anxious distress 2 or more : keyed up · restless · can't concentrate from worry · dread · fear of losing control Mixed features 3 or more manic symptoms during the depression (elevated mood, grandiosity, pressured talk, racing thoughts, more energy, risky activity, less need for sleep) Seen by others · a risk factor for bipolar disorder , not mania itself Melancholic 1 : pleasure lost or no mood reactivity + 3 : despair/emptiness · worse in the morning · early morning waking · agitation or slowing · weight loss · guilt Inpatients, psychotic, more severe cases Atypical Mood reactivity + 2 or more : weight gain · hypersomnia · leaden paralysis · rejection sensitivity Not melancholic or catatonic Psychotic Delusions or hallucinations Mood-congruent (guilt, disease, death, punishment) vs incongruent Catatonia 3 or more of 12 (stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia) Peripartum onset Onset in pregnancy or up to 4 weeks after delivery ~3% in pregnancy, 6% after · may be psychotic ( infanticide risk ) · recurrence 30-50% Seasonal pattern 2 major depressive episodes in 2 years tied to a time of year, with remission at a set time MDD only · hypersomnia, overeating, carbohydrate craving · higher latitude, younger age 4. Telling the depressive disorders apart Disorder Core rule Duration and timing Key exclusion or feature Major depressive disorder 5 of 9 , including low mood or anhedonia 2 weeks Never manic or hypomanic Persistent depressive disorder Low mood most days + 2 of 6 (appetite, sleep, energy, self-esteem, concentration, hopelessness) 2 years (1 year in children, mood may be irritable) · never symptom-free over 2 months - the rule of 2's Milder but longer · MDD criteria may be met throughout ("double depression") · never cyclothymic Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder Temper outbursts 3 or more times a week + irritable mood between 12 months , in 2 of 3 settings · onset before 10 · first diagnosed only between 6 and 18 Never a full manic or hypomanic episode over 1 day Premenstrual dysphoric disorder 5 symptoms in the week before menses, at least 1 mood symptom (lability, irritability, low mood, anxiety) Most cycles · improves within days of menses · confirmed by daily ratings over 2 cycles Not just a flare of another disorder Substance or medication-induced Prominent depressed mood or anhedonia During or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or a medication The substance can cause it · not only during delirium Due to another medical condition Prominent depressed mood or anhedonia — Direct physiological result of the illness on history, exam or labs · not adjustment disorder with depressed mood (where the illness is the stressor) · not only during delirium Other specified Full criteria not met - reason stated Recurrent brief (2-13 days, monthly for 12 months) · short-duration (4-13 days) · insufficient symptoms (2 weeks, fewer symptoms) Unspecified Full criteria not met - reason not stated e.g. emergency room, not enough information 5. Why depression happens Multifactorial and heterogeneous : genes × environment · early (childhood) onset = more psychosocial · later onset = more genetic Genetics : twin concordance 40-50% · first-degree relatives 2-3× · many small-effect genes, serotonin system best studied (e.g. the serotonin transpo

Pharmacology of antidepressants ⭐ SSRIs are first line because they are safe in overdose and well tolerated - never combine them with an MAOI (2-week washout, longer after fluoxetine). Fluoxetine: longest half-life, no discontinuation syndrome, least weight gain, most activating. Paroxetine: sedating, anticholinergic, discontinuation syndrome. Sertraline: diarrhea. Citalopram: avoid with QT or heart problems. Venlafaxine raises diastolic pressure; duloxetine helps neuropathic pain. Bupropion: no sexual effects or weight gain, but lowers the seizure threshold - avoid in eating disorders and brain injury. Mirtazapine: sleep and weight gain. TCAs: cardiac toxicity is the most serious effect. MAOIs + tyramine = hypertensive crisis. Serotonin syndrome = clonus and hyperreflexia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome = rigidity with reduced reflexes. Every antidepressant raises monoamines in the synapse; the classes differ in which ones, and in their side effects and interactions. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line because they are the safest; the older classes are limited by toxicity and interactions. 1. The classes at a glance Class Examples Mechanism Uses Adverse effects Cautions Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors ( SSRIs ) Paroxetine · sertraline · fluoxetine · citalopram · escitalopram Block serotonin reuptake → more serotonin at the postsynaptic neuron Most prescribed for major depression · response close to 70% Sexual (25-50%) · gastrointestinal (GI) · insomnia or sedation · headache · tremor · mania induction Never with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) or L-tryptophan (2-week washout, longer for fluoxetine) · interactions · liver disease Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors ( SNRIs ) Venlafaxine · desvenlafaxine · duloxetine Block serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake Depression and anxiety · efficacy and tolerability better than SSRIs ↑ diastolic blood pressure · nausea · sexual · discontinuation syndrome Taper slowly Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor Bupropion Blocks dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake Augmenting agent · second line for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder No weight gain, sexual effects or sedation · can cause anxiety, insomnia · psychosis at high doses ↑ seizure risk (450 mg+) · avoid in brain injury and eating disorders · does not treat anxiety · abuse potential Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitors Trazodone · nefazodone Block serotonin receptors + reuptake Mainly a sedative Dizziness · nausea · orthostatic hypotension · priapism (rare) Nefazodone withdrawn - liver toxicity Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant Mirtazapine Serotonin 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Augments SSRIs · hypnotic at low doses (antihistamine) Weight gain · very sedating · ↑ cholesterol and triglycerides Activating at 30 mg and above Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) Secondary (safer): nortriptyline, desipramine · tertiary: amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine Non-selective serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake block, plus many receptors Depression · pain · insomnia · headache Anticholinergic · antihistamine · orthostatic hypotension · cardiac toxicity (the most serious) · sexual Fatal in overdose · many CYP450 interactions Tetracyclics Amoxapine · maprotiline — Amoxapine: depression with anxiety or agitation Many side effects Not first line Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) Selective and non-selective · reversible: moclobemide Block breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine Usually third line : no response or intolerance · past good response · atypical depression Insomnia · sedation · headache · dry mouth Tyramine → hypertensive crisis · serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs · not in children 2. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors Safer than TCAs (far less risk of a fatal overdose) · starting dose ≈ therapeutic dose · better adherence Only fluoxetine has pregnancy-safety evidence (upper-year notes) Drug For it Against it Paroxetine Short half-life, no active metabolite · sedating - give at night for anxiety or insomnia Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor · most anticholinergic · weight gain · constipation · discontinuation syndrome Sertraline Few interactions · less sedating GI effects, especially diarrhea · absorbed best on a full stomach Fluoxetine Longest half-life - no discontinuation syndrome , missed doses matter less · activating · least weight gain Builds up (avoid in liver disease) · many interactions · activation → anxiety, insomnia, mania Citalopram Few interactions (low CYP450) · intermediate half-life Sedating · GI · avoid with heart disease : slow heart rate, long QT, low potassium or magnesium, recent heart attack, decompensated heart failure Escitalopram Less QT prolongation than citalopram Sleep problems · taste disturbance How an SSRI works: blocking the serotonin reuptake transporter leaves more serotonin in the synaptic cleft for the postsynaptic receptor Side effects by system : sexual 25-50% (delayed orgasm, ↓ libido, ↓ arousal) · GI (nausea 11-16%, diarrhea with sertraline, constipation with paroxetine, appetite loss with fluoxetine) · central nervous system (jitteriness, insomnia with fluoxetine, sedation with paroxetine and fluvoxamine, headache, tremor, mania ) the Introduction to Psychopharmacology note gives sexual dysfunction 50-80% (sources differ - check the slides) Interactions : fluvoxamine is a strong CYP450 inhibitor · paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6, lasting up to 5 weeks after stopping · choose the drug least likely to interact (e.g. citalopram) 3. Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors Drug For it Against it Venlafaxine Almost no CYP450 interactions · short half-life, fast renal clearance Dose-dependent ↑ diastolic pressure (10-15 mmHg) · nausea · discontinuation syndrome · QT prolongation · sexual (over 30%) Desvenlafaxine Active metabolite of venlafaxine · hot flashes in menopause ↑ diastolic pressure · nausea · more discontinuation syndrome Duloxetin

Introduction to psychopharmacology ⭐ Typical antipsychotics block D2 everywhere (→ parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia); atypicals block D2 mainly in the mesolimbic pathway plus serotonin 5-HT2 (→ metabolic syndrome, weight gain). Clozapine: agranulocytosis and the most weight gain. Risperidone: high prolactin. Antipsychotic symptoms improve in order: agitation → psychosis → negative symptoms; non-adherence is the #1 cause of relapse. Lithium: tremor, hypothyroidism, diabetes insipidus; not in kidney failure; Ebstein's anomaly in pregnancy. Benzodiazepines: wide safety margin but dependence; delirium in the elderly. Stimulants: avoid with tics. Psychotropic drugs act on the central nervous system by changing one step of neurotransmission at the synapse. The lecture tours the five families - antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines and stimulants - by indication and side effect. 1. Psychotropics and their targets Psychotropic = a drug acting on the central nervous system (sleep, wakefulness, sedation, hallucinations) that can cause dependence when misused · controlled by law (Controlled Drugs and Substances Act) Neuroplasticity = the nervous system reorganizing its structure and connections; synaptic plasticity changes the strength of transmission - underlies learning, memory and recovery Drugs can act at any step: synthesis · storage · metabolism · release · reuptake · degradation · the receptor · signalling inside the cell The ten places a drug can act at a synapse, from the presynaptic action potential through synthesis, storage, release and reuptake to the postsynaptic receptor System What it does Drugs that act on it GABA (main inhibitory) Calms firing · sleep, memory, seizures GABA-A modulators: benzodiazepines (sedative), barbiturates (anaesthetic) · GABA-B agonist baclofen (muscle relaxant) · valproate, tiagabine (seizures) · too much → coma Glutamate (main excitatory) Plasticity · overactivation → excitotoxicity Targets in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Dopamine Movement (nigrostriatal), reward, prolactin, nausea D2 antagonists = antipsychotics · D2 agonists for Parkinson's and high prolactin · reuptake inhibitors for depression, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, smoking cessation Serotonin Mood, sleep, appetite, sex, anger, gut Reuptake inhibitors (selective serotonin, serotonin-norepinephrine, tricyclic) · monoamine oxidase inhibitors · receptor agonists (migraine, anxiety) · antagonists (antipsychotics, antiemetics) · mirtazapine Norepinephrine Attention, arousal, mood, anxiety Reuptake inhibitors (tricyclic, serotonin-norepinephrine) · monoamine oxidase inhibitors · stimulants for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder 2. The families at a glance Class Examples Mechanism Uses Adverse effects Atypical antipsychotics Clozapine · olanzapine · quetiapine · risperidone · aripiprazole D2 block mostly in the mesolimbic pathway + serotonin 5-HT2 block Psychosis (positive and negative symptoms) · bipolar · add-on in depression Metabolic syndrome, weight gain · high prolactin · agranulocytosis (clozapine) Typical antipsychotics — D2 block throughout the brain Positive symptoms of psychosis Extrapyramidal (parkinsonism) from nigrostriatal block · tardive dyskinesia · high prolactin Antidepressants Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) · serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs: venlafaxine, duloxetine) · bupropion · mirtazapine Raise synaptic monoamines Depression, anxiety SSRIs: sexual dysfunction (commonest) · gastrointestinal (GI) upset · serotonin syndrome Mood stabilizers Lithium · valproate · carbamazepine · lamotrigine · atypical antipsychotics Lithium: unknown Bipolar disorder (treatment and prevention) Lithium: tremor · hypothyroidism · diabetes insipidus · teratogen Benzodiazepines Lorazepam · clonazepam · diazepam Bind GABA-A → open chloride channels → ↓ firing Anxiety · insomnia · alcohol withdrawal (lorazepam) · muscle relaxation (diazepam) Sedation · amnesia · delirium in the elderly · dependence, tolerance · respiratory depression Stimulants Methylphenidate · amphetamines · modafinil ↑ monoamines (modafinil blocks norepinephrine reuptake) Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder · narcolepsy (modafinil) Tics · abuse · psychosis with amphetamines 3. Antipsychotics Antipsychotics sit on the postsynaptic D2 receptor and block dopamine released from the presynaptic terminal Indications primary psychosis : schizophrenia · bipolar disorder · severe major depression secondary psychosis : dementia · substance use movement disorders : Tourette syndrome · Huntington's disease others: severe anxiety · aggression · some personality disorders · nausea and vomiting Principles : "start low and go slow" · judge effect at 4-6 weeks · treat 3-6 months past resolution , then ↓ dose 20% every 6 months if stable improvement order: ① anxiety, agitation, insomnia → ② delusions and hallucinations → ③ negative symptoms schizophrenia duration: first episode 2-3 years · recurrent 5 years · 3 or more episodes lifelong non-adherence is the #1 cause of relapse in schizophrenia Side effect Worst with Sedation (the commonest) Low-potency drugs: clozapine, quetiapine Anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, confusion; worse in the elderly) Chlorpromazine, thioridazine Orthostatic hypotension (alpha-adrenergic block) Risperidone, clozapine, quetiapine High prolactin (menstrual change, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction) Risperidone , amisulpride, haloperidol Weight gain (40% of patients → diabetes, hypertension, high lipids) Clozapine, olanzapine · least: ziprasidone, aripiprazole QT prolongation Chlorpromazine, thioridazine, ziprasidone Sun sensitivity Chlorpromazine Pregnancy : avoid in the first trimester if possible 4. Antidepressants SSRIs : block serotonin reuptake → more serotonin in the cleft · changing one monoamine shifts the others ✔ fewer side effects than tricyclics · safe with heart conduction disea

Suicide ⭐ Mental illness is the strongest predictor, but the red flags - active threats, seeking means, hopelessness - mark imminent risk. Egosyntonic, active ideation with a detailed plan and access to means is the highest-risk picture. Previous attempts are a huge risk factor - map the chain of events. Safety contracts are not acceptable; a patient-driven safety plan is. Admit only for acute stabilization; long admissions harm the chronically suicidal. Older men have the highest rate; women self-harm more. A suicide risk assessment weighs three things against each other: risk factors (who is vulnerable over a lifetime), warning signs (what is pushing them now) and protective factors (what holds them back). The disposition - admit or manage as an outpatient - follows from acuity, severity, risk and the patient's safety net. 1. Epidemiology Not rare : about 12% report suicidal ideation at some point Over 90% of people who die by suicide had a mental health condition - but suicide also happens with no known mental illness Highest-risk group: older men · men use more lethal means and are ~3× more likely to die · women self-harm more Indigenous (First Nations) rates are much higher - about 3×, 9× in youth (upper-year notes) 9th leading cause of death overall · 2nd at ages 10-29 (upper-year notes) 2. Principles of the assessment The therapeutic relationship is step #1 : unhurried, empathic, honest listening · validate and thank them for sharing · non-judgemental · a private setting Communication : clear language · reframe a question rather than let it be dodged Collateral history supports or challenges the story · privacy and culture can limit it · involve the circle of care for continuity Document (medicolegal and continuity) in a Suicide Risk Assessment : level of risk with the rationale · history · recent changes · previous attempts · risk factors, warning signs, protective factors Culture : both the patient's and the physician's (stigma, taboo) · individualize the plan 3. Risk factors, warning signs, protective factors Risk factors Warning signs Protective factors What they do Raise lifetime risk · persistent · some unchangeable (male sex) Promote or start suicidal behaviour now - imminent risk Lower risk , build resilience · usable in the plan Examples Mental illness - the strongest predictor , especially schizophrenia , personality disorders ( borderline ), major depression · physical illness: severe chronic non-cancer pain , chronic disease ( Parkinson's disease ) · psychosocial: guilt, shame, isolation, poor supports, poor coping, big life changes "IS PATH WARM" : Ideation · Substance use · Purposelessness · Anger · Trapped · Hopelessness · Withdrawal (social, not from drugs) · Anxiety · Recklessness · Mood changes Strong relationships · belonging · self-esteem · future orientation (goals) · clinical support and willingness to use it Red flags (highest-risk warning signs) : active threats · talking about wanting to die · seeking access to means · hopelessness Protective factors lose their weight when risk is severe 4. What the patient presents with Non-suicidal self-injury : not a cry for help - it serves a purpose · explore the motivation Ideation - two axes: Passive Active Effort No effort to consider, plan or act · may be intrusive and unwanted Effort to consider, plan, move to action Egodystonic Egosyntonic Fit with the self Clashes with identity and values · distressing, unwanted Fits current ideals · not distressing - red flag, high risk Plans : get a detailed description (never assume you have enough) · access to means Previous attempts - a huge risk factor : number (include this one) · method and intent · circumstances · how they survived · response to surviving · the chain of events leading up (where to intervene) an "impulsive" attempt may be a long-held plan suddenly activated - ask Underlying themes : control (of one's fate, or of others) · avoidance (escape from pain, money, legal problems, illness) · unbearable distress (abandonment, bereavement, chronic pain) 5. Disposition and management Tool Who drives it When Examples or verdict Coping plan Patient Everyday stress - prevents escalation to crisis Call a named person · write thoughts down · breathing · distraction Safety plan Patient In a crisis · active steps, more effort e.g. crisis centre, a friend Safety contract ("no-suicide agreement") Clinician — Not acceptable , especially for acute ideation in the emergency department · experts only, with a strong relationship Treating the underlying cause is the most important step (psychiatric or not) - it also prevents future risk Chronic ideation : hospital only for acute stabilization · long admissions build reliance on external control · explore the motives behind any self-harm 6. Neurobiology Heritable apart from mental illness : family studies · monozygotic > dizygotic twin concordance · adoptees resemble biological, not adoptive, relatives · no single "suicide gene" Epigenetics : life experience (trauma) alters gene expression (DNA methylation, histone modification, microRNA) Stress axis : hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity - the basis of the stress-diathesis model Serotonin : ↓ serotonin metabolite (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) in cerebrospinal fluid · imaging: ↑ serotonin receptor expression but ↓ binding in the prefrontal cortex · ↓ serotonin transporter binding Also: norepinephrine dysfunction · low serum cholesterol (may act through serotonin) Stress-diathesis model: the disorder appears once stress exceeds the threshold set by predisposition

Bipolar disorders ⭐ Bipolar I needs only one manic episode (≥ 1 week, or any length if hospitalized, or with psychosis); bipolar II needs hypomania (≥ 4 days, no psychosis, no admission) plus a major depression. Cyclothymia: 2 years of subthreshold highs and lows, never well over 2 months. Never an antidepressant alone in bipolar I depression - stop antidepressants and stimulants in mania. Lithium: kidneys, thyroid, parathyroid, Ebstein's. Lamotrigine: rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, slow titration. Valproate: neural tube defects. Clozapine and carbamazepine: agranulocytosis. Major depression is the commonest misdiagnosis. The bipolar disorders are sorted by how high the mood goes: full mania (bipolar I), hypomania with major depression (bipolar II), or neither reaching threshold for 2 years (cyclothymia). Treatment rests on mood stabilizers - and never on an antidepressant alone. 1. Epidemiology and course Lifetime prevalence (Canada): bipolar I disorder 0.87% · bipolar II disorder 0.67% (a 9-country study gives 0.6% and 0.4%) Onset : average 25 years , in three groups - early ~17 (~42%) · middle ~24 (~25%) · late ~32 (~34%) · ⅓ to ⅔ have their first episode in childhood or adolescence earlier onset → longer delay to treatment, more depression, anxiety and substance use Sex : women - more bipolar II, rapid cycling , seasonal pattern, longer depressions, episodes clustered in the reproductive years · men - more bipolar I, more substance use, more completed suicide Progressive course : each episode → ↑ recurrence, ↑ length and severity of later episodes, ↓ threshold for the next, ↑ dementia risk Morbidity : euthymic ~half the time · ill time is mostly depression (~70% in bipolar I, ~82% in bipolar II) Comorbidity is the rule : substance use 33-45% · anxiety 24-56% · personality disorders ~42% · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) 10-20% · treat the bipolar disorder first , then the comorbidity once mood is stable Stigma (public and self-stigma) delays and erodes treatment 2. The episodes Manic episode A: abnormally, persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood + increased energy or activity, most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 1 week (any duration if hospitalized) B: 3 or more (4 if the mood is only irritable) - mnemonic DIGFAST : Distractibility · Indiscretion (spending, sex, investments) · Grandiosity · Flight of ideas or racing thoughts · Activity ↑ or agitation · Sleep need ↓ (rested after 3 hours) · Talkative, pressured speech C: marked impairment, or hospitalization, or psychotic features D : not a substance or medical condition Hypomanic episode : the same symptoms for at least 4 days · an unequivocal change observable by others · not severe enough for marked impairment or hospitalization · psychosis makes it mania by definition An episode that starts on an antidepressant (or ECT) but persists beyond the drug's effect counts → bipolar diagnosis Mania Hypomania Duration ≥ 1 week (or any if admitted) ≥ 4 days Impairment Marked A change in function, but not marked Hospitalization May need it Never Psychosis May have it Never 3. Telling the bipolar disorders apart Bipolar I Bipolar II Cyclothymia Needs ≥ 1 manic episode ≥ 1 hypomanic + ≥ 1 major depressive episode Many hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms , neither reaching an episode Depression required? No (common, though) Yes Subthreshold only Duration rule Episode-based Episode-based ≥ 2 years (1 in youth) · symptomatic ≥ half the time · never well > 2 months Excludes — Any mania ever · psychosis · hospitalization Any full episode ever Specifiers include rapid cycling (≥ 4 episodes in 12 months) , mixed features, psychotic features, peripartum onset, seasonal pattern Mood over time in unipolar depression, bipolar I, bipolar II and cyclothymia 4. Diagnosis and differential Diagnosis often takes up to 10 years · major depressive disorder is the most frequent misdiagnosis (patients present depressed and don't recall or recognise hypomania) Psychotic disorders are the first diagnosis in 30% - psychosis without mood symptoms points there Others: borderline (true euphoria and long well intervals are extremely rare) · narcissistic (grandiosity without mood change) · antisocial · substance or medication (stimulants, steroids, L-dopa, antidepressants) · medical (brain injury, frontal tumours, multiple sclerosis, stroke, Cushing's, hyperthyroidism) Children : mania overlaps with ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) - in mania the change is episodic and mood-related , with ↓ need for sleep and no daytime sleepiness · older adults : depressive and cognitive symptoms dominate Workup : family history · collateral · prospective mood charting · Mood Disorders Questionnaire screens, does not diagnose · suicide risk assessment at every visit 5. Treatment Psychosocial (adjunct) : psychoeducation - the only first-line psychosocial treatment in maintenance (spot prodromes, stress, adherence, stigma) · cognitive behavioural therapy and family-focused therapy for acute depression and relapse prevention · interpersonal and social rhythm therapy for relapse prevention (little acute evidence) Choosing a drug : prior response · safety and tolerability · predominant polarity · prognostic features · discuss with patient and supports Antidepressants : second-line adjuncts only · avoid with past antidepressant-induced mania, mixed features or recent rapid cycling · never monotherapy in bipolar I depression the In-Class note names only quetiapine, cariprazine and lurasidone as approved for bipolar depression, while the guideline figure lists lithium and lamotrigine first line and cariprazine second (sources differ - check the slides) Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) : second line · refractory illness or need for speed (imminent suicide, catatonia, psychotic depression, medical instability) Light therapy : helps acute bipolar depression · does not cause switching · no evidence for remission Supplements : omega-3, N-ace
10 Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders

Psychotherapies in mood and anxiety disorders ⭐ CBT targets thoughts and behaviour with structured sessions and homework; IPT targets current relationships through one of four focus areas and never addresses transference; psychodynamic therapy interprets transference and the unconscious; DBT was built for borderline personality disorder. Supportive therapy bolsters defences; psychodynamic therapy challenges them. CBT and IPT are first line for major depression. Psychotherapy matches medication for many disorders and its effects last longer. Suitability needs motivation, psychological mindedness and ego strength - not psychosis. Each evidence-based therapy is defined by what it targets - the unconscious past (psychodynamic), thoughts and behaviours (CBT), current relationships (IPT) or emotional dysregulation (DBT) - and that target decides which patient it suits. Most work about as well as medication, and their effects last longer. 1. What psychotherapy is, and who it suits Treatment of mental illness with psychological interventions - usually talking, plus the therapeutic relationship and tailored strategies Evidence-based : psychodynamic · cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) · interpersonal therapy (IPT) · dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) · family · group effectiveness similar to medication, sometimes better (DBT beats any drug for borderline personality disorder) · effects outlast medication Common factors behind much of the benefit: accurate empathy · unconditional positive regard · genuineness · a strong working relationship · professionalism · goal-directed problem-solving Suitable patients : significant suffering · strong motivation · psychological mindedness (thinks abstractly about problems, capable of insight into their own role) · ego strength (intact reality testing - not psychotic, frustration tolerance, impulse control) · can form relationships (keeps a job, has relationships outside therapy) 2. The therapies compared Psychodynamic Supportive CBT IPT DBT Core idea The unconscious shapes patterns (psychic determinism) · make the unconscious conscious Bolster defences to help the person function Schemas → automatic thoughts → cognitive distortions drive feelings and behaviour Symptoms are a response to current relationship problems · medical "sick role" Emotional dysregulation + an invalidating environment → extreme behaviours (self-harm) to cope Focus Past (childhood) → present Present situation Present thoughts and behaviour Present relationships Behaviour, emotion regulation, acceptance Structure Little · free association · brief or open-ended Little · conversational Highly structured sessions + homework Structured · time-limited · treatment contract Multimodal · patient agreement · stages Transference Central - interpreted Not challenged Little emphasis Deliberately not addressed — Key tools Interpretation · confrontation · clarification · transference · defences · working through Praise · reassurance · reframing · advice · anticipatory guidance Socratic questioning · thought records · behavioural activation · behavioural experiments Interpersonal inventory · one of 4 focus areas Skills groups · chain analysis · validation · dialectics · phone coaching Indications (from the sources) Depression · personality disorders Not (yet) suitable for other therapy · adjustment disorder Major depression (first line) · anxiety (exposure) · bipolar depression and relapse Developed for depression - first line · peripartum depression (role change) Borderline personality disorder · suicidal behaviour 3. Psychodynamic (insight-oriented) therapy Freud's structure : id (unconscious drives) · superego (conscience, internalized rules) · ego (conscious self, balances reality against both) Process : free association → the therapist links past and present and finds recurring patterns · goal: change dysfunctional interpersonal patterns · the relationship is a "corrective emotional experience" techniques: observation (outside awareness) · confrontation (aware but avoided) · clarification · encouragement to elaborate · empathic validation · psychoeducation · advice and praise Transference : the patient casts the neutral ("blank screen") therapist in a role from their past · countertransference : the clinician's own reaction to the patient Object relations : past relationships re-enacted in the present Defence mechanisms reduce signal anxiety, can become pathological: displacement (emotion moved to another object) · reaction formation (into its opposite) · isolation of affect (idea split from feeling) · projection (own impulses attributed to others) Working through : repeated observing, clarifying, confronting and interpreting until the patient takes responsibility for their patterns Supportive therapy sits at the supportive end of this continuum: it bolsters defences where psychodynamic therapy challenges them 4. Cognitive behavioural therapy Beck, originally for major depression · thoughts, emotions and behaviours feed each other The CBT cycle: thoughts create feelings, feelings create behaviour, behaviour reinforces thoughts Session structure : greet → symptom check → set agenda → review homework → work on the agenda → teach the cognitive model → set new homework → summarize and get feedback Socratic questioning ("what is the evidence?") challenges cognitive distortions (cognitive restructuring): all-or-nothing · selective abstraction · personalization · magnification · minimization · arbitrary inference · overgeneralization Downward arrow questioning reaches the core belief ("she doesn't like me" → "no one likes me" → "I am a loser") Thought record : situation · thought · emotion · behaviour Behavioural activation : act before you feel better · activity scheduling rated for accomplishment and pleasure Behavioural experiments : test a belief · in anxiety, exposure Beck's cognitive triad: negative views of the self, the world and the future 5.
