11 Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses

Depression and anxiety in medical illness ⭐ Hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt, anhedonia and suicidal ideation are not normal in medical illness - they point to depression. Stroke carries the highest depression rate (22-50%). Adjustment disorder → supportive therapy; major depression → antidepressants; hypoactive delirium → treat the cause. Start low, go slow, but reach a therapeutic dose. Cardiac: sertraline first line; tricyclics and MAOIs contraindicated. Diabetes: SSRIs or SNRIs; tricyclics worsen glucose control. Depression in the medically ill is common, treatable, and missed because of myths - the discriminating question is whether the psychological symptoms (hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt, anhedonia, suicidal thoughts) are present, because illness alone does not cause them. Neither source covers anxiety in medical illness separately (check the slides). 1. Epidemiology Setting or disease Depression prevalence Outpatients 2-15% Inpatients 12-30% Diabetes 9-27% Stroke 22-50% - the highest Cancer 18-39% Myocardial infarction 15-19% Rheumatoid arthritis ~12-13% Parkinson's disease 10-37% Rates rise with the type, number and acuity of illnesses · in older patients, 3 comorbid illnesses = 3× suicide risk, 5 = 5× Bidirectional : major depression is a risk factor for diabetes , heart disease, stroke , hypertension , obesity , cancer and dementia Major depression raises mortality 60-80% , with or without chronic illness 2. Why it happens Disease factors : neurotransmitter changes · chronic pain · anxiety about recovery Psychosocial : grief for the pre-illness self · disability · trauma · isolation · money, housing, food Chronic stress : poor nutrition, low income, substance use · a sustained stress response → hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity → immune activation (pro-inflammatory cytokines) , sympathetic activation, corticotropin-releasing factor pathways Cytokine-induced "sickness behaviour" mimics depression : weakness · poor concentration · malaise · hypersomnia · anorexia · social withdrawal · anhedonia · heightened pain The stress response: corticotropin-releasing factor, adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol, and catecholamines, with their effects on behaviour and the body 3. Diagnosis Under-diagnosed and under-treated because of four myths: "anyone sick will be depressed" - still a minority , and depressed patients do worse and have far higher suicide rates "depression in the sick is untreatable" · " the sick can't tolerate antidepressants " - trials show efficacy and tolerability " you can't tell depression from the illness " - DSM criteria still work if you weigh psychological symptoms over neurovegetative ones · screening tools are validated (Beck, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Patient Health Questionnaire) Screen everyone : " Do you feel depressed? " Red-flag symptoms - not normal in medical illness : hopelessness · worthlessness · guilt · anhedonia · suicidal ideation Risk factors : family or personal psychiatric history · poorly controlled pain · more comorbidity and functional impairment Inclusive approach, low threshold · when in doubt, consultation-liaison psychiatry (psychiatric care for medical inpatients) Adjustment disorder Major depression Hypoactive delirium What it is "Situational depression" - excessive reaction to an identifiable stressor, within 3 months Persistent low mood and/or anhedonia, vegetative symptoms, possible suicidality Acute confusion with global inattention , slowed, lethargic Duration — At least 2 weeks Acute, fluctuating Treatment Supportive psychotherapy - responds poorly to medication Antidepressants Treat the underlying cause 4. Treatment principles "Under-treated depression is untreated depression" : start low and go slow, but reach a therapeutic dose - stop only for intolerable side effects Multidisciplinary, coordinate between specialists, include caregivers Options (adapt, ask if unsure): antidepressants · psychotherapy · electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) · transcranial magnetic stimulation · psychiatric admission Follow-up is paramount - side effects drive non-adherence 5. Cardiac disease Prevalence: cardiovascular disease ~15% · bypass surgery 20% · unstable angina 15% · catheterization 17-23% · post-myocardial infarction 15-23% · heart failure 14-20% Depression predicts mortality after myocardial infarction and in heart failure , and is an independent risk factor for coronary artery disease (relative risk 1.5-2, similar to smoking) Shared mechanisms : ↑ platelet reactivity · ↓ heart rate variability · ↑ inflammation (C-reactive protein) · HPA hyperactivity · immune activation · norepinephrine dysregulation First line Caution Contraindicated Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) - sertraline safe and effective after myocardial infarction or unstable angina (SADHART trial) · may normalize platelets and heart rate variability Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) MAOIs and tricyclics (QT prolongation, ↑ death) Educate on treating to remission · watch drug interactions · psychotherapy and ECT as indicated 6. Diabetes Bidirectional : diabetes → 3× risk of depression · high-risk depressed patients → ~2.5× risk of diabetes Disability is additive : diabetes 2.42 · depression 3.0 · both 7.15 (upper-year notes) Shared: HPA changes · inflammation · abnormal glucose metabolism Treatment : SSRIs or SNRIs first line (safe, effective) · tricyclics help neuropathic pain but worsen glycaemic control · other options may add weight and insulin resistance Remission is sustained in only ~10% over 5 years → lifelong follow-up · treating depression improves glycaemic control, pain and HbA1c
12 Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages

Mood disorders and reproductive life stages ⭐ Blues are common, mild and gone within weeks; peripartum depression starts in pregnancy or within 4 weeks of delivery; postpartum psychosis is a rapid-onset emergency whose strongest risk factor is bipolar disorder. PMDD needs 5 symptoms, at least one mood symptom, in the luteal phase, confirmed over 2 cycles - SSRIs or drospirenone pills; the progestin-only pill fails. Valproate and carbamazepine are avoided in pregnancy; lamotrigine is safe in pregnancy but contraindicated in breastfeeding. Sertraline is preferred when breastfeeding. Perimenopausal depression risk is 2-5× higher, driven by the transition, not age. Female vulnerability to mood disorders rises and falls with the reproductive hormones - puberty, the luteal phase, pregnancy and the postpartum, and perimenopause are each a window of risk. For each window: what it looks like, how to tell it from its look-alikes, and how to treat it safely for mother and baby. 1. Puberty: why depression is twice as common in females Lifetime major depression 2× higher in females across countries · the gap opens at puberty (pubertal stage, not age) and lasts through the reproductive years · equal in childhood, slightly higher in men in later life Explanations, likely combined: research artifact (women report more) - but the childhood and late-life ratios argue against it psychosocial : inequality, discrimination, objectification, victimization · women internalize, men externalize biological : estrogen and progesterone · episodes cluster at times of greatest hormone fluctuation · ↑ testosterone at puberty Risk factors around menarche : stressful events, abuse, violence, poor body image · family psychiatric history, prior anxiety, pubertal timing, illness · poor family relationships, low support, poor school connection 2. Menstruation: PMS vs PMDD Both: symptoms in the luteal phase , resolving within a few days of menses Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) How common ~30% 1-2% in the lecture note, 3-8% in the PMDD note (sources differ - check the slides) Mood symptoms May occur, not required Prominent psychiatric symptoms Function Less severe Clinically significant impairment · ↑ suicidality Mechanism — ↑ sensitivity to normal hormone changes PMDD criteria : 5 or more symptoms in the week before menses in most cycles, improving within days of onset and minimal the week after · at least 1 mood symptom (lability, irritability or anger, depressed mood or hopelessness, anxiety) · confirmed by prospective daily ratings over 2 cycles · not just a flare of another disorder Treatment : selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) - continuous or luteal-phase only · drospirenone combined oral contraceptives (clot risk; progestin-only pill does not work ) · cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT); dialectical behaviour therapy for suicidal behaviour · second line: gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues with hormone add-back · refractory: hysterectomy with both ovaries removed 3. Pregnancy and the postpartum Estrogen and progesterone affect monoamine metabolism and serotonin receptors · stressors pile up from pregnancy to 1 year postpartum Postpartum blues Peripartum depression Postpartum psychosis How common Up to 85% ~15% 1-2 per 1000 Onset A few days after birth Pregnancy or within 4 weeks of delivery (~half before delivery) Within 4-8 weeks · rapid Picture Mild, self-limited Depressive episode: crying, poor bonding, guilt as a mother, anxiety, egosyntonic thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby Confusion, disorganization, delusions about the baby , hallucinations · manic ~35%, depressive ~40% Key risk — Past depression (especially peripartum) , PMDD, family history, partner violence, poor support Bipolar disorder - the strongest (20-30% of women with it) · first pregnancy · prior episode Management Supportive care only Psychotherapy (supportive, CBT, interpersonal therapy (IPT)) · SSRIs first line - sertraline preferred in breastfeeding , avoid paroxetine · electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) relatively safe Psychiatric emergency - admit · benzodiazepine → antipsychotic → lithium (0.8-1.2 mmol/L) · lithium 9 months · prophylaxis next pregnancy Neonatal adaptation syndrome after in-utero SSRIs (~30%, 3-5 days) - tapering before delivery does not prevent it but raises the risk of depression Screen : Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (10 items, under 5 minutes) · "can you sleep when the baby sleeps? are you eating? any scary thoughts about you or the baby?" Untreated depression harms both : mother - poor self-care, substance use, preeclampsia, suicide (20% of maternal deaths in the first postpartum year) · infant - preterm birth, low birth weight , smaller head, lower Apgar, behavioural, language and attachment problems 4. Bipolar disorder in pregnancy and breastfeeding Relapse 70-85% without maintenance, 24-30% even with it · abrupt stopping (under 2 weeks) → 50-70% relapse Pre-conception counselling for every woman of childbearing age with bipolar disorder Clues: can't keep to bed rest · risk-taking · preoccupied with non-baby activities · postpartum depression preceded by agitation Drug Pregnancy Breastfeeding Valproate Avoid - up to 11% major defects · neural tube defects 5-6% , craniofacial, cleft lip or palate, limb, microcephaly Relatively safe Carbamazepine Avoid - up to 6% major defects, fewer neural tube defects than valproate Relatively safe Lithium High-risk pregnancy - Ebstein's anomaly (1 in 1000) Monitor levels in milk and infant Lamotrigine Safe - baseline 2-3% risk Contraindicated - Stevens-Johnson syndrome in the infant Atypical antipsychotics No evidence of ↑ risk (limited studies) Little evidence either way Rules : monotherapy at the lowest dose · folic acid, up to 4 mg a day on valproate or carbamazepine · options: switch to a lower-risk drug before conception, continue with known risks, or taper (e.g. through the first 12 weeks) Screen : alpha-fetop

In-class: mood disorders ⭐ Never an antidepressant in bipolar disorder - use quetiapine, cariprazine or lurasidone for bipolar depression. Bupropion: no serotonin, so no sexual dysfunction and good for smoking. Mirtazapine: appetite and weight gain. Fluoxetine: longest half-life, least weight gain. Aripiprazole or brexpiprazole are the first-line add-ons in major depression. A case session pulling the week together: which antidepressant for which patient, what is first line in major depression, and why bipolar depression is treated differently. Criteria and full treatment are in 05 - Depressive Disorders , 06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants and 09 - Bipolar Disorders . 1. Antidepressants to know Drug Class The fact that picks it sertraline (Zoloft) Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) Must know escitalopram (Lexapro) SSRI Must know paroxetine (Paxil) SSRI — fluoxetine SSRI Least weight gain · longest half-life (forgiving of missed doses) venlafaxine (Effexor) Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) Must know · SNRIs stronger than SSRIs - try one if an SSRI fails mirtazapine Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant Weight gain, appetite - useful in cancer with depression bupropion Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor No serotonin → smoking cessation , little weight gain, little sexual dysfunction trazodone — Insomnia (adjunct for sleep) Tricyclics · MAOIs Older classes Rarely used, more side effects · MAOIs: avoid tyramine (aged cheese) , best for atypical depression SSRI sexual dysfunction is loss of desire (serotonin) - sildenafil won't fix it → switch to bupropion quetiapine changes target with dose : ~25-50 mg sleep (histamine) · 150-300 mg depression · 600 mg or more psychosis (dopamine) lamotrigine → remember Stevens-Johnson syndrome 2. First line in major depression Lifestyle : supervised exercise · light therapy Psychotherapy : cognitive behavioural therapy · interpersonal therapy · behavioral activation Medication : SSRIs · SNRIs · norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitors · noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants Adjunct : second-generation antipsychotics aripiprazole or brexpiprazole (dopamine and serotonin) - not first-generation (dopamine only) Episode symptoms: SIGECAPS (depression) · DIGFAST (mania) 3. Bipolar depression is different No antidepressants in bipolar disorder - they can induce mania The session names 3 approved drugs for bipolar depression: quetiapine , cariprazine , lurasidone - the guideline figure in 09 - Bipolar Disorders also lists lithium and lamotrigine first line (sources differ - check the slides)

Anxiety disorders ⭐ The anxiety disorders differ by the focus of the fear: many things (GAD), the attacks themselves (panic), being judged (social anxiety), escape (agoraphobia), one object (phobia). Panic disorder needs 2+ unexpected attacks plus 1 month of worry or avoidance. GAD needs 6 months of uncontrollable worry plus 3 of 6 symptoms. Agoraphobia = 2 of 5 situations. Blood-injection-injury phobia drops the blood pressure. Rule out thyroid disease, low blood sugar, arrhythmia and caffeine before calling it panic. The anxiety disorders are told apart by one question: what is the fear about? Panic, generalized anxiety and social anxiety are the three the lecture asks you to compare. 1. Fear vs anxiety Fear = an intense reaction to an immediate threat - it saves your life now Anxiety = a negative emotion about the possibility of a future threat - it saves your life later · drives hypervigilance, worry and avoidance Risk factors family history · personal history of anxiety, mood disorders or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) childhood trauma · female sex · chronic medical illness (asthma, diabetes, obesity, heart disease) behavioural inhibition (a temperament reluctant to approach new things) 7 disorders in the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 5th edition), remembered as GPS-MAPS : G eneralized · P anic · S ocial · selective M utism · A goraphobia · specific P hobia · S eparation anxiety the first three matter most · selective mutism and separation anxiety are lower yield 2. The five to compare Disorder Core fear Key criteria Duration rule First-line treatment Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) Many everyday things (work, health, money, relationships) Excessive, uncontrollable worry most days + 3 of 6 : restless · tired · poor concentration · irritable · muscle tension · poor sleep (only 1 needed in children) 6+ months Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) · selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI): escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine · also venlafaxine, pregabalin, buspirone Panic disorder The panic attacks themselves and their consequences 2+ unexpected (untriggered) panic attacks + worry about more attacks or a change in behaviour to avoid them Worry or behaviour change for 1+ month after an attack CBT with interoceptive exposure · SSRI (also venlafaxine) Agoraphobia Being somewhere escape or help is hard if panic starts Fear of 2 of 5 : public transport · open spaces · enclosed spaces · crowds or lines · being outside home alone 6+ months As for panic disorder (often occur together) Social anxiety disorder Being judged negatively by others Fear of scrutiny in social or performance situations (talking, eating in front of others, speeches) · specifier: performance only 6+ months CBT with exposure · SSRI (also fluvoxamine, venlafaxine, pregabalin) Specific phobia One object or situation Fear out of proportion, almost always triggered, avoided · types: animal · natural environment · blood-injection-injury · situational 6+ months Exposure therapy · short-term benzodiazepine to get through an exposure The 6-month rule covers every one of them except panic disorder, where it is 1 month of worry after an attack Blood-injection-injury phobia is the odd one out: blood pressure and heart rate drop (vasovagal response, fainting) instead of rising A fear is only a phobia when it impairs function 3. Panic attacks and panic disorder Panic attack = an abrupt surge of fear that peaks within minutes , with 4 or more of 13 symptoms body: palpitations · sweating · trembling · shortness of breath · choking · chest pain · nausea · dizziness · chills or hot flashes · numbness or tingling mind: derealization or depersonalization · fear of losing control · fear of dying A panic attack is a symptom that can occur in any anxiety disorder; panic disorder needs attacks that come out of the blue Do not just ask "do you have panic attacks?" - ask for a sudden rush of fear with no obvious cause, and have them describe it Rule out medical and substance causes endocrine: hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism · low blood sugar · pheochromocytoma heart and lungs: arrhythmia · coronary disease · heart failure · asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease other: anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency · migraine, brain tumour · caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulants bloodwork: complete blood count · glucose · electrolytes · liver enzymes · thyroid-stimulating hormone · creatinine · B12 · urinalysis Epidemiology : 5% lifetime · 30-50% also have agoraphobia · more common in women · starts in late adolescence · often with depression · suicide risk about 20 times the general population 4. Telling them apart Panic vs social anxiety : panic fears the bodily symptoms · social anxiety fears other people's judgement (panic attacks may occur, but only in social situations) GAD vs depression : many symptoms overlap and they often occur together · separate them by the timeline and prominent low mood in depression Social anxiety vs avoidant personality disorder : avoidant personality is broader, with lower self-esteem · social anxiety is tied to particular situations Social anxiety vs paranoid personality : paranoid people believe others are critical · socially anxious people worry they might be Claustrophobia vs agoraphobia : claustrophobia fears being enclosed · agoraphobia fears panic symptoms with no escape

Obsessive-compulsive disorder ⭐ First-line OCD treatment is exposure and response prevention plus an SSRI at a higher-than-depression dose for 8-12 weeks; after 2 failed SSRIs, switch to clomipramine. Diagnosis needs more than 1 hour a day or real distress. OCD is ego-dystonic; obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is ego-syntonic. Insight is graded good, poor or absent; absent insight (4%) predicts a worse course and may need an antipsychotic add-on. GAD worries are about real-life events; obsessions are intrusive and themed. An obsession raises anxiety; a compulsion brings it down for a moment and so keeps the cycle going. Most people have some intrusive thoughts and rituals - OCD is the version that eats time and causes distress. 1. Obsessions and compulsions Obsession = a recurrent, persistent thought, urge or image that feels intrusive and unwanted (ego-dystonic) and causes marked anxiety the person tries to ignore, suppress or neutralize it common themes: contamination · symmetry · aggression or harm · somatic · religious · sexual Compulsion = a repetitive behaviour (washing, ordering, checking) or mental act (praying, counting, repeating words) done in response to an obsession or by rigid rules aims to prevent harm or reach a "just right" feeling not realistically connected to what it is meant to prevent, or clearly excessive Hallmarks: excessive doubt and intolerance of uncertainty 96% have both obsessions and compulsions Normal is common: about 80% of people have obsessions and 55% have compulsions · in OCD the thoughts carry more weight, are harder to dismiss, and compulsions become the learned way to relieve them 2. Diagnosis Criteria obsessions, compulsions or both time-consuming (more than 1 hour a day) or causing clinically significant distress or impairment not due to a substance or medical condition · not better explained by another mental disorder Insight specifier good or fair : knows the beliefs are definitely or probably untrue poor : thinks they are probably true absent or delusional : completely convinced ( 4% , worse outcome) Tic-related specifier: current or past tic disorder (30% have one, mostly men with childhood onset) Screening questions : unpleasant thoughts you cannot get rid of? · worry you might act on an impulse and harm someone? · counting, washing or checking over and over? Severity scale: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale 3. Epidemiology and course 2-3% lifetime · 60% women (pregnancy and postpartum raise the risk) · one-third severe Median onset 19 years · 21% start in childhood, more often boys 90% have another mental disorder (anxiety 76%, mood disorders) Core symptoms look the same across cultures Course: waxing and waning (better) or constant (worse) Worse prognosis : early onset · giving in to compulsions · bizarre compulsions · hospitalization · comorbid depression · poor insight or delusions · schizotypal personality 4. Telling OCD apart Condition How it differs from OCD Generalized anxiety disorder Worries about real everyday events , felt as reasonable (ego-syntonic), almost always thoughts, not resisted as hard · obsessions are intrusive, on specific themes, and can be images Delusional disorder Beliefs always of delusional intensity and ego-syntonic · OCD insight is often intact at times, and antipsychotics can worsen OCD Body dysmorphic disorder Focus is only on appearance , with shame and low self-esteem Hoarding disorder Driven by acquiring and distress at discarding, not by an obsession · OCD hoarding is unwanted Illness anxiety disorder Worry is only about illness , from misreading body sensations Impulse-control disorders Giving in to the urge is pleasurable · OCD compulsions only relieve anxiety Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder Ego-syntonic, no insight , little distress (perfectionism, rigidity, trouble discarding, tight spending) · only 25% of people with OCD also have it 5. Treatment Psychotherapy: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) exposure to the cue that triggers the obsession response prevention : resist the compulsion so the anxiety fades on its own (habituation) cognitive work on: thought-action fusion ("thinking it makes it more likely") · overvaluing thoughts · intolerance of uncertainty · emotional reasoning · inflated responsibility Medication first line: SSRIs - paroxetine, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram doses are higher than for depression · a fair trial is 8-12 weeks continue 6 months to 2 years after response; some need it for life Refractory = 3 failed SSRIs + failed add-on + failed CBT combined with medication Outcomes: 20-30% improve a lot · 40-50% moderately · 20-40% little or not at all
03 Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD

Management of anxiety disorders and OCD ⭐ First line for every anxiety disorder, OCD and PTSD is CBT plus an SSRI - escitalopram, sertraline or paroxetine ("ESP"). Interoceptive exposure is the one for panic disorder; imaginal exposure is the one for PTSD. Exposure must be planned, predictable, prolonged, paced and practised - and the quick fix (escape) undoes it. Benzodiazepines are short-term only: to get through a phobia exposure, or SSRI restlessness. Pregabalin when SSRIs are contraindicated, as in bipolar disorder. Clomipramine is OCD-only. Two first-line treatments cover every anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): an SSRI and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) built around exposure. 1. Medications First line almost across the board - "ESP" : escitalopram · sertraline · paroxetine (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, SSRIs) Which drug for which disorder: Drug Dose (mg/day) Generalized anxiety Social anxiety Panic / agoraphobia OCD PTSD Escitalopram 10-20 ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ — Sertraline 50-200 ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Paroxetine 20-60 ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Fluoxetine 20-80 — — ✔ ✔ ✔ Fluvoxamine 100-300 — ✔ ✔ ✔ — Citalopram 20-40 — — ✔ ✔ — Venlafaxine 75-300 ✔ ✔ ✔ — ✔ Pregabalin 75-300 twice daily ✔ ✔ — — — Buspirone — ✔ — — — — Clomipramine 100-200 — — — ✔ — Benzodiazepines : the only listed use is specific phobia , short term, to get through an exposure Pregabalin (not an SSRI): for when SSRIs are contraindicated (e.g. bipolar disorder ) or several SSRI trials have failed · also helps pain Clomipramine is for OCD only, after 2 SSRIs fail 2. SSRI side effects - "SSRIS" Side effect What helps (upper-year notes) S exual dysfunction Bupropion · sildenafil (Viagra) · buspirone S leep disturbance Trazodone R estlessness A short course of a benzodiazepine I ndigestion Mirtazapine S erotonin syndrome — (recognize it) 3. Cognitive behavioural therapy CBT is first line for every anxiety disorder, OCD and PTSD Changes both thoughts and behaviours - the patient learns to think and act differently from what the anxiety demands Thinking errors it targets: probability overestimation · catastrophizing · intolerance of uncertainty 4. Exposure therapy Face the feared thing until the anxiety falls on its own · each repeat starts lower and falls faster Do not take the "quick fix" (escaping, distraction, safety behaviours, compulsions) - it relieves anxiety now and keeps it going The 5 P's : planned · predictable and structured · prolonged (until anxiety drops naturally) · paced (gradual) · practised often and close together Fear peaks and falls during one exposure; after many exposures the peak is small and brief - escaping early (the quick fix) stops that from happening Type What it is Best for Example In vivo (situational) A real-life cue All of them Social anxiety: eat at a window seat · panic: crowded subway · OCD: touch an elevator button · phobia: drive over a bridge Interoceptive Bring on the body sensation that is feared Panic disorder Racing heart: spin, run on the spot · breathlessness: breathe through a straw · derealization: stare in a mirror · heat: hot drink, stuffy car Imaginal The situation in imagination only PTSD · fears you cannot recreate (flying) Retelling the trauma Virtual Computer simulation Specific phobia · social anxiety Thunderstorms, flying Combined interoceptive + in vivo Situation plus the feared sensations - faces the whole fear Panic, agoraphobia, social anxiety, phobias Hyperventilate in a car · wear a sweater to give a talk · hold your breath in an elevator Social anxiety : face the feared outcome , not just the situation - a talk that goes well teaches less than one that goes wrong shake on purpose during a speech · mispronounce a word · pause too long · spill food in a restaurant · ask directions to an obvious place

Post-traumatic stress disorder ⭐ PTSD needs a criterion-A trauma, then intrusion (1+), avoidance (1+), negative mood and thinking (2+) and arousal (2+) for more than 1 month; 3 days to 1 month is acute stress disorder. Delayed expression = criteria not met until 6+ months after. First-line drugs: fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine; prazosin for nightmares. Debriefing does not prevent PTSD. Imaginal exposure is the exposure type for PTSD. PTSD = a real trauma, then four symptom clusters - intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and thinking, and arousal - lasting more than a month. The clock (days vs a month vs 6 months) separates it from its neighbours. 1. The trauma (criterion A) Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence , in one or more ways: directly experiencing it witnessing it happen to others, in person learning it happened to a close family member or friend (must be violent or accidental) repeated or extreme exposure to its details (first responders, police) - not through media unless it is work 2. The four symptom clusters Cluster Need Examples Intrusion 1+ Intrusive memories · nightmares · flashbacks (dissociative reactions) · distress at reminders · body reactions to reminders (palpitations, dizziness) Avoidance 1+ Avoids memories, thoughts or feelings about it · avoids external reminders (people, places, conversations) Negative thinking and mood 2+ Cannot recall key parts (dissociative amnesia) · negative beliefs about self, others, the world · distorted blame of self or others · persistent fear, anger, guilt or shame · lost interest · detachment · cannot feel positive emotions Arousal and reactivity 2+ Irritability, angry outbursts · reckless or self-destructive behaviour · hypervigilance · exaggerated startle · poor concentration · poor sleep All must start or worsen after the event, last more than 1 month , cause distress or impairment, and not be due to a substance or medical condition Specifiers with dissociative symptoms : depersonalization (detached from your body) or derealization (things feel unreal) with delayed expression : full criteria not met until 6+ months after the event 3. Timing and the differential Condition How it differs from PTSD Adjustment disorder Stressor not severe enough, or not all PTSD criteria met Acute stress disorder Symptoms only 3 days to 1 month after the trauma Obsessive-compulsive disorder Intrusive thoughts not tied to a trauma Panic disorder Arousal and dissociation not tied to a trauma Generalized anxiety disorder Worry about a perceived future threat , not a past event Major depression Overlaps, but no intrusion or avoidance 4. Who gets it 76% of Canadians have had a traumatic event · 9.2% lifetime PTSD · more common in women Starts at any age, usually within 3 months · often follows acute stress disorder · lasts 3 months to years · flares with reminders, new trauma or failing health Suicide risk 2-3 times the general population 80% more likely to have another mental disorder : depression · anxiety · substance use · borderline personality disorder Risk factors before: prior mental illness · low income, family problems · female, younger age during: severity of the event · perceived threat · dissociation that persists after: negative coping · acute stress disorder · repeated reminders · further bad life events 5. Treatment Psychotherapy - aims at fear, loss and moral injury eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR): bilateral stimulation (eyes or hands) while holding the memory · first line, though some evidence is against it cognitive processing therapy : cognitive work plus written accounts · first line · an adapted version (a forgiving authority figure) for moral injury prolonged exposure : imaginal or in vivo, equally effective trauma-focused CBT for children 3-18 dialectical behaviour therapy when borderline personality coexists - reduces self-harm ⚠ Psychological debriefing right after a trauma does not help and may do harm Medication first line: fluoxetine · paroxetine · sertraline · venlafaxine second line: fluvoxamine · mirtazapine · phenelzine nightmares : prazosin 2-12 mg at bedtime (a blood pressure drug) · nabilone (synthetic THC) at bedtime, "50-100 mg" in both notes - check the unit on the slides · SSRIs cut rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which may reduce nightmares to avoid: alprazolam, clonazepam · citalopram · desipramine · divalproex · olanzapine · tiagabine

Personality disorders ⭐ Cluster A is odd (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), B is dramatic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic), C is anxious (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive) - and no drug is approved for any of them. Dialectical behaviour therapy is the treatment for borderline personality disorder. Antisocial needs age 18+ and conduct disorder before 15. Schizoid doesn't want people; avoidant wants them but fears rejection; schizotypal is odd. Obsessive-compulsive personality is ego-syntonic; OCD is ego-dystonic. Splitting = borderline; projection = paranoid. A personality disorder is a lifelong, inflexible way of thinking, feeling and relating that causes distress or impairment. Sort it into a cluster first (odd, dramatic or anxious), then find the one feature that names the disorder. 1. What makes it a personality disorder An enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that: deviates markedly from the person's culture is pervasive and inflexible starts in adolescence or early adulthood and is stable over time (tends to soften with age) causes distress or impairment Shows in 2 or more of: cognition (how you see yourself and others) · affect (range, intensity, fit of emotions) · interpersonal functioning · impulse control Not explained by another mental disorder, a substance or a medical condition Under 18 : traits must be present at least 1 year · antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before 18 2. The three clusters Cluster Nickname Disorders Shared style Runs in families with A "Mad" / weird Paranoid · schizoid · schizotypal Odd, eccentric, withdrawn · brief stress psychosis possible Schizophrenia and psychotic disorders B "Bad" / wild Antisocial · borderline · histrionic · narcissistic Dramatic, emotional, erratic Mood disorders (borderline) · alcohol use (antisocial) · somatization (histrionic) C "Sad" / worried Avoidant · dependent · obsessive-compulsive Anxious, fearful · inhibited, self-blaming, guilty Anxiety and depressive disorders Other diagnoses: personality change due to another medical condition (labile, disinhibited, aggressive, apathetic, paranoid) · other specified · unspecified Prevalence : any personality disorder 11% · clusters A and B 3.5%, cluster C 6.5% most common: borderline (28% of cases) , then dependent (15%) and avoidant strongly linked to impairment, slower recovery, worse physical health and mortality, and more health care use 3.
