Pairs that get confused Schizoid vs schizotypal vs avoidant : schizoid does not want people · schizotypal is odd (magical thinking) · avoidant wants people but fears rejection Paranoid personality vs paranoid schizophrenia or delusional disorder : no fixed delusion, not acutely psychotic - the suspiciousness is part of the personality Avoidant personality vs social anxiety disorder : avoidant has lower self-esteem and broader inadequacy · social anxiety is tied to particular situations Obsessive-compulsive personality vs OCD : person

Dissociation and dissociative disorders ⭐ Depersonalization-derealization keeps reality testing intact - that is what separates it from psychosis. Dissociative identity disorder = 2+ personality states plus recurrent gaps in everyday memory, with childhood abuse in about 90%. Dissociative amnesia is for autobiographical information, usually localized; fugue is its travel specifier. Dissociation also appears in borderline personality (stress-related), PTSD (dissociative subtype) and panic attacks. Rule out seizures, head injury, substances and transient global amnesia first. Dissociation is a symptom first and a disorder only sometimes. Faced with it, rule out substances, seizures and psychosis, check for trauma, panic and borderline personality, and only then call it a dissociative disorder. 1. What dissociation is A disruption or discontinuity in the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, movement and behaviour A spectrum : from ordinary absorption (lost in a book) to severe, disabling states Dissociative Experiences Scale ( Dissociative Experiences Scale II ): 28 questions, scored out of 100 · non-clinical average about 11 2. Disorders where dissociation is a symptom Borderline personality disorder : transient, stress-related severe dissociation (or paranoia) Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): the dissociative subtype (depersonalization, derealization) · flashbacks are dissociative reactions · amnesia for parts of the trauma Panic disorder : derealization or depersonalization during a panic attack Research links it to schizophrenia, eating disorders, mood disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorder 3. The dissociative disorders - dissociation is the main problem Disorder Core Key features Must not be Dissociative amnesia Cannot recall important personal information , usually traumatic or stressful, beyond normal forgetting Types: localized (a period of time - most common) · selective (parts of it) · generalized (whole life and identity - very rare) · systematized (a category) · continuous (each new event) · specifier: dissociative fugue (purposeful travel or bewildered wandering) · lasts minutes to years Seizures, transient global amnesia, head injury, substances, dementia Dissociative identity disorder 2 or more distinct personality states with breaks in sense of self and agency Recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events · may hear voices (a child, a spiritual being) · often with amnesia and fugue · childhood abuse or neglect in about 90% A cultural or religious practice · a child's imaginary playmate · intoxication blackouts · complex partial seizures Depersonalization-derealization disorder Persistent or recurrent depersonalization (detached, watching yourself from outside) and/or derealization (surroundings unreal, foggy, time distorted) Reality testing stays intact - not psychotic · episodes last moments or recur over years · can look like a panic attack Schizophrenia, panic disorder, depression, PTSD or acute stress disorder Treatment named in the notes: trauma-informed psychotherapy for dissociative identity disorder 4. Approach to a patient with dissociation Also on the differential for amnesia: factitious disorder and malingering · catatonia · normal age-related memory change

Approach to ADHD ⭐ ADHD needs 6 symptoms (5 if 17+) for 6 months, onset before 12, in 2+ settings, with impairment - and a checklist alone is never enough. Long-acting stimulants are first line and work at once; atomoxetine and guanfacine are second line. Rule out hearing, vision, thyroid, low blood sugar, lead, sleep problems and absence seizures. Girls present inattentive and are missed. Stimulants unmask tics but do not cause them; check heart rate and blood pressure. Treating ADHD lowers, not raises, substance use. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heritable brain disorder diagnosed on history from several sources - not on a checklist alone. Confirm the criteria, rule out the mimics, then treat: stimulants first, non-stimulants second, behavioural support throughout. 1. What ADHD is A neurodevelopmental disorder - an illness (harmful dysfunction), not bad parenting, television or video games smaller or less active prefrontal cortex (executive function), limbic system (memory, emotion regulation) and basal ganglia (planning, reward, motivation) Highly heritable - genetic coefficient 0.76 · polygenic affected: 25-35% of siblings · 78-92% of identical twins · 20-54% of children of a parent with ADHD About 20% acquired prenatal: maternal smoking or alcohol (risk ×2.5) · prematurity, especially with brain bleeding (45% get ADHD) · pregnancy complications after birth: head injury, hypoxia, tumour, infection · lead poisoning in the preschool years · surviving acute lymphoblastic leukemia (its treatment injures the brain) The most common neurodevelopmental disorder : 5-12% of children · boys 4:1 in the community, 9:1 in clinics (referral bias) · under 2:1 in adults girls more often inattentive , less disruptive, and are missed Persists into adulthood in about 60% 2. Diagnostic criteria (DSM-5) Inattention Hyperactivity-impulsivity Symptoms Careless mistakes · cannot sustain attention · seems not to listen · does not finish tasks · disorganized · avoids sustained mental effort · loses things · easily distracted · forgetful Fidgets · leaves seat · runs or climbs (restlessness in adults) · cannot play quietly · "on the go, driven by a motor" · talks excessively · blurts out answers · cannot wait turn · interrupts Need 6 of 9 ( 5 if 17 or older ) 6 of 9 ( 5 if 17 or older ) In adults becomes Procrastination · slow, inefficient · poor time management · trouble in meetings and paperwork Inner restlessness · workaholic · overscheduled · picks very active jobs · impulsivity: quits jobs, ends relationships, drives too fast Plus all of: 6+ months several symptoms before age 12 present in 2 or more settings (home, school, work, friends) clear impairment - without impairment there is no diagnosis not better explained by another disorder, and not only during psychosis Subtypes : inattentive (formerly "ADD") · hyperactive-impulsive · combined · specifiers: partial remission · mild, moderate, severe ADHD is inconsistent attention, not zero attention - worst on tasks that are not fun or easy 3. Approach Ask about settings, not symptoms : "what is homework like in the evening?" rather than "is your child easily distracted?" · "what is it like to take your child shopping?" Collateral history matters : adults recall their own childhood symptoms poorly Check current intellectual functioning and achievement - a full psychoeducational assessment only if a learning disorder is suspected Mostly assessed and treated in primary care ; comorbidities may need a specialist 4. What to rule out Medical : hearing or vision loss · hyper- or hypothyroidism (thyroid-stimulating hormone) · low blood sugar (glucose) · anemia (complete blood count) · lead (blood lead level) · head injury · absence seizures · sleep problems including obstructive sleep apnea · fragile X, fetal alcohol syndrome, phenylketonuria, neurofibromatosis · intellectual disability Psychiatric : anxiety · depression (a drop in mood vs ADHD's lifelong demoralization) · bipolar (episodic, grandiose) · oppositional defiant and conduct disorders · learning disorder · autism (30-70% also meet ADHD criteria) · personality disorders · substance use Comorbidity is the rule : only 25-40% have "simple" ADHD · commonest: oppositional defiant disorder · conduct disorder · mood · anxiety · learning disorders · substance use 5. Medication Stimulants (first line) Non-stimulants (second line) Drugs Methylphenidate (Concerta, Biphentin, Foquest; short-acting Ritalin) · amphetamine based (Adderall, Vyvanse, Dexedrine) Atomoxetine (reuptake inhibitor) · guanfacine extended release (alpha-2A agonist) How Release catecholamines and block their reuptake → more dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex Atomoxetine blocks reuptake · guanfacine boosts prefrontal signalling Onset Works immediately Atomoxetine about 2 weeks , then 24-hour cover Response High (sources differ: 90% in the medwiki note, 75% in the upper-year notes - check the slides) — Side effects Less appetite · insomnia · mood or anxiety, agitation · flattened affect · ↑ heart rate and blood pressure · can unmask tics · rarely hallucinations, cardiac death Atomoxetine: stomach upset, irritability, fatigue · guanfacine: sleepiness, dizziness, dry mouth Long-acting forms are preferred : fewer side effects, less misuse, more convenient Tics : stimulants unmask them, they do not cause them - continue if not disruptive Recommended 7 days a week, 12 months a year - ADHD affects social life and safety, not just school Medication alone, or with behavioural treatment, reduces core symptoms (MTA study: about 6000 children over 14 months) Where clonidine and bupropion sit (sources differ: second line in the upper-year notes, third-line off label in the medwiki note - check the slides) 6. Non-drug treatment Psychoeducation and dispelling myths ("boys will be boys", "my neighbour's kid was a zombie") Parent training : agree as caregivers · externalize time (timers), information (notes) and motivation (

Speech and language disorders ⭐ Language is the symbol system (what is said and understood); speech is making the sounds - and every workup starts with a hearing test. By age 3 a child should be 90% intelligible to strangers. Only 40-50% of late talkers catch up - don't wait and see. Apraxia = planning problem with inconsistent errors; dysarthria = muscle problem with drooling. Stuttering is normal at 2-4 years; treat if it lasts over 6 months, runs in the family, or bothers the child. Social communication disorder can only be diagnosed once autism is ruled out. First decide whether the problem is language (the symbol system - what is said and understood) or speech (making the sounds - what you hear). Whichever it is, check hearing first and refer to a speech-language pathologist. 1. Communication, language, speech Communication = any verbal or nonverbal behaviour that influences others - sending and receiving a message Language = conventional symbols (words, signs, writing, pictures) used by rules - a symbol system form : phonology (sound system) · morphology (units of meaning, like the "s" in cookies) · syntax (grammar) content : semantics (meaning) · use : pragmatics (social rules) expressive (producing a message) vs receptive (understanding one) Speech = producing the sounds - articulation · fluency · voice · resonance - making the oral signal Communication disorders: language (developmental, acquired), speech (articulation, voice, fluency) and other (swallowing, social communication, literacy) 2. When to worry Red flags : milestones not met · parents are concerned · struggling at school with no clear reason, or behaviour problems · child cannot be understood as expected · social difficulties How common : language disorders 5-10% (sources differ: 7% in the upper-year notes, 2-5% in the medwiki condition note - check the slides) · articulation 2-3% (falls with age) · voice 3% · fluency 1% (higher in preschoolers) Age Expected 6 months Loud tuneful vocalizing · turns to a familiar voice 9-10 months Responds to name · babbles, consonant sounds · purposeful gestures · understands "no", "bye-bye" 12 months First words with meaning · points · follows simple one-step directions 18 months Single words, mostly nouns (sources differ: 6-20 words in the medwiki note, at least 20 in the upper-year notes - check the slides) · points to body parts 18-24 months Once about 50 words , starts combining 2 words 2 years 50-100 words · understood about 50% of the time 3 years 3-word sentences · pronouns, plurals, past tense · 90% intelligible to strangers · a stutter is common 4 years Colours · multi-word sentences · make-believe play Do not "wait and see" in boys : the sex difference is only months · only 40-50% of late talkers catch up on their own Bilingual children show the same pattern in both languages - a true disorder shows in all of them 3. Language disorders Developmental language disorder (DSM-5 language disorder) persistent difficulty learning and using language: small vocabulary · limited sentence structure · poor discourse (connecting sentences) well below age expectations, with functional limits · onset in early development · not due to hearing loss, intellectual disability or another cause you notice: short answers · long pauses · fillers ("well, you know") · restarts · incomplete sentences · vague words ("she") · grammar errors · the listener cannot follow the message risk : boys 2-3:1 · twins · highly heritable (20-40% where there is a family history) prognosis : receptive problems fare worse · school-entry vocabulary predicts school success · oral language predicts reading and writing · secondary social, emotional and behaviour problems are often misread as the cause 40% of Canadian children aged 7-14 with psychiatric disorders have a language impairment Acquired language disorder (aphasia) after stroke, brain injury, tumour, infection, dementia - at least 30% of stroke patients Aphasia Problem Expressive (Broca) Knows what to say but cannot get it out in speech or writing Receptive (Wernicke) Hears or sees the words but cannot make sense of them Anomic Cannot find the right word for objects, places, events Global Cannot use, understand, read or write language 4. Speech sound disorders Sounds develop gradually · by 3 years every child should be 90% intelligible , even to strangers Articulation disorder : trouble making particular sounds (e.g. a lisp) · phonological disorder : patterns of substituting, dropping, adding or changing sounds ("dis" for "this", "do" for "dog") Speech sound disorder (DSM-5): persistent difficulty that hurts intelligibility · early onset · not from cerebral palsy, cleft palate, hearing loss or brain injury (genetic syndromes such as Down syndrome are not excluded) Childhood apraxia of speech Dysarthria Problem The brain cannot plan and coordinate the movements · no weakness Weak, slow, uncoordinated or numb speech muscles · abnormal muscle tone Errors Inconsistent Imprecise articulation (distortions, substitutions) Clues Little cooing or babbling · late first words · few sounds · trouble combining sounds · may look like an expressive language problem · often with aphasia when acquired Asymmetric face · drooling, eating difficulty · neurological conditions (stroke, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson's when acquired) Acquired speech disorders : structural (damage or removal of larynx, tongue, jaw) · motor ( dysarthria , apraxia ) 5. Voice, fluency and social communication Voice disorder = a voice that draws attention to itself (pitch, loudness, quality, resonance) causes: misuse · disease · congenital defects · laryngeal trauma or surgery · ageing · neurological (cerebral palsy, spasmodic dysphonia) laryngeal : rough, harsh, hoarse, breathy · resonance : hypernasal (too much nasal air - cleft ) vs hyponasal (too little - e.g. deviated septum) Stuttering (childhood-onset fluency disorder): repetitions, prolongations, blocks, broken words, word substitutions

Autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability ⭐ Every child with global developmental delay or intellectual disability (and autism with dysmorphic features or ID) gets a chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing - not a karyotype. Autism = all 3 social-communication deficits + 2 of 4 restricted, repetitive behaviours, from early development. Intellectual disability = IQ under about 70 plus adaptive deficits, onset in development; global developmental delay is the under-5 label. No drug treats the core of either; aggression is the main reason to medicate, usually with an antipsychotic. Vaccines do not cause autism. Autism is a disorder of social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviour; intellectual disability is low intelligence plus low adaptive function. They often coexist, share a genetic workup, and are managed the same way - no drug treats the core, so medication targets the problem behaviours. 1. Autism spectrum disorder - diagnosis One umbrella diagnosis in DSM-5, replacing autism, Asperger syndrome, childhood disintegrative disorder and pervasive developmental disorder A. Social communication and interaction - all 3 social-emotional reciprocity (no back-and-forth conversation, little sharing of interests or emotion) nonverbal communication (eye contact, gestures, facial expression) relationships (adjusting to context, imaginative play, interest in peers) B. Restricted, repetitive behaviour - at least 2 of 4 stereotyped movements, object use or speech (hand-flapping, lining up toys, echolalia) insistence on sameness (distress at small changes, rigid routines) fixated interests abnormal in intensity or focus over- or under-reaction to sensory input (indifferent to pain, upset by sounds or textures) C. Present in early development (may only show when social demands exceed capacity, or be masked later) · D. Impairment · E. Not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay both can be diagnosed together when social communication is below the child's general developmental level 2. Autism - who, why, and the workup About 1.7% of 8-year-olds · boys about 4.5:1 · rising, mostly from broader criteria and awareness Comorbidities : intellectual disability about a third (31% upper-year notes, 33% medwiki) · seizures 20% (early childhood or adolescence; more with fragile X, tuberous sclerosis) Causes neurodevelopmental - abnormal brain development, not degeneration · larger head circumference (up to 20% above the 97th percentile) and brain size, mostly white matter genetic : 10-15% have copy-number changes · sibling recurrence 5-10% leading psychological theory: missing "theory of mind" (inferring what others think and feel) no link with vaccines Assessment : developmental history from parents · reports from school or daycare · direct observation · speech-language and cognitive assessment · genetic testing with a chromosomal microarray (especially with dysmorphic features or intellectual disability) tools: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (screen) · Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (gold standard, expensive) Differential : hearing impairment · intellectual disability · severe language disorder · social communication disorder · ADHD (attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder) · social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder · Rett syndrome 3. Intellectual disability - diagnosis Intellectual deficits , confirmed by clinical assessment and standardized testing: reasoning · problem solving · planning · abstract thinking · judgement · academic learning · learning from experience IQ about 2 standard deviations below the mean - under about 70 Adaptive deficits that limit independence and social responsibility: communication · social participation · independent living (self-care, school, work) Onset in the developmental period · severity: mild · moderate · severe · profound Label Age When used Intellectual disability Any age Criteria met on testing - use it whenever the criteria are met Global developmental delay Under 5 Delay of 2+ standard deviations in 2 or more domains (motor · speech and language · cognition · social · daily living) and cannot yet be tested reliably · reassess later - most go on to intellectual disability Unspecified intellectual disability Over 5 Cannot be graded because of blindness, prelingual deafness, physical disability, severe behaviour or another disorder · reassess later About 1% of the population · boys 1.25:1 · higher with lower maternal education and income Comorbidities : hearing loss 10% · seizures (sources differ: a third of severe and 5-15% of mild in the upper-year notes, about 10% of mild in the medwiki note - check the slides) · cerebral palsy in 30-60% of severe · psychiatric disorders far more common but under-diagnosed 4. Intellectual disability - causes and workup The more severe, the more likely a cause is found : about 75% of severe vs under 50% of mild Group Examples Genetic (over 500 syndromes) Fragile X - most common genetic cause · Down syndrome · Rett syndrome Prenatal Teratogens : valproate, phenytoin · alcohol · radiation · infections : rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, HIV · inborn errors of metabolism · brain malformations · placental disease Postnatal (about 3.5%) Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy · meningitis, encephalitis · brain injury · infantile spasms · severe deprivation · lead or mercury poisoning First-line genetic tests : chromosomal microarray + fragile X testing in every child with global developmental delay or intellectual disability - not a karyotype Fragile X : CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene · features: long face, large ears, flat feet, lax joints, low tone · ADHD, autism, social anxiety, aggression · premutation carriers can later get a tremor-ataxia syndrome or early ovarian failure Workup of global developmental delay or intellectual disability: history, exam, hearing and vision first, then microarray and fragile X, then brain MRI and genetics or

Disruptive behaviour disorders ⭐ ODD = 6+ months of angry, defiant, vindictive behaviour (4 of 8) without violating others' rights; conduct disorder = 3 of 15 rights-violating behaviours in 12 months. Childhood-onset conduct disorder (before 10) has the worst prognosis and often leads to antisocial personality after 18. ODD severity counts settings: 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3+ severe. First line is structured psychosocial treatment with the parents; multisystemic therapy for conduct disorder. No drug for the disorder itself - treat comorbid ADHD, and risperidone for aggression. Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) defies and argues; conduct disorder (CD) violates the rights of others. Both are multifactorial, start early, overlap with ADHD (attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder), and are treated with structured psychosocial programmes that involve the parents - not medication. 1. Causes - risk factors in four domains Domain Risk factors Biological Family history of behaviour, substance use or mood disorders (genetic coefficient 0.5) · low birth weight · pregnancy and birth complications · brain injury or disease · male sex · autonomic under-reactivity (little anxiety about consequences) · underactive inhibitory regions (frontal lobe, amygdala, hippocampus) Individual Difficult temperament (fussy, hard to soothe) · low IQ · language and reading problems · inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity · aggression · reads threat into social situations · chronic illness or disability Family Parental antisocial behaviour or substance use · domestic violence · separation, single parent · maternal depression · maltreatment, neglect · poor supervision · harsh, coercive or inconsistent discipline Social Low income · delinquent peers · disadvantaged, high-crime neighbourhood · being bullied · peer rejection The most common reason for youth mental health referral (about 30%) · raise the risk of later psychiatric, social and legal problems 2. Oppositional defiant disorder A pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness for 6+ months - 4 or more of 8 , with at least one person who is not a sibling angry, irritable : loses temper · touchy, easily annoyed · angry and resentful argumentative, defiant : argues with authority · refuses rules or requests · deliberately annoys · blames others vindictive : spiteful at least twice in 6 months Usually feels justified · no major violation of society's rules Frequency : under 5 years → most days · 5 and over → at least weekly · must exceed what is normal for age, sex and culture Not only during psychosis, substance use, depression or bipolar disorder · disruptive mood dysregulation disorder excluded · over 18, antisocial personality disorder excluded Severity by number of settings : mild 1 · moderate 2 · severe 3+ Epidemiology : about 3.3% · boys 1.4:1 before adolescence, equal after · starts around 6-8 (preschool symptoms) · about 30% progress to conduct disorder , especially the vindictive and argumentative 3. Conduct disorder A persistent pattern that violates others' basic rights or major age-appropriate rules : 3 or more of 15 in 12 months , at least 1 in the last 6 months, with impairment Category Behaviours Aggression to people or animals Bullies, threatens · starts fights · uses a weapon · cruel to people · cruel to animals · steals while confronting a victim · forced sexual activity Destruction of property Deliberate fire-setting to cause damage · other deliberate destruction Deceit or theft Breaks into a house, building or car · lies to "con" others · shoplifting or forgery Serious rule violations Out at night against parents' rules before 13 · runs away overnight (2+ times, or once for long) · truant before 13 Onset specifier : childhood onset (before 10) - worse prognosis , more ADHD, aggression and family dysfunction · adolescent onset (after 10) · unspecified With limited prosocial emotions : 2+ over 12 months - no remorse or guilt · callous, no empathy · unconcerned about performance · shallow affect Severity mild · moderate · severe · not diagnosed when the behaviour is needed to survive (war, extreme poverty) Over 18 : diagnose antisocial personality disorder instead if its criteria are met Epidemiology : 2-10%, median 4% · boys 3-5:1 · progression to antisocial personality (sources differ: 30-50% in the upper-year notes, about 40% in the medwiki note - check the slides) 4. Telling them apart Versus How it differs ODD vs CD ODD has no aggression to people or animals, destruction or theft , but does include irritable mood · can coexist ADHD Impulsive, but does not violate others' rights or society's rules · can coexist Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder Same chronic negative mood and outbursts, but more severe Mood disorders More low-mood symptoms Intermittent explosive disorder Impulsive aggression not aimed at a goal Adjustment disorder Conduct problems that begin with a clear stressor Language disorder, hearing loss Does not follow directions because it does not understand them Social anxiety Defiance driven by fear of being judged 5. Comorbidities ODD: ADHD in about 50% , often seen first CD : up to 90% of early-onset CD had ODD · ADHD 40-70% · depression up to 40% · anxiety 30% · learning disabilities up to 20% · substance use · intellectual disability Consequences: incarceration · school dropout · teen pregnancy · family stress 6. Treatment Principles : individualized (causes vary) · earlier is better · structured psychosocial intervention is first line · involve the parents Parent training : Triple P (positive parenting - relationships, attitude, conduct) · parent-child interaction therapy (parent coached in real time) · collaborative problem solving (for ODD - flexibility and cooperation) Functional family therapy : tackles negative attributions, builds positive time together Individual therapy - works better in teens: CBT for social-thinking deficits · social skills · problem solving School : asses

Psychotic disorders and schizophrenia ⭐ Duration sorts the schizophrenia spectrum: under 1 month = brief psychotic disorder, 1-6 months = schizophreniform, 6+ months = schizophrenia. Schizoaffective needs 2+ weeks of psychosis without a mood episode; psychosis only during mood episodes = mood disorder with psychotic features. Delusional disorder: delusions for 1+ month, otherwise intact. Schizophrenia's criterion A needs delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech. Detailed visual hallucinations suggest an organic cause. Family history is the strongest risk factor; each relapse costs function. Psychosis is a set of symptoms, not a diagnosis. The disorders that cause it are told apart by how long the psychosis lasts and how it lines up with mood episodes . 1. What psychosis is Loss of contact with reality : trouble telling what is real from what is not · many causes besides the psychotic disorders Six domains change: Thinking : trouble concentrating, following conversation, remembering · thoughts jumbled · impaired working memory, attention, verbal and visual learning, reasoning, social cognition · slowed processing speed is the most common change · disrupted salience (cannot pick out what matters from what does not) Perception - hallucinations : false perceptions with no outside stimulus, made by the brain (a person born deaf can still hear voices) auditory, the most common : commenting (narrating) · conversing (voices talking to each other) · commanding (can drive harm) visual: rare, poorly formed shapes, shadows, lights · detailed visual hallucinations → think of an organic cause, pseudohallucination or malingering tactile: "inside out" (bugs under the skin) or "outside in" (being touched) · smell and taste: less common, usually foul Beliefs - delusions : fixed, false beliefs from a wrong inference about reality, out of keeping with the person's intelligence and culture, not correctable by reasoning types: persecutory · grandiose · somatic · religious · erotomanic · infidelity · reference · thought broadcasting, insertion, withdrawal Mood : swings, excitement, depression, anxiety, or very little emotion Behaviour : acting differently, often driven by hallucinations and delusions Insight : lacking in 50-70% , completely ("nothing is wrong") or partly ("it's just stress") · a neurological symptom like anosognosia, not tied to intelligence · poor insight → poor adherence 2. Positive vs negative symptoms Positive symptoms Negative symptoms What Something added that people do not normally experience A loss of normal function Examples Delusions · hallucinations · disorganized thinking · excitement, agitation Flat affect · alogia (less speech) · avolition (cannot start goal-directed activity) · anergia · anhedonia · asociality · inattention Prognosis Mostly positive symptoms → better outcome Negative symptoms → worse outcome, harder to treat 3. Telling the psychotic disorders apart Disorder Picture Duration What separates it Brief psychotic disorder Sudden psychotic symptoms (sources differ: the medwiki note lists 2 of schizophrenia's core symptoms, upper-year notes 1 or more - check the slides) 1 day to under 1 month Full return to baseline · often after a marked stressor · can start in pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum Schizophreniform disorder Schizophrenia's core symptoms (criterion A) 1 to 6 months Called "provisional" before recovery · almost all go on to schizophrenia Schizophrenia Core symptoms + decline in function 6+ months , with at least 1 month of core symptoms Mood episodes, if any, only for a minority of the illness Schizoaffective disorder Major mood episode at the same time as core symptoms, mood present for most of the illness - Psychosis for 2+ weeks with no mood episode · bipolar or depressive type Mood disorder with psychotic features Depression or mania with psychosis - Psychosis only during mood episodes Delusional disorder 1+ delusion , hallucinations minor and tied to its theme 1+ month Core criteria never met · function and behaviour not markedly odd apart from the delusion · resists medication alone Substance-induced psychosis Hallucinations and/or delusions during or soon after intoxication or withdrawal Settles within about 1 month of stopping Delirium excluded · alcohol, cannabis, phencyclidine, amphetamines, cocaine, hallucinogens, inhalants, sedatives · medications: steroids, interferon, mefloquine, diphenhydramine Schizoaffective disorder: psychosis runs alongside the mood episodes and also persists at baseline between them 4. Schizophrenia DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 5th edition) criteria A : 2+ of delusions · hallucinations · disorganized speech · grossly disorganized or catatonic behaviour · negative symptoms - for a significant part of 1 month (less if treated), and at least one must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech B : work, relationships or self-care well below the previous level (or failure to reach the expected level in a young person) C : 6 months of continuous signs, including 1 month of criterion A (the rest may be prodromal or residual symptoms) D-F : not schizoaffective or a mood disorder · not from a substance or medical condition · with past autism or a communication disorder, needs prominent delusions or hallucinations for 1 month Epidemiology : lifetime risk about 1% (any psychotic disorder about 3%) · same incidence worldwide , regardless of culture, class or background · men and women equally · first episode usually 18-24 (a second, late peak in women around 50-54) · 5-13% die by suicide Risk factors family history is the strongest (about 80% heritable): sibling 8% · one parent 12% · two parents 40% · non-identical twin 12% · identical twin 47% cannabis in early adolescence (12-18; higher-THC products carry more risk; use after 25 adds no risk) · birth complications · older father · childhood trauma, refugee migration · DiGeorge syndrome (25%) Course : brain changes are present near birth, but sympt

Treatment of psychotic disorders ⭐ Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic and the drug for treatment-resistant psychosis (2 failed trials of 4-6 weeks), but it needs blood monitoring for agranulocytosis. 1st generation = potent dopamine block, positive symptoms only, extrapyramidal effects; 2nd = sedation and weight gain; 3rd = partial agonist. Acute dystonia is an emergency; akathisia gets a beta-blocker; parkinsonism an anticholinergic. All antipsychotics can prolong the QT; risperidone is worst for sexual side effects. Stay on treatment 12-18 months after a first episode. Carers' critical comments are the 3rd biggest relapse risk. Antipsychotics treat psychosis by blocking dopamine; the three generations differ in how hard they block it, and that sets their side effects. Part 2 of the lecture is the reminder that medication is only one component: the psychosocial supports decide relapse. 1. Dopamine and psychosis Pathway Normal role In psychosis Blocking it gives Mesolimbic (limbic system) How we feel about what we notice, and remembering it Overactive → faulty salience, false connections, hallucinations → positive symptoms The antipsychotic effect Mesocortical Learning, memory, motivation, organizing behaviour (highly developed in humans) Underactive → negative and cognitive symptoms - Nigrostriatal Movement - Extrapyramidal (movement) side effects Tuberoinfundibular Controls prolactin release - Raised prolactin → sexual side effects Glutamate (NMDA receptors) and serotonin are involved too, but nothing yet treats them · the most effective antipsychotic, clozapine, is one of the least dopamine-blocking About 60% receptor blockade is enough · more is not better: stiffness, tremor, fatigue, sexual effects (upper-year notes) The four dopamine pathways: mesolimbic overactivity gives positive symptoms, mesocortical underactivity negative symptoms; nigrostriatal controls movement, tuberoinfundibular prolactin 2. Typical vs atypical antipsychotics 1st generation ("typical") 2nd generation ("atypical") 3rd generation Since 1960s 1990s 2000s Mechanism High-potency dopamine blockers Lower dopamine affinity relative to serotonin and histamine receptors Dopamine antagonist and partial agonist - balances dopamine rather than blocking it Examples haloperidol · zuclopenthixol · loxapine · flupentixol risperidone · quetiapine · olanzapine · ziprasidone · paliperidone · clozapine aripiprazole · lurasidone · asenapine · brexpiprazole Symptoms treated Positive only Designed to help negative symptoms too, but no more effective than 1st generation Designed for fewer side effects · not everyone responds Main side effects Extrapyramidal · sexual · low blood pressure · cognitive dulling Sedation · weight gain → metabolic syndrome (worst with clozapine and olanzapine) Restlessness · nausea · some weight gain · sexual Best use Emergency department · patients who cannot take or do not respond to newer drugs Widely used, also for sleep, bipolar disorder, add-on in depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder, severe ADHD, autism, dementia-related aggression - use judiciously given the metabolic risk - On 2nd generation drugs: routine metabolic bloodwork every 6 months In a first episode, 1st and 2nd generation drugs work equally well 3. Clozapine The most effective antipsychotic · the drug for treatment-resistant psychosis = 2 or more antipsychotics tried for 4-6 weeks each · works in about 2 of 3 such cases Very low potency, acts on dozens of receptors including serotonin Side effects: weight gain · sedation · fast heart rate · seizures · arrhythmia · rare but serious agranulocytosis (a rapid fall in white blood cells), so it needs blood monitoring 4. Side effects and their treatment Side effect What it looks like Most with Treatment Acute dystonia Sudden painful spasm: oculogyric crisis (eyes roll up) · blepharospasm · torticollis · trismus (jaw) · opisthotonus (back arches) · laryngospasm High-potency 1st generation An emergency : lower the dose + diphenhydramine, a benzodiazepine or an anticholinergic Parkinsonism Tremor · rigidity · slow movement · postural instability 1st generation Anticholinergic or a lower dose Akathisia Severe inner and physical restlessness · very distressing, linked to suicide 1st generation · restlessness with 3rd Beta-blocker (propranolol) or a benzodiazepine (lorazepam) Tardive dyskinesia Involuntary movements of face, lips, tongue, jaw, limbs, head Long-term dopamine blockade (also metoclopramide) - Metabolic Weight gain · metabolic syndrome Clozapine, olanzapine Bloodwork every 6 months Cardiovascular Fast heart rate · low blood pressure · QT prolongation → torsades de pointes All antipsychotics - Sexual Amenorrhea, cycle changes, breast enlargement or gynecomastia · erectile and ejaculation problems · low libido All, especially risperidone · less prolactin effect with 3rd generation - Heatstroke Cannot sense overheating All Teach hydration and sun protection 5. Using antipsychotics Onset : sleep and agitation improve in hours to days · a good response in about 2 weeks · full remission 4-8 weeks (sources differ: upper-year notes also give 2-3 weeks for the antipsychotic effect and 6-12 weeks for the maximum - check the slides) Start low, go slow Long-acting injectables (paliperidone, aripiprazole) help adherence - a few missed doses raise relapse risk After a first episode, continue for at least 12-18 months · relapse is highest in the first 2 years · most need a lower maintenance dose long term · no way to predict who can stop 6. Psychosocial treatment Aims : psychoeducation and normalizing · less distress · skills for stress and recovery · build on strengths and values · empowerment · a meaningful life Expressed emotion (carers' hostility, criticism or over-involvement) is the 3rd biggest relapse risk , after stopping medication and drug use Components case management : the first point of contact · coordinates housing, income, school, work, court and family · psychoedu
04 Consent, Capacity, and the Mental Health Act

Consent, capacity and the Mental Health Act ⭐ Form 1 = any physician who saw the patient in the past 7 days, holds 72 hours for assessment; Form 3 = a different physician, involuntary admission for 14 days. Form 2 comes from a justice of the peace; Form 4 renews for a month and may be the same physician. Box B (deterioration) needs prior response to treatment, incapacity and SDM consent. Capacity = understand + appreciate. Duty to warn: identifiable person, serious harm, imminent - permitted, not required. A known prior capable wish beats both the SDM and an emergency. Two Ontario laws answer two different questions. The Mental Health Act (MHA) decides whether a person can be held for psychiatric assessment or admission against their will; the Health Care Consent Act (HCCA) decides who agrees to treatment - for every kind of treatment, not just psychiatric. 1. Involuntary admission: the forms Form Who signs What it does How long Form 1 - application for psychiatric assessment Any physician who has examined the person in the past 7 days Allows the person to be held for a psychiatric assessment - not an admission, so the bar is relatively low Must be acted on within 7 days · holds for up to 72 hours Form 42 The Form 1 physician Tells the patient they are on a Form 1 and why Original to the patient, copy in the chart Form 2 - order for examination A justice of the peace , on information from anyone (often family) Police bring the person in for assessment (apprehension, not detention) Valid 7 days Form 3 - certificate of involuntary admission A different physician from the Form 1 (usually a psychiatrist) The person becomes an involuntary patient Up to 14 days Form 30 The Form 3 physician Notice of the right to rights advice - Form 4 - certificate of renewal Can be the same physician as the Form 3 Extends involuntary admission First renewal 1 month , renewable Community treatment order A physician, agreed to by the patient or substitute decision maker Treatment in the community instead of hospital 6 months, renewable · for 2+ admissions or 30+ days in hospital in the past 3 years Don't let a form expire : if it lapses before the next one, and the patient was not expressly told they are now voluntary, you are back to a Form 1 Rights : a Form 3 or 4 automatically brings a rights advisor to meet the patient privately · the patient can contest, with a hearing within 3-5 business days If a family member has been through the hard process of getting a Form 2, at least refer to psychiatry 2. Form 1 criteria: Box A and Box B Every Form 1 needs a mental disorder (very broad: any disease or disability of the mind) plus risk , in a person who will not or cannot be a voluntary patient · only one box needs to be met Box A - "serious harm" Box B - "deterioration" Past or present evidence Has threatened or attempted self-harm · has been violent or made others fear harm · has shown a lack of competence to care for self All of : previously treated for a recurring mental disorder · improved with that treatment · now has the same or a similar disorder · incapable of consenting and the substitute decision maker has consented Future opinion Likely and imminent serious bodily harm to self · to others · or serious physical impairment Likely serious harm to self or others, or substantial mental or physical deterioration Examples Planning suicide (writing a note, rehoming pets) · command hallucinations to harm · catatonic depression, not eating or drinking - Notes - Added in 2000 · not useful in a first episode or an emergency · police cannot use it The medwiki note labels the two parts a "past/present test" and a "future test" but maps them the other way round (sources differ - check the slides) 3. Breaking confidentiality: the duty to warn A permission, not an obligation , endorsed by the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Medical Protective Association and the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario All three must hold: ① a clear risk to an identifiable person or group ② a risk of serious bodily harm or death ③ the danger is imminent 4. Consent to treatment (Health Care Consent Act) Applies to all treatment (even physiotherapy) · valid consent is ① voluntary ② informed ③ capable Voluntary : no deception or coercion Informed : what a reasonable person would want to know - the nature of the treatment · expected benefits · risks, including rare but serious ones · side effects · alternatives · likely result of no treatment · and answers to all questions Capable - the two-part test : the patient must be able to understand the information relevant to the decision, and appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision, or of not deciding Who judges capacity : the clinician proposing the treatment · who consents for an incapable patient : the substitute decision maker (SDM) 5. Substitute decision makers Hierarchy : ① guardian → ② attorney for personal care → ③ representative appointed by the Consent and Capacity Board → ④ spouse or partner → ⑤ child or parent → ⑥ sibling → ⑦ other relative → ⑧ Public Guardian and Trustee spouses: married, or living together for 1 year, or parents of a child together, or with a cohabitation agreement siblings who cannot agree → the Public Guardian and Trustee decides To act, an SDM must be : capable for that treatment · 16 or older (unless a parent) · not barred by a court · available · willing How an SDM decides : a known, applicable prior capable wish must be followed · otherwise best interests, the patient's values and beliefs, and any incapable wishes Emergency treatment without consent is allowed when delay would prolong suffering or risk serious bodily harm · note the reasons and find an SDM · an emergency does not override a prior capable wish (e.g. a do-not-resuscitate order) Challenges : the patient can ask the Consent and Capacity Board to review a finding of incapacity or a detention, appeal its ruling to the courts, and challenge the choice of SDM

Eating disorders ⭐ Anorexia = restriction to a significantly low weight; bulimia = binges plus compensation; binge-eating disorder = binges with no compensation. ARFID restricts without any body-image concern. Russell's sign, enlarged salivary glands and enamel erosion point to purging. Daytime heart rate under 50 is one admission criterion on its own. Refeeding syndrome's hallmark is low phosphate - refeed slowly and check electrolytes often. Family-based treatment is first line in adolescents; fluoxetine has evidence in bulimia. Three questions sort the main eating disorders: is the weight significantly low, are there binges, and is there compensating (purging, fasting, exercise) afterwards? The second question for every patient is whether the body is safe enough to treat at home. 1. What an eating disorder is Definition : a persistent disturbance of eating or eating-related behaviour that changes how food is taken in or absorbed, and significantly harms physical health or psychosocial functioning When to be concerned : troubling weight-control behaviours · preoccupation with body, weight and food · fast weight loss · failure to meet expected growth or weight gain · distress from eating behaviours Risk factors family history (higher in identical twins and first-degree relatives) · perfectionist, rigid or impulsive traits · picky eating in childhood at-risk activities : sports with weight classes or a focus on looks (ballet, gymnastics, wrestling, diving, running, modelling) societal body ideals and dieting · abuse and post-traumatic stress disorder (bulimia) 2. Assessment Standard psychiatric assessment, plus insight and goals, then: Intake : restriction, rules, fasting, calorie counting, binge eating, sensory- or fear-based avoidance · Output : exercise, vomiting, laxatives, weight-loss substances Drivers : body image · fear of choking or vomiting · History : highest and lowest weight, puberty · review of systems for malnutrition · peers, online, at-risk activities, family food culture Collateral from parents : what they have seen · stressors · whether they can carry out treatment at home Investigations : complete blood count · electrolytes · glucose · creatinine · liver tests · thyroid-stimulating hormone · ECG Differential : depression · anxiety · irritable bowel syndrome · food insecurity · intellectual disability · neglect · medical conditions affecting intake or metabolism 3. Anorexia vs bulimia vs binge-eating disorder Anorexia nervosa Bulimia nervosa Binge-eating disorder Core Restriction → significantly low weight Binges + compensation Binges without compensation Criteria Restricted intake → significantly low weight for age, sex and growth · intense fear of gaining weight (or behaviour that blocks gain) · distorted body experience, self-worth tied to shape, or not seeing how serious the low weight is Binge = clearly more food than most would eat in a set period (about 2 hours) with loss of control · compensation: vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, exercise · both at least weekly for 3 months · self-worth unduly tied to shape and weight · not only during anorexia Binges at least weekly for 3 months , with 3 or more of: eating fast · until uncomfortably full · when not hungry · alone from embarrassment · disgust or guilt after · marked distress · no regular compensation Specifiers Restricting vs binge-eating/purging type (past 3 months) · severity by body mass index (BMI): mild 17+ · moderate 16-16.99 · severe 15-15.99 · extreme under 15 · youth: BMI percentile or ideal body weight Severity by compensations per week : mild 1-3 · moderate 4-7 · severe 8-13 · extreme 14+ Severity by binges per week , same cut-offs Who 1-2% of females · female to male 10:1 · onset 14-18 1-1.5% · 10:1 · slightly older onset (14-22), with dieting and stress · 10-15% move to anorexia Least sex skew · onset late teens to early adulthood · 5-30% of adults with obesity Signs Small portions, skipped meals, cutting food up · exercise · cold intolerance · constipation · amenorrhea · hair loss, lanugo · slow heart rate, low blood pressure · osteopenia · arrested growth or puberty Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) · enlarged salivary glands · dental enamel erosion · Mallory-Weiss tears · electrolyte disturbance · raised serum amylase Overweight, obesity, diabetes, chronic pain Treatment Level of care → medical stabilization → nutritional rehabilitation → family-based treatment (gold standard in adolescents) · medication only for comorbidity (SSRI, short-term benzodiazepine, olanzapine for distressing eating-disorder thoughts) Structured eating (3 meals, 3 snacks) · enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E) , family-based treatment, interpersonal therapy · fluoxetine · topiramate CBT (also guided self-help), interpersonal therapy, dialectical behaviour therapy · topiramate · lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) Outcome 80% improve, under half fully recover · 30-40% relapse · highest mortality of any psychiatric illness 50% remit with treatment · psychiatric comorbidity 88% · mortality 3.9% Most improve · psychiatric comorbidity 75% Anorexia mortality (sources differ: upper-year notes give 5-7%, the medwiki note 5-10% and 10% - check the slides) The medwiki note rates CBT's support as weak for anorexia and bulimia, while the upper-year notes make enhanced CBT the core therapy for bulimia (sources differ - check the slides) Anorexia affects every system: slow heart rate and low blood pressure, osteoporosis, low potassium and magnesium, amenorrhea, lanugo 4. Other feeding and eating disorders Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) : avoids food from lack of interest, its sensory features, or fear of choking or vomiting → weight loss or faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, dependence on tube feeds or supplements, or social impairment no body-image disturbance - the key difference from anorexia · more than picky eating equal in boys and girls · linked to autism, anxiety, depression, neglect, develo

Sleep disorders ⭐ Insomnia is a clinical diagnosis treated first with CBT for insomnia - a sleep study is not indicated. Obstructive sleep apnea is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness; CPAP is the treatment. Central apnea has no breathing effort during pauses. Cataplexy (emotion-triggered loss of tone) points to narcolepsy. NREM parasomnias: children, early night, no memory; REM sleep behaviour disorder: older men, late night, dream recalled, a warning sign for Parkinson and Lewy body disease. Restless legs = awake and voluntary, check ferritin; periodic limb movements = asleep and involuntary, needs a study. Sort the complaint first: can't sleep (insomnia), sleepy by day despite enough time in bed (sleep apnea, narcolepsy), strange behaviour during sleep (parasomnias), or an urge to move the legs at rest (restless legs). Only some of these need a sleep study - insomnia does not. 1. Normal sleep Two kinds of sleep : non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, about 75-80% · rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, about 20-25% Stage N1 : the transition from waking · 1-7 minutes, 2-5% of sleep · theta waves · easily disrupted Stage N2 : most of the night (45-55%) · sleep spindles and K-complexes , linked to memory consolidation · harder to wake Stage N3 (slow-wave sleep) : high-voltage slow delta waves · hardest to wake · growth hormone release · daily brain recovery · sympathetic activity falls REM : low-voltage fast "sawtooth" waves · muscle atonia so dreams are not acted out · vivid dreams · easy to wake Cycling : the first NREM-REM cycle is about 90 minutes , later cycles up to 120 · slow-wave sleep is concentrated in the first third of the night, REM in the last third Age : the need for sleep falls with age · REM falls with age · newborns sleep in chunks A night of sleep: deep stage 3 sleep early in the night, longer REM periods toward morning 2. Measuring sleep Polysomnography (overnight sleep study) : brain waves (EEG) · eye movements · chin and leg muscle activity (tibialis anterior, for leg movements) · airflow and chest and abdominal effort · oxygen saturation · ECG · snoring microphone · body position · rarely video Order it for : obstructive sleep apnea (90-95% of referrals) · narcolepsy · parasomnias Do not order it for insomnia or as a general look at sleep - only to rule out another sleep disorder 3. Comparing the main sleep disorders Insomnia Obstructive sleep apnea Narcolepsy Parasomnias Core Dissatisfied with sleep amount or quality despite the chance to sleep Upper airway closes during sleep → oxygen drops and brief arousals Irrepressible need to sleep by day Abnormal behaviour or experiences during sleep Criteria / features Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking early · 3 nights a week for 3 months · distress or impairment Snoring · witnessed apneas · most common cause of excessive daytime sleepiness · morning headache · poor concentration Sleep lapses 3 times a week for 3 months plus cataplexy , low hypocretin, or short REM latency · tetrad: sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations NREM type: incomplete waking from deep sleep, first third of night , no memory · REM type: dream enactment, last third , recalls dream Who Most common sleep complaint · about 10% meet criteria · comorbid with medical and psychiatric illness About 20% of the population · linked to resistant hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, coronary disease Rare (under 1%) · young NREM: mostly children · REM sleep behaviour disorder: older men Workup Clinical · sleep diary · actigraphy · sleep study only to rule out others Sleep study → apnea-hypopnea index: mild 5-14 · moderate 15-29 · severe 30+ · Epworth, STOP-BANG Sleep study + multiple sleep latency test : mean latency 8 minutes or less, REM at sleep onset Collateral history from bed partner or parent · video rarely captures events Treatment CBT for insomnia first (as effective as pills, fewer side effects) · cautious hypnotics CPAP · dental appliance · surgery (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty) · weight loss, less alcohol Stimulants · modafinil · venlafaxine or other antidepressants for cataplexy and paralysis · sodium oxybate (specialist) Safety of the sleep environment · avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol · clonazepam or melatonin 4. Insomnia Diagnosis by history : sleep-wake diary · actigraphy (a wrist tracker, not used much) · sleep study only to rule out another disorder Treatment CBT for insomnia is first line - few practitioners Sleep hygiene alone does not work - do not confuse it with the CBT elements that do (fixed wake time, bed only when sleepy, bed only for sleep) Medication: benzodiazepines and "z-drugs" (zolpidem, eszopiclone) with caution - dependence, falls in the elderly · melatonin helps about a third, minor effect · avoid alcohol and cannabis · over-the-counter antihistamines work but cause dependence Sedating antidepressants and antipsychotics: the medwiki note says avoid unless depression is present, the upper-year notes list them as options (sources differ - check the slides) 5. Sleep apnea Obstructive : the airway collapses, breathing effort continues until the patient gasps awake CPAP is the treatment of choice - pressure splints the airway open dental appliance (moves the jaw forward) for mild to moderate · surgery for selected patients · weight loss Central sleep apnea : the brain stops signalling to breathe - no breathing effort during the pauses causes: heart failure, stroke, opioids · treat the cause · bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), as CPAP can worsen it 6. Narcolepsy Cause : loss of hypothalamic neurons making hypocretin (orexin) , which keeps us awake - injury, autoimmune, infection Cataplexy : sudden loss of muscle tone (knees, face, neck) triggered by strong emotion , lasting seconds Hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking) hallucinations · sleep paralysis for seconds to minutes Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin: the upper-year notes give a cut-off of 100 pg/mL, the me

Sexual disorders and paraphilias ⭐ Paraphilia + (personal distress or harm to or non-consent of others) for 6 months = paraphilic disorder. Most people with paraphilias do not offend; fantasies are not illegal, acts like exhibitionism, voyeurism and pedophilia are. Psychological therapy (CBT, Good Lives Model) is first line; anti-androgens, LHRH agonists and SSRIs lower drive. Hypersexuality is not a DSM diagnosis - rule out mania, substances, brain lesions and personality disorders. Masochism = undergoing, sadism = inflicting. A paraphilia is an unusual sexual interest; it becomes a paraphilic disorder only when it causes the person distress or involves harm to, or the non-consent of, others. Most people with paraphilias never offend, and not every sex offender has a paraphilia. 1. Context Calling paraphilias a disorder is controversial - many object to pathologizing consensual adult sexual activity Distressed patients still come to general mental health services; the field is a "super-subspecialty" of forensic psychiatry (psychiatry + law: court testimony, risk assessment and management of sex offenders) Legality : pedophilia, voyeurism and exhibitionism are illegal only if acted on (fantasies are not illegal) · fetishism, cross-dressing and coprophilia are not illegal 2. Paraphilic disorders Paraphilia : any intense, persistent sexual interest other than in genital stimulation or fondling with physically mature, consenting human partners Paraphilic disorder (DSM-5) , over at least 6 months , either: personal distress about the interest (not merely from society's disapproval), or desire or behaviour involving another person's distress, injury or death , or unwilling persons or those unable to consent Disorder Focus Exhibitionistic Exposing the genitals to others Voyeuristic Watching others in private activities Frotteuristic Touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person Pedophilic Children Fetishistic Non-living objects, or a highly specific non-genital body part Transvestic Sexually arousing cross-dressing Sexual masochism Undergoing humiliation, bondage or suffering Sexual sadism Inflicting humiliation, bondage or suffering Epidemiology (upper-year notes) : 3.1% report at least one act of exhibitionism · 7.7% admit voyeuristic behaviour Associated factors : childhood sexual abuse · attachment difficulties · social incompetence · emotional dysregulation · disinhibition from low empathy and substance use Comorbidity (studied mostly in sex offenders): mood disorders · alcohol and other substance use · personality disorders Paraphilias are not generally linked to serious sexual violence, but up to 80% of sexual murderers have a history of paraphilic behaviour (upper-year notes) 3. Treatment of paraphilic disorders Psychological treatment is the gold standard CBT : social skills training · cognitive restructuring · victim empathy Good Lives Model : strengths-based - builds the skills to meet normal human needs in personally meaningful, socially acceptable ways Biological (evidence mostly from convicted offenders, and limited) historically surgical castration anti-androgens (cyproterone acetate) luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists (triptorelin, goserelin) SSRIs to lower libido 4. Sex addiction (problematic hypersexuality) Also called sexual compulsivity or impulsivity · not a DSM-5 diagnosis - usually coded as a paraphilic or other specified sexual disorder Problematic when : loss of control over fantasies, urges and behaviour plus adverse consequences or personal distress Research definition: 7 or more orgasms ("total sexual outlets") a week · upper-year notes add: for 6 months, 1-2 hours a day Three models : addiction · compulsivity (like obsessive-compulsive disorder) · impulsivity · in each the behaviour regulates emotional states Rule out and treat what mimics or drives it medical : temporal lobe lesions · brain injury · hypergonadal states · pituitary dysfunction substances : alcohol · amphetamines · cocaine · cannabis bipolar disorder · psychotic disorders personality disorders : antisocial · borderline Management follows the mechanism thought to drive the behaviour · lower impulsivity predicts a better outcome (upper-year notes)

The child welfare system ⭐ Every suspected abuse or neglect of a child must be reported to CAS: the duty overrides confidentiality, a good-faith report cannot be sued, and only 16-17 year olds are exempt. CAS shares little and owes you no report back. CAS cannot consent to treatment until a court places the child in its care. Admission medical within 72 hours, dental within 7 days. A capable child consents for themselves; surgery needs the caseworker's supervisor. Indigenous placement order: extended family → community → another Indigenous family; the band gets 60 days to plan before adoption. The lecture follows children through five cases, and each turns on the same three questions: what must the physician report, who is allowed to know, and who can consent to treatment? The Children's Aid Society (CAS) is the agency at the centre of all of them. 1. The Children's Aid Society and its terms CAS : investigates abuse, neglect and maltreatment of children aged 0-18 , and serious acting-out under age 12 · mandate from Ontario's Child, Youth and Family Services Act (2017) · about 50 non-profit branches in Ontario Kinship care : the child lives with another member of the biological family when the parents cannot cope (under an order of supervision or a temporary care agreement) Temporary care and custody order : the child is in CAS care for a set time · Long-term care : in care beyond that order, ideally with one foster family for the whole stay Crown (society) ward : CAS holds long-term guardianship Capable (the Health Care Consent Act definition): able to understand the information about a treatment and appreciate the foreseeable consequences of deciding or not deciding 2. Reporting and information (Case 1) Every suspected case of child abuse or neglect must be reported to CAS - a professional and legal duty that overrides confidentiality and any other law against disclosure a report made in good faith (not maliciously or without reasonable cause) is immune from civil action failing to report: criminal prosecution, civil liability, or professional misconduct (College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario) · Ontario fine up to $5,000 (across Canada $500-$10,000 and up to 1 year in jail) ages 16 and 17: reporting is not mandatory , though they can choose to receive services What CAS tells the physician : only relevant medical details and the general reason the child is followed · few details early in an investigation · no duty to report back after you raise a concern When CAS can decide about treatment urgent treatment refused by the parents → CAS can apprehend the child through an emergency court hearing non-urgent → CAS can apprehend and authorize a medical examination (an exam is not treatment) until a court places the child in CAS care, CAS is not a substitute decision maker 3. How a child comes into care 4. The team around the child (Case 2) Care needs a multidisciplinary team : physician · caseworker · foster parents · school · biological parents where appropriate Access visits : the court sets how often, whether supervised (by a CAS worker or relative), and where · CAS or the parents can ask the court to change or remove them · a crown ward with a long-term access order is usually not eligible for adoption Individual Education Plan (IEP) : written by educators for a child with special learning or developmental needs, naming everyone's role Who comes to appointments : the caseworker and foster parent attend (for information, adherence and feedback) unless the child prefers to be seen alone adolescents are always seen alone for part of the visit a possible abuse victim is seen alone, with a nurse present 5. Medical needs of children in care (Case 3) Admission medical within 72 hours of entering care · first dental check within 7 days (usually at the admission medical) · then dental check-ups every 6 months (sources differ: upper-year notes give every 12 months - check the slides) Severe dental caries can be a clue to neglect Problem Share affected Most common Chronic medical conditions 80%
