Anxiety (in-class session) ⭐ Beta-blockers are an as-needed treatment for performance anxiety; buspirone treats anxiety but not depression. The anxiety disorders reviewed: panic, generalized anxiety, social anxiety, agoraphobia. A short in-class review of the anxiety disorders and two medication points. The full charts are in Week 18: 01 - Anxiety Disorders (telling the disorders apart) and 03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD (treatment). 1. The anxiety disorders reviewed Panic disorder · generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) · social anxiety disorder · agoraphobia The note lists specific learning disorder as the fifth, which the Week 18 chart does not count among the anxiety disorders - it lists specific phobia there (sources differ - check the slides) 2. Medication points Buspirone : indicated for anxiety only, not for depression Beta-blockers for performance anxiety : taken as needed in social anxiety disorder, because they slow the heart rate The note also records "depression = serotonin (5-HT2) receptors" without context (check the slides)

Delirium ⭐ Inattention with acute, fluctuating onset is delirium until proven otherwise - CAM needs features 1 and 2 plus 3 or 4. Hypoactive delirium is the commonest and is mistaken for depression. Dementia is the strongest risk factor, and delirium speeds later decline. Use benzodiazepines only for alcohol withdrawal, physostigmine for anticholinergic toxicity; otherwise low-dose antipsychotic and only for distressing symptoms. Hallucinations in delirium are mostly visual; in depression and schizophrenia mostly auditory. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with a medical cause - it is a sign that something else is wrong. Screen for it, hunt for every trigger, and treat the cause; medication only manages symptoms. 1. Approach 2. Definition and subtypes DSM-5 criteria disturbance of attention (direct, focus, sustain, shift) and awareness (orientation) develops over a short time and fluctuates through the day · a change from baseline plus another cognitive disturbance : memory · orientation · language · visuospatial · perception not better explained by a neurocognitive disorder or coma · evidence of a medical cause , substance, medication or toxin onset: the medwiki note says hours to days, the upper-year notes days to weeks (sources differ - check the slides) Specifiers : substance intoxication or withdrawal · medication-induced · another medical condition · multiple causes · acute vs persistent Activity subtypes Hypoactive (most common, about 65%) : drowsy, withdrawn, refuses to eat or for care, approaching stupor - often missed or mistaken for depression Hyperactive (about 25%) : hypervigilant, loud fast speech, combative, pulls at lines - can look like mania Mixed (about 10%) : swings between the two Psychosis in about 42% : visual hallucinations most common , then auditory and tactile · poorly formed paranoid delusions · more in hyperactive 3. Who gets it Medical wards 10-20% · after surgery up to 50% · ICU up to 80% · elderly 10-15% at admission, 10-40% during it · up to 60% of nursing-home residents over 75 Risk factors : dementia (the strongest) · age over 65 · male · prior delirium · functional impairment · hearing or vision loss · polypharmacy (4 or more medications) · alcohol use disorder · dehydration, malnutrition · living in an institution Up to 40% preventable 4. Causes and pathophysiology Common culprit drugs : benzodiazepines, diphenhydramine, tricyclics, furosemide · anticholinergics · opioids · steroids · digoxin and many more Infection (lung, urine, skin, gut, central nervous system) · metabolic (sodium, calcium, glucose, thyroid, B12, thiamine, liver or kidney failure) · environment (night bloodwork, no clock or window, room changes, restraints, missing glasses and hearing aids) · structural (low oxygen, high carbon dioxide, heart attack, heart failure, stroke, seizure) · urinary retention · constipation · pain An older patient's heart attack may present only as delirium Pathophysiology (several hypotheses) low acetylcholine (leading theory) with excess dopamine, noradrenaline and glutamate neuroinflammation (peripheral inflammation activates brain cytokines) · oxidative stress · high glucocorticoids · disrupted circadian rhythm · network disconnection · aging lowers brain reserve Two-way link with dementia : dementia is the strongest risk factor, and delirium raises the risk of later cognitive decline 5. Assessment at the bedside History : baseline · onset, course and fluctuation · sleep · hallucinations ("have you seen anything unusual?") and paranoia ("is anyone hurting you?") · collateral from family and nursing · medications Observe first from the doorway: picking, pulling at lines, drowsiness, agitation Orientation out of 10 : year, season, month, date, day · country, province, city, building, floor Attention : tap at each "A" in "SAVEAHAART" · months backwards · serial 7s · spell WORLD backwards · digit span (sources differ: medwiki says 4 digits, upper-year notes 5 - check the slides) · clock drawing 6. Delirium vs dementia vs depression Delirium Dementia Depression Onset Acute Insidious Variable Course Fluctuating through the day Progressive · may worsen in the evening (sundowning) Variable Reversible Usually No Usually Consciousness Impaired Clear until late Mostly clear Attention Impaired - the core feature Intact until late (except frontotemporal) Mildly impaired Orientation Impaired Intact until later stages Intact Memory Poor Poor Mostly intact Hallucinations Mostly visual Mostly visual Usually auditory, if psychotic Delusions Poorly formed, paranoid Fixed, often paranoid Complex, mood-congruent 7. Management No drug treats delirium itself - treat the causes (medications, infection, fluids, immobility, pain, sensory deprivation) Non-drug care : reorient often, clocks and calendars · family involvement · familiar items · glasses and hearing aids · mobilize early · lights and blinds open by day, dark and quiet at night · avoid restraints and lines · fewer staff changes · hydration and nutrition · stop offending drugs Antipsychotics for distressing psychosis or agitation in hyperactive delirium: haloperidol (about 1 mg twice a day by mouth) or risperidone · check the QT · avoid in seizures, Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies Prognosis : higher mortality (upper-year notes: 10% at 3 months, 34% at 6 months), institutionalization and dementia · may last up to 12 months · many never return to baseline

Cognitive disorders in the elderly ⭐ Mild vs major neurocognitive disorder turns on one thing: is independence in everyday activities lost? Alzheimer: insidious, memory for new information first. Vascular: abrupt, stepwise, focal signs. Lewy body: fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism after the dementia, REM sleep behaviour disorder. Frontotemporal: young, behaviour or language first, memory spared. Rule out depression, hypothyroidism, delirium, medications and B12 deficiency. MoCA catches mild impairment that the MMSE misses. Two questions: does the decline cost the person their independence (major vs mild neurocognitive disorder), and which pattern of onset and symptoms does it follow (Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal)? Always look for the reversible causes first. 1. The neurocognitive disorders Core feature: an acquired decline in cognition · a spectrum of delirium → mild neurocognitive disorder → major neurocognitive disorder Six cognitive domains : complex attention · executive function · learning and memory · language · perceptual-motor · social cognition Mild neurocognitive disorder (mild cognitive impairment) : modest decline in 1 or more domains · independence preserved (more effort or strategies needed) 10-20% of adults over 65 · upper-year notes: 20-40% progress within 5 years · medwiki: about 10% a year, and over half stay stable or return to normal Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) : significant decline in 1 or more domains that interferes with independence (at least needs help with instrumental activities such as bills and medications) both: not only during a delirium · not better explained by another mental disorder such as depression severity: mild = trouble with instrumental activities of daily living (shopping, housework, money, medications, transport, phone) · moderate = trouble with basic activities of daily living (dressing, eating, bathing, toileting, transferring, continence) · severe = fully dependent Epidemiology : 5-7% of adults over 60 · 1-2% at 65-69, doubling every 5 years to about 30% over 85 · 65% female (longer life) 2. Normal aging vs dementia Normal aging : slightly slower processing · occasionally forgets but remembers later · short-term memory a little affected, long-term kept · language, abstraction and function preserved Red flags : memory loss that affects function · trouble with familiar tasks, language or abstraction · disorientation · poor judgement · change in mood, behaviour or personality · loss of initiative · misplacing items Risk factors : age (the biggest) · mild cognitive impairment · family history and genes · head injury · vascular risk factors · inactivity · alcohol · depression · chronic kidney disease · hearing loss · less education · social isolation - up to 40% of dementia is potentially preventable 3. Comparing the dementias Alzheimer disease Vascular dementia Dementia with Lewy bodies Frontotemporal dementia Share Most common, 60-90% Second, 15-30% Found in 20-35% of dementia cases (upper-year notes) Fourth · about 5% Onset 70s-80s · earlier with Down syndrome or genetic forms 0.2% at 65-70, 16% over 80 · more men 60-80 · more men · usually no family history Early, 40-60 · family history in about 40% Course Insidious, steadily progressive Abrupt, stepwise · highly variable Insidious · fluctuates within the day Insidious, progressive Hallmark features Memory for new information first (anterograde amnesia) · then aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, executive dysfunction Focal neurological signs · slowed processing and attention · executive dysfunction · mood and personality change Visual hallucinations (well formed) · parkinsonism starting after the cognitive decline · REM sleep behaviour disorder · falls · severe antipsychotic sensitivity Behavioural : disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality · language variant : early aphasia · memory relatively spared Pathology Beta-amyloid plaques (before symptoms) + tau neurofibrillary tangles → neuron loss, low acetylcholine · APOE4 Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke · usual vascular risk factors Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein inclusions) in cortex and subcortex Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy · tau or TDP-43 inclusions Survival 8-12 years (medwiki: mean 10) · often aspiration pneumonia Highly variable Rapid (sources differ: medwiki 3-5 years, upper-year notes 5-7 - check the slides) · falls, swallowing Sources differ: medwiki 5-10 years from onset, upper-year notes 6-11 - both about 3-4 years from diagnosis - check the slides Parkinson disease dementia : motor symptoms come at least a year before cognitive ones (the reverse of Lewy body dementia) · milder hallucinations · better levodopa response · dementia in 50-80% of Parkinson patients after 10-15 years 4. Workup Most common reversible causes : depression (pseudodementia) · hypothyroidism · delirium · medications · B12 deficiency Imaging : CT rules out tumour, chronic subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke · MRI gives more detail (small tumours, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease) Mnemonic for causes (upper-year notes) : AV DEMENTIA - Alzheimer · vascular · dementia with Lewy bodies, depression · ethanol · medical and metabolic · endocrine, ears, eyes, environment · neurologic · toxins, tumour, trauma · infection · amnesia, apnea, autoimmune 5. Screening tests Test Format Abnormal Strengths Weaknesses MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination) Out of 30 · about 7 minutes · orientation, registration, attention, recall, language Under 24 (26 or more could be normal) Quick · a baseline to track change Misses mild impairment (about 18% sensitivity), frontal and visuospatial deficits · biased by education MoCA (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) Out of 30 · about 10 minutes · more domains incl. executive Under 26 Best for mild impairment (about 90% sensitivity) · many languages, a version for the blind Longer · adjust for age and education Mini-Cog 3-word recall + clock draw Recalls 0 words, or 1-2 words with an abnormal

Maintaining boundaries ⭐ A crossing is harmless and non-exploitative; a violation exploits the patient through the relationship and harms them or their care. Sexual remarks alone count as sexual abuse under the RHPA. Sexual contact within 1 year of the relationship ending is still abuse. Report within 30 days to the professional's college, on reasonable grounds, without the patient's name unless they consent. Always offer a chaperone for intimate examinations. Does the departure from the usual professional role harm or exploit the patient? If not, it is a boundary crossing; if it does, it is a boundary violation. Sexual abuse of a patient is always a violation, and any physician who learns of it must report. 1. Boundaries Boundaries : the rules that keep the professional relationship separate from every other relationship Boundary crossing : a departure from usual practice that is harmless, non-exploitative , and may even support care Boundary violation : harmful or potentially harmful to the patient and the care, because it exploits the patient through the doctor-patient relationship 2. The CPSO Boundary Violations policy The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) requires physicians to set and keep appropriate boundaries Before any examination, treatment or procedure : explain its scope and reason in advance · explain why any question about sexual matters is being asked · obtain consent Always offer a third party (chaperone) for an intimate examination, whatever the gender of physician or patient · the patient may bring their own Preventing violations : sensitivity to gender and culture · know patient risk factors ( patients who have been abused are at higher risk of exploitation ) · know your own risk factors · recognize warning signs 3. The Regulated Health Professions Act (RHPA) Sexual abuse of a patient means any of: sexual intercourse or other physical sexual relations touching of a sexual nature behaviour or remarks of a sexual nature toward the patient A person is a patient if any one applies : the physician charged or was paid for care · contributed to their health record · they consented to care the physician recommended · the physician prescribed them a medication needing a prescription After the relationship ends : sexual contact within 1 year is still sexual abuse upper-year notes add: 5 years for psychotherapy , and it may be misconduct with someone closely associated with the patient, depending on the clinical problem, type of care and emotional dependence 4. Mandatory reporting Same logic as child-abuse reporting: the report must be reasonable, not proven Failure to report : fine of up to $25,000 and licence suspension of up to 6 months (medwiki note)
04 Management of Cognitive Disorders and Dementia

Management of cognitive disorders and dementia ⭐ Look for unmet needs and medical causes, and use non-drug approaches first - antipsychotics only for severe agitation, aggression or psychosis, or a safety risk. Citalopram is the best-supported antidepressant; risperidone the best-supported antipsychotic for BPSD. Lewy body dementia: be wary of antipsychotics, use cholinesterase inhibitors. Suspected dementia must be reported to the MTO; elder abuse must be reported only in long-term care. Wandering, undressing and vocalizing rarely respond to drugs. There is no cure, so the aim is function, safety, comfort and dignity for the patient and support for the caregiver. For behavioural and psychological symptoms, find the cause and try non-drug approaches first ; medication is for severe or dangerous symptoms. 1. General management of dementia Alliance with patient and family → disclose the diagnosis and prognosis, plan treatment, raise safety and legal issues Safety : the 3 Fs - fire, flood, falls · driving · medications · home Legal duties must report to the Ministry of Transportation (MTO) when dementia is suspected no legal duty to report elder abuse - unless it happens in a long-term care home Future planning : power of attorney · placement decisions (long-term care waiting lists are long) · advance care planning Community supports : home care (Ontario Health atHome) · Alzheimer Society · Meals on Wheels (especially after an MTO report for someone who lives alone or with a non-driving partner) · blister packs and medication delivery · day programs · caregiver support Risk reduction for further decline : nutrition · exercise · hearing · sleep · cognitive training · social engagement · frailty · vascular risk factors · minimize anticholinergics and polypharmacy Goals of medication : delay progression and functional decline · control symptoms · comfort · quality of life and dignity · treat comorbidities such as depression · support the caregiver 2. Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) About 90% of people with dementia have them · they arise from the brain disease, not from earlier psychiatric illness affective : depression · anxiety · elation or disinhibition · apathy behavioural : irritability · agitation or aggression · pacing, wandering · sleep disturbance · sexual disinhibition · vocalizing psychotic : hallucinations · delusions (paranoid or misidentification) By dementia type : frontotemporal → behavioural symptoms · Lewy body → visual hallucinations · vascular → depression and apathy · Alzheimer → delusions, mostly persecutory "Responsive behaviours" : every behaviour expresses something meaningful - a response to the person's surroundings, needs or misread information Causes : unmet needs (pain, thirst, hunger, toileting) · medical illness or delirium · medications · lower distress tolerance · learned behaviour · environment (over- or under-stimulating) · caregiver stress or lack of training Consequences : earlier long-term care · hospitalization · emotional and financial strain 3. Assessment and approach DICE : Describe · Investigate · Create · Evaluate · also ABC (antecedent, behaviour, consequence) and the PIECES caregiver training Rating scales : Neuropsychiatric Inventory · Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory · Brief Agitation Rating Scale · Pittsburgh Agitation Scale, among others 4. Non-drug management (always first) Reduce isolation, stimulate the senses, relax : talking and singing · family videos · pet and music therapy · multisensory (Snoezelen) room · aromatherapy · bright light · massage and touch Engagement : recreation · walking programs · group exercise Behaviour therapy : reward behaviours incompatible with the problem one · cueing · staff training Practical techniques (upper-year notes) : priming (predictable routine, familiar objects) · miming (communicate in more than one way at once) · timing (time of day, pacing) · environment (quiet, daylight) · gentle persuasion Limits : modest effect · weaker for aggression and psychosis Hard to treat with any drug : wandering · undressing · vocalizing · inappropriate urination · hoarding · eating non-food items 5. Medication for BPSD Older brains need lower doses and are more sensitive to side effects · minimize polypharmacy Drug Use Key adverse effects / notes Citalopram (also escitalopram, sertraline) Depression or anxiety - try first (low risk) · best-supported SSRI for BPSD Low sodium · avoid paroxetine (anticholinergic) and fluoxetine (long washout) Risperidone Psychosis, agitation, aggression (high risk, benefit must outweigh harm) · best for BPSD Most extrapyramidal effects of the atypicals Haloperidol (typical) Emergency when other intramuscular options are unavailable Most extrapyramidal effects Olanzapine - Sedating · most metabolic effects Quetiapine Lower doses in Lewy body dementia Sedating Aripiprazole - Akathisia Lorazepam, zopiclone Short-term only for sleep Sedation · confusion · tolerance Trazodone Sleep (short term) · frontotemporal dementia Sedation · orthostatic hypotension By type : frontotemporal → trazodone and SSRIs (citalopram) · Lewy body → cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine first for fluctuation, agitation and psychosis · extremely sensitive to antipsychotics (sources differ: the medwiki lecture note allows quetiapine or clozapine, its dementia with Lewy bodies note says do not use antipsychotics - check the slides) Severe cases : anticonvulsants or short-acting benzodiazepines (upper-year notes) The upper-year notes list atypical antipsychotics or antidepressants first; the medwiki note puts antidepressants first unless there is psychosis, aggression or risk (check the slides)

Pharmacotherapy of cognitive enhancers ⭐ Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild to severe Alzheimer, Parkinson disease dementia and Lewy body dementia; memantine only for moderate to severe Alzheimer. Cholinergic side effects: gut upset most often, but watch for bradycardia and syncope - a heart rate under 50 or heart block is a contraindication. No role in mild cognitive impairment. Titrate every 4 weeks, never stop abruptly, and taper by halves every 4 weeks. Loss of effect after years is progression, not a reason to switch. Two classes: cholinesterase inhibitors raise acetylcholine, memantine damps excess glutamate. They slow decline modestly but cure nothing - the art is choosing the right diagnosis and stage, titrating slowly, and knowing when to switch or stop. 1. The two classes Cholinesterase inhibitors block acetylcholine breakdown in the synapse; memantine blocks the NMDA glutamate receptor Cholinesterase inhibitors : donepezil , rivastigmine , galantamine Memantine Mechanism Block acetylcholinesterase , the enzyme that breaks acetylcholine into acetate and choline → more acetylcholine in the synapse (not reuptake inhibition) Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist → less activation by the excess glutamate of dementia → less calcium-driven cell damage Indication by diagnosis Alzheimer · mixed Alzheimer and vascular · Parkinson disease dementia · dementia with Lewy bodies · vascular alone: possible (sources differ: the lecture note and upper-year notes allow some benefit, the medwiki vascular dementia note says not for isolated vascular dementia - check the slides) Alzheimer only · not frontotemporal or pure vascular dementia Indication by stage Mild to severe dementia - all three equally effective, none superior Moderate to severe only Adverse effects Cholinergic excess (DUMBBELLS) : diarrhea, nausea and other gut effects (most common) · urinary incontinence · miosis · bronchospasm · bradycardia, syncope · emesis · lethargy · lacrimation · salivation · also insomnia, nightmares, muscle cramps, agitation, seizures Usually well tolerated · dizziness · headache · constipation · also agitation or sleepiness, hypertension, hallucinations Relative contraindications Heart rate under 50 , sick sinus, left bundle branch block, third-degree heart block · active peptic ulcer · severe asthma or COPD · epilepsy · delirium · angle-closure glaucoma · very low weight Severe renal impairment: lower the dose Metabolism Donepezil: liver (half-life about 70 hours) · galantamine: liver (± kidney) · rivastigmine: kidney per medwiki, hydrolysis per upper-year notes (check the slides) Kidney - adjust for low creatinine clearance Combination of both classes: the medwiki note says they can be combined, its Alzheimer note and the upper-year notes say the evidence is insufficient (sources differ - check the slides) No evidence in mild cognitive impairment - prescribe only for confirmed major neurocognitive disorder, but not so late that the neurons are already lost 2. Dosing Drug Start Usual / maximum Notes Donepezil 2.5-5 mg each morning 5-10 mg · max 10 mg a day Liver ("donepezi L = liver") Galantamine 8 mg a day (or 4 mg twice a day) 8-24 mg · max 24 mg a day Often twice daily Rivastigmine 1.5 mg twice a day 4.5 mg twice a day · max 6 mg twice a day Patch available · " R ivastigmine = renal" Memantine 5 mg once a day max 10 mg twice a day Renal dosing Titrate very slowly : raise the dose about every 4 weeks · a trial takes 3-6 months (about twice as slow as antidepressants) Memantine: the upper-year notes raise it by 5 mg weekly, reaching 10 mg twice a day by week 4 (sources differ: the medwiki note raises all these drugs monthly - check the slides) Never stop abruptly 3. Monitoring and expectations Before and during : cognition (MoCA or MMSE, serial) · function and behaviour · patient and caregiver report · ECG, heart rate, blood pressure · weight Expect modest benefit : they slow decline rather than stop it, so scores still fall upper-year notes: cognitive gains peak at about 6 months and return to baseline by 9-12 months · global measures peak by 3 months may prevent or ease neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, apathy) Side effects are usually mild - do not add another drug to treat them · try a lower dose or a shorter half-life agent 4. Switching and stopping Stop when : dementia worsens significantly over 6 months on treatment · no meaningful benefit · severe or end-stage dementia (total care) · intolerable side effects · poor adherence or monitoring not possible Taper : halve the dose every 4 weeks (twice as slow as SSRIs) · watch for rapid cognitive decline or responsive behaviours

Substance use disorders ⭐ Alcohol (and benzodiazepine) withdrawal can kill through seizures and delirium tremens, so it is scored with the CIWA-Ar and treated with benzodiazepines plus IM thiamine; opioid withdrawal is miserable but not fatal. Substance use disorder = 2+ of 11 criteria in 12 months; 6+ is severe. Pinpoint pupils in opioid overdose, dilated pupils in opioid withdrawal and stimulant use. Visual hallucinations in withdrawal point to alcohol. Methadone is a full agonist, buprenorphine a partial one, naloxone an antagonist. Naltrexone and acamprosate for alcohol use disorder; varenicline plus a patch for smoking. Substance use runs on a spectrum and becomes a disorder at 2 of 11 criteria in a year. Each drug class is then learned the same way - intoxication, withdrawal, treatment - and the question that matters at the bedside is which withdrawals can kill (alcohol and benzodiazepines) and which only feel like they might (opioids). 1. A spectrum, and a reward circuit 20% of Canadians aged 15+ have a substance use disorder at some point, most often alcohol or cannabis (upper-year notes: 1 in 15 over age 15, most commonly alcohol - sources differ, check the slides) The spectrum : beneficial → non-problematic → problematic (negative consequences: impaired driving, binges) → chronic dependence (habitual and compulsive despite harm) Neurobiology : dysregulated mesolimbic dopamine - the ventral tegmental area releases dopamine into the nucleus accumbens (reward), which keeps reward-seeking going · the mesocortical pathway is secondary (the transcluded condition note names the mesocortical pathway - check the slides) 2. DSM-5 substance use disorder At least 2 of 11 in the past 12 months , in four groups: control : more or longer than intended · cannot cut down · much time spent getting, using, recovering · craving social : failing work, school or home roles · use despite relationship problems · activities given up risk : use when physically hazardous · use despite a known physical or psychological problem pharmacological : tolerance · withdrawal Severity : mild 2-3 · moderate 4-5 · severe 6+ · remission : early after 3 months, sustained after 1 year · "on maintenance therapy" 3. Withdrawal syndromes compared Substance Intoxication Withdrawal Danger Managing withdrawal Use disorder treatment Alcohol Slurred speech · poor coordination · unsteady gait · nystagmus · poor attention or memory · stupor, coma Starts 4-12 h after the last drink: sweating, fast heart rate · tremor · insomnia · nausea, vomiting · agitation · transient hallucinations ( visual = red flag ) · seizures at 12-48 h · delirium tremens at 48-96 h Can be fatal - 20% mortality if missed CIWA-Ar score → benzodiazepine · IM thiamine + folic acid naltrexone · acamprosate Benzodiazepines Same picture as alcohol (DSM-5 groups them) Very similar to alcohol withdrawal As for alcohol No separate detail in the sources - Opioids Euphoria, then apathy · pinpoint pupils · drowsiness to coma · slurred speech · toxidrome: coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression , low blood pressure, low temperature, low reflexes Low mood · nausea, vomiting, diarrhea · muscle aches · tears, runny nose · dilated pupils · sweating · yawning · fever · insomnia Overdose kills; withdrawal is not fatal , but it drives re-use COWS score · opioid agonist · symptom relief: clonidine, ondansetron, loperamide, NSAIDs Methadone · buprenorphine-naloxone · naloxone kits Stimulants (cocaine, crack, methamphetamine) Euphoria, hypervigilance, anxiety, anger · fast or slow heart rate · dilated pupils · high or low blood pressure · sweating · weight loss · chest pain, arrhythmia, seizures · paranoia, psychosis "Crash": low mood + fatigue · vivid nightmares · too much or too little sleep · increased appetite · slowing or agitation Overdose: overheating, seizures, kidney injury · injecting raises suicide risk No medication given in the sources Harm reduction · psychoeducation Cannabis : withdrawal (sleep problems, irritability, restlessness, appetite loss) has no approved medication , nor does the use disorder · Nicotine : withdrawal handled with nicotine replacement 4. Alcohol Drinking guidance : older low-risk guidelines - women 10 a week (2 a day), men 15 a week (3 a day) · Canada's 2023 guidance: 1-2 a week low risk · 3-6 moderate · 7+ high Screening : the AUDIT (10 items, about 97% sensitive and 78% specific) beats CAGE and the single-question screen · AUDIT-C (3 items) measures consumption only Why withdrawal is dangerous : chronic alcohol leaves too little GABA and too much glutamate → a hyperexcitable brain → seizures, plus autonomic overdrive Alcohol withdrawal over days: minor withdrawal and hallucinosis peak at 1-2 days, seizures around day 1-2, delirium tremens peaks around day 3-4 Labs: point-of-care glucose · electrolytes with calcium, magnesium, phosphate · complete blood count · clotting · liver tests · blood alcohol The note says thiamine must be intramuscular because oral thiamine is poorly absorbed · thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy Agitated intoxication : antipsychotic with breathing monitored, not a benzodiazepine Alcohol use disorder : naltrexone once daily (cuts drinking up to 50%; not with liver dysfunction ) · acamprosate three times daily · motivational interviewing · peer support (Alcoholics Anonymous, SMART Recovery) · CBT · family therapy 5. Opioids Overdose → naloxone as soon as it is suspected Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) : scores withdrawal and guides buprenorphine induction Drug Type Route Key point Methadone Full agonist Oral Maintenance or taper · high dependence · sedation, respiratory depression, constipation Buprenorphine Partial agonist - its effect plateaus Sublingual Lower dependence and milder withdrawal Buprenorphine-naloxone (Suboxone) Partial agonist + antagonist Sublingual The naloxone discourages misuse Naloxone Antagonist Intranasal or intramuscular Reverses overdose · triggers withdrawal in a depend
07 Concurrent Mental Health and Substance Use Disorders

Concurrent mental health and substance use disorders ⭐ Treat both disorders together, and match the program to severity: both severe = a concurrent disorders program (quadrant IV). About half of people with a psychotic disorder have a substance use disorder; tobacco is the most used. In anxiety, the anxiety disorder usually comes first; panic links to alcohol, generalized anxiety to illicit drugs. Urine toxicology clarifies, it never punishes. Substance use makes psychosis start earlier, last longer and relapse more. A concurrent disorder means the patient meets the full criteria for both a mental disorder and a substance use disorder. Each worsens the other, so both are treated together , in a program chosen by how severe each one is. 1. How common, and why it matters Substance use disorders are among the most common comorbidities of severe mental illness about 50% of people with a psychotic disorder have one, against about 15% of the general population Substance use worsens the course of the mental illness and increases hospitalization 2. Assessment and recovery Diagnose both : each disorder must meet its own criteria Ask about : patterns of use · cravings and triggers · current coping · how emotional states change use · physical health, including acute or chronic pain · withdrawal symptoms History : substance history (age started, periods of not using) · psychiatric · family · medical · collateral · urine toxicology - to clarify what was taken, never punitive · assessment over time (longitudinal) Recovery = empowerment · self-management · engagement with community and care team · better functioning · a meaningful quality of life ① ask what the patient wants from recovery (e.g. going back to school) · ② expect setbacks, and keep hope and positive expectations VEAR model : V ulnerability → E xposure → A ddiction → R ecovery, marking the transition points and what to target at each VEAR model: vulnerability (genetic, childhood), exposure (adolescent risk factors), addiction (adult brain changes, aggravating and harm-reduction factors), then recovery and its treatments 3. The three main pairings Pairing The link Clinical approach Mood disorders + substance use (major depression, persistent depressive disorder, bipolar disorders) Each raises the risk of the other and changes its course Map mood changes against substance use · find what explains the overlap, especially mood lability · predisposing factors (genetic, environmental, psychological) · psychoeducation · treat both with an individual plan Anxiety disorders + substance use About 75% of people with an anxiety disorder use substances · the anxiety disorder usually comes first · 2-5× the risk of a substance use disorder · panic disorder → alcohol · generalized anxiety disorder → illicit drugs Predisposing factors · how withdrawal feeds anxiety · psychoeducation on substances and anxiety · treat both Psychosis + substance use Schizophrenia: 5× the risk of a substance use disorder · tobacco is the most used (55-85% have nicotine use disorder), then cannabis · more binge drinking · substances, especially crystal meth, mimic psychosis , sometimes beyond intoxication Substance use brings on psychosis earlier , makes symptoms more intense and longer, raises relapse and treatment resistance , and lengthens hospital stays 4. Matching care to severity: the quadrants of care Quadrant Mental illness Substance use disorder Where care happens I Less severe Less severe Community treatment program II More severe Less severe Mental health program III Less severe More severe Addictions treatment program IV More severe More severe Concurrent disorders program Social determinants of health shape whether a patient can succeed in treatment, so consider them for each patient

Somatic symptom and related disorders ⭐ Unconscious production with no gain = somatic symptom and related disorders; intentional production for the sick role = factitious disorder; intentional for an external reward = malingering. Illness anxiety has few or no symptoms - the fear of disease is the problem. Conversion disorder shows a mismatch with known neurology (Hoover's sign, improvement with distraction). Somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety both need 6+ months. Treatment aims at function and coping, started early, with a multidisciplinary plan. The suffering is real whether or not the symptom is medically explained. These disorders are told apart by two questions: is the symptom produced consciously, and what is gained from it? The aim of treatment is coping and function, not cure. 1. The problem of definition Medically unexplained symptoms : pain in several places · disturbed function of an organ system · fatigue may be a physiological disturbance, emotion, or a condition not yet diagnosed common: 15-25% in primary care · 39-50% in specialist clinics · over 60% in neurology Many names, depending on who sees the patient : psychogenic, psychosomatic, somatoform, functional, conversion, "hysteria" Functional disorders exist in every system : irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia · fibromyalgia · non-cardiac chest pain · chronic fatigue syndrome · tension headache, functional seizures and movement disorders · temporomandibular joint dysfunction more often female · overlap with anxiety and depression 2. Telling the disorders apart Somatic symptom disorder Illness anxiety disorder Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) Factitious disorder Malingering Core 1 or more distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours about them Preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness , with no or only mild symptoms Altered voluntary motor or sensory function incompatible with known disease Falsifies or induces illness in self or another, with no external reward Fakes or exaggerates for an external reward (time off work, drugs, avoiding arrest) Criteria At least 1 of: disproportionate thoughts about seriousness · persistently high health anxiety · excessive time and energy on symptoms · symptomatic for 6+ months (the symptom itself may change) High health anxiety · excessive checking or maladaptive avoidance · 6+ months · the feared illness may change Clinical findings show the mismatch · not better explained · distress or impairment Deception evident · presents self (or a victim) as ill or injured Not a DSM disorder Specifiers Predominant pain · persistent · severity (mild, moderate, severe) Care-seeking vs care-avoidant Symptom type (weakness, movement, seizures, sensory, speech, swallowing) · acute (under 6 months) or persistent · with or without stressor Single or recurrent episodes · imposed on self vs imposed on another (by proxy) - Symptom production Unconscious Unconscious Unconscious Intentional Intentional Gain None None Internal psychological gain (sources differ: upper-year notes say internal gain, the medwiki figure groups it with no gain - Hoover's sign (weak hip extension returns with opposite hip flexion against resistance) · tremor entrainment · controlled arm drop in a "seizure" Sorting unexplained symptoms by how they are produced, why, and for what gain 3. Cognitive enhancing medication have not shown any evidence at all for the treatment of neuropsychiatric symptoms. All the rest of the statements are true.
Q1 · Cognitive Disorders in the Elderly

Which is a good cognitive screening test to use if you suspect early cognitive changes or mild cognitive impairment? Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) Mini Mental Status Exam (MMSE) Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) All of the above The correct answer is C. The review's annotation: "MOCA is more accurate". The Week 20 study guide adds that the MoCA has higher sensitivity than the MMSE and is therefore better at detecting early cognitive impairment. The inherited Cognitive Disorders note agrees: the MoCA is better than the MMSE

Margaret is a 42-year-old patient with untreated depression. She is reluctant to begin antidepressant treatment due to concerns about treatment-induced weight gain. Which of the following antidepressant treatments is associated with the greatest risk of weight gain? Escitalopram Fluoxetine Mirtazapine Bupropion The correct answer is C. The review marks mirtazapine as carrying a HIGH risk of weight gain, and the Week 17 study guide notes that its increased appetite and sedation are more prominent than with other antidepressants. The inherited Pharmacology of Antidepressants note lists weight gain among mirt

A 36-year-old patient has only partially responded to his second monotherapy with a first-line antidepressant. Which of the following has the best evidence of efficacy for augmenting antidepressants in patients with inadequate response? Adding an atypical antipsychotic Adding buspirone Adding a stimulant The correct answer is A. The review's annotation: a low-dose atypical antipsychotic. The inherited Depressive Disorders note lists aripiprazole and brexpiprazole as the first-line add-ons when the response to an SSRI is incomplete.

A 24-year-old woman with no history of psychiatric symptoms presents with a major depressive episode and is prescribed an antidepressant. She quickly experiences improved mood and exhibits symptoms suggestive of hypomania. Recommendations from the International Society for Bipolar Disorders (ISBD) state that the patient’s antidepressant should be: Discontinued Maintained, but ONLY IF a mood stabilizer is added The correct answer is A. The review: antidepressant treatment is not recommended in bipolar depression because it can cause a switch to mania or hypomania. The inherited Bipolar Disorders note says antidepressants should be avoided, or used only cautiously, in patients with a history of antidepressa

A 38-year-old patient with depression presents with depressed mood, anhedonia, and loss of energy. These symptoms can be conceptualized as reflecting reduced positive affect; such a categorization is theoretically useful because it may direct treatment choice. Specifically, symptoms of reduced positive affect are hypothetically more likely to respond to agents that enhance: Serotonin and possibly dopamine function Dopamine and possibly norepinephrine function Norepinephrine and possibly serotonin function The correct answer is B. The review's annotation: positive affect = dopamine, negative affect = serotonin. Its table (adapted from Stahl) links loss of joy, loss of interest, low energy and poor concentration to dopamine and norepinephrine, and guilt, anxiety, hostility and irritability to norepinep
Q6 · Phenomenology and the Mental Status Exam

A 30-year-old man tells you his mood is "fine, maybe a 6 out of 10". Throughout the interview he is tearful and his facial expression barely changes. In the mental status exam, where do you record the tearful, restricted presentation you observe? Affect Mood Thought content Behaviour The correct answer is A. Affect is what the patient's emotional state looks like to you, in the moment (the weather); mood is the patient's own report of their state over time (the climate). His "6 out of 10" is his mood; the tearful, restricted expression is his affect, and you would also note that
Q7 · Phenomenology and the Mental Status Exam

A 22-year-old woman reports hearing a voice commenting on her actions when no one is present. Under which mental status exam heading does this belong? Thought content abnormalities Thought process abnormalities Level of consciousness Insight and judgement Perceptual abnormalities The correct answer is E. Hallucinations are perceptual abnormalities, not abnormalities of thought content. The review stresses this distinction; the inherited MSE note lists hallucinations and illusions under Perceptual Abnormalities.

A 45-year-old man has felt low on most days for the past three years. He sleeps poorly and has low energy, and he has never felt well for more than a few weeks at a time. He has never had five depressive symptoms at once. What is the most likely diagnosis? Major depressive disorder, recurrent Adjustment disorder with depressed mood Cyclothymic disorder Persistent depressive disorder Depression with melancholic features The correct answer is D. Persistent depressive disorder is depressed mood on most days for at least 2 years (1 year in children), never symptom-free for more than 2 months. Major depression needs 5 or more symptoms for 2 weeks; cyclothymia needs hypomanic periods as well.

A 34-year-old woman meets criteria for a major depressive episode. On most days of the episode she also has racing thoughts, talks much more than usual and sleeps little without feeling tired, but she has never met full criteria for hypomania. Which specifier applies? With melancholic features With mixed features With atypical features With anxious distress The correct answer is B. Mixed features means at least 3 manic or hypomanic symptoms during most days of a major depressive episode, without full criteria for mania or hypomania (which would make it bipolar I or II). It is a significant risk factor for later bipolar disorder.

A 29-year-old woman has a first episode of moderate major depression. Which of the following is NOT a first-line medication option? Sertraline Bupropion Amitriptyline Mirtazapine Venlafaxine XR The correct answer is C. SSRIs, SNRIs, the NDRI bupropion and the NaSSA mirtazapine are first line. TCAs (such as amitriptyline) and MAOIs are second or third line, not first-line medications.

A 38-year-old man has responded well to sertraline for depression but is distressed by delayed ejaculation and decreased libido. Which antidepressant is the best switch to avoid sexual side effects? Paroxetine Venlafaxine Bupropion Citalopram The correct answer is C. Bupropion causes no sexual side effects and no weight gain, so it is the switch the review recommends for SSRI-related sexual dysfunction or weight gain (it may be somewhat less effective). Venlafaxine causes sexual side effects in over 30% of patients.

A 26-year-old woman starting treatment for depression admits she often forgets to take her medications for several days at a time. Which SSRI is least likely to cause problems when doses are missed? Paroxetine Sertraline Escitalopram Fluoxetine The correct answer is D. Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of the SSRIs, so non-adherence causes fewer problems and it does not cause antidepressant discontinuation syndrome. Paroxetine, with its short half-life, is the classic cause of discontinuation syndrome.

A 55-year-old woman with congenital long QT syndrome needs an antidepressant. Which SSRI is contraindicated? Citalopram Sertraline Fluoxetine Paroxetine The correct answer is A. Citalopram is contraindicated in long QT syndrome, bradycardia, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, recent MI and decompensated heart failure. Its cousin escitalopram is less likely to prolong the QT interval.

A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has depression with prominent anxiety. Which antidepressant is most likely to worsen his blood pressure? Sertraline Venlafaxine Mirtazapine Escitalopram The correct answer is B. Venlafaxine causes a dose-dependent rise in diastolic blood pressure (10-15 mmHg). The review and the inherited note list it with nausea, QT prolongation and sexual side effects.

A 40-year-old woman on an SSRI starts a second serotonergic drug. Within 6 hours she is agitated and diaphoretic, with a temperature of 39.5°C, dilated pupils, hyperactive bowel sounds, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus in the legs. Besides stopping both drugs and giving supportive care, which specific medication is used? Dantrolene sodium Cyproheptadine Bromocriptine Haloperidol Physostigmine The correct answer is B. Rapid onset (under 12 hours) after serotonergic drugs, with hyperreflexia, clonus, mydriasis and hyperactive bowel sounds, is serotonin syndrome. Treat it by stopping the offending drugs, supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation, and the serotonin antagonist cyprohepta

A 25-year-old man started on haloperidol develops a shuffling gait, cogwheel rigidity and a resting tremor. Dopamine blockade in which pathway causes these effects? Mesolimbic Mesocortical Nigrostriatal Tuberoinfundibular The correct answer is C. Typical antipsychotics block D2 receptors throughout the brain. In the nigrostriatal pathway this causes extrapyramidal effects that mimic parkinsonism. Blocking the mesolimbic pathway is what treats positive symptoms.

A 45-year-old woman who has taken lithium for bipolar I disorder for 10 years reports passing large volumes of dilute urine and constant thirst. What is the most likely cause? Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Primary (psychogenic) polydipsia Hypothyroidism from lithium Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion Lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism The correct answer is A. Lithium's renal side effects include diabetes insipidus (mostly reversible) and polyuria. The study guide flags lithium toxicity, including nephrotoxicity and thyroid toxicity, and the need for regular blood-level monitoring.

Which of the following patients belongs to the demographic group at highest risk of dying by suicide? A 16-year-old girl A 35-year-old woman A 40-year-old woman A 78-year-old man The correct answer is D. The highest-risk group for suicide is older men. Women are more likely to attempt suicide, but men are more likely to die by it.

A 50-year-old man in the emergency department has depression and a detailed plan to end his life tonight. He refuses admission and tries to leave. What is the most appropriate next step? Complete a Form 1 Discharge with a no-suicide contract Book a follow-up in one week Refer him to a support group The correct answer is A. Active suicidal ideation with a plan can require admission, and when the patient refuses, a Form 1 allows him to be held for up to 72 hours for assessment. Safety contracts (no-suicide agreements) are not an acceptable solution for acute suicidal ideation in an emergency set

A 31-year-old woman has had two major depressive episodes. Between them she had a 5-day period of high energy, little sleep and rapid speech that her friends noticed but that did not impair her work or need hospital care. She has never had a longer or more severe episode. What is the diagnosis? Bipolar I disorder Bipolar II disorder Cyclothymic disorder Major depressive disorder The correct answer is B. Bipolar II disorder needs at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, and no manic episode ever. A manic episode (severe enough to impair function, need hospitalization or cause psychosis) would make it bipolar I.

A 27-year-old man describes 3 years of alternating periods of mild low mood and periods of increased energy and talkativeness. None of the episodes have met criteria for a major depressive, hypomanic or manic episode. What is the diagnosis? Persistent depressive disorder Bipolar II disorder Cyclothymic disorder Borderline personality disorder The correct answer is C. Cyclothymic disorder is at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents) of numerous hypomanic and depressive periods that never meet full criteria for a hypomanic or major depressive episode.

A 33-year-old woman with bipolar depression is starting lamotrigine. Why must the dose be titrated slowly? To reduce the risk of lithium toxicity To limit the risk of weight gain To prevent drug-induced hypothyroidism To reduce the risk of serious rash The correct answer is D. Lamotrigine can cause a serious rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome or TEN, 0.3-1%). Slow titration reduces that risk. Lamotrigine has a low risk of weight gain.

A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder presents with a major depressive episode. He is taking no medication. Which choice is inappropriate? Quetiapine alone Lithium alone Lamotrigine alone Lurasidone alone Sertraline alone The correct answer is E. Antidepressant monotherapy should not be used for bipolar I depression: it raises the risk of switching into mania or hypomania, rapid cycling and mixed features. Antidepressants are second-line adjuncts only, used with caution.
Q24 · Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders

A therapist treating depression focuses on the patient's conflict with her spouse, her recent move into retirement and the death of her mother, and does not work with transference. Which therapy is this? Interpersonal therapy Psychodynamic therapy Dialectical behaviour therapy Supportive therapy The correct answer is A. Interpersonal therapy (IPT) works on four areas: interpersonal role disputes, role transitions, grief (a real death) and interpersonal deficits. It solves problems in the present, and transference is intentionally not addressed.
Q25 · Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders

A family physician notices she feels unusually irritated and impatient with a patient who reminds her of her own demanding father. What is this called? Transference Projection Displacement Countertransference Reaction formation (defence) The correct answer is D. Countertransference is the provider's own reaction to a patient, shaped by the provider's past and emotions. Transference is the patient seeing the provider in a role from the patient's past.
Q26 · Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders

A high-school student who is strongly attracted to a classmate is consistently rude and dismissive toward her. Which defence mechanism is this? Displacement Reaction formation Isolation of affect Projection The correct answer is B. Reaction formation turns an undesirable feeling into its opposite. Displacement shifts an emotion onto a different object; isolation of affect separates an idea from its feeling; projection attributes one's own impulses to others.
Q27 · Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders

A 23-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder has recurrent self-harm and intense, rapidly shifting emotions. Which psychotherapy is the best-supported treatment? Psychodynamic psychotherapy Interpersonal therapy (IPT) Dialectical behaviour therapy Supportive psychotherapy Cognitive processing therapy (CPT) The correct answer is C. Dialectical behaviour therapy was developed specifically for borderline personality disorder, and it works better than any medication for it. It combines behavioural strategies with mindfulness and acceptance, through individual therapy, group skills training and phone coach
Q28 · Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses

A 62-year-old man has major depression 6 weeks after a myocardial infarction. Which is the most appropriate antidepressant? Amitriptyline Phenelzine Sertraline Venlafaxine The correct answer is C. SSRIs are first line in cardiac disease. In the SADHART trial, sertraline was the safest and most effective treatment after MI or unstable angina. SNRIs should be used cautiously, and TCAs and MAOIs are contraindicated.
Q29 · Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages

Four days after an uncomplicated delivery, a 30-year-old woman is tearful and irritable and cries easily. She is bonding with her baby, is functioning, and has no thoughts of harm. What is the most appropriate management? Start sertraline daily Reassurance and support Admit to hospital today Start an antipsychotic Refer for urgent ECT The correct answer is B. This is postpartum blues: very common, starting a few days after birth and resolving on its own within a few weeks. No treatment is needed beyond supportive care. Postpartum depression needs treatment; postpartum psychosis is an emergency.
Q30 · Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages

Two weeks after delivery, a 27-year-old woman is disorganized, is not sleeping and believes her baby is "defective" and must be taken away. What is the most appropriate next step? Repeat the EPDS screen in 2 weeks Start sertraline and follow up Reassure her that this will pass Arrange immediate hospitalization The correct answer is D. Postpartum psychosis (onset within about 4-8 weeks of delivery, with delusions often about the baby) is a psychiatric emergency that needs immediate hospitalization and treatment.

A 24-year-old man has had three sudden episodes of pounding heart, sweating, shortness of breath and fear of dying that came on without a trigger and peaked within minutes. For the past two months he has worried constantly about having another one and has stopped exercising. What is the diagnosis? Panic disorder Generalized anxiety disorder Specific phobia Social anxiety disorder The correct answer is A. Panic disorder is recurrent unexpected panic attacks (4 or more symptoms, peaking within minutes), followed by at least 1 month of worry about further attacks or a change in behaviour because of them. It carries about a 20-fold risk of suicide.

For the past 8 months a 41-year-old woman has worried, on most days and beyond her control, about her job, her children's health and money. She has muscle tension, tires easily and sleeps poorly. What is the diagnosis? Generalized anxiety disorder Panic disorder with agoraphobia Illness anxiety disorder Adjustment disorder with anxiety Obsessive-compulsive disorder The correct answer is A. GAD is excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things on most days for 6 or more months, with at least 3 of: muscle tension, restlessness, fatigue, irritability, sleep disturbance and poor concentration.

For 9 months, a 35-year-old woman has avoided buses and crowded shopping malls because she fears she would not be able to get out if she became panicky. She now leaves home only with her sister. What is the diagnosis? Social anxiety disorder Agoraphobia Specific phobia Separation anxiety disorder The correct answer is B. Agoraphobia is marked fear of at least 2 of 5 situations (for example public transit, enclosed places, crowds) because escape might be difficult if panic symptoms occur. The situations almost always provoke fear, and it lasts 6 months or more.
Q34 · Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD

A 30-year-old man has an intense fear of flying that has stopped him visiting his family abroad. What is the first-line treatment? Daily sertraline Pregabalin Exposure-based CBT Psychodynamic therapy The correct answer is C. CBT is first line for all the anxiety disorders, and exposure is its core technique for phobias. Virtual exposures are useful for feared situations that are hard to set up in real life, such as flying. SSRIs are the first-line drugs for most anxiety disorders, but not for sp
Q35 · Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD

A 20-year-old woman with OCD washes her hands for hours after touching door handles. Which psychotherapy technique is most important for her? Systematic desensitization alone Interpersonal therapy Supportive psychotherapy Exposure and response prevention The correct answer is D. In OCD, CBT uses exposure and response prevention: the patient is exposed to the trigger (starting small) and does not perform the compulsion, so she habituates.
Q36 · Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD

A 32-year-old man with OCD has taken fluoxetine 20 mg daily for 10 weeks with only a small improvement and no side effects. What is the most appropriate next step? Switch fluoxetine to bupropion Add a scheduled benzodiazepine Stop medication and observe him Refer for psychosurgery now Increase the fluoxetine dose The correct answer is E. In OCD the therapeutic SSRI dose is often higher than the antidepressant dose (fluoxetine up to 80-100 mg), and a trial takes 8-12 weeks. Augmenting with an antipsychotic is for absent insight or a failed response.

A 45-year-old accountant is rigid, perfectionistic and preoccupied with lists and rules, so that projects are never finished. He sees nothing wrong with this and thinks his colleagues are sloppy. He has no intrusive thoughts. What is the most likely diagnosis? Obsessive-compulsive disorder, poor insight Generalized anxiety disorder Autism spectrum disorder, level 1 Schizoid personality disorder Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder The correct answer is E. OCPD is a pervasive pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control that is egosyntonic (it fits the person's values). OCD involves true obsessions and compulsions that are egodystonic (intrusive and unwanted).

Ten days after a serious car crash, a 29-year-old woman has nightmares and flashbacks, avoids driving, is on edge and startles easily. What is the diagnosis? Acute stress disorder Post-traumatic stress disorder Adjustment disorder Generalized anxiety disorder The correct answer is A. Symptoms lasting 3 days to 1 month after the trauma are acute stress disorder. PTSD needs the symptoms to last more than 1 month.

A 38-year-old veteran with PTSD is doing better on sertraline but still has frequent trauma nightmares. Which medication is used specifically for the nightmares? Alprazolam Prazosin Olanzapine Divalproex The correct answer is B. Prazosin (an alpha-blocker, 2-12 mg at bedtime) is used for PTSD nightmares; nabilone is another option. Alprazolam, olanzapine and divalproex are all on the inherited note's list of medications to avoid in PTSD.

A 28-year-old man has few friends and dresses oddly. He believes he can sense other people's thoughts and that license plates carry messages meant for him, though he can be talked out of these ideas. He has never had hallucinations or fixed delusions. What is the most likely diagnosis? Schizoid personality disorder Schizophrenia, first psychotic episode Schizotypal personality disorder Avoidant personality disorder Paranoid personality disorder The correct answer is C. Schizotypal PD combines discomfort in close relationships with odd beliefs or magical thinking, ideas of reference (not delusions) and eccentric behaviour. Schizoid PD is detachment without the oddness: the schizoid avoids.

A 21-year-old student has repeated episodes of feeling as if she is watching herself from outside her body and that the world around her looks unreal and dreamlike. She knows the experience is not real. What is the diagnosis? Dissociative identity disorder Depersonalization/derealization disorder Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue Brief psychotic disorder Panic disorder with agoraphobia The correct answer is B. Depersonalization (observing oneself from outside) and derealization (the surroundings feel unreal), with reality testing intact, define depersonalization/derealization disorder. Intact reality testing separates it from psychosis.

An 8-year-old boy's teacher reports that he cannot stay seated, blurts out answers and loses his work. His parents and his hockey coach see none of this behaviour at home or at practice. What does this history show? He meets criteria for ADHD, combined type He meets criteria for ADHD, hyperactive type It does not meet ADHD criteria It is diagnostic of oppositional defiant disorder The correct answer is C. ADHD requires symptoms in at least 2 settings, present before age 12, for at least 6 months, with impairment. Symptoms seen only at school do not meet criteria; collateral from parents and teachers is essential.

A 9-year-old girl is diagnosed with ADHD. Her parents ask about medication. Which is first line? Long-acting methylphenidate Atomoxetine (non-stimulant) Guanfacine extended-release Bupropion sustained-release Clonidine at bedtime The correct answer is A. Stimulants (methylphenidate- or amphetamine-based) are first line, and long-acting forms have fewer side effects and are more convenient. Common side effects are insomnia and poor appetite. Atomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine and bupropion are second line.

A 17-year-old girl has a BMI of 15.8. She is terrified of gaining weight and says she is fat. Over the past 3 months she has binged several times a week and then made herself vomit. What is the diagnosis? Bulimia nervosa, purging presentation Binge eating disorder with purging Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder Other specified feeding or eating disorder (OSFED) Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type The correct answer is E. Low body weight, fear of weight gain and distorted self-evaluation make this anorexia nervosa. The restricting and binge-eating/purging subtypes belong to anorexia, not bulimia. Bulimia nervosa is not diagnosed when the disturbance occurs only during anorexia.

A 16-year-old girl with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted for nutritional rehabilitation. Which electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome? Hypernatremia Hypercalcemia Hyperkalemia Hypophosphatemia Hyperphosphatemia The correct answer is D. Refeeding syndrome is a potentially fatal shift in electrolytes and fluid when severely malnourished patients are refed, and hypophosphatemia is its hallmark. Severe malnutrition and rapid refeeding are the risk factors.

A 22-year-old woman of normal weight has binged and then vomited about 4 times a week for 6 months, and feels intense shame. Which treatment combination is best supported? Bupropion alone Olanzapine plus IPT Lisdexamfetamine alone CBT plus fluoxetine The correct answer is D. Bulimia nervosa is treated with CBT (CBT-E in particular) and fluoxetine. Bupropion should be avoided in bulimia because it raises seizure risk. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is used for binge eating disorder.

A 10-year-old boy eats only five foods because of their texture and gags on anything new. He has fallen off his growth curve. He has no concern about his weight or shape. What is the diagnosis? Anorexia nervosa, restricting type Rumination disorder Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder Pica Autism spectrum disorder with food selectivity The correct answer is C. In ARFID the restriction is driven by sensory features, fear of consequences such as choking, or lack of interest, not by concern about weight or shape. That separates it from anorexia nervosa.

A 23-year-old man has had auditory hallucinations and disorganized speech, with declining function, for 3 months. There are no mood episodes and no substance use. What is the diagnosis? Brief psychotic disorder Schizophreniform disorder Schizophrenia Delusional disorder Substance-induced psychotic disorder The correct answer is B. The disorders share the same symptom criteria and differ by duration: brief psychotic disorder lasts under 1 month, schizophreniform disorder 1-6 months, and schizophrenia more than 6 months.

A 52-year-old man has believed for 8 months that his wife is having an affair, despite no evidence. He works normally, has no hallucinations, and his speech and behaviour are otherwise unremarkable. What is the diagnosis? Delusional disorder Schizophrenia Schizotypal personality disorder Brief psychotic disorder The correct answer is A. Delusional disorder is at least one delusion lasting at least 1 month, with Criterion A for schizophrenia never met and functioning not markedly impaired apart from the delusion.

A 30-year-old woman has had several manic episodes with psychotic features. She has also had 4 weeks of auditory hallucinations and delusions at a time when her mood was normal. What is the diagnosis? Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features Schizoaffective disorder Schizophrenia Brief psychotic disorder The correct answer is B. Schizoaffective disorder needs delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, alongside mood episodes. In bipolar disorder with psychotic features, psychosis occurs only during mood episodes.

Two weeks after starting an antipsychotic, a 26-year-old man paces constantly and says he feels he cannot sit still inside his skin. Which treatment is most appropriate? Dantrolene Physostigmine Propranolol Clozapine The correct answer is C. This is akathisia, a severe inner and physical restlessness that is associated with suicide. Treat it with a beta-blocker such as propranolol, or a benzodiazepine.

A 19-year-old man given haloperidol in the emergency department develops sustained upward deviation of his eyes and painful twisting of his neck. What is the most appropriate treatment? A beta-blocker Switching to clozapine Increasing the dose An anticholinergic The correct answer is D. Acute dystonias (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonus) are an emergency. Reduce the antipsychotic dose and give an anticholinergic, diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine.

Two days after starting haloperidol, a 34-year-old man is febrile (40.5°C), confused, tachycardic and diaphoretic, with lead-pipe rigidity in all limbs and reduced reflexes. His creatine kinase is 8000 U/L. What is the first step? Stop the antipsychotic Give cyproheptadine orally Add benztropine Increase the haloperidol dose Start an SSRI The correct answer is A. Onset over 1-3 days on a dopamine antagonist, lead-pipe rigidity in all limbs, hyporeflexia and a very high CK point to neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not serotonin syndrome. Stop the antipsychotic and transfer to the ICU; dantrolene and bromocriptine are the specific treat

A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia has not responded to adequate trials of two antipsychotics. Clozapine is started. Why does it need regular blood monitoring? Risk of agranulocytosis Risk of hyponatremia Risk of hepatic failure Risk of hypothyroidism The correct answer is A. Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant psychosis (after 2 or more antipsychotics), but it can cause agranulocytosis, so it requires regular CBC monitoring and is reserved for later use.

A 24-year-old man is recovering from a first episode of psychosis. What is the biggest risk factor for relapse? Carer's critical comments Male sex Later age of onset Having only positive symptoms Stopping his antipsychotic The correct answer is E. Medication non-adherence is the biggest reason for relapse. After a first episode, patients should stay on medication for at least 12-18 months; long-acting injectables help adherence. Drug use and carers' critical comments come after it.
Q56 · Consent, Capacity, and the Mental Health Act

You complete a Form 1 on a patient in the emergency department. Which form must the patient then receive? Form 2 Form 42 Form 3 Form 14 The correct answer is B. A Form 1 lets the patient be detained for up to 72 hours for psychiatric assessment at a Schedule 1 facility, and the patient must receive notice of it on a Form 42. A Form 2 is issued by a justice of the peace.
Q57 · Consent, Capacity, and the Mental Health Act

A 70-year-old man with a gangrenous foot can accurately repeat what amputation involves and the risks of refusing it. He refuses, saying he is certain the infection will not spread to him because he is protected. Which element of capacity is he missing? Understanding the information Communicating a choice Appreciating the consequences Being over 16 years old The correct answer is C. To be capable, a patient must understand the information relevant to the decision and appreciate the reasonable, foreseeable consequences of deciding or not deciding. He understands the facts but cannot apply them to himself, so he fails appreciation.

A 48-year-old man answers yes to 2 of the 4 CAGE questions. What does this result mean? He has a confirmed diagnosis of alcohol use disorder He is in moderate to severe alcohol withdrawal He should start naltrexone today He has no alcohol problem He screens positive and needs further assessment The correct answer is E. CAGE is a screening test, not a diagnostic test, for alcohol use disorder. The AUDIT is more sensitive and specific. Diagnosis needs the DSM substance use disorder criteria.

A 55-year-old man with heavy daily alcohol use is admitted for withdrawal management. Besides CIWA-Ar-guided treatment, which supplement is essential? Oral vitamin B12 daily Oral vitamin D daily Intramuscular thiamine Intravenous iron sucrose Oral magnesium oxide The correct answer is C. Thiamine (and folic acid) is essential in withdrawal management. The inherited note specifies thiamine 100 mg IM for at least 3 days, because oral thiamine is poorly absorbed. The CIWA-Ar scores withdrawal severity to guide treatment.

A 44-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder has completed withdrawal and wants to stay abstinent. Which medication is first line? Disulfiram Baclofen Topiramate Naltrexone The correct answer is D. Naltrexone and acamprosate are the first-line medications for alcohol use disorder. Topiramate, gabapentin, baclofen and disulfiram are options only if first-line agents fail or are not suitable.

A 50-year-old man who smokes 25 cigarettes a day wants to quit. Which pharmacotherapy is considered best practice? Bupropion alone Varenicline plus a patch Nicotine gum as needed Nicotine patch alone Nicotine lozenges as needed The correct answer is B. Varenicline combined with a nicotine patch is considered best practice. Bupropion plus a patch is more effective than placebo; a patch suits a heavy daily smoker better than as-needed gum.

A 45-year-old woman has had trouble falling and staying asleep 4 nights a week for a year. She does not snore and has no leg symptoms or unusual behaviour in sleep. What is the most appropriate next step? Refer for CBT for insomnia Order polysomnography Start zolpidem nightly Give sleep hygiene advice only The correct answer is A. Insomnia is a clinical diagnosis, and polysomnography is not indicated for insomnia itself; it is for suspected OSA, narcolepsy or parasomnia. CBT is first-line treatment. Sleep hygiene on its own is largely ineffective.

A 19-year-old man falls asleep in lectures despite sleeping 8 hours a night. When he laughs, his knees buckle. Which test result supports the diagnosis? Short sleep latency and 2 or more SOREMPs Apnea-hypopnea index of 30 events per hour REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography Elevated CSF hypocretin Periodic limb movements in sleep The correct answer is A. Excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy is narcolepsy, caused by loss of hypocretin (orexin) neurons. On the multiple sleep latency test it shows a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less and 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods; CSF hypocretin is low.

A 67-year-old man's wife reports that he punches and shouts in his sleep in the early morning hours, acting out dreams of being chased. He wakes fully alert and remembers the dream. What does polysomnography typically show? Arousals from slow-wave sleep REM sleep without atonia Sleep-onset REM periods Repeated oxygen desaturations The correct answer is B. Dream enactment late in the night, with full alertness on waking, is REM sleep behaviour disorder, and polysomnography shows REM sleep without atonia. NREM parasomnias such as sleepwalking and night terrors arise from slow-wave sleep in the first third of the night.

A 32-year-old nurse is admitted repeatedly with hypoglycemia. Her C-peptide is low, and insulin syringes are found in her bag. She has no financial or legal gain from being ill. What is the diagnosis? Malingering Somatic symptom disorder Factitious disorder Conversion disorder The correct answer is C. Factitious disorder and malingering both involve intentionally produced symptoms, unlike somatic symptom, illness anxiety and conversion disorders. Factitious disorder has no external reward (the motive is the sick role); malingering involves clear external gain.

Which of the following is an example of a boundary crossing rather than a boundary violation? Starting a romantic relationship Borrowing money from a patient Repeatedly meeting a patient socially Accepting a small thank-you card The correct answer is D. A boundary crossing is a harmless, non-exploitative deviation that may even support the therapy, and it is usually isolated and discussable. A boundary violation is exploitative, usually repetitive, and harms the patient or the therapy.

Two days after hip surgery, an 84-year-old woman is quiet and drowsy, stares at the wall and cannot say the months backward. Her attention and level of alertness vary through the day. The team wonders whether she is depressed. What is the most likely diagnosis? Hypoactive delirium Major depressive disorder Alzheimer's disease Lewy body dementia The correct answer is A. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness. The hypoactive subtype is the most common (about 65%) and is often missed or mistaken for depression.

A 79-year-old man becomes acutely confused after starting a medication with strong anticholinergic effects. He is flushed, with dry skin, dilated pupils and urinary retention. Which treatment targets the cause? Haloperidol Lorazepam Quetiapine Diphenhydramine Physostigmine The correct answer is E. Antipsychotics are the usual first-line treatment for hyperactive delirium symptoms, with two exceptions: benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal and physostigmine for anticholinergic toxidrome.
Q69 · Cognitive Disorders in the Elderly

A 72-year-old retired teacher and her husband notice she forgets recent conversations and takes longer to balance the chequebook, though she still manages it, along with her medications and driving, on her own. Testing confirms a mild memory deficit. What is the diagnosis? Major neurocognitive disorder Mild neurocognitive disorder Delirium Pseudodementia The correct answer is B. Mild neurocognitive disorder (mild cognitive impairment) is objective cognitive decline without loss of independence: complex IADLs are preserved, even if they take more effort. In major NCD (dementia) the deficits interfere with independence.
Q70 · Cognitive Disorders in the Elderly

A 74-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes and atrial fibrillation has had three sudden drops in his thinking over two years, each followed by a plateau. What is the most likely diagnosis? Alzheimer's disease Frontotemporal dementia Vascular dementia Lewy body dementia The correct answer is C. Vascular dementia, the second most common cause of neurocognitive disorder, typically follows a stepwise course of sudden declines, and depends on the number, size and location of infarcts. Alzheimer's disease declines gradually and continuously.
Q71 · Cognitive Disorders in the Elderly

A 56-year-old man, previously reserved, has become disinhibited: he makes crude comments to strangers, overeats sweets and has lost interest in his family. His memory is relatively preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis? Alzheimer's disease Vascular dementia Lewy body dementia Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Frontotemporal dementia The correct answer is E. Frontotemporal dementia starts earlier than other dementias (often 40-60 years) and presents with behaviour and personality change, such as disinhibition and apathy, with relative sparing of memory.
Q72 · Management of Cognitive Disorders and Dementia

A 76-year-old man with fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations and parkinsonism has distressing psychosis despite non-drug measures. If an antipsychotic is needed, which is preferred? Haloperidol Risperidone Olanzapine Quetiapine The correct answer is D. Patients with Lewy body dementia are exceptionally sensitive to antipsychotics (severe reactions, including NMS), so quetiapine (or clozapine) at low doses is preferred. Always try non-drug approaches first.

A 81-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease has progressed to the moderate-severe stage. Which drug class is indicated specifically at this stage? An NMDA antagonist A cholinesterase inhibitor A dopamine agonist An SSRI The correct answer is A. Memantine, a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist, is used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. Donepezil, a cholinesterase inhibitor, is the most commonly prescribed dementia drug overall.

Which of the following is true? The Nipissing tool is a surveillance form so it is used continuously as a way to monitor the milestone development of low risk infants/children up to 5 years of age.
