Which of the following statements is true? If an asthmatic patient scores 4-7 on PRAM with FEV1 50-70%, they should be given continuous nebulized salbutamol and ipratropium for 60 minutes as well as IV steroids and magnesium sulfate. The three most common causes of bacterial pneumonia is H. influenzae, S. aureus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Bronchiolitis is most commonly caused by parainfluenza types 1 and 3. Symptoms include inspiratory stridor. It’s treated with oral dexamethasone (and nebulized epinephrine if severe). Inhaled ipratropium bromide should be added to even mild asthma exacerbations (PRAM 0-3; FEV1 >70%). Daily inhaled corticosteroids should be prescribed if patients have asthma symptoms (or waking up due to asthma) 2 times per month or more. The correct answer is E. E is correct. A describes what to do with a “severe asthma exacerbation” (PRAM 8-12, FEV1 <50%). B is incorrect because Strep pneumoniae is the most common cause. C describes croup. D - inhaled ipratropium bromide is only considered when PRAM reaches 6.

List three conditions on your differential diagnosis if a young child presents with a wheeze. Accepted answers: viral bronchiolitis, asthma, pneumonia, laryngotracheomalacia, foreign body aspiration, GERD, CHF, vascular ring, allergies, CF, mediastinal mass, tracheoesophageal fistula.

From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1 and 02 - Classification of Different Microbes (FoM Block 4). The correct answer is D. D is correct. B is incorrect because infant colic follows the rule of 3s and peaks at 6 weeks of age. NSAIDs are a common cause of duodenal ulcers, which are the most common cause of GI bleeds.

Since AB will be undergoing surgery soon, the stomach and intestines should be kept as empty as possible. Hence, the diet specification under AD DAVID should be nil per os (NPO).

Your hand is placed palm up on a table, with all your fingers completely fixed to the table except your middle finger. When you try to fully flex your middle finger, you cannot flex your DIP joint. What is the reasoning? Your flexor digitorum superficialis cannot be engaged because the rest of your fingers are fixed to the table Your flexor digitorum profundus cannot be engaged because the rest of your fingers are fixed to the table Your flexor digitorum superficialis tendon of the middle finger is ruptured You are part of the 15% population that does not have palmaris longus The correct answer is B. flexor digitorum profundus attaches to DIP and flexes at that joint. Sibyl spends over most of her day lying down on her couch or in bed, occasionally reading a book and watching reality TV with her brother Dorian has left his job and spends most of his time doing yoga, meditating & online shopping Henry is no longer able to travel to his clients and now spends most of his time working from home or chatting on MSN messenger Basil has not seen his friends or family in the past 2 weeks, presented previously with flat affect and has had trouble sleeping. Asterixis Hepatic encephalopathy (brain affected by liver failure) or kidney failure (uremia) · tremor of the hands later: PoM 1 Gastroenterology Steps Ask the patient to stretch both arms out in front Bend the wrists back and spread the fingers, as if stopping traffic Hold the position and watch the hands Positive A flapping of the hands (brief, irregular loss of wrist posture) ▶ Asterixis (AKA Flapping Tremor) (Med School Made Easy) Tap to reveal

Clubbing Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), celiac disease, cirrhosis Steps Look at each finger from the side Schamroth window : put the nails of two matching fingers back to back and look for the diamond-shaped gap Positive The angle between nail and nail fold is lost , the nail curves over the fingertip, and the diamond gap closes Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Liver stigmata (hands, face, chest)

Liver stigmata (hands, face, chest) Chronic liver disease Steps Hands : temperature, leukonychia (white nails), palmar erythema (red palms), Dupuytren's contracture (a finger pulled into a bent position), thenar and hypothenar wasting (thin thumb-side and little-finger-side muscles), Terry's nails later: PoM 1 Gastroenterology Face : scleral icterus, parotid enlargement (swollen glands in front of the ears), central cyanosis (blue lips), temporal balding later: PoM 1 Gastroenterology Chest : spider nevi (small spider-like blood vessels), and in a male gynecomastia (breast enlargement) Positive Any of these; Dupuytren's points to alcohol and smoking , leukonychia and palmar erythema to liver disease Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Inspection from the side and the foot

Inspection from the side and the foot Contour, asymmetry, scars, skin lesions, dilated veins, masses, pulsation, peristalsis, bulging flanks Steps Stand at the side of the bed : scars, skin, veins, contour, movement with breathing Look across the abdomen at skin level for asymmetry Go to the foot of the bed : bulging flanks and leg swelling Positive Distension, asymmetry, a visible mass or loops, caput medusae, bulging flanks, Cullen's or Grey Turner's sign Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Hernia check (head raise or cough)

Hernia check (head raise or cough) An incisional hernia (a bulge through an old scar) or a mass Steps Ask the patient to lift their head off the pillow, or to cough Watch the abdominal wall, especially along scars Positive A bulge appears or stands out Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Bowel sounds

Bowel sounds Present or absent , symmetric, how loud Steps Place the stethoscope in each of the four quadrants (RLQ, RUQ, LUQ, LLQ) Listen in each for long enough to hear a gurgle Say whether sounds are present or absent , symmetric, and how loud Positive Normal: intermittent gurgles , roughly every 5-10 seconds. Constant sound, or none for more than 1 minute = abnormal ▶ Bowel sounds, left lower quadrant (0:24) ▶ Left upper quadrant (0:22) ▶ Right upper quadrant (0:30) ▶ Bowel sounds, right lower quadrant (second volunteer) (0:16) ▶ Left lower quadrant (second volunteer) (0:16) ▶ Left upper quadrant (second volunteer) (0:16) ▶ Right upper quadrant (second volunteer) (0:16) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Bruits (aorta, renal, iliac, femoral)

Bruits (aorta, renal, iliac, femoral) A narrowed artery (stenosis) Steps Listen over the aorta , just above the umbilicus If you suspect arterial disease, also over the renal, iliac and femoral arteries Positive A whooshing sound (bruit) from turbulent blood flow Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Percussion of the four quadrants

Percussion of the four quadrants A mass or an enlarged organ (large dull areas) Steps Lay the middle finger of one hand flat on the abdomen Tap its middle joint with the tip of the other hand's middle finger Work through all four quadrants , painful area last Positive Normal = tympany (hollow drum note from gas; stool or normal fluid give small patches of dullness). Large areas of dullness = an underlying mass or enlarged organ (or ascites, section 10) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Light palpation

Light palpation Discomfort (tenderness), resistance from an organ or mass , superficial masses Steps One hand, palm and fingers together, gently Press lightly, all four quadrants , painful area last Watch the patient's face Positive Tenderness, resistance, or a superficial mass Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Deep palpation

Deep palpation Tenderness, enlarged organs or masses Steps Bend the hand at the knuckles (metacarpophalangeal joints) and press deeply, often one hand on top of the other All four quadrants For a mass note its location, size, shape, consistency, tenderness and whether it pulses Positive Tenderness, an enlarged organ or a mass Tap to reveal

Guarding Irritation of the abdominal lining (peritonitis) Steps Notice tensing of the muscles on palpation Help the patient relax (breathe out, bend the knees), then feel again Positive Guarding that goes away = voluntary . Guarding that stays = involuntary , which points to peritonitis Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Head-raise test for tenderness

Head-raise test for tenderness Whether tenderness is in the abdominal wall or inside the abdomen Steps Find the tender spot Ask the patient to lift their head off the bed (this tenses the abdominal wall) Press on the same spot again Positive Pain the same or worse = the wall itself (superficial) · pain less = the tensed muscles are shielding something deeper (deep) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Aorta width

Aorta width An enlarged aorta (abdominal aortic aneurysm, AAA) Steps One hand on each side of the aorta , in the upper abdomen just above the umbilicus Press firmly and deeply Estimate the gap between your hands Positive Wider than 3 cm (normal: about 2 cm) Tap to reveal

Kidneys (bimanual) The lower edge (pole) of each kidney Steps Palpate bimanually (one hand behind the flank, one hand in front) Feel for the lower margin of each kidney Positive A kidney you can feel (optional in the Gastroenterology session) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Liver span (percussion)

Liver span (percussion) Liver size Steps In the right midclavicular line , percuss upward from the RLQ until tympany turns dull = lower border Percuss downward from the right chest until resonance turns dull = upper border Measure the distance in centimetres Positive More than 12 cm = enlarged (hepatomegaly) (normal: 6-12 cm in the midclavicular line, 4-8 cm in the midsternal line) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Liver edge (palpation)

Liver edge (palpation) The lower margin of the liver Steps Hand in the RLQ, just outside the right rectus muscle , fingers pointing toward the costal margin (bottom of the ribs) Patient takes deep breaths : press gently on the breath in (the liver moves down) Move the hand up on each breath out, until you meet the edge or the costal margin Or the hooking technique : hook the fingers under the rib edge, press in and up, deep breath in Positive An edge that touches your hand below the costal margin on a deep breath = enlarged liver (normal: usually not felt; if felt, smooth) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Murphy's sign

Murphy's sign Inflamed gallbladder (cholecystitis) later: PoM 1 Gastroenterology Steps Patient breathes out Hand below the right costal margin Patient breathes in Positive Patient winces and stops breathing in (the gallbladder hits your hand) ▶ Murphy's sign - OSCE Tips (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Castell's sign (percussion)

Castell's sign (percussion) An enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) Steps Percuss the lowest intercostal space (about the 10th) in the left anterior axillary line Percuss again with the patient in full inspiration (deep breath held), and in full expiration Positive Note turns dull on the deep breath in (normal: tympanic throughout) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Spleen tip (palpation)

Spleen tip (palpation) The lower margin of the spleen Steps Start in the RLQ , lightly, just outside the left rectus muscle as you approach Press on the breath in; move up diagonally toward the LUQ on each breath out Near the ribs, your other hand lifts the lower left rib cage Not felt? Repeat with the patient rolled onto their right side, knees bent Positive A spleen tip you can feel = enlarged · if felt, measure its distance below the costal margin Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Shifting dullness

Shifting dullness Ascites, by percussion Steps Patient on their back: percuss from the midline out to the flank and mark where tympany turns dull Roll the patient onto their side and wait for the fluid to settle Percuss again and re-mark the border Positive The dull border moves toward the lower (dependent) side, more than 5 cm Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Fluid wave

Fluid wave Ascites (large amounts) Steps Patient (or a helper) presses the edge of their hand firmly down the midline (stops the wave travelling through fat) Tap one flank briskly Feel with your other hand on the opposite flank Positive An impulse felt on the other side , carried through the fluid ▶ Easily understand the fluid thrill test for your medical exams (Dr Matt Barrett) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Rebound tenderness
Rebound tenderness Peritonitis (irritated abdominal lining) Steps Press slowly and deeply Let go quickly Positive Pain is worse on letting go than on pressing Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · McBurney's point

McBurney's point Acute appendicitis Steps Find the point one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus Press deeply there Positive Deep, localized tenderness at that point Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Rovsing's sign
Rovsing's sign Appendicitis Steps Press in the left lower quadrant Positive Pain felt in the right lower quadrant ▶ Rovsing, Psoas, and Obturator Signs (OMMinutes) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Psoas test

Psoas test Appendicitis (the appendix lying on the psoas muscle) Steps Patient on their back Patient lifts the right leg against your hand's resistance (contracts the psoas) Positive Abdominal pain (the working muscle rubs the inflamed tissue) ▶ Rovsing, Psoas, and Obturator Signs (OMMinutes) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Obturator test

Obturator test Appendicitis (the appendix lying on the obturator muscle) Steps Patient on their back, hip and knee each bent to 90° One hand on the ankle, one on the knee Rotate the hip inward (pull the ankle out, let the knee fall in) Positive Abdominal pain ▶ Rovsing, Psoas, and Obturator Signs (OMMinutes) Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Leg edema

Leg edema Fluid in the legs (liver, kidney or heart failure, low albumin) Steps Patient still lying flat: look at both legs and feet for swelling Press firmly with a thumb over the shin or ankle for a few seconds Let go and look for a dent Positive A dent that stays = pitting edema Tap to reveal
Abdominal exam, in order · Inguinal nodes and hernias

Inguinal nodes and hernias Lymph nodes or a hernia in the groin extra Steps Feel along the inguinal ligament (groin crease) Ask the patient to cough while you feel Positive A node or a bulge Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Arms at sides

Arms at sides Skin, size and symmetry, contour, nipples Steps Patient sits, arms relaxed at her sides Compare the two sides Positive Redness, skin thickening, flattening, a mass, nipple asymmetry or retraction (normal: mild size difference) ▶ Breast examination, full walkthrough (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Arms over head

Arms over head Dimpling or retraction that is otherwise hidden Steps Patient raises both arms over her head Look at the contours again Positive Dimpling or a skin pull-in → suggests a cancer tethered to the skin and chest-wall tissue Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Hands pressed on hips

Hands pressed on hips Dimpling (tightens the pectoral muscles) Steps Patient presses her hands firmly against her hips Look at the contours again Positive Dimpling or retraction · occasionally benign (fat necrosis after injury, duct ectasia), but always investigate Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Leaning forward

Leaning forward Asymmetry of the breast or nipple Steps For large breasts: patient stands and leans forward , supported by a chair back or your hands Look at both breasts and nipples Positive Asymmetry, or retraction of the nipple and areola → suggests a cancer Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Lateral (outer) half

Lateral (outer) half Lumps in the outer breast Steps Patient rolls onto the opposite hip , hand on her forehead, shoulders kept flat on the table Start in the armpit ; palpate in a straight line down to the bra line Move the fingers inward, palpate up to the collarbone Keep going in overlapping vertical strips until you reach the nipple Positive A lump that feels different from the tissue around it Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Medial (inner) half

Medial (inner) half Lumps in the inner breast Steps Patient lies with shoulders flat , hand at her neck, elbow lifted level with the shoulder Palpate down from the nipple to the bra line, then back up to the collarbone Continue in overlapping vertical strips to the midsternal line Positive A lump that feels different from the tissue around it Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Nipple
Nipple Changes under the nipple Steps Palpate each nipple , noting its elasticity Positive Thickening and loss of elasticity → suggests an underlying cancer Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Mobility of a mass

Mobility of a mass What the lump is attached to Steps Gently move the breast near the mass and watch for dimpling Try to move the mass with the arm relaxed Try again with her hand pressed on her hip Positive Fixed with the arm relaxed → attached to the ribs and chest muscles between them · fixed only with the hand on the hip → attached to the pectoral fascia (the layer over the chest muscle) Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Axillary nodes

Axillary nodes Enlarged or hard lymph nodes in the armpit Steps Sit the patient up (preferable; lying down also works) Palpate the armpit on each side , and compare the two Cover each group: central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral , then the infraclavicular and supraclavicular nodes Positive Enlarged or hard nodes → suggests the breast cancer has spread to the nodes (a lump in the tail of the breast can be mistaken for a node, and the reverse) ▶ Axillary lymph node palpation (clip) (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Male breast: inspect and palpate
Male breast: inspect and palpate Nodules, swelling or ulcers Steps Inspect the nipple and areola Palpate the areola and the breast tissue Positive A nodule, swelling or ulcer Tap to reveal
Breast exam, look then feel · Enlarged male breast

Enlarged male breast Soft fat or a firm disc of gland Steps Feel the enlarged breast Tell apart soft fatty enlargement (obesity) from a firm disc of gland tissue ( gynecomastia : a hormone imbalance between estrogen and androgens, sometimes from a drug) Positive Firm disc of gland = gynecomastia · a hard, irregular, off-centre or ulcerated lump is not gynecomastia Tap to reveal

General inspection Is the patient unwell , short of breath or short of oxygen? later: PoM 1 Cardiology Steps Look at the patient while you talk and take the history Note colour (pallor, plethora, blue lips or tongue) Note breathing : nasal flaring, accessory muscles, pursed lips, can they finish sentences Look at nutrition and general state Positive Distress · pallor · central cyanosis (blue tongue and lips) · cachexia (wasting) Tap to reveal

Hands Heart and circulation problems showing in the fingers Steps Feel the temperature of the hands Look at the fingertips and nails: colour , clubbing (Schamroth window), splinter hemorrhages (thin dark lines under the nail) Look at the finger pads and palms for Osler's nodes (painful) and Janeway lesions (painless) Check capillary refill (section 7) Positive Cool, blue fingers (peripheral cyanosis) · clubbing · splinter hemorrhages , Osler's nodes , Janeway lesions (infection of the heart valves, endocarditis) Tap to reveal

Face and eyes Signs of anemia , cholesterol and blue lips Steps Pull down the lower eyelid: conjunctival pallor ; look at the sclera for jaundice Look at the lips and under the tongue: central cyanosis Look at the eyelids for xanthelasma ; look across the cheeks for a malar rash later: PoM 1 Cardiology Positive Pale conjunctiva · blue tongue · yellow plaques on the lids (high cholesterol) · flushed cheeks Tap to reveal

Chest wall inspection Scars , deformity, and the heartbeat showing through the skin Steps Expose the chest and look from the foot of the bed , then from the side Scars : a midline scar down the sternum (heart surgery), under the left breast or in the side of the chest Shape : pectus excavatum (sunken sternum), pectus carinatum (sternum sticks out), barrel chest , kyphosis (rounded upper back), scoliosis (sideways curve) Symmetry of the two sides of the chest as the patient breathes Look for the apical impulse and any abnormal pulsation Positive Scars · deformity · asymmetry · a visible apical impulse away from its usual spot, or pulsation in other places (normal: the apical impulse may be seen at the 5th space) Tap to reveal

JVP (jugular venous pressure) Right-sided heart pressure and fluid status Steps Patient reclined at 30° to 45° (PoM 1 Cardiology says 45° ), head turned slightly away , neck muscles relaxed Shine a light tangentially across the neck Find the pulsation between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (internal jugular vein) Check it is venous: it is not palpable , falls on breathing in and fades when you press just above the clavicle Measure the vertical height from the sternal angle (the bump where the manubrium meets the sternum) to the top of the pulsation, with a ruler If you cannot find it, lower the head of the bed later: PoM 1 Cardiology Positive More than about 3 cm above the sternal angle (normal: ≤ 3 cm; some sessions say < 4 cm) · distended veins at 45°: high right-sided pressure ▶ Measuring the JVP (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal

Hepatojugular reflux Right heart failure : a heart that cannot take the extra blood Steps Keep the patient reclined with the JVP in view Press firmly on the right upper abdomen for about 10 seconds Ask the patient to breathe normally (do not hold the breath) Watch the JVP later: PoM 1 Cardiology Positive JVP rises and stays up while you press (normal: a brief rise that settles) ▶ Testing the hepatojugular reflux (AMBOSS) Tap to reveal

Carotid pulse Rate, rhythm, contour and amplitude of the pulse at the neck Steps Listen over the carotid first for a bruit (a whooshing sound) Then place your finger pads between the larynx and the sternocleidomastoid on one side only Press gently, never both sides at once Note rate , rhythm , contour (the shape of the wave) and amplitude (strength) Compare with the other side Positive Bruit (narrowed artery, or a murmur radiating from the aortic valve) · weak and late pulse · bounding pulse · irregular rhythm Tap to reveal

Carotid bruit A narrowed carotid artery , or a murmur travelling up from the heart Steps Ask the patient to hold their breath for a few seconds Place the diaphragm over the carotid Listen on both sides Positive A whooshing sound (a murmur from aortic stenosis radiates up here) ▶ Auscultation of carotid arteries (Open RN) Tap to reveal

Apical impulse (PMI) Size and position of the heart , and how hard it works Steps Patient flat (or sitting forward if needed), chest exposed Place the pads of your first two or three fingers at the 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line If you cannot feel it, ask the patient to roll onto their left side Describe it: location (space and cm from the midsternal line), amplitude , duration (time it with your other hand on the carotid pulse), size Positive Displaced down and out (heart enlarged) · sustained (as long as the carotid pulse: pressure load, e.g. aortic stenosis) · diffuse (wider than a quarter: left ventricular hypertrophy) (normal: about 2-3 cm wide, the size of a quarter , a gentle tap in the first two-thirds of systole ) Tap to reveal

Heaves and lifts Right ventricular enlargement or a big left ventricle Steps Place the heel of the hand along the left sternal border , fingers lifted off the chest Ask the patient to breathe out and hold briefly Feel whether the heel of your hand is lifted with each beat Positive Heel of the hand pushed up with each systole ( parasternal lift ) ▶ Palpation of the precordium (Open RN) Tap to reveal

Thrills A murmur you can feel (loud, grade 4 or more) Steps Place the flat of your hand (or the base of the fingers) over each of the four areas : aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, mitral Feel for vibration , a buzzing Positive Buzzing under the palm (a thrill: a loud murmur) ▶ Palpation of the precordium (Open RN) Tap to reveal

Rub Inflamed pericardium (pericarditis) Steps Feel over the left sternal border and the apex Ask the patient to sit up and lean forward if you are unsure Positive A scratchy vibration felt with the beat ▶ Three-component pericardial friction rub (JAMA Network) Tap to reveal

Listening areas Which valve a sound comes from Steps Warm the stethoscope; patient reclined at 30° , you on their right Diaphragm : aortic , pulmonary , tricuspid , then mitral , at the sites above, a few beats at each Feel the carotid pulse with your other hand to tell systole from diastole (S1 comes just before the carotid pulse) Move laterally toward the mid-axillary line from the apex Then repeat with the bell , lightly Positive A sound you can place : where it is loudest, and when Tap to reveal
Cardiovascular exam · Rhythm, S1 and S2

Rhythm, S1 and S2 Regular or irregular rhythm; the loudness and splitting of S1 and S2 Steps At each site, note the rhythm: regular , regularly irregular or irregularly irregular Compare S1 and S2 loudness Splitting of S2 : listen at the pulmonary area while the patient breathes in later: PoM 1 Cardiology Positive Irregular rhythm (e.g. atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular) · quiet S2 · wide or fixed split S2 · loud S1 ▶ Hear it: two split S2 sounds (audio) Tap to reveal

Extra heart sounds Added sounds in systole or diastole: S3, S4, clicks, snaps, rubs Steps Switch to the bell at the apex Roll the patient onto their left side ( left lateral position ), which makes S3, S4 and the mitral-stenosis rumble louder Listen for gallop rhythm (three sounds, like a galloping horse), clicks , an opening snap , a rub Positive S3 or S4 (gallop) · systolic click · opening snap (mitral stenosis) · pericardial friction rub (a scratchy sound; sit forward and listen with the diaphragm) Tap to reveal

Describing a murmur What kind of murmur it is Steps Timing : systolic or diastolic (use the carotid pulse) Shape : crescendo-decrescendo, plateau ( pansystolic ), decrescendo Pitch (high with the diaphragm, low with the bell) and quality (blowing, harsh, rumbling) Grade 1 to 6 (1 barely audible; 4 has a thrill; 5 heard with the stethoscope tilted off the chest; 6 heard off the chest) Where it is loudest , how long it lasts, and where it radiates (to the carotids or the axilla) Draw it on a diagram Positive A murmur described by timing, shape, pitch, grade, location and radiation ▶ Heart murmur sounds (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal

Aortic regurgitation position The soft, high-pitched early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation Steps Patient sitting forward Ask the patient to breathe out fully and hold Diaphragm at the left sternal border , 2nd to 4th space later: PoM 1 Cardiology Positive Soft blowing decrescendo murmur starting right after S2 Tap to reveal

Carotid auscultation Radiation of a murmur or a bruit Steps Place the diaphragm over each carotid Patient holds their breath Positive Bruit or a systolic murmur radiating from the chest ▶ Auscultation of carotid arteries (Open RN) Tap to reveal

Radial pulse Rate and rhythm , and equal arms Steps Place the pads of two or three fingers on the thumb side of the front of the wrist , medial to the radial styloid Count for 30 seconds (or 15 seconds if you are sure it is regular), double it Note rhythm Compare both sides Positive Fast or slow rate · irregular rhythm · one side weaker Tap to reveal

Brachial pulse Amplitude and contour in the arm Steps Support the patient's arm slightly bent Feel inside the elbow, medial to the biceps tendon , with your thumb or fingers Compare both sides Positive Weak or bounding pulse · asymmetry Tap to reveal

Carotid pulse Same as section 4 Steps Check one side at a time between the larynx and the sternocleidomastoid Note rate, rhythm, contour and amplitude Positive Weak and late · bounding · irregular Tap to reveal

Femoral pulse Blocked flow to the legs; delay compared with the radial pulse Steps Patient lying flat, groin exposed with consent and drape Feel below the inguinal ligament , at the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis Press firmly; compare both sides Feel the radial and femoral pulses together to check for a delay extra Positive Weak or absent · delayed compared with the radial pulse (coarctation of the aorta) Tap to reveal

Popliteal pulse Flow behind the knee Steps Patient lying, knee slightly bent Both hands around the knee, fingers in the back of the knee Press deep Positive Absent or weak (deep, so hard to feel) ▶ Popliteal artery palpation (Emory University MSK) Tap to reveal

Posterior tibial pulse Flow to the foot Steps Foot relaxed Feel just behind the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus) Compare both feet Positive Absent or weak (narrowed leg arteries) ▶ Palpating the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses (Open RN) Tap to reveal

Dorsalis pedis pulse Flow to the foot Steps Feel on the top of the foot , between the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals , lateral to the big-toe tendon Compare both feet Positive Absent or weak Tap to reveal

Capillary refill Poor circulation in the fingers or toes Steps Press on a nail bed or fingertip for 5 seconds , then release Count how long the colour takes to return Positive More than 3 seconds (normal: less than 3) Tap to reveal

Peripheral edema Fluid in the tissues from heart failure or other causes Steps Look at both ankles, shins and feet for swelling Press firmly with your thumb for a few seconds over the shin bone and behind the inner ankle Look for a dent that stays ( pitting ) and note how high the swelling goes In a bed-bound patient, check the sacrum Positive A pit that stays after you lift your thumb · swelling up the legs or at the sacrum (right heart failure) ▶ Peripheral vascular exam (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal

Aortic stenosis Narrowed aortic valve : the left ventricle pumps against a block later: PoM 1 Cardiology Steps Diaphragm over the aortic area (2nd space, right sternal border) Listen to S2 (quiet) and for an S4 Follow the sound up to the carotids Feel the carotid pulse and the apex Positive Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur (diamond-shaped, peaks later the tighter the valve), radiates to the carotids · quiet S2 · S4 · weak, late pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) · sustained apex · shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting ▶ Hear it: aortic stenosis murmur (audio) Tap to reveal

Mitral stenosis Narrowed mitral valve : blood cannot leave the left atrium later: PoM 1 Cardiology Steps Roll the patient to the left side Bell at the apex Listen for a loud S1 and an opening snap Feel for a parasternal lift and look at the JVP Positive Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble (decrescendo-crescendo) after an opening snap · loud S1 · parasternal lift and raised JVP if severe · breathlessness Tap to reveal

Aortic regurgitation Leaking aortic valve : blood flows back into the left ventricle later: PoM 1 Cardiology Steps Sit the patient forward , breathe out and hold Diaphragm at the lower left sternal border Check the pulse and blood pressure Feel the apex Positive Decrescendo diastolic murmur starting at S2, high-pitched, blowing · wide pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic) · displaced, enlarged apex · S3 (and S4) Tap to reveal

Mitral regurgitation Leaking mitral valve : blood flows back into the left atrium later: PoM 1 Cardiology Steps Diaphragm at the apex Follow the sound into the armpit Ask the patient to breathe in to check the murmur does not change Feel the apex Positive Pansystolic high-pitched blowing murmur at the apex, radiates to the axilla , unchanged by breathing · displaced, enlarged apex · S3 Tap to reveal

Tricuspid regurgitation Leaking tricuspid valve : blood flows back into the right atrium extra Steps Diaphragm at the lower left sternal border Listen while the patient breathes in Look at the JVP and feel for a parasternal lift Positive Pansystolic blowing murmur, louder on breathing in , spreading to the lower right sternal border · raised JVP · parasternal lift Tap to reveal

Liver and aorta An enlarged, congested liver ; an aortic aneurysm Steps Patient lying with knees bent Palpate the aorta in the upper abdomen, just left of the midline Palpate the liver edge under the right ribs Positive Enlarged liver (hepatomegaly: right heart failure) · wide pulsatile mass (aortic aneurysm) later: PoM 1 Cardiology Tap to reveal
Ascites Fluid in the abdomen Steps Look at the flanks for bulging Ask if they feel bloated or if their waistband is tight Positive Bulging flanks later: PoM 1 Cardiology Tap to reveal
Cardiovascular exam · Lung bases and sacrum

Lung bases and sacrum Fluid backing up from the heart : pleural effusion, pulmonary edema, sacral edema Steps Patient sitting forward : percuss the lung bases , two spots on each side Auscultate for crackles Press over the sacrum for pitting Positive Dull bases (pleural effusion) · crackles (pulmonary edema) · pitting sacral edema later: PoM 1 Cardiology Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Penis: inspection

Penis: inspection Skin, hair, foreskin, meatus Steps Look at the pubic hair and skin Look at the shaft and glans If uncircumcised, ask the patient to pull back the foreskin (or do it gently), then return it afterwards Look at the position of the urethral opening Positive Ulcers, warts, rashes, lice · discharge from the meatus · meatus on the underside or top of the shaft rather than the tip · foreskin too tight to pull back , or ⚠ stuck behind the glans (normal: clean skin, meatus at the tip, foreskin retracts and returns easily) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Penis: palpation

Penis: palpation Structure of the shaft Steps Feel along the shaft between thumb and two fingers Gently squeeze the glans to open the meatus and look for discharge Positive Tender areas, hard lumps or plaques in the shaft · discharge (normal: soft, smooth, non-tender) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Scrotum: inspection

Scrotum: inspection Shape, size, skin Steps Lift the scrotum to see the back of it Compare the two sides Positive Swelling · redness · rashes, cysts, ulcers · ⚠ a testis sitting high or lying horizontally (normal: two sides roughly equal, left lower) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Testis palpation

Testis palpation Testes Steps Hold the testis gently between thumb and first two fingers Feel its size, shape, consistency and any lumps Repeat on the other side Positive ⚠ A firm lump within the testis (testicular cancer until proven otherwise) · tenderness · one testis missing from the scrotum (normal: smooth, rubbery, equal, mildly sensitive) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Epididymis palpation
Epididymis palpation Epididymis Steps Feel behind and on top of each testis Positive Tender swelling (epididymitis) · a separate cyst (normal: soft, non-tender ridge) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Spermatic cord and vas deferens

Spermatic cord and vas deferens Cord and vas deferens Steps Follow the cord up from the epididymis to the inguinal ring between thumb and finger Roll the vas deferens between your fingers Positive "Bag of worms" above the testis ( varicocele , enlarged veins; usually left, best felt standing) · thickening or tenderness (normal: smooth cord with a firm string-like vas) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Transillumination

Transillumination Whether a swelling is fluid or solid extra Steps Darken the room Shine a penlight from behind the swelling Positive Glows red = fluid (hydrocele) · does not glow = solid (consider a tumour) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Cremasteric reflex

Cremasteric reflex Whether the testis rises (testicular torsion screen) extra Steps Patient standing or lying, thigh slightly turned out Stroke the skin of the inner upper thigh with a finger or blunt tool Watch the testis on that side Positive Testis does not rise (reflex absent) ⚠ often absent in torsion , the twisting of the testis, a surgical emergency (normal: the testis rises a little) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Groin inspection with Valsalva

Groin inspection with Valsalva Visible hernia Steps Look at both groins at rest Ask the patient to bear down as if having a bowel movement (Valsalva) or cough Watch both groins and the scrotum Positive A bulge in the groin or scrotum that appears or grows with straining (normal: no bulge) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Inguinal canal palpation

Inguinal canal palpation Small hernia Steps Use the index finger on the same side (right for right) Start low on the scrotum and push the loose scrotal skin up with your finger, folding it inward along the spermatic cord to the external inguinal ring (just above and beside the pubic bone) Ask the patient to bear down or cough Repeat on the other side Positive A bulge or impulse pushing against your fingertip or the side of your finger when the patient strains (normal: nothing felt, or the ring just tightens) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Inguinal lymph nodes

Inguinal lymph nodes Enlarged nodes extra Steps With the pads of your fingers, roll gently over the skin above and below the inguinal ligament Positive Enlarged, hard or tender nodes (infection or cancer in the legs, genitals or anus) (normal: small, soft, mobile nodes can be felt) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Anus: inspection

Anus: inspection Superficial anal disease Steps Gently spread the buttocks Look at the skin around the anus Ask the patient to bear down to bring out anything hidden Positive Hemorrhoids (swollen veins) · skin tags · fissure (a split in the skin) · fistula opening · warts · rash · bleeding (normal: puckered, darker skin, nothing protruding) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Digital rectal exam (DRE)

Digital rectal exam (DRE) Anal tone, rectal wall Steps Lubricate the gloved index finger Place the pad of the finger on the anus and wait for the muscle to relax Slowly insert it, pointing toward the belly button Ask the patient to squeeze around your finger (anal tone) Sweep around the rectal walls Positive Weak squeeze (poor anal tone) · a mass in the rectal wall · tenderness (normal: firm squeeze, smooth walls) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Withdrawing and the glove
Withdrawing and the glove Blood, stool Steps Withdraw slowly Look at the glove Positive Blood (fresh red or black) or mucus (normal: brown stool, no blood) Tap to reveal
Male genital and rectal exam · Prostate palpation

Prostate palpation Size, consistency, surface, tenderness Steps Turn the finger to the front wall (toward the bladder) Feel both lobes and the groove between them Note size, consistency, surface and tenderness Positive Enlarged, smooth, rubbery, groove lost (benign prostatic hyperplasia, BPH) · ⚠ hard nodule or irregular, hard gland (prostate cancer) · very tender, boggy (prostatitis) (normal: walnut-sized, smooth, rubbery, two lobes with a groove, non-tender) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Position and drape

Position and drape A comfortable, dignified position with the vulva reachable Steps Back on the table, head slightly raised Heels in the footrests, knees bent and apart Slide down until the buttocks reach the table edge Drape from the abdomen over the knees, pressed down between the knees so you can see her face Positive Patient tense, guarding or unable to relax : pause, check in, adjust (normal: relaxed, covered, able to see you) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Inspect the vulva

Inspect the vulva Labia, clitoris, urethral opening, vaginal opening, perineum Steps Say what you are about to do, then touch the inner thigh first Look at the labia majora and minora , clitoris, urethral opening , vaginal opening and perineum Note colour, swelling, discharge, lesions, ulcers, skin changes Positive Redness, swelling, ulcers, warts, discharge or skin changes (normal: symmetrical, moist, no lesions) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Speculum insertion

Speculum insertion Getting a view with the least discomfort Steps Tell the patient, then touch the inner thigh first with the back of your hand Gently separate the labia Insert the closed blades slowly, angled slightly downward (toward the back) , pressing on the back wall, not the front (where the urethra is) Rotate the blades level as you go in Positive Pain or distress : pause, check in, and stop if asked (normal: pressure, not pain) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Viewing the cervix

Viewing the cervix Cervix and its opening (os) Steps Open the blades slowly Tilt or re-angle until the cervix sits between the blades Lock the speculum Look at colour, the os, discharge, bleeding and any growths Positive Lesions, ulcers, a mass, abnormal discharge or bleeding (normal: smooth pink cervix; small round os if never given birth vaginally, slit-shaped if they have) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Speculum removal

Speculum removal Vaginal walls Steps Unlock and draw back until the blades clear the cervix Let the blades close as you withdraw , never pinching the cervix or walls Look at the vaginal walls on the way out Positive Redness, lesions, discharge (normal: pink, moist folds) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Cervical screening sample (HPV test)

Cervical screening sample (HPV test) Human papillomavirus (HPV) and abnormal cervical cells Steps Place the brush or broom in the opening of the cervix Rotate it so it samples the transformation zone (where cervical cancer starts) Rinse it into the vial as the kit directs; label it with the patient's full name, date of birth and collection date Positive High-risk HPV positive : the lab then checks the cells (normal: HPV negative) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Other swabs

Other swabs Infection Steps Swab the cervix for chlamydia and gonorrhea when indicated Swab the vaginal walls for discharge (yeast, bacterial vaginosis) when indicated Positive Positive culture or test Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Cervix

Cervix Consistency, tenderness Steps Find the cervix with your fingertips Feel its consistency Gently move it side to side Positive ⚠ Cervical motion tenderness (sharp pain when the cervix moves): pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or ectopic pregnancy (normal: firm like the tip of the nose, moves without pain) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Uterus

Uterus Size, shape, position, tenderness Steps Fingers below the cervix , lift it upward Abdominal hand presses down just above the pubic bone Feel the uterus between your hands Positive Enlarged (pregnancy, fibroids) · irregular or lumpy (fibroids) · fixed or tender (normal: pear-sized, smooth, mobile, non-tender; tilted forward = anteverted , tilted back = retroverted , both normal) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Adnexa (ovaries and tubes)

Adnexa (ovaries and tubes) Masses, tenderness Steps Move the vaginal fingers to one side of the cervix (lateral fornix) Abdominal hand sweeps down and inward from the hip bone on that side Repeat on the other side Positive A mass (ovarian cyst or tumour, ectopic pregnancy) or tenderness (normal: nothing felt, or a small mobile ovary that is mildly tender) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Position and drape (obstetrical)

Position and drape (obstetrical) A position that is comfortable and safe for her and the baby Steps Empty the bladder first On her back, head raised, tilted slightly to her left so the uterus does not press on the large veins Uncover the abdomen from the bottom of the ribs to the pubic bone Drape over the pelvis and legs Positive Light-headed, short of breath or pale when lying flat : turn her onto her left side (normal: comfortable) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Symphysis-fundal height (SFH)

Symphysis-fundal height (SFH) Fetal growth Steps Find the top of the uterus (fundus) : lay the side of your hand across the abdomen high up and walk it down until you meet the uterus Tape from the top of the pubic bone (symphysis pubis) to the fundus Record it in centimetres and plot it against gestational age Positive More than 2-3 cm less than the weeks of pregnancy : the baby may be growing too slowly (intrauterine growth restriction) (normal: after 20 weeks , SFH in cm ≈ weeks of pregnancy ) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Leopold's 1: fundal grip

Leopold's 1: fundal grip Fetal lie and presentation: what is at the top Steps Face the patient's head Both hands feel the top of the uterus Positive Round, hard, movable = head (breech baby) · soft, irregular = bottom (usual, head-down baby) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Leopold's 2: lateral grip

Leopold's 2: lateral grip Where the baby's back is Steps Hands on each side of the abdomen Hold one hand steady while the other presses; then switch Positive Firm, smooth = back · small knobbly parts = limbs · back running up and down = longitudinal lie ; across = transverse lie Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Leopold's 3: pelvic grip (Pawlik's)

Leopold's 3: pelvic grip (Pawlik's) What is presenting above the pelvis Steps Grasp the lower abdomen just above the pubic bone between thumb and fingers of one hand Positive Should be the opposite of grip 1 · head that moves easily = not yet engaged in the pelvis Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Leopold's 4: deep pelvic grip

Leopold's 4: deep pelvic grip Whether the head is flexed, and how far it has descended Steps Turn to face the patient's feet Slide the fingers of both hands down the sides of the uterus toward the pubic bone Positive The side where the fingers meet resistance = the brow · brow opposite the back = flexed head (normal) Tap to reveal
Pelvic exam and obstetrical abdominal exam · Fetal heart rate

Fetal heart rate Fetal well-being (discuss) Steps Use the lie and back from Leopold's to place a handheld Doppler over the baby's back Check you are hearing the baby, not the mother's pulse (feel her wrist at the same time) Count the rate Positive Outside 110-160 beats per minute (normal: 110-160 ) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Inspect the eyes and eyelids

Inspect the eyes and eyelids Exophthalmos, ptosis, eyelid swelling, xanthelasma, jaundice and inflammation Steps Sit at the patient's eye level in good light Look at the eyes from the front and the side: does either bulge forward (exophthalmos) ? Look at the eyelids: drooping (ptosis) , swelling (edema) , yellow plaques (xanthelasma) Gently pull the lower lid down; look at the conjunctiva and sclera for colour Compare left with right Positive Bulging eye, drooping or swollen lid, yellow plaques, yellow sclera (jaundice) or red conjunctiva (inflammation) (normal: eyes level and symmetric, white sclera, pink moist conjunctiva) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Pupils and light reflex

Pupils and light reflex Also a cranial nerve test: II and III · Pupil size, regularity and reaction to light compared with the other pupil Steps Look at the size, shape and symmetry of both pupils Patient looks into the distance Shine the light into one eye from the side Watch that pupil (direct) and the other pupil (consensual) Repeat on the other eye Near reaction : patient shifts focus to your finger brought toward the nose Positive Unequal, irregular, or slow or absent constriction (normal: both pupils constrict almost immediately, directly and consensually, and on near focus) ▶ Pupillary Light Response and RAPD (1:31) ▶ Cranial Nerve Exam Pupillary Light Response and RAPD (0:44) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Eye movements

Eye movements Also a cranial nerve test: III, IV, VI · Range of eye movement in six directions, nystagmus, and double vision in all directions Steps Hold your finger about 45–60 cm (18–24 inches) away Patient keeps the head still and follows with the eyes only Trace an "H" : far right, up, down, then far left, up, down Ask about double vision in each direction Watch for nystagmus at the end of each movement Positive Limited movement, misalignment, double vision in one direction, or nystagmus (normal: full, smooth movement, no diplopia) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Visual fields by confrontation

Visual fields by confrontation Also a cranial nerve test: II · Visual fields, tested with your index finger Steps Sit at the patient's eye level, about an arm's length away Patient covers one eye; you close your opposite eye (mirror them) Patient looks at your nose Bring your index finger in from the edge toward the centre in each of the four quadrants , halfway between you Patient says when they first see it; repeat for the other eye Positive Patient sees the finger later than you do, or not at all, in a quadrant (normal: you both see it at the same time) ▶ Testing Visual Fields (1:15) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Visual acuity

Visual acuity Also a cranial nerve test: II · Visual acuity with a pocket-size chart Steps Patient keeps on any distance glasses (note them) Hold the pocket chart at the distance printed on it Cover one eye; patient reads the smallest line they can (more than half of the letters) Repeat with the other eye Positive Worse than expected or different between the eyes (normal: 20/20; the top number is the test distance, the bottom the distance at which a normal eye reads that line) ▶ Near Visual Acuity (1:16) ▶ Near Visual Acuity, view 2 (1:01) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Ophthalmoscope: front of the eye, then the fundus

Ophthalmoscope: front of the eye, then the fundus The fundus part is also a cranial nerve test: II · Iris, pupil and lens; then the optic disc (colour, sharpness, elevation), arterioles and veins, the retina between the vessels, and the macula Steps Dim the room ; set the lens dial to 0 , finger on the dial to focus Patient fixes on a point in the distance From about 15° to the side of their line of sight, look at the iris, pupil and lens , and the red reflex Move in close; find a vessel and follow it to the optic disc Note the disc's colour, margins (sharpness) and any elevation , then follow the arterioles and veins outward, the retina between them , and the macula (to the temporal side of the disc) Positive Disc swollen with blurred margins (papilledema, raised pressure inside the skull) , haemorrhages, or a missing or interrupted red reflex (normal: sharp round or oval disc, pale pink to yellow-orange, cup less than half the disc; veins larger and darker red than arteries ) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Swinging flashlight test

Swinging flashlight test Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) : an optic nerve problem in one eye later: T2C Ophthalmology Steps Dim the room; patient looks into the distance Shine the light into one eye for a few seconds Swing it quickly to the other eye Swing back and forth several times, watching the pupil you are lighting Positive Pupil dilates when the light swings onto it (that eye's optic nerve "sees" less light) (normal: each pupil stays constricted as the light arrives) ▶ Pupillary Light Response and RAPD (1:31) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Red reflex

Red reflex Opacity in the eye (such as cataract), a large refractive error, or misaligned eyes (strabismus) later: T2C Ophthalmology Steps Dim the room; ophthalmoscope at 0 Stand back about an arm's length Shine the light into both pupils while the patient looks straight ahead Positive Dull, uneven or absent red glow, or a white pupil (⚠ a white pupil in a child can mean retinoblastoma ) (normal: equal bright red reflex in both eyes) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Slit lamp

Slit lamp Corneal clouding or scratches, depth of the anterior chamber, blood or pus in the anterior chamber later: T2C Ophthalmology Steps Dim the room; patient seated with the chin on the rest and forehead against the bar Look through the microscope with a thin, bright beam , from the eyelid to the cornea to the anterior chamber For a scratch, add fluorescein dye and a cobalt blue light Shine the beam at the edge of the cornea to judge how deep the anterior chamber is Positive Cloudy cornea · green-lit abrasion · shallow anterior chamber (acute glaucoma) · blood (hyphema) or pus (hypopyon) (normal: clear cornea, no dye uptake, deep clear chamber) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Inspect the external ear

Inspect the external ear Name the parts; deformity, skin lesions, inflammation, tenderness Steps Look at the pinna from the side and behind: name the helix, antihelix, tragus and lobule Look for deformity, skin lesions, redness and discharge Press in front of the ear and over the mastoid behind it, and move the pinna , noting tenderness or masses Compare the two ears Positive Deformity, lesion, redness, swelling or tenderness (normal: symmetric, non-tender, no discharge) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Otoscopy

Otoscopy Ear canal (patent?) and eardrum, both ears Steps Hold the otoscope like a pencil , your hand braced on the patient's head Pull the pinna back (up and back in an adult) to straighten the canal Insert gently into the outer (cartilage) part only Look at the canal: wax, discharge, redness, foreign body, swelling Find the eardrum landmarks: handle (manubrium), lateral process and umbo of the malleus , cone of light , pars tensa and pars flaccida Positive Red (inflammation; also fever or crying) · bulging (pus, acute infection) · pulled in (retracted) (Eustachian tube problem or fluid) · hole (perforation) · poor movement (fluid behind it) (normal: intact drum with the landmarks and cone of light visible, canal open) ▶ Otoscopy and hearing assessment (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Whisper or finger-rub test

Whisper or finger-rub test Also a cranial nerve test: VIII · Hearing loss in one ear Steps Patient closes their eyes; block one ear (or rub your fingers beside it to mask it) Stand so they cannot see your lips Whisper numbers , or rub your fingertips by the open ear Repeat on the other side Positive Cannot repeat the numbers or hear the rub → go on to Weber and Rinne (normal: hears both sides equally) ▶ Hearing and balance assessment (CN VIII) (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Weber test

Weber test Which ear and which kind of hearing loss Steps Strike a 512 Hz fork Place it on the top of the head (midline) Ask: "Do you hear it in both ears, or louder on one side?" Positive Louder in the bad ear = conductive loss · louder in the good ear = sensorineural loss (normal: heard equally, in the middle) ▶ Rinne and Weber test (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Rinne test

Rinne test Conductive hearing loss Steps Place the vibrating fork on the mastoid bone behind the ear Patient says when the sound stops Move the prongs beside the ear canal straight away Ask if they can hear it again Positive Cannot hear it beside the ear (bone conduction louder than air) = conductive loss in that ear (normal: hears it again, air conduction louder than bone) ▶ Rinne and Weber test (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Nostril patency

Nostril patency Whether air passes through each nostril Steps Patient sits facing you Press one nostril closed with your finger Ask them to breathe in through the other Repeat on the other side Positive Little or no airflow through one nostril (swelling, a bowed septum or a polyp) (normal: air moves freely through both) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Septum and turbinates

Septum and turbinates Septal deviation and turbinate size Steps Tilt the patient's head back a little Use the otoscope with a wide speculum (or a nasal speculum and light), lifting the tip of the nose Look at the septum , and avoid touching it Look at the inferior and middle turbinates : size and colour Check the mucosa for polyps or ulcers; repeat on the other side Positive Septum bowed to one side · swollen turbinates (purplish with clear discharge in allergic rhinitis) · polyps or ulcers (normal: septum central, turbinates small, mucosa pink, moist and smooth) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Lips, tongue, teeth, gums and throat

Lips, tongue, teeth, gums and throat Masses, ulcers and colour change Steps Look at the lips : colour, cracks, ulcers, masses Patient opens wide: look at the teeth and gums (colour, swelling, bleeding, ulcers) Look at the top of the tongue , then ask them to lift it and look at the underside and floor of the mouth Look at the inside of the cheeks , including the parotid duct opening near the upper second molar With a tongue depressor, look at the soft palate, uvula, pillars and tonsils Positive Mass, ulcer, white or red patch, swelling or exudate (normal: pink, moist, intact; tonsils not enlarged or coated) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Palate rise

Palate rise Also a cranial nerve test: IX, X · Movement of the palate Steps Patient opens wide (tongue depressor if needed) Ask them to say "ahh" Watch the soft palate and uvula Positive Palate rises on one side only, uvula pulled to one side (normal: palate rises evenly, uvula stays in the midline) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Tongue

Tongue Also a cranial nerve test: XII · Movement of the tongue Steps Look at the tongue resting on the floor of the mouth : wasting, twitching (fasciculations) Patient sticks the tongue straight out Then moves it side to side Positive Tongue points to one side when stuck out (toward the weak side), wasting or fasciculations (normal: midline, moves freely) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Hair and skin

Hair and skin Texture and distribution of hair; skin colour and lesions Steps Look at the hair : amount, distribution (patchy loss?) and texture (coarse, fine, brittle) Look at the scalp and the skin of the face and neck : colour, pigmentation, scaling, lumps, lesions Positive Patchy or diffuse hair loss, very coarse or fine hair, abnormal colour or a skin lesion (normal: even distribution, normal texture, clear skin of even colour) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Facial movements

Facial movements Also a cranial nerve test: VII · Facial nerve (CN VII) weakness Steps Wrinkle the forehead (raise the eyebrows) Close the eyes tightly ; try gently to open them Bare the teeth in a broad smile Puff out the cheeks Pucker the lips Positive One side weaker or flatter ; whole side = lower motor neuron, lower face only = upper motor neuron (normal: symmetric, strong) ▶ Facial Power Exam (CN VII) (0:27) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Shoulder shrug and head turn

Shoulder shrug and head turn Also a cranial nerve test: XI · Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid strength Steps Patient shrugs and holds it while you push down on both shoulders Patient turns the head to each side against your hand Positive Weakness or wasting on one side (normal: strong, equal) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Neck inspection

Neck inspection Venous distention, masses, lymph nodes, salivary gland and thyroid enlargement Steps Patient sits with the neck exposed and the head straight, in good light Look from the front and both sides at the neck veins , any visible mass , the lymph node areas , the parotid and submandibular glands and the thyroid area Compare left with right Positive Distended neck veins, visible swelling or asymmetry (normal: symmetric, no visible mass or swelling) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Lymph node palpation

Lymph node palpation Lymph nodes or masses in the neck and supraclavicular area Steps From the front, use the pads of the index and middle fingers in small circles, light then firmer Feel both sides together to compare Go through every group in order (list above) Do the anterior cervical chain one side at a time (so you never press both carotid arteries) Positive Enlarged, hard, fixed or tender node (normal: none felt, or small, soft, mobile, non-tender) ▶ Head and neck lymph node palpation (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Salivary glands

Salivary glands Parotid and submandibular enlargement and tenderness Steps Parotid : feel in front of the ear, over the angle of the jaw Submandibular : feel under the jaw, in from its lower edge Compare the sides Positive Swelling or tenderness of a gland (normal: not enlarged, non-tender) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Thyroid inspection

Thyroid inspection Thyroid at rest and with swallowing Steps Stand in front Look at the lower neck at rest Patient takes a sip of water and swallows Watch the thyroid rise with the swallow Positive Swelling on both sides (goitre) or one side (a thyroid mass) (normal: not visible, or a symmetric rise) ▶ Thyroid status examination (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
Head and neck, eye and ear · Thyroid palpation

Thyroid palpation The isthmus and the left and right lobes, from behind Steps Stand behind the seated patient Find the thyroid cartilage , then the cricoid Just below the cricoid, feel the isthmus rise as the patient swallows a sip of water One lobe at a time : gently push the trachea toward the other side, and feel the lobe between the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid while they swallow Repeat on the other side Positive Enlarged, asymmetric, nodular or tender (normal: symmetrical, non-nodular, non-tender) ▶ Thyroid status examination (Geeky Medics) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Spurling's maneuver

Spurling's maneuver Cervical nerve root compression (radiculopathy) Steps Patient sits Extend the neck and turn the head toward the painful side Press gently straight down on top of the head Positive Shooting pain or tingling down the arm (neck pain alone does not count) ▶ Spurling's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Cervical distraction

Cervical distraction Nerve root compression Steps Patient lies on their back (or sits) Cup the back of the head and the chin Gently lift the head to pull the neck long Positive Arm symptoms ease ▶ Cervical Distraction Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Straight leg raise (Lasègue)

Straight leg raise (Lasègue) L5/S1 nerve root tension (sciatic nerve), usually a disc herniation Steps Patient lies on their back Hold the heel and lift the leg with the knee straight Note the angle where symptoms start Positive Pain shooting below the knee between 30° and 70° · back pain only = negative ▶ Straight Leg Raise Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Bragard's sign

Bragard's sign Confirms a positive straight leg raise Steps Raise the leg until the pain starts Lower it just until the pain goes Dorsiflex the ankle (pull the toes up) Positive Leg pain returns ▶ Braggard's Sign Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Bowstring sign

Bowstring sign Confirms a positive straight leg raise Steps Raise the leg until the pain starts Bend the knee slightly until the pain eases Press on the nerve behind the knee (popliteal fossa) Positive Leg pain returns ▶ Bowstring Sign Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Crossed straight leg raise

Crossed straight leg raise Disc herniation Steps Patient lies on their back Lift the unaffected (pain-free) leg straight Positive Pain in the affected leg (very specific for a disc herniation) ▶ Crossed Straight Leg Raise Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Femoral stretch test

Femoral stretch test Upper lumbar roots (L2-L4) Steps Patient lies face down Bend the knee , bringing the heel toward the buttock Optionally lift the thigh to extend the hip Positive Pain in the front of the thigh ▶ Femoral Stretch Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Modified Schober's test

Modified Schober's test Inflammatory back disease (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis) restricting lumbar flexion Steps Patient stands; mark the spine between the dimples of Venus (lower back dimples) Mark 10 cm above it Patient bends forward, knees straight , and you remeasure Positive Distance increases by less than 5 cm ▶ Modified Schober's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Adam's forward bend test

Adam's forward bend test Scoliosis Steps Stand behind the patient Patient bends forward, arms hanging Positive One side of the ribs or back sits higher ▶ SRS Educational Video: Scoliosis Screening Exam (Scoliosis Research Society) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · FABER test (Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation)

FABER test (Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation) SI joint or hip Steps Patient lies on their back Ankle on the opposite knee (figure-4) Hold the opposite pelvis (ASIS) and press the bent knee down Positive Back-of-pelvis pain = SI joint · groin pain = hip ▶ FABER Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Thigh thrust

Thigh thrust SI joint Steps Patient lies on their back; hip bent 90° One hand under the sacrum Push down along the thigh Positive Buttock (SI joint) pain ▶ Thigh Thrust Test | Sacroiliac Joint Provocation (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Thomas test

Thomas test Hip flexion contracture Steps Patient lies on their back Patient hugs one knee to the chest (flattens the low back) Watch the other thigh Positive Other thigh lifts off the table ▶ Thomas Flexion Contracture Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · True and apparent leg length

True and apparent leg length Leg length difference Steps Patient lies straight True : tape from the ASIS to the medial malleolus Apparent : tape from the belly button to the medial malleolus Positive True difference = bone length · apparent only = pelvic tilt or contracture ▶ True leg length measurement Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Painful arc

Painful arc Impingement (rotator cuff) Steps Patient lifts the arm out to the side and overhead , thumb up Then lowers it slowly Positive Pain between 60° and 120° ▶ Painful Arc - Rotator Cuff Impingement Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Neer's test

Neer's test Impingement Steps Stand behind; hold the scapula down Turn the arm in (thumb down) Lift the straight arm forward as high as it goes Positive Pain at the front or side of the shoulder ▶ Neer's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Hawkins test
Hawkins test Impingement Steps Raise the arm forward to 90°, elbow bent 90° Support the elbow Rotate the forearm down (internal rotation) Positive Pain in the shoulder ▶ Hawkin's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Empty can test

Empty can test Supraspinatus Steps Arms out to 90°, angled 30° forward Thumbs pointing down ("emptying a can") Push down while the patient resists Positive Pain or weakness ▶ Empty Can Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Resisted external rotation

Resisted external rotation Infraspinatus, teres minor Steps Elbows at the sides, bent 90° Patient pushes the hands outward against yours Positive Pain or weakness ▶ External Rotation Test - Shoulder Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Lift-off test

Lift-off test Subscapularis Steps Patient puts the back of the hand on the lower back Asks to lift the hand off the back (against resistance) Positive Cannot lift it off , or pain ▶ Lift Off Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Belly press test

Belly press test Subscapularis (when the arm can't reach behind the back) Steps Hand flat on the belly, elbow bent Press into the belly, keeping the elbow forward Positive Elbow drops back or wrist bends to cheat · pain or weakness ▶ Belly Press Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Bear hug test

Bear hug test Subscapularis extra Steps Patient puts the hand of the tested arm flat on the opposite shoulder , fingers straight, elbow held forward Try to lift the hand off the shoulder (pull it outward, at right angles to the forearm) while the patient resists Positive Cannot keep the hand on the shoulder , or clearly weaker than the other side (subscapularis tear) ▶ Bear Hug Test | Subscapularis Tear (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Drop arm test

Drop arm test Full-thickness supraspinatus tear extra Steps Lift the patient's straight arm out to the side (to about 90° or higher) Ask them to lower it slowly to the side Positive Arm drops suddenly or cannot be lowered smoothly ▶ Drop Arm Test / Sign | Supraspinatus Tear (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · External rotation lag sign

External rotation lag sign Infraspinatus (± supraspinatus) tear extra Steps Elbow bent 90° at the side Turn the forearm outward almost as far as it goes Let go of the wrist and ask the patient to hold it there Positive Forearm springs back inward (a lag) ▶ Lateral Rotation Lag Sign⎟Infraspinatus Weakness (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Speed's test

Speed's test Biceps tendinopathy Steps Arm straight forward, palm up , elbow straight Push down while the patient resists Positive Pain in the bicipital groove (front of the shoulder) ▶ Speed's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Yergason's test

Yergason's test Biceps tendinopathy Steps Elbow bent 90° at the side , palm down "Shake hands"; patient turns the palm up against your resistance Positive Pain in the bicipital groove ▶ Yerguson's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Apprehension test

Apprehension test Anterior instability Steps Patient lies on their back Arm out to 90°, elbow bent Slowly rotate the hand back (external rotation) Positive Apprehension: fear the shoulder will dislocate (pain alone is weaker) ▶ Apprehension Test (Shoulder) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Relocation test (Fowler's sign)

Relocation test (Fowler's sign) Confirms anterior instability Steps At the point of apprehension Press the front of the shoulder backward Positive Apprehension goes away ▶ Fowler's Sign (Relocation Test) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Scarf test (cross-arm)
Scarf test (cross-arm) AC joint Steps Bring the arm across the chest toward the opposite shoulder Push it a little further Positive Pain on top of the shoulder (AC joint) ▶ Scarf Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Valgus and varus stress

Valgus and varus stress Medial (ulnar) collateral and lateral collateral ligaments Steps Elbow bent 20-30° ; hold the upper arm still Valgus : push the forearm outward (tests the medial ligament) Varus : push it inward (tests the lateral ligament) Positive Pain or more gap than the other side ▶ Elbow Valgus and Varus Stress Tests Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow")

Lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow") Wrist extensor tendons Steps Elbow straight, fist made Resisted wrist extension (and resisted middle finger extension) Then passively bend the wrist down (stretch) Positive Pain at the lateral epicondyle ▶ Lateral Epicondylitis Tests Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Medial epicondylitis ("golfer's elbow")

Medial epicondylitis ("golfer's elbow") Wrist flexor tendons Steps Elbow straight Resisted wrist flexion Then passively bend the wrist back (stretch) Positive Pain at the medial epicondyle ▶ Medial Epicondylitis Tests Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Tinel's sign (elbow)

Tinel's sign (elbow) Ulnar nerve (cubital tunnel) Steps Find the groove between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon Tap over the nerve Positive Tingling into the ring and little finger ▶ Tinel's Sign (Elbow) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Tinel's sign (wrist)

Tinel's sign (wrist) Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve) Steps Tap over the carpal tunnel at the wrist crease Positive Tingling in the thumb, index, middle (and half the ring) finger ▶ Tinel's Sign - Median nerve (Carpal Tunnel) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Phalen's test
Phalen's test Carpal tunnel syndrome Steps Backs of the hands pressed together , wrists fully bent Hold for 60 seconds Positive Same median-nerve tingling ▶ Phalen's Sign Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · 1st CMC grind test

1st CMC grind test Thumb base osteoarthritis Steps Hold the thumb's metacarpal Push it into the joint and rotate Positive Pain or grinding at the thumb base ▶ 1st CMC Grind Test ▶ Thumb circumduction (the movement the CMC joint allows) (0:05) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Finkelstein's test

Finkelstein's test De Quervain's tenosynovitis Steps Thumb tucked inside a fist Bend the wrist toward the little finger Positive Sharp pain over the radial styloid (thumb side of the wrist) ▶ Finkelstein's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Tinel's sign (elbow)

Tinel's sign (elbow) Ulnar nerve (cubital tunnel) Steps Find the groove between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon Tap over the nerve Positive Tingling into the ring and little finger ▶ Tinel's Sign (Elbow) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Thomas test

Thomas test Hip flexion contracture Steps Patient lies on their back Patient hugs one knee to the chest (flattens the low back) Watch the other thigh Positive Other thigh lifts off the table ▶ Thomas Flexion Contracture Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Trendelenburg sign

Trendelenburg sign Weak gluteus medius Steps Stand behind; hands on the iliac crests Patient stands on the tested leg , lifts the other foot Positive Pelvis drops on the lifted-leg side = the standing side is weak ▶ Trendelenberg Sign Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Stinchfield test

Stinchfield test Inside the hip joint (e.g. arthritis) Steps Patient lies on their back Lifts the straight leg to about 30° Push down on the thigh; patient resists Positive Groin pain ▶ Stinchfield's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · FABER test (Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation)

FABER test (Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation) SI joint or hip Steps Patient lies on their back Ankle on the opposite knee (figure-4) Hold the opposite pelvis (ASIS) and press the bent knee down Positive Back-of-pelvis pain = SI joint · groin pain = hip ▶ FABER Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Thigh thrust

Thigh thrust SI joint Steps Patient lies on their back; hip bent 90° One hand under the sacrum Push down along the thigh Positive Buttock (SI joint) pain ▶ Thigh Thrust Test | Sacroiliac Joint Provocation (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Ober's test

Ober's test Tight IT band Steps Patient lies on the good side , tested leg on top Bend the top knee 90°; take the leg back and out Let it drop toward the table Positive Leg stays up (does not drop) ▶ Ober's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · True and apparent leg length

True and apparent leg length Leg length difference Steps Patient lies straight True : tape from the ASIS to the medial malleolus Apparent : tape from the belly button to the medial malleolus Positive True difference = bone length · apparent only = pelvic tilt or contracture ▶ True leg length measurement Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Wipe (bulge) test

Wipe (bulge) test Small effusion (also called the fluid wave test) Steps Stroke up the inner knee 2-3 times Then stroke down the outer side Positive Bulge of fluid appears on the inner side ▶ Brush / Stroke / Bulge / Swipe Test⎟Knee Swelling (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Patellar ballottement

Patellar ballottement Moderate to large effusion Steps Squeeze down from above the knee Tap the patella down Positive Patella bounces ("floats") ▶ Patellar Tap Test / Ballottement Test⎟Knee Swelling (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Valgus / varus stress

Valgus / varus stress MCL (medial) / LCL (lateral) Steps Test at 0° and at 30° of knee bend Valgus : push the knee inward (tests medial) Varus : push it outward (tests lateral) Positive Pain or gapping vs the other knee ▶ Knee Valgus and Varus Stress Tests Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Lachman test
Lachman test ACL (most accurate test) Steps Knee bent 20-30° Hold the thigh still Pull the shin forward Positive More forward movement, soft end point ▶ Lachman Maneuvers Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Anterior drawer

Anterior drawer ACL Steps Hip 45°, knee 90° ; sit on the foot Hands behind the top of the shin Pull the shin forward Positive More forward movement than the other side ▶ Anterior Drawer (Knee) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Posterior drawer
Posterior drawer PCL Steps Same position as the anterior drawer, then push the shin backward Positive More backward movement ▶ Posterior Drawer Sign (PCL) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Posterior sag sign
Posterior sag sign PCL Steps Both hips 45°, knees 90° Look from the side at the shin Positive Shin sags back vs the other side ▶ PCL Sulcus and Sag Signs Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · McMurray's test

McMurray's test Meniscus tear Steps Fingers on the joint lines; bend the knee fully Medial : turn the foot out , then straighten Lateral : turn the foot in , then straighten Positive Painful click or catch on the joint line ▶ McMurray's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Thessaly's test

Thessaly's test Meniscus tear Steps Patient stands on the tested leg , knee bent 20° , holding your hands Twists the body in and out 3 times Positive Joint-line pain , locking or catching ▶ Thessaly's Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Crouch compression (duck walk)

Crouch compression (duck walk) Meniscus tear Steps Patient squats fully Waddles forward in the squat Positive Joint-line pain (pain in front = patellofemoral) ▶ Crouch Compression Test (Knee) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Patellar apprehension

Patellar apprehension Patellar instability Steps Knee slightly bent, thigh relaxed Push the patella outward (laterally) Positive Patient tenses or fears it will dislocate ▶ Patellar Apprehension Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Patellar grind (Osmond-Clarke)

Patellar grind (Osmond-Clarke) Patellofemoral pain Steps Knee straight Press the top of the patella down toward the feet Patient tightens the thigh Positive Pain behind the patella ▶ Patellar Grind Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Anterior drawer (ankle)

Anterior drawer (ankle) ATFL Steps Ankle slightly pointed down Hold the shin still Pull the heel forward Positive More forward movement than the other side ▶ Anterior Drawer - Ankle (ATFL) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Talar tilt
Talar tilt CFL Steps Ankle at 90° Tip the heel inward (invert) Positive Pain or more tilt than the other side ▶ Talar Tilt Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Lateral ankle ligament stress

Lateral ankle ligament stress Which lateral ligament is torn Steps Hold the shin still Point the foot down and tip the heel inward: tests the ATFL Foot at 90° , tip inward: CFL Foot pulled up , tip inward: PTFL Positive Pain or more give than the other side ▶ Lateral Ankle Ligament Tests Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Passive external rotation

Passive external rotation High ankle sprain (syndesmosis) Steps Knee bent 90°, ankle at 90° Turn the foot outward Positive Pain above the ankle , between tibia and fibula ▶ Dorsiflexion External Rotation Stress Test | Syndesmosis Injury (Physiotutors) Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Thompson test
Thompson test Achilles tendon rupture Steps Patient lies face down , feet off the bed Squeeze the calf Positive Foot does not point down ▶ Thompson Test Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Homan's sign
Homan's sign Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) Steps Knee slightly bent Pull the foot up (dorsiflex) Positive Calf pain (a weak test: never rules a DVT in or out) ▶ Homan's Sign Tap to reveal
MSK exam, by region · Metatarsal squeeze
